Though it is the custom of printers to prefix their list of errors <note>original: "Errata"</note> to the books they publish, I hope the lack of one here will not cause this work to be considered more imperfect. ...a distorted and unpleasant view. Nevertheless, I trust so much in the generous disposition of the fair-minded and honorable <term>original: "ingenuous"; meaning noble-minded or high-born in character</term> reader that I believe once he has thoroughly weighed the evidence in the *balance of the sanctuary* <note>A biblical metaphor for weighing truth by God’s standards rather than human prejudice.</note>—those most authentic testimonies which justify the truth of every essential part of the following discourse so clearly that he who runs may read it—I shall find such favor in his eyes as to be counted among the number of the most sincere and faithful historians (though perhaps not the most talented) who have ever appeared in public, excepting only the writers of the Holy Scriptures. Indeed, all I ask of you, whoever you are, is to measure out your judgment according to the evidence of the matter contained here. And then, if you think I owe you ten thousand talents <note>A talent was a massive unit of weight or currency; this is a reference to the Parable of the Unforgiving Servant in Matthew 18.</note> of truth, only have patience with me, and I will pay you everything.

It has now been more than nineteen months since the cry of the blood of the poor *Protestants* in the valleys of *Piedmont* was heard in every corner of the *Christian* world. This was especially true throughout the *English* nation, where letters arrived one after another—just like *Job's* messengers <note>In the Book of Job, messengers arrived in quick succession to deliver news of various disasters.</note>—bringing the sad and mournful news of the most strange and unheard-of cruelties. I would almost dare to challenge the best-equipped historians (both ancient and modern) to find parallels for them. Some of their women were raped and then staked down to the ground through their private parts. Others were brutally violated, and then their bellies were stuffed with stones and rubbish. The brains and breasts of others were boiled <note>original: "sodden"</note> and eaten by their murderers. It was as if the design of those bloody cannibals and barbarous man-eaters <note>original: "Anthropophagi"</note> was not only to wipe those poor creatures out of this world, but also—as far as they were able by such a strange mixing and confusion of bodies—to prevent them from even existing in the world to come. 

Others had their flesh sliced from their bones while they were still alive, until they became mere skeletons. Many helpless and elderly people, ninety and a hundred years old, were most cruelly burnt in their beds. No respect was shown to their snow-white heads and gray hair, even though the *All-wise Creator* has frequently marked these with signs of honor in His sacred Word. If two female bears were commanded to tear forty-two little children into pieces for mocking the *old prophet* merely with the term "*bald-head*" <note>A reference to the biblical story of Elisha in 2 Kings 2:23–24.</note>, Lord, what shall be the end of these murderers of grown men? They took such pleasure and delight in torturing and tormenting so many poor, helpless, and elderly people by fire and sword.

There is no one who understands what it means to be grieved by the *afflictions of Joseph* <note>A reference to Amos 6:6, describing those who are indifferent to the suffering of God's people; here, the author means the English people were NOT indifferent.</note> who will not easily imagine how closely this bloody and barbarous massacre then touched all the tender hearts of the *English* nation. This was especially true of the heart of that most serene Prince and *heroic* captain <note>Likely referring to Oliver Cromwell, the Lord Protector, who intervened on behalf of the Waldensians.</note>, the depth of whose most *Christian* compassion for the poor afflicted...

...Saints of *Jesus*, are by no means to be measured by any of my slender and brief expressions.

The truth is, he <note>Referring to Oliver Cromwell, the Lord Protector of England.</note> has been a victorious Prince in all his undertakings; yet I am confident it would be much easier to surpass him in anything else than in his tenderness and compassion toward the poor members of *Christ* in misery and affliction. As soon as the news of this massacre reached His Highness's ears, he rose up like a lion from his lair and, through various moving and stirring letters, awakened the whole *Christian* world and moved their hearts to pity and compassion. Of these letters from His Highness, the humblest of his servants <note>The author, Samuel Morland.</note> had the honor to be the bearer of two: one to the King of *France*, to engage (if possible) his Most *Christian Majesty* <note>A traditional formal title for the King of France.</note> to use his power and influence on behalf of the survivors of those miserable people; and the other to the Duke of *Savoy*. According to His Highness's commands, I delivered this letter, along with an earnest verbal plea in His Highness's name, asking that the Duke would be pleased to revoke those merciless and inhuman edicts <note>The legal decrees that authorized the persecution and displacement of the Protestants.</note> and restore his poor, afflicted subjects to their ancient liberties and homes.

Now, when I had executed the commands of His Highness (my master) at *Turin* according to my limited capacity, I retired to the city of *Geneva*. This place is no more pleasant for its lovely location than it is eminent for the sincere, constant, and diligent preaching of the *Word* and administration of the sacraments in no fewer than three different languages (*French, Italian*, and *German* <note>original: "High Dutch"</note>). To complete this heavenly harmony, the preaching is accompanied by a singular piety and *Christian* behavior in general from both the governors and the people.

I had not remained many months in this place before I received a letter from the Right Honorable Mr. Secretary *Thurloe* <note>John Thurloe (1616–1668), Cromwell’s Secretary of State and head of intelligence.</note>, in which he was pleased to suggest to me how usefully I might employ my spare hours during my retirement, both for the present age and for future generations. Specifically, he suggested I should compile an accurate history of all that had lately happened to the poor *Protestants* in the valleys of *Piedmont*, beginning with the *Order of Gastaldo* <note>The 1655 decree by Andrea Gastaldo that sparked the crisis by ordering the Protestants to leave their ancestral lands or convert to Catholicism.</note> and then proceeding to set down all the particulars in a distinct and clear method.

Now, when I had sat down and seriously considered the contents of this letter—combined with the strict charge given to me by the late, deceased Lord Primate of *Ireland* <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), the Archbishop of Armagh and a highly respected scholar.</note>, one of the wonders of our recent age, regarding the same subject—I began to persuade myself that just as there were many sincere-hearted *Christians* in the *English* nation, so there were also many noble-minded <term>original: "ingenuous"</term> souls in other parts of the world. Indeed, even among the more moderate party of the adversaries themselves, there were those who were exceedingly curious and almost impatient to know more specifically who these people were and what their lineage <note>original: "fathers house"</note> was—people whose lives and liberties have been so extremely precious in the thoughts of *His Highness*, and whose bleeding miseries so effectively moved him to exert his utmost...

And indeed, upon these and similar considerations (Providence having then blessed me with a singular opportunity), I knew no better way to serve my generation or succeeding ages than by collecting and organizing into an exact and entire history whatever concerns the antiquity, doctrine, life, or persecutions of those poor *Evangelical Churches* <note>The "Evangelical Churches" here refers specifically to the Waldensians (or Vaudois) of the Piedmont valleys.</note>, from the days of *Christ* and his *Apostles* to this very time. To tell the truth, I promised myself no small pleasure and satisfaction at the beginning of this undertaking. 

But alas, I had no sooner made significant progress into the work than I found it to be, from one end to the other, one of the saddest tragedies that has ever been acted in the *Christian world*. It is a story so lined and interwoven with horrible attempts, such bloody edicts, such profound stratagems, and barbarous persecutions against the poor, harmless, and innocent flock of that Great Shepherd of our souls, that the reader can hardly fix his eye upon any part of it without finding reason for weeping and lamentation. I say, whichever way he turns, he shall find treacheries plotted, desolations predetermined, the *pit dug*, and the *net of destruction spread*. In conclusion, *whole families were miserably ruined, and the innocent blood of the saints was poured out and spilled like water upon the ground*. 

Indeed, my spirit has often grown cold within me, and my heart has even failed me—yes, my very hand has trembled as if with a fit of the palsy—while writing this. To be honest, I would soon have been discouraged from proceeding in this design if it were not a work that I knew might justly be expected from me by His Highness <note>Oliver Cromwell, the Lord Protector.</note> and all the good people of the *English* nation. I am bound to them by all the obligations of both nature and conscience to give an account of my time and opportunities. 

Furthermore, I knew it would be a most acceptable, satisfactory, and useful work to the whole *Christian world*—both for themselves, their children, and their children's children in future generations. Beyond all this, the examples of *Moses* and the prophets, of the Evangelists and *Apostles*, as well as the greatest doctors <note>original: "Doctours"; meaning learned theologians and scholars of the church.</note>, both ancient and modern, who have published to the world and left in writing the various dispensations of Divine Providence toward His people in this world, are more than abundantly sufficient to authorize and encourage me (however unequal I may be to follow them) in such an important undertaking. 

I am certain that whoever reads with an appropriate understanding and due attention the treacherous stratagems and horrid cruelties contained herein must have a heart of adamant and bowels of brass <note>A 17th-century idiom meaning a lack of compassion; the "bowels" were then considered the seat of pity and emotion.</note> if they are not touched with a fellow-feeling for their brothers' misery. Indeed, I am much mistaken if they do not remain astonished and amazed to think that a Prince—or rather, indeed, his royal mother <note>Duke Charles Emmanuel II and his mother, Christina of France, who acted as regent and was a driving force behind the persecutions.</note>—who ought to be as a nursing father and a nursing mother to their subjects, should so miserably comply with the spirits of malicious men who are wholly transported with rage and passion, and inflamed with a vehement thirst after

And they should do such violence to their own moderate inclinations as to listen to—and even support—those urgent requests that tend toward the ruin of their country and the division of their people. This has not only made them unappealing to all the princes and states of the Protestant <note>original: "Reformed"</note> Churches, but has also brought significant blame upon them from those of their very own religion.

Not to mention any other than the King of France, who surely must see that this recent attack in the valleys was a mere strategy to gain possession of Pragela <note>Pragelato, a valley in the Piedmont region.</note>, and thereby block his most Christian Majesty’s <note>A traditional title for the King of France.</note> passage into Italy. It is also unlikely that such violent actions committed by the Pope and his agents <note>original: "Emissaries"</note> are offensive to France alone. They are likely just as poorly received by politically-minded Catholics themselves, who know very well that this can only serve to unite the Protestant party more firmly. Consequently, when a fair opportunity arises, this may very likely throw everything into confusion and lead to their utter overthrow. However that may be, it cannot help but stir the compassion <note>original: "melt the bowels," a common 17th-century idiom for deep emotion.</note> of all tender and sympathetic souls toward the poor, afflicted saints of Jesus.

This, O intelligent reader, is what I am bold enough to present to you now, out of a genuine care for your immortal soul (though it is possible your principles and mine may differ). I hope that the undeniable truths contained here may serve as a precious eye-salve <note>A reference to Revelation 3:18, meaning a remedy to help one see the spiritual truth.</note> to anoint your eyes, so that you may see and discover the many remarkable acts of Divine Providence toward His poor Church militant <note>The "Church militant" refers to the Christian church on earth, struggling against sin and temptation, as opposed to the "Church triumphant" in heaven.</note> in this world. I also hope it may persuade you, in
<margin>Revelation 18:4</margin>
*this your day of visitation, to come out of Babylon, so that you may not share in her sins, nor receive any of her plagues.* By "Babylon," I mean that generation of vipers who, by their barbarous and unheard-of cruelties, have clearly revealed themselves to be the firebrands of Hell itself and fiends of internal darkness.

<margin>Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book 5, chapter 20, page 418. Printed in Geneva by Jean de Tournes, 1613.</margin>
"There is a vast difference between butchery and godliness; truth cannot be joined with force, nor justice with cruelty," <note>original Latin: "Longè diversa sunt carnificina & pietas, nec potest aut veritas cum vi, aut justitia cum crudelitate conjungi"</note> as Lactantius elegantly expresses it on this subject. Do you believe this, O tender-hearted reader? I know that you do, and therefore I desire to lay the following history before you. I beseech the God of Truth and Righteousness to remove all the stumbling blocks and biased thoughts that might be suggested to you—whether by the frailty of the author's understanding and youth, or the seemingly small importance of the poor people of the valleys who are the subject of his work.

The truth is, if you look only at the outside of these poor wretches and their physical appearance, you will be ready to cry out, *Lord, what are these men, that you should be mindful of them? Or their descendants, that you should have any regard for them?* <note>A reference to Psalm 8:4, questioning why God cares for such humble people.</note> Likewise, if you visit their ancient houses and dwellings in such a dark and obscure corner of the world (being, as it were, divided from the rest of the habitable earth) in deserts and solitary places among the craggy rocks and snowy mountains, they may seem to you to have been held in low regard by the great Creator of the world, as the most insignificant part of his handiwork. 

But when you *enter into the sanctuary of God* <note>original: "Sanctuary of God," a biblical phrase meaning to gain spiritual insight or see things from God's perspective.</note> and seriously consider the lifestyle and behavior <note>original: "conversation"</note> of these people, along with their principles and religious practices in all ages and generations—and that from the extensive testimony of their declared enemies—when you consider their loyal submission to their sovereign prince, their Christian patience and courage <note>original: "magnanimity"</note> in their afflictions, and the doubling of their heroic zeal in the depth of their tribulations (*as they do not consider these sufferings worthy to be compared with the joys which are to be revealed* <note>A reference to Romans 8:18.</note>), and when you also consider, on the other hand, *how the Lord has many times chosen these foolish things to shame the wise, and these weak things to shame the mighty, and these lowly things, and things which were despised—yes, and things which essentially were not—to bring to nothing things that are;* <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 1:27–28.</note> 

When you have seen how they have always been preserved like *lambs among wolves*, even though they have often been furiously assaulted by the *Anakims* <note>In the Bible, the Anakims were a race of formidable giants; here used to represent powerful and terrifying oppressors.</note> and sons of violence—so much so that neither the deliverance of the *Israelites* at the *Red Sea*, nor *Jonah* in the *whale’s belly*, nor *Daniel* in the *lions' den*, nor the *three children* in the *fiery furnace* was ever more miraculous—I say, when you have well considered and taken to heart all these things, then perhaps you will conclude with me that these are not the people who have been portrayed to you by their slanderous <note>original: "black-mouth'd"</note> enemies, and that they have in no way deserved to be so cruelly treated by their persecutors. 

You will then conclude with me that all the bitter accusations against both their doctrine and their behavior are nothing more than total deceptions. And you will see that the description of this recent *massacre* has fallen very short of expressing its true rage and horror. Likewise, you will see that cunning has not been lacking in any kind of trickery, nor is there any false scheme or passionate fury that the *Court of Rome* <note>The papal government or administration in the Vatican.</note> and their followers have not devised and carried out for the total destruction <note>original: "extirpation"</note> of the *Christian religion*. This should be a strong motive for us to unite ourselves more closely to resist their bloody force and undermine their strategies.

But alas! Why do we need to search any further than the late bloody massacre to furnish the reader abundantly regarding these two points of cruelty and luxury? I can hardly persuade myself that the likes of it can be found in any history. Certainly, the ancient heretics, Mohammedans, and pagans—had they lived now—would have been very much ashamed to see themselves so outstripped in foulness by the bloody butchers of our own day in the invention of such strange and unheard-of cruelties! 

Indeed, these are such deeds as the Lord, the righteous judge, will most certainly one day repay into the authors' bosoms with as great a variety of punishments, either in this world or that which is to come! *Shall not God avenge his chosen elect, who cry day and night unto him? I tell you, he will avenge them, and he shall do so speedily! Though the kings of the earth may for a time set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together against the Lord and against his Anointed, yet he shall one day break them with a rod of iron, and dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel.* 

Though the wicked in their pride may for a time persecute the poor, and though they may eat up the Saints as they eat bread and do not call upon the name of the Lord, yet when he makes an investigation for blood, he will surely remember them. Yes, upon the wicked he shall rain snares, fire, and brimstone, and a horrible tempest—and this shall be the portion of their cup. When they spring up like the grass and flourish like the green herb, alas, it is so that they should be destroyed forever! *For lo, your enemy, O God—for lo, your enemies shall perish; and all the workers of iniquity shall be scattered. But the righteous shall flourish like the palm tree and grow like the cedar in Lebanon.*

It is most certain, though it be not a thing so commonly noticed...

In the end, the extremity of his torment made him loathe both the sight of food and the smell of wine. As his body was consumed bit by bit, he closed his eyes, being forced to frequently acknowledge during his sickness *that it was the just judgment of God upon him for his cruelties*.

If I were to attempt to list all the terrifying judgments of God upon the persecutors of his Church and people in the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh centuries—meaning the Persians, Greeks, Romans, and other nations—it would require a volume as large as the *Book of Martyrs*. <note>Referring to John Foxe's *Actes and Monuments*, a massive and famous 16th-century history of Christian martyrs.</note>

I ask the patient and polite Christian reader for permission to add a word regarding the disciples and followers of the aforementioned Muslims—I mean the Saracens. Although they were a most cruel people toward Christians, they were sometimes repaid sevenfold for their actions. To give just one example: the Battle of Abdiram <note>likely Abdul Rahman Al Ghafiqi</note> against Charles Martel near Tours, where 375,000 men were killed on the spot in the year AD 730. In truth, it is a terrifying thing to read about the end of the Saracen kingdom, in which one may see, as if in a mirror, clear evidence of God's wrath. Selim I <note>original: "Selym"</note>, the father of Suleiman <note>original: "Solyman"</note>, was the man who destroyed and ended that kingdom. Afterward, Selim <note>Selim I (reigned 1512–1520), the Ottoman Sultan who greatly expanded the empire.</note> led all his forces to Cairo, where another battle took place within the city itself. This fight continued for two days and two nights before he could capture all its forts. It is hard to believe how great the spilling of blood was then, and how horrible the cruelties acted upon the *Saracens* <note>In this context, the author refers to the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt.</note>! The castle of the town mentioned above was won on January 25, 1517. The Sultan fled and hid himself among the reeds in the marshes <note>original: "Moors"</note>, from which he was dragged and brought before *Selim*. After many intense <note>original: "exquisite"</note> tortures, he was put upon a camel and led through all the streets of the town for greater disgrace <note>original: "ignominy"</note>, and at last hanged at one of the gates. This happened on April 13, 1517. I leave the reader to think how sorrowful a spectacle it was then to see that mighty Emperor of *Syria* and *Egypt* so shamefully hanged in the sight of his own people. (*This Sultan was the last Prince of the Saracens and proud Mamluks.*) So did the just and righteous God make them feel the power of His hand, revenging upon them the blood of His beloved ones! And He will certainly one day remember the *Turks* themselves, when He seeks justice for blood <note>original: "makes inquisition for bloud," an allusion to Psalm 9:12.</note> because of all their inhumane butcheries of His faithful servants.

<margin>The Popes of Rome.</margin>
<margin>Onuphrius Panvinus.</margin>
But here it may be that the Popes of *Rome*, and successors of *Boniface* <note>Likely referring to Pope Boniface VIII, whom Protestant authors often cited as a peak of papal arrogance.</note>, may take offense that in such a lengthy <note>original: "prolix"</note> discussion of God’s judgments against the persecutors of the Church, there should be no notice taken of their *Holinesses*. The truth is, they have for a long time been a scourge to the true followers <note>original: "Professors"</note> of the Gospel; yet they have not always escaped without punishment <note>original: "scap’d scot-free"</note>, but have felt the heavy hand of vengeance upon them. Indeed, when they have lacked enemies from abroad to harm them, they have run against one another with their *Bulls'* horns <term>A pun on a "Papal Bull"—a formal decree—and the physical horns of a bull.</term>, which have produced all kinds of violence, wars, murders, and other strange confusions. *Onuphrius* <note>Giacomo Panvinio (1529–1568), an Augustinian historian who wrote about the Popes.</note>, in his abridgment of the history of the Popes, lists seven great schisms <term>Schism: A formal split or division within a religious body.</term> in the *Roman Church* from the time of *Gregory VII* until *Urban VI* (a space of 294 years). During this time, there were no fewer than seven instances of two Popes reigning at once, and toward the end there were three—every one of them, nonetheless, calling himself the true *Pope* and accordingly excommunicating and condemning his competitors.

<margin>Theodoricus.</margin>
<margin>That the Popes have been for the most part but short-lived.</margin>
After that came the eighth and Great Schism, which began in the time of *Urban VI* and *Clement VII* and lasted thirty-nine years until the Council of *Constance*. During this time, the *Popes* fought <note>original: "bandied"</note> against one another with such impudence and fury—using *Bulls*, *Briefs* <term>Brief: A papal letter less formal than a Bull.</term>, and slandering pamphlets <note>original: "defaming Libels"</note>—that if any other person had done so, he would have endangered his life; they called one another schismatics, heretics, and other hateful names. If anyone desires to see their actions, let him read the five books of *Theodoricus* <note>Dietrich of Niem (c. 1340–1418), a historian and clerk in the papal court who wrote an eyewitness account of the Great Schism.</note>, who was a servant and very familiar with the *Popes*, and consequently a man whose account is the more to be believed. But neither is this all! If we cast our eyes upon the histories of the Popes, we shall find that a great number of them have not been very long-lived. For from *Gregory VII* to *Gregory XIII*, there were nearly 68 Popes; during which same time, from *Henry IV* to *Maximilian I* <note>The text likely refers to the Holy Roman Emperors to show that multiple Popes reigned during the span of far fewer Emperors.</note>, there

# An Introduction to

<margin>God's judgments upon the Germans for persecuting the Church.</margin>
The **Germans** who were allied with the **Goths**, after they had destroyed and desolated the churches of **Italy**, met various ends. Some were killed in the war, while others—heavily burdened with loot—were slain and cast headlong down the mountains by the **Huns** and other tribes. The remainder died of the plague in the places where they had retreated.

<margin>Lutarius and Bultinus.</margin>
As for their captains, specifically **Lutarius** and **Bultinus**: the first went mad, and after tearing his own flesh with his teeth, died "drunk" with his own blood. The second was overthrown and killed along with his army of thirty thousand men, of whom only five escaped by fleeing early.

<margin>Antharis. Paul the Deacon, Book 3, *On the Deeds of the Lombards* <note>original: "Paul. Diac. l. 3. de gest. Lomb."</note></margin>
**Antharis**, King of the **Lombards** and a great adversary of the Christians, was poisoned in **Pavia** as a just judgment from God for his cruel actions.

If I were to attempt to list all the fearful judgments of God upon the persecutors of His church and people in the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh centuries—including the **Persians**, **Greeks**, **Romans**, and other nations—it would require a volume as large as the *Book of Martyrs* <note>A reference to John Foxe’s famous 16th-century work detailing the sufferings of Protestants.</note>.

<margin>Mahomet <note>Muhammad, the founder of Islam.</note></margin>
What shall we say of **Mahomet**, the Eastern **Antichrist**, and **Phocas**, the Western **Antichrist**? The first left nothing but an abominable stench behind him; although he boasted that his body would not need burial because it was to rise on the third day, his carcass rotted upon the earth so severely that no one could endure being near it.

<margin>Phocas. <note>Phocas was a Byzantine Emperor (reigned 602–610).</note> Cedrenus. Zonaras. <note>References to Byzantine historians George Kedrenos and Joannes Zonaras.</note></margin>
The second, Phocas, after he had most treasonously put to death the Emperor **Maurice**, his wife, and his children, faced a conspiracy by the Roman Senate and his own son-in-law. They cut off his hands, feet, genitals, and head, and then placed him into a bronze ox <note>A torture device designed to roast victims alive.</note> along with all his children and kindred. This was the end of that execrable murderer, who had granted to **Boniface III**, Bishop of Rome, the title of "Primate" and "Supreme" over all the churches, approximately 600 years after the death of Christ.

<margin>The Saracens.</margin>
I beg the Christian and courteous reader’s patience to add a word concerning the disciples and followers of the aforementioned Mahometans—I mean the **Saracens**. Being a most cruel people toward Christians, they were sometimes repaid seven-fold for their actions.

<margin>Abdiram <note>Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, the Umayyad commander.</note></margin>
To give one instance: the Battle of **Abdiram** against **Charles Martel** near **Tours**, where 375,000 men were slain on the spot in the year of our Lord 730 <note>Modern historians usually date the Battle of Tours to 732.</note>. After this, in the year 736:

<margin>Athin. Amorrheus.</margin>
**Athin**, King of the Saracens, entered **France** with an innumerable company, but Charles overthrew him and his army near **Avignon**. Finally, **Amorrheus**, another of their kings who was bringing reinforcements to Athin, was killed and his troops utterly defeated. The truth is, it is a fearful thing to read of the end of the Saracen kingdom, in which one may see, as if in a mirror, an evident testimony of the wrath of God.

<margin>Paulus Jovius in his *History of Our Times*.</margin>
**Selim I**, father to **Soliman** <note>Suleiman the Magnificent.</note>, was the man who finally destroyed and extinguished that kingdom. He first won two battles against the Sultan **Tuman bay** <note>original: "Tomumbei," the last Mamluk Sultan of Egypt.</note> under the leadership of **Sinan Pasha**. One battle was near **Gaza** in **Syria**, and the other was in **Egypt** near **Grand Cairo**.

Afterward, **Selim** <note>Selim I (reigned 1512–1520), the Sultan of the Ottoman Empire.</note> led all his forces to **Cairo**, where another battle took place within the city itself. It continued for two days and two nights before he could capture all its fortifications. It is hard to believe how great the bloodshed was then, and how horrible the cruelties committed against the **Saracens** <note>A term used historically by Europeans to refer to Muslims.</note>! The citadel of the town mentioned above was won on January 25, 1517. The Sultan <note>Tuman bay II, the last Mamluk Sultan of Egypt.</note> fled and hid himself among the reeds in the marshes <note>original: "Moors"</note>, from where he was dragged and brought before **Selim**. This happened on April 13, 1517. I leave the reader to imagine what a woeful spectacle it was to see that mighty Emperor of **Syria** and **Egypt** so shamefully hanged in the sight of his own people. <margin>The **Mamluks** <note>A caste of warrior-slaves who ruled Egypt and Syria for centuries until the Ottoman conquest.</note>.</margin> (*This Sultan was the last Prince of the* **Saracens** *and proud* **Mamluks**:*) So did the just and righteous God make them feel the power of His hand, taking revenge upon them for the blood of His beloved ones! And He will certainly one day remember the **Turks** themselves when He judges those responsible for bloodshed <note>original: "makes inquisition for bloud"</note>, because of all their inhumane butcheries of His faithful servants.

<margin>The **Popes of Rome**.</margin>
But at this point, perhaps the **Popes of Rome** and the successors of **Boniface** <note>Likely referring to Boniface VIII or Boniface III, often cited by Protestant authors as key figures in the expansion of papal power.</note> may take offense that, in such a lengthy discourse on God’s judgments against the persecutors of the Church, there should be no notice taken of their **Holinesses**. The truth is, they have for a long time been a scourge to the true believers <note>original: "Professors"</note> of the **Gospel**, yet they have not always escaped without punishment. They have felt the heavy hand of vengeance upon them; indeed, when they lacked enemies from abroad to harm them, they have charged at one another with their **Bulls’** <note>A "Bull" is a formal decree or edict issued by the Pope, named after the lead seal (*bulla*) attached to it.</note> horns, which have produced all kinds of violence, wars, murders, and other strange confusions. <margin>**Onofrio Panvinio** <note>original: "Onuphrius Panuinus," a 16th-century Italian historian and Augustinian friar.</note>.</margin> **Onofrio**—in his abridgment of the history of the **Popes**—counts seven great schisms in the **Roman Church** from **Gregory VII** to **Urban VI** (a span of 294 years). During that time, there were no fewer than seven instances where two **Popes** reigned at once, and toward the end, there were three. Every one of them, nonetheless, called himself the true **Pope**, and accordingly excommunicated and condemned his competitors.

After that came the eighth and great schism, which began in the time of **Urban VI** and **Clement VII**, and lasted thirty-nine years until the **Council of Constance**. During this time, the **Popes** attacked <note>original: "bandied"</note> one another with such impudence and fury through **Bulls**, **Briefs** <note>A "Brief" is a less formal papal letter than a Bull.</note>, and defaming **libels**, that if anyone else had done so, he would have endangered his life. They called each other "Schismatics," "Heretics," and other hateful names. <margin>**Dietrich von Nieheim** <note>original: "Theodoricus," an ecclesiastical official and historian who was an eyewitness to the Great Schism.</note>.</margin> If anyone desires to see their actions, let him read **Dietrich's** five books; he was a servant and very familiar with the **Popes**, and consequently, his account is the more to be believed. <margin>That the **Popes** have been for the most part short-lived.</margin> But this is not all! There were only 26 Kings or Emperors of the *Romans* <note>In this context, the author is referring to the Popes, whom he views as worldly rulers of Rome.</note>: thus their lives were extremely short, and certainly not very sweet! We find that the majority of them were tormented with grievous diseases, and many were surprised by sudden death. Some were driven from their thrones and taken prisoner; others were murdered by poison. *Lucius* II was stoned by his own people. *Lucius* III was banished from the city, and his servants were beaten to death. *Adrian* IV was choked by a fly. *Pope John* VIII—or rather *Joan* I (if we may give any credit to *Platina* <note>Bartolomeo Platina (1421–1481), a papal historian who recorded the legend of Pope Joan.</note> and many other notable Catholic writers)—met a scandalous end. After she had given a very fitting and complete exposition on the 17th chapter of *Revelation* concerning the **GREAT WHORE** AND **THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS**, she went into labor and gave birth to a child during a *procession* as she was going to the Church of *Lateran* <note>The Archbasilica of Saint John Lateran in Rome.</note>. In full view of the people, she died immediately, with as much shame and disgrace as the villainy and wickedness in which she had lived. This accident (as the same historians tell us) led to the creation of the *Trying-stool* called the *Porphyry Chair* <note>A chair with a hole in the seat, allegedly used to physically verify that a newly elected Pope was male, though modern historians consider the "Pope Joan" story a legend.</note> for her successors. However, the truth is that the greatest part of them ever since have given sufficient proof of their "abilities" in that regard, evidenced by the multitude of *nephews* <note>original: "Nephews" — a common euphemism for the illegitimate sons of Popes (the origin of the word "nepotism").</note> who have called them *fathers*. *John* XII was stabbed by a *Roman* who by chance caught ***His Holiness*** in bed with his ***wife*** (a great argument, without doubt, for that Pope's *sinfulness* <note>original: "peccability"</note> and an even greater one for his *fallibility*, to be caught in the act!). *Pope John* XXI was killed by the collapse of a vaulted ceiling. *Boniface* VIII, who came to the Popedom like a fox and governed like a lion, at last died like a dog.

I suppose it is now high time to draw to a conclusion; I shall therefore only make a very brief reflection upon a few of those cruelties that have been exercised against the professors of the Gospel <note>A term for Protestants.</note> in our neighboring countries.

<margin>
Henry II of France.
D'Aubigny in his *Universal History, Amsterdam Edition.*
</margin>
It is observed that *Henry* II of *France*, being incensed against the Protestants by his mistress, the Duchess of *Valentinois*, once took an oath that he would see with his own eyes the burning of *Du Bourg* <note>Anne du Bourg (1521–1559), a French magistrate and Protestant martyr.</note>. But the wise God had disposed of affairs otherwise. During a jousting tournament with *Count Montgomery*, a splinter from the Count's lance rebounded and glanced into the King's eye, wounding him so severely that he died within a few days. And what is even more remarkable: as they carried him from the field, he turned his face toward the Bastille and, with a deep sigh, confessed *that he had most unjustly persecuted and afflicted the honest and good people who were imprisoned there.*

<margin>
Philip II of Spain.

*Philip* II of *Spain*, who married *Elizabeth* of *France* (the daughter of *Henry* II), arrived in *Spain* after the death of his father, *Charles* V. He issued a summons for all prisoners held on account of religion in all parts of *Spain* to be gathered for two *Acts of Faith* <note>original: "Acts" (Autos-da-fé) — public ceremonies where the Inquisition handed out sentences to heretics.</note>. Likewise, a multitude of other eminent persons—disguised in yellow robes painted with crosses and devils (which they call *Sanbenitos* <note>original: "St. Benedicts habits"; these were the penitential garments worn by those condemned by the Spanish Inquisition</note>)—were burned alive in the month of *May*.

The second *Act of Faith* <note>original: "Act"; referring to an *Auto-da-fé*, the public ritual of penance and execution performed by the Inquisition</note> was proclaimed at *Seville* in the King's presence. There, they burned *Juan Ponce de León*, son of *Rodrigo, Count of Bailén*; *Juan Gil* <note>original: "John Bayley"; Juan Gil was a famous Seville theologian known as Dr. Egidio</note>, a theologian of *Seville*; and *García Arias*, a man esteemed as the most excellent and able doctor in *Spain*, together with a great number of men and women. His body was carried about *in effigy* <note>as a statue or likeness representing him</note>, dressed in the robes of a clergyman, and thus presented to public view.

This King <note>Philip II of Spain</note>, having reigned about 40 years, caused his only son <note>Don Carlos</note> and his wife *Elizabeth* <note>Elizabeth of Valois</note> to be put to death on the advice of the Inquisition! But now, mark his end! He was seized by four abscesses <note>original: "Apostemes"</note> in the four corners of his stomach which, when opened, poured forth such a prodigious quantity of lice that the surgeons could never find a remedy for him. And thus he died most miserably, being eaten up by lice.

<margin>Francis II</margin>
*Francis II*, son of *Henry II*, having persecuted the *Protestants* at the instigation of the *Guises* <note>original: "Guisars"; the powerful Catholic Ducal House of Guise</note>, also seized the *Prince of Condé* and was very near to cutting off his head. This was after he had made a vow (which he intended to confirm by oath to the *Virgin Mary*) for the total destruction of the *Protestants* and all their supporters, or anyone who had favored that party in any way. However, he was overtaken by a fever, and having an abscess burst in one of his ears, he died suddenly in the month of *December*.

<margin>Charles IX</margin>
*Charles IX*, son of *Henry II* and brother to *Francis II*, caused the execution of the Massacre of *St. Bartholomew* (which they call the *Parisian Matins*) contrary to the faith of his promise. About eight days later, a prodigious multitude of crows arrived, making a hideous noise upon the great *cupola* <note>original: "Lanthorn"</note> of the *Louvre* palace, so that both the King and the entire Court were greatly frightened. That very same night, about two hours after the *King* had gone to bed, he leaped up suddenly and ordered those in his chamber to rise immediately and call his brother-in-law, among others, to hear a strange and hideous noise in the air. It sounded like a great multitude of voices—some crying and groaning in a most lamentable manner, others threatening and blaspheming—not unlike that confused noise heard on the night the *Massacre* was carried out.

<margin>Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a famous French historian</note> book 57, page 990.</margin>
After this *Bartholomew*-tide, this Prince found no true rest but was always interrupted by startings and groanings, which ended in words of distrust and despair, and the most extreme pains from a disease that seized him. Indeed, blood was observed to spring forth from almost all the passages of his body, so that he died thus wallowing and weltering in his own gore.

He felt a fire already in his body, as a taste of those eternal flames prepared for such enemies of the Church <note>original: "fire-brands of the Church"; a term for those who incite destruction or are destined for hellfire</note>.

Gaspar de Renialme.

**Gaspar de Renialme**, one of the magistrates of the city of **Antwerp**, having sentenced certain poor **Protestants** to death, was struck by God in that very place. He was led home in a state of near despair and died in a terrible manner, often crying out and saying that *he had condemned innocent blood.*

<margin>
Du Prat.
Idem, book 6, page 473.
</margin>
The Chancellor **du Prat**, who was the first to grant jurisdiction to Parliaments to proceed against the poor **Protestants**, died in his own house while swearing and cursing against God himself. His very stomach was later found to have been gnawn and eaten through by worms.

<margin>
John Morin.
Ibid.
</margin>
**John Morin**, *Lieutenant of the Provost of Paris* <note>original: "Lieutenant de la Prevosté de Paris"</note>, a strange and cruel monster, after putting a great number of martyrs to death, was struck with the disease called the **Wolf** <note>original: "the Wolf"; likely referring to lupus or a form of gangrene or eating ulcer</note> in both his legs. He died of this, blaspheming and renouncing God in a most hideous manner.

A certain Counselor.

The same author mentions a certain counselor who, having been involved in certain legal cases managed by the *Lieutenant of the Châtelet of Paris* <note>original: "Lieutenant du Chastelet de Paris"; the Châtelet was a major judicial and detention center in Paris</note>, died a very strange death. During his sickness, he would often cry out to those who visited him in the following terms: *Why do we put to death these poor people, who pray to God so well?*

<margin>
Ibid.
Oliver the Chancellor.
Idem, book 7, page 558.
</margin>
During the cruel executions at **Amboise** <note>original: "Amboise"; referring to the mass executions following the failed Protestant "Conspiracy of Amboise" in 1560</note>, carried out against those who had gathered to reveal to the King the secret plots then being hatched against him, **Oliver** the Chancellor fell ill. Oliver had drafted the legal proceedings against these poor people and had also proceeded in the former persecutions directly against his own conscience (which for a long time had been enlightened by the knowledge of the truth). He was at length seized by a grievous disease, during which he let out most lamentable sighs and bitter groans. In this torment, he was visited by the **Cardinal of Lorraine**, to whom he cried out in these words: *Ah, Cardinal! You are causing us all to be damned!* <note>original: "Ha! Cardinal! Tu nous fais tous danner"</note>. It is said, moreover, that he mentioned with profound regret the death of **Mr. Anne du Bourg**, who not long before had been burnt for his testimony to the truth.

<margin>
The Bailiff of Nancy in Lorraine.
Idem, book 7, page 579.
</margin>
The **Bailiff of Nancy** in **Lorraine**, having without any form of legal trial caused a man named **Florentin** to be hanged, was struck with terror. Florentin, a native of **Cologne**, had been a faithful servant and minister of **Jesus Christ**. The Bailiff also demolished the church where Florentin used to preach and administer the Sacraments. It happened that as the Bailiff was walking out after dinner (not knowing the location where this poor martyr had been executed), he came directly upon the very place where he was hanging. As soon as he saw him, he was struck with such a dismal terror that it stayed with him until his grave. Not long after, his body became as dry as parchment rolled upon wood. Besides this, he was severely tormented in his conscience, so much so that he often demanded...

<header>An Introduction to</header>

...asked many honest people during his final illness <note>original: "languishment"</note> whether God would pardon a man for sins he repented of without confessing the specific cause of his remorse (likely out of fear of upsetting the princes and powerful men). However, when he made his last Will and Testament, he clearly revealed the cause of his torment and horror of conscience by assigning 500 francs <note>original: "Francks"</note> to the daughter of the martyr **Florentin**, mentioned earlier. His executors actually paid this sum to her later.

<margin>John de Roma, an Inquisitor. Ibid, book 1, p. 67.</margin>
**John de Roma**, an Inquisitor in **Provence**, invented a horrific way to torture the poor Saints: he made them put on a type of "Boots" filled with boiling grease to drive them to despair through extreme pain. Later, he was struck by a terrible and disgusting disease. No one dared go near him because of the stench and rot of his illness. His only comfort was a wish to die, and he spoke only words of despair. His complaints were like these:

> *Alas, what a miserable state I am in! What am I suffering! I truly remember the evils I did to those poor people, and I know very well why I am being tortured like this on every side. Who will deliver me from this distress? O, kill me quickly so I no longer suffer in this misery.*

<margin>Dr. Lambert, Prior of the Augustinian Friars. French Book of Martyrs, book 7, p. 617.</margin>
One **Dr. Lambert**, Prior <note>original: "Priour"</note> of the **Augustinian Friars**, was preaching loudly against the faithful followers of Christ (whom he called **Calvinists** and **Lutherans**). Suddenly, he lost his voice in the pulpit and his senses failed him in a strange way. He was immediately carried out of the assembly, and a few days later, he was found dead in a ditch.

<margin>Poncher, Archbishop of Tours, book 6, p. 473.</margin>
**Poncher**, the Archbishop of **Tours**, was overseeing the execution of a famous martyr when he was struck by a "fire from Heaven." It began at his heel, and he was forced to have his limbs amputated one by one <note>original: "cut off one member after another"</note> until he died miserably. No one could ever determine the cause of his illness.

<margin>Thomas Arundel. Foxe’s Book of Martyrs, p. 541.</margin>
**Thomas Arundel**, the Archbishop of **Canterbury**, who sentenced **Lord Cobham** (an early witness to the Truth) to death, died before Cobham did. Before his death, his tongue swelled so much in his mouth that he could neither eat nor speak.

<margin>Dr. Foxford, 962.</margin>
**Dr. Foxford**, Chancellor to **Stokesley**, the Bishop of **London**, had his intestines <note>original: "guts"</note> fall out of his body while he was sitting in his chair.

<margin>Morgan of St. Davids, 1902.</margin>
**Morgan**, the Bishop of **St. Davids**, who judged **Ferrar** the Martyr and stole his position <note>original: "usurped his place"</note>, was struck with a disgusting disease. The food he ate would constantly come back up, sometimes through his mouth and sometimes through his nose, until he died.

<margin>Justice Morgan, 1902.</margin>
**Justice Morgan**, who sat in judgment over **Lady Jane Grey**, went mad. In his fits of rage, he always cried out, "*Take away the Lady Jane! Take away the Lady Jane!*" and died in that state.

<margin>John Fetty's Wife, 1824.</margin>
The wife of **John Fetty** betrayed her own husband and then lost her mind.

<header>the following History.</header>

<margin>Alexander the Keeper of Newgate, 1003.</margin>
Alexander, the Keeper of **Newgate** Prison in the days of the Martyrs, died in a most terrifying <note>original: "formidable"</note> manner; his body became swollen and as monstrous as his actions, and as rotten as his principles.

<margin>Gardiner Bishop of Winchester 1824.</margin>
**Gardiner**, the Bishop of **Winchester**—the Devil's chief cabinet messenger <note>original: "Courier du Cabinet"</note>—would by no means go to dinner on the day that **Ridley** and **Latimer** were burnt at **Oxford** until his servant arrived by post from there with the news that he saw the fire set to them at the stake. But before this cursed murderer had sat long at the table, he was seized with such an intolerable pain in his bowels, and the heat within his body was so violent, that his tongue was swollen and turned black in his mouth. When this wicked wretch was reminded by one of the bishops standing by him of the death and merits of **Christ**, he answered, *"Open that door to the people, my lord, and all is gone! You may speak of it to those in my condition, but open that door to the people, and all is gone."* <note>This likely refers to Gardiner's fear that if the common people were allowed access to the Gospel and Protestant teachings, the power of the Catholic Church would be destroyed.</note>

<margin>Queen Mary.</margin>
I shall end all with that reproach of her sex, Queen **Mary**, who never prospered once she began to persecute the saints, and at last died of a swelling of the abdomen <term>tympany</term>. This miserable wretch told one of her maids of honor *that if they opened her after she was dead, they should find Calais lying at her heart.* <note>Mary I famously lost the last English territory in France, Calais, shortly before her death.</note> But I am persuaded she was mistaken, and that it was rather the *fire*, the *scalding lead*, and *red-hot irons* with which she had put the poor martyrs to death.

The truth is, the instances that might be cited for the confirmation of this truth are almost innumerable. And I do truly believe that there has hardly been any famous persecutor of the Church in almost any age or place of the world who has gone down to his grave without some remarkable tokens of divine vengeance upon him in some respect or other.

I might here, in the conclusion of this discourse (and it would not be at all off-topic if I should), descend to some particular instances in **Savoy** itself. By these, it would plainly appear to all the world that even they, as they have in a very prominent manner played their parts in the persecution of the saints, have likewise been met with judgments from heaven. I say, I might provide examples of several persons of quality and note, some of whom have had their *"candles strangely put out,"* <note>An idiom meaning they died a sudden or mysterious death.</note> and others who are now living and have already tasted in some measure the first fruits of their bloody deeds, as an earnest <note>original: "earnest," meaning a down payment or deposit</note> of a heavier curse, without serious and timely repentance. I would not wish to be misunderstood here or thought to bluntly strike at or attack the princely persons of their **Royal Highnesses** (I mean the **Duke** and his **Mother** now reigning). The tender years of the one, and those few observations I myself have sometimes made of the natural kindness and mildness of the tempers and dispositions of both, forbid me to believe them to be otherwise—or any further guilty of those horrid cruelties and persecutions—than by listening (more is the pity) to the black slanders of malicious men, and by allowing themselves to be persuaded that whoever kills and destroys those poor **Protestant** subjects thereby saves their own souls, and does...

<meta>This page continues the conclusion of the preface, following the mention of Queen Mary's death. [...who believed they were doing] God a unique and meritorious service; and on those grounds, most unhappily set their hands to many a cruel and bloody edict. No! They are a generation of **Jesuitical** spirits <term>Jesuitical: at this time, the term implied being cunning, deceitful, or plotting on behalf of the Catholic Church</term> to whom I direct this discourse—men who love cruelty in its purest form <note>original: "in the Abstract"</note> and hunt after blood as naturally as the eagle hunts its prey. But I shall instead be sparing and gentle in this regard and only pray for them, as **Stephen** did for his murderers: *“Lord, do not hold this sin against them!”* Or in the words of our **Savior** for the **Jews**: *“Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”* Yet let me tell them that the cry of those souls who are now under the **altar** <note>A reference to Revelation 6:9-10, where the souls of martyrs cry out for justice.</note> is strong and loud—those whom they have so cruelly and barbarously slain for the testimony of **Jesus**. Let them take heed that these cries do not eventually persuade the **Lord, Holy and True**, to judge and avenge their blood upon those who dwell on the earth.

These are the introductory (and I hope timely) thoughts and suggestions...

# The Contents

In the volume marked with the letter **C**, the following treatises are contained:

1. *An exhortation to confess our sins to one another and to God.*
2. *A sermon regarding the fear of the Lord.*
3. *A sermon regarding the accusation of sinners before God in judgment.*
4. *A treatise regarding tribulations.*
5. *A treatise regarding the martyrdom of the Maccabees <note>original: "Machabees"</note> and others.*
6. *A treatise concerning the sufferings and steadfastness of Job.*
7. *An extract of the history of Tobit <note>original: "Tobias"</note>.*

***

In volume **D** are many excellent and heavenly meditations concerning the miseries, tribulations, and shortness of this life; as likewise of repentance, good works, and the like. These were written in the language of the ancient inhabitants of the Valleys <note>The Alpine Occitan or Piedmontese dialect of the Waldensians.</note> on parchment, though the lettering is almost worn out with age. According to many probable circumstances regarding the place and manner of its preservation, it is judged to have been written at least six or seven hundred years ago.

***

In the volume marked **E** are contained:

1. *A Latin grammar of the ancient Barbes <term>original: "Barbes"; the term for Waldensian pastors or ministers</term>.*
2. *The Proverbs of Solomon and Ecclesiastes.*
3. *A pious piece of poetry in the language of the ancient inhabitants of the Valleys.*
4. *A treatise concerning the love and fear of God, and the manner of life which Christians ought to live.*
5. *A treatise of morals in Latin.*
6. *A treatise of arithmetic <note>original: "Arithmetick"</note>.*

***

In volume **F** are collected and written on parchment, in that which is called the *Waldensian Language*, in a very ancient but beautiful and distinct script:

*The Gospel of Matthew.*
*The first chapter of Luke.*
*The Gospel of John.*
*The Acts of the Apostles.*
*The first Epistle to the Corinthians.*
*The Epistle to the Galatians.*
*The Epistle to the Ephesians.*
*The Epistle to the Philippians.*
*The first Epistle to the Thessalonians.*
*The second Epistle to Timothy.*
*The Epistle to Titus.*
*The eleventh chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews.*
*The first and second Epistle of Peter, but incomplete.*

# [A Catalog] of the following History

The volume marked with the letter **G** contains the following manuscripts:

1. *A legal record <note>original: "verbal Process," from the French "procès-verbal"</note> against the Waldensians, by the Archbishop of Embrun <note>original: "L'Ambrun"</note>, in the years 1497 and 1502, written in the French language.*
2. *A papal bull of Pope Innocent against the Waldensians, in the year 1487, written in Latin.*
3. *A Latin treatise titled, "The Origin of the Waldensians and the proceedings carried out against them" <note>original: "Origo Valdensium & processus contra eos facti"</note>, dated 1501.*
4. *Various reports and examinations taken by the Archbishop of Évreux <note>original: "Evereux"</note> and others of the Pope's commissioners against the Waldensians of Freissinières <note>original: "Fraffinere"</note> and other places, in the years 1478, 1479, 1483, 1486, and 1501. These contain many very remarkable passages, worthy of being diligently studied by all curious readers.*

***

->In Volume **H**, the following manuscripts are contained:<-

1. *Various extensive and very remarkable trials <note>original: "Processes"</note> and cruel inquisitions against the people of Freissinières and other places, in the years 1487, 1488, 1489, 1492, and 1494.*
2. *A papal bull of Pope Alexander, dated April 1, 1501, for the absolution of the Waldensians, etc., to encourage them to abandon and renounce <note>original: "revolt and abjure"</note> their religion.*
3. *A papal bull of the same Pope Alexander, dated April 5, 1501, for the absolution of usurers <note>those who lend money at interest</note>, etc.*
4. *A papal bull of the aforementioned Pope Alexander, dated October 7, 1501, for the absolution of all sorts of crimes and sins, particularly that of heresy.*
5. *An edict of Louis, King of France, dated October 12, 1501, for the restoration of the property <note>original: "restitution of the goods"</note> of those in Freissinières.*
6. *Letters patent <term>official documents or charters issued by a monarch</term> obtained from Louis, King of France, by the people of Freissinières, dated October 12, 1501.*
7. *A decree of the Great Council <note>original: "Arrest du Grand Conseil"</note> dated May 27, 1502, in favor of those in Freissinières, Vallouise <note>original: "Val Loyse"</note>, l'Argentière, and other inhabitants of Dauphiné <note>a province in southeast France</note> who converted to Catholicism.*

***

->In Volume **I**, the following manuscripts are contained:<-

<meta>This page continues the table of contents for Samuel Morland’s collection of documents related to the history of the Evangelical (Protestant) churches in Piedmont. <header>The Contents</header>

In the black box marked "x" are contained the several printed tickets and other papers and pictures which were found in the pockets of some of the soldiers in Piedmont who had previously massacred the Protestants.

->Namely,<-

In Paper *A* are several forms of blessings, consecrated to be carried on their persons for protection; as for example:

1. By the power of God the Father, the wisdom of God the Son, and the virtue of the Holy Spirit, through the intercession of the most holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, Saint Francis, and the blessed Diego and Salvatore, may the Lord deliver you from every fever, plague, and sudden death. Amen. <note>original Latin: "Potentia Dei Patris, Sapientia Dei Filii, Virtus Spiritus Sancti, per intercessionem Sanctissimæ Virginis Dei genitricis Mariæ, Sancti Francisci, & Beatorum Didaci, & Salvatoris liberet te Dominus ab omni Febre, Peste, & improvisâ morte. Amen."</note>
2. "Make the men sit down," from the Cathedral of Casale, 1649. <note>original Latin: "Facite homines discumbere, ex Cathed. Casalens. 1649." This is a quote from the miracle of the loaves and fishes in the Gospel of John, here used as a ritual charm.</note>
3. "There is a boy here," from the Cathedral of Casale, 1648. <note>original Latin: "Est puer unus hic, ex Cathed. Casalens. 1648." Also a Gospel quote used as a religious token.</note>

In Paper *B* is a certain powder which they call "Virgin’s Milk" <note>original Italian: "Latte della Madonna"</note>, or the Milk of the Virgin Mary.

In Papers *C, D, E, F, G, H, I, and K* are enclosed small pieces of the bones of several martyrs, etc., with the following inscriptions on the back of the papers:

*   *C, Saint Justine, Virgin Martyr.* <note>original: "Sancti Justine Vierge Martyre"</note>
*   *D, Saint Lucius the Hermit.* <note>original: "Sancti Lucii Eremitæ"</note>
*   *E, Saint Dindarus the Martyr.* <note>original: "Sancti Dindari Martyris"</note>
*   *F, Saint Blaise, Bishop and Martyr.* <note>original: "Sancti Blasii Episcopi Martyris"</note>
*   *G, Saint Anthony the Abbot.* <note>original: "Sancti Antonii Abbatis"</note>
*   *H, Saint Anthony the Martyr.* <note>original: "Sancti Antonii Martyris"</note>
*   *I, Saint Pancras.* <note>original: "Sancti Pancratii"</note>
*   *K, Of the Holy Sepulcher.* <note>original: "De la Sancta Sepulcra"; referring to the tomb of Jesus in Jerusalem.</note>

In Paper *L* are the pictures of several saints, as well as of Christ and the Virgin Mary; among these, there is one remarkable image, the title or inscription of which is: <term>For the Conversion of Heretics</term> <note>original Latin: "PRO CONVERSIONE HÆRETICORUM"</note>; all painted in a cloudy color.

Besides these papers and tickets, there are in the said black box these original documents:

1. The Marquess of Pianezza’s grant of immunity <note>original: "indemnity"</note> and various privileges to a certain person for renouncing his religion.
2. The certificate of Prospero da Tarano, delivered to the Marquess of Pianezza, confirming that the person mentioned above had indeed renounced <note>original: "abjured"</note> his religion.

Inasmuch as it is my purpose in the following discourse to give a faithful and accurate account of those many notable and remarkable events of Divine Providence <note>Divine Providence: The belief in God's intervention in and guidance of the world.</note> which have, in almost every age, accompanied the poor Protestants of Piedmont (otherwise known by the name of Waldenses <note>Waldenses: A medieval Christian movement, originating in the 12th century, that sought to return to apostolic poverty and simplicity; they are often seen as precursors to the Protestant Reformation.</note>), and especially regarding that bloody and cruel massacre in the year of our Lord 1655 (the woeful cry of which has been heard throughout the entire Christian world), I shall ask the kind reader to spend a few minutes with me in viewing

<header>The Location and Extent of Book I.</header>

<margin>The pleasant location and great fertility of the Province of *Piedmont*.</margin>
viewing the situation of those *Valleys*, where not only those poor people lived at that time, but where, in all human probability, their forefathers and ancestors have both resided and professed the same religion ever since the days of the *Apostles*.

<margin>The derivation or origin of the word *Piedmont*. The borders of *Piedmont*.</margin>
Now, because these valleys are for the most part enclosed within the borders of *Piedmont*, it will not be out of place to first give a brief description of the entire *Province*. It is indeed but a small spot of earth by comparison and of very limited size, yet it is as pleasant in its location and as incredibly fertile as any province in *Europe*, bringing in a proportionately large revenue to its Prince.

<margin>The extent of the entire Province of *Piedmont*.</margin>
This Province of *Piedmont*—so called because it is situated *at the foot of the mountains* <note>original: "a pede montium"</note>, specifically at the feet of the *Alps* which separate *Italy* from *France*—has for its borders: on the East, the Duchy of *Milan*, *Monferrato*, and the Republic of *Genoa*; on the South, it is bounded by the *Mediterranean Sea*; on the West and North, it has the *Alps* for a wall or bulwark, which separate it on the West from *Provence* and *Dauphiné*, and on the North from *Savoy* and the country of *Valais* <note>original: "Valley"</note>.

<margin>The four great Rivers that cross *Piedmont*: 1. *Po*. 2. *Tanaro*. 3. *Stura*. 4. *Dora*.</margin>
Its longest extent from East to West is from the Valley of *Barcelonnette* (which is about nine miles <note>original: "three Leagues"</note> from *Embrun*) to *Cairo*, which is located on the *Bormida* river toward *Monferrato* and the *Genoese* territory. It is almost entirely covered with high mountains: the *Alps* (specifically the *Pennine*, *Graian*, and *Cottian* ranges, the last of which is now named after the *Val d'Aosta*), *Mont Cenis*, *Mont Genèvre*, as well as the *Apennine* hills.

The province is crossed by four great rivers: the *Po* (which has its source or head near *Monte Viso*, one of the highest mountains in *Europe*), the *Tanaro*, the *Stura*, and the *Dora*. But besides these four, there are about twenty-eight other rivers, large and small, which water the land like a pleasant garden. These rivers make it exceedingly productive in livestock, wine, grain, hay, nuts, and almost all other goods in great abundance.

The truth is, this is a part of the world containing many remarkable things which, if treated individually, would fill a large volume. But as my design is not to dwell too long on this subject, I shall content myself for the sake of brevity to give only a general description of the *Valleys* of *Piedmont*. This is intended to better prepare the noble-minded <note>original: "ingenuous"</note> reader to understand the location of that region which, before the recent *massacre*, was inhabited by the Protestants.

<margin>The principal Valleys that enrich *Piedmont*.</margin>
The principal *valleys* that enrich *Piedmont* are, in the Northern part, the two valleys of *Aosta* and *Susa*; on the Southern side, the Valley of *Stura* and several others; and in the central region, *Luserna*, *Angrogna*, *Roccapiatta*, *Pramollo*, *Perosa*, and *San Martino*.

<margin>The location of the Valley of *Clusone*.</margin>
The Valley of *Clusone*, otherwise called *Pragelato*—meaning the High and the Low Community—is located at the descent of the *Alps* on the East side and empties its river, the *Clusone*, into the Valley of *Perosa* (which is on the West side of *Pinerolo*). In ancient times, it was and still is a part of *Dauphiné* as far as *La Cappella*, which is seated at the

lower end of it, and divides it from *Perosa*. Likewise, it was the usual passage for the *French* armies into *Italy*.

<margin>How the valleys of *Piedmont* are naturally and strongly fortified.</margin>
These valleys—especially those of *Angrogna*, *Pramol*, and *San Martino*—are naturally strongly fortified because of their many difficult passages and barriers of rocks and mountains. It is as if the all-wise Creator had from the beginning intended that place to be a display case <note>original: "Cabinet"</note> in which to place some priceless jewel, or, to speak more plainly, to preserve many thousands of souls who would not bow the knee before *Baal* <note>A biblical reference to those who remained faithful to God and refused to worship idols.</note>.

<margin>Which valleys were previously inhabited by the Protestants.</margin>
But to return to our main subject: of these valleys of *Piedmont*, several were inhabited and peopled by those Protestants who have now, for over five hundred years, been called <note>original: "stiled"</note> *Waldenses*—specifically *Lucerna*, *Perosa*, and *San Martino*.

<margin>A description of the Valley of *Lucerna*.</margin>
The Valley of *Lucerna* (which is also the name of a county) is fifteen Piedmontese miles long, or seven *French* miles. That is to say, from its lowest part in the east, which is bordered by *Garcigliana* and *Campiglione*, to the highest part in the west, where the Fort of *Miraboco* stands. The highest communities <note>original: "Communalty"</note> there—namely *Bobbio*, *Villar*, and *La Torre*—are mostly mountainous, as the valley is not very wide. However, the lower parts—*Lucerna*, *San Giovanni*, *Fenile*, *Campiglione*, and *Garcigliana*—extend into a very beautiful plain, though they have small mountains on both their north and south sides.

<margin>*Angrogna*, *Rorata*, *Vallon*, *Roccapiatta*, *Pramol*.</margin>
*Angrogna*, which is a small valley on the north side of *Lucerna*, as well as *Rorata* and *Vallon*, which are to the south <note>original: "Meridional"</note> of the Valley of *Lucerna*, are entirely within the mountains. So are *Roccapiatta* and *Pramol*, which are enclosed between the valleys of *Lucerna* and *Perosa*.

<margin>A description of the community of *La Torre*.</margin>
The community of *La Torre* took its name from an ancient high tower that stood on a small hill near *Bourg*. *Francis I*, King of *France*, realized that this citadel—located near where the *Lucerna* and *Angrogna* rivers meet <note>original: "conflux"</note> in the very center of the Valley of *Lucerna*—might greatly harm French interests and the safety of *Pinerolo* <note>original: "Pignerole"</note>, so he ordered it to be demolished. This is the same place where the Duke of *Savoy* rebuilt that citadel in 1652, which previously served as a slaughterhouse where so many innocent souls were murdered.

<margin>*Bricherasio*.</margin>
*Bricherasio* <note>original: "Bricheras"</note>, being adjacent to the Valley of *Lucerna*, lies to the east of *Angrogna* and *San Giovanni*, and on the south side of *Roccapiatta*; it is located almost entirely on the plain.

<margin>*Perosa*, *San Martino*.</margin>
The valleys of *Perosa* and *San Martino* are north of *Lucerna*, *Angrogna*, and *Roccapiatta*. They are situated so that the Valley of *Perosa*, being at the lower end and to the east of the valleys of *San Martino* and *Pragela*, receives their two rivers: the *Clusone* and the *Germanasca* <note>original: "Germanacha"</note>.

<margin>A description of the Valley of *Perosa*.</margin>
The Valley of *Perosa*, being about six miles long, consists partly of mountains and partly of beautiful plains and very fertile hills. At its lower end, it contains the communities of *Porte*, *San Germano*, and *Villar*.

## CHAP. II.

### A Description of the Evangelical Churches in the Valleys of Piedmont.

<margin>The fourteen Churches in the Valleys of *Piedmont*, distinguished into two *Classes*.</margin>
Before the recent, horrible dispersion <note>Referring to the "Piedmontese Easter" massacres and forced exile of 1655.</note> of those poor Protestants in the year 1655, there were fourteen *churches* in the said valleys which were populated by *Waldenses*. These churches composed two *Classes* <note>A regional governing body of churches, similar to a presbytery.</note> or *Colloquies* <note>original: "Colloques"</note>, and those two *Classes* formed one *Synod*.

<margin>The first *Classis* comprising the 7 churches: 1. *San Giovanni*. 2. *La Torre*. 3. *Villar*. 4. *Bobbio*. 5. *Rorà*. 6. *Angrogna*. 7. *Roccapiatta*.</margin>
One of these two was called the *Colloquy* of the Valley of *Lucerna*, comprising the churches of *San Giovanni*, *La Torre*, *Villar*, *Bobbio*, *Rorà* <note>original: "Rorata"</note>, and *Angrogna*, which belong to the Valley of *Lucerna*, and the church of *Roccapiatta*, which is between the Valley of *Lucerna* and *Perosa*. It is situated upon those little hills which separate the two valleys and is attached to the said *Colloquy* of the Valley of *Lucerna*.

<margin>The other *Classis* comprising the seven Churches.</margin>
The other *Colloquy*, which was called the *Colloquy* of the Valley of *Perosa* and *San Martino*, contained the other seven churches: namely, four in the said Valley of *Perosa* and three in the Valley of *San Martino*.

<margin>
A description of the Church of *San Giovanni*.
</margin>
The Church of *San Giovanni* <note>modern: San Giovanni Pellice</note> includes a very beautiful plain and small hills. It is very fertile and produces plenty of grain, vines, chestnuts, figs, olives, and all sorts of fruits. However, because the entire area is used for farming, there is a lack of pastures and woods. For this reason, they do not keep much cattle there, except for the oxen used to till their ground and to carry their wine to sell in *Turin* and other places in *Piedmont*.

<margin>
The places annexed to the Church of *Lucerna*.
</margin>
The Church of *Lucerna* also has several places attached to it: *Lucerna*, *Lucernetta*, the vineyards of *Lucerna*, *Fenile*, *Bubiana*, and *Bricheras*. In the city of *Lucerna*, which gives its name to the whole valley, a third of the inhabitants belonged to the Reformed Religion <note>Protestantism</note>. Similarly, in *Lucernetta* and the vineyards of *Lucerna*, almost all the inhabitants have identified as Reformed since time immemorial.

*Fenile* is located even lower on the southern side of the River *Pelice*. Its soil is richer and more fertile than any part of *San Giovanni*, producing all kinds of fruits and grain.

*Bubiana* is similar to *Fenile* regarding its plains, and the two are close neighbors. However, the Protestants there have historically been gradually hunted and driven out of much of that area. What they still possessed in this community was mostly in the hills bordering *Fruzzafca* <note>original: "Fruzzafca," likely modern Frossasco</note>, *Bagnolo*, and *Barge*. Little corn or wine grows there, as the land is covered in chestnuts. The Protestant inhabitants of this place (consisting of about fifty-five families) were mostly poor, living primarily by sheer hard work and the profit they made from selling wood in the towns of *Bubiana* and *Lucerna*.

The hills of *Bricheras*, where Protestant families have always lived, are similar to those of *San Giovanni*.

<margin>
A description of the Church of *La Torre*.
</margin>
The Church of *La Torre* <note>modern: Torre Pellice</note> is similar in location and quality to *San Giovanni*. It contains a plain where the town of *La Torre* is situated, as well as hills decorated with the same kinds of fruits found in the district of *San Giovanni*.

<margin>
A description of the Church of *Villaro*.
</margin>
The Church of *Villaro* is adjacent to *La Torre* but is slightly higher up toward *Dauphiné* <note>original: "Dauphine," a province in southeast France</note>. it contains a small plain where the town is located, while the remaining hills are full of vines and chestnuts.

<margin>
A description of the Church of *Bobbio*.
</margin>
The Church of *Bobbio* borders *Villaro*. It is situated slightly higher toward the mountains to the west but is just as fertile in every way as *Villaro*. Because these places are surrounded by many mountains and rich pastures, the inhabitants kept a great number of oxen, cows <note>original: "Kine"</note>, and smaller livestock. This provided them with an abundance of milk and wool, which returned a considerable profit. They also made a profit from chestnuts, which they dried and cleaned to sell or exchange for other goods.
