# A Summary <note>original: "Abbreviation"</note> of that Confession of Faith which was presented to Ladislaus, King of Bohemia, etc., in the Year of our Lord 1508, by his subjects falsely called Waldenses, wherein they declare the reason for their separation from the Church of Rome.

## And since that time expanded <note>original: "amplified"</note> and explained by the same people, and presented to Ferdinand, King of Bohemia, etc., in the Year of our Lord 1535.

***

->The Preface<-

> Although in times past, our clergy have [given an account] of this faith which we hold, etc. <note>original Latin: "Quanquam retroactis temporibus, ab Ecclesiasticis nostris, hujus quam tenemus fidei, &c."</note>

Although our ministers and clergy <note>original: "Ecclesiasticks"</note> in former ages have often given an account of the faith, religion, and doctrine which we now hold and profess to several kings and princes—and indeed, to everyone who has demanded a reason for it by virtue of their church or government authority—it still seems very necessary to us (for many important reasons) to present to Your Royal Majesty an account of the doctrine we received from our ancestors. We will do this in as brief and concise <note>original: "compendious"</note> a manner as possible in the following articles, which we consider (especially at this moment) to be of general importance and great consequence. 

We do this so that everyone may see how unjustly we have been persecuted by the enemies of this doctrine, and how we are now being falsely accused before Your Royal Majesty in an attempt to make us and our families <note>original: "ours"</note> vulnerable <note>original: "obnoxious"</note> to further suffering and violence.

The preface explains that they are documenting their beliefs to clear their names of false accusations and justify their separation from the Roman Catholic Church.</summary>

## ARTICLE I.

### Concerning the Holy Scriptures.

"In the beginning, all of our people teach with unanimous consent that the Holy Scriptures, etc." <note>original Latin: "Principio, nostri omnes unanimi consensu docent Scripturas sacras, &c."</note>

In the first place, all those of our profession <note>meaning their specific branch of the Christian faith</note> teach and declare with unanimous consent that the Holy Scriptures—which are contained and included in the *Bible*, received by the Church Fathers, and established by canonical authority—must be regarded as undeniably and beyond all controversy most true and certain. In all things and for all reasons, they ought to be preferred over any other writings whatsoever, just as holy things are preferred over profane ones and divine things over human ones. They are to be entirely and absolutely believed, and all the rules of truth concerning our justification <note>the process by which a person is made righteous in the eyes of God</note> and salvation by faith must be sought there and derived from them. 

Furthermore, we believe they were delivered and inspired by God himself, as is affirmed by *Peter, Paul,* and others. They are publicly read and recited in all our churches (especially the Epistles and Gospels) in our native language <note>original: "vulgar Tongue," meaning the common language of the people</note>, following the manner and custom of the *early <note>original: "Primitive"</note> Church*, primarily so that they may be understood by everyone. Finally, from these Scriptures arise points of doctrine and encouragement <note>original: "Exhortation"</note> suitable for all affairs and occasions; and sermons are frequently preached in public to the people.

## ARTICLE II.

### Concerning Catechisms.

"From here they teach the Catechism, which is this Catholic and Orthodox doctrine of the Fathers, etc." <note>original Latin: "Hinc Catechismum docent, hoc est Catholicam hanc & Orthodoxam Patrum, &c."</note>

From these Scriptures, they derive the Catechism—that is, the universal <note>original: "Catholick"</note> and orthodox <note>conforming to the established and traditional faith</note> doctrine of the Fathers. This is one and the same as the Decalogue <term>the Ten Commandments</term> of God's commandments, and the *Apostles' Creed* (organized into *twelve articles* and delivered as a statement of faith <note>original: "Symbol"</note> by the Council of *Nicaea*), which has been similarly explained and confirmed by others. Finally, it also contains the *Lord's Prayer*. Now, they constantly affirm all these things to be most holy, good, and well-pleasing in the eyes of God.

Moreover, they teach that all these things ought to be followed in practice and with the whole heart, seeing that the Law is spiritual; as also

...that the Articles of Faith ought undoubtedly to be believed, confessed with the mouth, and demonstrated through works. They also enforce and support these Articles with the Scriptures to the best of their ability, endeavoring to teach their genuine sense. Where anything occurs that is abstruse or difficult, they attempt to unfold its true scope and meaning fully and plainly.

They teach likewise that God alone is to be prayed to, and invoked only through the name of *Christ* the Mediator <note>A "mediator" is an intermediary; in Christian theology, Jesus is seen as the bridge between God and humanity</note>. They also teach that prayers and supplications ought to be made for all governors of the Church, and all others who are placed in positions of eminence and authority for the government of others.

## ARTICLE III.

### Of Faith in the Holy Trinity.

->*Furthermore, they teach that God is known by faith through the Scriptures, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Præterea fide nosci Deum Scripturis docent, &c."</note><-

Furthermore, they teach that God is known by faith in the Scriptures to be one in the substance of his divinity, and three persons: namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. They teach that as to the persons there is a difference, but as to the essence and substance, there is co-equality and no distinction. This the Catholic <note>Here "Catholic" refers to the "universal" or "whole" Christian Church, not specifically the Roman Catholic Church</note> faith, the consensus of the Council of *Nicaea*, the decrees and sanctions of other Councils, and the confession or creed of *Athanasius* <note>The Athanasian Creed is a Christian statement of belief focusing on Trinitarian doctrine</note> clearly testify.

Hence they also teach the great power, wisdom, and goodness of this one and only God, as well as those three most excellent works agreeable to him alone, and which are applicable to none but him: namely, the works of Creation, Redemption, and Conservation <note>preservation</note> or Sanctification. Moreover, they teach that this true God—in one essence of divinity and a blessed trinity of persons—is alone to be worshipped (*Deuteronomy 6, etc.*).

## ARTICLE IV.

### Of Sin, its Fruits, and the knowledge of oneself.

->*Here they teach that we should not be ignorant of the sins which are committed both against neighbors and against God, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Hic docent, ne peccata ignoremus quæ cum in proximos, tum in Deum, &c."</note><-

Here they teach that we should not be ignorant of our sins, which are committed and acted out both against God and our neighbor.

First, they teach that people ought to acknowledge that they are conceived and—

...and are born in sin, and so are sinners immediately and naturally from the womb. Thus, straying <note>original: "prevaricating," meaning to act or speak evasively or to transgress</note> from their childhood against the Law of God in heart and deed, they are pressed and burdened with the weight of sin, as it is written: *The Lord looked down from Heaven to see whether there was anyone who was wise, or sought after God; but they have all gone out of the way, they have all corrupted themselves, there is none who does good, no, not one.* <note>Psalm 14:2–3</note> Again, *God saw that the wickedness of man was great upon the earth, and that all the thoughts and imaginations of his heart were wholly evil, and that continually.* <note>Genesis 6:5</note> And again the Lord says, *that the conception and thought of man's heart is evil from his youth.* <note>Genesis 8:21</note> And Paul likewise says, *We were by nature the children of wrath even as others.* <note>Ephesians 2:3</note>

Next, they teach from the Scriptures that men ought to acknowledge that—because of this depravity and corruption, and for the sins arising and springing up from this root of bitterness <note>a biblical metaphor for a source of sin or trouble</note>—the fearful vengeance of God and utter destruction deservedly hang over their heads. They teach that, according to these deeds, the pains of hell are most justly set before them; for, as Paul says, *the wages of sin is death.* <note>Romans 6:23</note> And the Lord says in the Gospel, *They that have done ill shall go into eternal punishment, where there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.* <note>Matthew 25:46</note> They teach further that it is necessary for all to consider and know their weakness, their extreme need, and the disasters into which they have fallen because of their sins. They must realize that they can in no way save or justify themselves by any works or efforts of their own, nor have anything to trust in but Christ alone, through whom they may be redeemed and freed from sin, Satan, the wrath of God, and eternal death. Also, there is nothing in man by which one may help another before God, seeing that all are equally lacking the righteousness of God and are subject <note>original: "obnoxious," which in this period meant "liable to" or "exposed to punishment"</note> to his wrath because of sin.

---

### ARTICLE V.
### Of Repentance.

->*In this place, they teach that repentance is that which is born from the acknowledgment of sins and divine wrath, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Hoc loco docent Pœnitentiam esse, quæ ex peccatorum & ira divina agnitione nascitur, &c."</note><-

In this place, they teach repentance to be that which comes from the acknowledgment of sin and God's anger, which—through the Law of God—first strikes the conscience with sorrow and terror. Because they are inwardly convinced of sin by the Word of God, the mind becomes affected with an evil conscience: unquiet, exceedingly sorrowful, and despairing. The heart is anxious, broken, and contrite, so that a man cannot be raised up or find comfort by his own efforts, but is altogether afflicted. His spirit is dejected, trembling, shaken, and shattered with exceedingly great horror through

the sight of God's wrath, (as David says of himself): *There is no health in my flesh because of your indignation, nor is there any rest in my bones because of my sin. I have become miserable, and am bowed down, and go mourning all day long.* <note>Psalm 38:3, 6</note> But yet despite this, they teach that being thus frightened, they ought nevertheless not to despair, but rather to return to God with their whole heart through faith in Christ, which is also a part of Repentance; taking hold of Mercy, and grieving that they have sinned. For although they are devoid of righteousness, they still ought to beg for Divine Grace and Mercy, so that he would have mercy on them and pardon their sins for the sake of Christ and his merits—who for our sake was made sin and a curse, so that he might satisfy the justice of God for our sins, etc.

## ARTICLE VI.
### Of the Lord Christ, and Faith in him.

> First of all, they teach that a certain and firm faith must be held concerning Christ the Lord, etc. <note>original: "Omnium primò docent, certam firmámque fidem habendam de Christo Domino, &c."</note>

First of all, they teach that we ought to have a certain and firm faith concerning the Lord Christ—namely, that he is true God by nature, and also true man, by whom all things were made, visible and invisible, in heaven and earth. John, calling him the *Eternal Word*, interprets him to be God, *Light*, the *only begotten*, abiding in the bosom of the Father, full of grace and truth. The same author, in his first Epistle and fifth chapter, says, *This is the true God and Eternal Life.* <note>1 John 5:20</note>

They also declare his works performed for our salvation: his incarnation, birth <note>original: "Nativity"</note>, passion, death, burial, resurrection, and ascension into heaven; his sitting at the right hand of God, and his return to judge the living <note>original: "Quick"</note> and the dead. They teach that through the Word and Sacraments, good fruits are derived to us, by which we may be saved, as the Scriptures show.

They teach further that Christ is not now in the world, nor will he ever appear until the world has ended in the same sensible and physical manner in which he previously lived as a man upon the earth—suffering himself to be betrayed, tormented, crucified, and put to death, and afterwards rising again in a glorious manner, making his way through the hard rock and the sealed door of the tomb <note>original: "Sepulcher"</note>. But they teach that he is now in heaven in such a way that every tongue ought to confess him, and all the godly should worship him together with the Father. To this the Article of Faith <note>referring to the Apostles' Creed</note> clearly bears witness: *He ascended into heaven, where he sits at the right hand of God the Father Almighty, from which he shall come to judge both the living and the dead.* Just as Paul says in the 4th chapter of 1 Thessalonians: *The Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God.* <note>1 Thessalonians 4:16</note>

<summary>This page concludes the section on repentance, emphasizing that believers should not despair but seek mercy through Christ, and begins Article VI, which defines the Waldensian belief in the divinity, humanity, and redemptive work of Jesus Christ.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the confession of faith regarding the nature of Jesus Christ, moving from his divinity and incarnation (on the previous page) to his ascension, his ongoing presence in the Church, and the doctrine of justification by faith alone.</meta>

God. Peter likewise in the Book of Acts says, *Whom heaven must receive until the times of the restoration of all things.* <note>Acts 3:21</note> And in the last chapter of Mark, *Therefore the Lord, after he had spoken to them, was received up into heaven, and sat on the right hand of God.* <note>Mark 16:19</note> And the angels who stood by said to them, *This same Jesus, who is taken up from you into heaven, shall come in the same way as you have seen him going into heaven, etc.* <note>Acts 1:11</note>

They also teach that the Lord Christ—in this, his other manner of being, which we call "invisible"—is present in the ministers of his Church, the Word, and the Sacraments. Through these means, all people hereafter ought to receive him by faith, so that he may dwell and remain in them by the Spirit of Truth, concerning whom he has said, *He shall be in you.* And again, *I will come to you, etc.*

Moreover, they hold that by faith in Christ, people are—through mercy—freely <term>justified</term> <note>Justified: In a legal or theological sense, being declared righteous or "not guilty" before God.</note> and attain salvation and the forgiveness of sins through Christ, without any human help or merit.

They likewise hold that all confidence and hope is to be fixed in him alone, and that all our worries ought to be cast upon him. To these points they further add that for his sake only, and for his merits alone, God is pacified and reconciled to us, loves and preserves us, and adopts us to be his children; and that eternal life is in him, and as many as believe in him shall enjoy it through him. John 6: *He that believes in me has eternal life, etc.*

They also teach that no one can have this faith by any power, will, or pleasure of their own; it is indeed the gift of God. He works it in a person by his Spirit when and where it pleases him, so that they may receive whatever is rightly administered to them by the outward Word and the Sacraments established by Christ for the purpose of salvation.

Of this faith, John the Baptist says that no one can have anything unless it is given to him from above. And Christ himself says, *No one can come to me, unless the Father, who sent me, draws him.* And a little later he adds, *Unless it is given to him by my Father*—that is to say, by the Holy Spirit.

Furthermore, they teach that people are justified before God by faith alone, or trust in Jesus Christ, without their own endeavors, merits, or works, according to that saying of Paul: *Moreover, to him who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness.* <note>Romans 4:5</note> Again, *But now the righteousness of God is revealed without the Law, being witnessed by the Law and the Prophets. And this righteousness is through the faith of Jesus Christ.* <note>Romans 3:21–22</note>

## ARTICLE VII.

### Concerning Good Works.

->*To these points they add that those who are justified by the grace of God alone, and through faith in Christ, etc.* <note>original Latin: "His addunt, ut qui sola Dei gratia, fidéque in Christum, justificati sunt, &c."</note><-

To these points they add that those people who are justified only by the grace of God and through faith in *Christ* do perform those good works which God commands. Every person should walk in these works as is appropriate for them, according to their <term>calling</term> <note>Calling: One's station in life, profession, or social role, viewed as a task assigned by God.</note> in any kind of life, condition, or age whatsoever. For the Lord says in *Matthew*: *Teach them to observe all things which I have commanded you.* <note>Matthew 28:20</note> But because there are many things written in various places of the *Scriptures* concerning this matter, we refrain from expanding further.

Indeed, they also teach for what specific reason and with what purpose good works are to be done. They are not to be done for the purpose of people thinking they can obtain justification, salvation, or the forgiveness of sins through them; for even the Lord himself says, *When you have done all the things which are commanded of you, say, "We are unprofitable servants."* <note>Luke 17:10</note> Again, *Paul* says, *By the works of the Law shall no flesh be justified in his sight.* <note>Romans 3:20</note> So also *David* says, *Lord, do not enter into judgment with your servant, for in your sight shall no man living be justified.* <note>Psalm 143:2</note>

However, they teach that good works are to be done so that faith may be proven by them. Good works are sure testimonies, seals, and evidences of a living faith lying hidden within; they are the fruits of that faith, by which the tree is known to be good or bad (*Matthew 7*). Also, works are done so that through them people may make their calling sure and certain, and be saved in that state without sin; according to what *Peter* says in his *second Epistle, chapter 1*: *Brethren, give diligence to make your calling and election sure.*

Furthermore, they teach that we should know there is a difference between works ordained by men and works which are commanded by God. They also teach how both may be performed and observed, because the works commanded by God are in no way to be neglected for the sake of human traditions. The Lord severely <term>reproves</term> <note>Reproves: Criticizes or corrects; expresses disapproval.</note> those who do the opposite: *Why do you transgress the commandment of God for your traditions?* And, *In vain do they worship me, teaching the doctrines of men as commandments.* <note>Matthew 15:3, 9</note>

They teach, moreover, that there is no man who can indeed perfectly perform the works commanded by God. Also, there is no man who does not sin, even if he carefully exercises himself in good works and in the Law of God; as it is written: *There is no one upon earth who does good and does not sin, etc.* <note>Ecclesiastes 7:20</note>

<sig>H</sig>
<meta>catchword: ARTIC.</meta>

<summary>This article explains that while good works do not earn salvation or justification, they are necessary as evidence of a living faith and as an act of obedience to God's commands. It distinguishes between God's laws and human traditions, noting that human nature is inherently prone to sin even when attempting to do good.</summary>

# ARTICLE VIII.

## Of the Holy Catholic Church.

->*They teach first, that Christ the Lord, by his own merit, grace, and truth, is the head and foundation of the Church, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Docent primùm, Chriſtum Dominum ſuo merito, gratiâ & veritate, Eccleſiæ caput & fundamentum eſſe, &c."</note><-

They teach first that the Lord *Christ*, through his own merit, grace, and truth, is the Head and Foundation of the Church. She is built up in him through the Holy Spirit, by the Word and Sacraments; as *Christ* said to *Peter*: *And upon this Rock (that is, myself) I will build my Church.* And *Paul* says in 1 Corinthians 3: *No man can lay any other foundation besides that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.* The same Apostle says in another place that he is the Head of the Church, who fills all in all.

They also teach that we must believe and confess that the holy Catholic <note>In this historical context, "Catholic" refers to the "universal" or "whole" Christian church throughout history and the world, rather than specifically the Roman Catholic denomination.</note> Church, as it is currently gathered, consists of all *Christian* people throughout the world, in whatever nations they live or wherever they may be scattered. These people are gathered together out of all nations, peoples, tribes, and languages by the sacred Word of the Gospel into the same faith in *Christ* and the holy Trinity, regardless of their rank, age, or condition. This is according to what was written by *John* in the *Apocalypse* <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>: *After these things I looked, and behold, a great multitude, which no man was able to number, etc.* And the Lord says: *Where two or three shall be gathered together in my Name (in any nation or people whatsoever), there am I in the midst of them.* For wherever *Christ* is preached and received, and wherever his Word and Sacraments are administered and received according to his appointment and will, there is a holy Church, a *Christian* society, and the people of God, whatever their number may be. But where *Christ* is absent and his Word is rejected, there can be neither a true Church nor a people who please God.

Regarding their own congregation, they believe and teach that it—just like other congregations, whether large or small—is not the holy universal Church itself, but only a part and member of it. This is as the *Corinthians* were, of whom the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 12: *Now you are the body of Christ, and members in particular, etc.*

Besides this, they teach that those who are clearly ungodly, unrepentant, and stubborn—that is to say, those who do not listen to the warnings of the Church—may be restricted by the Church's discipline and punishment. In common usage, this is called *Anathema* <note>A formal curse or excommunication by a religious authority.</note> or excommunication. This ought to be done without favoritism <note>original: "without respect of persons"</note> against all those whose wickedness is known and who are addicted to notorious sins, and who persist in their sins even after being warned many times.

Furthermore, they teach that *Antichrist*, that "man of sin," sits in the temple of God (that is, in the Church), of whom the Prophets and

<summary>This article defines the Church as a universal body of believers gathered from all nations, with Jesus Christ as its sole head and foundation. It also outlines the practice of church discipline and excommunication for unrepentant members.</summary>

### ARTICLE IX.

->Of the Ecclesiastical Order, or the Overseers, or Ministers of the Church.<-

They teach that the Ministers of the Church, to whom the administration of the Word and Sacraments is entrusted, ought to be properly ordained, etc. <note>original Latin: "Docent Ministros Ecclesiæ, quibus administratio Verbi & Sacramentorum demandatur, ritè institutos esse oportere, &c."</note>

They teach that the ministers of the church, to whom the administration of the Word and the sacraments is entrusted, ought to be properly ordained according to the rule prescribed by the Lord and his apostles. To undertake this office, men full of faith and without blame may be called from among the godly and faithful people—specifically those who possess the gifts necessary for this ministry and are of honest life and conduct. These men are to be tested first. Then, after prayer is offered by the elders, they are to be confirmed in their office within the congregation by the <term>imposition of hands</term> <note>The practice of "laying on of hands," a formal act of blessing and authorization for ministry.</note>, etc.

Therefore, no one among us is permitted to perform the office of a <term>priest</term> <note>original: "Priest"; in this Waldensian context, this refers to a pastor or ordained minister rather than a sacrificial priest in the Roman Catholic sense.</note> unless he is properly called and ordained according to this rule. Next, they teach that it is the duty of those chosen for the ministry of the church to have a diligent care for the souls committed to their charge, to faithfully administer to them the Word of the Gospel and the sacraments according to Christ’s institution, to provide a good example for all people to follow, and to pray to God for them, that they may be delivered from their errors and offenses, etc.

### ARTICLE X.

->Of the Word of God.<-

Furthermore, they teach that the preaching of the Word of God or the Gospel is a ministry appointed and commanded by Christ, in the last chapter of Matthew: etc. <note>original Latin: "Deinde docent, quod verbi Dei, seu Evangelii prædicatio est Ministerium à Christo institutum & præceptum, Matthæi ultimo: &c."</note>

Furthermore, they teach that the preaching of the Word of God or the Gospel is a ministry appointed and commanded by Christ in the final chapter of *Matthew*: *Go into all the world, and preach the Gospel to every creature.* Peter also says in *Acts* 10: *The Lord commanded us that we should preach, etc.*

They teach also, that we ought to hold a difference between the

For that reason, they read the Gospels themselves and the other Scriptures in the common language <note>original: "vulgar Tongue"</note> in their churches.

## ARTICLE XI.
### Of the Sacraments.

-> They teach especially that the sacraments instituted by Christ are necessary for salvation, etc. <note>original Latin: "Docent imprimis, Sacramenta per Christum instituta, ad salutem necessaria esse, &c."</note> <-

First, they teach that the sacraments ordained by *Christ* are necessary for salvation, as they are the means by which believers are made partakers of the merits of *Christ*. However, if any person willfully despises or does not worthily value them, or uses them in any manner other than what *Christ* has willed and commanded, they declare that he sins grievously against *Christ*, the author of those sacraments.

But if it should happen that a person truly desires to receive the sacraments according to the mind and command of *Christ*, yet is hindered by sickness, or carried away captive into foreign lands, or is oppressed by the adversaries and enemies of the faith, etc., so that he is unable to satisfy his own godly desire—in such cases, if he sincerely and entirely believes the Gospel, he shall undoubtedly be saved by faith in *Christ* alone.

They next teach that the sacraments do not confer grace or justifying faith by the mere act of performing them <note>original Latin: "ex opere operato," a theological term meaning "from the work worked," implying the sacrament works automatically regardless of the recipient's heart</note> upon those who are not first endowed with good intentions and inwardly given life by the Holy Spirit, etc.

## ARTICLE XII.
### Of Baptism.

*They teach also that baptism is a saving administration, instituted by Christ, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Docent item, quod Baptismus sit salutaris administratio, à Christo institu- ta, &c."</note>

They teach also that baptism is a saving administration <note>original: "administration," here meaning a formal religious rite or service</note> instituted by **Christ** and added to the **Gospel**, by which he purifies, cleanses, and sanctifies his Church in his own death and blood. As **Paul** says, **Christ loved his Church, and gave himself for it: that he might sanctify it, being cleansed by the washing of water through the Word, etc.**

Likewise, they teach that **children** are to be baptized for salvation and to be consecrated to **Christ** according to his Word: **Allow little children to come to me, and do not forbid them, for of such is the Kingdom of God, etc.**

## ARTICLE XIII.
### Of the Lord's Supper.

*That the Lord's Supper, or the Sacrament of the Eucharist, is a ministry established by Christ, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Dominicam Cœnam, seu Sacramentum Eucharistiæ, Ministerium esse à Christo, &c."</note>

They teach that the Lord's Supper, or Sacrament of the Eucharist, was a ministry <note>original: "Ministerium"</note> appointed by **Christ**, afterward by his Apostles, and by them—through his grace and goodness—delivered to the whole Church for the common use and salvation of all people. As the Evangelists bear witness, and also the Apostle whose words are used by all the Church: **For I have received from the Lord that which I also delivered to you: how the Lord Jesus, in the same night in which he was betrayed, took bread, etc.** And a little after: **Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat (that is, this Supper), wait for one another.**

Furthermore, they also teach here that people must believe with the heart and confess with the mouth that the bread of the Lord's Supper is the true body of **Christ**, which was delivered for us, and that the cup is his true blood, which was shed for us for the remission <note>original: "Remission," meaning the forgiveness or cancellation of a debt or penalty</note> of sins, as the Lord **Christ** expressly says: **This is my body; This is my blood, etc.**

They further teach that in administering this sacrament, nothing else is to be done but what is set forth and commanded by these express words of **Christ**, who, giving bread to his disciples, said: **Take, eat; this is my body.** And taking the cup, he gave thanks and said: **Drink you all of this; for this is my blood of the New Testa-**

But if any man, out of arrogance, attempts anything contrary to this institution of **Christ**, he sins against **Christ** the author of it, and against his will expressly revealed in the Scripture.

## ARTICLE XIV.
### Of Ecclesiastical Power, or the Keys.

*And here they teach that it should be believed that the keys were handed over by Christ to the church, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Et hic docent, ut credatur Claves à Christo Ecclesiæ traditas esse, &c."</note>

And here they teach how it ought to be believed that the keys were delivered by **Christ** to the church, concerning which he said to **Peter**, on behalf of all the apostles, **I will give you the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven.** They teach that these keys represent an administration delivered to the church of **Christ** and its ministers. This authority continues in the church to this present day and is not to end before the dissolution of the world.

The duty and authority of this administration, according to the command and intent of **Christ**, is (as the Scriptures express) to correct and bind those who are wicked and unrepentant in the church, and to shut the Kingdom of Heaven against them. This means excluding them from **Christ** and from the fellowship and communion of the church. 

On the contrary, its duty is to absolve those who are truly penitent, restore them to peace of conscience, and place them in a sure hope and belief of salvation. By doing so, they open the Kingdom of Heaven to them and instruct and strengthen them against all the temptations, assaults, and cunning devices of the enemy. They ought to do this not by their own power and pleasure, but as stewards <note>original: "Dispensers"</note> of the mysteries of God, acting as ministers and servants of **Christ**. They act by his authority, through the Word and sacraments, etc.

## ARTICLE XV.
### Of Human Traditions.

*They teach that human traditions, rites, and customs, which are in no way contrary to piety, are to be observed in public assemblies, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Humanas traditiones, ritus & consuetudines, quæ nihil pietati adversantur, in publicis conventibus servanda docent, &c."</note>

They teach that human traditions, rites, and customs, which

...are not against piety, are to be observed in public congregations, and so on.

But they teach that such traditions, rites, and ceremonies which obscure the glory of **Christ** and his grace, lead the people away, and draw them back from the truth and faith, are to be avoided and rejected. This also applies if these rituals are made equal to or preferred over divine institutions, or if any man violates God's commands for the sake of these ceremonies and abandons the sincere use of the Word of God.

They teach next that because of the differences in ceremonies, customs, and rites which are seen in several Christian churches—and which are not harmful or hurtful to piety—believers ought not to be offended by one another, nor should they despise <note>original: "contemn"</note>, hate, or persecute one another, and so on.

## ARTICLE XVI.
### Of the Secular Power.

*It is taught here among us according to the Scriptures, that the higher power, or the secular magistrate, is an ordinance of God, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Docetur hic apud nos juxta Scripturas, quod sublimior potestas, seu Magistratus secularis, Dei ordinatio sit, &c."</note>

We teach here, according to the Scriptures, that the higher power or secular magistrate <note>a civil official or government authority</note> is an ordinance of God, established so that the people may be governed in those things which are political and temporary. Concerning this, that passage from **Paul** is excellent: *For there is no power but from God; the powers that exist are ordained by God.*

They teach, moreover, that those who are in power, or hold public office and magistracy of any degree, should understand that they do not do their own work, but the work of God. He is the sovereign Lord and King over them and all others. They should also remember that they must give an account of their stewardship <note>their management of the authority entrusted to them</note> on the Last Day.

They teach also that it is commanded in the Word of God that all men should be subject to the higher powers in all things, provided they are such things as are not contrary to God and his Word, and so on.

But regarding those things which concern souls, faith, and salvation, they teach that we ought to listen to God’s Word only, and his ministers, as **Christ** himself says: *Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.*

And if any man endeavors to compel them to do things that are against God and contrary <note>original: "repugnant"</note> to his Word, which endures forever, they teach that we ought to follow the example of the Apostles, who gave this answer to the magistrate at **Jerusalem**: *We ought (they said) to obey God rather than men.*

## ARTICLE XVII.

### On the Worship of Saints.

*They teach at the beginning that since the creation of man, none of them ever existed, nor is there now, nor will there ever be, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Initio docent quòd post creatos homines nullus eorum unquam extitit, nec nunc quoque est, nec aliquando futurus est, &c."</note>

They teach first that since the creation of mankind, there has never been anyone—nor is there now, nor will there ever be—who can be holy or righteous by any strength, merits, efforts, or works of their own. Even as holy **Job** says, "*What is man, that he should be pure, and he who is born of a woman, that he should appear righteous?*"

But whatever good things are found in the saints, they ought to be acknowledged as received from the bounty and goodness of God. For the fact that they are holy and acceptable to God is something that happens to them without any merit of their own, but solely through His divine will and pleasure, etc.

They teach, moreover, that the honor and worship due to God must not be transferred to the saints, nor to their images; as it is written in **Isaiah**: "*I am the Lord, that is my name; I will not give my glory to another,*" etc.

---

## ARTICLE XVIII.

### On Fasting.

*Our people teach that fasts are a certain external worship among the godly, to be offered to God alone, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Jejunia nostri cultum quendam externum in piis esse, Deo soli exhibendum, &c."</note>

Those of our persuasion teach that fasts are a kind of outward worship among the godly, to be offered only to God Himself. These should be observed according to the circumstances of people, nations, places, and affairs, by everyone, without superstition and hypocrisy.

They teach next that fasting does not consist in a distinction between types of food <note>original: "difference of Meats," referring to religious rules forbidding meat on certain days</note>, but in a sparing use of them, including sobriety, temperance, the disciplining <note>original: "afflicting"</note> of the body, and humiliation before God. It is, however, a matter of great importance with what mindset or purpose a person fasts, because fasting is only good when it is pleasing and acceptable to God, as you may read in **Matthew 6** and **Isaiah 58**.

## ARTICLE XIX.

### On Celibacy, or the Unmarried State.

*They teach concerning celibacy that no one should be forced into it, nor discouraged from it, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Ad cœlibatum docent, neminem cogendum, aut ab eo retrahendum esse, &c."</note>

They teach that no one should be forced into a single life, nor kept from it, because God has neither commanded nor forbidden it to anyone. Instead, He has left it to every person's own will and choice to live unmarried or to marry.

They teach, moreover, that no one should choose a single life with the intention of thinking they might merit the forgiveness of sins and eternal life for themselves or others. For neither a single life nor any work of ours can obtain these things for us; they come only through the death and grace of **Christ** alone.

---

## ARTICLE XX.

### On the Time of Grace, in which God's Favor Should be Sought and May be Found.

*Finally, in this section they teach that people should know that for as long as they are alive, there is a time given by God, which is a time of grace, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Hoc demùm loco docent, ut sciant homines tantisper dum in vivis sunt, tempus à Deo, quod gratiæ est, &c."</note>

Lastly, they teach here that people must understand that as long as they live in this world, a time is given to them by God—a time of grace—so that they may seek Him and His grace, goodness, mercy, and kindness. Through His promise, they may find these things and thereby achieve blessedness and salvation. They also teach that every person, while this time of grace lasts, should repent for their past life, be reconciled to God, and calm, quiet, and reassure their own conscience through faith in **Christ** and through His ministry in the church. 

Following this, firmly believing that their sins are pardoned and that God is reconciled for the sake of **Christ**, and being established in His grace while walking and persevering in good works, they should confidently expect that when the soul is released from the prison of the body, it shall not pass into any punishment. Instead, like poor **Lazarus** <note>A reference to the parable in Luke 16:19–31, where the beggar Lazarus is carried by angels to Abraham's side after death.</note>, it will be carried into eternal happiness and remain there with the Lord **Christ** forever, etc.

### A Testimony taken from Dr. Martin Luther's Preface to the Confession of the Waldenses,
#### In the Year of our Lord 1533.

->*But among these people there also appeared those Brethren whom they called Pighards, who are no longer as hateful to me as they once were, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Inter hos autem occurrebant & isti Fratres, quos Pighardos vocabant, jam mihi non ita invisi, &c."</note><-

But among these I observed also those Brethren whom they called *Pighard Brethren* or *Picards*, who are not now hateful to me as they were in the days when I was a Papist <note>original: "Popery"; referring to Luther's time as a Roman Catholic monk</note>. In a word, I found among them that one great and wonderful thing, which is hardly ever heard of in the Pope’s Church: namely, that by laying aside the doctrines of men as far as they were able, they meditated on the law of the Lord night and day. I found that they were skilled and ready in the Scriptures, whereas under the Papacy, our own masters completely neglected the Scriptures; they were puffed up with the name of the *Bible*, yet some of them had never even seen one at any time. 

And yet, it could not be any other way than that various passages remained obscure to them, because not only the *Greek* and *Hebrew languages*, but *Latin* as well, were essentially lost to them. It remained a fault among them that, while they endeavored to avoid the briars and bogs in which the sophists <note>original: "Sophisters"; a term for university-trained theologians whose complex logic Luther often criticized</note> and monks were entangled, they completely abstained from all study of the liberal arts. They were also pinched by poverty, which they relieved by the labor of their hands.

But now they appear much better instructed and more free—I may also say more enlightened and improved—so that I hope they will be neither unwelcome nor unpleasing to those who are truly *Christian*. Therefore, it behooves us to give very great thanks to God the Father of our Lord *Jesus Christ*, who, according to the riches of His glory, has commanded this light of His Word to shine out of darkness, thereby to destroy death in us and restore life. We ought to rejoice also, both on their behalf and our own, that we—who were at a distance from each other—have now, upon throwing down that dividing wall of jealousy <note>original: "Jealousie"; here meaning mutual suspicion or sectarian animosity</note> by which we seemed like heretics to one another, been made near and brought together into one sheepfold. We are under that one Shepherd and Bishop of our souls, who is blessed for ever. **Amen.**

<summary>This page contains a 1533 testimonial from Martin Luther praising the Waldensian Brethren (Picards) for their dedication to the Bible despite their lack of formal education and poverty. Luther celebrates the reconciliation between his followers and the Waldensians, viewing them no longer as heretics but as fellow members of Christ's flock.</summary>

## The testimony given by Philip Melanchthon <note>original: Philip Melancthon; a key leader in the German Reformation and collaborator with Martin Luther</note> to the Waldenses <note>A medieval Christian group often considered precursors to the Protestant Reformation</note>, in a letter addressed:

### To the Reverend Brother in Christ Mr. Benedict, and the rest of the Waldensian Brethren in Bohemia.

> Grace and peace, etc. I believe, distinguished man, that your brothers in this meeting of ours have come to understand my opinion on many things better, etc. <note>original Latin: "Gratia & pax, &c. Existimo, vir eximie, Fratres tuos in hoc nostro congressu in multis rebus melius meam sententiam cognovisse, &c."</note>

Grace and Peace, etc. I believe, worthy Sir, that your brethren at this meeting of ours have come to know and thoroughly understand my opinion on many things—perhaps better than I myself understood your affairs in the past. Therefore, since we agree on the main articles of the Christian faith, let us mutually embrace each other in love, for no difference or variety of rites and ceremonies should divide our minds. The Apostle Paul speaks often regarding ceremonies and forbids Christians from disagreeing because of a variety of rituals, even though the rest of the world argues fiercely about them. Indeed, I do not dislike that stricter way of practice <note>original: "Exercise"</note> or discipline used in your churches; I wish to God it were observed a little more strictly in our churches as well. As for my own feelings toward you, I want you to know that I earnestly wish that those who love the Gospel and desire the name of Christ to be glorified would support one another with mutual love. Together, we should use our learning for the glory of Christ, rather than destroying ourselves through private enmities or arguments—especially about matters that do not require such conflict. Farewell; pray for me and for the glory of Christ.

->Given at Wittenberg, in the year 1533.<-

->Philip Melanchthon.<-

### Another excerpt from *Martin Bucer's* <note>Martin Bucer (1491–1551) was a prominent German Protestant reformer based in Strasbourg who influenced many different denominations</note> book, titled, *Two Written Replies to Latomus, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Scripta duo Adversaria Latomi, &c."</note> in the chapter regarding the authority of the Church, page 159.

->*That certainly is the best method which the Picard Brothers observe, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Illa certe ratio optima est quam observant Fratres Picardi, &c." The "Picard Brothers" was a common name for the Waldenses in Bohemia and Moravia.</note><-

They have also maintained the discipline of *Christ* among them. The reality of their practice compels us to give them this praise, so that we may honor the Lord, who works in them this way—even though those brethren are despised by some men who are "perversely learned" <note>A reference to scholars who prioritized academic hair-splitting over practical Christian living</note>. The practice they follow in this matter is as follows:

Besides the ministers of the Word and the Sacraments, they have a certain council <note>original: "College"</note> of men who excel in wisdom and seriousness of spirit. Their office is to warn and correct brothers who have done wrong, to reconcile those who disagree, and to judge in their disputes <note>original: "Causes"</note>, etc.

...to look upon us as true members of the mystical body of *Christ*, suffering for his name's sake, despite our poverty and low status; and to continue to grant us the help of their prayers to *God*, and all other effects of their charity, as we have previously found and felt in abundance. ### A short Justification, relating to those points for which the doctors <note>original: "Doctours"—meaning learned theologians or teachers</note> of the *Roman* Church are accustomed to accuse us and other Reformed Churches, which are nevertheless condemned by us all as being full of impiety and to be detested by all *Christians*.

First, we are commonly accused:

1. That *God* is the author of sin.
2. That *God* is not omnipotent.
3. That *Christ* was not impeccable <note>original: "impeccable"—meaning incapable of sinning</note>.
4. That *Jesus Christ*, while upon the cross, fell into despair.
5. That man is like a block of wood <note>original: "stock"</note> or a stone in the actions toward which he is moved by the Holy Spirit for his own salvation.
6. That on account of predestination, it is a matter of indifference whether we live well or not.
7. That good works are not necessary for salvation.
8. That repentance and confession of sins are absolutely condemned among us.

<column-break/>

<note>This column is a translation of the original Italian text provided on the page.</note>

...to regard us (despite our poverty and lowliness) as true members of the mystical body of Jesus Christ, who suffer for his name, and to continue the help of their prayers toward God, and all other effects of their charity, as we have already experienced in abundance. Therefore, we thank them with all possible humility, praying to the Lord with all our heart that he may be their rewarder, spreading over them the most precious blessings of grace and glory, in this life and in that which is to come. Amen.

### *A short justification regarding those points for which the doctors of the Roman religion are accustomed to accuse our churches and the other Reformed ones: which are also condemned by everyone as being full of impiety, and worthy of the detestation of Christians.*

*We are commonly accused of believing:*

*1. That God is the author of sin.*
*2. That God is not omnipotent.*
*3. That Jesus Christ was not impeccable <note>original: "impeccabile"—incapable of sinning</note>.*
*4. That Jesus Christ, on the cross, fell into despair.*
*5. That man is like a stick or a stone in the actions to which he is moved for salvation by the Spirit of God.*
*6. That by virtue of predestination, it is a matter of indifference whether one lives well or poorly.*
*7. That good works are not necessary for salvation.*
*8. That penance and the confession of sins are absolutely condemned among us.*

# CHAPTER 5

## The Ancient Discipline of the Evangelical Churches in the Valleys of PIEDMONT.

### Extracted from various authentic manuscripts, written in their own language several hundreds of years before either Calvin or Luther.

---

### ARTICLE 1
### Concerning Discipline.

<columns>

Discipline contains within itself all moral doctrine, according to the teaching of Christ and his Apostles, showing in what manner each person ought to live in their calling by faith, and walk worthily in current <term>present</term> righteousness.

Holy Scripture recites various doctrines regarding this discipline, and shows not only how everyone in particular ought to live—of whatever status <term>estate</term>, age, or condition they may be—but also what the union, agreement, and bond of love in the communion of the faithful ought to be. Now, if anyone desires to have knowledge of these things, let them read what the Apostle says in his Epistles, and they shall find it there—

<column-break/>

*Discipline contains within itself all moral doctrine according to the teaching of Christ and of the Apostles, in what manner each one in their calling, living by faith <note>original Occitan: "vivent per se," which the adjacent English column translates as "living by Faith"</note>, can walk worthily in current <term>present</term> righteousness.*

*And regarding this discipline, the Holy Scriptures recite abundant teachings, and not only in what way each one by themselves <note>original: "depersi"</note> ought to live—of every state, age, and condition—but what should be the unity, the unanimity, and the bond of love in the community of the faithful. And regarding this, if anyone wishes to know, let him read the Apostle in the Epistles and there you will find them laid out abundantly and specially—* <note>original: "special-", which concludes on the following page as "specialment" (specially)</note>

</columns>

## ARTICLE II.
### Concerning Pastors or Ministers.

*All those who are to be received as Pastors among us, while they are still with their people, they ask if it pleases our people to receive them into the ministry, and that they would be pleased to pray to God afterward so that they might be made worthy of such a great office. However, those making the request do not do these things for any other reason than to demonstrate humility.*

*We assign them lessons and make them learn by heart <note>original: "empenre de cor"</note> all the chapters of St. Matthew and St. John, and all the Epistles that are called Canonical, and a good part of the writings of Solomon, David, and the Prophets.*

*And afterward, having good testimonials, they are received with the laying on [of hands]...*

<column-break/>

...amply set down, especially in what manner every one is bound to keep himself in unity, and to walk in such a way that he is not a cause of scandal and ruin to his neighbor, either by sinful words or actions. In that way, he is bound not only to avoid evil, but the occasion and appearance of it as well; and when anyone has fallen, he must use his best endeavor to restore him and bring him to an amendment of life.

By various such general doctrines, those who are of the household of faith ought to be instructed, so that they may walk worthily in the house of the Lord, and not make it a *Den of Thieves* by their profane and perverse conversation, and by their toleration of evil.

All those who are to be received as Pastors among us, while they remain with their brothers, are to entreat our people to receive them into the ministry, and likewise ask that they would be pleased to pray to God for them, that they may be made worthy of so great a charge. This they are to do to give proof or evidence of their humility.

We also appoint them their lectures and set them their tasks, so that they may learn by heart all the chapters of *St. Matthew* and *St. John*, with all the *Epistles* which are called *Canonical*, and a good part of the writings of *Solomon*, *David*, and the *Prophets*.

And afterwards, having good testimonials and being well approved...

</columns>

<columns>

[...of hands,] they are received with the imposition (or *laying on*) of hands and the preaching of the Word.

The person who is received last <note>referring to the most recently ordained minister</note> should do nothing without the permission of the one who was received before him. In the same way, the senior minister should do nothing without the consent of his associate, so that all things may be done among us in good order.

Our daily food and the clothing with which we are covered are provided and given to us freely as alms, sufficient for our needs, by the good people whom we teach and instruct.

Among other privileges which God has given to His servants, He has given them this: to choose their leaders and those who are to govern the people, and to appoint elders in their charges, according to the variety of the work within the unity of Christ. This is clear from the words of the Apostle in the Epistle to Titus, chapter 1: *“For this reason I left you in Crete, that you should set in order the things that are lacking, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed you.”*

When any one of us, the aforementioned pastors, falls into any serious <note>original: "gross"</note> sin, he is both excommunicated and forbidden from preaching.

### ARTICLE III.

### Concerning the Instruction of Youth.

Those children who are born of earthly <note>original: "carnal"</note> parents ought to be made spiritual toward God through discipline and instruction, as it is said in Ecclesiasticus: *“He who loves his son causes him to frequently feel the rod, so that he may have joy in him at the end, and may not be ashamed before his neighbor.”* <note>original: Sirach 30:1</note>

<column-break/>

[...laying on] of hands, in the office of preaching. <note>original Occitan: "de las mans, en l' offici de la predication."</note>

the junior minister <note>original: "lo sequend"</note> must not do anything without the permission of the senior; and similarly, the seniors must not do anything without the permission of their companion, so that all things may be done among us in good order.

The nourishment and the things by which we are covered are provided to us and given freely, as alms, quite sufficiently, by the good people whom we teach.

Among the other powers God gave to His servants is that they choose rulers of the people and priests <note>original: "preires," used here in the sense of elders or ministers</note> in their offices, according to the diversity of the work in the unity of Christ. And the Apostle similarly proves this in Titus 1: *“I left you in Crete for the sake of these things that are lacking, and that you might ordain priests in the cities, as I commanded you.”*

When any of our aforesaid pastors falls into a sin of dishonesty, he is cast out of our company and prohibited from the office of preaching.

Children who are born of earthly parents must be returned spiritually to God by discipline and through loving instruction, as it is said in Ecclesiasticus: *“He who loves his son frequently applies the rod to him, that he may rejoice in the end, and not feel shame before his neighbor.”*

</columns>

# Chapter V. In the Valleys of Piedmont <note>original: "Piemont"</note>.

<columns>

<note>original: The left column contains the original Occitan text, and the right column contains the Early Modern English translation. The following is a modernization of that text.</note>

He who instructs his son shall have praise in him and shall gain commendation in the midst of his household. He who teaches his son makes his enemy jealous and gains honor among his friends. Though his father dies, it is as though he were not dead, for he leaves behind someone like himself. While he lived, he saw and rejoiced in him; and when he died, he was not confounded or sorrowful before his enemies. For he left behind those who shall uphold his house against his enemies, and children who shall return kindness to his friends. <note>This passage is a translation of Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 30:2–7.</note>

Instruct your son in the fear of the Lord, and in the ways of tradition <note>original: "costumas"</note> and of the faith.

Do not despair of your child if he will not willingly receive your correction, or if he does not become good immediately. For the farmer does not gather all the fruit of the earth as soon as he casts the seed into the ground, but waits for the appointed time.

In the same way, a man ought to correct and watch over his daughters. Do you have daughters? Guard their bodies so that they do not wander; for Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, was violated <note>original: "corrotta" / "ravished"</note> because she appeared in public <note>original: "mostrar se a li olli strang" / "shewing her self abroad"</note> to strangers.

...know him, serve him, and be saved by his grace.

*Minister:* In what does your salvation consist?

*Answer:* In three fundamental <note>original: "substantial"</note> virtues, which are essential for salvation.

*Minister:* Which virtues are they?

*Answer:* Faith, Hope, and Charity <note>original: "Charity" here means Christian love (Agape).</note>.

*Minister:* How can you prove that?

*Answer:* The Apostle [Paul] writes in 1 Corinthians 13: *Now abide Faith, Hope, and Charity—these three.*

*Minister:* What is Faith?

*Answer:* According to the Apostle in Hebrews 11: *It is the substance of things hoped for, and the evidence of things not seen.*

*Minister:* How many kinds of faith are there?

*Answer:* There are two kinds, namely, a Living Faith and a Dead Faith.

*Minister:* What is a Living Faith?

*Answer:* It is the faith that works through charity.

*Minister:* What is a Dead Faith?

*Answer:* According to Saint James, faith without works is dead. Furthermore, faith is void without works. Or, a dead faith is to believe that there is a God, to believe facts about God, and yet not to believe *in* him <note>The author distinguishes between intellectual assent (believing God exists) and saving trust (believing in God).</note>.

*Minister:* What is your faith?

*Answer:* The true Catholic <note>The term "Catholic" is used here in its original sense of "universal" or "orthodox," rather than specifically Roman Catholic.</note> and Apostolic faith.

*Minister:* What is that?

*Answer:* It is that which, in the Apostles' Creed <note>original: "Result (or Symbole) of the Apostle"</note>, is divided into twelve Articles.

*Minister:* What is that Creed?

*Answer:* I believe in God the Father Almighty, etc.

*Minister:* By what means can you know that you believe in God?

*Answer:* By this: that I know and I keep <note>original: "observe"</note> the Commandments of God.

*Minister:* How many Commandments of God are there?

<column-break/>

<note>The following is a translation of the original Occitan (Waldensian dialect) text provided in the source's second column.</note>

...[know] him, and worship [him], and by having his own grace, be saved. <note>original Occitan: "me, & cola, & avent la gratia de luy meseime sia salvà."</note>

*The Minister <note>original: "Lo Barb." — "Barba" was the traditional title for Waldensian pastors, meaning "uncle."</note>:* In what does your salvation consist?

*Answer:* In three fundamental virtues essentially pertaining to salvation.

*The Minister:* Which are those?

*Answer:* Faith, Hope, and Charity.

*Question:* By what thing will you prove this?

*Answer:* The Apostle writes in 1 Corinthians 13: *These things remain: Faith, Hope, and Charity.*

*Question:* What thing is Faith?

*Answer:* According to the Apostle in Hebrews 11: *It is a substance of the things to be hoped for, and an argument for those things not appearing.*

*Question:* In how many ways does faith exist?

*Answer:* In two ways: that is, living and dead.

*Question:* What thing is living faith?

*Answer:* It is that which works through charity.

*Question:* What thing is dead faith?

*Answer:* According to Saint James, faith, if it has no works, is dead; and again, faith is idle without works. Or, dead faith is to believe God exists, to believe of God, and not to believe in God.

*Question:* Of which faith are you?

*Answer:* Of the true Catholic and Apostolic faith.

*Question:* Which is that?

*Answer:* It is that which, by the counsel of the Apostles, is divided into twelve Articles.

*Question:* Which is that?

*Answer:* I believe in God the Father Almighty, etc.

*Question:* By what thing can you know that you believe in God?

*Answer:* By this: because I know and keep the commandments of God.

*Question:* How many are the commandments of God?

# The Ancient Discipline of the Evangelical Church: Book I

<columns>

The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son and is one Person of the Trinity. According to his Divinity, he is equal to the Father and the Son.

**Minister:** You believe in God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit; therefore, you have three Gods.

**Answer:** I do not have three.

**Minister:** Yes, but you have named three.

**Answer:** That is because of the distinction between the Persons, not because of the essence of the Divinity. For although there are three Persons, there is nevertheless only one Essence.

**Minister:** In what way do you adore and worship the God in whom you believe?

**Answer:** I adore him with both internal and external worship. Externally, I worship by kneeling, lifting up my hands, bowing my body, and through hymns and spiritual songs, fasting, and prayer. But internally, I worship through holy affection and a will that conforms to everything that is pleasing to him. I serve him through Faith, Hope, and Charity <note>original: "Charity," referring here to the theological virtue of divine love or *Agape*</note>, according to his Commandments.

**Minister:** Do you adore and worship anything else as God?

**Answer:** No.

**Minister:** Why?

**Answer:** Because of his commandment, which strictly commands:
> *“You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.”*

And again,
> *“I will not give my glory to another.”*

Again,
> *“As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow before me.”*

And Jesus Christ says,
> *“The true worshippers shall come, who will worship the Father in spirit and in truth.”*

Also, the Angel would not be worshipped by Saint John, nor Saint Peter by Cornelius.

<column-break/>

[The Holy Spirit] proceeding from the Father and the Son <note>original Occitan: "cedent del Paire, & del filli"</note> is one person of the Trinity; and according to the Divinity, is equal to the Father and the Son.

**Question:** You believe God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit are three in persons. Therefore you have three Gods?

**Answer:** I do not have three.

**Question:** Yet you have named three?

**Answer:** This is by reason of the difference of the persons, but not by reason of the essence of the Divinity. For although he is three in persons, yet he is one in Essence.

**Question:** In what way do you adore and worship that God in whom you believe?

**Answer:** I adore him by the worship of *latria* <note>original: "latria," a theological term for the supreme worship offered to God alone, as opposed to "dulia" offered to saints</note> both exterior and interior. Exteriorly, by the bending of the knees, the lifting of hands, by bowing, by hymns, by spiritual songs, by fasts, and by prayers <note>original: "Envocationas"</note>. But interiorly, by pious affection and a will prepared for all things pleasing to him; and I worship through Faith, through Hope, and through Charity in his commandments.

**Question:** Do you adore any other thing or worship it as God?

**Answer:** No.

**Question:** Why?

**Answer:** Because of his commandment which he strictly commands, saying:
> *“You shall adore your Lord God and serve him alone.”*

Furthermore:
> *“I will not give my glory to others.”*

And likewise:
> *“As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall be bowed to me.”*

And Jesus Christ says:
> *“The true worshippers shall be those who adore the Father in Spirit and in truth.”*

And the Angel did not wish to be adored by Saint John, nor Peter by Cornelius.

</columns>

# Chapter V: In the Valleys of Piedmont

<columns>

**Minister:** In what way do you pray? <note>original Occitan: "En qual modo oras?"</note>

**Answer:** I pray by reciting the prayer given by the Son of God, saying, "Our Father, who art in heaven," etc. <note>original Occitan: "Yo oro de la oration liord per le filli de Dio difont, Noſtre Paire qui fies in li cel."</note>

**Minister:** What is the other essential virtue belonging to salvation? <note>original Occitan: "Qual es l’autra vertù fobſtantial de neceſsitâ pertinent à ſalù?"</note>

**Answer:** It is Charity. <note>original Occitan: "Lo es Caritâ."</note>

**Minister:** What is Charity? <note>original Occitan: "Qual coſa es Charitâ?"</note>

**Answer:** It is a gift of the Holy Spirit, by which the soul is reformed in its will and enlightened by Faith; through this, I believe all things that should be believed, and I hope for all things that should be hoped for. <note>original Occitan: "Lo es un don del Sanét Eſperit, per loqual es Reformâ l’arma en volontà, enlumenâ per Fè..."</note>

**Minister:** Do you believe *in* the Holy Church? <note>original Occitan: "Crees tu en la Sanéta Gleifa?"</note>

**Answer:** No, for it is a created thing; but I believe there is a Church. <note>original Occitan: "Non car illi es creatura ma yo creo de ley meſcima."</note>

**Minister:** What do you believe regarding the Holy Church? <note>original Occitan: "Qual coſa crees tu dela Sanéta Gleifa?"</note>

**Answer:** I say regarding it that the Church is understood in two ways: one in terms of its substance, the other in terms of its ministry. In terms of substance, the Holy Catholic Church consists of all the elect of God, from the beginning to the end, living in the grace of God through the merit of Christ. They are gathered by the Holy Spirit and predestined to eternal life. Only he who chose them knows their number and their names. Finally, in this Church, no one remains who is a reprobate <term>reprobate: those rejected by God or destined for damnation</term>. But the Church according to ministerial truth consists of the ministers of Christ along with the subject people, using the ministry through Faith, Hope, and Charity. <note>original Occitan: "Yo demando de ley meſcima que la Gleifa es de doas manieras..."</note>

**Minister:** By what should you recognize the Church of Christ? <note>original Occitan: "Per qual coſa deves conoiſſer la Gleifa de Chriſt?"</note>

**Answer:** By suitable ministers and the people participating in truth in the ministry. <note>original Occitan: "Per li miniſtres convenivols & lo poble participant en verità en li meneſter."</note>

<column-break/>

**Minister:** In what way do you pray?

**Answer:** I pray, reciting the prayer given to me by the Son of God, saying: "Our Father, who art in heaven," etc.

**Minister:** What is the other essential <note>original: "substantial"</note> virtue belonging to salvation?

**Answer:** It is Charity.

**Minister:** What is Charity?

**Answer:** It is the gift of the Holy Spirit by which the soul is reformed in its will and enlightened by faith. By this, I believe all that ought to be believed, and hope for all that ought to be hoped for.

**Minister:** Do you believe *in* the Holy Church?

**Answer:** No, for it is a created thing <note>original: "creature"</note>, but I believe that there is one.

**Minister:** What is it that you believe concerning the Holy Church?

**Answer:** I say that the Church is considered in two ways: the one Substantially, and the other Ministerially. As it is considered Substantially, the Holy Catholic Church refers to all the Elect of God, from the beginning of the world to the end. By the grace of God through the merit of Christ, they are gathered together by the Holy Spirit and foreordained to eternal life. The number and names of these people are known only to him who has elected them; and in this Church, no one remains who is a reprobate. But the Church, as it is considered according to the truth of the Ministry, is the company of the ministers of Christ, together with the people committed to their charge, practicing the ministry through Faith, Hope, and Charity.

**Minister:** How do you recognize the Church of Christ?

**Answer:** By the ministers who are lawfully called, and by the people who truly participate in the ministry.

**Minister:**
</columns>

# The Ancient Discipline of the Evangelical Churches. Book I.

<page-num>80</page-num>

---

<columns>

**Minister:** But by what signs do you recognize the ministers?

**Answer:** By the true understanding of Faith, by sound doctrine, by a life of good example, by the preaching of the Gospel, and by a proper administration of the Sacraments.

---

**Minister:** By what signs do you recognize false ministers?

**Answer:** By their fruits, by their blindness, by their evil works, by their corrupt doctrine, and by their improper administration of the Sacraments.

---

**Minister:** How do you recognize their blindness?

**Answer:** When, not knowing the truth which is necessary for salvation, they follow human inventions as if they were the ordinances of God. Of them, that which Isaiah says is proven true, and was also cited by our Lord Jesus Christ in Matthew 15: "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. But in vain they do worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men."

---

**Minister:** By what signs do you recognize evil works?

**Answer:** By those obvious sins of which the Apostle speaks in Galatians 5, saying, "They which do such things shall not inherit the Kingdom of God."

---

**Minister:** By what sign do you recognize corrupt <note>original: "perverse"</note> doctrine?

**Answer:** When it teaches things contrary to Faith and Hope. Such is idolatry of several sorts—namely, toward a rational <note>original: "reasonable," meaning a being with the faculty of reason, like an angel or human</note>, sensible, visible, or invisible creature. For it is the Father alone, with his Son and the Holy Spirit, who ought to be worshipped, and not any creature whatsoever. But on the contrary, they attribute [divine honor] to man and to the work of his hands, or to his words, or to his authority, in such a manner that men ignorantly believe they have satisfied God through a false religion and by satisfying the greedy simony <note>term: Simony — The buying or selling of spiritual things, such as church offices, pardons, or sacraments.</note> of the priests.

<column-break/>

---

**Question:** But by what thing do you recognize the ministers? <note>original Occitan: "Ma per qual cosa conoisses li ministres?"</note>

**Response:** By the true sense of the Faith, and by sound doctrine, and by a life of good example, and by evangelization, and by the proper administration of the Sacraments. <note>original Occitan: "Per lo veray sen dela Fè & per la sana doctrina..."</note>

---

**Question:** By what thing do you recognize false ministers? <note>original Occitan: "Per qual cosa conoisses li fals ministres?"</note>

**Response:** By their fruits, by their blindness, by evil operations, by corrupt doctrine, and by the improper administration of the Sacraments. <note>original Occitan: "...per l'encequetà, per mala operation, per perversa doctrina..."</note>

---

**Question:** By what thing is blindness recognized? <note>original Occitan: "Per qual cosa se conois l'encequetà?"</note>

**Response:** Since they do not know the truth of necessity pertaining to salvation, they keep human inventions in the likeness of God’s commandments; of whom is verified that saying of Isaiah which Christ spoke in Matthew 15: "This people honors me with their lips <note>original: "cum labias"</note>, but their heart is far from me, but they worship me without cause, teaching the doctrines and commandments of men."

---

**Question:** By what thing is evil operation recognized? <note>original Occitan: "Per qual cosa es conoissua la mala operation?"</note>

**Response:** By the manifest sins of which the Apostle says in Galatians 5: "Those who do such things shall not follow <note>original: "consegren," meaning to attain or inherit</note> the kingdom of God."

---

**Question:** By what thing is corrupt doctrine recognized? <note>original Occitan: "Per qual cosa es conoissua la perversa doctrina?"</note>

**Response:** When it teaches against the Faith and Hope, in the form of idolatry done in many ways to the rational, sensible, visible, or invisible creature. For the Father alone with his Son and the Holy Spirit must be worshipped, and no other creature whatsoever. But against this they attribute [divine power] to man, and to the work of his hands, or to words, or to his authority, so that men, believing blindly, estimate themselves to be justified before God by a false religion and by the greedy Simony of the priests.

</columns>

### ARTICLE V.
### Concerning Elders, the Distribution of Alms, and Ecclesiastical Assemblies.

| Modernized English (from original English) | Modernized English (translated from original Occitan) |
| :--- | :--- |
| Rulers and Elders are chosen from among the people, according to the diversity of the work, in the unity of *Christ*. The Apostle proves this in the Epistle to *Titus, chapter 1*: *For this cause I left you in Crete, that you should set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed you.* | Rulers <note>original Occitan: "Regidors"</note> are chosen from the people, as well as Elders <note>original: "Preire"</note>, according to the diversity of the work in the unity of *Christ*. | When the drunkard goes to the tavern, he walks upright; but when he returns, he reels and staggers, having as it were lost his sight, hearing, and speech. Behold the miracles which the Devil performs in the tavern! The lessons learned in this school of the Devil are drunkenness, swearing, lying, perjury, blasphemy, the denial of God, and the commission of many other sins. This is the place where, for the most part, all quarrels, slanders, disputes, and murders are provoked. Those who keep the taverns and allow this are participants in all those sins and evils committed there. For certainly, if anyone should offer to speak as insultingly of their father and mother in the presence of these men as they allow to be spoken of God, the glorious Virgin, and the saints in Paradise—simply to sell a penny's worth <note>A "penny-worth" refers to a very small or trivial amount of wine.</note> of wine—they would never allow them to remain so peacefully in their houses. Such are the miracles that the Devil knows how to perform in the tavern. The lessons that are read in this school of the Devil are gluttony, swearing, perjury, lying, blasphemy, and renouncing God, and saying and doing many other sins. For in the tavern are prepared brawls, slanders, disputes, and homicides; and the tavern keepers who allow it are partners in all the sins and the evil done there. For if someone said as many insults of a father or mother, or wife, as they allow of God, the glorious Virgin, and the holy men and women of Paradise—just to sell a penny’s worth of wine—they would not tolerate them there in peace. Therefore it is said in *Ecclesiasticus* that the tavern keeper shall not be justified from sin <note>original: "non sere justifica de pecca"</note>. |
