And Balaam also chose them to cast out the sons of Israel <note>referring to the women of Moab; see Numbers 31:16.</note>. Just as women caused Samson, David, and Absalom to sin. The Devil tempts man through women in three ways: by touching, by seeing, and by hearing. In these three ways, he tempts unwise men at the ball: by the touching of hands, by the display of beauty, and by the sweetness of the song and sound. The fourth reason is that those who dance break the agreement they made with God at baptism, when their godparents said on their behalf, "I renounce the Devil and all his pomps." The ball is the pomp and the Mass of the Devil, and whoever enters the ball enters into his pomp and his Mass. For the woman singing at the ball is the Devil's prioress, those who respond are his clerks, and those who watch are the parishioners. The music and the flutes <note>original: "calamelas"; reed pipes or shawms.</note> are the bells, and the musicians who play are the Devil's ministers. For just as when pigs are scattered and their shepherd makes one of them squeal <note>original: "quialar."</note> so that the others gather together, so the Devil makes a woman sing at the ball or plays the flute so that all his pigs (that is, the dancers) gather together. | ...consume men's estates <note>original: "fume mens Estates."</note>. The third reason is that in balls, the Devil makes use of his best armor of proof <note>Armor of proof: armor tested to withstand specific weapons; here, the Devil's most effective tools.</note>. Now the strongest weapons the Devil has are women; this is shown by the fact that the Devil chose a woman to deceive the first man. Similarly, Balaam chose women to cause the children of Israel to be rejected. Through women, the Devil caused Samson, David, and Absalom to sin. The Devil tempts man through women in three ways: by touch, sight, and hearing. In these three ways, he tempts unwise men at balls: by the touching of hands, by beautiful looks, and by the sweetness of the voice. The fourth reason is that those who dance break the agreement they made with God at their baptism, when their godfathers and godmothers promised on their behalf to renounce the Devil and all his pomp <note>Pomp: in this context, the "pomps and vanities" of the world as renounced in the baptismal covenant.</note>. Balls are the pomp and the Mass of the Devil, and whoever enters a ball enters the Devil's pomp and Mass. For the woman who sings at the ball is the Devil’s prioress, those who respond are his clerks, and those who watch are the parishioners. Likewise, the cymbals and flutes are the church bells, and the musicians are the ministers of the Devil. For just as when pigs are scattered and the swineherd gives a shout, they immediately flock together to him; so the Devil causes one woman to sing at the ball or play music so that all the swine (that is, the dancers) may immediately gather into a group. |

## CHAPTER VI.

### Extracts of several very authentic and rare treatises, composed by the ancient inhabitants of the valleys of Piedmont; a great part of these were written about four hundred and twenty years ago, others above five hundred and fifty years ago, and the rest in all probability are of a far more ancient date.

### The true originals of all these were collected with significant effort and industry by the author of this history during his stay in those parts; upon his return, he presented them to the public library of the famous University of Cambridge.

It would now, without any question, be both distasteful <note>original: "nauseous"</note> and harmful <note>original: "injurious"</note> to intelligent readers if the author presumed to intermingle his own private commentaries <note>original: "Glosses"</note> or reflections upon the subject of the preceding chapters. It is sufficiently evident what a conformity both the doctrine and discipline of the ancient inhabitants of these valleys bear to the doctrine and discipline of all the Reformed Churches at this very day. 

I must certainly confess that this is a point which I chiefly labored to be clearly and fully informed about from the very beginning—partly for my own private satisfaction, and partly to answer the earnest desire of that pillar of learning and model of piety, the late Lord Primate of Ireland <note>This refers to James Ussher (1581–1656), the Archbishop of Armagh, a highly influential scholar and collector of ancient manuscripts.</note>. A few days before my departure for Savoy, he sent for me specifically to come to his chamber, and there gave me a very serious and strict charge to use my utmost diligence in inquiring after, and to spare no expense in the purchase of, all those manuscripts and authentic documents which might shed any light on the ancient doctrine and discipline of those churches,

<meta>catchword: churches,</meta>

<summary>This page introduces Chapter VI, documenting the author’s efforts to collect ancient Waldensian manuscripts from the Piedmont valleys. It highlights the support of James Ussher, the Lord Primate of Ireland, in preserving these historical records for the University of Cambridge.</summary>

<keywords>Piedmont, Waldensians, James Ussher, Cambridge University, manuscripts, Reformed Churches, church history, Vaudois</keywords>

<page-num>95</page-num>
<header>Chap. VI. In the Valleys of Piedmont.</header>

Churches; adding that there was nothing in the world he was more curious and impatient to know, as it was a point of exceedingly great weight and importance for stopping the mouths of our Roman Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> adversaries, and discovering the footsteps of our religion in those dark intervals of the eighth, ninth, and tenth centuries. This earnest request <note>original: "serious Injunction"</note> from that Reverend and worthy man, together with my own natural inclinations, caused me to leave no stone unturned and to lose no opportunity during my stay in those parts to actually accomplish this. And though the Pope’s agents <note>original: "Emissaries"</note> had already gathered the choice clusters and first ripe fruits, I still found at least the "grape-gleanings of the vintage." By this, I mean various pieces of antiquity, some of which had been buried under dust and rubbish for a long time, while others had been scattered about the Valleys—some here, some there—in deserted and obscure places; without a singular providence, they would never have come to light. Now, to insert them all at full length would make this book <note>original: "the Work in hand"</note> grow into too large a volume; therefore, I have only thought it fit to include a simple catalogue of the whole, and from that to pick a few to present to the reader, so that he may better judge the rest.

---

## A Catalogue of various manuscripts, written by the ancient inhabitants of the Valleys (the greatest part of them in their own language) collected by the author of this history during his stay in those parts; the true originals of all of which may be seen in the public library of the famous University of Cambridge.

### The volume marked with the letter *A* contains the following treatises:

1. The history of the Creation and the Flood <note>original: "Deluge"</note>, written in their own language.
2. An excellent treatise of various profitable instructions which a person ought to learn from the nature of different animals.
3. *The Treatise on Sin* <note>original: "Lo tracta de li pecca"</note>, which is an allegorical and moral explanation of the Beast described in Revelation 13.
4. A treatise on the Word of God, and its power and effectiveness; also how it ought to be received. At the end, the date of either the work or at least the copy is attached: In the year of our Lord 1230 <note>original: "Anno Domini 1230"</note>.
5. Several Latin pieces, which are certain collections <note>original: "Rhapsodies"</note> concerning priests and friars.
6. A treatise against human traditions <note>original: "Tramettament"</note>, or the ordinances of men, as they are not consistent with the Holy Scriptures.

<header>Several Treatises of the Evangelical Churches Book I.</header>

7. An exhortation to *Herman* to convert himself to God and not to created things.
8. Concerning Pharisaical plantations <note>The author uses this term, referencing Matthew 15:13, to describe religious institutions he believes were not established by God.</note> which the Father has not planted, namely <note>original: "viz."</note> the orders and sects of monks, *Franciscan Friars, Dominicans*, and the like, which are not ordained by God.
9. A *Latin* treatise *On the Duties of Spouses, Husband and Wife* <note>original: "De Officiis Conjugum, Viri & Uxoris"</note>.
10. A *Latin* treatise *On the Apostles' Creed* <note>original: "De Symbolo Apostolico"</note>.
11. A *Latin* treatise *On the Building of Cities, the Origin and Progress of Idolatry, and its Overthrow through the Preaching of the Gospel* <note>original: "De Ædificatione Urbium, Idololatriæ ortu & progressu, ejusque eversione per Evangelii prædicationem"</note>.
12. A *Latin* treatise, *By Which Ways Sin is Committed* <note>original: "Quibus Modis peccatum fiat"</note>.
13. A *Latin* treatise *On the True Cleansing of Sin* <note>original: "De verâ peccati purgatione"</note>.
14. A *Latin* treatise titled *Let Us Strive to Please God Alone* <note>original: "Uni Deo placere studeamus"</note>.
15. A *Latin* treatise titled *Three Truths* <note>original: "Tres veritates"</note>: **1. Of Doctrine. 2. Of Justice. 3. Of Life.**
16. A *Latin* treatise titled *That Controversies of Faith are to be Determined Only by God’s Written Law* <note>original: "Solâ Dei Lege scriptâ definiri Fidei Controversias"</note>.

---

In the volume marked with the letter *B.* are contained the following treatises, all written in that which is called the *Waldensian* language <note>This is an old form of Occitan, the language spoken by the Vaudois in the Alpine valleys.</note>, on parchment, and in a very ancient but excellent handwriting <note>original: "Character"</note>.

1. *The Father’s Commentary* <note>original: "Glosa Pater"</note>, or the explanation of the Lord's Prayer.
2. *The Thirteen* <note>original: "Trecenas"</note>, or various passages from the Evangelists and Epistles.
3. *The Teacher* <note>original: "Doctor"</note>, that is, various sayings and testimonies of the Church Fathers concerning repentance.
4. *Punishments* <note>original: "Penas"</note>, or a treatise concerning the punishment of sin.
5. *The Joys of Paradise* <note>original: "Li Goy de Paradis"</note>, a treatise concerning the joys of paradise.
6. An epistle to all the faithful.
7. A poem titled *New Comfort* <note>original: "Novel Confort"</note>.
8. A poem titled *New Sermon* <note>original: "Novel Sermon"</note>, containing many wholesome instructions for the people.
9. A poem titled *The Noble Lesson* <note>original: "La Noble Leyçon," a foundational 12th-century Waldensian poem summarizing their history and beliefs.</note>.
10. A poem titled *Eternal Father* <note>original: "Pair eternal"</note>.
11. A poem titled *The Boat* <note>original: "Barca"</note>, concerning the misery and shortness of man's life and his arrival at the haven of salvation.
12. An explanation of the Ten Commandments.
13. An explanation of the articles of the Apostles' Creed.
14. A treatise concerning vice and mortal sins.
15. A treatise concerning the seven gifts of the Spirit, Isaiah 11.
16. A treatise concerning the three theological and the four cardinal virtues <note>The theological virtues are faith, hope, and charity; the cardinal virtues are prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance.</note>.
17. A treatise concerning the benefits <note>original: "Goods"</note> of fortune, nature, and grace.

In Volume *D.* there are many excellent and heavenly meditations regarding the miseries, tribulations, and shortness of this life; as well as on repentance, good works, and similar topics. These were written in the language of the ancient inhabitants of the valleys <note>This refers to the Old Occitan or Waldensian dialect, a Romance language used by the Vaudois in the Middle Ages.</note> on parchment, but the lettering is almost worn out with age. According to many probable circumstances regarding the place and manner of its preservation, it is judged to have been written at least six or seven hundred years ago.

# Chapter VI. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

The noble lesson written in the language of the ancient inhabitants of the valleys in the year 1100. Extracted from a most authentic manuscript, the true original of which can be seen in the public library of the famous University of Cambridge.

<note>original: "La Nobla Leyçon"; a rhythmic poem in the Waldensian (Old Occitan) dialect that summarizes biblical history and Waldensian ethics. The date "1100" mentioned in the poem was historically used by the Waldensians to argue that their movement began long before Peter Waldo (c. 1140–1218).</note>

*O brothers, listen to a noble lesson.* <note>The following is an English translation of the original Waldensian dialect text shown in the first column of the source.</note>

*We must often watch and remain in prayer.*

*For we see this world is near its end.*

*We should be very diligent in doing good works,*

*Since we see this world approaching its conclusion.*

*Already, eleven hundred years have fully passed*

*Since it was written, "For we are in the last time."*

*We should desire little, for we are at the remainder.*

*Every day we see the signs coming to fulfillment,*

*In the increase of evil and the decrease of good.*

*These are the perils of which the Scripture speaks,*

*Which the Gospel recounts and Saint Paul also:*

*That no man living can know the end.*

*Therefore we should fear more, for we are not certain*

*Whether death will take us today or tomorrow.*

*But when the Day of Judgment comes,*

*Every person shall receive their full payment:*

*Those who have done evil and those who have done good.*

*But the Scripture says it, and we must believe it.*

<column-break/>

O Brothers, listen to a noble lesson.

We should always watch and pray,

For we see the world is near its conclusion.

We should strive to do good works,

Seeing that the end of this world approaches.

There are already one thousand one hundred years fully accomplished,

Since it was written thus, *For we are in the last time*.

We should desire little, for we are at what remains, *namely*, at the later end.

We see daily the signs being fulfilled,

And that in the increase of evil and the decrease of good.

These are the perils which the Scripture mentions,

In the Gospels and Saint Paul’s writings:

As also, that no man living can know the end.

And therefore we should fear more, as we are not certain

Whether we shall die today or tomorrow.

But when the Day of Judgment comes,

Every one shall receive their full reward:

Those who have done either well or ill.

Now the Scripture says it, and we ought to believe it,

### That all men shall travel two ways.
---

The good go to glory, and the wicked to torment.
But whoever does not believe in this separation <note>original: "Departure"; here referring to the final judgment and the parting of souls</note>,
Let him search the Scripture from the very beginning,
From the time Adam was formed until this present time;
There he shall find, if he has understanding,
That those who are saved are few compared to the rest.
Therefore, everyone who wishes to do good works
Should make the honor of God the Father their first guiding principle.
They should likewise pray for the aid of his glorious Son, the dear Son of the Virgin Mary,
And the Holy Spirit who enlightens us in the true way.
These three (the Holy Trinity), being but one God, ought to be called upon,
Full of all power, wisdom, and goodness.
This we should often beg and pray for:
That he would enable us to face our enemies,
And overcome them before our end,
Which are the world, the devil, and the flesh;
And that he would give us wisdom accompanied by goodness,
That we may know the way of life,
And keep pure the soul which God has given us—
Yes, both soul and body in the way of charity,
So that we love the Holy Trinity,
And our neighbor, for God has commanded it.

<column-break/>

### *That all the men of the world shall travel by two paths.* <note>The following is an English translation of the original Waldensian/Occitan text: "Que tuit li home del mont per dui chamin tenren."</note>
---

*The good shall go into glory, the wicked into torment.*
*But he who will not believe in that separation,*
*Let him look at the Scripture from the very beginning,*
*From when Adam was formed until this present time.*
*There he will be able to find, if he has understanding,*
*That those who are saved are few compared to the rest.*
*But every person who wishes to work well,*
*The honor of God the Father must be at the beginning.*
*And quickly call upon the glorious Son, the dear Son of Saint Mary,*
*And the Holy Spirit, who gives us the good way.*
*These three, the Holy Trinity, as one God, must be worshipped <note>original: "aurà," from the Latin "adorare"</note>,*
*Full of all power, and of all wisdom, and of all goodness.*
*This [Trinity] we must often worship and petition,*
*That he may give us strength against the enemies,*
*That we may be able to overcome them before our end—*
*Which are the world, and the Devil, and the flesh—*
*And give us wisdom accompanied by goodness,*
*That we may be able to know the way of truth,*
*And keep pure the soul that God has given us,*
*The soul and the body in the way of charity,*
*In such a way that we love the Holy Trinity,*
*And our neighbor, for God has commanded it.*

Not only those who do us good,
but even those who do us harm.
And to have firm hope in the heavenly King,
That at the end he may house us in his glorious home.
But he who will not do what is contained in this lesson,
Will not enter into the Holy House.
But this is hard to keep for the wretched people,
Who love gold and silver,
And hold the promises of God in contempt.
They do not keep the law nor the commandments,
Nor can they allow any good people to keep them,
But according to their power, they cause hindrance.
Why is this evil among the human race?
Because Adam sinned at the very beginning,
For he ate of the apple against the prohibition <note>original: "otra defendement"</note>,
And in others sprouted the grain of the evil seed;
He acquired death for himself and for his followers.
We can well say that it was a bitter bite <note>original: "mal bocon"</note>,
But Christ has redeemed the good by his passion.
But we find in this lesson,
That Adam was unfaithful to God the Creator;
And here we can see that now they have done worse—
Those who abandon God the Father almighty,
And believe in idols to their own destruction.
That which the law forbids, which was from the beginning,
Called the law of nature <note>original: "Ley natural"</note>, common to all people,
Which God placed in the heart of the man whom he first formed.

| We have sinned against the Creator and offended the creation <note>original: "creature"</note>. | We have sinned against the Creator and offended the creature. |

But the new [law] counsels keeping virginity, <note>original Occitan: *M. la novella cosellia gardar vergenetá*</note>

The old law forbids only perjury <note>original: swearing falsely</note>,

The old law commands fighting against enemies and returning evil for evil,

And let those who would do you harm live in peace,

For if you do not pardon, you shall not find salvation.

No one ought to kill or hate any person,
Much less should we mock simple or poor men,
Nor hold in contempt the stranger who comes from another's country.
For in this world, we are all pilgrims. <note>original: *pellegrin*</note>

This is the new law which Jesus Christ said we ought to keep.

Then a people was newly converted;
They were called Christians, because they believed in Christ.
But we find what the Scripture says,
The Jews and Saracens <note>original: "Saraçins" — a medieval term for Muslims.</note> persecuted them very severely.
But the Apostles were so strong in the fear of the Lord,

That because of [their enemies] they did not stop their deeds or their words,

Great were the torments according to what is written,
Only because they showed the way of Jesus Christ.
But those who persecuted them were not so much to be blamed;
Because they did not have the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ,
As compared to those who now seek occasion and persecute so much;
Who ought to be Christians, but make a poor show of it.

Who showed the way of Jesus Christ our Savior.
But some are still found in this present time,
Who are known to very few people,
Who would very much like to show the way of Jesus Christ,
But they are so persecuted that they can do little,
So much are the false Christians blinded by error,

Then there was a people newly converted;
They were called Christians, for they believed in Christ.

That the Jews and Saracens persecuted them grievously.
But the Apostles were so strengthened <note>original: "fortified"</note> in the fear of the Lord,

The torments were great, according to what is written,

So much are the false Christians blinded with error,

And even more than the rest are those who are pastors,

That if anyone loves those who are good, he must necessarily love God and Jesus Christ.
Such a person will neither curse, swear, nor lie;
He will neither commit adultery nor kill; he will neither defraud his neighbor,
Nor take revenge on his enemies.
Now such a person is called a Waldensian <note>original: "Waldensian" — members of this movement were often identified by their strict adherence to biblical morality, which stood in contrast to the perceived corruption of the medieval church.</note> and is considered worthy of punishment;
And they find opportunities through lies and deceit
To take from him what he has earned through his honest labor.

Then he shall have a wealth of glory as a reward for all such dishonor.

That those who curse, lie, and swear,

| *Of the Fear of the Lord.* | *Of the Fear of the Lord.* |
| *The fear of the Lord casts out sin. Through the fear of the Lord, many good things are born. Therefore Solomon says, "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom." And again he says, "The man is blessed who is always fearful [of God]." For through the fear of the Lord, souls are delivered from the pains of hell. And through the fear of the Lord, the joys of paradise are found. For the love of God and of one's neighbor is charity; and he who has charity has God. And he who has God turns away from worldly things; and he who loves God fears the pains of hell and desires the joys of paradise, which he hopes to reach and in which he hopes to remain. In that place, there is no fear of death, nor fear of enemies. Here is life without death. Therefore, through the love of God and of one's neighbor, this eternal life is acquired. And St. Paul says, "The love of God and of one's neighbor does no evil." And he who does these things shall not fall into sin. But he who leans toward temporal <term>temporal: earthly or worldly possessions, as opposed to eternal or spiritual things</term> things distances himself from the love of God. For riches cannot be acquired without sin in this world. For if one does not lose, another cannot gain; and he who gains rejoices, while he who loses is saddened. But there are many who hope to give alms <note>original Occitan: "almosna"</note> from the sweat of others; they strip one person to clothe another. But alms given with iniquity are despised before God. As Saint Au—* <note>original: "Sant Au-" likely referring to Saint Augustine.</note> | The fear of the Lord drives away sin. Much good is gained by the fear of the Lord. As Solomon says, *The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.* And again, *Happy is the man who always thus fears.* For by the fear of the Lord, his soul is delivered from the pains of hell, and by the fear of the Lord, he finds the joys of heaven. The love of God and of our neighbor is charity; and he who has charity is of God. He who is of God is weaned from the things of this world; and he who loves God fears the pains of hell and thirsts after the joys of heaven, which he hopes to enjoy <note>original: "have the fruition"</note> and in which he hopes to live, where there is no fear of death or of enemies, and where there is life without death. Therefore, through the love of God and of our neighbor, eternal life is obtained. And St. Paul says that the love of God and of our neighbor works no evil. And he who shall do those things shall never fall. Whereas he who lets his heart run after temporal things departs from the love of God. For riches cannot be heaped up in this world without sin, because what one gains, another loses; and where the gainer rejoices, the loser is made sad. Now there are many who hope to give alms out of the sweat of other men's brows, stripping one to clothe another; but such alms-deeds are not at all acceptable before God, according— |

# A Treatise of Tribulations.

---

| ->Of Tribulations.<- <note>original Occitan: "De las Tribulacions"</note> | ->Of Tribulations.<- |
| :--- | :--- |
| Many are the tribulations of the righteous, but the Lord will deliver them from them all. And Saint Paul says, through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God; and whoever has no part in tribulations shall have no part in consolations. The Lord says in the Gospel, "Love your enemies, and do good to those who hate you." And Augustine says, "As much as your enemy hurts you, so much more you ought to love him." For <note>original: "C." an abbreviation for "Car" or "Because"</note> through such love you will be able to have eternal life. Because if the evil man wants to hurt you, even before he has done the evil, he will be wounded in his own heart; and all the evil that he wished to do to you will return upon him. And if the criminal <note>original: "fellon"</note> takes your property through his wickedness, he loses more than you who lose your property—for it is he who loses his soul. Those who see with the eyes of the heart recognize the damnation of the soul. There are many who have eyes to recognize gold and silver, but they do not have eyes to recognize the damnation of their own souls. The Lord comforts good men, saying, "Do not fear those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul." All those who oppose you are out of their minds, for they neither see nor know themselves; they act just like a madman who, having a sword <note>original: "glay"</note> in his hand, cuts the hem <note>original: "gonella"; a tunic or cloak</note> of another’s garment, and afterwards would be... | Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the Lord will deliver them out of them all; and St. Paul says that through many tribulations we must enter into the Kingdom of God; and whoever does not have a share of persecutions shall not share in the comforts. Our blessed Savior says in the Gospel, "Love your enemies, and do good to them that hate you"; and St. Augustine says, "The more your enemy hurts you, the more you ought to love him, for in doing so you shall inherit eternal life." For even when the wicked person seeks to do you harm, his conscience accuses him before the action, so that all the evil and mischief he plans against you returns upon his own head. And if a thief robs you and takes away your property from you, he suffers the greater loss of the two; for, alas, he loses his own soul. Those who see with the eyes of the heart both know and fear the damnation of their souls. There are many men who are quick-sighted enough to recognize gold and silver, but have no eyes to recognize the damnation of their own souls. The Lord comforts the righteous when he tells them not to fear those who can only kill the body but cannot hurt the soul. Our adversaries are surely out of their minds, for they neither see nor know themselves; they act just like a madman who, holding a naked sword in his hand, first cuts off the hem of his neighbor's garment, and then sheaths... |

| ...because he *suffered tribulation among wicked men:* or, as Saint Paul calls it, *Perils among false brothers.* All other afflictions and persecutions in this world may possibly cease, but those with which the ungodly persecute the righteous will never cease; and if you do not believe this to be a truth, just once begin to do well, and you shall quickly see how the wicked will persecute you. The *Wise Man* <note>original: "Wise man"; likely referring to Solomon, the traditional author of Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, or the author of the Book of Wisdom</note> tells us that the friends of God ought to have three sorts of patience: the first consists in suffering patiently all the evils that are both done and said against them. The second is the patient bearing of their own infirmities, and whatever tribulations it pleases God to inflict on them in this world. And the third is in resisting the Devil, who always strives to turn them aside from doing good works. Now, no one must expect to receive a crown who has not fought faithfully for it, and where the greatest combat is, there is the greatest reward and the most noble crown (as the *Wise Man* says). I speak to you according to the patience of God. For he who is most patient in adversities and under the persecutions of wicked men shall have the greater recompense; just as those grapes yield the most wine which are the most pressed and bruised; or as the olive, when it is most squeezed, the skins all slip aside and the oil remains pure and clear; or as the wheat, when it is well threshed and beaten, is thereby separated from the chaff. The first is in all the evils that are either done or said against them. The second is in their infirmities, and in all the labors that God allows to come to them in this world. The third patience is against the devil, who strives to turn them away from their good works. But no one receives a crown if he does not fight faithfully. And where there is a greater battle, there is greater salvation and a more noble crown. Therefore the Wise Man says: "I speak to you according to the patience of God." For <note>original: "C."; an abbreviation for "car" meaning "for" or "because"</note> he who is patient under the whip and in the persecutions of evil men shall have a greater reward. Just as the grape, when it is most pressed, yields the most wine. Just as the olive, when it is most squeezed, the dregs go to one side and the oil remains clear. Just as the wheat, when it is most threshed, the chaff goes to one side and the grain to the other. But if you want to be good while you are in this life, suffer the evil men near you in patience. And the Wise Man says: "The truly patient man hopes to have the brotherhood of the angels." The truly patient man does not become angry. For it is a certain thing that God loves those who hate the world for his love. |

### The first Petition.

The first request is *Hallowed be your Name*. In this request, we desire that the sin of lust <note>original: "Lust"</note> may be removed, and that the virtue of chastity may be given to us. For we bear the name of *Christ* and are called *Christians*, which is nothing other than being disciples, servants, and children of *Christ*. But your name is polluted, vilified, and blasphemed in us when we live in impurity and luxury <note>original: "luxury"; in this period, the word specifically referred to lust or lewdness</note>. On the contrary, it is sanctified and purified when we abstain from all pollutions of heart, mouth, and body, and wash and purify our past sins through true repentance. For those *Christians* who do indeed bear the name of *Christ* are purified—that is, they are made saints. Now, a saint is one who is without stain; but the sin of lust is rightly called a stain because, just as a stain takes the natural color from cloth or wool, so the sin of lust takes from the soul the benefit of baptism and all graces. Again, as a stain passes through the cloth, inside and out, so lust defiles a person inside and out. It first of all defiles a person at the heart by base and vile thoughts and consenting to pleasures; likewise the eyes by unchaste looks; the ears with filthy words that heat and inflame one toward sin; the nose by the unpleasant smells of ointments, which serve as allurements to sexual immorality <note>original: "whoredom"</note>, with which some women, being possessed by the devil, paint themselves to please their lovers; the mouth by unchaste words, kisses, and excessive delicacies, by which lust is nourish[ed]—

<column-break/>

[...present life and in the one to come; but let us take at present for our edification a rough and simple exposition.] <note>original: *ruda e grosa exposicion*</note>

### [The First Request]

[*The first request is: your name be sanctified.* In this request we ask to be removed from the sin of lust <note>original: *peccà de luxuria*</note>, and for the virtue of chastity to be given to us; for we bear the name of Christ, and we are called Christian, which is nothing other than being a disciple, servant, and child of Christ. But that name is soiled, made vile, and blasphemed in us when we live filthily and lustfully. But it is sanctified and cleansed when we abstain from all the filth of the heart, the mouth, and the body, and wash and purify past sins through true repentance. For in this way, the Christians who bear the name of Christ are purified—that is, they are made saints—for "saint" is said to mean "without stain" <note>original: *sant es dit sença tentura*</note>. But the sin of lust is called a stain; for just as a stain takes from the cloth or the wool its natural color, so the sin of lust takes from the soul the innocence of baptism and all the virtues. Just as a stain passes through the cloth inside and out, so lust soils the whole person inside and out. It soils the person first in the heart by filthy and impure thoughts, delights, and consent. Afterward, the eyes by unchaste looks; and afterward, the ears by curious words that inflame one to sin; afterward, the nostrils by the filthy smells of prostitute-like <note>original: *meretricienç*</note> ointments with which devilish women paint themselves to please their lovers. Afterward, the mouth by unchaste words, by kissing, and by delicate and excessive eating, by which lust is nourished and set on fire.]

<summary>This page provides a moral exposition of the first petition of the Lord's Prayer, "Hallowed be thy Name," equating the sanctification of God's name with the practice of chastity and the rejection of lust. It describes how sin—specifically "luxury" or lust—acts as a stain that defiles the soul and the physical senses.</summary>

They are fitly called "poor in spirit"—that is, voluntarily, not constrained or out of any necessity in this life—which is also consistent with what St. Bernard says: that there are three sorts of poverty, namely feigned, constrained, and voluntary. We ought to endure constrained poverty patiently and embrace voluntary poverty with all our heart, and so we shall become poor in spirit. 

Of this poverty St. James speaks: "Has not God chosen the poor of this world, rich in faith, and heirs of the Kingdom which God has promised to those who love him?" And Augustine says in the person of Christ: "I have something to sell, but what? The Kingdom of God, Heaven, the Kingdom of Heaven. In what fashion is it to be bought? By poverty. He says well "poor in spirit," that is, by will and not by force or by necessity in life; and as St. Bernard says, there is poverty of three kinds: that is to say, feigned, needy [constrained], and voluntary. We must sustain the needy [constrained] poverty patiently and embrace the voluntary with all the heart; in this way they are made poor in spirit. 

Of this poverty St. James says: "Therefore has God not chosen the poor in this world rich in faith, heirs of the kingdom, which God has promised to those loving him?" So will all the good and rich to whom it shall be said at the Day of Judgment: *“Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world.”* But no one can excuse themselves from the purchase of this kingdom; for as *Gregory* <note>Saint Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a prominent theologian and Pope.</note> says: “The kingdom of God is worth as much as you have.” It cost the holy *Apostles* their ship and their nets; it cost *Zacchaeus* <note>original: "Zaquio"</note> half of his goods; it cost a widow two mites <note>original: "doas poyfas," small copper coins of minimal value.</note> which she placed on the altar of God; and it cost another a cup of cold water. ...may be taken from us, which is an enemy to all goodness; for it begets lusts, feeds the belly, sows detractions, and causes trouble for that which is good—that is, when we are troubled to do anything ourselves, or to see others do well. Or, if we do anything that is good, we do it idly, coldly, and unpleasantly; and so, instead of obtaining a blessing, we get a curse, as *Jeremiah* says: *“Cursed is he who does the work of God negligently.”* <note>original: "faith" (says); citing Jeremiah 48:10.</note> Therefore, heedlessness or idleness is when we do not finish the good which we have begun; and therefore we do not receive the wages; for it is the end that crowns the work, and not the battle. 

Idleness is directly opposite to the command of the Law, in which it was enjoined to offer up the entire sacrifice—*the head with the tail.* <note>A metaphorical interpretation of Levitical law regarding whole burnt offerings, symbolizing perseverance from beginning to end.</note> The sacrifice is every good work which we sanctify to God, doing it for his honor; the head is the beginning of the work, and the tail is the end. We offer the sacrifice to God (*the head with the tail*) when, persevering, we continue good works to the end. 

Now, the negligent and idle would prefer not to do anything, but to be always idle, which is exceedingly dangerous for both body and soul. And so it is said in the *Book of Wisdom*: *“Idleness begets much evil,”* <note>original: "Wisedom"; likely referring to Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 33:27: "Send him to work, that he be not idle; for idleness teacheth much evil."</note> for the belly of man can scarcely be idle; for when it is not employed in good, it is employed in evil. And *St. Bernard* says that idleness is the bilge <note>original: "the hold or storehouse"; Bernard of Clairvaux used the Latin word *sentina*, referring to the foul water that collects in the bottom of a ship.</note> of all evils. The bilge is the lowest place in the ship, where serpents and creeping things are easily bred; likewise, it is often seen that in the idle soul are bred evil thoughts, consents to sin, and delights in sin. And *Gregory* <note>Pope Gregory I (the Great).</note> says: *“The reason why the heart of Solomon forsook the wisdom of God so quickly was because no outward discipline kept him in check.”* Again, it is necessary for a man to be very watchful...

The sin of sloth <note>original: "lo pecca d'acidia"; acidia is the medieval term for spiritual apathy or sloth.</note>, which is a distaste for good; for this opens the way for lust, nourishes gluttony, sows detractions and contentions—that is, a distaste for good—which is to say, when we are loath to do good, or we are loath to see others doing good. Or, if we do any good thing, we do it lazily, lukewarmly, and contemptuously; and so, where we should acquire a blessing, we acquire a malediction; even as *Jeremiah* says: *“Accursed is he who does the work of God lazily.”* 

For this reason, sloth is when we do not bring to an end the good which we began. Therefore, we do not obtain the reward, for the end crowns the work, not the battle. And the lazy act against the commandment of the law, in which it is commanded to offer the entire sacrifice—the head with the tail. The sacrifice is every good work which we sanctify to God, which we do for the honor of God; the head is the beginning of the work, but the tail is the end. To God we offer the sacrifice, the head with the tail, when, persevering, we bring the good work to the end. 

And the slothful and the lazy would not want to do anything, but to be always idle; which thing is a great danger to the body and to the soul. In this same way, it happens frequently that in the idle soul are born evil thoughts, consents, and delights. # CHAP. VII.

->*An extract of those famous treatises written by the ancient inhabitants of the Valleys concerning Antichrist, Purgatory, the invocation of saints, and the sacraments.*<-

## ARTICLE I.

->*Of Antichrist.*<-

This book concerning *Antichrist* exists in an old manuscript containing many sermons of the *Barbes* <note>original: "Bardes"; the Barbes were the pastors and elders of the Waldensian church. The term means "uncles," used to distinguish them from the Catholic "fathers."</note>, collected in the year 1120. It was therefore written before the time of Peter Waldo and around the time of Peter de Bruys <note>original: "Peter de Bruis"; a 12th-century French reformer whose followers were known as Petrobrusians.</note>, who taught in the Languedoc region where he was burned at the stake—specifically at Saint-Gilles—before Waldo left Lyon <note>original: "Lions"</note>. Since that time, this treatise has been preserved among the Waldensians of the Alps, from whom Mr. Jean-Paul Perrin <note>original: "Mr. Paul Perrin"; a 17th-century historian who wrote "History of the Ancient Christians."</note> obtained it, along with many others.

| <note>This column contains the original Occitan (Vaudois) dialect used by the Waldensians.</note> ...placed within itself the way of truth, of justice, of faith, of hope, of charity, and the moral life, and the ministerial truth of the Church—ministered by the false apostles and stubbornly defended by both the one and the other arm <note>The "two arms" refer to the Secular (state) and Ecclesiastical (church) powers.</note>. Or it is a hidden deceit of the truth of salvation in things substantial and ministerial; or it is a fraudulent opposition to **Christ** and his **Spouse**, and to every faithful member. And so it is not any one special person ordained in any degree, office, or ministry, considering it universally. But falsehood itself sets itself against the truth, which covers and adorns itself with beauty and piety outside the Church of Christ—such as by names of offices, of Scriptures, of Sacraments, and many other things. Iniquity of this sort, with its ministers great and small, along with those following the law of an evil heart, etc.—such a congregation taken together is called **Antichrist**, **Babylon**, or the **fourth beast**, or the **whore**, or the **man of sin**, the **son of perdition**. | **Christ**, and his **Spouse**, contrary to the way of Truth, Righteousness, Faith, Hope, and Charity, as likewise to moral Life, and to the ministerial Truth of the Church, administered by the false Apostles, and resolutely upheld by the one and the other Arm of Secular and Ecclesiastical Power; or else we may say, **Antichrist** is a Deceit which hides the Truth of Salvation in substantial and ministerial matters; or, that it is a disguised contrariety to **Christ** and his **Spouse**, and every faithful member thereof. And so it is not any one particular person, ordained to such a Degree, Office, or Ministry, it being considered universally; but it is **Falsehood** itself, in opposition to the Truth, covering and adorning itself with a pretense of Beauty and Piety, not suitable to the **Church of Christ**, as by the Names, and Offices, the Scriptures, the Sacraments, and many other things may appear. Iniquity thus qualified with all the Ministers thereof great and small, together with all them that follow them, with an evil heart, and blindfold; such a Congregation comprised together, is that which is called **Antichrist**, or **Babylon**, or the **fourth Beast**, or the **Whore**, or the **Man of Sin**, the **Son of perdition**. |

### What are the Works of Antichrist?

The first work of Antichrist is to take away the truth and to change it into falsehood, error, and heresy. The second work of Antichrist is to cover falsehood with a semblance of truth, and to assert and maintain lies in the name of faith and grace, and to spread falsehood—

<column-break/>

...to these things, making the people commit idolatry, fraudulently serving the idols of all the world under the names of saints, relics, and their services <note>original: "menestier"</note>. Thus the people, wandering disastrously <note>original: "peissament"</note> from the way of truth, think they serve God and do well; yet this stirs up that people to hatred, anger, and malice against the faithful and against those who love the truth, and causes murders and homicides. 

And so the Apostle speaks the truth: that he is the "man of sin" made complete, and that he raises himself above all that is called God or that is worshipped, and that he opposes all truth, and that he sits in the temple of God (that is, in the Church), showing himself as if he were God. He comes with all deception to those who are perishing. And if that wicked one <note>original: "felon"</note> has already come perfectly, he is no longer to be sought, for by God’s permission he is already made old and even now decreases. For his power and authority are diminished, and the Lord Jesus kills this wicked one by the spirit of His mouth in many people of good will, and sends a power contrary to him and those who love him, and destroys his places and possessions, and divides this city of Babylon in which the entire generation had the strength of malice.

# Chapter VII. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

<language>Modernized from the original Occitan and Early Modern English</language>

...intermingled with spiritual things for the people under his subjection, whether through his ministers, his ministry, or in any other way relating to the Church. 

Now, it is certain that these two ways of acting contain such perfect and complete wickedness that no tyrant and no power in the world has ever been able to achieve anything like it from the creation until the time of Antichrist. Christ never had an enemy like this—one so capable of perverting the way of truth into falsehood and falsehood into truth, and who likewise corrupted the followers of both truth and falsehood. 

The result is that our holy mother the Church and her true children are entirely trodden underfoot, especially regarding the truth, the true worship of truth, the ministry and its practice, and the children who participate in it. This causes her to weep bitterly, using the words and complaints of Jeremiah <note>Jeremy: an archaic form of the name Jeremiah, referring here to the Book of Lamentations 1:1</note>, saying: *"Ah, how desolate you are, O city of the heathen and uncircumcised people! She has become a widow"*—meaning she is deprived of the truth of her Bridegroom <note>The "Bridegroom" is a traditional metaphor for Christ as the head of the Church</note>. 

Once the lady of the people, she is now subject to errors and sin; once the princess of provinces, she now conforms to the world and the things that are in the world. Weep and look around you, and you will find these things are being fulfilled at this very time: for the holy Church is treated as a synagogue <note>original: "Synagoga"; used here in a derogatory sense to mean a gathering of the wicked or unbelievers</note> of miscreants, while the assembly of the wicked is considered the mother of those who rightly believe in the Word. Falsehood is preached as truth, iniquity as righteousness <note>original Occitan: "eygaleza" (equity)</note>, injustice passes for justice, error for faith, sin for virtue, and lies for the truth.

<column-break/>

...intermingled with spiritual things for the people under his subjection, whether through his ministers, his ministry, or in any other way relating to the Church. 

Now, it is certain that these two ways of proceeding contain such perfect and complete wickedness that no tyrant and no power in the world was ever able to accomplish the like since the creation, until the time of Antichrist. And Christ had never any enemy yet like this, so able to pervert the way of truth into falsehood, and falsehood into truth, and who in like manner did pervert the professors of the one or the other—namely, of truth and of falsehood. 

In so much that the holy mother the Church, with her true children, is altogether trodden underfoot, especially in the truth and in what concerns the true worship in the truth, and the ministry and its exercise, and the children partaking of it. This causes her to weep bitterly, in the language and complaints of Jeremiah, saying: *"Ah, how desolate you are, O city of the heathen and uncircumcised people! She has become a widow"*—namely, being destitute of the truth of her Bridegroom; Lady of people, by reason of the subjection to errors and to sin; Princess of provinces, by partaking with the world and the things that are in the world. 

Weep and look abroad just a little, and you shall find those things now accomplished at this time: for the holy Church is accounted a synagogue of miscreants, and the congregation of the wicked is esteemed the mother of those who rightly believe in the Word. Falsehood is preached up for truth, iniquity for righteousness, injustice passes for justice, error for faith, sin for virtue, and lies for the truth.

...and his Spouse <note>The "Spouse" refers to the true Church of Christ</note>, however small she may appear, as far as our understanding is able to comprehend. This essential truth is the inward knowledge of the only true God and the unity of the Divine Essence in three persons—a knowledge which "flesh and blood" <note>Human nature or effort alone</note> does not provide. The good ministers mentioned urge faith and a good life; they are examples of proper conduct and obedience, and watchfully follow the example and work of the Lord toward the flock.

The things which the ministers are obliged to do for the service of the people are these: the preaching of the word of the Gospel; the sacraments joined to the word, which testify to the intent and meaning of the word and confirm hope in Christ for the faithful; the ministerial communion <note>The fellowship and shared participation in the rites of the church</note> possesses all things through the essential truth. As for the Antichrist, he has already reigned for a long time in the Church by God’s permission.

The errors and impurities of the Antichrist forbidden by the Lord are these: a diverse and endless idolatry, against the express command of God and Christ. To these creatures, they offer the service or worship of faith and hope, works, prayers, pilgrimages, alms, offerings, and expensive sacrifices. And therefore, we are committed to speaking about this Purgatory and presenting what we understand about it.

First, then, we say that the souls of those who are to be saved must finally be purged of all their uncleanness, according to God’s ordinance declared in Revelation 21: *No unclean thing, or anything that gives itself up to abomination and lying, shall enter into Heaven.* Now, we hold that faith and the Scriptures promise us many and various ways of purging or cleansing those who are in this present life of all their sins. But Saint Peter shows in Acts 15 that hearts are purged by faith, and that faith is sufficient to cleanse evil without any other outward means. This is made plain by the case of the thief on the right hand of Christ, who, by believing and sincerely acknowledging his sins, became worthy of Paradise. 

The other way of purging the Spouse of Christ <note>The "Spouse of Christ" is a traditional metaphor for the Church or the body of believers.</note> is through repentance, as spoken of in Isaiah 1, where the Lord commands: *Wash yourselves, make yourselves clean; remove the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes; stop doing perverse things. And afterwards: Though your sins were like scarlet, they shall be made as white as snow; though they were as crimson, they shall be as white wool.* In this passage, the Lord presents himself to the truly penitent in the manner described above, and those who were guilty of sin shall be made as white as snow.

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<page-num>164</page-num>
<header>Several Treatises of the Evangelical Churches Book I.</header>

<column>
...what others will do for us after our death, we should do the same for ourselves while we are still alive. It is a much happier thing for a person to depart from this world in a state of freedom than to seek for liberty after they have been fettered.

In addition to what has been said, we maintain that it cannot be proven by any explicit passage of the Holy Scriptures (the Law of God), nor by any holy teachers whose views are grounded in those Scriptures without twisting them, that there has ever been a common consensus that the faithful must necessarily believe and publicly profess as an article of faith that there is a place like Purgatory. They claim this is a place entered after this life for sins committed after the Ascension of **Christ**, specifically by those souls who—though they are destined to be saved—have not made full satisfaction <note>In this context, "satisfaction" refers to the medieval Catholic doctrine that a person must perform penance or suffer punishment to "pay" for the temporal effects of sin.</note> in this life for the sins they committed. In this place, they are said to endure intense physical pains after leaving their bodies until they are cleansed; some are said to leave sooner and some later, some at Judgment Day and others before. 

Regarding the first point—scriptural proof—there is none at all to be found throughout the Bible. Let us examine the entire Law of God, and we will not find a single passage that obliges or binds a Christian to believe, as an essential article of faith, that after this life there is such a place as Purgatory, as some claim. There is not one place in all the Holy Scriptures to show it; nor can any evidence be produced that any soul ever entered such a Purgatory and came out again.

Therefore, it is something that should not be credited or believed. As proof of this, **St. Augustine** in the book titled *Mille Verba* <note>original: "Mille verba" (Latin). This likely refers to a medieval compilation of Augustine's sayings known as "The Thousand Words."</note> writes: "We believe by the universal faith..."
</column>

<column>
<gloss>...as one hopes will be done by others after their death, they should do it for themselves while they live, as it is a more blessed thing to die free than to seek liberty after being bound.</gloss>

<gloss>These things previously stated, we say that it is not expressly found in the Holy Scriptures of the Law of God, nor in the holy Doctors founded upon those same Scriptures (and not avoiding the truth), that there is any consensus of opinion that the faithful must be compelled by necessity to believe, hold, or publicly confess as an Article of Faith that there is such a place as Purgatory after this life for sins. They say that after the ascension of Christ to heaven, souls—especially those who are to be saved but did not satisfy for their sins in this life—suffer sensible pains upon leaving the body to be purged; from which some leave sooner, some later, some at the day of judgment, and some even before the day of judgment.</gloss>

<gloss>Regarding the first part, which is of Scripture: this cannot be deduced according to the law itself. This is clearly apparent because, searching through the whole Law binding Christians, there is no express Scripture of the Law by which the faithful are required to believe as an Article of Faith that after this life there is such a place as Purgatory, as some say. Nor has the primary meaning of any part of Holy Scripture been given to it, nor can any evidence be made of any soul that has entered said Purgatory and left it.</gloss>

<gloss>Therefore, it is not to be believed or held by faith. In confirmation of this, Augustine in the book called *Mille Parlament* <note>original: "Mil Parlament" (Occitan), a vernacular title for Augustine’s *Mille Verba*.</note> writes: "Because we believe by the Catholic Faith..."</gloss>
</column>

# Several Treatises of the Evangelical Churches, Book I.

[purga]tory, and since the Apostles left us no instructions about it; and since the Primitive Church <note>The early Christian church, specifically during the first few centuries when it was perceived to be most faithful to the Gospel</note>—governed according to the Gospel and by the Apostles themselves—left no ordinance or commandment regarding it; and seeing that Pope Pelagius <note>Pelagius I, who reigned from 556 to 561 AD; the text attributes the formalization of prayers for the dead in the Mass to him</note> first began this institution 508 years after Christ, ordaining that remembrance of the dead should be made in the Mass; it follows that because there is no single express proof for it in the Law of God, it is unnecessary to believe in Purgatory as an Article of Faith, or that such a place exists after this life.

But why is it (one might wonder) that people nowadays are so taken with this opinion of assisting the dead? For in all the Scriptures, there is nothing expressly taught concerning it, unless it be in the Book of Maccabees <note>The Books of the Maccabees are part of the Apocrypha/Deuterocanon; the Waldensians, like later Protestants, rejected their status as inspired Scripture</note>, which does not belong to the Old Testament nor is it canonical. Neither Christ, nor any of his Apostles, nor any of the Saints who immediately succeeded them, ever taught anyone to pray for the dead. Instead, they were all very careful to teach that the people who lived blamelessly should be holy. Therefore, answering this question <note>original: "Quære"</note>, we say that the primary cause for this is the deceit and craft of the priests, which proceeds from their greed and avarice. These priests did not teach and instruct the people to live well, as the Prophets and Apostles of Christ did; they only taught them to give generous offerings and to place their trust and hope for deliverance and salvation in Purgatory.

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the original Occitan (Waldensian) version of the text above.</note>

...any express instruction. Nor has the primitive Church—living according to the Gospel, of which the Apostles were the rulers—handed down anything to us by ordinance or commandment. But it is read that Pope Pelagius, 558 years after the Lord, ordained that in the Mass there should be a remembrance of the dead. The remainder of the Scripture, taken expressly from the Law of God, shows that it is not necessary to believe—as an Article of Faith—that such a place as Purgatory exists after this life, etc.

---

But the doubt remains as to why modern men have such an affection for the assistance of the dead, since in all the Holy Scripture the Lord does not teach this expressly, except for the Book of Maccabees, which is not part of the Old Testament, nor is it Canonical. Neither Christ, nor the Prophets, nor his Apostles, nor the Saints who were their immediate teachers, taught us to pray for the dead. Instead, they taught very diligently that the living people should be holy and without sin. Therefore, answering the aforementioned doubt, we add that the first cause is the deception and fraud of the Priests, proceeding from greed, who did not diligently teach the people to live well in the manner of the Prophets and Apostles of Christ, but instead taught them to offer much, placing their hope of liberation and blessedness in Purgatory.

<summary>This page argues that Purgatory is a human invention established by Pope Pelagius rather than a biblical doctrine, suggesting that the practice of praying for the dead was promoted by priests out of greed.</summary>

### Of the Invocation of Saints.

| Now we must speak of the invocation of the saints, which the Masters <note>original: "Maistre"; referring to religious leaders or teachers</note> and their assistants preach and promote with great diligence, publishing it as an Article of Faith. They say that the saints existing in the celestial homeland <note>original: "patria celestial"</note> should be prayed to by those of us still living, in the manner that priests and other common people usually do by their instruction. They enjoin them to do this and other things to aid their invocation. Through this invocation, authorization, and magnification, the people are seen to perceive things in a worldly and erroneous way <note>original: "carnalment & arrivolment"</note>. They believe that just as it is done before an earthly king who is angry—where others who are not angry intercede to mitigate his anger before him—the people estimate it is done before God: that the saints, turning toward the sinner, mitigate God's anger toward them. | Now we shall also speak regarding the Invocation of Saints <term>Invocation of Saints</term>, concerning which some of our Masters and their followers <note>original: "Adherents"</note> preach and create a stir to publish it as an Article of Faith. They say that the saints who have departed and now possess the heavenly kingdom <note>original: "Countrey"</note> ought to be prayed to by us, in the same manner that the priests do, and other people by their instruction. They command them many other things to further and facilitate their invocation. By this invocation, and the way it is authorized and magnified, the people believe in a worldly <note>original: "carnally"</note> way and err greatly; conceiving that as it is practiced in the courts of earthly kings—where if a king is provoked or angry, those about him who are not in the same passion intercede for others and mitigate his displeasure—so it must also be with God himself. That is to say, that the deceased saints must soothe God’s anger when it is kindled against a sinner. |
| And this is not to be believed, as it would not be seen as true harmony <note>original: "conformita"</note> between the will of the saints and the will of God; for it would not seem right that they themselves would turn toward God on behalf of one with whom God was indignant. | But we ought to believe no such matter; for if that were true, there would be no true harmony <note>original: "conformity"</note> between the will of the saints and that of God. For it would appear as if the saints were not moved with indignation against the person who provokes God to indignation. |
| Secondly, through this magnification and invocation of the saints, the people fall into idolatry, trusting more in some of the saints than in God, and serving them more affectionately than the only God. And they demonstrate this through the elaborate decoration of altars with more precious ornaments, and through sounds... | And secondly, by this magnifying of and praying to the saints, the people fall away into idolatry, putting more trust in the saints than in God himself, and serving them with more affection than the only God; which they do effectively make appear by the adorning of their altars most... |

| ...is dispersed through the multitude of the Saints <note>original: "Sanct"</note>, so that the affection is distanced from Christ, and consequently it decreases as it is spread among many. And it appears to many that when prayer is directed specifically to that one mediator <note>original: "personna mezana"</note> for spiritual help, then the Church <note>original: "Gleisa"</note> would profit and grow more than it does now, when the mind finds many intercessions. Therefore, it would be seen as great folly to abandon the most ready fountain and turn to the troubled and distant river. These things are thus declared: 1. That nothing can be obtained from God except through Christ the mediator <note>original: "mecengier"</note>. 2. That it would be more beneficial to adore Christ among men simply, for he is the best and most kind Mediator and Intercessor between both extremes <note>i.e., between God and humanity</note>. 3. That to speak with him, one does not need the intervention of other Saints, as he is more ready to help than any other Saint, having been ordained by God for this purpose: that the plea or intercession be through him, who is more merciful than the others. For he knows what is a just thing to pray for them, since he shed his precious blood <note>original: "feo sang"</note> for them, which he never forgets, having written them on his hands and on his breast. 4. That he would be a fool who would require another intercessor. 5. That in the early Church <note>original: "primitiva Gleisa"</note> prayer was uniquely directed to that one mediator for spiritual help. 6. That then the Church profited and grew more than it does now, having found many intercessors, who are like clouds without water, darkening— | ...all, so that the spirit of the one who prays must be distracted and straying through the multitude of Saints to be prayed to; thus, the affection must decrease and grow weak toward Christ, being divided among so many. There are many who think that addressing one's prayer to one alone, making him the sole Intercessor <note>original: "Intercessour"</note>, proves more beneficial in spiritual matters; yet certainly the Church would advance and improve much more if she acknowledged no such multitude of newly invented intercessors. It would be great folly indeed to abandon the Fountain of Living Water and go to the rivulets <note>original: "Rivolets"</note> that are not nearly as clear or ready at hand. Thus it is evident that nothing is obtainable from God’s hand except through Christ the Mediator <note>original: "Mediatour"</note>. 2. It would be far more beneficial to adore Christ alone of all men, as he is absolutely the best and kindest Mediator and Intercessor in every kind of extremity. 3. By keeping to his Word, we do not need to address any other Saints as intercessors, because he is much more ready to help us than any other Saint; he was ordained by God for that very purpose—that our address and intercession should be made through him, who is more merciful than all others. He knows for whom it is most fitting to intercede, having shed his blood for them, which he can never forget; they are written on his hands and on his breast. 4. ## ARTICLE IV.

### Of Baptism and the rest of the Sacraments in the Church of Rome.

| [Modernized from Occitan] | [Modernized from Early Modern English] |
| :--- | :--- |
| Outside of what is necessary regarding the administration of baptism, there are the exorcisms, the breathing, the sign of the cross on the breast and forehead, the putting of salt in the mouth, the anointing with spittle on the ears and nose, the anointing on the breast, the capuchin <note>original: "scapupchin"; a baptismal hood or cloth</note>, the anointing of the crown with chrism, and similar things consecrated by the bishop, the giving of candles into the hands, the putting on of the white garment, the blessing of the water, the dipping three times, and the requirement of godparents. Many take these as an occasion for great error and superstition rather than for the building up <note>original: "edification"</note> of salvation, and according to some doctors, they are of no power or profit. | That which is of no necessity in the administration of baptism is the exorcism, the breathing on, the sign of the cross upon the infant's breast and forehead, the salt which they put into his mouth, the spittle applied to his ears and nose, the anointing of his breast, the capuchin <note>A white cloth or hood placed on the head of the newly baptized</note>, the anointing on the crown of the head, and all the rest of those things consecrated by the bishop: putting wax candles in their hands, dressing them in white, blessing the water, plunging the infant three times, and seeking for godfathers. All these things commonly practiced in the administration of this sacrament are needless, as they are not at all part of the substance of, nor required in, the sacrament of baptism. These things only give occasion for many to fall into error and superstition, rather than being built up by them toward salvation; which made some doctors declare that there was no power or benefit to be had from them. |

# Several Treatises of the Evangelical Churches: Book I.

| [Modernized from Early Modern English] | [Modernized from Occitan] |

| Regarding Christ’s body being eaten figuratively, Christ said, "Whenever you do this, do it in remembrance of me." If it were not a figurative eating, Christ would have bound himself to be eaten continually; for we are, in a sense, always in need of feeding on him spiritually. As Augustine <note>original: "Austin"</note> says, "He truly eats Christ who believes in him." And Christ says that to eat him is to abide in him. In the administration of this sacrament, the following things are profitable: prayer, charity, the preaching of the Holy Scriptures in a language people understand <note>original: "known Tongue"</note> for their spiritual growth <note>original: "Edification"</note>, and whatever else is established for that purpose according to the Law of the Gospel to increase peace and charity among the people. However, as for other things—beyond the consecration of the Eucharist—such as the actions of priests during the Mass, the chanting of the clergy in the choir <note>original: "Quire"</note> from the beginning to the end, and the vestments <note>original: "Ornaments"</note> used by the Roman Church and its followers, these are not necessary for this Holy Supper. | ...Christ saying, "Whenever you do this, do it in my remembrance." For if this were not an eating in a figure <note>original: "en figura"</note>, Christ would have made himself obligated to this continually; for spiritual [feeding] is almost always necessary, as Augustine says: "He truly eats Christ who believes in him." And Christ says that eating him is remaining in him. Regarding the celebration of this sacrament, these things are profitable: prayer, love, and the preaching of the Holy Scriptures in the vernacular <note>original: "volgar"</note> and for edification; and whatever other things were ordained for this, according to the Gospel law, so that peace and charity might increase among the people. But the other things besides the consecration of the Eucharist—such as the things the priests do in the Mass, or what the clerk sings in the choir from the Introit <note>original: "introito"; the opening of the Mass</note> to the end, and the ornaments of the priests as they are currently used by the Roman Church and its followers—these are not necessarily relevant to the Holy Supper. |

| ->**Of the Chrism, or Confirmation.**<- | ->**Of the Chrism, or Confirmation.**<- |
| Now we must speak of the Chrism <note>original: "Cresima"; anointing oil mixed with balm</note>, which is currently called the Sacrament of Confirmation, lacking a foundation in Scripture in this regard: that it must first be consecrated by the Bishop, and made of olive oil and balm, applied to the baptized person on the forehead with the sign of the cross in this form of words: "I sign you with the sign of the cross, and confirm you by the sign of salvation: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit" <note>original Latin: "In nomine Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus Sancti"</note>. This is performed with the laying on of hands <note>original: "alpisation de mans," likely a typo for "imposition"</note> and the tying of a white garment <note>original: "vestiment blanc"</note> to the head. This, which they now call the Sacrament of Confirmation, is not seen to have been ordained by Christ or his Apostles. For Christ, the pattern for the whole Church, was not personally confirmed, and he did not require such an anointing <note>original: "Chresima"</note> at his baptism, but only water. Therefore, such a sacrament is not seen as necessary for salvation; through it, God is blasphemed, and it was introduced by the Devil’s instigation, so that the people might be deceived in the faith of the Church and might believe more in the solemnity or necessity of the Bishops. | Now to speak of the Chrism <note>term: a mixture of oil and balsam used in sacramental anointing</note>, which they also call a sacrament, having no ground at all in Scripture for this purpose: that first, it must be consecrated by a Bishop, and composed of olive oil and of balm to be applied to the person baptized, upon the forehead with the sign of the cross, and with these words: ["I sign you with the sign of the cross, and confirm you by the sign of salvation, in the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost."] Which is performed by the laying on <note>original: "imposing"</note> of hands, and with a white garment <note>original: "Attire"</note> fastened to the head. This is that which they call the Sacrament of Confirmation, which we find was not instituted by either Christ or his Apostles. For Christ, the pattern of all his Church, was not confirmed in his person, and he does not require that there should be any such anointing <note>original: "Unction"</note> in baptism, but only pure water. And therefore such a sacrament is not found necessary for salvation; by it God is blasphemed, and it was introduced by the Devil's instigation to seduce the people and to deprive them of the faith of the Church, so that by such means they might be drawn more to believe the ceremonies and the necessity of the Bishops. |

### Of the Extreme Unction.

| [Modernized from Early Modern English] | [Modernized from Occitan] |
| :--- | :--- |
| The seventh Sacrament of the Church of Rome is the **Extreme Unction** <note>original: "Extreme Unction of the Sick"; the final anointing before death</note>, which they attempt to prove by the saying of the Apostle **St. James**. There is no evidence to show that **Christ** or his Apostles instituted any such thing. For, if this physical anointing were a Sacrament, as they would have us believe, **Christ** or his Apostles would not have passed over the evidence of its practice <note>original: "putting the same in ure"</note> in silence. Upon deliberate consideration of this, we do not dare to presume to hold or profess as an Article of Faith that this Sacrament was instituted by **Christ** or any of his Apostles. | The seventh Sacrament of the Roman Church is the **extreme Anointing** <note>original: "extrema Unction"</note> of the sick, which they strive to base on the words of Saint James the Apostle. It is not seen to be ordained by Christ or his Apostles. For if this physical anointing were a Sacrament, as is imagined, Christ or the Apostles would not have kept silent about the proper demonstration of its practice. Thinking well on these things, [we] must not dare to hold or confess as an article of faith that this Sacrament was ordained by Christ and the Apostles. |

### Of Fasting.

| [Modernized from Early Modern English] | [Modernized from Occitan] |
| :--- | :--- |
| It follows now to say something also of **Fasting**, which is twofold: namely, the bodily and the spiritual. The spiritual is to abstain from sin; the bodily is to abstain from food. But the **Christian** is at liberty to eat at all times, just as they are to fast at any time, provided they do not observe the Fast superstitiously, as if it were a virtue of abstinence. And observe that there are some Fasts which ought not to be kept nor commended by the Faithful, but rather to be abhorred and avoided. Such are the Fasts of the Scribes and of the Pharisees, and those instituted by **Antichrist**, which favor <note>original: "favouring"</note> Idolatry; the Fasts of Heretics and superstitious people, observed by Enchanters, Sorcerers, and Necromancers; and the Fasts dedicated to creatures and not to the Creator, which have no ground in the Law of God. Those Fasts are inordinate which are kept by feeding only on rarer, costlier, and... | Now it follows [to speak] of **Fasting** <note>original: "Dejuni"</note>, which is twofold: that is, spiritual and bodily. The spiritual is to abstain from sins; the bodily is to abstain from eating. But freedom is given to the Christian to eat at all times, as every day is a time for fasting <note>original: "com tuit li jorn sian act de dejunar"</note>, not observing it superstitiously as a virtue of self-control <note>original: "continenza"</note>. Note that there are some Fasts which are not to be held nor praised by the faithful, but especially are to be rejected <note>original: "scommingar"; literally "excommunicated"</note> and fled from. Such are the Fasts of the Scribes and Pharisees, and those ordained by the **Antichrist**, smelling of <note>original: "sabent"; literally "tasting of"</note> idolatry. [Also] the Fasts of the heretics and superstitious, which are observed by enchanters, sorcerers, and necromancers; and the Fasts dedicated to creatures and not to the Creator, not founded in the Law of God. The Fasts are inordinate in eating (especially [of foods] more rare, more precious, and de- <note>original: "lica-"; referring to delicacies</note>... |

### Of Fasting (continued)

| [Modernized from Occitan] | [Modernized from Early Modern English] |
| :--- | :--- |
| ...delicious things; such as sea creatures, figs, raisins, grapes, and almonds, of which the poor are deprived and the rich gorge themselves, and the alms are taken away from the poor. If, instead, they fasted on lighter and more common foods, they could more easily and readily provide for their own families and for other poor people. Because fasting does not consist of abstaining from any bodily food as if it were evil or unclean. For all things are clean to the clean, and nothing is to be refused which is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by the word of God and by prayer. All those pre-determined fasts are to be rejected <note>original: "excommingas"; likely meaning excommunicated or cast out from practice</note> and not promoted by the faithful. For these things, they should not be blamed or accused. | ...choicer foods <note>original: "Meats"; in this context, "meat" refers to food in general</note>, such as all manner of sea fish, figs, raisins, and almonds, of which the poor are deprived and with which the rich abound, while alms are withdrawn from the poor. Whereas if they fasted so as to eat afterwards more common and less expensive <note>original: "chargeable"</note> food, they would be able to provide better both for their own families and for the poor. It is plain, then, that fasting does not consist in abstaining from any bodily food as if it were unclean, because all things are clean to those who are clean; and nothing is to be refused if it is taken with thanksgiving, or sanctified by the Word of God and by prayer. It follows that all these aforementioned fasts are to be detested and rejected by the faithful; and of such things they ought to be guiltless and remain unspotted. |
