# An Epistle of the Barbe <note>original: "Barbe"; a term used by the Waldensians for their pastors, literally meaning "uncle" to distinguish them from the "fathers" of the Roman Catholic priesthood</note> Bartholemi Tertian, written to the Evangelical Churches of Pragela <note>A region in the Cottian Alps, now part of Italy</note>.

->*Jesus* be with us.<-
->*Jesus be with us.* <note>original Occitan: "Jesus fia con nos"</note><-

To all our faithful and beloved brothers in *Jesus Christ*. I salute you all. *Amen.*

This letter <note>original: "Epistle"</note> is to notify your brotherhood, as I fulfill the duty committed to me by God regarding the salvation of your souls, according to that light of truth which has been given to us by the Most High. I ask that every one of you please maintain, increase, and cherish to your utmost—and by no means weaken or diminish—those good principles, forms, and customs which were left to us by our ancestors, even though we were unworthy of them. 

For it would be of very little benefit to us to have been renewed by the fatherly encouragement of God himself and the light which he has given us, if we were now to surrender ourselves to a worldly, demonic, and fleshly way of life <note>original: "Conversation"</note>, forsaking the principal Good (which is God) and the salvation of our own souls for a short and temporary life. For the Lord has said in the Gospel, *What will it profit a man to gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?* And, *It would have been better never to have known the way of righteousness, than having once known it, to turn away from it.* Indeed, we shall be altogether without excuse, and our condemnation will be more severe, because there will be greater punish—

To all our faithful and beloved ones, as well as brothers in Jesus Christ: Salvation be to you all. Amen.

This present letter is to advise your brotherhood, as I pay my debt from me to you on behalf of God, especially regarding the care of the salvation of your souls in the light of truth, distributed to us by the Most High. May it please every one of you to maintain, increase, and favor it according to your ability, and not to fall short of all those good principles, uses, and customs given to us by our ancestors, of which we are not worthy. For it would profit us little to be changed by the fatherly insistence and the light given to us by God, if we were to give ourselves over to worldly, demonic, and fleshly conduct, abandoning the most important thing, which is God, and the salvation of our souls, for this brief and temporary life. For the Lord says in the Gospel: *What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and suffers the destruction of his own soul?* For it would be better for us not to have known the way of justice than, having known it, to do the opposite. ...strongly, and to those who know most. Purge from among you every defect and failing that disturbs peace, love, and concord, and every cause that takes away your liberty in the service of God, your salvation, and the administration of truth—if you desire that God prosper you in temporal <note>original: "ben temporals"; material or worldly goods</note> and spiritual goods. And if you desire to be heirs of His glory, do what He says: *If you wish to enter into life, keep My commandments.* Also, ensure that among you there is no fostering of games <note>original: "juoc"; likely referring to gambling or vain pastimes</note>, gluttony, debauchery, dancing, or other disorders, nor disputes, deceit, fraud <note>original: "barat"</note>, usury, ill-will, or discord. Do not support or sustain among you persons of bad life, nor those who give scandal and a bad example. But let charity <note>original: "carita"; meaning brotherly love</note> and faithfulness reign among you, along with every good example, treating one another just as each would want to be treated. For otherwise, it is not possible for anyone to be saved, nor to have the grace of God or of man in this world, nor glory in the next. All this is the principal duty of the Rulers <note>original: "Regidors"</note> and Governors to maintain and encourage. For when the heads are sick, all the members suffer along with them. If you hope and desire to inherit eternal life, and to be in good esteem and credit, and to prosper in the world—regarding both *temporal* <note>original: "Temporal"; relating to worldly or material life</note> and *spiritual* good things—cleanse yourselves from every disorderly way among you. But know for certain that God does not dwell with sinners, nor does he in his soul cling to evil-doing or to the person who is a slave sold under sin. Therefore, let everyone rectify the way of his own heart and shun dangers, if he does not wish to perish in them. I shall not add more for the present, except this: see to the performance of these things, and may the God of *peace* be with you all. # Chapter VIII. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

<margin>
The Synodical Assemblies of the *Barbes*, or ancient pastors of the Evangelical Churches of *Piedmont*. *Book 1, chapter 5, Article 4.*
</margin>
<margin>
*A brief history of the affairs of the Waldenses of the Valleys. 1587.* 140 *Barbes* seen together at a General Council in the *Chisone Valley <note>original: "Val Clusone"</note>, page 15.*
</margin>
It is true that, regarding the specific details of the form of discipline among those *Barbes* <note>original: "Barbes"; a term for Waldensian pastors, meaning 'uncles'</note> in those times—specifically their *consistories* <term>consistory: a local church council or governing body</term> and *synodical constitutions*—those remnants of their ancient records which the *Pope's emissaries* have left us (or rather, which have been miraculously preserved from the fires) are somewhat dark and imperfect. However, what has come into my hands concerning this matter, I shall faithfully share with the *Christian* reader. As to their *synodical constitutions*, the above-mentioned manuscripts tell us that the *Barbes* (or pastors) assembled once a year to manage their affairs in a General Council. The *Italian manuscript* (the original of which can be seen with the rest in the University Library of *Cambridge*, dated 1587) tells us that this Council was constantly held in the month of *September*. It also notes that some hundreds of years ago, no fewer than 140 *Barbes* were seen assembled together in one synod held at *Valone del Lauso* in the *Chisone Valley*. The same manuscript adds that they always had their *consistories* and a form of discipline among themselves, except during times of persecution. In those times, the *Barbes* held their *consistories* in secret and also preached to their congregations during the winter season in their own private houses, and in the summer time, upon the tops of mountains while the people were there feeding their flocks.

<margin>
*page 16, page 17.*
</margin>
<margin>
*page 17.*
</margin>
<margin>
*page 16. Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho against the Jews <note>original: "Justin Mart. Dial. Triph. contr. Jud."</note>.*
</margin>
Of these *Barbes*, some were married to demonstrate their approval of the state of matrimony; others kept themselves single for the sake of convenience, because they were often obliged to move and change their homes and (as the need arose) to undertake long and tiring journeys to spread the *Gospel* in remote countries. They maintained a particular and constant correspondence with these regions after the year 1160—namely, in *Bohemia*, *Germany*, *Gascony*, *Provence*, *Dauphiné*, *England*, *Calabria*, and *Lombardy*. The *Barbes* went to these places by turns as *traveling preachers* <note>original: "Itineraries"</note> to visit their brethren there and to preach the Gospel of *Christ* among them. Those *Barbes* who remained at home in the *valleys* (besides their official duties and labor in the work of the *ministry*) took upon themselves the task of disciplining and instructing the youth—especially those who were appointed for the *ministry*—in Grammar, Logic, Moral Philosophy, and Divinity. Moreover, the greatest part of them dedicated themselves to the study and practice of medicine <note>original: "Physick"</note> and surgery <note>original: "Chirurgery"</note>. In this, they excelled to an admirable degree (as their histories tell us), thereby making themselves most able and skillful physicians of both soul and body. Others among them also worked in various mechanical arts, in imitation of **St. Paul**, who was a *tent-maker*, and *Christ* himself, who until the time of his public appearance worked with his recognized father *Joseph*, as *Justin Martyr* reports in a certain dialogue of his with *Trypho against the Jews*.

Here I suppose it will not be unwelcome to insert the names of all those *Barbes* or *pastors* of the *Evangelical Churches* of *Piedmont* which are found scattered here and there in their *writings*, not knowing what use they may be to any future discoveries of their *ancient records*.

### ARTICLE I.

<margin>Rainerius, *Concerning the Waldensians* <note>original: *de Valdensibus*</note></margin>
The Evangelical Churches of the *Valleys* of *Piedmont*, as well as those of *Dauphiné* <note>A historical province in southeastern France</note>, have indeed been severely persecuted from the very beginning by the ecclesiastics <note>original: "Ecclesiasticks"; church officials</note>. This has occurred ever since the apostasy <note>The abandonment of original Christian principles; a "falling away"</note> of the *Roman* Church has taken place in the world, and all because they would by no means comply with its beliefs and customs. Rainerius <note>Rainerius Saccho, a 13th-century Inquisitor and author who wrote about the Waldensians</note>, in his treatise *Concerning the Waldensians* <note>original: *de Valdensibus*</note>, tells us *that among all those that have*

<header>The Persecutions of the Evangelical Churches Book II.</header>

<margin>Rainerius, chapter *Concerning the zeal for perverting others, and the method of teaching* <note>original: *de studio pervertendi alias, & modo docendi*</note>, page 98.</margin>...have rebelled against the Church of *Rome*, there have been none so pernicious as the *Waldensians*. And truly, we may say on the other side, with as much justice and truth, that of all the enemies that have opposed the true Evangelical doctrine and worship of those poor *Christians*, there have been none so cruel and malicious as the *Popes* of *Rome* and their emissaries are. This is for no other reason than this: that those poor people did, upon all occasions, openly bear witness against the luxury, greed <note>original: "avarice"</note>, and errors of the said *Popes* and their followers, who had so subtly and serpent-like wound and insinuated themselves (first the head, and then the whole body) into the true Church of *Christ*.

And because they taught and maintained (as *Rainerius* himself confesses) that those were the true successors of the *Apostles* who imitated their life, and that the *Pope*, the *Bishops*, and that tribe <note>original: "true," likely an OCR error for "tribe" or "crew"</note> of other *clergymen*—who hunted after and took possession of the riches and treasures of this world—were not the true *shepherds*. Neither was it ever *Christ's* intention to commit the care of his chaste and dearly beloved Spouse <note>The Church</note> to those who would so shamefully prostitute her by evil examples and wicked works.

The very truth is, *this little flock of Christ in the Valleys of Piedmont*, by reason of the remoteness and obscurity of their country and homes—adding to that the natural character <note>original: *genius*</note> of those plain and simple people, which was not at all to pursue high status—did for many *centuries* together peaceably enjoy, or at least preserve among them, the purity of that *doctrine* which was left to them by *Christ* and his *Apostles*. Therefore, when once the seven-horned beast <note>A reference to the beast in the biblical Book of Revelation; original OCR "leasen horn'd," likely "seven-horned"</note> rising out of the bottomless pit began to show itself in the world, and corruption was foisted into the *Church* by the *Roman clergy*, those true *Nathaniels* <note>A biblical reference to people of sincere faith without deceit; see John 1:47</note> could by no means swallow <note>original: "drink down"</note> such abominations. Instead, they resisted and opposed them with all their might, and often even to the point of shedding blood; and for this account, and this alone, they first became the objects of their enemies' hatred and afterwards the subjects of their *Antichristian* fury.

<margin>Pope Alexander III's efforts to exterminate the Waldensians</margin>The first means they used to exterminate and uproot <note>original: "extirpate"</note> them were their thunderbolts and excommunications <note>original: *Anathemas*</note>; their *church laws* <note>original: "Canons"</note>, *constitutions*, and *decrees*, along with whatever might make them hated by the *kings*, *princes*, and people of the earth. They prohibited them from all manner of communion and social interaction with any of their own kind, sentencing them as men unworthy and incapable of the least responsibility <note>original: "charge"</note>, honor, profit, or inheritance; they were even denied so much as a burial place among other *Christians*! 

They confiscated their goods, disinherited their children, and tore their houses down to the ground. These very sentences are to be seen today, together with several letters of *Pope Alexander III* and many others after him, containing the formal instructions which were given by them to those instruments whom they then employed for the completion of that work. They also included the strict commands they laid upon *kings*, *princes*, *magistrates*, *consuls*, and *people* to conduct an exact *Inquisition*, to shut the gates of their *cities*, and to lay violent hands upon and slay without mercy those poor innocent *lambs*—giving their accusers a third, or thereabouts, of their goods...

# Chapter I. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

possessions, and imposing punishments on all those, whoever they were, who should attempt to hide any one of them.

However, as time went on, these measures were judged too mild and gentle for carrying out a task of such magnitude. Despite all their efforts, these people began to multiply greatly. Their ministers did not stop teaching and preaching to their respective congregations that the **Pope** was the **Antichrist**, the **Mass** an **abomination**, the **Host** an **idol**, and **Purgatory** a **fable**. Consequently, **Innocent** (who succeeded Pope **Celestine** by name), around the year 1198, took a faster and more effective course for their total destruction. He gave certain inquisitors, appointed specifically for that work, absolute power: first to build their legal cases as they saw fit, and then to deliver the accused to the magistrate to be hurried to the stake or the gallows. By these means, in a few years, they filled the greatest part of **Christendom** with the most terrifying and tragic spectacles of their barbaric and unchristian cruelties.

<margin>The unlimited power of the inquisitors for the prosecution of the Waldensians.</margin>
It is plain from their constant practices that the power of these inquisitors was unlimited. They had the power to assemble the people whenever they pleased at the sound of a bell! They had the power to proceed against the bishops themselves, if they saw fit, and to manage the legal cases themselves! Yes, they had the power to imprison or release whomever they wished. Every kind of accusation was considered valid by them. A sorcerer or a prostitute was a sufficient witness to take the life of any **Waldensian** heretic! 

Even worse, there was no necessity of confronting parties with one another or properly examining the case. It was enough to present a bill before the inquisitor without any witness or legal process whatsoever. If a man was rich, his wealth was enough proof to either convict him of heresy or at least brand him a supporter of it. No lawyer dared to plead their cause, nor could any notary record any legal act on their behalf. When anyone was caught in this net of the Inquisition, they were certain never to escape. If by chance they were let out, it was only in mockery, to bring them back in again—much like a cat plays with a mouse for a while before crushing its bones between its teeth. 

As if taking their lives were too small a punishment, one can still see many sentences from those bloody inquisitors directed against the very bones of those poor **Waldensians**. <margin>The bones of some Waldensians were dug up thirty years after they had been buried.</margin> They would dig them up at least thirty years after they had been buried and then burn them in the open streets and other public places. The children of parents who were prosecuted in this way did not dare inherit their lands and possessions for fear of being condemned—fearing that by inheriting the property, they would be seen as also inheriting the supposed heresies.

To keep the people in even greater awe <term>awe: here meaning terror or fearful respect</term>, those "holy fathers" used to lead their prisoners and captives in triumph whenever they went in procession. They forced some to whip and lash themselves as they marched through the streets. Others were forced to wear red cassocks <term>cassock: a long, close-fitting garment worn by clergy or those performing penance</term> with yellow crosses, under the name of **Benedictine Converts**, to signify thereby

others were told they were convicted of some well-known errors and warned that for the next fault they committed, they would be condemned as heretics without any hope of mercy. Some were forced to follow the Inquisitors wearing only their shirts, barefoot and bareheaded, with a green withe <note>A "withe" is a tough, flexible branch, often willow, twisted into a rope and used here as a symbol of the gallows.</note> around their necks and a bundle of straw in their hands. In this miserable condition, people of every social rank and both sexes were forced to parade publicly (to the great grief and terror of all who saw them). They were prohibited from entering their churches during services or even casting their eyes upon the *Host* <note>The "Host" refers to the consecrated bread used in the Catholic Mass, which the Waldensians were accused of disrespecting.</note> when the priest lifted it up. 

In a practice no less cruel than the rest, many were ordered as an act of penance to take journeys as far as the *Holy Land* or other remote corners of the world at their own expense for a set period. They did not even dare to ask upon their return what had become of their estates or what intimacy those "holy fathers" had with their wives during their absence, for fear that they would be labeled as relapsed and impenitent <term>impenitent</term><note>Meaning someone who is not truly sorry for their "sins" or "heresy," which usually led to execution.</note> and thus become impossible to pardon.

In addition to these practices, they used a specific set of clever devices and subtle strategies to manage all their legal cases against the poor *Waldensians*. These can be seen in the following maxims, or rules of caution, which Providence has allowed to come to light—however secretly they were devised by those "Sons of Darkness" in hidden corners, like the rest of their plans.

### An Extract of certain Rules of Caution, whereby the 
### Inquisitors formerly regulated their Prosecution 
### of the Waldenses.

1. *It is not helpful to debate matters of faith in front of laypeople.*
2. *No one should be considered truly repentant unless they reveal the names of everyone they know who holds the same principles and profession as themselves.*
3. *Anyone who accuses others but does not reveal those of his own profession should be cut off from the Church as a rotten and decayed member, lest he corrupt and infect the rest.*
4. *After anyone is delivered over to the secular power <note>The "secular power" refers to the civil government or state authorities, who carried out the actual executions that the Church decreed.</note>, he must not be allowed to excuse himself or declare his innocence before the people. If such a person is put to death, it upsets the laypeople; if he escapes, it brings prejudice against our religion.*
5. *Great caution must be taken when promising life to any man who has been condemned in front of the people. No heretic would ever be burned if he could escape by virtue of a promise. If he should promise repentance before the people and then be put to death regardless, it would necessarily scandalize the people and make them believe such people were wrongfully executed.*

<meta>This page continues a list of instructions or "maxims" used by Inquisitors to interrogate Waldensians. It follows a section describing the public humiliations and forced penances imposed on those accused of heresy.</meta>

### Chapter 1: In the Valleys of Piedmont.

6. The Inquisitor ought always to presuppose the fact of the crime and (setting that aside) only inquire concerning the circumstances of the act, in this manner: *How many times have you confessed yourself to heretics? In what room of your house did they stay?* And other such questions.

7. The Inquisitor must hold some book before the accused party during the examination, as if he had the person's entire life story written there.

8. He must threaten the prisoner with death if he will not confess, telling him that he is a dead man and that he ought to think of his soul and wholly renounce his heresy. He should say that since the prisoner must die, he ought to take whatever happens to him patiently. And if the prisoner answers, *Since I must die, I would rather die in this, my faith, than in that of the Roman Church,* then be sure there is no hope at all for such a person, and therefore he must be delivered immediately to justice. <note>original: "delivered forthwith to Justice"; in this context, "Justice" refers to the secular authorities who carried out the death penalty, as the Church itself technically did not execute people.</note>

9. There is no hope at all of convincing heretics through knowledge of the Scriptures or learning. Indeed, it often happens that very learned men are confounded by them. Because of this, the heretics strengthen their own resolve when they find that even learned men are deceived by their arguments.

10. Heretics must never be allowed to answer any question directly. When they are pressured by frequent questioning, they have a habit of answering that they are poor, ignorant men, incapable of answering. If they perceive that the bystanders are moved with any compassion toward them—seeing them as poor, harmless men who are wrongfully accused—then they take courage. They pretend to cry and act like miserable wretches, flattering and smoothing over the judge to try and escape the Inquisition, saying: *Sir, if I have offended in anything, I shall willingly do penance; but I beseech you, help me and deliver me from this infamy which has been cast upon me out of pure malice and envy, and is altogether undeserved.* But then the courageous Inquisitor must not yield or be moved by these flatteries, nor give the least bit of credit to any such stories.

11. Lastly, the Inquisitor must get ahead of them by assuring them that they will gain nothing by swearing falsely, because he has sufficient proof to convict them otherwise; therefore, they should not think they can escape a death sentence that way. However, he must also promise them that if they freely confess their error, they shall find mercy. In such a state of distress, many will confess their error in hopes of escaping.

***

These were the inhumane practices of these "Sons of Violence" from the year 1206 to the year 1228. During this time, such a great number of the Waldensians <note>original: "Waldenses"</note> were arrested throughout most parts of Europe that the Archbishops of Aix, Arles, and Narbonne, meeting at Avignon <note>original: "Navignon"</note> in the year 1228, had compassion on such a great multitude of miserable wretches. They told the Inquisitors that they had arrested so many Waldensians that it was not possible to get enough lime and stone to build prisons for them all; they therefore asked them to refrain—

# Of the Persecutions of the Evangelical Churches: Book II.

...endured their imprisonment until they heard further from the Pope. The truth is, we need no better proof for this than what came directly from the mouths of the Inquisitors themselves. When the question was put to them whether those who received the Sacrament with the Waldensians <note>original: "Waldenses"</note> were excusable, or if they might pretend ignorance by claiming they did not know the people were Waldensians, it was answered:

> *That there had been so vigorous and open a persecution of Waldensians of all ranks and sexes—so many of them put to death, and so many constantly standing in a most forlorn condition before the doors of their chapels and churches—that it was not possible for any man to pretend ignorance in such a case.*

<margin>Vignaux in his *Memoirs of the Vaudois*. Paul Perrin, *History of the Waldensians*, Book 2, Chapter 3. Pierre Gilles, *Ecclesiastical History*, Chapter 4.</margin>

If I should undertake here to speak at length about all the persecutions that ever befell those poor people, I would certainly restrict myself too much in the account of what remains to be told. Therefore, I shall be content to begin only with the year 1400, when the inhabitants of the Valley of Pragelato <note>original: "Pragela"</note> were attacked by their Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> neighbors around Christmas time. This attack was so violent and furious that those poor creatures were forced to flee in great haste with their wives and little ones in their arms to one of the highest mountains in the area. This mountain has been called the *Albergean* ever since, from the Italian word *albergo* (meaning "shelter" or "inn"), because the poor people made it their place of refuge. 

In this flight, a very great number of them were overtaken by their pursuers, whose feet were swifter to shed blood than the feet of the victims were to fly, and so they were most barbarously murdered. The remainder, being overtaken by the night, wandered up and down in the snow until their joints were frozen and became stiff from the extreme cold. Consequently, there were found the next morning, lying on the snow, no fewer than eighty <note>original: "fourscore"</note> small children, with most of their mothers lying beside them, all frozen to death—a most miserable spectacle to behold.

At this time, and for many years after, the Archbishop and the Inquisitors of Turin employed all their strength and power against the Waldensians of Piedmont. Indeed, they compelled some of those who had fallen into their hands to promise that they would change their religion. However, these new converts were unable to continue in that state with a good conscience. On the other hand, fearing to fall again into the "paws of the lion and the bear" <note>A biblical metaphor for a dangerous enemy or predator.</note>, they quickly settled their affairs as well as the circumstances of that situation would permit and retreated—some into Provence, and the rest into Calabria and the adjacent places. 

When this became known to Jean de Compesio, Archbishop of Turin, and to Andrew of Acquapendente <note>original: "Andrew d' Aqua-pendente"</note>, the Inquisitor, several Papal Bulls were issued against them on November 28, 1475. By virtue of these decrees, although most of those poor wretches found a way to escape, many nevertheless suffered martyrdom in a most cruel and bloody manner throughout most towns and cities of Piedmont. Jordan Tertian was burnt at Susa; Hippolite Roussier at Turin. When Hugo Chiamp of Fenestrelle was brought to Turin, they pulled his guts

A while after, when the Pope saw that his persecutions of specific individuals had not achieved his goals, he resolved to resort to widespread violence. To that end, he appointed Albert de' Capitanei <note>original: Albertus de Capitaneis</note>, the Archdeacon of Cremona, to be his Legate <term>A personal representative of the Pope empowered to act on his behalf.</term> and Commissioner General for that affair. He sent him with Papal Bulls <term>Official edicts or charters issued by the Pope, named after the lead seal (*bulla*) used to authenticate them.</term> and patents to all the lords and princes in whose territories any Waldensians were found. He did this to incite them to assist the Legate with sufficient forces to exterminate all the Waldensians—or the "Poor Men of Lyon" <note>An early name for the Waldensian movement, referencing their founder, Peter Waldo of Lyon.</note>—who lived in their domains. So that the world may be satisfied regarding the contents, I have inserted here a true copy of that famous Bull of Pope Innocent, given to the said Albert de' Capitanei in the year 1487. I direct all who are curious about matters of this nature to the University Library of Cambridge, where they may see and compare it with the actual original document.

# Translation of a **Latin Manuscript**, titled *Origo Waldensium, etc.*: The **Origin** of the **Waldenses**, and the **Legal Proceedings** against them.

->The true **original** of which may be seen, together with the rest, in the **Public Library** of the famous **University of Cambridge**.<-

To you, the Most Reverend Father in Christ and Lord, the Lord Rostagnus, Archbishop of Embrun <note>original: "Ebredunensi Archi-episcopo". The text later spells this "Evereux," but the Latin refers to Embrun in the Alps.</note>, and to you Reverend Fathers and Lords: Brother Lawrence, Bishop of Citeaux <note>original: "Cistavicensi"</note>, and Thomas Paschal, Official of Orleans, the Apostolic Commissary, acting under the authority of the King and the Dauphinate, send greetings. 

Concerning the case of those "Poor Men of Lyon"—commonly called Waldenses after Waldo, a citizen of the aforementioned chief city of Lyon—which is currently pending in the town of Val-Grisent <note>original: "Val-grant"</note>: know that the said Waldo, being wealthy and the leader <note>original: "Prince"</note> of this heresy, was, according to historians, the first author of the heresy of the sect of the Waldenses. 

Renouncing worldly goods, he and his accomplices began to lead an "Apostolic life" characterized by the cross and poverty. Despising the clergy <note>original: "Ecclesiastical Men"</note>, he gathered many disciples to himself, who were thereafter called the "Poor Men of Lyon." While pretending to live under Apostolic obedience, they actually separated themselves from it. When reproved, they stubbornly answered that they ought to obey God rather than man; for this, they were at last (and deservedly) condemned by the Church Militant <term>the Christian Church on earth, viewed as engaged in spiritual warfare against sin and error</term>. 

However, not being fully wiped out <note>original: "extirpated"</note>, they fled from Lyon and retreated to the farthest parts of Dauphiné, in the dioceses of Embrun and Turin, among the Alps and in the caves of the mountains—places exceedingly difficult to reach—where more than fifty thousand of them lived. In these places, through the great diligence of the "Sower of Tares" <note>A biblical reference to the Devil (Matthew 13:25), suggesting the rapid spread of what the author considers "weeds" of heresy.</note>, they became so numerous in a short space of time that they sent out colonies from there into Liguria, Italy, and beyond Rome into Apulia <note>original: "Puglia"</note>. 

And just as Christ our Redeemer sent his disciples out two by two to preach, so was the master of that cursed and beastly sect accustomed to sending other inferior pastors—created and approved by himself (whom we commonly call *Barbes* <term>from the regional word for "uncles," the title given to Waldensian spiritual leaders</term>)—two by two to preach and teach the aforementioned doctrine. Now, these *Barbes* used to be ordained <note>original: "created"</note> by their great master (or Chairman) in the city of Aquila, in the...

the Kingdom of Naples <note>This refers to Waldensian colonies established in Calabria, southern Italy, which were part of the Kingdom of Naples.</note>, and in the appointment <note>original: "creation"</note> of them there was usually great solemnity; they had their names changed when they were admitted to this office, in derision of the Bishop of Rome, whose doctrine and worship the followers of this most damnable heresy—namely, the men and women of the Valley of Clusone in the diocese of Turin, along with all the males and females of the valley of Freissinières <note>original: "Fraissimere"</note>, Argentière <note>original: "Argenteria"</note>, and Vallouise <note>original: "Loysia"</note> in the diocese of Embrun <note>original: "Evereux," referring to the Archbishopric of Embrun</note>—have from time immemorial been opposed to (as more than a hundred of them have confessed, and that of their own accord). They are accused of the following articles which are contrary to the faith they claim to have held, and which they inviolably observe. And so that this may be evident and appear more clearly, the prosecutor <note>original: "Procurator"</note> of the place and surrounding areas in the regions of Briançon and Embrun, for the maintenance of the Christian faith and for the honoring of his native country against each and every person of the said Valley of Freissinières, presents and exhibits the following articles, which he desires may be admitted as evidence (to avoid the burden of excessive <note>original: "superfluous"</note> proof, to which he does not intend to limit himself). In reference to this, by way of a formal charge, he solemnly protests against them all and each individual person.

*First, he posits and says, and intends to prove, that the same men of the Valley of Freissinières have been [heretics] for a hundred years, more or less, and, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Inprimis, ponit & dicit, & probare intendit, quôd ipſi homines Vallis Fraxininieræ fuerint a centum annis, citra & ultra, ac, &c." Note that while the Latin says "one hundred years," the English text below says "six hundred."</note>

1. First, he alleges and says, and intends to prove, that the said men of the Valley of Freissinières have been heretics for these six hundred years <note>The English translation here expands "centum" to "six hundred," reflecting the Waldensian claim to ancient apostolic roots.</note>, or thereabouts, and for that term and beyond—even from time immemorial—have been and currently are heretics; and they have held, and do hold, the following points of doctrine contrary to the Catholic faith. And this is a truth that is notorious, public, and manifest.

2. Also, that at present they are commonly held, esteemed, and reputed to be heretics and Waldenses by all who have knowledge of them, their lives, manners, or conversation. This also has been and is a truth that is notorious, public, and manifest.

3. Also, that this has been and is the common rumor <note>original: "voice and fame"</note>, not only among their neighbors but even among those who are more distant from the said valley, for a distance of a hundred leagues <term>A league was a unit of distance, usually about three miles.</term> around and more. This also is true, notorious, public, and manifest.

4. Also, that they have been and currently are infamous throughout the whole world for the heresy and most damnable sect of the Waldenses, which is contrary to the Christian faith. And this has been and is true, notorious, and manifest.

5. Also, that for this reason, their neighbors in the adjacent parts (though they are true Catholics and faithful Christians) are everywhere slandered because of the faults of these people. Indeed, they sometimes suffer great losses and are barred from many honors and profits merely from a suspicion and jealousy of their being tainted with the heresy of the men of Freissinières. And this has been and is true, notorious, public, and manifest.

### **Their Accusations comprised in the following Particulars.**

1. *First, because they call the* Church of Rome *a* Church of Malignants <note>original: "Malignants"; here meaning a gathering of those who are rebellious or evil-doers</note>, *defaming and reproaching it; and this is their damnable belief, contrary to the* Catholic Faith. *This also is true, public, notorious, and manifest.*

2. *Also, because they believe, and have believed, that the* Church of God *is made up only of those who live in poverty, believing as their* Creed *that the holy* Church *is without spot or wrinkle. And this is true.*

3. *Also, because they have damnably believed, and do believe, that their teachers, the* Barbes <term>Barbes</term> <note>The term "Barbe" (meaning "uncle" in the local dialect) was the title given to Waldensian pastors or elders to distinguish them from Catholic priests.</note>, *have the power of* Binding and Loosing <note>original: "Binding and Loosing"; referring to the biblical authority to forgive or retain sins mentioned in Matthew 16:19</note>, *and that accordingly, sins are to be confessed to them and not to the* priests *of the* Roman Church, *which is contrary to the* Faith. *This also is true.*

4. *Also, because they have believed, and do believe, that it neither has been, nor is lawful for the* prelates *of the* Roman Church *to have* patrimony <note>original: "patrimony"; landed property or inherited wealth</note> *or temporal* jurisdiction <note>political or legal power over worldly affairs</note> *in this world, and that since the time of* St. Sylvester <note>Pope Sylvester I (reigned 314–335 AD). The Waldensians believed the Church became corrupt when it accepted the "Donation of Constantine" and gained worldly power during his reign.</note>, *there has not been a true* Pope. *And this is true.*

5. *Also, because they have believed, and do believe, that no one has a greater degree of* power *and* authority *in the* Church *than the level of* holiness *they possess, which is contrary to the* Faith. *And this is true.*

6. *Also, because they have believed, and do believe, that the* sacraments *administered by the* priests *of the* Roman Church *have no efficacy or virtue, which is contrary to the* Faith. *And this is true.*

7. *Also, because they have believed, and do believe, that* tithes <note>a tenth of one's income given as a tax to the church</note> *are not to be paid to the said* priests *of the* Roman Church, *nor are* offerings *to be given to them, which is contrary to the* Faith. *And this is true.*

8. *Also, because they have believed, and do believe, that the* censures and penances <note>church punishments or disciplinary actions like excommunication</note> *inflicted by the* prelates *of the* Roman Church *are to be ignored* <note>original: "slighted"</note>; *for they believe these punishments do not compel or bind the conscience because of the prelates' lack of holiness, seeing as they do not walk in the footsteps of* Christ, *which is contrary to the* Faith. *And this is true.*

9. *Also, because they have believed, and do believe, that the* Roman Church *is a* house of confusion, Babylon, *the* Whore, *and the* synagogue of the Devil, *contrary to the* Faith. *And this is true.*

10. *Also, because they have believed, and do believe, that no one ought to yield obedience to the said* Roman Church *or its* prelates; *and that all who obey them are damned, which is contrary to the* Faith. *And this is true.*

11. *Also, because they have believed, and do believe, that there is no* purgatory <note>a place of temporary suffering for purification after death in Catholic doctrine</note> *in the next world, but that the* living *are purified* <note>original: "purged"</note> *in this life only; and that when a* person *dies, they either immediately ascend into* Heaven *or are cast down into* Hell: *affirming that the* Roman Church *was motivated by a...*

<meta>This page continues the list of articles or formal charges of heresy brought against the Waldensian communities. # Of the Persecutions of the Evangelical Churches Book II.

11. Also, for believing that it was a principle of greed <note>original: "Covetousness"</note> to invent Purgatory; and that because of this, the dead are not to be prayed for, which is contrary to the Faith. *And this is true.*

12. Also, for believing and continuing to believe that it is not lawful to swear an oath for any reason, whether the statement be true or false, which is contrary to the Faith. *And this is true.*

13. Also, for believing and continuing to believe that it is lawful to meet and socialize together indecently <note>original: "wantonly"</note>, and that any persons may associate even if they are closely related by blood or marriage <note>original: "Consanguinity and Affinity"</note>—provided they are all of the same sect—during the time of their preachings, and likewise afterward when the lights are put out, which is contrary to the Faith. <note>This was a common, though usually baseless, accusation made against religious minorities in the middle ages to portray them as immoral.</note> *And this is true.*

14. Also, for believing and continuing to believe it to be as profitable to pray to God in a stable as in a church, which is against the Faith. *And this is true.*

15. Also, for believing, etc., that only God is to be prayed to, and not the Virgin Mary nor the saints, because they are at such a great distance from us that they cannot hear our prayers, which is contrary to the Faith. *And this is true.*

16. Also, for believing and having believed that rainwater has as much power <note>original: "virtue"</note> as the Holy Water found in the church, because all waters were blessed by God, which is contrary to the Faith. *And this is true.*

17. Also, for believing and continuing to believe that secular rulers <term>temporal Lords</term> <note>referring to kings, dukes, or landlords rather than church officials</note> are not to be obeyed unless they belong to their own sect, which is contrary to the Faith. *And this is true.*

18. Also, for believing and continuing to believe it to be an unforgivable <note>original: "irremissible"</note> sin for any man to turn in or expose <note>original: "detect"</note> another member of the said sect, which is contrary to the Faith. *And this is true.*

19. Also, for believing, etc., that outside of their sect no one shall be saved, and that those of their own sect are the true saints, which is contrary to the Faith. *And this is true.*

20. Also, for believing, etc., that no one ought to observe the feast days of saints which were established by the Roman Church, and that it is lawful to do any manual labor <note>original: "servile work"</note> on every one of the six days, which is contrary to the Faith. *And this is true.*

21. Also, for believing, etc., that it is lawful to eat meat <note>original: "Flesh"</note> anywhere and at all times; and that the fasts established by the Roman Church are not to be kept (specifically those who begin their Lent on the second day after the first Lord’s Day in Lent), which is contrary to the Faith. *And this is true.*

22. Also, for believing and continuing to believe that it is not lawful for the "heretics" of their sect to be married <note>original: "given in Matrimony"</note> to Catholics; and they have held, believed, and preached many other outrageous and wicked things, according to their own confessions, which are contrary to the Faith. *And this is true.*

Chap. I. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

### Efforts Used to Root Out the *Waldensians*.

1. Also, for that reason, both the most reverend *Bishops* and *Prelates* of *Évreux* <note>Though the text says "Evereux" (a city in Normandy), this historically refers to the Archbishopric of Embrun in the French Alps, which had jurisdiction over these valleys.</note>, and the *Inquisitors* of heretical wickedness <note>original: "pravity"</note>, have in the past taken great pains to root out the mentioned heretical sect from those areas, even until the days of the Right Reverend Father in Christ and Lord, the Lord *John, Archbishop* of *Évreux*, who recently died. *And this is true.*

2. ### Chapter I. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

<margin>Philip VII, Duke of Savoy and Prince of Piedmont.</margin>

The army was strangely shattered and broken to pieces, and Divine Providence so assisted His people in every place that the remainder of that army wandered up and down, in and about the valleys, for nearly a year, to the great damage of the whole country. Finally, Philip VII, *Duke of Savoy and Prince of Piedmont*, put an end to that war, which he perceived to be so disadvantageous to all his subjects. Indeed, the history tells us that it pleased God to touch his heart with compassion for those poor people, so that he spoke openly, saying that because he had always found them to be most faithful and obedient subjects, he would not allow them to be treated with such force of arms in the future. 

Only for what was past, he ordered for the sake of formality that twelve of them should come to *Pinerolo* <note>original: "Pignerol"</note>, where he was then staying, to beg his pardon for having taken up arms in their own defense. This they accordingly did, and His Highness received them courteously, freely forgiving them all that had happened during the time of the war. He gave them to understand that he had been misinformed regarding both their persons and their principles. 

Furthermore, he desired to see some of their small children, because there were some who had made him believe that they were strange and monstrous creatures, having only one eye in their forehead, four sets of black teeth, and many other such fictions. When some children were brought before him and he found them, on the contrary, to be well-proportioned and handsome, he openly declared how dissatisfied he was with the slanders and lies of their malicious adversaries. Thereupon, he not only confirmed their privileges and liberties but also made them a gracious promise to settle and establish those rights for the time to come. 

This was undoubtedly the real intention and resolution of that Prince at that time. However, he was afterward influenced (or at least deceived) by the subtle schemes of the <term>Inquisitors: officials of the Catholic Church tasked with identifying and suppressing heresy</term>, who had the boldness, despite all the gracious promises of their Prince, to continue prosecuting those poor *Waldenses*. They laid violent hands on them and delivered them up to the secular powers, who in most places were not at all reluctant to lend their helping hands.

Among others, *Marguerite de Foix, Marchioness of Saluzzo* <note>original: "Saluces"</note>, at the urging and request of the Roman clergy, most cruelly persecuted the faithful *Waldenses of Pravillesia*. They were all forced to abandon their own country to retreat into *Val Lucerna*. There, after they had petitioned for five years for the restoration of their estates—which had been seized by their Popish enemies—and found that all their entreaties were fruitless, they resolved at length to take courage in the Lord. By that means, they regained their lands by force of arms, which they subsequently enjoyed for the space of a hundred years afterward.

In the year 1534, Charles, *Duke of Savoy*, was so pressured by the Archbishop and by the Inquisitor of Turin to persecute his Protestant subjects and deliver them over to the secular power, that he appointed a certain gentleman named *Sieur Pantaleon Bersour* of...

Of the Persecutions of the Evangelical Churches: Book II.

The Lord of Roccapiata, near Pinerolo <note>original: "Pignerolo"</note>, was appointed as his Commissioner to carry out that plan. This gentleman, being very eager to prove himself honorable in such a great trust, organized his affairs and laid his plans so that the following year he secretly led about five hundred men—both cavalry and infantry—into the valleys. There, they looted, plundered, and destroyed everything in their path. To be honest, the news of this sudden and violent attack initially surprised those poor people. However, once they regained their composure, they took courage. Every man left his plow and all other work, rushing in haste to stop the enemy's retreat. Armed with slings and other weapons that came to hand, they attacked the soldiers so fiercely that the enemy was forced to flee, leaving their loot behind, along with many of their men dead on the battlefield.

<margin>George Morel's *Memoirs*, written in 1550.</margin>
When His Highness saw that the life of one Protestant was likely to cost him a dozen of his other subjects, he would no longer allow them to be openly harassed by military force. Instead, he thought it better to gradually wear them down and consume them. For this purpose, he stationed certain soldiers to lie in ambush for them as they came down from the mountains into Piedmont <note>original: "Piemont"</note> in small groups of two or three to conduct their ordinary business. While it is true that those who were trapped in this way rarely escaped with their lives, this did not stop the people from persevering in their faith in both life and death. 

A witness to this was Catelan Girard of San Giovanni in Luserna <note>original: "St. Giovanni in Lucerna"</note>. When he was condemned to be burned at Revello <note>original: "Revel"</note>, he called for two pebbles while standing on the woodpile. Holding them in his hands, he told his persecutors, "You think," he said, "to abolish and destroy our churches by these persecutions; but it will be no more possible for you to do it than it is for me to crush these stones into powder with my hands, or to swallow and digest them." Indeed, despite so many general and specific persecutions against the Waldenses, George Morel confesses in his *Memoirs* (written in the year 1530) *that at that very time there were over eight hundred thousand persons professing the religion of the Waldenses.*

In the year 1536, after King Francis I of France conquered Piedmont, Pope Paul III urged and persuaded the Parliament of Turin to take legal action against the Waldenses as highly dangerous heretics. Accordingly, that Parliament burned many of those poor people, following the example of the other parliaments of France. When the poor people sent humble petitions to the King, their condition grew much worse; the King ordered them to live according to the laws of the Roman Catholic Church, giving them to understand that otherwise he would have them punished as heretics. He added that he *did not burn the Lutherans in all other parts of France only to allow a pocket of heretics to remain in the Alps.* The Parliament also commanded them, under penalty of death, to send away their ministers and to receive in their place certain priests to sing Masses. To this, the Waldenses replied that they could by no means obey any...

### Chapter 1: In the Valleys of Piedmont

...any commands that were contrary to the laws of God. They preferred to be obedient to God in everything concerning His service, rather than following the minds and fancies of men.

Since the King had many other concerns at the time <note>original: "many irons in the fire"</note>, the Parliament <note>The French *Parlement*, which acted as a high court of justice.</note> only pursued them through the Inquisition, burning those who were turned over to them by the monks. Among others, they burned a bookseller named **Bartholomew** <note>original: "Bartlemy"</note> **Hector**. This poor man died (as recorded) very steadfastly, greatly encouraging the faith of those watching. He drew many tears from their eyes and words of compassion from their mouths. This execution took place at **Turin** on June 20, 1555, in the Castle square.

However, not long after, this same Parliament sent a presiding judge <note>original: "President"</note> named **De St. Julien**, along with a legal associate <note>original: "Collateral"</note> named **De Ecclesia**. They were given power and instructions to exterminate the **Waldensians**. In pursuit of this goal, they went to **Perosa** and issued a proclamation in the King’s name, commanding the inhabitants to attend Mass under penalty of death. Afterward, they went to **Pinerolo** <note>original: "Pignerol"</note>, where many people were summoned to appear before them. Among them was a poor plowman whom the judge commanded to have his child rebaptized <note>That is, baptized into the Catholic Church, as the Waldensians performed their own baptisms.</note>. 

The poor man first asked for some time to seek God in prayer. After finishing his prayer, he told the judge that he was willing to have his child rebaptized, provided that the judge would give him a signed note taking responsibility for the sin he would be committing. The judge would have to promise to answer for it before God for himself and his descendants, and to suffer all the pains and punishments that would be inflicted for it. Hearing this, the judge thought he had enough sins of his own to answer for without taking on those of other men. He sent the man away with insults, without pressuring him any further.

After conducting many legal proceedings against various people living in these valleys, the judge found that the results were not meeting his expectations. He then tried to entice them through the preaching of the monks, whom he brought into the Valley of **Angrogna** <note>original: "Angrognia"</note> for that purpose. Finding this method just as ineffective as the first, he returned to **Turin**. There, he reported on the great danger of trying to force these people into submission through extreme measures. He added that such an undertaking was better suited for the King, who alone had the power to exterminate them. He suggested that the best course of action was to send all the information and documents to His Majesty, leaving the management of such a dangerous and difficult task entirely to the King's wisdom and will.

Since royal courts usually move slowly in important matters, it was more than a year before the poor people received another warning. Eventually, however, an express order arrived from the King’s court via the same judge mentioned before. Arriving in **Angrogna**, he commanded them in the King's name to attend Mass, under the penalty of the loss of their lives <note>original: "Confiscation of Body"</note> and the seizure of their property. To this, it was

--- Page 336 ---
<meta>This page continues the response of the Waldensian Deputies and Elders to the French Parliament in Turin and details the subsequent executions and political shifts between 1557 and 1559.</meta>

The Deputies and Elders of those Evangelical Churches answered that they were not bound to obey such commands, because they proceeded from man and not from God. They argued that it should be considered that they all worshiped the same God and Savior, *Jesus Christ*, and followed the same Law and held the same hopes as their neighbors. Furthermore, seeing that *Jews* and Muslims <note>original: "Mahometans"</note>—who were regarded as blasphemers and enemies of the name of *Christ*—were nevertheless permitted to live among them in peace and in the quiet enjoyment of their own separate religions, it was far more reasonable that those who worship the true God in *Christ* should be allowed to live in peace among their hills and mountains. This was especially true considering they were ready to accept anything proved to be in accordance with the Word and Will of God, and were prepared to show all due obedience to their superiors and sovereign magistrates. They protested that they would live and die by this resolution.

This answer so incensed the Parliament of *Turin* <note>The French-controlled high court in the region.</note> against them that they burned as many of them as they could catch in *Piedmont* <note>original: "Piemont"</note> and on the frontiers of the Valleys. Among others, Mr. **Geoffrey Varvaille** <note>original: "Jefferey Varvaille"</note>, the minister of **Angrogna** <note>original: "Angrognia"</note>, was burned in the year 1557. His death was a great source of encouragement <note>original: "edification"</note> to those who watched; he was executed in the Castle Square before a great number of people who saw him continue calling on the name of God until his very last breath. **Nicholas Sartoris** of **Chieri** <note>original: "Quiers"</note> in *Piedmont*, a divinity student supported by the Lords of *Bern*, was burned for the same cause at the **Aosta Valley** <note>original: "Val d'Oste"</note> on the fourth of May, 1557, after valiantly overcoming all the temptations they tried to set before him.

During these troubles, Duke **Emanuel Philibert** <note>The Duke of Savoy, who regained his territories after the Italian Wars.</note> was restored to his estates by the general Peace of 1559 <note>The Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis.</note>. He was persuaded by the monks of **Pinerolo** <note>original: "Pignerol"</note> to condemn all the *Waldensians* of the Valleys to the fire and faggot <note>A term for being burned at the stake.</note>, and to grant the plunder taken from them to the neighboring garrisons. # An Extract of the Humble Petition of the Poor *Waldenses*.

### To the Most Serene and Most High Prince *Philibert Emmanuel*, Duke of *Savoy*, Prince of *Piedmont*, our most gracious Lord.

Festus, the Governor of *Judea*, when requested by the chief priests and elders of the people to put the Apostle *Paul* to death, answered no less wisely than justly: that it was not the custom of the *Romans* to put anyone to death before they had brought the accused face to face with his accusers and given him time to answer for himself. *We are not ignorant, Most Gracious Prince, that many accusations are laid against us, and that many slanders are cast upon us to make us loathsome to all the princes and monarchs in the Christian world. But if the Roman people (though they were pagans) were so fair as to not condemn any man before they had known and understood his reasons, and if the law condemns no man (as Nicodemus testified in John 7) before he has been heard and before it is known what he has done—and since the matter now in question is of such great importance (namely, the glory of the most high God and the salvation of so many souls)—we implore your mercy, Most Gracious Prince, that you will be pleased to listen willingly to your poor subjects in so just and righteous a cause.*

First, we declare <note>original: "protest"</note> before the Almighty and all-just God, before whose tribunal we must all appear one day, that we intend to live and die in the holy faith, piety, and religion of our Lord *Jesus Christ*, and that we abhor all heresies that have been and are condemned by the Word of God.

We embrace the most holy doctrine of the Prophets and Apostles, as well as the *Nicene* and *Athanasian* Creeds; we subscribe to the four Councils <note>The first four Ecumenical Councils: Nicaea (325), Constantinople (381), Ephesus (431), and Chalcedon (451).</note> and to all the ancient Fathers in all such things that are not contrary to the "analogy of faith" <note>A principle of interpretation meaning that any particular passage of Scripture must be understood in the light of the whole of Scripture.</note>.

We most willingly yield obedience to our superiors; we have always endeavored to live peaceably with our neighbors; we have wronged no one, even when provoked, nor do we fear that anyone can reasonably complain against us.

Finally, we were never stubborn in our opinions, but rather cooperative and always ready to receive all holy and pious advice, as appears by our *Confession of Faith*.

And we are so far from refusing a debate, or rather a free council,

The deputies and elders of those Evangelical churches answered that they were not bound to obey such commands, since they proceeded from man and not from God. They asked that it be considered that they all worshipped the same God and Savior, our *Jesus Christ*, and shared the same law and the same hopes as their neighbors. Furthermore, seeing that the Jews and Muslims <note>original: "Mahometans"</note>—who are considered blasphemers and enemies to the name of *Christ*—were nevertheless permitted to live among them in peace and in the quiet enjoyment of their own separate religions, it was far more reasonable that those who worship the true God in *Christ* should be allowed to live in peace among their hills and mountains. They emphasized that they were ready to embrace anything proved to be suitable to the Word and Will of God, as well as to yield all due obedience to their superiors and sovereign magistrates, protesting that they would live and die in this resolution.

This answer so enraged the Parliament of *Turin* against them that they burned as many of them as they could catch in *Piedmont* and along the frontiers of the Valleys. Among others, Mr. *Jeffrey Varaille*, minister of *Angrogna* <note>original: "Angrognia"</note>, was burned in the year 1557. His death was a great inspiration <note>original: "of much edification"</note> to the onlookers; he was executed in the castle square, where a great number of people saw him persist in calling on the name of God until his very last breath. *Nicholas Sartoris* of *Chieri* <note>original: "Quiers"</note> in *Piedmont*, a student of divinity supported <note>original: "entertained"</note> by the Lords of *Bern*, was burned for the same cause at the *Aosta Valley* <note>original: "Val d' Oste"</note> on the fourth of May, 1557, having bravely overcome all the temptations they could devise to place before him.

During these troubles, Duke *Philibert Emmanuel* was restored to his territory <note>original: "Estate"</note> by the General Peace of 1559 <note>The Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis</note>. He was persuaded by the monks of *Pinerolo* <note>original: "Pignerol"</note> to condemn all the *Waldenses* of the Valleys to the fire and woodpile <term>fire and faggot: a common phrase for execution by burning at the stake</term>, and likewise to give their plundered goods to the neighboring garrisons. ## An Extract of the Humble Supplication of the Poor Waldenses.

->To the most Serene and most High Prince Philibert Emmanuel, Duke of Savoy, Prince of Piedmont, our most gracious Lord.<-

*Festus, Governor of Judea, being required by the chief priests and elders of the people to put the Apostle Paul to death, answered no less wisely than justly that the Romans were not accustomed <note>original: "wont"</note> to put anyone to death before they had brought his accusers face to face and given him time to answer for himself. *...wherein all things may be established by the Word of God, which we desire with all our hearts, etc.*

> We likewise beg your Highness to consider that this religion we profess is not only ours, nor was it invented by men in recent years, as is falsely reported. Instead, it is the religion of our fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, and of our even more ancient predecessors. It is the religion *of the blessed martyrs, confessors, prophets, and apostles. If anyone can prove the contrary, we are ready to submit and yield to it, etc.* The Word of God shall not perish but remain forever. Therefore, if our religion is the true Word of God (*as we are convinced*) and not a human invention, no human force shall be able to extinguish it, etc.
>
> Your Highness knows that this very same religion has been most severely persecuted in all places for many ages past. Yet, it is so far from being abolished or rooted out that it has instead increased daily. This is a certain argument that this work and purpose is not the work and purpose of men, but of God, and therefore cannot be destroyed by any violence. Besides, it is no small sin to fight against God; witness all those who have until now persecuted the people of God and His holy Word. Therefore, we beg your most Serene Highness (*most Illustrious Prince*) to consider what it is to undertake anything against God, so that you may not stain <note>original: "imbrue"</note> your hands in innocent blood! Jesus is our Savior. We will religiously obey all your Highness’s edicts as far as conscience will permit; but when conscience says "No," your Highness knows we must obey God rather than man. We sincerely confess that we ought to give Caesar what belongs to Caesar, provided we also give to God what is due to him <note>The authors are referencing Matthew 22:21, balancing civic duty with religious devotion.</note>.
>
> There are likely those who will endeavor to incite the generous mind and courage of your Highness to persecute our religion by force of arms. But, O magnanimous Prince! You may easily guess why they do it: it is not out of zeal for God's glory, but rather to preserve their own worldly status, pomp, and riches. Therefore, we beg your Highness not to regard or favor their sayings.
>
> The Turks, Jews, Saracens <note>original: "Saracens," a term historically used by Christians to refer to Muslims</note>, and other nations, though ever so barbarous, are allowed to enjoy their own religion and are forced by no man to change their manner of living or worship. Since we serve and worship the true and Almighty God in faith, and our true and only Sovereign, the Lord Jesus Christ—confessing one God and one baptism—shall we not be allowed to enjoy the same privileges?
>
> We humbly implore your Highness’s goodness, for the sake of our only Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, to allow us (your most humble subjects) the most holy Gospel of the Lord our God in its purity, and that we may not be forced to do things against our consciences. For this, we shall pray with all our hearts to our Almighty and all-good God to preserve your Highness in prosperity.

# Chapter I. In the Valleys of Piedmont. 229

...village of *San Germano* <note>original: "St. Germano"</note>, whereupon many of the poor people, receiving the alarm, retreated to the mountain. Among these, there were about twenty-five who, after they had sought <note>original: "fought," likely an OCR error for "sought"</note> God in prayer, assaulted the enemy so courageously that the enemy's hearts began to fail them. This was especially because they had observed the Waldenses falling down upon their knees before they began to fight; indeed, this fear grew to such a height that many, as they were fleeing in terror, were drowned in a small brook which they had to cross during their retreat.

Soon after, the Duke sent a complete army against them under the command of the Lord *of La Trinité* <note>original: "Lord de la Trinité"; this was Charles de Chevron-Villette, Count of Trinità</note>. Seeing his men discouraged and beaten in several encounters, he began to flatter the poor *Waldenses* with smooth words. Having persuaded them to lay down their arms and to send away their ministers, he secretly stationed garrisons in many places and afterwards treated the people most unmercifully. However, this barbarous and shameful cruelty did not astonish the people enough to cause their hearts to fail. On the contrary, it increased their constancy even more and made them resolve to take up arms again in hope of new victories, as may be seen in the following letter written by a certain minister of the Valleys named *Scipio Lentulus, in the year of our Lord 1561* <note>original: "Anno Domini 1561"</note>.

#### Chapter I. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

> "it comes to **pass** that very few of them are ready, upon any urgent occasion, to defend themselves against public injuries. Furthermore, the Valleys themselves lie so remote from each other that they cannot help one another until it is too late. And although these towns and villages have their counts or lords (as they call them), yet the Duke of Savoy is lord over them all.
> 
> "Before this Duke came from **Nice** into **Piedmont**, he diligently gave orders to those counts and lords of places that they should advise the inhabitants of the Valleys to submit to him and the Pope; that is, that casting off their ministers, they should admit Popish preachers and the abominable Mass. Whereupon, our people sent a certain messenger to Nice, together with their <term>Confession of Faith</term> and petitions to the Prince, beseeching him that he would take it well if they were resolved to die rather than lose the true <term>Religion of Jesus Christ</term>, since they had received it through a very ancient <term>passage of time</term> <note>original: "Tract of Time"</note>, as if by hand from their ancestors. ### Chap. I. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

> "At Villaro and Taillaretto <note>modern: Villar Pellice and Taylare, villages in the Piedmont valleys</note>, a small number of our people put a very large body of the enemy to flight and killed about thirty of them. For these reasons, that most crafty fox, the Lord of La Trinità <note>original: "Lord de la Tyrannitie," referring to Count George Costa de la Trinità, the military commander leading the campaign against the Waldenses</note>, realized that this task was much more difficult than he had previously imagined. He had assumed our men would be terrified by the mere name of an army, but instead they fought stoutly and most valiantly, even though they were poorly armed, few in number, and lacked military experience.
>
> Wherefore he thought it necessary to resort (as is his habit) to deceitful practices. To this end, he employed people to offer hope of peace if they would lay down their arms. Consequently, certain 'false brothers'—acting to serve their own private interests, as experience has since shown—persuaded the people to trust the false promises of their enemies. Although almost all the ministers protested against it, the people were convinced that by laying down their arms and sending deputies to the Prince to promise obedience and beg for pardon in the name of all the people, they might redeem both themselves and their religion for 16,000 <term>crowns</term> <note>a significant sum of gold or silver currency</note>.
> 
> As soon as the overly trusting people yielded to and promised these things (with the consent of some men who should not have agreed to it) through a vain hope of obtaining peace and religious freedom, our deputies arrived at Vercelli <note>original: "Versello"</note>. From there, they were taken by the Lord of La Trinità to a certain cloister to stay for two months, so that there would be time to collect the money. At length, throwing themselves at the feet of the Prince and the Pope's <term>Legate</term> <note>the Pope's official representative</note>—who were both there, attended by many nobles and commoners—they were forced to supplicate the Prince first, and then the Pope's Legate, to take pity on the people who sent them. They were also forced to swear an oath that they would be ready to do everything commanded of them.
>
> The Prince, growing confident because of this solemn promise, immediately sent people to command our people to receive and embrace that 'horrible idol' of the **Mass** <note>the central act of Catholic worship, which the Waldenses, as early Protestants, viewed as idolatrous</note>. Upon realizing the inconsistency of their deputies and discovering the deceit—or rather, the extreme treachery—of the tyrants, the people flatly refused to ratify the agreement. They argued that their deputies had acted recklessly through their own weakness and without the consent of the people; for they had been sent on the condition that they should only do things in the name of the whole people that would lead to peace while ensuring the safety of their religion.
>
> When the <term>Tyrant</term> <note>The Duke of Savoy</note> learned of this, he was more inflamed with anger—or rather, outrageous fury—against our people than ever before. Reassembling a rabble of an army, he commanded the Lord of La Trinità to waste and destroy everything by fire and sword, without any regard for gender or age.
>
> Consequently, houses were everywhere set on fire and goods were plundered; there was no kind of evil so great that it was not committed by those most wretched villains. By these means, they forced our people with

# Of the Persecutions of the Evangelical Churches Book II.

> “...with their wives and children, they were forced to seek refuge in the craggiest parts of the mountains—a truly heartbreaking sight to witness! At the very first attack, they were essentially stunned. Having been stripped of both their weapons and their possessions and living in extreme poverty, they could not see how they would be able to endure such a massive and difficult war.
>
> “But finally taking heart and trusting in the mercy and help of God, as well as the justice of their cause—and being emboldened by the wickedness and betrayal of their enemies—they resolved once again to defend themselves. To this end, they stationed guards and garrisons, fortified various locations, and blocked mountain passes. They were completely determined to die rather than obey a treacherous and wicked Prince in such a loathsome matter. In short, things reached a point where, over the course of several battles, more than 900 of the enemy were killed, while on our side, barely fifteen men were lost.
>
> “I must also inform you that during that time, eight of those leaders whom the Prince held in the highest regard fell in battle. These men were esteemed for their extraordinary bravery and military skill, which they had proven primarily in the war against the King of France. Among them was **Charles Trusset**, Lord of a town called **Runclaret** <note>original: "Runclaret"; modern: Rodoretto, a village in the Prali valley</note>. He was a man of great strength and daring, who had been trained in arms since childhood and was generally considered very courageous in action. This man led two regiments, consisting of about six hundred men, toward a side where our people least expected an enemy to approach. He advanced his men to the top of a mountain where he could look down upon our party. 
>
> “As soon as our people saw them, they offered prayers to the Lord (for they always have a minister with them). Although they were fewer than thirty in number, they courageously advanced against the enemy, who came down the mountain joyfully, as if they had already won the victory. No sooner had they engaged in battle than six of our <term>slingers</term> <note>soldiers who used slings to hurl stones with great accuracy and force</note> found a path unknown to the enemy and immediately took control of the mountaintop, which the others had carelessly abandoned. Crying out loudly from there, **'Let Jesus Christ be glorified!'**, they rushed down upon them with such force that the enemy's strength and courage completely failed, while our men became even more active and brave. 
>

The same Prince (as reported by D'Aubigné <note>Theodore Agrippa d'Aubigné (1552–1630), a French Protestant poet and historian</note> in his *Universal History*) borrowed from the King a commander named Maugiron with ten companies of infantry, and Monsieur La Mothegondrin with some trained bands <note>local militia units</note>.

But the Waldensians <note>original: "Waldenfes"</note>, not lacking courage when the occasion arose, besieged the fortress of Villar <note>original: "Villaro"</note>—which had been built to oppose them—right in front of the French. After eight days, the fortress was surrendered to them upon terms of agreement <note>original: "Articles of Composition"</note>.

The next day, the Lord of La Trinità <note>original: "Mr. De la Trinité"</note> was held back from morning until night with his entire army by those peasants. Later, the Pra del Tor <note>original: "Pré de la Torre"; a natural mountain stronghold in the Angrogna valley</note> was attacked by 7,000 men for four consecutive days, but with the loss of 400 soldiers, including several colonels and captains. Consequently, the Lord of La Trinità sent for artillery and several Spanish troops to assist him, but all in vain; for those poor shepherds fell upon the army so fiercely that they completely routed them, killing many on the spot. Not content with that, they later attacked the rear and pursued the victory as far as Angrogna.
