# Of the Persecutions of the Evangelical Churches: Book II.

At Turin, a man named Chaffincourt, who was then the Gentleman-Usher to the Duchess (as D’Aubigné <note>Theodore Agrippa d'Aubigné (1552–1630), a French historian and poet</note> relates it), began to question the deputies, asking: *How they ever dared to be so impudent—poor wretches as they were—as to appear before their sovereign Prince to negotiate with him after they had made war against him? And with what confidence did they dare to contradict him regarding that religion which was supported by the whole world, or contend against so great a Prince who had the advice of so many doctors <note>original: "Doctors," referring to learned theologians or legal scholars</note>, while they were but poor shepherds, ignorant of all things?* In short, he told them that since they were so ill-advised, they could expect no other result from all their foolishness and folly <note>original: "sottishnes"</note> than to end up on the gallows. To this, one of the aforementioned deputies answered him as follows:

"Sir, what gives us the boldness to appear before our Prince is that his goodness encourages and calls us to do so. Our defense of ourselves has been just, because we have been forced to do it, and God has justified it by His wonders. As for our property, we have suffered the loss of it without resistance; but when we saw that the plan was to oppress our consciences and utterly abolish the true service and worship of God among us—and when we saw our Prince unwillingly executing (as we charitably believe) the Pope's commands and acting by the will of others, contrary to his own natural inclination, and therefore exercising judicial power not as a sovereign but as an inferior lord who has another sovereign over himself—we thought that defending ourselves was only to oppose that supreme power and tyranny which the enemies of God have usurped over our sovereign Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. 

This is the supreme power that ought to be preferred above all the powers of the world; and having once been bound to Him by an oath, we are thereby released from all others that are contrary to it. As for that simplicity with which you are pleased to reproach us, God Himself has blessed it to show that He does not need the greatness of the world to perform great things; the most lowly and humble instruments have often been the most pleasing to Him. As for advice, that which we receive from His Spirit is wise enough, and those hearts which He animates are sufficiently courageous; those arms strengthened by Him cannot lack any strength. We are ignorant, it is true, and aim for no other eloquence than to pray in faith. As for the death with which we are threatened, the word and honor of our Prince is more precious than our lives; however, even death itself is not in the least able to dismay those who have the fear of God deeply engraved in their hearts."

These and similar expressions so deeply touched the heart of Chaffincourt that they led him to become a Protestant. Furthermore, these and similar expressions and the conduct of these deputies of those poor people obtained the following edict in the year 1561.

But in the year 1565, another Edict, dated the tenth of *June*, was published at the persistent <note>original: "importunate"</note> request of the *Catholic* <note>original: "Popish"</note> party. By this decree, all men who lived within the *Duke* of *Savoy's* Dominions and would not conform to the *Roman Catholic* Religion were commanded to come and declare the same to the respective Magistrates of their several habitations within ten days after the publication. Two months later, they were required to leave the country, having been given one year to sell or dispose of their goods, both movable and immovable; during which time they could keep the income from them. As for the Magistrates, they were commanded to watch and observe diligently who were stubborn and rebellious <note>original: "refractory"</note>, and having done so, to send their reports to his Highness so that he might proceed against them according to his will and pleasure.

Now the news and tidings of this cruelty so moved the hearts of the Protestant Princes of *Germany* that they sent an embassy to his Highness of *Savoy* to intercede on their behalf. Among them, the Prince Elector of the Palatinate was exceedingly zealous. Upon the return of one *John Junius*—one of his senior <note>original: "ancient"</note> Councilors of State and a person of singular worth, whom he had sent as his Ambassador to the Duke of *Savoy* purely for that reason—the Elector heard Junius's report of the shameful and dishonorable treatment <note>original: "unworthy and unhandsome dealings"</note> of that Court. Finding that, despite all the fair and golden promises they had made to his Ambassador, they did not cease at all to persecute and molest the poor people, he wrote a very sharp and powerful <note>original: "smart and significant"</note> letter to the Duke, which indeed is fit to be shared with posterity.

### ARTICLE 5.

# A Copy of a Notable Letter, Written by the Prince Elector Palatine to the Duke of Savoy, in favor of the Evangelical Churches of the Valleys of Piedmont. 1566.

*I received with great contentment and satisfaction, (my most dear cousin) the report which my Junius <note>Franciscus Junius the Elder (1545–1602), a prominent Reformed theologian and diplomat sent by the Elector.</note> has made to me of your good affection toward me and your great civility toward him. You have likewise given an ample testimony of this by your promise to release and set free for my sake, and for the sake of the other Protestant Princes, those who were imprisoned and in the galleys <note>original: "Galleys" — a common form of forced labor for prisoners on naval vessels.</note> on account of their religion.*

*But this contentment of mine has been somewhat mingled with grief and trouble by that Act of the Senate of Savoy <note>The Sovereign Council of Savoy, the high court of the Duchy.</note>, who have had the boldness to diminish the benefit which you had granted to me and to the other Protestant Princes. They have done this by condemning those nine poor innocent souls, who were detained as prisoners at Chambéry <note>original: "Cambery"</note>, to perpetual exile as if they were guilty of sedition and treason.*

*For I myself am not the kind of person who, having once granted Your Highness any kindness, would ever have permitted any of my subordinates to make the least reduction of my generosity <note>original: "Liberality"</note>; rather, I would much more have enlarged it (as is both customary and proper in the acts of Princes). But now, I do not only believe the above-mentioned persons to be altogether innocent of the crimes laid to their charge, but it is something of which I am fully persuaded.*

*For, by the letters signed by Your Highness’s own hands, and the hands of your Chancellor and Secretary, and sealed with the seals of both, I perceive that it is undoubtedly so. For by the said letters, they are so far from being accused that they are excused and justified from having in the least conspired against Your Highness. Indeed, if they would but have accepted those letters, they would have long ago been set at liberty. But they could not consent to do so with a good conscience, because Your Highness required from them such conditions as would have obliged them to follow, for the time to come, the customs and superstitions of the Church of Rome. This truly is a matter no less distressing to them, or to any of God’s faithful people, than if you should pressure them to renounce Jesus Christ himself!*

*Consequently, I easily judge that it is by the persuasion of the Pope and his counselors that Your Highness accuses them of sedition. I have sufficient ground to believe that they are so carried away with hatred and furious passion against our religion that they invent and seek out every imaginable occasion, right or wrong, to add affliction to the misery of those poor creatures. These people, nonetheless, desire nothing more than to yield all manner of obedience and fidelity to Your Highness, provided they are not forced in matters of religion to violate their consciences. And this I easily perceived (though to my great trouble) by Your Highness’s...*

their hearts. *After the coming of Christ, the Roman Emperors, even after they had persecuted the Christians in various ways and charged them with all sorts of slanders <note>original: "Calumnies"</note>, nevertheless saw that their numbers always increased. Since they could not find enough executioners <note>original: "Hangmen"</note> to torment them, they were forced to allow them to live in the Empire (as history bears witness), granting them the free exercise of their religion. What is more, they even allowed them their temples, as is reported of Alexander Severus, who permitted this at Rome. Indeed, the same was done by several others, who prohibited their subjects from injuring or slandering the Christians, even though they did not approve of their religion at all, but hated the name of Christ from their very hearts.*

*Similarly, among the Pagans, how great must the diversity of their religion have been, considering some did not even know the names of the gods of others? Was the Roman Empire troubled and divided because of it? Are there not today, under the rule of the Turks <note>The Ottoman Empire</note>, Jews, Persians, Muslims <note>original: "Mahometans"</note>, and Christians, who all follow different religions that are extremely contrary to one another? And yet, we see how that empire has grown and increased. Now, if religious diversity was the cause of rebellion <note>original: "Seditions"</note> and unrest, the empire of the Turks would surely not have grown so large, to the harm and detriment of the Christian world.*

*Your Highness sees the state of Germany, France, Poland <note>original: "Polonia"</note>, Scotland, Switzerland, and other countries where both religions are found; nevertheless, they live in sweet peace and tranquility. Therefore, your Highness should not fear that allowing or permitting the profession of the Reformed religion in your country will cause rebellions and unrest. On the contrary, you should fear the outcome of doing the opposite! I say this as one who desires your Highness to follow good advice, and who would be very sorry if any trouble should happen to you because of this.*

*But I entreat your Highness not to resist God, who has decreed to plant his Gospel in your country. I ask that you would consider the examples of those who tried to stop the progress of the Gospel in its infancy, and the evils they brought upon their own heads by doing so; follow instead the advice of Gamaliel <note>A reference to Acts 5:38–39, where Gamaliel advises the Jewish council not to persecute the Apostles, arguing that if their work is of God, it cannot be overthrown.</note>. Let your Highness see and consider what has been done for the faithful and those who fear God; for if this counsel were of men, it would not stand—it would certainly have dissolved on its own and been extinguished long ago. But since God is the author, it cannot be abolished or dissolved by any torments or persecutions whatsoever.*

For no violent thing lasts long, and we must not always "follow the wolf into the woods" <note>A proverb meaning to pursue a dangerous enemy too far or to push someone to the point of desperation</note>. It is justly to be feared that *Patience*, being so often vexed and provoked, will become *Fury*, and that the evil and mischief of it will result in harm to the *Public*. *Poverty* and *Hunger* are no small torments, nor is it an easy thing to lead such a long and miserable life in exile, being robbed of all our *Goods* and *Estates*. It is the highest of injustice and misery to be constrained to submit to the yoke and tyranny of the *Bishop of Rome* <note>The Pope</note> and be prohibited from worshipping *God* according to his *Word*. Indeed, it is altogether insupportable for good and faithful *Subjects* to be accused as *Rebels* and seditious persons.

*Your Highness* ought to consider these things much more than lending an ear to those who are biased by their passions and who are sworn enemies of the truth and true *Evangelical* <note>Protestant</note> doctrine, achieving their own goals under the pretext and cover of the *Roman Religion*. Neither ought your *Highness* to consent to these passions and furies which are so implacably bent against *Gospel-worship*.

Now, to better apply a speedy remedy to all these evils, your *Highness* cannot find a more proper one (without offering violence to your own natural clemency and gentleness) than to promise your poor *Subjects* the free exercise of their *Religion*—which is the only thing they request from your hands. This is esteemed the only true way to avoid those dangers and miseries which have befallen *France* and other parts on this account, and which may well befall your *Country* if they proceed as they have begun. This is the true means to retain your *Subjects* in their due obedience and ready execution of your commands.

But perhaps your *Highness* will tell me that there is no enduring two *Religions* under the same *Prince* and in the same *Country*, objecting to that common proverb, *One Law, one Faith, one King* <note>original: "Une foi, une loi, un roi," a contemporary French maxim for absolute monarchy</note>. This would truly be a very desirable thing; but since the true *Religion* and *Faith* is the gift of *God*, infused and engraved in the hearts of men—which (as *I* have already said) no man can extinguish but *God* alone—those men are extremely inconsiderate who think it is necessary that every individual of a *Country* (or the whole *Christian* world) should be brought to be of the same *Religion* by force of *Arms* or persecutions. Perhaps it might be so if *Religion* were founded upon the *Authority* and good will of men; yet that would not be a *Religion*, but rather *Hypocrisy* and insincerity. For since true *Religion* has *God* for its *Author*, it cannot be brought about by any force or reason that those who have received this conviction from *God* should ever suffer themselves to be drawn aside from it in the least.

Indeed, it has never been seen since the beginning of the world that everyone was of the same *Religion*, exactly agreeing in their *Customs* and *Ceremonies*, as is evident in the *Family* of our *First Father* <note>Adam</note>. Likewise, before the coming of *Christ*, in the *Kingdoms* of the *Egyptians*, *Assyrians*, *Chaldeans*, *Medes*, and *Persians*, those *Kings* and *Lords* were forced to tolerate <note>original: "countenance"</note> the *Jews* in their *Kingdoms* with the exercise of their *Religion*, although they abominated it in

...their hearts. *After the coming of Christ, the Roman Emperors, after they had in various ways persecuted the Christians and charged them with all sorts of false accusations <note>original: "Calumnies"</note>, nevertheless—seeing that their number always increased and that they could not find enough executioners <note>original: "Hangmen"</note> to torment them—were forced <note>original: "fain"</note> to permit them in the Empire (as historical records testify). They granted them the free exercise of their religion and (what was more) allowed them their temples, as is reported of Alexander Severus, who permitted this at Rome. Indeed, the same was done by various others, who prohibited their subjects from injuring or slandering the Christians, even though they did not in any way approve of their religion but detested the name of Christ from their very hearts.*

*In the same way, among the pagans, how great must the diversity of their religion have been, given that some did not even know the names of the gods of others? Was the Roman Empire troubled and divided because of it? Are there not today under the Turkish <note>The Ottoman Empire</note> dominions Jews, Persians, Muslims <note>original: "Mahometans"</note>, and Christians, who are all of various religions and extremely opposite to one another? And yet, despite this, we see how that empire has grown and increased. Now, if diversity of religion were the cause of rebellions <note>original: "Seditions"</note> and riots <note>original: "Tumults"</note>, surely the empire of the Turks would not have grown so large, to the harm and detriment of the Christian world.*

*Your Highness sees the state of Germany, France, Poland <note>original: "Polonia"</note>, Scotland, Switzerland, and other countries, where both one and the other religion are found, yet nonetheless they live in sweet peace and tranquility. Therefore, Your Highness should not fear that allowing or permitting the profession of the Reformed religion in your country will give rise to rebellions and riots. On the contrary, you should rather fear the outcome of a contrary proceeding!*

*And I say this as one who desires Your Highness to follow good advice, and who would be very sorry if any trouble should happen to you on this account. But I urge Your Highness not to resist God, who has decreed to plant his Gospel in your country. Please set before your eyes the examples of those who tried to hinder the course of the Gospel in its infancy and the evils they brought upon their own heads as a result, and follow the advice of Gamaliel <note>A reference to Acts 5:34-39, where the Pharisee Gamaliel advises the Jewish council that if a movement is of human origin it will fail, but if it is from God, it cannot be stopped.</note>. But since God is the author, it cannot be abolished or dissolved by any torments or persecutions whatsoever.*

*Do not let Your Highness think it is a proper thing to resist or fight against God; for he will be the winner, no matter what happens. Let me urge this one thing upon Your Highness: since your magistrates cannot hide <note>original: "dissemble"</note> the hatred they bear toward the faithful because of their religion—oppressing those poor people by every means imaginable and accusing them of the crimes of rebellion and sedition merely for gathering with no other intention than to pray to God in sincerity and to hear or read his Word (or if they hear sermons outside of Your Highness's territories, thus provoking Your Highness against them)—I ask that you would not permit those magistrates to judge matters of religion, but instead reserve that authority for yourself alone. <header>Of the Persecutions of the Evangelical Churches Book II.</header>

By this means, you would easily know that those men are not as they have been represented to your Highness. For if we carefully consider both sacred and secular <note>original: "profane"</note> history, we see that it is a constant cause of all riots and unrest <note>original: "Tumults"</note> when the governors of provinces and their officers take the liberty—even against the decrees of princes—to treat poor people however they please, merely to satisfy the passions of private individuals, to the great harm of public peace and stability. Regarding other matters, I understand (and not without grief) that almost none of the promises your Highness made to my representative, Junius, in person <note>original: "with your own Mouth"</note> have been kept. Those poor souls who were held in the galleys <term>galleys: sea vessels where prisoners were forced to row as a form of hard labor</term> because of their religion—whose names he had delivered to your Highness—are still being held. This clearly shows me that these are the actions of your Highness's counselors, who are carried away by a deadly hatred for our religion. I know this not only by hearsay, but have experienced it through the example of two people who have been driven away into banishment.

But this severity (to put it mildly) pleases neither God nor man. Nor is it the way to lead people to the true knowledge of God; that must be done through persuasion and evidence from the Scriptures, not by persecution. Your Highness will perhaps reply that our religion has been condemned for a long time. But by whom? And how? By one who has violated and corrupted all rights, both divine and human, making himself both a participant <note>original: "Party"</note> and a judge, and who has lately confirmed at the Council of Trent <term>Council of Trent: a major Roman Catholic council held between 1545 and 1563 to counter the Protestant Reformation</term> all his idolatries, superstitions, and abuses introduced into the Church. 

But let your Highness read and examine the Holy Scriptures and seek the truth, and you shall find that this is so. Never allow yourself to be deluded by those deceivers who uphold their idolatries and superstitions for no other reason than to serve their own appetites <note>original: "Bellies"</note>, so that they may lead the lives of pleasure-seekers <term>Epicures: followers of a philosophy associated with sensory pleasure; here used as a derogatory term for those living in luxury</term>. 

Consider, your Highness, that you must one day appear before the judgment seat <note>original: "Tribunal"</note> of Christ to give an account for the souls of your subjects. At that time, saying "I thought so" or "I believed it to be so" will not be enough. For God has revealed His will in His Word and desires that we follow it without turning either to the right or to the left. Now, the Word of God is clear and plain; if your Highness will only hear and embrace it, you will easily discover the whole truth. 

I say all this as one who desires the good of your Highness's soul, wishing for you as much as I do for myself. I beg the Lord incessantly that He will please enlighten your understanding and call you home to His true light, so that you may discern truth from falsehood. Then, having knowledge of the horrible abuses of the Church of Rome, you may serve God in truth and sincerity. 

Therefore, I pray that your Highness will give us a sign and evidence of the esteem you have for us by releasing those poor people who are now in the galleys, and by recalling those who have been lately banished by the Senate of Savoy—just as you promised my representative Junius and myself in your letters. Have compassion upon so many poor wandering exiles, deprived of all their goods and estates! Call them home...

# Chap. I. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

...home, and restore them to their houses and homes, and grant both them and the other inhabitants of your Highness's countries the public exercise of their religion, which they consider to be more necessary than their daily food! Absolve those poor people of the Valleys who have been falsely accused, so that all of them may live in peace and tranquility under your Highness's government! Establish terms of peace with them that may be maintained without change! Keep them in peace and quiet in the practice of the religion you have allowed them. Be their protector by controlling and restraining the bitter hatred that their Governor, Castrocaro <note>Sebastiano Grazioli, known as Castrocaro, was a notoriously harsh governor of the Piedmont valleys who frequently persecuted the Waldensians despite the Duke's official edicts of tolerance.</note>, directs against them. Warn him not to harass them anymore, as he has done until now, and command him to stop making false accusations against them, which he uses to disguise his tyranny. Such actions are not at all fitting for a magistrate and governor, who should be a father to those committed to his care. 

If your Highness is pleased to grant the things I now request with such sincerity and earnestness, I do not doubt that you will personally experience the favor and blessing of God, and you will find us ready to assist you in all matters. If not, you will both provoke God to lift His hand against you and alienate the affection and loyalty of all those who wish to serve you. Let your Highness value the favor of God and the goodwill of other princes more than the promises of the Pope and his followers <note>original: "Creatures," meaning those dependent on or serving the interests of another.</note>. Do not allow yourself to be used as an instrument for their insatiable desires to spill the blood of Christians! Do not support their cruelty and inhumanity against those who are not at all rebellious <note>original: "perverse"</note> but are true Christians. They desire nothing more than to serve God purely and sincerely under your Highness’s government, paying all the obedience and loyalty due to you, and dedicating themselves entirely—their goods, bodies, and lives, if necessary—to your service. 

May it please you to have compassion on them, and you will always find them even more faithful and obedient. By doing so, you will do what is most acceptable to God, and you will earn the eternal gratitude of those poor people. You will also find us even more ready to do you any service with all that we have. Therefore, I entreat your Highness to listen to these requests. In the end, you will know beyond doubt that we have sought nothing so much as your own benefit and the peace of your lands. May the great and all-powerful God guide and govern your Highness by His Holy Spirit, and keep and defend you in long health and safety.

Absolve those poor people of the **Valleys** who have been falsely accused, so that all of them may live in peace and tranquility under your **Highness's** government! Make such articles of peace with them as may be maintained without change! Preserve them in peace and quiet in the exercise of that **religion** which you have permitted to them, and be their defense, controlling and restraining the bitter hatred which their governor, **Castrocaro** <note>Andrea Castrocaro was a governor notorious for his harsh and often personal crusade against the Waldensian communities.</note>, exercises against them. Warn him to harass them no more in the future as he has done until now, and command him to refrain from charging them with false crimes and accusations, by which he attempts to justify his **tyranny**. Such things are not at all appropriate for a magistrate and governor, who ought to be a father to those committed to his care. 

If your **Highness** is pleased to grant me those things which I now desire of you with so much affection and earnestness, I do not doubt that you will find by experience the favor and blessing of **God**, and you shall find us ready to serve you in all things. If not, you will both provoke **God** to lift up his hand against you and also alienate the affection and courage of all those who desire to do you pleasure and service. Let your **Highness** then value the favor of **God** and the goodwill of **Princes** more than the promises of the **Pope** and his followers. Do not make yourself an instrument of their insatiable desires to spill the blood of **Christians**! Do not support their cruelty and inhumanity against those who are in no way rebellious, but are sincere **Christians**—those who desire nothing more than to serve **God** purely and sincerely under your **Highness's government**, and to pay all the obedience and loyalty that is due to you, and to devote themselves entirely (their goods, bodies, and lives, if necessary) to your service. 

May it please you then to have compassion on them, and you will always find them to be even more faithful and obedient. In doing so, you will do what is most acceptable to **God**, and you will forever oblige those poor creatures to you. You will also find us always more ready, with all that we have, to do you any favor on all occasions. Therefore, I entreat your **Highness** to please listen to these requests, and in the end, you will know abundantly that we have sought nothing so much as your own advantage and the tranquility of your **dominions**. *May the great and all-powerful God guide and govern your Highness by his Holy Spirit, and keep and defend you long in health and safety.*

->Dated and signed thus in the original,<-

->**Augsburg**, 1566. <note>original: *Augustæ Vindelicorum*</note> Your Devoted Cousin, the **Palatine Elector**. <note>original: *V. D. Consanguineus Palatinus Elector*</note><-

### ARTICLE VI.

To gain a more specific understanding of why the Elector Palatine made such heavy complaints in his letter regarding the *failure to observe* what his ambassador had been promised, it should be noted that *Castrocaro* was extremely troubled that the ambassador had obtained several promises at court for the benefit of the poor people. Immediately after the ambassador's departure, *Castrocaro* caused two ordinances to be published throughout the Valley of *Lucerna*. One of these was dated the twenty-first of *April*, 1566, by which he commanded all inhabitants throughout his government who were not natives to depart within one day after its publication, under penalty of death and the forfeiture of their property. By the other ordinance, he prohibited those of the Reformed Religion inhabiting *Lucerna*, *Bobbio*, *Campiglione*, and *Fenile* from hearing sermons at *San Giovanni* <note>original: "St. Giovanni"</note> under the same penalty. 

Despite this, the poor people were not discouraged from continuing their accustomed worship, as they had been permitted to hold public meetings there by a formal agreement <note>original: "Capitulation," referring to the Treaty of Cavour in 1561</note> with his Highness in the year 1561. In response, *Castrocaro* imprisoned and tormented a great number of them in the Castle of *Torre Pellice* <note>original: "La Torre"</note>. Because of this, the poor people made an appeal to the Duchess <note>Margaret of Valois, Duchess of Savoy, who was known for her mediation and sympathy toward the Waldensians.</note>, who had pity on them. She wrote a letter to the said *Castrocaro* on their behalf, commanding him in the Duke's name to *release the prisoners and to stop harassing them in the enjoyment of their ancient homes and privileges*.

This letter from the Duchess did indeed restrain the fury of *Castrocaro* for a time, though it was far from working any change in his spirit or principles. This is clearly evident by his later actions and his rude behavior toward them, especially in the year 1571. At that time, he so incensed the Governor of *Bobbio* against the poor inhabitants of the valley that the Governor not only grievously harassed them whenever they fell into his clutches, but also wrote bitter letters to his Highness against them, using the best of his abilities and power to ruin and exterminate them. Certainly, *Castrocaro* would have brought his designs to their desired end had not the Duchess—following the joint supplications and requests of all the Evangelical Churches—very effectively intervened for them and secured the continuation of their just and certain rights and privileges.

Here, incidentally, the Christian reader may be pleased to take notice of the great blessing from Heaven upon the sweet harmony and unity that existed at that time among those Evangelical Churches. This unity always appeared—but now more especially—through their constant empathy for one another's miseries and sufferings, and their marvelous readiness to support each other's needs, often even at the risk of both their estates and lives. ### An Extract of a League or Agreement made between the Evangelical Churches of the Valleys of Piedmont, in the Year 1571, for mutual assistance in Times of Trouble and Persecution.

1. *We promise by an oath to persist without fail in that ancient union that has been continued from father to son among the faithful of the Evangelical Churches of the Valleys until our own times; and not to depart from it under any condition whatsoever, according to the following conditions and promises:*

2. *To all continue in the profession of the true Christian Reformed Religion, which we have embraced to this day. This religion consists of believing in and worshipping the only true God, and the only head of the Church and mediator between God and man, Jesus Christ. It also consists of the only rule for believing and living well, which is contained in the canonical books of the Old and New Testament, together with the two sacraments instituted by our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, namely, Baptism and the Lord's Supper. We promise, according to the Word, to yield obedience to all external <note>original: "exteriour"</note> order and discipline already established and previously observed among us, rejecting all heresies and false doctrines which are contrary to this Word of God contained in the books of the Old and New Testament.*

3. *Also <note>original: "Item"</note>, we promise to be faithful and obedient to His Serene <note>original: "S."</note> Highness and to those magistrates who shall be appointed by him to govern and rule over us, in everything that either human or divine laws shall require of us, according to the Word of God.*

4. *Also <note>original: "Item"</note>, because there are always some who—contrary to the agreements <term>capitulations</term> and concessions granted to them by the mercy of His Highness through the mediation of the Duchess—endeavor to disturb the peace of their churches and their members, and to violate their concessions, we all promise to use our utmost power and influence on all occasions as judged necessary to maintain all the said churches in general, and each member in particular, in the enjoyment of these concessions. This will be done by constantly appealing to His Highness for as long as is thought necessary, as well as by all other lawful ways and means justifiable by the Word of God in such circumstances. All the churches in general shall undertake the lawful protection and defense (so far as it concerns them) of each church, and every individual person and member of the same, who shall be harassed <note>original: "molested"</note> for the cause of religion, by contributing their advice, goods, and their very persons if there be a need.*

5. *Also <note>original: "Item"</note>, that just as in those requests made regarding matters of religion and related issues, or requests that may be made by the churches in general, all the said churches shall answer unanimously and give consent as if with one voice. Furthermore, if any specific church happens to be harassed <note>original: "molested"</note> concerning any matter of religion or their granted rights, no individual church shall undertake to give any answer without taking a sufficient period of time to communicate with all the rest of the churches and members of this union. This is to ensure they take counsel concerning their common interest, and to answer and act by common consent and advice, with all the modesty, candor, and sincerity suitable to good Christians, according to the guidance of a good conscience and for mutual edification.*

6. *Finally, we all and every one of us voluntarily submit—should anyone fail to keep any of these terms (which God forbid) against the declaration of this union—to censure, or even correction and ecclesiastical discipline. Such a person shall be accounted by the rest of the body of the union as a <term>schismatic</term> <note>Someone who promotes division or separation within the church</note> and a perjured person, if the fault requires such a severe punishment, and this shall be without exception of persons. And so we all promise, with our hands lifted up to Almighty God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.*

->Made and ratified the 11th day of November, 1571.<-

### An Extract of a League or Agreement made between the Evangelical Churches of the Valleys of Piedmont, in the Year 1571, for the mutual assistance of each other in Times of Trouble and Persecution.

*1. We promise by an oath to persist without fail <note>original: "inviolably"</note> in that ancient union which has been continued from father to son among the faithful of the Evangelical Churches of the Valleys until our time. We will not depart from it under any condition whatsoever, according to the following conditions and promises.*

This religion consists of believing in and worshipping the only one true God, and the only one Head of the Church and Mediator between God and man, Jesus Christ. It also follows the only rule for belief and living well, which is contained in the canonical books of the Old and New Testaments, along with the two sacraments instituted by our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ: namely, Baptism and the Lord’s Supper. We promise, according to the Word of God, to obey all external order and discipline already established and previously observed among us. We detest all heresies and false doctrines that are contrary to this Word of God contained in the books of the Old and New Testaments.*

*3. Also <note>original: "Item"</note>, we promise to be faithful and obedient to His Serene Highness <note>original: "S. Highness," referring to the Duke of Savoy</note> and to those magistrates he appoints to govern and rule over us, in everything that either human or divine laws require of us, according to the Word of God.*

*4. Also <note>original: "Item"</note>, because there are always some people who—contrary to the agreements <note>original: "Capitulations"</note> and concessions granted to them by the mercy of His Highness through the intervention <note>original: "Intercession"</note> of the Duchess <note>Margaret of France, Duchess of Savoy, who often advocated for the Waldensians</note>—try to disturb the peace of these churches and their members and violate their rights, we all promise to use our utmost power and influence whenever necessary. We will do this to maintain all the said churches in general, and each member in particular, in the enjoyment of these concessions. This includes making constant appeals to His Highness for as long as necessary, as well as using all other lawful ways and means justified by the Word of God. All the churches together shall undertake the lawful protection and defense (so far as it concerns them) of every church and every individual member who is harassed <note>original: "molested"</note> for the cause of religion, by contributing their advice, property, and personal service if the need arises.*

*...among one another, and established everyone in their rights, of which they might have been deprived because of those troubles (during which passion affected the patient as much as the disease itself). The subject and expressions of this letter were not only satisfactory to those for whom it interceded, but also to all other faithful people of the Valleys and neighboring areas, because of the great hopes they had for future peace <note>original: "tranquillity"</note>. However, this lasted only until their enemies found an opportunity to harass them. They greedily seized this chance upon hearing news of the horrible massacres in *France* <note>This refers to the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre of August 1572, where thousands of French Protestants (Huguenots) were killed.</note>. *Castrocaro* <note>The Governor of the Valleys</note> then so threatened the poor Protestants under his jurisdiction that they retreated with their families and belongings to the tops of the neighboring mountains and all other places where they hoped to be most secure. 

But the Duke of *Savoy*, appearing not to approve at all of the cruelties committed against the Protestants in *France*, sent word to those subjects who had fled, commanding them to return to their houses and homes. He gave his word that they would suffer no harm or incur the least danger by doing so. Indeed, their sufferings were not very great from that time forward, as long as the Duchess was alive (whom all historians have recommended to posterity as one of the most prudent, moderate, and charitable princesses of her age). She was always the sanctuary and refuge for those poor Evangelical churches whenever they found themselves oppressed by their adversaries.

After the death of this Princess (which happened on the nineteenth of *October*, 1574), the Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> party came forth like lions out of their dens and were not lacking in their efforts to devour and destroy—

...[to de]stroy the poor people upon all occasions, but the goodness of God was so great toward them that they constantly found very influential friends to stand in the gap <note>original: "stand in the Gap"; a biblical idiom (Ezekiel 22:30) meaning to advocate for or defend the vulnerable.</note> and to incline the heart of the Duke who then reigned toward much gentleness and moderation. However, after the death of Philibert Emmanuel, which happened on August 30, 1580, his son Charles Emmanuel invaded the Marquisate of Saluzzo <note>original: "Salusses"</note>. In response, Monsieur de Lesdiguières <note>original: "l'Esdiguieres"</note> seized the Valleys of Piedmont as a retaliatory measure. The French army had no sooner gone home than a great rumor spread throughout the Valleys that the Duke was resolved to take this opportunity to wipe out all the Protestant churches because they had taken an oath of loyalty to the King of France. This rumor was not entirely without basis, for the plan was actually proposed in the Duke’s Council. But it pleased God to order affairs so that the leading men among them did not approve of the business at all; indeed, the Duke himself extremely disliked it. After he had retaken Mirabouc <note>original: "Mirebouc"</note>, he greatly revived the spirits of the representatives of the Protestants of Luserna <note>original: "Lucerna"</note>, who met him at Villar <note>original: "Villaro"</note> specifically to assure His Highness of their loyalty and fidelity and to beg for the continuation of his grace and favor. In the presence of a great number of lords and courtiers, he spoke the following terms:

> "Be but faithful to me, and I shall be sure to be a good Prince, and even a father to you. As for the liberty of your consciences and the exercise of your religion, I shall be so far from introducing any changes against those liberties in which you have lived until this present, that if anyone offers to molest you, have your recourse to me, and I shall effectively relieve and protect you."

These words, being spoken in the presence of so many influential persons and in such an obliging manner, were exceedingly advantageous to the interests of the poor people. They served not only for the present but also for some time after, often serving to counterbalance the threats of their fiercest enemies. However, the memory of this promise did not last forever. There were those among the Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> party who thought it an unpardonable sin to allow them even one year’s respite; on the contrary, they believed it a significant service to disturb and harass them, sometimes by secret strategies and other times by open force and violence.

This was the condition of these poor people from the year 1595 to the year 1602. At that time, all the masters of families in the Valley of Luserna who professed the Protestant religion were summoned to appear before the Lord Count Charles of Luserna, Governor Ponte, Archbishop Broglia, and several others. They were commanded in the Duke’s name either to go to Mass or to leave Luserna and abandon all their legal claims <term>pretensions: legal claims to property or status</term> there, without the slightest hope in the world of ever obtaining leave to return. They were likewise told (in case of disobedience to the said order) to prepare themselves for unavoidable mischiefs and calamities. These threats were pressed so hard that they caused many of the poor creatures to submit to (at least) a seeming change of their religion, though many others of them instead chose...

<summary>Following the death of Duke Philibert Emmanuel, the Protestant Waldensians were initially reassured of their safety by his successor, Charles Emmanuel, despite political tensions with France. However, by 1602, local Catholic authorities and the Archbishop of Turin intensified their persecution, forcing families in the Valley of Luserna to choose between their faith and their homes.</summary>

# Of the Persecutions of the Evangelical Churches Book II.

The faith took deeper root by being thus shaken. From *Luserna* <note>original: "Lucerna"; a key town in the Waldensian Valleys</note>, the lords mentioned above soon after moved their seat to *Bibiana* <note>original: "Bubiana"</note>, where they found the Reformed <note>The "Reformed" refers to the Protestant Waldensian community</note> so firm in their principles that they were not able to move them a hair's breadth. Therefore, they caused the leaders of the community to be summoned to appear at *Turin* before His Highness, thinking that the Duke's presence might prevail upon them better than all their threatening speeches. 

Those who were thus summoned were *Mr. Valentine* and *Matthew Boule* his brother, along with one *Pietro Meresc* and *Samuel Falc*. They were brought in separately, one after another, before His Highness. The first was *Mr. Valentine*, to whom the Duke spoke in this manner: 

> *That his desire was to see all his subjects profess the same religion as he did; and knowing also how much Valentine was able to contribute to that goal because of his great reputation among those of his party, he had sent for him to exhort him to embrace the Catholic and Apostolic Roman Religion, which he (who was his Prince) followed. Afterwards, he expected Valentine to lead his Protestant neighbors by his exhortations and example to do the same. In doing so, besides the spiritual profit he would reap, he would also receive such rewards that he would realize he had done his Prince no small or insignificant service.* 

To this, *Mr. Valentine* answered: 

> *That he entreated His Highness to be assured that, next to the service of God, he had no greater desire than to obey and please His Highness. He would willingly employ and risk his person and his goods in the Duke's service (according to his duty) whenever there was an occasion. But as for his religion, which he knew to be true and established by the Word of God himself, he could not abandon it without disobeying God and wounding his conscience in such a way that he could never enjoy any comfort in his soul afterward. Therefore, he humbly entreated His Highness to be satisfied with such things as he could do with a good conscience, and to leave him in the liberty of his religion, which he valued above his own life.* 

Whereupon the Duke replied: 

> *That he also was careful for his own soul, and that he was likewise persuaded that his religion was the true religion; otherwise, he would neither follow it nor induce any other to embrace it. And withall, he added this: that he would indeed show those who embraced it that they had greatly pleased him by doing so, but he would, nonetheless, force the conscience of no man.*

Thereupon, the Duke gave him leave to depart. However, Valentine was not allowed to speak or have any conversation with the other three men, lest he should spoil the plan. Furthermore, to better disguise the business, a rumor was spread that the said *Valentine Boule* had promised to turn Papist <note>A derogatory term for a Roman Catholic, referring to loyalty to the Pope</note>, which was completely untrue.

During the reign of Emperor *Charles* <note>referring to Duke Charles Emmanuel I of Savoy</note>, not a single year passed in which the monks did not attempt, both secretly and openly, to undermine the Protestant religion in the Valleys. And although the said Prince, together with his son *Victor Amadeus* <note>original: "Victor Amedeo"</note>, always gave smooth and promising words to the deputies of the Valleys—assuring them that they would be maintained in their ancient privileges and concessions—the churchmen, being urged on by the Pope, never gave them rest. Instead, they employed all along both force <meta>and</meta>

# CHAPTER II.

## A Description of the Marquisate of Saluzzo, with its several Troubles and Persecutions.

What and how great the miseries of the poor Protestants have been—not only in the Valleys of Piedmont properly so called, but also in all the dominions of the Duke of Savoy where there were any of that profession—we need look no further for a lively proof than in the neighboring country called the Marquisate of Saluzzo <note>original: "Saluces"; a historical region now part of the Italian province of Cuneo</note>. As soon as they were under the Duke's jurisdiction, they had nothing but the "bread of sorrow" given them to eat and the "waters of affliction" to drink <note>These are biblical metaphors for extreme suffering and hardship, found in Psalm 127:2 and Isaiah 30:20</note>. It is true that they were harassed several times while under the King of France, which lasted until the year 1588, but never in the same manner as afterward. They found by woeful experience that the first [the French] only chastised them with whips, but the last [the Savoyards] chastised them with scorpions <note>A reference to 1 Kings 12:11, implying that the new rulers were far more cruel than the old ones</note>.

<margin>The Situation of the Marquisate of Saluzzo.</margin>
The Marquisate of Saluzzo is on the south side of the Valleys of Piedmont, containing several cities, significant valleys, and plains that are extremely fertile in all sorts of fruits. Its most northern <margin>The Valley of Po.</margin> valley is the Valley of the Po—so called because the famous River Po has its rise and source there. Only a single mountain separates it from the Valley of Lucerna on the north side. In this Valley of the Po were <margin>The Churches of Pravillelm, Biolets, and Bietone.</margin> those ancient churches of the Waldenses <note>original: "Waldenfes"</note>, namely Pravillelm, Biolets, and Bietone, who retained the purity of the Christian religion there for several hundreds of years and lived in great union and communion with their neighboring churches of the same profession. The truth is, the Reformed religion was received in various parts of this Marquisate of Saluzzo as soon as it was published and tolerated <margin>The Church of Dronier.</margin> in other countries. For example, in the year 1561, the church of Dronier (which was always one of the most flourishing) understood that the public exercise of the Reformed religion was permitted in France by an Edict of January <note>The Edict of Saint-Germain (1562), which provided limited tolerance to French Protestants (Huguenots)</note>. They obtained letters from the King’s Council for Sieur Louis of Birague, Governor of that country in the absence of the Duke of Nevers, by which he was ordered to provide the petitioners a convenient place for the public exercise of their religion. But not long after, their adversaries prevailed so far through their persistence that the said letters were revoked. Whereupon they sent...

# Chapter II (Continued): With its several persecutions.

<margin>
Lord <note>original: "Sieur"</note> Francois Galatée.
</margin>
They sent Lord Francois Galatée, one of their ministers, as a deputy to **France**, along with several others, to recover (if possible) their former privileges. However, this journey took place during the first religious wars in **France**. Although they managed to get the favorable support of various people of high rank and status, all they were able to obtain were empty promises. In the meantime, they received many letters of encouragement and comfort from many of the leading ministers of the French churches—including those of **Grenoble** and **Lyon**, specifically **Mr. Viret** of **Nîmes** and others—who tried by all means to persuade them to have patience and to persevere in the truth they had embraced. The Lord enabled them to do this, despite all the malice and trickery of their adversaries, who repeatedly issued the same old decrees <note>original: "Edicts"</note> against them. Thus, their churches were sustained and upheld; proper order was established for the preaching of the Word, the administration of the Sacraments, the exercise of church discipline, and other sacred duties. The only thing they lacked in several places was the freedom to hold general assemblies and public sermons.

<margin>
Synods held at Pravillelm and at Dronero in 1567. Lord Galatée's assignment. Mr. Second’s assignment. Mr. Fr. Truchi’s assignment. Andrew Lancianois's assignment. Peter Gelido, Lord Jacques Iloard, and Mr. Bertrand's various assignments.
</margin>
For the better safety and security of their ministers in the most dangerous areas, one pastor was given charge of the faithful in several cities and communities. This made their residence and their religious exercises less visible to their enemies. This practice is also shown in the records of their Synods <note>A synod is a council or assembly of church officials</note>, which they held at **Pravillelm** on June 2, 1567, and at **Dronero** <note>original: "Dronier"</note> in the palace of the Lords of **Montauraux** on October 14 of that same year. The aforementioned **Lord Galatée** was the pastor of the faithful in **Saluzzo**, **Savigliano**, **Carmagnola**, **Levaldigi**, and **Villafalletto**. **Mr. Second Masseran** looked after those in **Verzuolo**, **Alpease**, and **Costigliole**. **Mr. Francois Truchi** was the pastor of the church in **Dronero**. **Andrew Lancianois** served those in **San Damiano**, **Pagno** <note>original: "Palliar"</note>, and **Cartignano**. **Peter Gelido** served **Acceglio** <note>original: "Aceil"</note>. **Lord Jacques Iloard** served **San Michele**, **Prazzo**, and **Canosio** <note>original: "Chanues"</note>. **Lord Francis Soulf** served **Pravillelm**. **Mr. Bertrand Jordan** served **Biolè** and **Bietoné**, and **N.N.** <note>A Latin abbreviation used when a specific name is unknown</note> was the pastor of the churches of **Demonte** and **Festiona**.

The progress of the Gospel at Dronero and other places. The Church of Acceglio.

The church of **Acceglio**, located at the highest point of the **Maira Valley** <note>original: "Val de Mairi"</note>, was exceptionally well-populated and enjoyed more liberty than the others because of its remote location. Nevertheless, Satan—the enemy of the church and the kingdom of **Jesus**—seeing such growth and increase of the Reformed religion in those places, did not stop using all his force and trickery to hinder it. Whenever the church had even the slightest bit of peace, he would set himself to writing strange things and crying out against the abuses of Catholicism <note>original: "Popery"</note>. # The Marquisate of Saluces described Book II.

<margin>
The Lord of Valgrane, a supporter of Baronius.

...persuade and draw others to do the same, by which means he gained a multitude of followers. Among others was a certain Lord of **Valgrane** and **Cervignale**, called **Maximilian de Saluces**, who lent his name to *Baronius* to add more prestige <note>original: "lustre"</note> to his writings against the ministers. He reproached them and threw it in their teeth <note>An idiom meaning to insult or mock someone by reminding them of a past failure</note> that because they would not allow any deception <note>original: "dissimulation"</note> among their disciples, they thereby exposed them to great hardships. To prove his point, he cited the destruction <note>original: "dissipation"</note> of the neighboring church of **Caraglio** <note>original: "Caraill"</note>. This Lord had some learning and knowledge of the truth; however, to avoid "bearing the cross" <note>A biblical metaphor for enduring suffering or persecution for the sake of one's faith</note>, he thought it convenient (along with *Baronius*) to act the hypocrite and condemn those who in any way opposed the Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note>. However, **Lord Gelido**, the minister of **Acceglio** <note>original: "Aceil"</note>, opposed them both very learnedly and in strong terms through several letters that he wrote to them. **Lord Truchi**, the minister of the church of **Dronero** <note>original: "Dronier"</note>, did the same, together with other pastors from neighboring places. They demonstrated, by the testimony of the Holy Scriptures and by the doctrine and practice of the early Church <note>original: "Primitive Church"</note>, that they had done only what every faithful soul ought to do, and that consequently the opinion of *Baronius* and his disciples was very harmful <note>original: "pernicious"</note> to the Church in times of persecution.

<margin>
The second sort of instruments the Devil used to hinder the progress of the Gospel in the Marquisate of Saluces.
</margin>
<margin>
Their designs were chiefly against the ministry.
</margin>

The other instruments that the great enemy of souls used in those days to hinder the progress of the Church of *Christ* in this place were the *Roman Clergy*, along with their angry and fervent converts <note>original: "cholerick and passionate Proselytes"</note>. These people would have gladly done to these people—if it had been in their power—what their "partners in crime" <note>original: "Brethren in iniquity"</note> had done to their neighbors in the territories of the Duke of **Savoy**. That is to say, they wished to banish, imprison, and put the Protestants to death, and confiscate their goods. Because the *King* had, by his Edicts, guaranteed his subjects in **Saluzzo** who professed the *Reformed Religion* a peaceful life without being molested for their conscience or religion, or questioned for anything they did in their private houses (provided they abstained from the public exercise of their religion), the ministers had opportunities to assemble in small groups, perform baptisms and marriages, comfort the sick, and instruct individuals privately. This was the reason why their adversaries directed their plots chiefly against the ministers; they thought that if they could find a way to eliminate <note>original: "extirpate"</note> them, they could easily overcome the uneducated people, especially when there would be no one left to encourage or instruct them.

<margin>
Their edict of October 19, 1567.
</margin>

Accordingly, they caused an Edict to be published on October 19, 1567, in the name of the **Duke of Nevers**, Lieutenant General of the King on this side of the mountains <note>Referring to the Italian side of the Alps</note>. By this decree, everyone of the Reformed religion living or staying within his jurisdiction who was not a native-born subject of the King was commanded to depart with their families within three days of the publication of the Edict. They were never to return to live, pass through, or stay there without a special safe-conduct, upon penalty of death <note>original: "pain of life"</note> and the confiscation of their goods.

## Chapter II. with its several Persecutions.

But now, since the greatest part of the above-named ministers were not natural-born subjects of the **King**, and consequently it was necessary that they should either leave the **Marquisate** <note>The territory of Saluzzo</note> according to the **Edict** <note>official decree</note>, obtain a safe conduct, or else forfeit the penalty specified above, they found themselves in an unhappy **legal predicament** <note>original: "premunire," a legal trap or dilemma where one is caught between conflicting laws</note>. For on the one hand, they could by no means obtain a safe conduct because of their official positions, and on the other hand, they felt bound in conscience not to abandon their people and congregations. Therefore, while striving to remain in their positions, two of them were imprisoned: **Mr. Francois Truchi**, a native of **Cental**, and **Mr. Francois Soulf**, a native of **Cuni**. They were held in prison at **Saluzzo** <note>original: "Salutres"</note> for four years, four months, and some odd days. The poor people were unable by any means to secure their release, despite their continual appeals to **Lord Ludovic de Birague**, their governor, and others who had undertaken the management of these affairs. However, the Lord always manifested his fatherly care toward these faithful servants, not permitting their enemies to take the life of any of them (a thing which was much pressed for by their passionate and biased enemies). Indeed, little by little, a more spacious and convenient prison was obtained for them than the one in which they were first confined.

<margin>
Mr. Francis Truchi and Mr. Fr. Soulf imprisoned four years and four months, and odd days.
</margin>

At length, to procure their full and absolute release <note>original: "deliverance"</note>, the churches of the Marquisate sent their petitions to the **King** by the hands of the above-named minister **Galatée**, with another person to accompany him. They set out on July 27, 1571, and went as far as **La Rochelle** <note>original: "Rochel"</note> to beg for the intercession of the **Queen of Navarre** <note>Jeanne d'Albret, a key leader of the French Huguenots</note>, as well as to entreat the assistance of various others in several places. Moreover, the great patrons of the Reformed religion argued their cause before the King. In the end, they obtained letters signed by his own hand and the hands of his secretaries, **Neufville** and **Lomenie**, by which the prisoners' release <note>original: "enlargement"</note> was granted on October 14, 1571. 

But the Chancellor **René Birago**, cousin to the Governor of the Marquisate, made such difficulty in signing the letters that they were forced to wait several months before they could have them processed <note>original: "expedition"</note>. The Chancellor always alleged as a pretext that before the business could be signed, it was necessary to have a verbal conference with the King, who had then made a journey into **Brittany** <note>original: "Bretagne"</note>. This was despite the fact that the **Admiral** <note>Gaspard de Coligny, the primary military leader of the French Protestants</note> never ceased petitioning and continually assisting the said **Mr. Galatée** through his secretary or other members of his household. Also, perceiving that Galatée was forced to travel back and forth on foot, and so spend and exhaust himself, the Admiral gave him 50 Francs to support himself on his journeys.

At length, the **King** having returned from Brittany, the Chancellor spoke with him and afterwards signed the said letters. He insisted on sending them himself to the Marquisate, to his cousin **Birague**, who by virtue of those letters finally caused the prisoners to be released and set free.

A little after, **Mr. Galatée** arrived, being overjoyed as much for the

# Chapter II. With its several Persecutions.

<margin>Mr. Francis Truchi and Mr. Fr. Soulf were imprisoned for four years, four months, and some odd days.</margin>

But now, because most of the ministers named above were not native subjects of the **King**, it was necessary for them to either leave the **Marquisate** <note>The Marquisate of Saluzzo, an Alpine territory then under French control.</note> according to the **Edict**, obtain a safe-conduct, or else pay the penalty mentioned above. They found themselves in an unhappy legal trap <term>præmunire</term> <note>original: "præmunire"; a legal term referring to a situation where one is caught between conflicting laws or jurisdictions</note>. On one hand, they could not obtain a safe-conduct because of their office; on the other hand, they felt bound in conscience not to abandon their people and congregations. Therefore, while striving to remain in their positions, two of them were imprisoned: **Mr. François Truchi**, a native of **Centallo** <note>original: "Cental"</note>, and **Mr. François Soulf**, a native of **Cuneo** <note>original: "Cuni"</note>. They were held in prison at **Saluzzo** <note>original: "Salutres"</note> for four years, four months, and some odd days. The poor people were unable to secure their release by any means, despite their constant appeals to **Mr. Ludovico de Birague**, their Governor, and others who managed these affairs. However, the Lord always showed his fatherly care toward these faithful servants, not allowing their enemies to take the life of any of them (a course of action which was strongly urged by their bitter and committed enemies!). Indeed, bit by bit, a larger and more comfortable prison was obtained for them than the one where they were first confined.

Finally, to secure their full and absolute release, the churches of the Marquisate sent their petitions to the King by the hand of the minister **Galatée**, who was accompanied by another representative. They set out on July 27, 1571, and went as far as **La Rochelle** <note>original: "Rochel"</note> to seek the help of the **Queen of Navarre** <note>Jeanne d'Albret, a key leader of the French Huguenots.</note>, and to ask for the assistance of various others in several places. Moreover, the great patrons of the **Reformed Religion** argued their case before the King. In the end, they obtained letters signed by the King's own hand and by his secretaries **Neufville** and **Lomenie**, which granted the prisoners their release on October 14, 1571. But the Chancellor **René Birago**, cousin to the Governor of the Marquisate, made such difficulties in signing the papers that they were forced to wait several months before the documents were processed. The Chancellor always used the excuse that before the matter could be signed, it was necessary to have a personal meeting with the King, who had then gone on a journey to **Brittany** <note>original: "Bretagne"</note>. This delay occurred even though the **Admiral** <note>Likely Admiral Gaspard de Coligny, a prominent Protestant leader.</note> never stopped petitioning and assisting Mr. Galatée through his secretary or other members of his staff. Also, seeing that Galatée was forced to travel everywhere on foot and was thus exhausting himself, the Admiral gave him 50 Franks to pay for transportation and supplies on his journeys.

Finally, when the King returned from Brittany, the Chancellor spoke with him and afterward signed the letters. He insisted on sending them himself to the Marquisate to his cousin **Birague**, who, by the authority of those letters, finally caused the prisoners to be released and set free.

### The Marquisate of Saluzzo Described: Book II.

<margin>The Lord of Valgrana, a supporter of Baronius.</margin>
[But] persuade and draw others to do the same, by which means he had a multitude of followers. Among others, there was a certain Lord of **Valgrana** and **Cervignale** called **Maximilian of Saluzzo**, who lent his name to **Baronius** to add more prestige to his writings against the ministers. He rebuked them and threw it in their faces <note>original: "casting in their teeth"</note> that because they would not allow any outward conformity <note>original: "dissimulation"</note> among their disciples, they thereby exposed them to great hardships. To support this, he cited the destruction <note>original: "dissipation"</note> of the neighboring Church of **Caraglio** <note>original: "Caraill"</note>. 

This Lord had some level of learning and knowledge of the truth, but to avoid **carrying the Cross** <note>a common metaphor for suffering or facing persecution for one’s faith</note>, he thought it convenient (along with **Baronius**) to act the hypocrite and condemn those who in any way opposed the Papists. However, **Mr.** <note>original: "Sieur"</note> **Gelido**, the Minister of **Acceglio** <note>original: "Aceil"</note>, opposed them both very learnedly and in vivid terms through several letters that he wrote to them. Likewise, **Mr. Truchi**, Minister of the Church of **Dronero** <note>original: "Dronier"</note>, along with other pastors from neighboring areas, did the same. They demonstrated by the testimony of Holy Scripture, and by the doctrine and practice of the Early Church, that they were doing exactly what they ought to do, and that every faithful soul was required to do the same. Consequently, they argued that the opinion of **Baronius** and his disciples was very harmful to the Church in times of persecution.

<margin>The second type of instrument the Devil used to hinder the progress of the Gospel in the Marquisate of Saluzzo.</margin>
The other instruments which that arch-enemy of souls <note>Satan</note> used in those days to hinder the progress of the Church of **Christ** in this place were the **Roman** clergy, along with their angry and passionate converts. These people would have gladly done to these inhabitants (if it had been in their power) what their **partners in crime** <note>original: "Brethren in iniquity"</note> had done to their neighbors in the territories of the **Duke of Savoy**—that is to say, banish, imprison, or execute them and seize the property of the Protestants. 

Because the **King**, through his Edicts, had guaranteed a peaceful residence to those subjects in **Saluzzo** who followed the **Reformed** religion, they were not to be harassed for their conscience or religion, nor questioned for anything they did in their private houses (provided they did not practice their religion publicly). 

<margin>Their designs were mainly against the ministry.</margin>
Because of this, the ministers had opportunities to assemble in small groups, perform baptisms and marriages, comfort the sick, and instruct individuals privately. This was why their adversaries directed their plots mainly against the ministers. They believed that if they could find a way to root them out <note>original: "extirpate"</note>, they could easily overcome the uneducated people, especially when there would be no one left to encourage or instruct them.

<margin>Their edict of October 19, 1567.</margin>
Accordingly, they arranged for an Edict to be published on October 19, 1567, in the name of the **Duke of Nevers**, the **King’s** Lieutenant General on this side of the mountains. This edict ordered all those of the [Reformed] religion living or staying within his jurisdiction who were not the King’s native-born subjects to depart with their families within three days of the edict's publication. They were never to return there to live, pass through, or otherwise stay without a special safe-conduct, under penalty of death and seizure of their property.

### Chapter II. With its several Persecutions.

<margin>Mr. Francis Truchi and Mr. Francois Soulf imprisoned four years, four months, and several days.</margin>

But now, because the majority of the ministers named above were not natural-born subjects of the King, it was necessary for them to either leave the Marquisate according to the Edict, obtain a safe-conduct, or else face the penalties mentioned previously. They found themselves in a difficult **legal trap** <note>original: "premunire"; a legal term referring to a difficult situation or a conflict of authority</note>. On one hand, they could not obtain a safe-conduct because of their official positions as ministers; on the other hand, they felt bound in conscience not to abandon their people and congregations. 

While striving to remain in their positions, two of them were imprisoned: **Mr.** <note>original: "Sieur"; a title of respect</note> **Francois Truchi**, a native of **Centallo** <note>original: "Cental"</note>, and **Mr. Francois Soulf**, a native of **Cuneo** <note>original: "Cuni"</note>. They were held in prison at **Saluzzo** <note>original: "Saluces"</note> for four years, four months, and a few odd days. The poor people of their congregations were unable to secure their release by any means, despite their constant appeals to **Mr. Ludovico de Birague**, their Governor, and others who were managing these affairs. However, the Lord always showed his fatherly care toward these faithful servants by not permitting their enemies to take their lives (a course of action strongly urged by their passionate and prejudiced enemies!). Indeed, bit by bit, a more spacious and convenient prison was obtained for them than the one where they were first confined.

At length, to secure their full and absolute release, the Churches of the **Marquisate** sent their petitions to the **King** by the hand of the minister **Galatée**, accompanied by another man. They set out on July 27, 1571, and traveled as far as **La Rochelle** <note>original: "Rochel"</note> to beg for the intervention of the **Queen of Navarre** <note>Jeanne d'Albret, a prominent leader of the French Huguenots</note>, as well as to seek the assistance of various others in several places. Furthermore, the great patrons of the Reformed Religion argued their case before the King. 

In the end, they obtained letters signed by the King’s own hand and the hands of his secretaries **Neufville** and **Lomenie**, which granted the prisoners their release on October 14, 1571. However, the Chancellor **René Birago**—cousin to the Governor of the Marquisate—made such difficulties about signing the documents that they were forced to wait several months before they could complete the process. The Chancellor repeatedly used the excuse that before the business could be signed, it was necessary to have a verbal conference with the King, who had then gone on a journey into **Brittany** <note>original: "Bretagne"</note>. This delay occurred even though the **Admiral** <note>likely Admiral Gaspard de Coligny</note> never stopped advocating for them and continually assisted Mr. Galatée through his secretary or other members of his household. Also, seeing that Galatée was forced to travel everywhere on foot and was exhausting himself, the Admiral gave him 50 Franks to help him with his travels.

Finally, after the King returned from Brittany, the Chancellor spoke with him and afterward signed the letters. He insisted on sending them himself to the Marquisate to his cousin, Governor Birague, who, by virtue of those letters, finally caused the prisoners to be released and set free.

A short time later, Mr. Galatée arrived, filled with joy, both for the...

The prosperous success and outcome of his negotiations and voyage (though it was otherwise very long and tedious), as well as the great hopes he had for a profound peace, were based on the King's smooth words and kind treatment, and on the alliance formed by the marriage of his sister to the King of **Navarre**. Therefore, they judged that it would be enough to simply secure the people listed and postpone the execution for a while. In the meantime, they would inform the King that these were honorable people, faithful to His Majesty, who lived peaceably with their neighbors and were (except for their religion) entirely beyond reproach. The Churches of the Marquisate, having received this letter, returned an answer to the Duke in a lengthy document in the form of a formal request, which contained two main points:

In the first point, they expressed their gratitude to His Highness because he had, until then, allowed them to practice their religion in peace. He had permitted this in the same manner as he found them in the year 1588, when he first took possession of the Marquisate.

In the second place, they most humbly petitioned him to continue providing them with that benefit, as well as his protection. They argued that their religion was founded upon the Holy Scriptures, and that they ordered their lives and conduct <note>original: "conversation"; in the 17th century, this referred to one's general behavior and social dealings</note> according to those scriptures in such a way that no one had any just reason to be offended by them. Furthermore, they pointed out that since even the Jews and other enemies of Christ were permitted to live in peace and enjoy their own religion, they were confident that those who were found to be Christians and faithful to both God and their Prince would not be denied the same privilege.

After this answer was delivered, they were left in peace for a while. During that time, the Duke took a journey to France, which was followed by a war in Savoy. During this period, the churches continued as they had before. However, after the exchange of the Marquisate was finalized, along with the territory of Bresse <note>The Treaty of Lyon (1601), in which the Duke of Savoy traded Bresse and other French-speaking lands to France in exchange for undisputed control of the Marquisate of Saluzzo</note>, the "smooth and soft letters" were replaced by sharp edicts. These edicts expressly commanded everyone of the Reformed religion in the Marquisate:

<margin>A sharp and severe edict against all those of the Marquisate in July 1601.</margin>

That every person must go and declare to their local magistrate, within the following fifteen days, whether or not they would renounce their religion and attend Mass. In the case of those who converted, they were promised not only that they could remain peaceably in their homes, but would also be favored in many other ways. But if, on the other hand, they were resolved to persist in their religion, they were ordered to withdraw and depart from His Highness's dominions within two months of the publication of this edict, and never to return without express permission. This was commanded upon pain of death and the confiscation of all their property. However, they were permitted to transport their goods as they saw fit within that two-month period, provided they did not violate the terms of their obedience.

When this unexpected edict was published throughout the Marquisate at the end of July 1601, it greatly troubled those of the Reformed faith...
