## Chapter II, with its several persecutions.

The members of the Reformed Religion <note>Protestantism, specifically the Calvinist tradition practiced by the Waldensians and Huguenots.</note> in that country immediately sent deputies to His Highness <note>Charles Emmanuel I, Duke of Savoy.</note> to obtain either a revocation (or at least a moderation) of the Edict. They were given so much hope by various persons of quality that many of the poor people, resting upon this "broken reed" <note>An unreliable support; a biblical reference to Isaiah 36:6.</note>, let a great part of the set deadline pass without putting their affairs in order for their departure. Because of this, they were even more surprised and amazed when they learned, not many days before the time expired, that all hope of a remedy was now completely gone. However, the majority of them prepared for their departure—some entrusting their goods to relatives and friends who remained in the country, and others leaving all they had behind at random, except for what they could carry with them to serve their immediate needs.

But during these two months, those who were resolved to depart (in case there was no other remedy) were perpetually pressured by their friends and relatives with every imaginable persuasion and motive to divert them, if possible, from their resolution. This was especially true when they appeared before the magistrate to submit their answer in writing. For this purpose, they were obliged to do so in a certain pew in public view, where the magistrates had either monks or other Roman Catholic clergy <note>original: "Roman Ecclesiasticks"</note> and prominent men who did not stop proposing and urging everything they could possibly imagine to shake the faith and constancy of these poor people.

Among others, a certain Capuchin friar named Philip Ribot—who shortly before had exercised his tactics in the same manner in the Valley of Perosa—was now employed in the Marquisate and was very diligent. He ran from place to place to make as many converts <note>original: "Proselytes"</note> as he possibly could, using every imaginable subtlety, especially among those whom old age, the "weakness of their sex" <note>A common 17th-century trope used to describe women as more spiritually or intellectually vulnerable.</note>, or poverty might make more easily influenced. Besides all this, they caused them to be brought before the magistrate one by one so that the steadfastness of some might not encourage others. Indeed, husbands were hardly permitted to speak for their wives or children, and they so thoroughly interrogated the young and vulnerable <note>original: "sift the tender ones"; "sifting" is a biblical term for rigorous testing or interrogation.</note> that it was very hard to escape without "making shipwreck" of their faith and religion. Furthermore, to accomplish their designs, they prohibited everyone, under pain of death, from in any way discouraging anyone from converting <note>original: "revolting"; in this context, it refers to turning away from the Reformed faith to the Roman Catholic Church.</note>.

However, it pleased the Lord to strengthen those people so much that a great number of them departed unshaken, going forth as Providence guided them, *not knowing where they were going*. Some steered their course beyond the Alps to France, Geneva, and other places. Others retired into the Valleys of Piedmont, where the freedom of the Reformed Religion was still continued and where they remained without trouble, despite the Edict stating that they should depart from the territories of His Highness.

Now, in the beginning of this general persecution, their adversaries...

# The Marquisate of Saluces described, Book II.

[Authori]ties fearing some bold and resolute union of these poor persecuted people, and wanting to prevent any uprising or disturbance, spread word among the churches of the mountains that—though the terms of the Edict were general—the actual intention was only to remove all those who lived in the lower plains, the great villages, and other public places. They were told that all those who lived among the mountains could be assured of living in peace and quiet.

<margin>Those of the church of Pravillelm persecuted and banished.</margin>
This deceptive <note>original: "Cautelous"</note> dealing caused a situation where, at first, there was not such a universal union of those of the Reformed Religion in all the areas destined for slaughter as they could have desired. However, in the end, the discovery of this fraud caused a closer union among them. For the truth is, at last they spared those in the mountains no more than those on the plains, except that they made no initial show of investigation into the Church of *Pravillelm* <note>Pravilelmo, a historic Waldensian community in the upper Po Valley.</note> and the surrounding areas. When the people of those places saw this, and trusting in the long history of their land ownership <note>original: "Ancientness of their possessions"</note>, they never troubled themselves to make any declaration before the magistrate or to prepare for their departure, acting as if the Edict did not concern them at all. Indeed, they were not disturbed at all until all the rest who persevered in their religion had departed from the province and were scattered abroad in various places. 

At length, they were seriously informed that because they had not yielded obedience to the Edict, they had become liable <note>original: "obnoxious"</note> to the punishments specified within it. At this point, some people warned them to look out for themselves, both as a community and as individuals. Consequently, once they had considered their situation, they—as members of the community—begged the Syndics <note>Elected local officials or magistrates representing a municipality.</note> of the said community to intercede for them. They argued that they believed they were not included in the Edict, and therefore they had not disobeyed out of any malicious intention.

These Syndics accordingly (whether seriously or just for show, the Lord knows) made many journeys regarding this business, but they always returned with sad and discouraging messages and orders that the people were forced to follow in the end. One part of them (the men having given orders to the families they left in their houses) retreated into the Western Mountains. Those who were capable of bearing arms—about two hundred in number—retreated with their weapons into the district of Château-Dauphin <note>original: "Chastellenie de Chasteau Dauphin"; a mountain fortress area on the border of France and Savoy.</note>, which was not far away. But those from Dauphiné <note>A province in southeastern France.</note>, and those who were less prepared, retreated into their highest forests.

Now, before their departure, they had informed their Roman Catholic <note>original: "Papists"</note> neighbors that, being forced to retreat by the threats made against them for the sake of their religion and being unable to take their families with them, they entreated the neighbors to look after them. They promised to eventually return either the good or the evil that was done to their relatives, whether by the neighbors themselves or by anything done with their permission. Upon this, the Roman Catholics, either out of fear or for some other reasons, did petition...

### Chapter II: Regarding its various Persecutions

...that in the end, they succeeded so well with their superiors that the others were granted the freedom to return to their ancient homes with a guarantee that they would not be harassed, and they remained there for many years together.

<margin>Sieur Dominique Vigneaux, a famous minister of Villar.</margin>
During this persecution, Sieur <note>A title of respect, similar to "Sir" or "Lord."</note> Dominique Vigneaux—pastor of the church of Villar in the Luserna Valley <note>original: "Val Lucerna"</note> and one of the most venerable and respected figures in the churches of the Valleys at that time—being a man of excellent character, wrote many important letters. These were sent to their poor, persecuted brethren to encourage them to persevere with patience, offering them spirited comfort. He also wrote to several noblemen of high rank to ask them to intercede on the people’s behalf. Specifically, he wrote to Lord De la Mente, Governor of the Marquisate, with whom he shared a personal friendship. To him, he fully explained the justice of the persecuted people’s cause, presenting many significant motives and reasons in an attempt to persuade the Lord to offer them his protection.

## CHAP. III.

### The Cunning Artifices and Wicked Practices Used Both Formerly and Presently to Consume and Destroy the Remainder of the Faithful in the Valleys of Piedmont.

In the preceding chapters, we have seen the enemy of our salvation represented to us as a *roaring lion* <note>A biblical reference to 1 Peter 5:8, describing the devil's predatory nature</note>; in this chapter, he is shown as a *cunning serpent*, subtly intruding himself and secretly wounding the faithful. And indeed, although it is extremely difficult (as the wise man observes <note>A reference to Proverbs 30:19, which mentions "the way of a serpent upon a rock" as something difficult to understand</note>) to find out the *way of a serpent upon a rock*, the poor Evangelical Churches have from time to time had sufficient experience with—and tasted the woeful and bitter fruits of—his deadly malice and hatred. In this, he has not only utilized the wickedness of several private men, but has also found a way to make public authority subservient to his goals, often transforming himself into an *angel of light*.

The instruments he used to carry out his designs upon those poor people were, for the most part, the priests and monks, who continually burdened them with dark slanders to make them appear hateful and abominable in the sight of all men. Indeed, they did not only represent them as heretics, but also as *Infernal Monsters* <note>original: "Monstri Infernali"</note> (this is <term>Prior Rorenco’s</term> <note>Marco Aurelio Rorengo, a 17th-century Catholic official and historian who wrote extensively against the Waldensians</note> own expression in the Italian language)—that is, the most cursed creatures that Hell itself affords.

The treacheries, lies, and deceptions suggested by those who were secretly employed by the Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> clergy to gradually exterminate those poor people are innumerable. Indeed, nothing is more certain than that they had in those days—and at this very day continue to have—several persons on their payroll whose business it is to stir up strife and quarrels among the Protestants and to involve them in lawsuits against one another. When they see them reduced to poverty and despair, they then come and secretly offer to each of them separately all the favors imaginable and an absolute victory over their enemies, provided they will either openly renounce their faith <note>original: "revolt"</note> or remain as spies among their brethren to betray them. To better prepare and incline them toward this by degrees, they assure them that if they employ certain churchmen to recommend their affairs to the judges, they will undoubtedly obtain their desires. But if they cannot persuade either the one or the other to renounce their faith or to betray their

### Chapter III: In the Valleys of Piedmont.

They stir up quarrels within the Protestants' own group, embittering and inflaming their spirits more and more by using their usual "incendiaries"—meaning those who fan the flames of conflict. These are the gentlemen, lawyers, attorneys, and Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> notaries, most of whom receive payments from Rome for this very purpose. These men eventually try to make the parties fight it out, promising help to each side. Their goal is to bring both the people and their estates to ruin under a pretense of friendship. They continue to flatter both sides, using a third person to give them a high opinion of their supposed legal rights and persuading them that if they were to come to a *friendly* agreement (as they are encouraged to do by their ministers), they would do themselves great wrong and injury. 

By this course of action, they often oppose and hinder the good efforts of the ministers and elders, whose only desire is to preserve peace and Christian unity among their brothers. Indeed, these "kindlers of discord" misrepresent and twist the ministers' exhortations—which are taken from the Word of God—doing everything they can to persuade the magistrates and judges themselves that such advice threatens their authority and ruins their legal practice. 

Worst of all, the priests and monks never stop investigating and inserting themselves into all the discontents and divisions that arise at any time between husband and wife, master and servant, or father and child. After incensing them against one another as much as possible, they try to persuade the weaker party to rebel. To put that person in a better position to take revenge, the monks and their associates offer them every imaginable assistance through the authority of the Catholic magistrates. These magistrates are intentionally preferred for public office over the Protestants and given superior power, so that they may control and overrule them as they wish.

The Catholic clergy also know by experience that young men are prone to falling in love, an emotion that usually binds and captivates reason. Through their agents, they frequently propose that these young men marry a Roman Catholic, exaggerating the dowry and other advantages with "dutiful" lies <note>original: "officious lies"—lies told with the intent to be helpful to one's own cause</note>. In this way, they trick many innocent souls, sometimes without the knowledge of their parents and friends, and sometimes by open force against their will. 

When there is someone among the Protestants so wicked and rebellious that they refuse to listen to warnings and advice—forcing the ministers to proceed to more severe church discipline or <term>excommunication</term> <note>Expulsion from the church community and denial of the sacraments</note>—these monks and priests then typically criticize the <term>Consistories</term> <note>The local governing bodies of the Reformed/Protestant church, made up of ministers and elders</note>. They do everything they can to persuade the "young man void of understanding" <note>A biblical reference to Proverbs 7:7</note> to abandon the group by whom he is supposedly being treated so badly. They urge him to embrace the Catholic religion, where he will not only find a safe shelter from those who pursue him for his crimes and offenses, but will also be placed over them in political offices and employment, so that he may have the power to get revenge. This was certainly practiced by the monks in the years 1640, 1641, 1642, and so on, even toward some who were manifestly convinced...

# Practises to destroy the Evangelical Churches Book II.

...convicted of witchcraft, who, having converted <note>original: "revolted"</note> at the persuasion of the monks, had their lives spared and were set at liberty. And because the monks could not deny that those miserable creatures were actually witches—especially in the valleys where they were known by the name of *Maschi* <note>original: "Maschi" - an Italian term for male witches or sorcerers</note>—whenever they were upbraided for supporting such wretches, they answered in a jeering (and, as they thought, witty) manner, "*We know how to unmask them*" <note>original: "Sapiamo dismascarli", meaning they had a device to make witches stop being witches</note>. This was the secret of those men of whom the Prophet Isaiah speaks, saying, *“Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness...”* [Isaiah 5:20]. It is even as Cardinal Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a powerful Jesuit and defender of the Catholic Church</note> boasts that the Pope has the power to make *from sin, no sin* <note>original: "de peccato non peccatum", meaning to declare that which is sin to be no sin</note>. 

Thus, those sorcerers and witches frequently enjoyed the very same exemption from all charges and accusations which is granted by His Royal Highness to all others who convert or change their religion. Not only that, but they have also often been rewarded for their wickedness with presents of money, merchandise, and other things, according to their various abilities and occupations. Where any such apostates were owners of land, they were exempted from all types of taxes so that they might enrich themselves. To this end, the gentlemen and other rich Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note> are accustomed to making counterfeit sales of their farms and tenements to these converts. They send them the legal deeds and rent-rolls, and afterward, they secretly split the profits arising from the tax exemptions and other such payments. 

When the Protestants complained about this—as they had good reason to, since the tax burden fell just as much heavier on their shoulders as it was lightened for the others—His Royal Highness did give them a favorable answer in an edict dated June 30, 1649, but they could never manage to have it actually enforced.

The truth is, of all the ways and means in which public authority (both church and state) has worked together for the last sixty years to root out and utterly ruin the poor Protestant churches in the valleys of Piedmont, there has been none like that of the *Missionaries*. These were established by Pope Clement VIII in the year 1596, as Rorengo mentions in his *Memoirs*, Chapter 29, page 135, and Chapters 30 and 31, etc. Indeed, the monasteries of those "firebrands" <note>original: "Firebrands" - people who passionately stir up conflict</note> (as Rorengo observes on page 142) have always been like citadels in the valleys. Within them have been harbored many legions of evil spirits who have never ceased to plot and contrive mischief through their meddlesome lies, slanders, and false reports. They have filled the ears of the magistrates and princes with these stories. For the most part, the rulers have given more credit to the monks' fake protestations than to the real and better-grounded complaints of the poor Reformed churches in their own just defense. Accordingly, the rulers have either issued bloody edicts against them themselves or, at the very least, have signed those suggested and *contrived by the priests, the missionary monks, or the Congregation.*

### Chapter 3: In the Valleys of Piedmont

-> *Concerning the extirpation of heretics* <note>original Latin: "De extirpandis hæreticis"</note>. <-

And although the **Protestants** have repeated their humble petitions and laid them at the feet of His Royal Highness, the innocence and boldness of those **missionary** "beasts" has, from that time until now, so increased and reached such a height that it is altogether unbearable. What makes them even more confident and insulting is that they know they will [not] be punished by any magistrate, no matter what they say or do to the Protestants—not even when they kidnap their very children! 

In contrast, the **Protestants** are put to death by the magistrates if they speak even the slightest word against the **missionary** priests, or if they attempt to talk even their own <term>domestics</term> <note>household servants</note> out of turning Catholic. <margin>Rorenco, 1636, pages 136–137.</margin> This can be seen in the Duke's Edict (which **Rorenco** mentions in his *Memoirs*, pages 136 and 137), which was undoubtedly forced from the Duke by these missionaries. ### Chapter III. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

*Concerning the extermination of heretics.* <note>original Latin: "De extirpandis hæreticis"</note> Although the **Protestants** have repeatedly sent their humble petitions and laid them at the feet of His Royal Highness <note>The Duke of Savoy</note>, the local **missionary** priests—those "beasts"—have grown so bold and unrestrained that their behavior has become completely unbearable. #### Practices to destroy the Evangelical Churches: Book II.

Both in the streets and in public places—even in the very churches during the sermon—they would assault the **Protestant** ministers with the most base, vile, shameful, and unbearable speeches they could possibly devise to spew against them. They did this knowing that no one dared to punish their **Catholic** zeal, let alone testify against their Reverences <note>original: "Fatherhoods"</note> on behalf of the **Protestants**, for fear of incurring excommunication and other penalties ordained against those who favor heretics. On the contrary, if by such provocations they could at any time draw a single word out of a minister’s mouth (or the mouth of any other man) that did not please them, they had their hired witnesses ready to bring the poor minister or other **Protestant** to the stake without any hope of mercy.

There can be no other reasonable interpretation of the edict which they cunningly obtained from Madame Royale <note>Christine of France, Duchess of Savoy and Regent for her son</note> on January 16, 1642. It was printed at **Turin** by **John Sinibaldo**, printer to the **Duke**. They made **His Royal Highness** believe that the **Catholics** <note>original: "Papists"</note> were being forced to contribute toward the maintenance of Protestant ministers, along with other such fictions and false tales. Based on these lies, they obtained an order from **His Royal Highness** for the local officials, called *Castellani* <term>Castellans: Governors or administrative officials of a castle or district</term>, to give the **missionaries** all the legal documents they might desire or demand. The order stated: "Commanding the castellans to send, without difficulty, all the writings that the Father Missionaries should request of them." <note>original Italian: "Commandato alli castellani di dover spedir senza difficultà tutte le scritture che dalli Padri Missionari gli fossero richieste."</note> 

By this means, the **missionaries** usurped the supreme power of the Prince over these *Castellani*, and consequently over the poor **Protestants**. They compelled the *Castellani* to issue the most unjust ordinances imaginable against those poor people, and dictated to them as many helpful lies <note>original: "officious lies," meaning lies told to serve a specific purpose or "duty"</note> as they pleased. I leave it to others to consider whether a Prince may justly place his **Protestant** subjects under the power of their sworn enemies, to whom he gives authority over the magistrates themselves. Is it right that **Protestants** should be bound in conscience to obey magistrates who are merely the secretaries—or rather, the servants—of those who are themselves slaves to the Pope? These officials are sold to serve the desires of those **missionaries** without any moral hesitation or questioning the justice of such proceedings, thereby exposing the Prince's poor, harmless subjects to all manner of wrongs and oppressions.

What actions, however base and harmful to human society, might private men not carry out when invested with this kind of power? To speak more directly about the **missionary** priests, it is well known that they frequently used this power to prevent Catholics from testifying to the truth when they tried to support their **Protestant** neighbors, even when the matter was completely obvious and clear. For example, when the question concerns where someone lives, the **missionaries** persuade those who come to testify to the truth that doing so would "favor heretics." They tell them they would then fall irrevocably under the penalty of excommunication. Meanwhile, they claim it is a meritorious work to testify against Protestants by using the helpful lies dictated to them by the **Catholic** <note>original: "Popish"</note> clergy. Indeed, they will...

### Chapter 3: In the Valleys of Piedmont

They will not allow even the judges to prosecute a **righteous cause, or to judge with righteous judgment**, whenever it reflects in the slightest upon the **Catholic party**. Furthermore, judges are not permitted at all to carry out any legal executions <note>In this context, "executions" refers to the seizure of property or the enforcement of legal judgments</note> upon such **commoner lands** <term>original: "Roture-Lands"; lands held by non-nobles, which were typically subject to taxes and legal seizure</term> as are given to the **Roman clergy**. By making those lands free of taxes and charges, they lay that entire financial burden upon the necks of the poor **Protestants**. 

To ensure they have the best opportunity and pretext to negotiate with those of the **Reformed Religion**, all the monks and friars of the neighboring cloisters usually procure from **His Royal Highness** every year the **assignments of grain** <term>Legal authorizations to collect a portion of the harvest as tax or payment</term> and other taxes—collecting as much as they possibly can. They do this so that those of the **Reformed Religion**, being forced to make their payments into the hands of these **tax collectors** <note>original: "Publicans"; a biblical reference to the often-corrupt tax collectors of the Roman Empire</note>, provide the clergy with the advantage of showing favor and giving ample rewards to those who will comply with their idolatry and superstitions, while laying heavy loads upon the backs of those who stand fast to their principles. By these means, the one party grows powerful almost imperceptibly, while the other is proportionally weakened and impoverished. This has been their practice for many years together at **La Torre**, **San Martino**, and various other places.

I might also mention their frequent invasions into the said **Valleys** with troops of armed men, under the pretense of quartering there (as they did in the years 1560, 1561, 1624, and 1655), in order to miserably surprise and prey upon the inhabitants. I could likewise mention the crafty wiles and cunning stratagems which they have always used in their treaties. These agreements have consistently been as full of deceits and **Jesuitical** equivocations as they were of lines and sentences—witness the last unhappy agreement made at **Pinerolo**—following the maxim of **Rome**: **"That is, never to keep faith with heretics"** <note>original: "Never to keep Faith with Hereticks"; a reference to the controversial Catholic principle *Fides hereticis non est servanda*</note>.

To this I may add their diligent search and strict inquiry after all **Protestant** books and writings, which they commit with much devotion to the flames, lest these books should discover the rottenness of their principles and the wickedness of their actions to the world. They fear that, as a consequence, those **craftsmen's** wares and trade might be in danger of being valued at nothing, **"and the magnificence of their great goddess Diana despised, and those Demetriuses not have so quick a market for their silver shrines"** <note>A reference to Acts 19:24–27, where the silversmith Demetrius incited a riot against the Apostle Paul because the spread of Christianity threatened his business of making shrines for the goddess Diana</note>.

But I cannot pass over one of their most notorious stratagems to allure and induce those who care more for their bodies than their souls—and **love the world above God**—to defect. This is done in imitation of the Devil when he tempted our blessed Savior. As soon as they see a **Protestant** reduced to poverty and very hungry, they immediately take him and set him **"upon the pinnacle of the temple, and show him all the riches, glory, and promotions of this world"** <note>A reference to the Temptation of Christ in Matthew 4</note>, offering to give him all these **if he will only fall down and worship their idol**. To give the business a better appearance, just as it was the Prince of this world who tempted our Savior, these offers are most commonly made and published in the **Prince's** name (through the great subtlety of **Jesuitical** minds) and presented as his bounty and beneficence. For this purpose, they dexterously manipulate orders out of...

> To encourage all the aforementioned heretics <note>The Catholic authorities referred to the Protestant Waldensians as "heretics"</note> to convert to Catholicism, it is our pleasure, and we do hereby expressly command, that all those who either converted this past year, or shall in the future embrace the holy faith, shall enjoy an exemption and immunity from each and every tax (whether property tax or personal tax) to be imposed on them. Now, it is remarkable that despite the order mentioned above, where His Royal Highness promises them exemption for only five years, he has—as the occasion arose—doubled and extended these five years to ten, and sometimes even to fifteen years. However, the secret purpose <term>original: "the Mystery"</term> of all this is (as has been specified above) that those burdens which are taken off the shoulders of the converts should be laid upon the backs of those who persevere in the true religion, the better to break and destroy them.

But as if all this were not enough to achieve their goals against the poor Protestants, they came up with an admirable and complete invention to speed up the process. This can be gathered from Belvedere's <note>Theodore Belvedere, a Catholic missionary and author who focused on the conversion of the Waldensian valleys</note> own report, page 286, where he says:

# Chapter III. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

<sig>Nn 2</sig>

It was this same Congregation for the Extirpation of Heretics <note>original: *de extirpandis Hereticis*</note>, which in the year 1655 undertook to judge the rights of the Protestants. Their meeting place was in the Archbishop's own house, the Bishop himself presiding. With him were the Confessor of His Royal Highness, the Abbot of la Monta, the Prior Rorengo <note>Marco Aurelio Rorengo, a Catholic prior and historian who wrote extensively against the Waldensians</note>, the Marquess of Pianezza <note>a military leader and statesman infamous among Protestants for his role in the 1655 massacres</note>, the Great Chancellor, and the Chief President of the Chamber, named Filippo Ferraris. Also present were the Chief President of the Senate, along with Presidents Beletis and Nomis. Every one of them was hired by the Court of Rome to undermine the liberty of the Protestant churches by robbing them of their ancient privileges under various pretenses and based on false and wicked information, sometimes in one regard and sometimes in another. 

To better cloak and disguise their actions, they usually surprised the Duke with heavy and serious accusations, suddenly obtaining several edicts against the poor Protestants before they could even be heard in their own defense. You can see this in Rorengo’s book titled *Narrative of the Introduction of the Heretics into the Valleys of Piedmont* <note>original Italian: *Narratione dell’ introduttione de gl’ heretici nelle valli del Piemonte*</note>, which was printed at Turin in the year 1632. In that work, he explicitly says that the intention of His Royal Highness is to restrain, rather than enlarge, the limits prescribed to the Protestants, boldly attributing his own design to the Prince.

<margin>Rorengo, *Narrative of the Introduction of the Heretics into the Valleys of Piedmont*.</margin>

It was to this Council that all those were sent who might have any claim to preserving their property after the revolt in 1650. This is clearly shown by the orders published at that time against those who claimed the right to live outside their fixed boundaries. These orders are essentially the same as those from the year 1655. After the account of the declaration of the confiscation of goods—and out of malice toward those who would not yield obedience—there are these expressions:

> *With the declaration that such a restriction shall remain limited, and thus cause no prejudice to those who—before the most Excellent Council established in Turin by His Royal Highness for the advancement and preservation of the Catholic faith—shall testify to having converted to Catholicism, etc., within fifteen days.* <note>original Italian: *Con Dichiaratione, che tal riduttione restarà circonscritta, e così di nissun pregiudicio, in quanto à quelli, che faranno fede inanzi l' Eccellentissimo Consiglio da S. A. R. eretto in Torino, per l' aumentatione, e conservatione della fede Catolica d' essersi catolizati, &c. fra giorni quindeci.*</note>

It was at the earnest suit and request of men such as these that Emmanuel Philibert <note>Duke of Savoy from 1553 to 1580</note>, on June 10, 1565, commanded all those who would not attend Mass to depart from his territories within two months. As for the inhabitants of the Valley of Barcelonnette <note>original: "Barcelona," a valley in the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence then under Savoyard control</note>, they were ordered to depart within one month, as related by Rorengo in his *Historical Memoirs*, pages 74, 76, and 107.

<margin>Rorengo, *History*, pages 74, 76, & 107. Belvedere.</margin>

However, the Duke soon after perceived that the order was very unjust. He gave them leave to stay and to enjoy those ancient liberties, which he himself has since confirmed to them.

In the very same workshop, and by the same hands, the following edicts were fabricated. These are described at length by the aforementioned Rorengo in his narrative. One was dated February 25, 1602, in which they make Charles Emmanuel <note>Charles Emmanuel I, Duke of Savoy (reigned 1580–1630)</note> speak and say that he will utterly destroy the said religion (which they pretend is heretical). To that purpose, he orders the Protestants, upon pain of death, to banish from among them all types of schools, whether private or public. This is exactly what Julian the Apostate <note>A 4th-century Roman Emperor who attempted to revive traditional Roman religion and suppress Christianity by forbidding Christians from teaching</note> did formerly to root out the Christian religion, as witnessed by Ammianus Marcellinus in his twenty-second book. He also forbade them from receiving any strangers among them who might serve as ministers or schoolmasters. And in another edict of December 18, 1622, he forbids them from sending their youth to any foreign schools suspected of being infected with this "pretended heresy," as witnessed by Rorengo on page 233. By this, it clearly appears that the design was indeed to destroy the Protestant religion.

In the aforementioned edict of February 25, 1602, he excludes (for the same purpose) all Protestants from public offices, whether high or low. I shall insert his very own words:

> We prohibit any heretic of the said pretended religion from holding public office in any community, town, or place within our domain; and those who currently hold them must leave them, nor shall they be admitted to the office of notary, etc. <note>original Italian: "Prohibiamo che alcuno eretico della detta pretenduta Religione, possi haver officii publici in alcuna communità, ò terra, ò luogo del dominio nostro, e quelli che lihanno debbino lasciarli, ne esser ammessi all’ufficio di nodaro, &c."</note>

<margin>Rorengo, pages 192, 193.</margin>
From this very cause proceed all other edicts issued against the Protestants of Saluzzo <note>original: Saluces</note>, by which they are forced and compelled to go to Mass whether they want to or not. Father John of Moncalieri, a missionary monk, maintains this practice to be lawful, as witnessed by Rorengo in his aforementioned book, pages 192 and 193. Here we must observe, in passing, that both the said missionary and Prior Rorengo—along with all the doctors of the Roman Church who have read and approved that book—have not noticed which epistle Paul uses to relate the institution of the Holy Supper, where he says, *"For I received from the Lord that which I also delivered to you, etc."* <note>original Latin: "Ego enim accepi à Domino, quod & tradidi vobis, &c." This is found in 1 Corinthians 11:23.</note> For the same book says on page 194 that it is in the Epistle to the Hebrews. It is a pity those "Seraphic Doctors" <note>A title of honor often given to eminent medieval Catholic theologians</note> are no better versed in the Scriptures.

<margin>Rorengo, page 152.</margin>

And by another edict in 1602, the same was commanded, but only fifteen days' time was given to depart. # Practices to Destroy the Evangelical Churches: Book II

<margin>page 235.</margin>
In his *Memoirs, page 235*, he records that they abducted many people in the year 1655 during the time of the Massacre. They refused to return them afterward, even though His Highness had promised to do so in his official decree <note>original: "Patent"</note>. To continue this practice with legal cover, those wicked men ensured that the relevant article of the decree was written as follows:

> *No person belonging to the <term>pretended Reformed Religion</term> <note>original: "Religion pret. Rifor." – a derogatory legal term used by Catholic authorities to describe Protestantism</note> shall be forced to embrace the Catholic, Apostolic, Roman Religion. Neither shall their children be stolen or taken away from their parents while they are minors—that is to say, males under the age of twelve and females under ten.* <note>original: "Non potra alcuno di detta Religione pret. Rifor. esser sforzato d' abbracciar la Religione Catholica Apostolica Romana, n' ei figliuoli potranno esser tolti alli loro parenti, mentre che sono in età minore, cioè li maschi di dodici, & le femine di dieci anni."</note>

The truth is, this is the most detestable of all "Turkish" tyrannies. For the Turks, in some of their provinces, do steal away the children of Christians and infect those tender infants with the teachings of Muhammad <note>original: "Impieties of Mahomet"</note> to gradually root out the Christian religion. However, there is this difference: the Turks only do this to their own subjects, whereas the Pope's ministers do it to those over whom they have no legal right at all.

In short, the cunning schemes and strategies used to wipe out the poor <term>Waldenses</term> <note>A medieval Christian movement that faced centuries of persecution; they are often considered predecessors to the Reformation</note> are too numerous to be included in a short discourse. It is not necessary to dwell on this point any longer, as the rest of this history consists of almost nothing else. Although the Court of Savoy refuses to acknowledge that religion was the true fundamental cause of the recent troubles in those valleys, the results plainly show it to be so. Very few of those who were killed or taken prisoner were not pressured to the utmost to renounce their faith. I will satisfy myself by providing two very sad examples where the subtle manipulations and persuasive arguments of Jesuitical spirits—using every kind of unrighteous deception—demonstrated their great power and influence. I must confess, I would be very reluctant to bring other men's weaknesses into public view, but since the following declaration was written by the individuals themselves for that very purpose, and because it contains many lessons from which the Christian reader can benefit, I have included it here in its original expression, as follows:

### *The Restorative Declaration*
<note>original French: "La Declaration reparative"</note>

*Which Messrs. Pierre Gros and François Aguit, formerly Pastors in the Valley of Luserna in Piedmont, made in a full assembly on August 25 and 29, 1655, at the village of Pinache in the Valley of Perosa, to testify to the extreme sorrow they felt for their previous apostasy <note>original: "revolte"</note>, into which they were led through weakness while they were held in the prisons of Turin, along with a renunciation of Catholicism <note>original: "Papisme"</note>.*

---

->*Gentlemen and most Honored Fathers and Brothers in the Lord,*<-

We could have wished that a less painful subject had forced us to appear in public, and that a more favorable occasion had called us to make ourselves known to the world by some remarkable deed, the memory of which might have been a blessing <note>original: "in benediction"</note> in the Church. But since our names must be made famous only by the extreme misfortunes that have overwhelmed us, and by the horrible scandal that we have just given to the Church of God, we now emerge from the dungeons of our own shame and confusion. We present ourselves before men to show our conversion and repentance to the whole world, and to give certain proof of the grief we feel for having been so cowardly as to abandon our former profession of faith.

<column-break/>

### *A Restorative Declaration*

*Made in a full Congregation on August 28 and 29, 1655, at Pinache in the Valley of Perosa, by Mr. Peter Gros and Mr. Francis Aguit, formerly Ministers in the Valley of Luserna in Piedmont; to testify to their extreme sorrow for their falling away <note>original: "defection"</note> through weakness <note>original: "infirmity"</note> from the true Religion during the time of their imprisonment at Turin, together with their renunciation of Catholicism <note>original: "Popery"</note>.*

---

->*Most Honored Fathers and Brothers in the Lord,*<-

WE could have wished that a less sad subject had caused our appearance in public, and that a more favorable occasion had made us known to the world by some notable action, the memory of which might have been a blessing in the Church. But since our names cannot be famous except by the extreme misfortunes which have overwhelmed us, and by the horrible scandal which we have given to the Church of God, we now come forth out of the dark dungeons of our own shame and confusion. We present ourselves before men to testify to all the world our conversion and repentance, and to give unquestionable <note>original: "indubitable"</note> proof of our grief for being so base as to forsake our former profession.

<page-num>278</page-num>
<header>Practices to Destroy the Evangelical Churches, Book II.</header>

In his *Memoirs, page 235,* <note>Refers to the memoirs of Jean Léger or a similar contemporary chronicler of the Waldensian persecutions.</note> they stole away very many in the year 1655, during the time of the massacre, whom they would not afterward restore, despite the fact that his Highness <note>The Duke of Savoy.</note> had promised it by his Patent <note>original: "Patent"; a formal legal document or decree issued by a monarch.</note>. To continue that trade with legal permission, those wicked men caused that article of the Patent to be written thus:

> *No person of the said pretended Reformed Religion <note>original Italian: "Religione pret. Rifor."; a standard Catholic term used at the time to refer to Protestantism.</note> shall be in any way compelled (or forced) to embrace the Catholic, Apostolic, Roman Religion. Neither shall their children be stolen or taken away from their parents while they are in their minority—that is to say, males under twelve years of age, and females under ten.* <note>original Italian: "Non potra alcuno di detta Religione pret. Rifor. esser sforzato d' abbraciar la Religione Catholica Apostolica Romana, n'ei figliuoli potranno esser tolti alli loro parenti, mentre che sono in età minore, cioè li maschi di dodeci, & le femine di dieci anni."</note>

The truth is, this is the most wretched of all the *Turkish* tyrannies <note>A reference to the Ottoman Empire's "devshirme" system, where Christian children were taken to be raised as Muslims and soldiers.</note>. For the *Turks*, in some of their provinces, do steal away the *Christians'* children and infect those tender infants with the impieties of *Muhammad* <note>original: "Mahomet"</note>, thereby rooting out the *Christian* religion by degrees. But there is this difference: namely, that the *Turks* do so only to their own subjects, whereas the Pope's ministers do it to those over whom they have no right at all.

In summary, the cunning wiles and stratagems used to exterminate the poor *Waldensians* <note>original: "Waldenfes"; a proto-Protestant group in the Alps persecuted by the Catholic Church.</note> are too numerous to be included in a short discourse. Nor is it indeed at all necessary to dwell upon this point any longer, because the rest of this history consists of almost nothing else. Although the Court of *Savoy* will by no means acknowledge that religion was the true fundamental cause of the late troubles in those valleys, the effects plainly show it to be so. There were very few of those who were either killed or taken prisoner who were not tempted to the utmost to renounce their religion. I shall only content myself by providing two very sad examples where certainly (if ever) the subtle windings and insinuating arguments of *Jesuitical* spirits, with *all manner of deceptive unrighteousness*, clearly evidenced their great power and influence. I must confess, I would be very hesitant to bring other men's weaknesses <note>original: "Infirmities"</note> onto the stage, but since the following declaration was written by the parties themselves for that very purpose—and because there are many lessons contained within it from which the *Christian* reader can gain much satisfaction and advantage—I have inserted it in its original expressions, as follows.

<header>Chapter III. In the Valleys of Piedmont.</header>

<image-desc>A decorative horizontal headpiece featuring repeating ornate floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>

### The corrective declaration <note>original: "Declaration reparative"; a public statement intended to repair a scandal or rectify a spiritual lapse.</note> that Messrs. Pierre Gros and François Aguit, formerly Pastors in the Valley of Lucerna in Piedmont, made in a full assembly on the 25th and 29th <note>The French text says the 25th and 29th, while the English text says the 28th and 29th.</note> of August 1655, at Pinache in the Valley of Perosa, to testify to the extreme regret they felt for their previous lapse <note>original: "revolte"; here meaning a turning away from their faith.</note>, to which they were driven by weakness while held in the prisons of Turin, including a renunciation of Catholicism <note>original: "Papisme"; a derogatory historical term for the Roman Catholic Church.</note>.

---

-> Gentlemen and most Honored Fathers and Brothers in the Lord, <-

We wish that a less painful subject had compelled us to appear in public, and that a more favorable occasion had called us to make ourselves known to the world through some remarkable action—the memory of which might have been a blessing to the Church. But since our names must become famous only through the extreme misfortunes that have overwhelmed us, and by the horrible scandal we have just given to the Church of God, we now emerge from the depths of our own shame and confusion. We present ourselves before all people to demonstrate our conversion and repentance, and to give undeniable proof of the grief we feel for having been so cowardly as to abandon our former profession of faith.

<column-break/>

### A corrective declaration made in a full Congregation on the 28th and 29th of August 1655 at Pinache in the Valley of Perosa, by Mr. Peter Gros and Mr. Francis Aguit, formerly Ministers in the Valley of Lucerna in Piedmont; to testify to their extreme sorrow for their abandonment of the faith <note>original: "defection"; the act of deserting a cause or religion.</note> through weakness <note>original: "infirmity"; likely referring to the physical and mental exhaustion of imprisonment and the threat of execution.</note> during their imprisonment at Turin, together with their renunciation of Catholicism.

---

-> Most Honored Fathers and Brothers in the Lord, <-

WE could have wished that a less sad subject had caused us to appear in public, and that a more favorable occasion had made us known to the world by some notable action, the memory of which might have been a blessing in the Church. But since our names cannot be famous except for the extreme misfortunes which have overwhelmed us, and the horrible scandal which we have given to the Church of God, we now come forth out of the dark dungeons of our own shame and confusion. We present ourselves before all men to testify to the whole world our conversion and repentance, and to give unquestionable proof of our grief for being so cowardly as to forsake our former profession.

When we reflect upon those advantages with which the Lord has blessed us, above so many others—such as being born in his Church, drinking in piety with our mother’s milk, receiving the grace of his saving knowledge, and being taught true happiness—and finally having been called to the highest office that men can have in this world, namely, to be the heralds of God’s justice and preachers of his truth, we cannot speak of our offense without horror. We must confess that it is a sin all the more hateful because, having known our Master’s will, we nonetheless withdrew our support <note>original: "withdrawn our shoulder"; a metaphor for refusing the yoke of service</note> from his service to act in total opposition to his commandments.

It was during these recent disasters that have overwhelmed our country that we met with spiritual disaster <note>original: "made shipwrack"</note>, after we had lost our liberty and all our possessions. When the enemies of the truth, having resolved to completely wipe out the *Reformed Religion* in the *Valleys of Piedmont*, committed the most barbaric cruelties against our countrymen, we fell into their hands. After they showed us how far their inhumanity could go, as a final proof of it, they threw us into prison. There they prosecuted us and sentenced us to death as guilty of treason and as leaders of the rebellion. They did not stop setting before our eyes the torments and punishments to which we were condemned, to make us more vulnerable to the enticements of the *Jesuits* <note>The Jesuits were a Catholic religious order often at the forefront of efforts to convert Protestants during the Counter-Reformation.</note>, who constantly pressured us to accept a pardon they would obtain for us, provided we would only—

<column-break/>

*When we reflect on the advantages with which the Lord had favored us above countless others, having caused us to be born into his Church and to suckle piety with our milk; having also honored us with his saving knowledge and taught us the path of true happiness; and finally, having called us to the highest of positions with which he honors men in this world—making us heralds of his justice and announcers of his truth—we can only speak with horror of our mistake. We frankly admit that it is a sin all the more enormous and detestable because, having known the will of our master, we pulled our shoulders back from his service to do the exact opposite of what he commands us.*

*It was in these recent calamities that flooded our country that we were shipwrecked, after having lost our liberty along with all our goods. When the enemies of truth, having intended to entirely exterminate the Reformed Religion in the Valleys of Piedmont, exercised their barbarities and cruelties upon our compatriots; having fallen into their hands, after they made us experience just how far their inhumanity could go, to give us the final proof of it, they had us moved to prisons. There, a case was built against us, and we were sentenced to death as criminals of High Treason <note>original: "leze Majesté"</note> and leaders of rebellion. They never stopped proposing the torments and the execution to which they destined us, to make us all the more pliable to the summons of the Jesuits and others, who never tired of soliciting us to receive the grace they promised to obtain for us, provided that we embrace—*

...embrace Popery <note>original French: "fassions le Papisme"; a derogatory term for Roman Catholicism used by Protestants at the time</note> by abjuring our religion.

At the first attacks, it seemed that, far from succumbing, we had enough strength and vigor to despise everything that superstition could place as frightening before our eyes. We believed that those funeral shadows of death with which we were threatened did not have enough power to extinguish that celestial light that radiated in our souls. But we have learned, to our extreme regret, how great human fragility is, and we have recognized how deceptive the prudence of the flesh is. To make us enjoy a decaying and fleeting life, it made us renounce the unutterable blessings prepared for the children of God and the eternal joy in which those who persevere to the end participate. It was this prudence which—through a desire to preserve this "house of clay" and this "earthly dwelling" <note>biblical metaphors for the mortal body</note>, and to save ourselves from a shameful death and an infamous punishment in the eyes of the world—led us to a shameful revolt and to turn our backs on him who is the source of life. We gave our ear to this deceptive Delilah <note>a biblical reference to the woman who betrayed Samson; here it represents the temptation to prioritize physical safety over spiritual truth</note>. Even though there was no reasoning so powerful that it could in any way obscure the truth we were professing, we freely confess that the fear of death and the horror of the punishment shook our courage and broke our strength. We have flowed away like water, for not resisting even to the point of shedding our blood, as the profession not only of Christians, but moreover of pastors of the Church, obliged us to do.

Persuaded by a deceptive reasoning that our life was better...
</column>

<column-break/>

...embrace Popery <note>original English: "imbrace Popery"</note> and abjure our religion.

At their first onsets, we were confident that, being far from yielding to them, we had strength and constancy enough to despise whatever superstition could present as dreadful or terrible before our eyes. We believed that the dark and mournful shadows of death itself, with which they threatened us, were not powerful enough to extinguish that heavenly light which then shone in our souls. But we have learned, to our deepest grief, how frail our nature is and how deceptive the wisdom of the flesh can be. For the enjoyment of a fragile and fleeting life, this wisdom made us abandon those inexpressible blessings that God has prepared for his children—that everlasting joy shared by those who persevere to the end. It was this worldly <note>original: "carnal"</note> wisdom which—out of a desire to preserve this "house of clay" and this "earthly tabernacle" <note>metaphors for the human body</note>, and to avoid a shameful death and an ignominious punishment in the eyes of the world—led us to a shameful falling away and to turn our backs on him who is the fountain of life. We listened to this deceitful Delilah <note>original: "Dalilah"</note>. Although no arguments were offered that were strong enough to obscure the truth we professed, we freely confess that the fear of death and the horror of torments shook our courage and broke our strength. We have wasted away and dried up like water, not resisting to the point of bloodshed <note>original: "not resisting to bloud"; a reference to Hebrews 12:4</note>, as the profession not only of Christians, but (what is more) of ministers of the Church, obliged us to do.

Having been persuaded by deceptive reasoning that life was better...

<header>Chapter III. with its several Persecutions.</header>

<columns>

<note>original: French</note>
...calls the sinner to repentance to give him life, we take the boldness to present ourselves before His face and to humble ourselves in His holy presence, to bewail the greatness of our crime and to make a free confession of our iniquity. Our sin, which is not ordinary or common, demands an extraordinary repentance; and as we recognize it as one of the greatest committed in the world, so we also wish that our repentance might reach the final degree of humiliation, so that the acts of our contrition <note>original: "contrition"; sincere remorse for sin</note> might be known to the whole earth. If David, for lighter faults, desired that his laments and deep repentance be perpetual in the Church, we shall not be ashamed to publish to men the inconsolable regret remaining in us for having offended God, scandalized the assembly of the saints, and imprinted on our forehead the mark of an eternal disgrace through a miserable revolt. We wish to keep this memory alive forever, if only we can demonstrate the extreme displeasure we have felt for it, and disavow everything that fear forced us to do against the dictates of our conscience. We hope that He who pardoned Saint Peter for his denials in the court of Caiaphas will grant us the same graces, since we come to ask Him for a very humble pardon with tears in our eyes, confession in our mouths, and contrition in our hearts; and that, as there is joy in heaven for one sinner who comes to repentance, there will also be joy in the assembly of the faithful when they see our conversion to the Lord.

<page-num>285</page-num>
<header>Chapter IV. In the Valleys of Piedmont.</header>

<columns>
<column>
<note>original: French</note>
...a physical and spiritual captivity in which we were stagnating, so that you might set us at liberty to be able to call upon you. You have heard us from the deep places and have given us new cause to rejoice in your goodness and bless your holy name. May eternal glory be given to you at all times and throughout every age. Amen.

Faithful souls, who see how we bring a contrite heart and a broken spirit before the Eternal to humble ourselves before his face: have pity on our lamentable state! Learn by our example to recognize what human frailty is, and into what a precipice we fall when God withdraws his grace from us. Consider that, just as it has been an extreme misfortune for us to have fallen into such a great sin, you have reason to rejoice in God for the grace he gives you to still stand firm. Watch and pray so that you do not enter into temptation. Hold fast to what you have, so that no one takes your crown from you. Christians, who see us return into the heart <note>original: "bosom"</note> of the Church, lend us your helping hand, and let your arms be opened to embrace us, seeing that we beg your pardon for the scandal which we have given you. # CHAPTER IV.

### *The grounds or motives of the late persecution in the year 1655, with the publication of Gastaldo's bloody order and the flight of the Protestants in the middle of winter.*

<margin>
The grounds or motives of the late persecution in the year 1655.
</margin>
I have often pondered in my more private thoughts (because such an effect cannot happen without a moving cause) what might be the ground or reason why the Devil is always so extremely malicious against the sons and daughters of men. Humans are his poor fellow creatures and were originally of a lower rank and degree—indeed, they were likely never in a position to give him a proportionate provocation. In the same way, it is possible that the Christian reader may be just as curious and inquisitive in their own reflections as to what motives could provoke the Court of *Savoy* to persecute and prosecute their own poor natives and countrymen with such rancor and violence. These were people of the humblest rank and quality, whose poverty and need <note>original: "indigency"</note> could never have sparked envy, nor could their abilities <note>original: "parts"</note> or education in any age have threatened deep political designs. They have, in short, never been guilty of disturbing their Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> adversaries any more than the lamb in the fable was guilty of troubling the waters where the wolf was drinking.

<margin>
The Order of Gastaldo.
The flight of the Protestants.
The middle of winter.
</margin>
Naturalists observe of the monkey that once he begins to gnaw and feed upon his own tail, it is a certain sign not only that he is diseased, but that his illness is incurable. Truly, for my part, I could never yet learn any satisfactory reason why certain Jesuit spirits of that Court—whom I may (without stretching the metaphor) aptly call the Pope's monkeys—should thus continually gnaw and devour their own flesh (meaning their Protestant brothers and countrymen). Furthermore, they chose to devour the leanest and poorest part of them, driven by nothing other than that incurable disease of malice and envy with which the Devil has infected them. However, I shall faithfully relate here the opinions of others who are more intimately acquainted with these affairs, using their own expressions (the original documents of which I have in my possession). I leave the probability or improbability of these reasons to the discerning reader. According to their descriptions and representations of this matter, the reasons are of two sorts: the first more general, and the other more specific.

# Motives of the Persecution, 1655. Book II.

->The general grounds are:<-

<margin>The first general reason why the Court of Savoy persecutes the poor Protestants.</margin>
1. Their pretended zeal for the religion of the Church of Rome. Because these men believe that to be the true Church, and consequently believe that what we profess is a most detestable heresy, they look upon themselves as obligated in conscience to use every effort for the total destruction <note>original: "extirpation"</note> of the same. As Christ himself forewarns his disciples in John 16:2: *The time comes that whoever kills you will think he does God service.*

<margin>2. General reason.</margin>
2. The belief they hold that, in matters of heresy, all princes ought to conform themselves to the judgment of the Pope and the clergy. This is despite the fact that they well know that the Reformed Churches accuse the Pope himself of many notorious heresies, idolatries, and impieties. The question is whether the Pope should be his own judge in this matter, or whether any prince ought to rely so heavily upon, or comply with, another person’s conscience as to condemn his own subjects because of it. Indeed, they condemn them before the prince is even certain whether the cause for which he condemns them is good or evil, especially when the condemned parties offer to prove the truth of both their principles and practices.

<margin>The particular motives for the late persecution in the year 1655.</margin>
But to come more closely to our purpose, the more specific grounds which (according to their own authors) move and incline some of the chief officers and gentry of *Savoy* to attempt to wipe out the Reformed party are:

<margin>1. Particular motive.</margin>
1. To the end that by mistreating the Reformed Churches, they may preserve the Papal authority, which they often need so much—specifically to cover and cloak their incestuous marriages <note>These were marriages between close relatives that were normally forbidden by church law but allowed with a special permit (dispensation) from the Pope.</note>, contracted through dispensations from the *Pope*. Thus, they become committed to defending and maintaining Popery for fear of being declared guilty of incest; though, for all I know, the first sin (persecution) may be the worse of the two.

<margin>2. Motive.</margin>
2. By persecuting the Reformed party, those courtiers receive (as "a reward for their wickedness" <note>original: "a Reward of Iniquity"</note>) various church offices such as prebendaries, bishoprics, abbeys, and priories—especially those who are members of the Council *for the Propagation of the Faith and the Extirpation of Heretics* <note>original: "De propaganda fide & extirpandis hereticis"</note>.

<margin>3. Motive.</margin>
3. Under this pretext, the poor people of the Valleys become a continual prey to the courtiers mentioned above, who daily rob and spoil them by extorting the best part of their livelihood through all sorts of strategies and clever devices.

<margin>4. Motive.</margin>
4. The gentry of *Lucerna* (who are otherwise very poor) do what they can to promote this work through constant slanders <note>original: "calumnies"</note> against the Reformed party, either in general or against individuals. By performing such "good services," they make themselves eligible to earn and receive those pensions assigned to them by the Court of Rome for that very purpose.

<margin>5. Motive.</margin>
5. For this reason in recent years—so that they might leave no means untried for the absolute ruin and destruction of those Protestant Churches—they have influenced the gentlemen of the respective Valleys...

### Chapter IV. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

These valleys are under the authority of monks and Catholic priests, who usually dictate what the people must do. This includes giving false testimony against their fellow Christians <note>original: "Brethren"</note>, sowing discord among them, murdering one another, arranging assassinations, or assisting in the kidnapping and carrying away of their children, and other such harmful acts. Unless the people readily perform these tasks, the priests refuse to pay them their annual pensions.

6. In the sixth and final place, the primary reason why the Court of Savoy strives so hard to eliminate <note>original: "extirpate"</note> these poor people is their plan to seize Pinerolo <note>original: "Pignerolio"</note> from the King of France. The presence and freedom of the Protestant people is a major obstacle to this goal. Because they live in the areas surrounding Pinerolo—both in the plains and the mountains—and because their consciences prevent them from conspiring or making any agreement with the Spanish faction to attack or surprise that city, the Court of Savoy seeks every possible excuse and pretext to uproot them. This is especially true for the residents of Lucerna, Fenile, Bobbio, Campiglione, Bricherasio, and San Secondo, which are near Pinerolo. For this very reason, the fortress of La Torre was previously built in the heart of the Lucerna and Angrogna valleys, near the junction of two great rivers. This was intended to better block off Pinerolo from that side and deprive it of the supplies <note>original: "Commodities"</note> it receives from that valley, which alone usually provides it with more than all the other neighboring valleys belonging to the Duke combined.

<margin>The interest of France in preserving the interests of the poor Protestants.</margin>
The Court of Savoy believes that by exterminating these people and replacing them with men willing to carry out their plans, they could easily seize Malange—a narrow pass above Pinerolo on the side facing France. In that spot, a very few people would be able to prevent the French army from reinforcing Pinerolo. Because of this, many sensible people believe that France, on the contrary, has a significant interest in protecting these poor people in their ancient homes in the valleys. Their reasons are:

<margin>The first reason why France is concerned with preserving the interests of the poor Protestants.</margin>
1. A large number of the inhabitants of the valleys are of French descent, their ancestors having moved there about five hundred years ago. They feel a natural obligation to be faithful to the French Crown and are certainly much better suited to live there than those of the Spanish faction, who would undoubtedly take their place if the Protestants were wiped out.

<margin>2. Reason.</margin>
2. The valleys are naturally very well-defended; it would be almost impossible to remove an enemy once they took possession of them.

<margin>3. Reason.</margin>
3. Because these places are inhabited by people loyal to French interests, they serve as sentinels and fortifications <note>original: "Centinels and Bulwarks"</note> (which cost the French nothing) to guard the border. They also constantly provide the French with food, hay, oats, and wood.

<margin>4. Reason.</margin>
4. Furthermore, this is a very convenient passage for the French into Italy. It is the same route that Hannibal used in ancient times...

#### Motives of the Persecution 1655. Book II.

of, and since that time, various Kings of *France*, especially *Charles* 8.

<margin>5. Reason.</margin>
5. Since the Duke of *Savoy* handed everything over to the King of *France*, and the King of *France* was bound to the arrangement by a formal Treaty made in the year of our Lord <note>original: "Anno Domini"</note> 1535, it is assumed that his Most *Christian* Majesty <note>A traditional title for the King of France</note> will consider himself interested and obligated to uphold the Acts and Edicts of his predecessors. He should take into consideration that the promises of Kings and Princes are sacred things and ought to be as unchangeable as the Laws of the *Medes* and *Persians* <note>A biblical reference to laws that cannot be altered or repealed</note>.

Based on these and similar grounds, according to many knowledgeable people, the Court of *Savoy* and its agents <note>original: "Creatures"</note> have from time to time sought the destruction of those poor Protestant Churches. It is true that in all the persecutions they have raised against them (and more especially in this last one of 1655), those *ravening wolves* have always approached in *sheep's clothing* to better disguise their bloody actions and to fall upon those *innocent lambs* when they are unaware. 

It is evident that the Evangelical Churches of the Valleys had, long before this fatal year of 1655, cleared themselves of those slanders <note>original: "Calumnies"</note> which the Council *for the Extirpation of Heretics* <note>original: "De extirpandis hæreticis"</note> had tried to discredit them with. This Council was an assembly made up of those on the payroll of *Rome* <note>original: "Pensioners of Rome"</note> who, in order to receive their promised payments, had endeavored to slander the Protestants and thereby make them hateful in the eyes of their sovereign Prince. 

Indeed, his Royal Highness <note>The Duke of Savoy</note> had already given ample testimony that he was fully satisfied on this point, having granted them an authentic Decree, printed and published in the year 1649, confirming their rights <note>original: "Concessions"</note>. These were again confirmed and expanded by his Royal Highness on the second and fourth of *June*, and the twenty-ninth of *December* 1653, establishing their right to the grants given to them in 1603 and 1620. This was done without any addition or subtraction, expansion or restriction, as may be seen by the following copies of their petitions <note>original: "Requests"</note> and the Decrees of his Royal Highness regarding them. An authentic copy of the true original document can be seen in the public library of the famous University of *Cambridge*.

# Chapter IV. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

The most faithful and most humble subjects of Your Royal Highness, practitioners of the Reformed Religion in the Valleys of Lucerna, Perosa, San Martino, Roccapiatta, San Bartolomeo, Prarustino, and the surrounding areas, prostrate at your feet, etc. <note>original Italian: "Li fidelissimi & humillimi sudditi di V. A. R. professanti la Religione Riformata nella Valli di Lucerna, Perosa, Martino, Roccapiatta, S. Bartolomeo, Prarustino, & luoghi anessi, prostrati alli piedi di quella, &c."</note>

*The most faithful and most humble subjects of your Royal Highness—the practitioners of the Reformed Religion in the Valley of Lucerna, Perosa, San Martino, Roccapiatta, San Bartolomeo, Prarustino, and the neighboring regions—prostrating ourselves at your feet, do in all humility pay our respects to you. We beseech His Divine Majesty to grant you a happy and prosperous reign, under which we desire to live quietly and peaceably. We intend to offer you every form of obedience due from true subjects to their lawful and natural Prince, just as our people have always done under the blessed rule of your most serene predecessors of famous memory. Now, renewing our petition to Your Royal Highness, we most humbly request that, according to your accustomed generosity and mercy <note>original: "bountie and clemencie"</note>, you would be pleased to grant us the following Articles. We shall continue to pray to God for the prosperity of Your Royal Highness and your entire Royal Family, and for the growth and expansion of your territories.*

---

->centered text<-
The First Article.

May it please you to confirm the favors and privileges granted to them, which were frequently confirmed and officially registered by your most serene predecessors of glorious memory, etc. <note>original Italian: "Si compiaccia confirmar luoro le gratie & privilegii a luoro concessi, & piu volte confirmati & interinati da serenissimi suoi Predecessori di gloriosa memoria, &c."</note>

*That you will be pleased to confirm for us the immunities and privileges previously granted, which were often confirmed and officially registered <term>interinated: a legal term meaning to formally ratify or register a decree in a court of law</term> by your most serene predecessors of glorious memory. We specifically ask for those granted by your grandfather, the late most serene Duke Charles Emanuel, dated April 9, May 14, and September 29, 1603; registered on June 20, 1620; and confirmed by Your Royal Highness in your answers to the Memorial of the seven Articles on June 30, 1649. We ask this so that your subjects may peaceably enjoy the benefits of these rights, together with all the privileges that the rest of your subjects enjoy without distinction, just as they did under the happy reign of your aforementioned predecessors, without hindrance or harassment of any kind, regardless of any orders made—or to be made—to the contrary.*

> His Royal Highness graciously confirms to the Petitioners all their privileges, according to their form and tenor, and as they are legally registered <term>interinated: formally recorded or registered in the official records of a court or government</term>, without the least alteration. For the benefit of the Petitioners, his intention is that they shall enjoy these privileges without any disturbance, according to the conditions contained and included within them. Furthermore, they shall not make use of any foreign ministers, nor accept any strangers of the Reformed Religion to dwell, or even stay among them, for more than ten days at a time without the special permission of His Royal Highness. Likewise, they shall not perform any religious functions—whether preaching or any other kind—outside the limits graciously tolerated for them. Neither shall they hinder or in any way disturb the Most Reverend Missionary Fathers in their duties, nor cause them or their attendants the slightest trouble in their churches, missions, or anywhere else. Above all, they must punctually observe the contents of the tolerations graciously granted to them, both by His Royal Highness and by his most famous predecessors. If any of these conditions are broken or violated on their part, all such grants, favors, and tolerations are declared to be void and of no effect.

### Royal Highness

The most faithful and most obedient subjects of Your Royal Highness, professing the Reformed Religion in the Valleys of Lucerna, Perosa, St. Martino, Roccapiatta, St. Bartholomeo, Prarustino, and annexed places, being prostrate at your feet, etc. <note>original Italian: "Li fedelissimi & obedientissimi sudditi di V. A. R. professanti la Relig. riformata..."</note>

> *The most faithful and most obedient subjects of your Royal Highness, professing the Reformed Religion in the Valley of Lucerna, Perosa, St. Martino, Roccapiatta, St. Bartholomeo, Prarustino, and the annexed places, being prostrate at your feet, return you their most humble thanks for the favorable answers which it has pleased you to give to their memorial and articles of the second of June last past, which were somewhat expanded and declared on the fourth of the same month. However, because there are certain conditions never before inserted in their concessions—which, if wrongly interpreted by those who are ill-disposed toward us, might cause strange troubles to your petitioners, to the prejudice of their consciences and against the true meaning and intention of your Royal Highness—and because we desire nothing more than that we may live quietly under your happy dominions and render you all that obedience and fidelity which is due from true and faithful subjects to their lawful and natural Prince, we renew our address to you on this ground.*

### The Duke’s Answer to the Second Particular

When it happens that in the Valleys of San Martino, Perosa, and Luserna, anyone of the pretended reformed religion is found sick outside the tolerated places and limits, etc. <note>original Italian: "Quando il caso porti che nelle Valli di S. *When it happens that in the Valleys of San Martino, Perosa, and Luserna, any of the pretended reformed religion <note>The Duke’s administration used the term "pretended reformed religion" as a legal label for Protestantism, indicating it was not a recognized state church.</note> fall sick outside the said places and limits which are tolerated—which must not be thought enlarged in any way by the present concessions—His Royal Highness is willing (in case of instant danger of death through some sharp fit of sickness) that a Minister, accompanied by one other person who is not a minister, may travel to the place where the sick party is to visit and comfort him. This is provided that he remains in such a place outside the limits for no longer than one day, or two at the most; and also that he does not catechize or perform any other function (either public or private) relating to the pretended reformed religion, but that he confines himself to and intends only the said visit.*

*That your Royal Highness will be pleased to permit the exercise of public offices in the said three Valleys without distinction, as is specified in the Concessions of April 9, 1603, Article 4, and confirmed in the year 1620.*
