<page-num>302</page-num>

# Motives of the Persecution 1655. Book II.

Therefore, until May 19, 1654, no one can say that those of the Reformed Religion had committed any act that would deprive them of the benefits of their concessions. It is not worth the time to mention certain monks and friars, or the childish games of some young children in **La Torre** (some of whom were Catholic and some Protestant). Their adversaries attempted to use these incidents to form a criminal accusation, but it was soon revealed to be a matter so irrelevant, false, and maliciously twisted to the disadvantage of those poor people that the Legate **Gastaldo**, after conducting a specific inquiry at their request, declared plainly and openly that it was not worth noticing and that he would neither speak nor hear any more about it. 

The truth is, neither he nor the **Marquess of Pianezza**, in all their orders and letters—where they nevertheless gathered every possible thing they could imagine to be prejudicial to them to make them appear hateful and provide some plausible excuse for the late massacre—ever made the slightest mention of those childish stories. Therefore, all that **Gastaldo** and the Marquess accused those poor Protestants of were matters for which they had already cleared themselves, and which had been settled a long time before the said confirmation in the year 1654. Furthermore, the principal point—namely, their right of habitation—was an undoubted right they had enjoyed from time immemorial. 

All of this plainly argues that nothing happened on the Protestants' part that should have altered the intention and good pleasure of **His Royal Highness**, or hindered and delayed the <term>interination</term> <note>original: "interination"; the formal process of a court or chamber registering and validating a sovereign's decree</note> of their concessions. In addition to all this, the poor people (despite the heavy expenses of the legal process) did not stop petitioning the Court with all possible diligence and urgency, presenting the original records of the decrees. They agreed to pay all the <term>regales</term> <note>original: "Regales"; royal fees or taxes paid to the sovereign</note> amounting to 800 livres <note>original: "livers"</note>, deferring to the wishes of the Chamber; in short, they satisfied every single demand. 

Furthermore, the Chamber distributed the papers and sent the decrees to the <term>Advocate Patrimonial</term> <note>original: "Advocate Patrimonial"; a high-ranking state attorney responsible for the ruler's legal and financial interests</note>, who was supposed to sign the conclusions and report them back to the Chamber daily to finalize the process. However, the opposing party—who believe they perform a great service by contradicting and obstructing anything concerning the interests of those poor people—suggested that the decrees could not be officially registered because they had never been passed by the Chamber or the Senate, and consequently, they could not be trusted. 

In reality, they believed that the Protestants had completely lost the original registration documents from 1620 and that the copies they currently held were not authentic; they claimed that if those of the Reformed Religion could produce them, no further difficulty would remain. The poor people overcame this obstacle as well and produced their authentic papers. Nevertheless, after being led on for a long time with false hopes and nearly ruined by expenses, an order was published on January 25, 1655—contrary to all expectation—which I have set down word for word in its original language.

<page-num>305</page-num>
# Chap. V. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

It is easy for anyone to imagine the great evils and hardships of fleeing in the middle of winter, especially for such a people, many of whom were elderly and frail, many sick and diseased, besides a multitude of pregnant women or those who had recently given birth, along with a number of vulnerable infants. Yet all were forced to flee, with no one being in a position to help or assist another.

<margin>*Matthew 24*</margin>
This is why our Savior *Jesus Christ* taught his disciples to pray that their flight would not be in the winter, so that in that general calamity, they might at least have the benefit of a favorable season—thus teaching them to pray for a moderation of such a violent persecution. But the Council for the Propagation of the Faith <note>original: *de Propaganda fide*</note>, driven by principles completely opposite and offensive to the spirit of gentleness and kindness in *Jesus Christ*, manifested to the world the inhumanity of this persecution. They purposefully and by design chose the most violent and rigorous winter season to suddenly chase and drive these poor people out of their homes. These people had hardly any clothes to cover their nakedness, much less the supplies needed to survive the extremes of cold and hunger. The Council thought by this means either to force them to change their religion, or else to cause them to perish and die among the craggy rocks and snowy mountains. Indeed, they were so maliciously clever, or rather so cleverly malicious, as to choose those very days and that exact moment when, because of the flooding in the plains and the snow upon the mountains, they judged it absolutely impossible for those poor, innocent sheep <note>original: "silly sheep." In this period, "silly" meant helpless, innocent, or deserving of pity.</note> to ever escape.

Now, these poor people considered that the <term>apostasy</term> <note>the total abandonment of one's religious faith</note> proposed to them by their enemies was a cliff that would lead them to eternal damnation. They chose instead to follow *Jesus Christ* by *bearing his cross*, even though the path was full of *thorns and briars*, and to risk their earthly lives rather than lose their souls forever. Nevertheless, so that they might leave no lawful and just means untried to avoid the sad effects of this cruelty, immediately after the issuance of the cruel decree, they sent their representatives to the Delegate <note>The official carrying out the order, Andrea Gastaldo</note> to explain what a strange command this was: to force them and their entire families to abandon their homes. They also explained that it was absolutely impossible for so many people to survive in the places where they were confined by the decree, as those areas were hardly sufficient to support the people already living there. Furthermore, they argued that this command was expressly contrary to all their legal rights and agreements <note>original: "Concessions"</note>. On these grounds, they made their formal protests and appealed to *His Royal Highness*, their sovereign prince. But the said Delegate, knowing well the intention and design of the Council for the Extirpation of Heretics <note>original: *de Extirpandis hereticis*</note>, would by no means allow either the one appeal or the other. Therefore, the poor people, seeing they could obtain nothing they sought (no matter how just and fair), entreated him to grant them...

<summary>This page describes the immense suffering of the Waldensian people as they were forced to flee their homes in the dead of winter, 1655. It highlights the calculated cruelty of the Catholic Council in choosing a season of extreme weather to force either conversion or death.</summary>

<page-num>305</page-num>
# Motives of the Persecution 1655. Book II.

They hoped, at the very least, to have some time to appeal to *His Royal Highness* <note>Charles Emmanuel II, Duke of Savoy</note> through humble petitions. But even this was refused them, unless they would agree to write their petition according to a specific template that was to be dictated to them. This template was harmful to both their legal rights and their consciences—neither of which they felt they could rightfully sacrifice. 

I say, these poor people, seeing that they could obtain nothing, decided to remove any excuse for accusing them of rebellion (which was being used as a cover to ruin and destroy them). They hoped that eventually they might find a way to bring their grievances before *His Royal Highness*, and that his mercy and justice would eventually restore them to the rightful possession of their property and homes, from which the said Delegate <note>Andrea Gastaldo, the official who issued the expulsion order</note> had driven them. They chose to endure this violence rather than resist; therefore, they withdrew their formal protest to demonstrate their profound respect for their Prince. Leaving behind their houses and goods, they retreated with their families: wives and children, great and small, young and old, healthy and sick. In many places, this included the disabled, the lame, and the blind, along with many young children. They dragged all those who were infirm, whether by sickness or age, through the rain, snow, ice, and a thousand other difficulties.

Here I leave all compassionate souls who are in any way moved by *the afflictions of Joseph* <note>A biblical reference from Amos 6:6, referring to those who are indifferent to the suffering of God's people</note> to imagine the bitter tears and wringing of hands, the beating of breasts, the mourning, sighs, and lamentations in the families of these miserable and distressed creatures. They were now reduced to the greatest extremity imaginable. Before them lay a multitude of violent and roaring waters—though not a Red Sea—and on either side stood most treacherous and snowy mountains! Behind them were men seven times worse than the *Egyptians*, waiting to butcher and destroy them! Yet, recommending themselves, their souls, and their lives to the protection of the *God of their souls and lives*, they were resolved to undergo the worst of temporary miseries rather than incur the pains of eternal fire by abandoning their religion.

The steadfastness and determination of these poor saints provided great comfort to the other churches. On the other hand, it was a matter of great astonishment to their persecutors—especially considering the great advantages to be gained in those parts by leaving the *Reformed Religion* and embracing Catholicism. For example, if they were criminals, they received pardons (as has already been mentioned); if they were prisoners, they were given their liberty. They were also granted exemptions from taxes and duties, as well as from all financial charges, whether property-based or personal, for five years after the day of their <term>abjuration</term> <note>original: "abjuration"; the formal renunciation of their Protestant faith</note>. This was according to the Order of the *Royal Mother and Guardian of His Royal Highness* <note>Christine Marie of France, the Duchess Regent</note>, dated *January* 26, 1642. In practice, this exemption even extended to lands that were transferred to them through false and counterfeit deeds. By such tricks, the poor people who remained constant in their profession of the true religion were burdened with the weight...

# Chap. IV. In the Valleys of Piedmont.
<insert>8307</insert>

...which they took off from the backs of others, to the point that they were completely ruined and undone by it.

In short, they had no sooner departed from their houses than a vast number of thieves and robbers (God knows who incited them) entered their homes, spoiling and pillaging whatever those poor souls <note>original: "Wretches"</note> had left behind. This was a condition far worse than that of the Israelites, who instead of losing anything when they left, actually plundered the Egyptians <note>A biblical reference to Exodus 12:35-36, where the fleeing Israelites took gold and silver from their former masters.</note>. These robbers pulled down their houses, cut down all their trees, and turned the sites of their ancient homes into a chaotic and desolate wilderness. All of this happened without any prohibition or order from the Delegate <note>Andrea Gastaldo, the official overseeing the expulsion</note> to prevent this violence. On the contrary, the Delegate claimed the property was under the protection of *His Royal Highness* <note>Charles Emmanuel II, Duke of Savoy</note>, which clearly shows the hostile intentions of their enemies in this undertaking.

Indeed, when the poor people complained of this violence, the only answer they received from *His Royal Highness* was that they must identify the specific individuals responsible for these acts. Anyone can see at a glance that this was impossible for these poor people, who had been driven two, three, or four leagues away from their homes <note>A league is an archaic unit of distance, usually measuring about three miles.</note>.

Based on this answer, the poor people at least concluded that *His Royal Highness* did not actually intend for them to be driven from their houses, but rather that they should remain there until their case could be heard and judged. With this hope, they gradually began to return to their houses to protect them from these robbers and to farm their lands so they would have the means to pay their taxes. Because of this, they were labeled as rebels <note>original: "branded with Rebellion"</note>, even though their actions gave no cause for suspicion. They had not taken up arms or committed any act of hostility; everyone lived peaceably in their homes without offending anyone.

# CHAPTER V.

## The most humble and earnest supplications of the Evangelical Churches in the Valleys of Piedmont to their Prince, seeking justice against the inhumanity of Gastaldo’s Order.

---

After Gastaldo had driven those poor people out of their ancient <note>original: "antient"</note> inheritances—without either summoning them in a formal and legal way or hearing them plead in their own defense, and (what is more) without allowing them even the slightest time to prepare for such a sorrowful journey—their last refuge was to turn to the Lord through fervent prayers and to their Prince through humble petitions. In these appeals, both those whom Gastaldo had driven from their houses and the rest of the members of the *Reformed Religion* (the cause being common to them all) joined together and drafted their addresses and requests in the following terms.

->May it please your *Royal Highness*,<-

The most faithful and obedient subjects of your *Royal Highness*, who profess the *Reformed Religion* in the Valleys of *Luserna*, *Perosa*, *San Martino*, *Roccapiatta*, *San Bartolomeo*, *Prarostino* <note>original: "Parustino"</note>, and the annexed areas, declare: 

At the very moment they thought they had obtained the <term>ratification</term> <note>original: "Interination"; this refers to the formal legal registration of an edict or grant</note> of their *Ancient Concessions* <note>original: "Concessions"; these were the historical legal rights and religious freedoms granted to the Waldensians by previous dukes</note> confirmed to them by your *Royal Highness*, they were unexpectedly summoned. Those of *Luserna*, *San Giovanni*, *Fenile*, *Bubbiana*, *San Secondo*, *Torre*, *Bricherasio*, and the *borders* of the *Country of Bonetti* were served an *Order* published under the direction of the most Illustrious Lord *Auditor*, Master of the *Chamber* and *Deputy* of your *Royal Highness*, *Andrew Gastaldo*.

This order commanded them to leave their houses and estates within three days under penalty of death, unless they could prove they had become *Catholics* within twenty days. Consequently, all have been forced from their homes. This was done so that they would not have even the slightest failure or default held against them, yet it was done without prejudice to their aforementioned *Concessions*.

There now remain several hundred *families* miserably reduced to the extremes of hunger and cold among the *mountains* and *snow*, where they find no shelter or help. After suffering so much destruction, both now and in the past, they are forced into total desperation. They cannot believe these actions proceed from your *Royal Highness’s* natural character or intention, but rather from some misleading information you have received. Therefore, prostrating themselves at your feet, they most humbly beg you to be pleased to grant the articles written below. They shall continue to pray to God for the prosperity of your *Royal Highness* and your *Royal Family*, and for the expansion of your *dominions*.

1. That you will be pleased to cancel the aforementioned *Order*, as well as every other *Order*—whether already made or yet to be made—by which the petitioners have been harassed because of their *religion*. This includes all *confiscations*, *legal proceedings*, or declarations of punishment, thereby restoring all things to their ancient and peaceful state.

2. To command the most *Illustrious Audit Office* <note>original: "Chamber of Accompts"</note> to *ratify* their *Ancient Concessions*. These were previously *ratified* on August 17, 1620, and your *Royal Highness* confirmed them again on September 29, 1653, with an express declaration not to add to or take away from them. This will allow them to peacefully enjoy the fruits of those rights, just as they did during the happy *reign* of his *Highness Charles Emmanuel*—*your Royal Highness’s uncle* of glorious memory. He made a formal promise to the undersigned deputies in the name of the *natives* and *inhabitants* of the respective *valleys* and *communities*, and confirmed the same to them without any innovation or change.

3. That because of their extreme *desolations*, both past and present, your *Royal Highness* would be pleased to have enough compassion to grant the *ratification* of these requests for free <note>original: "gratis"</note>.

*May it please your Royal Highness,*

*The most faithful and obedient subjects of Your Royal Highness, who profess the Reformed Religion in the Valleys of Luserna, Perosa, San Martino, Roccapiatta, San Bartolomeo, Prarostino, and the surrounding areas, declare: that at the very moment they expected to obtain the <term>interination</term> <note>interination: the formal legal registration or ratification of a document by a sovereign or court</note> of their ancient rights <note>original: "concessions"</note>, which Your Royal Highness had confirmed for them, they were unexpectedly summoned. Therefore, having all been evicted—complying only so that no fault or disobedience could be charged against them, and without giving up their legal rights—several hundred families now remain miserably reduced to the extremes of hunger and cold among the mountains and snow. They cannot believe these actions proceed from Your Royal Highness’s own natural character or intentions, but rather from some malicious <note>original: "sinister"</note> misinformation. Therefore, kneeling at your feet, they most humbly beg you to be pleased to grant them the following articles; they shall continue to pray to God for the prosperity of Your Royal Highness and your entire Royal Family, and for the expansion of your dominions.*

That you would be pleased to revoke both the aforementioned order and every other order, whether already made or yet to be made, by which the petitioners have been harassed because of their religion. This includes all confiscations, legal proceedings, or declarations of punishment, thereby restoring all things to their former peaceful state.*

*2. To command the most illustrious Chamber of Accounts <note>original: "Chamber of Accompts"; the government body responsible for financial and legal records</note> to formally register <note>original: "make an Interination of"</note> their ancient rights. These rights were formerly registered on August 17, 1620, and Your Royal Highness also confirmed them on September 29, 1653, with an express declaration neither to add to nor take away from them. This would allow them to peaceably enjoy the benefits of those rights, just as they did during the happy reign of His Highness Charles Emmanuel (Your Royal Highness's uncle of glorious memory), who made a formal promise to the undersigned deputies in the name of the natives, inhabitants, and communities of the respective valleys, and confirmed those rights to them without any innovation or alteration whatsoever.*

*3. That because of the extraordinary devastation they have suffered both in the past and present, Your Royal Highness would be moved to compassion and grant the registration of these requests free of charge <note>original: "gratis"</note>.*

# Chapter V. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

May it please your *Royal Highness*,

The most faithful and obedient subjects of your *Royal Highness*, professing the *Reformed Religion* in the *Valleys of Luserna*, *Perosa*, *San Martino*, *Roccapiatta*, *San Bartolomeo*, *Prarostino*, and the annexed places, declare: 

At the very moment they thought they had obtained the *ratification* <term>original: "Interination"; the official registration and legal validation of a decree</term> of their *Ancient Concessions*—which were confirmed to them by your *Royal Highness*—they were unexpectedly summoned. Specifically, those of *Luserna*, *San Giovanni*, *Fenile*, *Campiglione*, *San Secondo*, *Torre*, *Bricherasio*, and the *borders* near the *Town of Bonetti* were served an *Order* published by the direction of the most *Illustrious Lord Auditor*, *Master of the Chamber* and *Deputy* of your *Royal Highness*, *Andrea Gastaldo*. This order commanded them to leave their houses and estates within three days, upon pain of *death*, unless they could prove they had become *Catholics* within twenty days. 

Consequently, they have all been dislodged. They complied only so that no fault or default could be held against them, and without giving up their rights to the aforementioned *Concessions*. There now remain several hundreds of *families* miserably reduced to the extremes of hunger and cold among the *mountains* and *snow*. They find no shelter or help there, which—after so many ruins suffered both now and in the past—has forced them almost to total despair. They cannot believe these actions proceed from your *Royal Highness’s* natural inclination or intention, but rather from some *malicious reports* <note>original: "sinister Information"</note>. 

Therefore, prostrating themselves at your feet, they most humbly Beseech you to be pleased to grant the following *Articles*. They shall continue to pray to God for the prosperity of your *Royal Highness*, your *Royal Family*, and for the expansion of your *Dominions*.

1. That you will be pleased to recall both the aforementioned *Order* and every other *Order* whatsoever, whether already made or yet to be made, by which the *Petitioners* have been harassed on account of their *Religion*. This includes reversing all *confiscations*, *legal proceedings*, or declarations of punishment, thereby restoring all things to their ancient and peaceful state.

2. That you give a command to the most *Illustrious Chamber of Accounts* to formally *ratify* <term>original: "Interination"</term> their said *Ancient Concessions*. These were previously *ratified* on August 17, 1620, and your *Royal Highness* also confirmed them on September 29, 1653, with an express *declaration* not to add to or take away from them. This will allow them to peacefully enjoy the *benefits* of those rights, just as they did during the happy *reign* of his *Highness Charles Emmanuel*, *Your Royal Highness’s Uncle* of *glorious memory*. He made a formal promise to the undersigned *Deputies* in the name of the *natives* and *inhabitants* of the respective *Valleys* and *communities*, and confirmed the same to them without any innovation or alteration whatsoever.

3. That in light of their strange *devastations* past and present, your *Royal Highness* would be pleased to have compassion on them and grant the *ratification* <term>original: "Interination"</term> of these requests *without cost* <note>original: "gratis"</note>.

Supplications of the Evangelical Churches, Book II.

In this way, those poor distressed churches used every lawful means imaginable for their survival, having recourse to their Sovereign Prince. He certainly should have shown himself to be their **Nursing-father** <note>A biblical reference to Isaiah 49:23, implying a ruler's duty to protect and nourish his subjects</note> in this time of great misery and oppression, and should have protected them under his wings *from the blast of the terrible ones, which was now like a storm against the wall.* <note>A reference to Isaiah 25:4</note> But alas, they found both his ears, and the ears of all men, closed to their woeful cries, with no possibility of even entering into his **Royal Highness’s** presence.

Among many other schemes and subtle tricks used by their malicious adversaries for this purpose, a new plot was hatched five days after the publication of Gastaldo’s Order (dated January 30, 1655). To further anger and embitter the spirits of both his **Royal Highness** and the **Duchess** his mother against their poor **Protestant** subjects—and consequently to disgust them from listening to their requests—Jean Ange Ressan, President of the Province of Pignerolio, devised a strategy. Ressan, a most persistent persecutor of the **Protestants** and a person in the pay of **Rome**, used a tactic not unlike the one **Nero** used against the ancient **Christians** to make them hated by all people and to wipe them off the face of the earth. 

Just as that wicked **Nero** first caused the city of **Rome** to be set on fire and then spread a report that the **Christians** were the authors of it, so this wicked Ressan acted. Having held a deadly grudge against the Priest of **Fenile** for many years (as was well known to all the neighbors), he took this opportunity to *kill two birds with one shot*. He hired someone to assassinate the priest. At the same time, he ordered his secretary to spread a report throughout the entire country—both by letter and by word of mouth—that the **Protestants** (who had been driven out of **Fenile** about five days earlier) were the authors of that murder. 

This report, though entirely false, came from the mouths and pens of the **Roman Catholics**. It was received with such general applause among the **Catholics** living in distant parts that it was believed to be as authentic as the **Sibyl’s Oracles** <note>original: "Sybils Oracles"; ancient prophecies that were considered divinely inspired and unquestionable</note>. Soon after, the story was presented to the world through the *magnifying* and *multiplying lenses* of the ***Parisian Gazette*** <note>An early influential newspaper (Gazette de France) that often carried biased reports of the conflict</note>. 

However, on the scene, the **underlying cause** <note>original: "Causa causati"</note> or chief author of this assassination and murder was so well known that whatever reports were raised, they could not convince the dead priest's friends and relatives. Nor did the rumors stop them from arresting both the secretary and his master. By this means, the innocence of the **Reformed** party was made manifest to the world. Indeed, the **Marquess of Pianezza**, in those very letters where he sought every pretext he could devise to accuse them, was too shrewd to mention this incident at all, for fear of ruining the credibility of all his other claims.

After this, it happened that a man named **Berru** most inhumanely assassinated **Pietro Revoir**, the **Consul of Meana** (which adjoins **La Cappella**, belonging to the **King**). Afterward, he fled to **Pignerolio**, where he...

Despite the propaganda, the plot was exposed when the priest's own family suspected Ressan, proving the Protestants' innocence in the matter.</summary>

# Chap. V. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

[Berru] was met with by this **Reissan**, who had now returned from **Turin**, where he had been detained as a prisoner for a long time. He had obtained his liberty only by providing very significant security <note>meaning: he was out on bail</note>, because the aforementioned **Berru** and others had not long before sworn under oath that both **Reissan** and his secretary **D'Agot** were guilty of the assassination mentioned above. 

But after some private meetings and conversations, **Reissan** so manipulated the miserable wretch **Berru** with gifts and promises that he finally persuaded him to return with him to **Turin**. There, **Berru** was to not only retract and recant his former testimony, but also to swear that he had been pressured to lie by the two pastors, **Leger** and **Michelin**, as well as by **Antonio** and **Francisco Danna**, the chief elders of the church of **San Giovanni**. In short, by means of this **wicked retraction and slander**, both **Reissan** and his secretary were discharged and cleared in the month of **July 1655**. This occurred during the very heat of the war between the **Catholics** and the **Protestants**, so they had the freedom to forge whatever lies they pleased against the Protestants at both **Luserna** and **Turin** without the slightest opposition; which they certainly did to great effect. 

At **Luserna**, two personal citations <note>legal summons</note> were published at that same time against **Leger**, **Michelin**, and **Danna**. As for **Berru**, he was also released and set free at the same time as a reward for the perjury **Reissan** had procured from him, even though he had been convicted of two assassinations: the one we have already mentioned, and another at **San Giovanni**, where he murdered a Protestant named **Giovanni Bertot**. 

After this treacherous and base action, **Berru** came—like **Sinon** to the **Trojans** in **Virgil's** *Aeneid* <note>Sinon was a Greek spy who pretended to be a victim of his own people to trick the Trojans into accepting the wooden horse</note>—to the said **Leger** and a great number of the pastors and leaders of the Valleys. Leaning upon his staff and bemoaning his condition, he protested, *“That he was hardly able to stand upright because of the many blows and knocks he had received from the Papists to make him swear falsely against Leger and the rest. But,”* he claimed, *“as he could not in conscience do such a wicked thing, he had resisted them to the utmost, telling those who pressured him plainly that he would rather endure being torn to pieces by wild horses. Seeing his constancy, they had beaten him most unmercifully and then cast him out into the middle of the open street, where he would have miserably died if a certain Jew had not had compassion on him, picking him up as he lay groveling on the ground, ready to die.”*

In the meantime, the Treaty of Peace was finalized at **Pinerolo** <note>original: "Pigneroglio"</note> in the month of **August 1655**. Mr. **Leger** and the others, against whom the legal proceedings had been made as if they were criminals—something they never even dreamed of!—were staying at **Pinerolo** and came to hear the news. They immediately went to the Prefect **Reissan**, who was the chief minister of justice (or rather, injustice) in that province, and earnestly entreated him to tell them if it were true that **Berru** had accused them. He answered them in such vague and doubtful terms that they began to have a very great suspicion <note>original: "jealousie"</note> of the matter, so much so that they thought it high time to seek immediate help from the Senator...

Perrichini <note>original: "Perrashino"</note>, who had been appointed shortly before by his Royal Highness to investigate the assassination of the priest, was urged by the Protestant leaders with all possible persistence to explain the truth of the entire matter and to set a time and place for them to present their defense. 

Upon this request, the Senator told them plainly that **Berru** had indeed accused them of bribing him to swear falsely against **D’Agot** <note>Reissan’s secretary</note> and his master. He then showed them a **copy of the summons against the said Leger** and the rest of his accomplices. The substance of the summons was **to banish them from the territories of his Royal Highness if they did not appear in person at Turin to answer the interrogations regarding that business.**

Faced with this, the **Pastor Leger**, with the assistance of the minister **David Leger**, managed the situation so that they immediately had **Berru** arrested in the plain of **Angrogna**. Berru had recently arrived there and was lurking by the roads where **Leger** usually traveled, specifically intending to assassinate him at the first opportunity. This wretch, finding himself caught by surprise, used every trick he could to escape their hands, even though they assured him they intended nothing more than to make him verify what he had previously confessed before a full assembly of their ministers and others.

When the **Pastor Leger** was certain that **Berru** was in secure custody, he went and openly declared the whole story to the **Senator Perrichini**, to the **Referendary Tarquin** <note>a high-ranking administrative and legal official</note>, and even to **Reissan** himself, who was suddenly very surprised by the news. After that, he told the **French Ambassador** and the **Ambassadors of the Swiss Protestant Cantons**. In the end (though with much difficulty), he obtained permission to bring the perjurer to **Pinerolo** <note>original: "Pigneroglio"</note>, where he hoped to get permission to face him in open court. To that end, he strongly petitioned all the ministers of his Royal Highness, as well as the **French** and **Swiss Ambassadors**, for their mediation. The Swiss ambassadors openly declared that if a trial were refused, they would formally complain **regarding the denial of justice** <note>original Latin: "De denegatâ Justitiâ"</note>. 

However, the plain truth is that the only satisfaction the injured parties received was a promise **that a letter would be written to Turin about it**. A while later, the **answer from Turin was that nothing could be done in the matter.** 

Thus, **Leger** was forced to be satisfied with the honor of having captured a perjurer and with being declared innocent. Indeed, both he and the others accused by the Royal Ministers were declared—in the presence of the **Ambassadors** and all the deputies of the **Valleys**—by the mouth of **Monsieur Balcet**, a notary of **Pragelato**, to be entirely innocent and clearly justified **against the accusations Berru had made**. 

But as for any other formal annulment of the charges, they were led to believe that since the third **summons** had not yet been published, Berru's accusation was not legally valid, and therefore they should just let the matter rest. After this, **Berru was taken to Turin**, from where he was reportedly sent to the **Venetian Galleys** <note>a harsh sentence of forced labor rowing on warships</note>, even though he had been convicted (as has been already...

Indeed, the young man described all the circumstances of the event so simply and clearly that he left not the least doubt or hesitation in their minds about the truth of his words. Besides all this, the mother-in-law and wife of this **Berru** assured them that the matter happened exactly as it was described. 

Certainly, although it is very difficult to penetrate the depths of the devil's schemes <note>original: "Depths of Satan"</note>, this business looks very suspicious. For if **Berru** had testified justly and rightfully against those ministers, why would he have refused to be brought face-to-face with them to bring those impostors and bribers <note>original: "suborners"</note> to justice? On the contrary, if the ministers were innocent, why should a man charged with no less than two assassinations and two counts of perjury be allowed to escape? No, even if there had been no stronger arguments than those sad complaints and those bitter tears alone, which that poor widow of **Meun** poured out at **Pinerolo** <note>original: "Pigneroglio"</note> while demanding justice from **Monsieur de Servient**, they were enough (one would have thought) to have moved the very stones in the walls to have pity and compassion for her. 

To conclude, it is all too evident that some more mighty and powerful adversary of the Reformed party, waiting in ambush, was the true mastermind of this murder to create a better excuse <note>original: "pretext"</note> for all their cruel dealings. However, it may have been immediately carried out by inferior hands, who—had they not been protected by such powerful interests—would have certainly received no better reward for their efforts than **Giovanni Odin** of **Angrogna** did not long before. Based on these and similar frivolous and fabricated accusations, the representatives <note>original: "Deputies"</note> of those poor people and their petitions <note>original: "Supplications"</note> were unhappily and miserably rejected by the Court of *Savoy*. After they had gone to *Turin* to present their request, and to urgently beseech the chief ministers of state to favor them with an audience in His Royal Highness’s presence so they could cast themselves at his feet, their path was blocked. The Council for the Propagation of the Faith and the Extirpation of Heretics <note>original: *De propaganda fide & extirpandis hereticis*</note>—which was composed of the *Archbishop* of *Turin*, His Royal Highness’s Confessor, the *Abbot of La Monta*, the *Prior Rorenco*, the *Lords of Lucerna*, the *Marquess of Pianezza*, the Great *Chancellor*, the Chief *President* of the Chamber, the Chief of the Senate *Ferrais*, and the other Presidents, *Beletis* and *Nomis*—prevented the representatives from having an audience with their prince. Contrary to all justice and equity, this Council took legal control of <note>original: "usurped the cognizance of"</note> this affair, which in no way belonged to them, as they were the opposing party. 

Thus, the people were forced to seek justice from their own oppressors! Even then, something might have been achieved with that Council if the representatives could have only obtained a hearing; it is not impossible, nor even improbable, that some of their consciences might have rebuked them, or that the sight of such misery combined with persistent pleading might have moved them. Yet even this was denied to the poor representatives. They were not even allowed to appear personally before the Council for the Extirpation of Heretics; instead, they were forced to send in their attorney <note>original: "Procurator"</note>, *Gibellino*, a Catholic <note>original: "Papist"</note>. *Gibellino*, knowing full well that excommunication was the certain punishment for anyone who favored the Protestant <note>original: "Heretical Protestant"</note> party in any way, did not dare speak a word until he had fallen on his knees and begged permission from the *Archbishop*, who served as President of the Council. 

The final decision was this: *Those of the Valleys were commanded to make no more requests to His Royal Highness regarding this business, unless they sent representatives with legal authority and power to accept and promise—a poor reward for such a long delay—everything that should be ordered for them.* This answer made the poor people almost despair of ever making another appeal. However, like the persistent widow in the Gospel, they sent their representatives to *Turin* once more with their request, ordered to try and get an audience with His Royal Highness. To this end, among other pleas, they urgently requested *Madam Royal* <note>Christina of France, the Duchess of Savoy and mother of the Duke</note> to have pity on them and help them gain an audience, writing her a letter as follows:

In the year 1638, Your Royal Highness was pleased, according to your justice and clemency, to confirm those ancient grants of the deceased Lord, Duke Charles Emmanuel, your father-in-law of glorious memory, and your most serene predecessors. By your special grace, you have kept us—throughout the time of your most happy reign—without the slightest innovation or change, in a peaceful condition and quiet enjoyment of the same, for which we offer you our most humble acknowledgments. 

Now, may it please Your Royal Highness, our most gracious Princess and Lady: despite that same confirmation of our grants, we face new troubles. Through the sinister and malicious misinformation of those who hate us and bear us ill-will—claiming we have exceeded the boundaries allotted to us by those grants and our ancient customs (the complete opposite of which we shall clearly prove in due time and place)—Auditor Gastaldo <note>Andrea Gastaldo, a judge and official, issued the "Gastaldo Edict" on January 25, 1655, which triggered the humanitarian crisis described here.</note> published an order this past January 25th. 

By this order, all inhabitants of Lucerna, Lucernette, Fenile, Bubiana, Campiglione, San Giovanni, La Torre, Bricherasio, and San Secondo who would not convert to Catholicism <note>original: "turn Catholicks"</note> were commanded to abandon their houses and estates within three days, under penalty of death. Not only that, but they were forced to flee—some to the tops of the mountains in the middle of snow and ice, and many into caves for lack of shelter. 

When they sought relief through most humble requests to Your Royal Highness, they were rejected by your Excellencies, the principal and chief ministers of state. These ministers ordered them to appoint commissioners with sufficient power of attorney <note>original: "Procuration and Authoritie"</note> to make and accept new propositions and conditions; otherwise, we were never to return or appear in their presence again. 

But we are unable to undergo such conditions for several significant reasons learned from the experience of past evils. We judge these new conditions unnecessary because we demand nothing but a confirmation of those grants that were already confirmed in the year 1620 by Your Royal Highness, and to enjoy them as we have done for many ages and from time immemorial under the happy reigns of your most famous predecessors. We refuse to act against our consciences, following the true intent and purpose of our grants, though in all other things we have constantly behaved ourselves as becomes faithful and most obe-

# Chap. V. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

The same was likewise confirmed by a third *Edict* in the year 1620, which was duly registered <note>original: "interinated", meaning the formal registration of an edict by a sovereign court to give it the force of law</note>. Indeed, His Royal *Highness*, who by the grace of God reigns today, after a long and costly <note>original: "chargeable"</note> debate, has confirmed these very same *Concessions* to us with a formal Declaration. He promised not to add to or take away from them, as shown by his Decree of December 29, 1653. 

Yet, despite all this, while we were continuously petitioning for the official registration of those rights and satisfying all the demands of the most Illustrious Chamber of Accounts for that purpose, at the very moment we hoped to obtain our requests according to those laws, Auditor *Gastaldo* arrived. He came with orders to force us to leave our homes in *Fenile*, *Bibiana*, *San Secondo*, *Luserna*, *Lucernetta*, *Bricherasio*, *San Giovanni*, and *La Torre*. In these places, by virtue of the aforementioned concessions—and from time immemorial <note>original: "time out of mind"</note>—we have lived in peace. 

Because of this, more than a thousand families—and very large ones at that—who never did anything against the orders of Your Royal *Highness*, are already ruined by the various disasters they have undergone. They must now perish miserably among the snowy mountains, where they have only the canopy of *heaven* for their shelter and cover. 

Now, being crushed by so many tragedies, all stemming from pure hatred for the *religion* we profess, we had resolved to offer our most humble petitions and flee for refuge to the mercy of His Royal *Highness*, our most serene Prince and Lord. However, we were rejected by their Excellencies, the chief and principal ministers, who threatened never to accept another petition in the future if we did not first submit to certain conditions never required under the happy reign of your most serene *predecessors*. Specifically, they demanded we immediately send *Commissioners* with full power <note>original: "plenipotentiarie power"</note> to conclude and accept new *conditions* which we are completely unable to fulfill. We ask for nothing except that His Royal *Highness* be pleased, according to his frequent gracious promises, to let us enjoy the same *Concessions* we previously enjoyed under his ancestors—especially since there has been no change since the death of the father of Your Most Serene *Highness*, except for changes that have been to our disadvantage.

In these desperate times and calamities, lacking any other counsel in the world except what *Despair* usually suggests to men driven from their homes—and seeing themselves meanwhile plundered by their malicious neighbors, whose goal is to provoke them to some act of revenge so that His Royal *Highness* may have an excuse to be even more angered against them (having already been falsely informed about us to promote our final exile)—and having no freedom of access to His Royal *Highness*, we throw ourselves at the feet of Your Most Serene *Highness*. We turn to you as a *sanctuary*, humbly begging that you would allow yourself to be moved with compassion toward so many hundreds of small and innocent Christian babies. ->Your Royal Highness,<-

From the experience of that singular grace and bountiful favor *which lately moved your* Royal Highness's *clemency to cause an answer to be made to one of our letters (dated February 20th) which we took the boldness to present to you; we hope (as with all humility we request) that you will deign to listen to the present reply which we, your poor subjects, being prostrate at your feet, do here humbly offer to you. *First, while it is alleged that the places prohibited in the order published by* Auditor Gastaldo <note>Auditor Gastaldo: Andrea Gastaldo, the official who issued the January 1655 decree ordering the Waldensians to abandon their homes in specific communes or face death and land confiscation.</note> *have always been opposed and excepted, this cannot be proved regarding the places of* San Giovanni, La Torre, San Secondo, *and the others. On the contrary, they have always granted and permitted us that liberty in all the accustomed places of the three Valleys. Only* Roccapiatta, San Bartolomeo, *and* Prarustino *are named as towns not belonging to the three Valleys, as may be plainly seen in the first article of that grant dated May 14, 1603. ...became disturbed, **His Royal Highness Charles Emanuel** [Charles Emmanuel I, Duke of Savoy] of glorious **memory**, did yet by another **Grant** dated **April 9, 1605**, in the third and sixth **Articles**, permit them to move back into those places. Indeed, in another grant of **September 29** of that same year, it is expressed in formal terms in the very first **Article** that those who owned **property** <note>original: "Goods"</note> outside the prescribed **limits** (that is to say, the **limits** appointed for **preaching**, according to the **Grants** of **1561**) should be permitted to return to their dwellings. In these said **Grants**, the **limits** for **preaching** are often found to differ from those for **habitation**. These **limits** for **habitation** are extended to all the **towns** and places belonging to the three **Valleys**, along with their adjacent areas, as can be seen in the eighth, ninth, eleventh, and twentieth **Articles**, which we shall not repeat here to avoid being tedious.

These facts being represented to his said **Royal Highness** (**Charles Emanuel** of glorious **memory**) made him inclined to revoke the **orders** published against the people of **Fenile, Lucerna,** and **Bubbiana**, and to restore everything to a peaceful condition. He confirmed this with an irrevocable **Edict** dated **August 17, 1602**, for which they paid 6,000 Ducatons <note>original: "Ducatons"; a large silver coin used in Europe at the time</note>, as appears by the decree made and formally registered <note>original: "interinated," meaning officially ratified or recorded</note> at that time by the most Illustrious **Chamber** [of Accounts] and most serene **Senate**.

By all this, it is evident that we are far from having justly deserved the accusation of overstepping the **limits** or abusively seizing the least privilege. On the contrary, we have strictly kept ourselves within our just measure and boundaries, as the *Catastri* <note>original: "Catastri"; official land surveys and tax registers used to prove ownership and residency</note> of the **communities** may sufficiently testify for us.

In the second place, we are accused of many outrages and excesses; but we are not aware of the least offense (after the clearing up of the incident at **Villaro** upon the arrival of **Count** <note>original: "Conte"</note> **Todesco**), except for that forged one at **La Torre**. That incident was so ridiculously invented and interpreted that **Auditor Gastaldo** himself, having discovered its absurdities, promised no more words would be spoken of it. Furthermore, even if any crime had been involved in it, it could not in any way be blamed on those of **Lucerna, Fenile, Bubbiana, Campiglione, Bricherasio, San Secondo**, and the rest. For by the **Grant** of **September 29, 1603 (Article 3)**, as also by that of his **Royal Highness** [Charles Emmanuel II] now reigning by the **Grace of God**, dated **June 4, 1653**, it is plainly declared that the innocent are not to suffer with the guilty, but that **Justice** shall be upheld with a strong hand for the suppression of the rebellious.

As to the escape of **Berruto**, we might truthfully allege that, having secured him in the very place required upon the first demand of **Mr. Collateral** <note>original: "Collateral"; a high-ranking judicial official</note> **Perrachione**, we ought not to be questioned or asked for any further account of him. We were in no way accessories to his escape, especially since we spared no effort to recapture him immediately after that accident happened. It clearly appears by various and sundry **examinations** that he broke **prison** for no other reason than to escape the great hardships and tortures he was in some way threatened with. The great noise and rumor of this, together with the imprisonment of **Berruto**, might well be the reason why others would say little, as they did not dare to bear witness to the **truth** for fear of similar danger. By all these events, your **Royal Highness** may easily see...

# A supplicatory Letter of the poor distressed Churches of the Valleys of Piedmont, to the Marquess of Pianessa, March 16, 1655.

->*Most Excellent Lord,*<- <note>original: *Excellentissimo Segnor*</note>

*The kindness and patience with which Your Excellency deigned to answer the letters that we were so bold as to address to you on the 8th of last February, makes us hope that you will also look upon this present reply, which we come to present to you with due reverence, etc.* <note>original: *La benegnita & pazienza con laquale V. Eccellenza si e degnata risponder alle lettere che s' inardissimo addrizzarle sotto li, 8. cadutto Feb. ci fa sperare che anche adochiera la presente replica, che con la debita riverenza veniamo a presentarle, &cc.*</note>

The kindness and patience with which Your Excellency graciously deigned to answer the letters that we were emboldened to write to you, dated the eighth of last February, gives us some ground to hope that you will accordingly cast your eyes upon this present reply. We present this to you with all due reverence, solely for the purpose of better informing you regarding certain points or articles. We humbly beg your pardon for our slowness in responding, which has been caused—against our will—by the distance between our locations and the difficulty in assembling our people.

First, Your Excellency accuses us of being guilty of many excesses and outrages, and claims that we have given just cause for the publication of the order issued by Auditor Gastaldo <note>Andrea Gastaldo was the official who issued the 1655 decree ordering the Waldensians to convert to Catholicism or leave their homes in the lower valleys within three days.</note>. However, after clearing ourselves of the incident at Villar <note>original: Villaro</note>—which was sufficiently done when Count Tedesco arrived—we have not heard of the slightest misconduct laid to our charge. The only exception might be if Your Excellency were to hold against us that foolish business at Torre Pellice <note>original: La Torre</note>. That was carried out by a group of youths (a large portion of whom were the children of Catholics) and did not reflect poorly on the Catholic Church at all. It did not have the least appearance of being an insult either to the Mass or to those who performed it, as Auditor Gastaldo was very well informed. Indeed, he promised us that nothing more would be said of it. 

Furthermore, even if there had been any offenders involved in such an incident, His Royal Highness declared in the first article of the Act of June 4, 1633—which explained the concessions of September 29, 1603—that it is not at all his intention that the innocent should be punished along with the guilty, provided that we always conduct a severe investigation into the latter (which we have never refused to do). 

Regarding the boundaries of our settlement <note>original: "Limits of Habitation"</note>, Your Excellency has been informed that we claim our defense on the grounds that these boundaries were established after the grants made at Racconigi. Since this is supposedly not true, it is claimed that our dwelling places remain illegally occupied. We entreat Your Excellency with all humility, and for the love of God, to graciously believe that our evidence shows quite another thing. We also argued, on the contrary, that our boundaries have actually been narrowed in some places. We will not even mention our banishment from the Marquisate of Saluzzo, Praviglielmo, Festeone, and many other cities and towns of Piedmont which are not specifically listed here.

*...or expressed in the said grants (even though all those places have been tolerated in the past), but particularly because the Valley of Meana was mentioned in them, along with Campiglione and the town of Bibiana <note>original: "Bubiana"</note>. These were included as part of the towns of the three valleys <note>The "three valleys" historically refers to the Waldensian strongholds of Pellice, Perosa, and San Martino.</note> that were tolerated at that time, and where the Count of Raconigi <note>original: "the reverend Raconigi"</note> resettled us after the wars.*

*His Royal Highness confirmed this in his grants of 1603 and had them legally registered <term>interinated; from the Italian 'interinare', to formally register a decree</term> in the year 1620. It is evident from the answers to the third and sixth articles of the first petition <note>original: "Memorial"</note> dated April 9, 1603, which were given to the people of Fenile, Bibiana, and Luserna—whose residency was the only one facing opposition at that time—that they were permitted to be re-established. This was because those towns and places were common and tolerated within the three valleys designated as the boundaries for living.*

*In the first article of the grant dated September 29 of the year mentioned above, it can be clearly seen that everyone was allowed to return to their respective homes within those three valleys without any exceptions, even if their estates were outside the boundaries designated for preaching. This was confirmed on August 17, 1620, and legally registered in 1620, along with a specific act for the payment of six thousand ducatoons <term>large silver coins used across Europe</term> for that very purpose. Thus, the residency of those living beyond the Pellice River <note>original: "Pelice"</note> was made peaceful, firm, and permanent—even if it was not entirely free from various harassments brought upon them by their ill-intentioned neighbors.*

*Furthermore, Roccapiatta, San Bartolomeo, and Prarustino were not named separately in the third article of the concessions of May 14, 1603, or the first article of those from 1620, for any reason other than that those towns did not belong to the "three valleys," as may be found there. This is a manifest proof that regarding our dwelling or residency, no town belonging to the three valleys that was frequented and tolerated before suffered the slightest opposition.*

*Besides all this, the agreement made by the Lord of Raconigi—which only establishes the limits for preaching (the same limits now being used to define residency)—also permits living outside and beyond the boundaries of preaching in all the other towns of the three valleys and their adjacent parts. When your Excellency's important and serious business allows you to read Articles 8 through 14, 20, and 21 (which we will not detail here to avoid being tedious), we are fully convinced you will see the distinction. Since the limits for preaching have been so often distinguished from the limits for residency—the latter having no boundaries other than the three valleys and their adjacent parts—your Excellency will not blame us for trying to defend the just title of our homes against any misleading <note>original: "sophistical"</note> interpretations and distinctions.*

*Truly, we are far from acting as our own judges in the interpretation of such grants (which belongs only to the Sovereign who makes them). Instead, we submit ourselves entirely to the intentions of the Sovereigns who granted those acts, to the specific terms of their concessions, and to the actual use, practice, and observance of them under their successful government. Nor can it be truthfully claimed that we have in later times encroached upon or expanded our said limits. On the contrary, they have been every*

These and similar ones were the repeated petitions <note>original: "Supplications"</note> of the deputies of those poor, distressed churches, who nevertheless did nothing all the while but *sing to the deaf* <note>original: "Surdo canere"; a Latin proverb meaning to waste words on someone who refuses to listen</note>. They could not possibly obtain an audience with the Duke’s court unless they would agree to give their deputies <term>plenipotentiary power; absolute authority to make decisions and sign agreements without needing to consult their community further</term> as mentioned before. To do this without any limitations, and according to what the Marquess had prescribed for them, they knew very well could have no other result than this: to silently agree to giving up and renouncing their former grants and other privileges. 

In short, when they saw themselves forced into it, they chose their deputies and gave them instructions as thorough as they possibly could. These were signed by all the pastors and deputies of their churches, who were likewise authorized by the governing power of Luserna <note>original: "Lucerna"</note>. The substance of those instructions, after their due declaration of loyalty and obedience, was that they sent their deputies to Turin to accept and promise everything that it should please His Royal Highness to appoint for them, according to their ancient grants and the rules of a good conscience. But just as there is no reasoning with a lion that is greedy for its prey, so were all the pleas and requests in the world of little use in softening the Marquess of Pianessa’s <note>original: "Pionessa’s"</note> stony heart, as he thirsted so violently after the blood of those poor creatures. Accordingly, he brushed aside this last petition of theirs—

He treated their petition with as much disdain as he had the previous one. However, so that he might not too openly reveal the dark plan of the Council for the Propagation of the Faith and the Extirpation of Heretics <note>original Latin: *De propaganda fide & extirpandis Hæreticis*</note> before the moment of its execution, he tried to hide all his answers to the poor people in such cryptic <note>original: "ænigmatical"</note> language—not unlike the way the Devil once spoke through ancient oracles. Though he gave them little comfort, he still left them with a faint hope that they would eventually have a formal hearing <term>Day of Audience: a scheduled formal meeting for a petitioner to present their case to a person of authority</term> to present their grievances and complaints. ## CHAPTER VI.

### A brief and most authentic narrative of some part of those extraordinary cruelties which were exercised against the poor Protestants of the Valleys of Piedmont, during the heat of the late massacre, in the year of our Lord 1655, in the month of April.

Every particular circumstance of this account was abundantly verified to the author during his stay in those parts. This was done both by word of mouth and by the formal attestations and signatures of those very persons who were both eye and ear witnesses of those inhuman cruelties. The author has placed the original documents of some of these accounts on public display in the library of the University of Cambridge <note>Sir Samuel Morland, the author, donated the "Morland Manuscripts"—a collection of Waldensian documents—to Cambridge in 1658</note>; for several important reasons, he has kept the rest in his own custody, ready to give any sincere <note>original: "ingenuous"</note> person full and clear satisfaction.

In the former chapter, the Christian reader received a large account of the Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> design against the poor Evangelical churches of the Valleys; this chapter gives a distinct and faithful narrative of the execution of that plan. Truly, the execution was as perfectly matched to the plan (in terms of cruelty) as a wax impression is to the seal.

On Saturday, April 17, 1655, while the poor deputies of the Protestants were—through the trickery <term>artifice: clever or cunning devices used to deceive</term> of the Marquess of Pianessa—detained at Turin to wait for an answer to their requests (where the fifth and last chapter leaves them), a great army arrived at San Giovanni. This town, together with La Torre and all the lower parts, was by now uninhabited and in a most desolate and lamentable condition. This army encamped for several hours in a place called San Giorgio, and in the dusk of the evening, they entered the borough of La Torre, where they did not meet even a single soul of the Protestants,

...except for a small company of eight or ten people. Unaware that the enemy was there, they were searching around for something to satisfy their hunger. But as soon as they approached the convent, they were immediately spotted by the monks and the soldiers <note>original: "Troopers"</note> who had been hiding there for several days for that very purpose. To show the "kindness" they had for them, the soldiers greeted them with a heavy volley of gunfire, killing Giovanni Combe of Villaro on the spot and wounding Pietro Rostain of La Torre. At this, the rest of the group, seeing themselves surrounded on every side, immediately fled for their lives.

On the following Lord's Day, which was April 18, the enemy roamed up and down throughout the communities of La Torre and San Giovanni <note>original: "St. Giovanni"</note>, plundering and looting at their pleasure. And on the 19th (the army having now become larger like a rolling snowball, their numbers increasing to about fifteen thousand), they attacked the Protestants in several quarters among the hills of San Giovanni and La Torre. 

However, the poor people had long foreseen this plan. Prompted by the law of nature to defend themselves, they took courage and stood their ground. The enemy was vigorously opposed on every side: in one place by Captain Fabier, and in other places by the officers and troops of San Giovanni, Angrogna <note>original: "Angrognia"</note>, and Roccapiatta <note>original: "Roccapiaita"</note>. 

The next day, which was Tuesday, the Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> army made three separate attempts to seize the bell of San Giovanni and to burn the church. This was despite the church being located within the borders of Angrogna—a place the Marquess of Pianezza <note>original: "Pionessa"</note> had always promised to protect, as it was specifically excluded from Gastaldo's order and designated as a retreat for those he had banished and driven from their homes. 

Nevertheless, as a distraction, they attacked the people of San Giovanni who had gathered about a mile away at a place called Castelluzzo <note>original: "Castelus"</note>, on the side of Mount Bricherasio <note>original: "Briquer as"</note>, as well as at La Torre toward Tagliaretto <note>original: "Taliaret"</note>. But the poor people who were then under arms resisted them so courageously that the enemy was forced into a shameful retreat, losing about fifty of their men. Had their cavalry not defended the plain, they would have been utterly defeated. Meanwhile, none of the Protestants were killed, except for one man from Roccapiatta (whose corpse they brutally desecrated <note>original: "upon whose dead Carkase they sufficiently revenged themselves"</note>) and another, namely Giovanni Brocher of San Giovanni. 

On the 21st of the same month—which was the terrible, fatal day for the poor Protestants—the Marquess of Pianezza, using a hellish trick <note>original: "stratagem"</note>, held the deputies of the Luserna <note>original: "Lucerna"</note> Valley in negotiations <note>original: "Parley"</note> until noon. He then treated them to a large dinner, after which they went their way with much satisfaction and cheerfulness; their minds were as full of good hopes as their bellies were of meat. Indeed, the Marquess of Pianezza had fully persuaded them with his smooth language and solemn promises <note>original: "asseveration"</note> that no harm would come to anyone, except for those of San Giovanni and La Torre, as those were the places specified in Gastaldo's order to...

...be prohibited to those of the Reformed party. But as for all the rest, if they would only receive and quarter a few troops as a token of their obedience, and that for only a short time, they could set their hearts at rest without fear or suspicion <note>original: "jealousie"</note> of the slightest trouble <note>original: "inconvenience"</note>. Thereupon, the agents of *Angrogna* went to the leaders of those who were allegedly only supposed to go and quarter in those places. They did their best <note>original: "bestirred themselves"</note> with every possible persuasion to keep the men of their own party from making even the slightest resistance. Those of *Villaro* and *Bobbio* <note>original: "Bobio"</note> did the same, never dreaming of the sad consequences of such great recklessness <note>original: "unadvisedness"</note>. 

But the enemy's men had no sooner entered than the inhabitants found (when it was too late) how poorly the Catholics keep faith with those they call heretics. For after using every possible trick to draw the rest within their reach, they immediately closed their nets <note>original: "clapt to their Nets"</note> and divided the prey. They put everything to fire and sword, slaying everyone they met who even had the likeness of a human being <note>original: "Mankinde"</note>, and doing so in the most barbarous manner they could possibly devise. For a general description of this, I shall refer the reader to an extract from one of their own letters before I provide a more detailed account of those horrid and unheard-of cruelties.

“...proposals, or instructions sufficient to empower them to promise and accept, on behalf of their respective churches, whatever his Royal Highness chose to grant or bestow upon them. By the instigation and planning <note>original: "contrivance"</note> of the Roman Catholic clergy, an army of six thousand men was secretly set in ambush. Suddenly—encouraged by the presence and vigorous efforts of the Marquis of Pianezza—they violently attacked the people of San Giovanni and La Torre.

“Once this army had entered and established a foothold, it grew rapidly. It was joined by a multitude of neighboring inhabitants from throughout all Piedmont. Hearing that we had been given over as prey to plunderers, they fell upon the poor people with impulsive fury. Added to these were countless outlaws, prisoners, and other offenders who believed that by doing this, they could both save their souls and fill their purses. To better execute their plan, they were forced to receive five or six regiments of the French Army, along with some Irish soldiers—to whom, it is reported, our country was promised. They also took in several other troops of highwaymen and vagabonds under the pretext of coming into the valleys for a *rinfresco* <note>Italian: "refreshment"; here used as a military term for seeking fresh quarters or re-provisioning</note>.

“This vast multitude, authorized by the Marquis of Pianezza, was animated by the monks and led into this work by our wicked and unnatural neighbors. They fell upon us with such violence from every side and in such a horribly treacherous manner—especially in Angrogna, Villar, and Bobbio. The Marquis had promised <note>original: "engaged himself"</note> these towns that if they would only agree to house and quarter a single regiment in each community, they would be kept safe from all harm or violence. Yet, in a single moment, everything was turned into a heap of confusion. After some skirmishes fought in self-defense, the inhabitants were forced to flee for their lives with their wives and little children. This included not only those from the plains who had sought refuge in the mountains, but also the mountain dwellers themselves, who would otherwise have been betrayed and surprised. 

“Despite all the diligence they could possibly use for their preservation, it was not sufficient to prevent the destruction of a very large number of them. In many places, such as Villar and Bobbio, they were so hemmed in on every side—the enemy having seized the Fort of Mirabouc <note>original: "Miraburg"</note> and blocked the passage—that there was no way left to escape. They were most dreadfully massacred and put to death. In one location, they cruelly tormented no fewer than 150 women and small children, later chopping off the heads of some and dashing the brains of others against the rocks. As for a large portion of the prisoners they took, aged fifteen years and up, who refused to attend the Catholic Mass <note>The Waldensians were Protestants being forced to convert to Catholicism</note>, they

I presume the Christian reader is now somewhat prepared, by what has been already hinted, to behold with greater steadfastness <note>original: "constancy"</note> those doleful spectacles which he shall have presented here before his eyes. The truth is, the cruelties related here would far exceed the belief of any man (except for the authors and perpetrators of them) were they not accompanied by such authentic proofs that he who denies their truth must, at the same time, deny his own reason and understanding. 

For if the formal testimonies <note>original: "Attestations"</note> of those who were eyewitnesses and bystanders may carry any weight with us; if the strong and woeful cries of so many desolate and poor wretches—who have been miserably robbed and deprived of their relatives, houses, lands, and all other comforts—may in any way gain our belief; in a word, if the formal sworn statement <note>original: "deposition"</note> of one of the chief commanders of that very army who performed those cruelties, signed with his own hand in the presence of two sufficient witnesses, may persuade us to give any credit to such a report; or (which is yet one degree closer) if the voluntary confession of one of the soldiers themselves—one who had his own hands soaked <note>original: "embrewed"</note> in the blood of those poor creatures—boasting to some of his comrades that he had many times during the heat of the massacre surfeited <note>original: "surfetted"; meaning he ate to the point of illness</note> by eating the boiled brains of those <term>Barbets</term> (or Protestants)...

<margin>Note here that in Piedmont they call those "Barbets" whom they call "Huguenots" in France.</margin>

...I say, if the voluntary confession of such cannibals as these may be accepted as authentic proof, then I do not doubt I can give full satisfaction to everyone—as well to those who would prefer not to believe as to those who cannot yet easily believe such monstrous cruelties. I have inserted here the true copies of the said depositions and attestations (which are indeed worthy of being shared with posterity) and have presented the very original signed documents <note>original: "Subscriptions"</note> to the public library of the famous University of Cambridge.

<page-num>333</page-num>
<header>Chapter VI. In the Valleys of Piedmont.</header>

## The Declaration of Monsieur du Petit Bourg, first Captain of the Regiment of Grancey, regarding the cruelties that were exercised upon persons of all ages and sexes among the poor Protestants of the Valleys of Piedmont, signed with his own hand at Pinerolo <note>original: "Pignerol"</note>, November 27, 1655, in the presence of two other commanders.

The true original of which is to be seen, together with the rest, in the Public Library of the famous University of Cambridge.

<note>The following text was originally printed in two columns: French on the left and a contemporary English translation on the right. Both have been modernized and combined here for clarity.</note>

I, Sieur <note>A title of respect, similar to "Sir" or "Lord"</note> du Petit Bourg, first Captain of the Regiment of Grancey and commander of the same, received directions from *Prince Thomas* to go and join with the *Marquis* of *Pianezza* <note>original: "Pianeſſe"</note> and to receive his orders (the *Marquis* was then at *La Torre*). ...easing of the situation <note>original: "mitigation of Affairs"</note> that this or any other consideration I could offer him produced. As for what he claims in the same declaration—namely, that no harm was done to anyone except during the fight, nor the least outrage committed against any persons unfit to bear arms—I assert and will maintain that this is not so. I saw with my own eyes several men killed in cold blood, as well as women, elderly persons, and young children miserably murdered.

When prisoners were brought to the Marquis of Pianezza, I saw orders given that everyone must be killed, because His Highness wanted no people of the [Protestant] religion in all his lands.

Regarding all that he protests in the same Declaration, that no one was ever touched except in combat, nor the least outrage done to persons unfit for arms, I maintain that this is not true, since I have seen with my own eyes men murdered in cold blood, and women, the elderly, and small children miserably killed.

### Sara Rastignole des Vignes.

**S**ara Rastignole des Vignes, about sixty years of age, was overtaken in a certain place called Eyvals by several <note>original: "divers"</note> soldiers. She was commanded by them to say her prayers, which after she had done, they urged her to repeat *Jesus Maria* <note>Latin: "Jesus Maria" (Jesus Mary), a Catholic invocation the Protestant Waldensians refused on theological grounds</note>. But the poor woman refusing to do it, one of the soldiers thrust a sickle into

<image-desc>An engraving illustrating the martyrdom of Sara Rastignole des Vignes. In the center, a naked woman lies prostrate on the ground and is being dragged by her feet by several soldiers armed with halberds and wearing 17th-century style armor and hats. To the left, another woman is shown kneeling in prayer while being accosted by a soldier. The scene takes place in a mountainous landscape with a small stone building in the distance.</image-desc>

the lower part of her belly and ripped her up to the navel. Afterward, they dragged the poor, miserable creature across the ground while she was half dead, until another of them came and severed her head from her body. The daughter-in-law of this poor woman—who was forced to hide herself in the snow for two days afterward without any help <note>original: "succour"</note> or nourishment—was an eyewitness to this horrible butchery.

### Martha Constantine of St. Giovanni.

A certain woman of *St. Giovanni* <note>Modern: San Giovanni Pellice</note>, whose name (as it is credibly believed) was *Martha Constantin*, the wife of *Jacopo Barral*, after she had seen several others before her most cruelly put to death, was herself first raped <note>original: "ravished"</note>, and then had her breasts cut off, as well as her private parts <note>original: "privities"</note>, by some of the soldiers. They also carried these remains to *Macel* <note>Modern: Massello</note> in *Piedmont*, where they fried them and set them before some of their other comrades whom they met there by accident, making them believe that they were tripe. But after they had eaten a good portion of them, the soldiers told them plainly that they were nothing other than women's breasts <note>original: "dugs"</note>, etc. This

<image-desc>An engraving depicting a scene of wartime atrocity. In the foreground, three soldiers in 17th-century military attire (broad-brimmed hats and boots) are assaulting a woman on the ground. was taken so extremely ill by those who had been thus deceived <note>original: "beguiled"</note>, that a quarrel immediately arose because of it—and indeed not without sufficient reason. For all those who had eaten the flesh found it to be of such poor digestion, and it lay so heavy in their stomachs, that they straightway became severely sick from it, and some of them died soon after. This is certified by a man from *Dauphiné*, a *Roman Catholic* (whom it would be easy to name if necessary), and he related the story to one *Andrea Pavel* of *Pinasca* <note>original: "Pinachia"</note>.
