### The Servant of Jacopo Michalino of Bobbio

A certain man from Trassiniere, a servant of Jacopo Michalino of Bobbio <note>Modern: Bobbio Pellice</note>, was taken prisoner on the 8th of May. He received several stabs with a dagger in the soles of his feet and in his ears at the hands of one Guglielmo Roche—a notorious murderer <note>original: "Massacrer"</note> of Luserna—and another man named Mandolin. These men afterwards cut off his genitals <note>original: "privy Members"</note> and then applied a burning candle to the wound, searing it with the flame so that the blood might be stopped and the torments of that miserable creature prolonged.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting scenes of religious persecution and torture. On the left, a man is tied by his wrists and suspended from a wooden frame. In the center and right, several soldiers dressed in 17th-century attire, including wide-brimmed hats and breeches, carry halberds and swords. One figure appears to be dragging or attacking a victim on the ground near a stone building. The background shows a sparse landscape with hills.</image-desc>

Once they were satisfied with this, they tore off his nails with hot pincers to see if they could force him by any means to renounce his religion. When nothing worked, they tied one of his legs to the Marquess of Luserna’s mule and dragged him through the streets until he had almost ended his painful life. Then, binding his head with a cord, they tightened and twisted it with a staff so hard that it caused his eyes and brains to drop out of his head. 

In the end, when they had sufficiently satisfied their appetites with all the various cruelties they could devise, they cast the dead carcass into the river, so that both elements <note>The author refers to the classical elements—in this case, Earth and Water—as witnesses to the crime</note> might be better able one day to bear witness against their barbarous and inhumane actions.

### *Martha Constantine of San Giovanni.*

A certain woman of *San Giovanni* <note>Modern: San Giovanni Pellice</note>, whose name (as it is reliably believed) was *Martha Constantine*, the wife of *Jacopo Barral*, witnessed several others before her being most cruelly put to death. She herself was first raped <note>original: "ravisht"</note> and then had her breasts cut off, as well as her private parts <note>original: "Privities"</note>, by some of the soldiers. These soldiers also carried the severed parts to *Macello* <note>original: "Macel"</note> in *Piedmont* <note>original: "Piemont"</note>, where they fried them and served them to some of their comrades whom they happened to meet there. They led them to believe the meat was *tripe* <note>original: "Tripes"; animal stomach lining used as food</note>. But after the comrades had eaten a good portion of it, the soldiers told them plainly that it was nothing other than *women's breasts* <note>original: "Dugs"</note>.

<image-desc>An engraving depicting a scene of extreme violence and cruelty. In the foreground, a group of soldiers in seventeenth-century attire are attacking a woman. This was taken so extremely poorly by those who had been thus deceived <note>original: "beguiled"</note> that a quarrel immediately broke out, and with good reason. All those who had eaten the meat found it so impossible to digest, and it lay so heavy in their stomachs, that they immediately became gravely ill, and some of them died soon after. This account is certified by a man from *Dauphiné* <note>A province in southeastern France</note>, a *Roman Catholic* (whom it would be easy to name, if necessary), and he related the same story to one *Andrea Favel* of *Pinache* <note>original: "Pinachia"; a town in the Chisone Valley</note>.

### Jacopo Perrin and his brother David, of Villaro

Jacopo Perrin, an elder of the church of *Villaro*, and his brother *David*, were taken prisoner in their beds in a village called *La Baudine*. They were carried from there to *Lucerna*, where they were thrown <note>original: "clapt up"</note> into the Marquess's prison and treated most barbarously and inhumanely. Among other things, the bloody butchers of that place stripped the skin from their arms and legs in long slices, shaped like leather laces <note>original: "Leathern points"; these were narrow strips or cords used to fasten clothes</note>, until the flesh was left completely bare. At length, they were miserably starved to death in that same prison, where their carcasses were left to lie and rot <note>original: "putrifie"</note>.

### A poor Woman of Villaro, with her young Infant

Giovanni Tolafano, a merchant <term>original: "mercer"; a dealer in textile fabrics</term> of Villaro, was passing by the Hill of St. Julian when he saw a poor woman fleeing from the soldiers. She carried a cradle upon her head, in which was a young nursing child. Seeing that she was likely to be overtaken by them, she left her cradle in the middle of the path, truly believing that those butchers could not possibly have hearts of stone <term>original: "Adamant"; a legendary rock or mineral of unbreakable hardness</term> enough to lay violent hands upon the poor innocent babe. She then hid herself not far from that place in the cleft of a rock.

### *Jacopo Michelino of Bobbio.*

*Jacopo Michelino*, one of the primary Elders of the Church of *Bobbio*, was taken prisoner. His hands were tied to his genitals <term>original: "privy Members"</term>, and he was afterwards hung from a certain gate in a most shameful position. But alas, the shame was nothing compared to the torture; because the entire weight of his body hung from such a sensitive area, the pain was agonizing and almost beyond belief. All this was done to force him, if possible, to renounce his religion. However, seeing that they could not prevail, they carried him away along with other prisoners, where—

<image-desc>A black and white engraving illustrating the torture of Jacopo Michelino. In the center, a man is suspended from the inner arch of a large stone gateway by a rope tied to his genitals, his hands bound behind his back. To the left, a group of prisoners is being marched away by armed guards wearing 17th-century style hats and carrying pikes. The background shows a fortified stone tower and other buildings under a cloudy sky. In the foreground, a large, rough-hewn log lies on the ground.</image-desc>

—after enduring a world of other cruelties with incredible steadfastness <note>original: "constancy"</note>, he exchanged the sufferings of this miserable life for the joys of the next <note>meaning: he died and went to heaven</note>. In a similar manner, *Pietro Gras*, during the time he was a prisoner, saw two of the poor Protestants a little above *La Sarcena* hanging in a most hideous manner, supported solely by their genitals with their hands tied behind them. They remained there until at last their very internal organs <term>original: "bowels"</term> were almost torn out, and they died in horrible pain and anguish.

### *Jacopo di Ronc*

**Jacopo di Ronc**, a schoolmaster of **Rora** <note>original: "Roras"</note>, was stripped stark naked. After they had torn off his nails with pincers and made a thousand holes in his hands with a dagger's point, he was dragged by a rope fastened around his waist through the town <note>original: "Bourg"</note> of **Lucerna**. With every step he took, one of the soldiers on one side cut off a piece of his flesh with a <term>falchion</term> <note>original: "Fauchion"; a broad, curved medieval sword</note>, and another soldier on the other side gave him a heavy blow with a staff, crying out, "Well, **Barbet** <note>A derogatory term used by Catholics for the Waldensian pastors, literally meaning "uncles"</note>, will you go to Mass now?" <note>original: "E ben Barbet andares tu à la Meſſa?"</note> To which the poor creature, with incredible constancy as long as he was able to speak, answered, "Death is much better than the Mass! Kill me quickly for the love of God!" <note>original: "Piu preſt la Mort, que la Meſſa! amaſſeme preſt per amour di Dio!"</note> 

<image-desc>An engraving depicting the torture and martyrdom of Jacopo di Ronc. In the center, a naked man is tied with a rope around his waist and is being dragged forward. Several soldiers in seventeenth-century attire surround him; one on the left strikes him with a heavy staff, while others carry halberds. To his right, a soldier raises a sword to strike him. In the background, other figures are being pushed into a river, and armed men stand on the hilly banks. The scene illustrates the violent persecution described in the text.</image-desc>

Shortly after, a famous persecutor named **Villelmin Roche** arrived. As soon as he saw him, he cried out, "Look, here is the minister of **Rora**!" and gave him a deadly blow across the head with a <term>back-sword</term> <note>A sword with a single sharpened edge and a thick back</note>. After this, he had him brought to the **L’ayal** bridge, and cutting off his head, threw him into the **Pellice** <note>original: "Pelis"</note> River. The river rolled the dead body down as far as **Bibiana** <note>original: "Bubliana"</note>, where it was eventually found and buried.

### Paolo Garnier

**Paolo Garnier** of **Rora** <note>original: "Roras"</note>, having been captured by those murderers, first had his eyes violently pulled out. They then cut off his genitals <note>original: "privy Members"</note> and thrust his penis <note>original: "Yard"</note> into his mouth; in this condition, they exposed him to public view for several days.

<image-desc>An engraving depicting scenes of brutal torture in a 17th-century setting. Not satisfied with this, they later skinned this poor soul alive <note>original: "stript this poor Creature alive"</note> in a most barbaric <note>original: "butcher-like"</note> manner. Then, cutting his skin into four pieces, they hung them in the windows of four of the principal houses in **Lucerna**.

# In San Giovanni.

->*Michel Gonet*<-

Michel Gonet of *Lucernetta*, a man at least ninety years of age, was burned alive in a place called *Sarcena*, toward the mountains of *Bobbio*, where he had fled and hidden himself.

->*Bartholomeo Frasche*<-

*Bartholomeo Frasche*, of *Fenile*, was captured by the soldiers. After they had slashed and sliced his legs all over, they thrust a poisoned knife through his heels; in this miserable condition <note>original: "woeful plight"</note>, they dragged him to the common prison at *Turin*, where he died soon after.

->*Giovanni Baptista Oudri*<-

*Giovanni Baptista Oudri*, an old man of *San Giovanni*, was cruelly murdered at a place called *La Sarcena* after he had been treated very barbarously.

->*Magdalena la Peine*<-

*Magdalena la Peine*, a woman of about thirty-five years of age, was closely pursued by the enemy. Knowing what treatment <note>original: "measure"</note> she would receive from them, she chose to throw herself down a terrifying <note>original: "formidable"</note> cliff rather than fall into the hands of such bloody butchers.

->*Marguerita Revella*<-

*Marguerita Revella*, a woman about eighty-five years old, along with another woman named *Maria di Pravillerm*—who was ninety and blind from old age—were burned to death.

->*Maria Davi*<-

*Maria*, the daughter of *Jacopo Davi*, was murdered by the soldiers.

->*Michele Bellino*<-

*Michele Bellino*, along with *Anna di Pol Bochiardino* and their servant *Giovanni Pietro Marguet*, were beheaded by the hands of *Cattalino* and *Francisco Lemna* of *Bricherasio* <note>original: "Briqueras"</note>.

->*Daniele Pellene*<-

*Daniele Pellene* was massacred in *Angrogna* <note>original: "Angrognia"</note>.

### *Michele Parife*

*Michele Parife* was beheaded at Cavour <note>original: "Cavor"</note>.

### *Giovanni Danna*

*Giovanni Danna* was burned alive in a barn at a certain place called La Maria, in Angrogna <note>original: "Angrognia"</note>.

### *Daniele Gonin and David Chianforan*

*Daniele Gonin* and *David Chianforan* of La Piene were cruelly massacred.

### *Pietro Mallanot’s Daughter*

The daughter of *Pietro Mallanot*, a counselor of San Giovanni, was thrown from the top of a precipice to the bottom. She fell with her brother, an infant only eight months old, in her arms. Two days later, they were found by their father dead upon the snow; the girl still held her little brother in her arms.

### *Giovanni, Son of Pol Parife*

*Giovanni*, the son of *Pol Parife*, was terribly murdered along with his wife and child, as was the daughter of *Giovanni Prin*. Most notably, the wife of *Pol Parife* was thrown down a massive cliff <note>original: "mighty Rock"</note> with an infant in her arms. Three days later, she was found dead with the little child still alive, held tightly in the cold and stiff arms of the dead mother. Those who found them had a great deal of trouble removing the young child from her grasp.

### *Paolo Chiariet’s Wife*

The wife of *Paolo Chiariet*, along with two small infants, was inhumanely put to death.

### *Josepho Chiariet and Paolo Garniero*

*Josepho <note>original: "Fosepho"</note> Chiariet*, who had been wounded in a fight shortly before, was flayed <note>original: "flay’d"; to have the skin stripped off</note> at Luserna <note>original: "Lucerna"</note>, and the fat <note>original: "Grease"</note> was taken out of his body. The same was also done to *Paolo Garniero*.

### *Maria Peul*

*Maria Peul* was massacred.

### *Mattheo Turin*

*Mattheo Turin*, having been captured at Angrogna, was taken from there and massacred at Lucernetta, close to the bridge of Luserna. His carcass was afterward eaten by dogs.

### *Marguerita Saretta*

*Marguerita Saretta* was stoned to death, and her dead body was thrown into the river from the bridge of Balfre in Angrogna.

## In San Giovanni <note>original: "S. Giovanni"</note>.

### *Michel Gonet*

Michel Gonet of Lucernetta, a man at least ninety years of age, was burned alive in a place called Sarcena, toward the mountains of Bobbio <note>original: "Bobio"</note>, where he had fled and hidden himself.

### *Bartholomeo Frasche*

Bartholomeo Frasche of Fenile was captured by the soldiers, who, after they had all slashed and sliced his legs, thrust a poisoned knife through his heels; in this woeful state, they dragged him to the common prison at Turin, where he died soon after.

### *Giovanni Baptista Oudri*

Giovanni Baptista Oudri, an old man of San Giovanni, was cruelly murdered at a place called La Sarcena after he had been very barbarously treated.

### *Magdalena la Peine*

Magdalena la Peine, a woman about thirty-five years of age, was pursued closely by the enemy. Knowing what treatment she would receive from them, she chose to throw herself down a formidable precipice rather than fall into the hands of such bloody butchers.

### *Marguerita Revella*

Marguerita Revella, a woman about eighty-five <note>original: "fourscore and five"</note> years of age, together with another woman of ninety who was blind from old age named Maria di Pravillerm, were burned to death.

### *Maria Davi*

Maria, the daughter of Jacopo Davi, was murdered by the soldiers.

# Chapter VI. In the Valleys of Piedmont <note>original: "Piemont"</note>.

->Michele Parise<-

**Michele Parise** was beheaded at Cavour <note>original: "Cavor"</note>.

->Giovanni Danna<-

**Giovanni Danna** was burned alive in a barn at a certain place called La Maria, in Angrogna <note>original: "Angrognia"</note>.

->Daniele Gonin and David Chianforan<-

**Daniele Gonin** and **David Chianforan**, of La Piene, were cruelly massacred.

->Pietro Mallanot's Daughter<-

The daughter of **Pietro Mallanot**, a counselor of San Giovanni <note>original: "S. Giovanni"</note>, was rolled from the top of a precipice to the bottom with her brother, a little infant of eight months old, in her arms. Two days later, they were found by their father quite dead upon the snow—both the girl and the little infant brother still in her arms.

->Giovanni, Son of Pol Parise<-

**Giovanni**, son of **Pol Parise**, with his wife and child, as also the daughter of **Giovanni Prin**, were all fearfully murdered. This was especially true of the wife of **Pol Parise**, who was hurled down a great rock with a little infant in her arms. Three days later, she was found dead with the little child still alive, but fast-clasped between the arms of the dead mother. Her arms were so cold and stiff that those who found them had a very difficult time <note>original: "had much ado"</note> getting the young child out.

->Paolo Chiairet's Wife<-

The wife of **Paolo Chiairet**, together with two small infants, was inhumanly put to death.

->Josepho Chiairet and Paolo Garniero<-

**Josepho Chiairet**, who had been wounded in the fight shortly before, was flayed <note>original: "flay'd"; to be skinned alive</note> at Luserna <note>original: "Lucerna"</note>, and had the grease <note>original: "Grease"; likely referring to body fat</note> taken out of his body. The same was likewise done to **Paolo Garniero**.

->Maria Peul<-

**Maria Peul** was massacred.

->Mattheo Turin<-

**Mattheo Turin**, being taken at Angrogna, was carried from there and massacred at Lucernetta, close by the bridge of Luserna, and his carcass was afterwards eaten by the dogs.

->Marguerita Saretta<-

**Marguerita Saretta** was stoned to death, and her dead body cast into the river from the bridge of Balfre in Angrogna.

## In Angrogna <note>original: "Angrognia"</note>.

### *Jacopo Simond* and *Catharina Coissone*

Catharina Coissone, a poor lame woman and eighty years old <note>original: "fourscore years old"</note>, was dragged barefoot to a certain place called Chiodet, where they cut off her head and left her body unburied in the snow. The same was also done to *Jacopo Simond*.

### *Isaiah Ricca* and *Catharina Simond*

*Isaiah Ricca* and *Catharina* (the wife of Pietro Simond), a frail old woman, were grabbed by the feet and thrown down the precipices of jagged rocks in a manner dreadful to see. The last of these, Catharina, had her brains dashed out against the rocks before she was thrown down the cliffs.

### *Jeanna Praessuch*

*Jeanna*, a poor innocent woman and the sister of Antonio Praessuch, had her head cut off in a certain place called Gachet, and her body was thrown into a crevice of a rock, from which it was recovered with great difficulty some days later.

### *Bartholomeo Odin*

*Bartholomeo Odin*, a poor man at least eighty years old, was first thrown down a section of the rocks. Because he did not die from the fall, he was afterward brutally killed <note>original: "dispatcht"</note> by the soldiers, who left his naked body unburied.

<center>***Matteo Peloux***</center>

# Chapter 6: In the Valleys of Piedmont

The widow of the late **Giovanni Paglias** and [another victim] were both massacred, and their dead bodies were afterwards devoured by wild beasts.

**Marguerita Chialmis** and **Marguerita Bonetta** were both murdered.

**Pietro Richiardon**, together with the wife of **Giovanni Allova** (also known as **Ben**), and **Marguerita Copin**, were all massacred.

->**Giovanni Pallias**<-

**Giovanni Pallias**, a poor peasant from the community of **La Torre**, was taken prisoner by the soldiers. After enduring all kinds of insults and scorns cast upon him by those of the convent and the town, both in words and actions, he was—by special order of the **Marquis of Pianezza**—dragged by the executioner <note>original: "Hangman"</note> to a certain place near the convent where the Marquis was personally present. When he arrived, the Marquis acted as an under-sheriff (an ironic role for a gentleman of his status) and commanded the executioner to place the poor peasant at the foot of a ladder set against a tree and prepare everything for the execution. 

At that moment, the monks and Catholic priests <note>original: "Mass-priests"</note> who had led the condemned innocent man from his prison to the gallows—and who really should have shown him the way up the ladder themselves—did not stop using every argument that the Devil or their own invention could provide to shake the faith and constancy of this poor man. But it was all in vain. Far from being frightened by the pale face or terrors of death, his expressions and outward gestures clearly showed the inward ecstasy and joy of his heart, seeing himself worthy to suffer for the cross of **Christ**. 

Even though they repeatedly pressured him to remember the sad condition in which he would leave his children and family, he always replied that it was his sincere prayer to Almighty God that his children might follow in their father's footsteps and die as he did. When the priests saw that all their persuasion and temptations were as useless as "sounding brass and tinkling cymbals" <note>A biblical reference to 1 Corinthians 13:1, implying their words were empty noise</note>, they helped the executioner end the poor man's miserable days. Because they could not shake him from his principles, they hurried to push him off the ladder.

->**Paolo Clement**<-

This **Mr. Paolo Clement** <note>original: "Sieur," a title of respect</note>, an elder of the church of **Rossana**, was brought by the monks and priests to the very same place not many days after the execution of the aforementioned **Pallias**. They showed him the dead body of the other man, thinking it would scare him out of his principles and faith. But the good man answered them with undaunted courage, saying *that although they might be able to kill the body, they could never harm the soul of a true believer.* However, he assured them that God would avenge all the innocent blood they had spilled: "God will take revenge for so much innocent blood" <note>original Italian: "Iddio farà la Vendetta di tanto sangue innocente"</note>...

# Chapter VI. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

The widow of the previously deceased *Giovanni Paglias* was massacred, and her dead body was afterward devoured by wild beasts.

Marguerita Chialmis and Marguerita Bonetta were both murdered.

Pietro Richiardon, together with the wife of *Giovanni Allova* (also known as *Ben*) and *Marguerita Copin*, were all massacred.

->*Giovanni Pallias*<-

**Giovanni Pallias**, a poor peasant of the community of *La Torre*, was taken prisoner by the soldiers. After enduring all kinds of insults and scorn from those in the monastery and town—expressed in both words and actions—he was dragged by the executioner to a place near the monastery by special order of the Marquess of *Pionessa*. The Marquess himself was present there. At that location, the Marquess acted as an under-sheriff (a lowly role for a gentleman of his rank) and ordered the executioner to place the poor peasant at the foot of a ladder set against a tree and prepare everything for the execution. 

During this time, the monks and Mass priests who had led the condemned innocent man from his prison to the gallows (and who really should have shown him the way up the ladder himself) did not stop using every argument that either the devil or their own imaginations could provide to shake the faith and the constancy of this poor man. But it was all in vain. He was far from being frightened by the pale face or the terrors of death; instead, all his expressions and outward gestures clearly showed the inward ecstasy and joy of his heart to see himself considered worthy to suffer for the *Cross of Christ*. 

Even though they often urged him to remember the sad condition in which he would leave his children and family, he always replied that it was his sincere prayer to Almighty God that his children might follow their father’s footsteps and die as he did. When the Mass priests saw that all their persuasion and temptation were nothing more than "sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:1, implying their words were empty and meaningless noise.</note>, they helped the executioner end the poor man’s miserable days. Because they could not shake him from his principles, they hurried to turn him off the ladder.

->*Paolo Clement*<-

This **Paolo Clement**, an elder of the church of *Rossana*, was brought by the monks and Mass priests to the very same place not many days after the execution of the previously mentioned *Pallias*. They showed him the dead body of the other man, thinking it would scare him into abandoning his principles and profession of faith. However, the good man answered them with undaunted courage, stating *that they might be able to kill the body, but they could never harm the soul of a true believer.* He assured them that God would be the avenger of all the innocent blood they had spilled ("God will take vengeance for so much innocent blood" <note>original: *Iddio farà la Vendetta di tanto sangue innocente*</note>).

# Chapter VI. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

The widow <note>original: "dow," completing the word "widow" from the previous page</note> of the previously deceased *Giovanni Paglias* was massacred, and her dead body was afterwards devoured by wild beasts.

*Marguerita Chialmis* and *Marguerita Bonetta* were both murdered.

*Pietro Richiardon*, together with the wife of *Giovanni Allova* (also known as *Ben*) and *Marguerita Copin*, were all massacred.

->**Giovanni Pallias**<-

*Giovanni Pallias*, a poor peasant from the community of *La Torre*, was taken prisoner by the soldiers. After enduring all kinds of insults and mockery from the members of the monastery and the townspeople—both in words and actions—he was dragged by the executioner by special order of the Marquess of *Pionessa* to a certain place near the monastery where the Marquess himself was present. When he arrived, the Marquess acted as the Under-Sheriff <term>a lowly administrative official; the author is mocking the high-ranking Marquess for performing such a grim, base task</term> and commanded the executioner to place the poor peasant at the foot of a ladder set against a tree and to prepare everything for the execution. 

At that time, the monks and Catholic priests who had escorted the condemned innocent man from his prison to the gallows—and who really should have shown him the way up the ladder themselves—did not stop using every argument that either the Devil or their own imagination could provide to shake the faith and the constancy of this poor man. But it was all in vain. He was so far from being frightened by the pale face or the terrors of death that all his expressions and outward gestures clearly showed the inward ecstasy and joy of his heart to see himself considered worthy to suffer for the cross of *Christ*. 

Despite the fact that they often pressured him to remember the miserable state in which he would leave his children and family, he always answered them that it was his sincere prayer to Almighty God that his children might follow in their father's footsteps and die as he did. Consequently, when the priests saw that all their persuasion and temptations were nothing more than "sounding brass and tinkling cymbals" <note>a reference to 1 Corinthians 13:1, meaning their words were hollow and meaningless</note>, they lent the executioner their own hands to help end the poor man's miserable days. Because they could not shake him from his principles, they hurried to push him off the ladder.

->**Paolo Clement**<-

This Mr. *Paolo Clement*, an Elder of the Church of *Rossana*, was brought by the monks and priests to the very same location not many days after the execution of the aforementioned *Pallias*. They showed him the dead body of the other man, thinking they could scare him into abandoning his principles and his faith. However, the good man answered them with undaunted courage, saying that *they might be able to kill the body, but they could never harm the soul of a true believer*. Furthermore, he assured them that God would be the avenger of all the innocent blood they had spilled ("God will take vengeance for so much innocent blood" <note>original Italian: *Iddio farà la Vendetta di tanto sangue innocente*</note>).

# Chapter VI. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

The widow of the late *Giovanni Paglias* was massacred, and her dead body was afterward devoured by wild beasts.

*Marguerita Chialmis* and *Marguerita Bonetta* were both murdered.

*Pietro Richiardon*, together with the wife of *Giovanni Allova* (also known as *Ben*) and *Marguerita Copin*, were all massacred.

### *Giovanni Pallias*

*Giovanni Pallias*, a poor peasant of the community of *La Torre*, was taken prisoner by the soldiers. After enduring all kinds of insults and scorn from those of the convent and town in both words and actions, he was dragged by the executioner—by special order of the Marquis of *Pianezza*—to a certain place not far from the convent where the Marquis himself was present. When he arrived, the Marquis acted as an under-sheriff <note>The author is being sarcastic here, suggesting that such a high-ranking noble was demeaning himself by personally overseeing a common execution</note> and commanded the executioner to place the poor peasant at the foot of a ladder set against a tree and to prepare everything for the execution. 

During this time, the monks and priests who had led the condemned, innocent man from his prison to the gallows (and who really should have shown him the way up the ladder as well) did not stop using every argument that either the Devil or their own imagination could provide to shake the faith and constancy of this poor man. But it was all in vain; he was so far from being terrified by the pale face or the horrors of death that all his expressions and outward gestures clearly showed the inward ecstasy and joy of his heart. He saw himself as worthy to suffer for the cross of *Christ*. 

Despite their frequent pressure on him to remember the sad state in which he would leave his children and family, he always answered them that it was his hearty prayer to Almighty God that his children might follow in their father's footsteps and die as he did. When the priests saw that all their persuasions and temptations were nothing more than "sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal" <note>A biblical reference to 1 Corinthians 13:1, meaning empty or meaningless noise</note>, they lent the executioner their own hands to end the poor man's miserable days. Because they could not shake him from his principles, they hurried to turn him off the ladder <term>original: "turn him off the ladder"; a common idiom for hanging someone</term>.

### *Paolo Clement*

This Lord *Paolo Clement*, an elder of the church of *Rossana*, was brought by the monks and priests to the very same place not many days after the execution of *Pallias*. They showed him the dead body of the other man, thinking it would scare him out of his principles and profession of faith. But the good man answered them with undaunted courage, saying that *they might be able to kill the body, but they could never prejudice the soul of a true believer*. Furthermore, he assured them that God would be the avenger of all the innocent blood that they had spilled (*God will be the avenger of so much innocent blood* <note>original: "Iddio sarà la Vendetta di tanto sangue innocente"</note>).

<summary>This page details the steadfastness of Waldensian martyrs Giovanni Pallias and Paolo Clement, who refused to renounce their faith even when faced with the gallows and the sight of other victims.</summary>

...innocent blood which is shed) <note>original: "cente che si spande"</note>. Thereupon, after first offering some spiritual prayers <note>original: "Ejaculations"</note> and preparing himself to yield up his soul to *God who gave it*, he asked the executioner to finish his work. 

Three or four days after the death of this holy and devout man, the *Marquis of Pianezza* happened to pass that way. One of his soldiers fired a musket at the dead body, and immediately a stream of fresh-colored blood gushed out. Upon seeing this, the *Marquis* told those near him, "This blood cries for vengeance" <note>original: "Questo sangue crida vendetta"</note>. 

After this, both of their dead bodies were hung by one foot from a tree near the gate of *La Torre*. Whenever any prisoner of the *Reformed* <note>Protestant</note> party passed by that way, they were forced to go and kiss the dead men’s genitals, intending to heap the same disgrace upon both the living and the dead. However, because of the many bullets fired at the bodies by soldiers passing by, it was not long before the corpses fell completely to pieces.

*Andrea Gillio* (son of *Pietro Gillio*, the pastor of *La Torre*) and *Bartolemi Copin* were both cruelly massacred.

### *Magdalena Juliano*

*Magdalena*, the wife of *Stephano Juliano*, was first wounded by a gunshot and then had her body cut into pieces.

## In Villaro

### *Daniele Rambaut*

*Daniele Rambaut* of *Villaro* <note>modern: Villar Pellice</note>, a man burdened with a large family, was taken prisoner and carried to *Païsana* along with several of his neighbors. After he had been imprisoned for a while, the monks and priests <note>original: "Mass-Priests"</note> tried to persuade him to say the words "*Jesus Maria*." Although they pressured him with many threats and tricks, he could not be moved. Consequently, the tormentors first cut off his fingers one by one, then both of his hands, and finally gave him a fatal wound with a shot to the stomach. But, as was their usual custom, not contenting themselves without venting their malice on the dead bodies of the *Protestants*, they dragged his carcass to the riverbank, where it was eaten and devoured by dogs and wild beasts.

### *Pietro Chabriolo*

*Pietro Chabriolo*, the son of *Josepho Chabriolo* of *Villaro*, was captured by the soldiers near the house of a man named *Laurentio Durant*. They placed...

### *Pietro Bertino Maghit*

*Pietro Bertino Maghit* of *Villaro* was massacred in the village of *Pertusel*. He was first severely wounded with many slashes and cuts across most of his body.

### *Pietro Mondon*

*Pietro Mondon* of *Villaro* (where he had previously fled for refuge) was overtaken by the enemy while fleeing his own house toward the mountains of *Chiapelet*. There, he was cruelly murdered by them.

### *Giuditha Rostagnol*

*Giuditha*, the widow of the late *Daniele Rostagnol* of *Villaro*, first had her head chopped off in a cave at *Chastelus*, and afterward her body was thrown down the rocks.

### *David Geimet and his Mother*

*David Geimet* of *Villaro*, along with his mother who was extremely aged and infirm <note>original: "decrepit"</note>, was barbarously murdered by the soldiers among the villages of *Moussa*.

### *Daniele Fellipone*

*Daniele Fellipone* had his head hacked off from his body while he was lying in bed in the house of *Giovanni Fiantino* at *Villaro*.

### *Antonio Calieris*

*Antonio*, the son of the late *Samuele Calieris* (a man who was mute and simple-minded <note>original: "a dumb and innocent Creature"</note>), was most inhumanely butchered while sitting by the fireside at a place called *Clotillart*.

### *Peiron Minan*

*Peiron Minan* was caught by the soldiers while attempting to escape from his own house; he was killed in a very cruel manner on the spot where he was caught.

### *Pietro Moninat*

*Pietro Moninat* and his wife, who were both extremely sick and weak, were butchered at the alpine pasture <note>original: "Alpe"</note> of *La Roussa* by the soldiers. Finding one of their children in the same house—a poor, lame, and disabled infant—the soldiers cut off its legs and left it in that miserable condition. There was also another of their children in the house, a poor girl who had been mute from birth; she was found by some neighbors not long after, having starved to death for want of food.

### *Susanna Fantino*

*Susanna*, widow of the late *David Fantino*, was cruelly murdered in the village of *Liuzza*.

### *Davide Fontano*

*Davide Fontano* of *Villermino*, a man who was extremely old and frail, was massacred in the village of *Bezza*. Afterward, his body was dragged back and forth by the soldiers in a most disgraceful manner.

### *Giovanni Gaio*

*Giovanni Gaio*, son of the late *Antonio Gaio* of *Pravillerm*, who had earlier fled to *Villaro* for refuge, was massacred while fleeing toward the mountains of *Balmedaut*.

### *Daniele Benech* and his two small children

*Daniele Benech*, a resident of *Villaro*, was captured by the soldiers in one of the villages of *La Cercena*. They first cut off his nose, his ears, and other parts of his body until they had killed him <note>original: "dispatched him"</note>. Afterward, they left the mangled pieces of his body hanging on the hedges and bushes of that place. There were also two small children belonging to the aforementioned *Daniele Benech* who suffocated in the snow at the same time, for lack of a father to lead and guide them.

### *Daniele Garre*

*Daniele Garre*, son-in-law to the Lord <note>original: "Sieur"</note> *Mondonis*, was most unmercifully murdered in the village of *La Cercena* by the same soldiers who had killed the aforementioned *Benech*.

### *Maria Gril*

*Maria*, widow of the late *Daniele Gril Bourgoin* of *Villaro*, was horribly murdered by the soldiers at *Macanail* near *La Cercena*. Her body was afterward eaten and devoured by wild beasts.

### *Pietro Berardo*

*Pietro Berardo* of *Villaro*, while being closely pursued by the soldiers toward the mountains of *Balmedaut*, unfortunately slipped in a narrow passage as he was fleeing. He fell down the side of a high cliff, where he was later found dead.

### *Maria Pelanchion*

*Maria*, the widow of the late *Daniele Pelanchion* of *Villaro*, was captured by the soldiers at *La Combe delli Carbonieri*. After they had abused her, they shot her and left her for dead, then threw her into the river of *Valguichiart*. This poor woman, who was not quite dead, managed with great pain and many pitiable efforts to get out of the river again. She lay down in the sun, hoping to be somewhat revived and refreshed by its heat; but the soldiers...

## Of Bobbio

->*Giovanni di Savetto*<-

Giovanni di Savetto of La Combe and La Feriera, in the commune <note>original: "Communalty"</note> of Bobbio, was found dead upon the snow. He had been massacred along with a little infant (whom the murderers, it is probable, had spared) who was found sleeping in its father's arms. Thus, though the father was murdered, the young infant was preserved by a special Providence <note>God's intervention or protective care.</note>.

->*Paolo Armand*<-

*Paolo Armand*, who was extremely sick and weak, was captured by the soldiers at a place called *La Vota di Crosouna* and hacked into pieces.

->*Andrea Bertono* and *Josepho Catalino*<-

*Andrea Bertono*, a very elderly and lame man, was captured at a certain place called *Serre de Cruel*. There, his breasts were first cut off, and then he was cruelly murdered by those bloody butchers. To demonstrate their hatred against him for his perseverance in his religion, they cut out his bowels after his death and hacked his dead body into pieces with their halberds <note>A combined spear and battle-axe.</note>. Not far from the place where this was done, *Josepho Catalino* was also massacred.

->*Daniele Michialino*<-

*Daniele*, the son of *Davide Michialino*, was captured by the soldiers in the very same place where *Catalino* was massacred. Besides other ill and cruel usage, he had his tongue plucked out with great violence and torment.

->*Martha Giraudina*<-

*Martha Giraudina*, an old woman of about eighty <note>original: "fourscore"</note> years of age, had her head chopped off by some of the murderers.

->*Constantia Bellione*<-

*Constantia Bellione of Sibaud*, after having her body hacked and mangled in most parts, was killed with several bullets shot into her abdomen <note>original: "Bowels"</note>. After she was dead, they split her head with a hanger <term>hanger</term> <note>A short, slightly curved sword often worn by infantry or sailors.</note>.

->*Juditha Mondon*<-

*Juditha Mondon* was beaten to death in a most savage manner with clubs and staves.

### Davide Paglias and Paolo Genre, with two infants.

*Davide Paglias* and *Paolo Genre*, while attempting to escape each carrying a small infant in their arms, eventually grew exhausted. They were overtaken by their pursuers, and both the men and the infants were cruelly put to death.

### Stephano Billior.

### Giovanni Rovetto.

[Ludovico was car]ried to *La Torre* <note>Modern Torre Pellice</note>, where after the tormentors had sufficiently afflicted him to their satisfaction by burning matches between his fingers, his lips, and other parts of his body until he died from sheer pain and anguish, they ordered his dead body to be carried out by two of his fellow prisoners and thrown into the River *Pelice*. However, afterward, reconsidering how they might further take revenge against the corpse and believing the river to be too honorable a burial place for a heretic, they compelled the men who had thrown him in to fetch him out again and lay him at the riverbank. There, after they had exposed the body to all manner of insults and indignities, it was finally eaten by dogs.

# In Rora

## The Wives of Josepho Garniero, Josepho Pellenc, and Stephano Revellio.

The wife of *Josepho Garniero*, the wife of *Josepho Pellenc*, and the wife of *Stephano Revellio* were all brutally assassinated and murdered at the time when the army fell upon the borders of *Rora*. Among other events, there was one very remarkable incident concerning *Marguerita*, the wife of *Josepho Garniero* and sister to Captain *Joshua Gianavel*. Having received a gunshot in one of her breasts while she was breastfeeding a small child with the other, she remained so brave and courageous that she exhorted her husband with many moving <note>original: "pathetical"</note> expressions to endure the cross with patience and to hold out until the end. She did not ask for any favor from the killers except to spare the life of her innocent baby. They did spare the child, but they immediately shot the mother again in the body, from which she died. Afterward, the infant was found alive in its dead mother's arms, miraculously preserved.

## Isaiah Mondon.

Isaiah Mondon, having hidden himself for a long time in the cleft of a rock—where for many days he had nothing but a few leaves of unwholesome herbs to eat—was at last discovered by the soldiers near the bridge of the river called *La Luserna*. He was most unmercifully treated by them. From there, they dragged him (being nearly half dead) toward the town of *Luserna*. When the poor man was unable to march any further, he fell down upon his knees, begging his executioners to kill him quickly. They were "civil" enough to grant his request; using their swords and pistols, they soon ended his miserable days, crying out in a scoffing and mocking manner:

> "Kill this <term>Barbet</term>! Kill this Barbet, who refuses to become a Christian!"
<note>The term "Barbet" (meaning "uncle" in the local dialect) was originally a respectful title for Waldensian pastors, but it was used by their persecutors as a derogatory slur for the Waldensians themselves.</note>

All of this took place near the *Rock of Luserna* <note>original: "Rocca di Lucerna"</note>.

## In Rorà <note>original: Roras</note>.

### The wives of Joseph Garniero, Joseph Pellenc, and Stephen Revellio.

The wife of Joseph Garniero, the wife of Joseph Pellenc, and the wife of Stephen Revellio <note>original: Stephano Revellio</note> were all most outrageously assassinated and murdered at the time when the army attacked the borders of Rorà. Among other events, there was one very remarkable incident concerning Marguerita, the wife of Joseph Garniero and sister to Captain Joshua Gianavel. Having received a gunshot in one of her breasts while she was breastfeeding a small child with the other, she remained so stout-hearted and courageous that she exhorted her husband with many moving expressions **to endure the Cross with patience, and to hold out to the end.** She did not ask for any favor from the killers, except to spare the life of her innocent babe. They did so, but immediately shot the mother again in the body, which killed her. Afterward, the infant was found alive in its dead mother's arms, miraculously preserved.

### Isaiah Mondon.

Isaiah Mondon, having hidden himself for a long time in the crevice of a rock—where for many days he had nothing to feed upon but a few leaves of unwholesome herbs—was at last discovered by the soldiers. Near the bridge of the river called La Lucerna, he was most unmercifully handled by them. From there, they dragged him (being little more than half dead) toward the town of Luserna <note>original: Lucerna</note>. When the poor man was able to march no further, he fell down upon his knees, beseeching his executioners to dispatch him quickly. They were "civil" enough to grant his request; with their swords and pistols, they soon ended his miserable days, crying out in a scoffing and deriding manner, *"Kill this Barbet! <term>Barbet: A derogatory nickname for the Waldensians, originally meaning "uncle," used to refer to their pastors.</term> Kill this Barbet, who refuses to become a Christian!"* All of this took place near the Rocca di Lucerna.

### Giovanni Barrolino and his Wife.

Giovanni Barrolino and his wife were thrown alive into a pond or pool, where they were repeatedly plunged and forced under the water with prongs and pitchforks, and at last killed with stones and pieces of brick <note>original: "brick-batts"</note>.

---

### Maria Revel.

Maria Revel, having been shot in the body, fell down as if dead. However, she later regained enough strength to get onto her knees to pray to God, at which point the enemy killed <note>original: "dispatched"</note> her.

---

### Giovanni Salvagiot.

Giovanni Salvagiot was returning from Bagnolo <note>modern Bagnolo Piemonte</note> after the peace treaty had been concluded. As he passed by a Catholic chapel without removing his hat or bowing in respect to it <note>original: "making obeysance thereto"</note>, he was murdered and his body was left unburied.

---

### Giovanni Gayo and two of his children; Daniele Garniero and his son; a daughter of Giovanni Moglio; Giovanni Feliero; Giovanni Miroto; Bartholemi Moglio; and Giovanni Salvagiot (another man of the same name as the one mentioned above).

Giovanni Gayo and all the others named above were cruelly massacred in a certain **cave**, where they had hidden themselves, thinking they would be more secure there than in any other place. When these poor people found they had been discovered, they fell to their knees and begged for their lives from their executioners. They had known most of these men personally for a long time, and the killers had always claimed to be their very good friends; indeed, they were none other than their neighbors from Luserna <note>original: Lucerna</note>, Bubbiana, Barges, Bagnolo, Cavour, and the surrounding areas. 

But because the mercy of those men was entirely cruel, the kindest greeting they offered their old acquaintances was with muskets, swords, and pistols. When the poor people realized this, and not wishing to see the tragic sight of one another's suffering, they knelt down in a circle and thrust their heads (with their faces toward the ground) into some fern bushes <note>original: "Fearn-brakes"</note> and other similar material they had brought into the cave to use as beds. In this position, they were all wretchedly shot to death, and their corpses were afterwards horribly mutilated and cut into pieces.

<header>Chapter 6: In the Valleys of Piedmont.</header>

## In Roccapiatta.

### *Jacopo Barral, and his Wife.*

Jacopo Barral and his wife, having been taken prisoner by the Earl of San Secondo, were carried out of the prison three or four days later to a place about a quarter of a Piedmontese mile away. There, they were shot to death. These same executioners also cut off the woman’s breasts.

### *Giovanni Bonino.*

*Giovanni Bonino* (also known as <term>Grangiot</term>) was captured while fleeing by French troops near the Perosa Valley <note>original: "Val Perosa"</note>. He was miserably hacked to pieces with their short swords <term>Hangers</term>.

### *Antonio Guigou.*

*Antonio Guigou* had come to Periero intending to change his religion at the prompting <note>original: "instigation"</note> of Count <note>original: "Conte"</note> Borichard. However, it pleased God to touch his heart so that he repented of his decision and tried to escape. He was caught again by the troops of the Marquis <note>original: "Marquess"</note> of Galeazzo <note>original: "Galeas"</note> and treated with extreme cruelty because he would not yield to attend Mass. As they were leading him prisoner toward Prali, they passed a precipice. To escape the hands of his tormentors, the poor man leaped down the side of a cliff <note>original: "Rock"</note> and was dashed to pieces.

---

In addition to the cruelties named above, many other accounts <note>original: "Relations"</note> were brought to the author’s hands. Because he had not sufficiently verified them, he thought it better to omit them rather than include them among those he found to be undoubtedly true. Furthermore, the honest <term>ingenuous</term> reader cannot expect that every cruelty committed against these poor creatures in so many dark corners and remote places could ever be brought to light. In truth, those recorded here are more than enough to demonstrate the cursed and hellish cruelties of their bloody Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> enemies. Therefore, all that I shall add here is a catalog of the names of some of those poor Protestants who miserably perished in prison or while defending themselves, along with those who were held prisoner. they are listed in order as follows:

devil himself) his due. On the other hand, so that the reader may not have one eye open and the other shut, and so he may better be enabled to make a right judgment of all things after a serious hearing and weighing the reasons of both sides—according to the words of the Tragedian <note>original: "Tragedian"; referring to the Roman philosopher and playwright Seneca</note>:

> *He who decides anything without hearing the other side, even if his decision is just, is not a just judge.* <note>original Latin: "Qui statuit aliquid, parte inauditâ alterâ, Æquum licet statuerit, haud æquus est judex." — Seneca, *Medea*</note>

I say, upon this ground and for this reason, I thought it might be very acceptable, and indeed necessary—after I have given an ample narrative of the late massacre (though supported and propped up with the most evident and authentic proofs)—to insert also what the Court of **Savoy** pleads in its own vindication for such horrid and barbarous cruelties.

I imagine I hear the noble and **Christian** reader debating the matter and guessing the reasons for it in his own private thoughts: *“I would gladly know what the behavior of those in the Court of* **Savoy** *was in this affair, and how they could ever think to handle the matter so as to satisfy the world! Did they plainly and openly deny the* **fact**? *That would be to deny a truth as clear as noonday and to deceive the world in too gross a manner! Or did they openly admit it? Certainly they would be more protective of their own reputation than to expose themselves and their Prince to the hatred of the whole world by a voluntary confession!”*

The plain truth is, this could only be a very critical time for those of that Court. They knew very well that the cry of the poor people’s blood had already gone out into every corner of the world, and that it was now high time to think of some way to influence the minds of men—at least with some plausible excuses to justify their proceedings—and where the business was too foul, to disguise and cover it up! A summary of this apology was drawn to the life by a Jesuitical pen (which the reader may as easily detect in this writing as **Daniel** did the footprints in the **House of Bel** <note>A reference to the biblical story of Bel and the Dragon from the Apocrypha, where Daniel exposes the deception of priests by spreading ashes on the floor to reveal their footprints.</note>) and was afterwards published in **Italian**, **Latin**, and **French**. 

If the author had not possessed certain advantages in investigating and, to some extent, reaching the bottom of those designs—and in proving their contradictions and falsehoods by the undeniable arguments that will appear later in this discourse—it might possibly have gained some credit and belief in the world. At the very least, it could have done nothing less than significantly diminish the reputation of the previous chapter. Now, so that the author may not hereafter be criticized for having either added, diminished, or in any way corrupted or falsified the genuine sense of their report, he has included it in its original expressions, as follows:

### A Report of the Events that occurred in the Valley of Lucerna, in the year 1655.
<note>original Italian: "Relatione de' Successi seguiti nella Valle di Luserna..."</note>

His Royal Highness, on January 25, 1655, commanded his subjects of the so-called Reformed Religion <note>original Italian: "Religione pretesa riformata"; a term used by the Catholic authorities to deny the legitimacy of the Protestant Waldensian faith</note>, by means of an order from Auditor Gastaldo <term>Auditor Gastaldo</term>—Andrea Gastaldo, a high-ranking judge and official representing the Duke of Savoy—to withdraw within three days, under penalty of death, into the valley and borders of Angrogna, and into the lands of Rora <note>original: "Rorata"</note>, Villaro, and Bobbio with their villages. They were required to abandon their homes and property in the other lands of the said valley. They were, however, given the power to sell these assets, even though said properties were confiscated for being acquired against the express provisions of the laws. Regarding the justice of this command—which is the foundation of everything—a separate document is provided, so as not to make this report excessively long.

The aforementioned members of the so-called Reformed Religion obeyed the order by withdrawing. At the same time, they sent representatives to His Royal Highness to demonstrate that the order was contrary to their granted rights, and petitioned him to revoke it.

His Royal Highness replied to them that the order was in accordance with justice and the provisions of previous laws. Despite this, he was content to hear whatever they might allege against it, and even to grant them some favor, whenever—

</column>
<column>

### A Narrative of the various Transactions in the Valley of Lucerna, in the year 1655.

His Royal Highness, on January 25, 1655, commanded his subjects of the so-called Reformed Religion, by virtue of an order from his Auditor Gastaldo, to relocate themselves within three days, under penalty of death, into the Valley and borders of Angrogna, the lands of Rora <note>original: "Rorata"</note>, Villaro, Bobbio, and the villages belonging to them. Likewise, they were to leave their homes and the goods they possessed in other parts of the said Valley. Nevertheless, they had the liberty to sell those goods, even though they were technically confiscated (as having been purchased contrary to express orders). We have demonstrated the justice of this command—which is indeed the basis for everything else—in a separate document to avoid being too long-winded in this one.

In obedience to this command, those of the so-called Reformed Religion accordingly retired within the prescribed limits. At the same time, however, they sent deputies to His Royal Highness, declaring this command to be contrary to their ancient concessions <term>concessions</term>—the historic legal rights and religious freedoms previously granted to the Waldensians by the Dukes of Savoy—and therefore petitioned that it might be revoked.

His Royal Highness’s answer to them was that this order was consistent both with justice and the intent of their former concessions. Yet nevertheless, he was graciously willing to hear what they could argue to the contrary, and moreover—

</column>
</columns>

...that he would still be favorable to them in case they would send deputies to **Turin**, furnished with a full commission drawn up in a due and legal form. With these deputies, the concessions <term>concessions</term><note>Legal privileges or grants previously awarded to the Waldensian communities by the Dukes of Savoy.</note> might be examined, and afterward, whatsoever should be found equitable might be concluded and ratified. But withal, in receiving these favors from his Royal Highness, they should promise inviolably to observe the conditions annexed thereunto; and in the meantime, they were warned not to be disobedient, or return to the places which they had then relinquished.

This admonition was reiterated by various ministers of state and members of a committee constituted for that very end and purpose—consisting of the chief counselors of state and of justice—as also by the **Marquess of Pianezza** <note>original: "Pionezza"; the commander of the ducal troops during the subsequent massacre.</note>, partly by word of mouth and partly by a long letter. In this letter, he exhorted them not to omit sending deputies with such letters of procuration <term>procuration</term><note>A formal legal document giving a deputy the power of attorney to act on behalf of the community.</note>. And besides all this, **Christophoro, Earl of Lucerna**, (as he was commanded) expressly mentioned to them the favors that his Royal Highness would be inclined to accord unto them.

Notwithstanding, they always refused to send letters of procuration in a due form; indeed, on the contrary, they often sent deputies with letters that never so much as passed through the hands of a notary and were invalid. They had given themselves up to the advice of certain seditious persons who were ringleaders in the rebellion, whose goal was not to suffer themselves to be wrought upon so far as to come to an accommodation in anything, even though they knew the same to be ever so just and necessary according to the true meaning and interpretation of the concessions...

</column>

<column-break/>

<column>

*...that they had sent to Turin deputies provided with a power of attorney in good and legal form, with whom, after the examination of the concessions, what was to be done could be established; and receiving these favors from His Royal Highness, they would validly promise the observation of the conditions attached to those favors; warning them, however, not to be disobedient in the meantime, and not to return to the places already abandoned.* <note>original Italian: "ta havesse mandati à Torino Deputati provisti di Procura..."</note>

*The same was repeated to them by various ministers, by the body of an entire congregation composed of the principal Counselors of State and of Justice, and by the Marquess of Pianezza in person and in writing with a long letter, in which he exhorted them not to fail to send their deputies with such a power of attorney; and furthermore, Count Christoforo of Lucerna expressed to them (as he had orders to do) the favors that His Royal Highness wished to grant them.* <note>original Italian: "L'istesso fù loro replicato da diversi Ministri..."</note>

*However, they always refused to send said powers of attorney in good form, and several times they sent deputies, but with powers of attorney not received by a notary and invalid; being persuaded by some seditious persons and leaders of the rebellion not to bring themselves to a point of adjusting anything, which according to the disposition of the...* <note>original Italian: "Ricusarono però essi sempre di mandar dette Procure..."</note>

</column>
</columns>

# Chapter I. In the Valleys of Piedmont.

To address this matter, the inhabitants of the valleys organized and held a general assembly. The residents of **St. Martin** and **Perosa** attended and, along with the others, consulted about the business (and the letters were read openly). The truth is that the entire assembly—especially those from **St. Martin** and **Perosa**, along with some of the leading instigators <note>original: "Incendiaries"</note> of this rebellion—gave sufficient proof that their respect for their own natural Prince <note>The Duke of Savoy.</note> was much less than that of the ministers of **Geneva** toward the **Duke of Savoy**.

In short, their conclusion was never to obey any such order, and that they would take up arms whenever they were forbidden from returning to the houses they had recently left. They also decided that the estates they had illegally purchased beyond the established <note>original: "prefixed"</note> limits should not be sold to any Catholic whatsoever, and that anyone who spoke to the contrary or showed the slightest inclination to become a Catholic should be severely punished. To ensure all of this, they all took a solemn oath, with the ministers adding a decree of excommunication <term>Excommunication</term><note>A formal religious penalty that excludes a person from the community and the sacraments of the church.</note> against anyone who sold their estates to Catholics.

Once this was done, they returned by their own authority to the prohibited places. Even so, they continued to conduct their business through deputies <note>official representatives</note>, acting as if they had no intention of starting an open rebellion. This was done with such great contempt for His Royal Highness’s authority that it cannot be adequately expressed.

*They therefore concluded never to obey such an order, to take up arms whenever it was attempted to force them not to return to the abandoned houses, not to sell any of the land illegally acquired outside the limits to any Catholic, and to mistreat anyone who spoke to the contrary or considered becoming Catholic. Regarding this, they took a universal oath <note>original Italian: "giuramento univerſale"</note>, and the ministers added an excommunication <note>original Italian: "Scommunica"</note> for whoever sold property to Catholics.*

By giving orders to those same troops, he took control of the place by force with very little bloodshed. The rebels fled under the cover of night into the mountains, without being pursued.

All the troops then took up quarters in that town. No more harm was done to the town than what even friends usually do when a large body of soldiers enters an uninhabited village—which is to make use of the things found there. However, its outlying hamlets continued their hostilities, even sending musketeers into the mountains for many days to attack the army’s main headquarters in the town. These hamlets were conquered by force and plundered. As a result, the Marquess was forced to reinforce his army, which he did with some regiments from the French army that had arrived in Piedmont.

Although this insolent and unexpected resistance forced the Marquess to take harsh measures, he nevertheless wanted to try kindness first. He attempted to persuade them through a letter sent to those stubborn <note>original: "indurati," meaning hardened or obstinate.</note> people, who did not know how to choose a path to escape their deserved punishment by giving His Royal Highness <note>Sua Altezza Reale (S.A.R.), referring to Charles Emmanuel II, Duke of Savoy.</note> some satisfaction.

He stated that as their brothers had committed a most grievous crime by refusing to <term>quarter</term> <note>original: "quartering" - providing housing and food for soldiers.</note> soldiers (a rebellion which they had also assisted), they now ought to endeavor to repair that fault. On the other side, where the Pelice Valley lies and where the villages of Villaro and Bobbio are located, they sent several troops commanded by the Marquess Galeazzo Villa. These included the Villa Regiment and the Chamblay Regiment. The major of the latter is named Monsieur de Montafon <note>original: "Monfù di Montafon"</note>. He, along with several other officers who belong to the so-called Reformed Religion <note>original: "Religione pretesa riformata"; the Catholic Savoyard government used this term to refer to the Waldensian Protestant faith</note>, can testify whether any cruel actions were either committed or commanded by anyone. 

The lands of Villaro and Bobbio offered no resistance to the quartering of troops, but the men almost entirely abandoned their homes. They retreated to the upper towns and settlements with all their provisions. Because of this, the soldiers were forced either to die of hunger or to go searching for food with their muskets in those upper towns. It was never possible—despite the patience shown or the formal appeals sent to them—to obtain peaceful access or, failing that, some food supplies. Instead, those towns chose to be taken by force, looted, and burned one by one, even though they had the example of Villaro and Bobbio before them. Those people chose rather to suffer themselves to be looted and burned, one after another, although they had as a precedent before their eyes the inhabitants of Villaro and Bobbio, who remained untouched and lived in peace (at least that little handful of them who were left behind). # Chapter 1: In the Valleys of Piedmont

...besides a very few men from Angrogna, and those found dead on the scene were bearing arms. <note>original: "ssimi huomini, etiandio portanti le armi d’Angrogna"</note>

On the other side, where the Valley of Pelice lies along with the villages of Villaro and Bobbio, some troops were sent under the command of the Marquis Galeazzo Villa. Both the Regiment of Villa and the Regiment of Chamblay—whose Major is named Monsieur de Montafon—included several other officers who profess the "so-called Reformed Religion." <note>original: "Religione pretesa riformata"; a derogatory term used by Catholic authorities to refer to Protestantism.</note> These officers can testify whether any cruel actions were ever committed or commanded in those places.

The people of Villaro and Bobbio offered no resistance to the quartering of the soldiers. However, they almost entirely abandoned their homes, retreating with all their provisions into the villages and districts of the upper valley. This put the soldiers in a difficult position: they had to either die of hunger or go and seek food with their muskets in those upper villages. 

Despite all the patience the soldiers tried to exercise and the formal appeals <term>remonstrances</term> made to the villagers, it was never possible to gain peaceful access, let alone persuade them to share any food supplies. These people chose to allow their villages to be taken by force, looted, and burned one by one, even though they had a clear example before their eyes: the lower towns of Villaro and Bobbio remained untouched. In those towns, the small handful of inhabitants who had stayed behind lived in peace. They were eventually joined by others who had initially fled to the Valley of Queiras <note>A valley in the French Alps that served as a frequent refuge for Waldensians during times of persecution.</note> but later returned to their own country. To these people was also given...

They were afterwards distributed throughout all Piedmont, and a register was kept of their names, the places where they were sent, and the persons to whom they were given <note>Historically, the Waldensians viewed this "distribution" as the kidnapping of their children for forced conversion to Catholicism.</note>. Or, if they desired it, they were placed in domestic service in Piedmont, and a roll or register was also kept of them. This was the greatest death toll <term>mortality</term> that occurred, which nonetheless did not exceed 200 people, even when adding together those who perished in the snow, those who died from the cold, and those who were killed by the sword. <header>Chap. I. In the Valleys of Piedmont.</header>

<language>English, Italian</language>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>

From this, <note>original Italian: *tutto si può vedere*—"from all this it can be seen"</note> it will easily appear how false the slanders <note>original: "calumnies"</note> of the rebels are. To make themselves objects of pity and to make those who punished them hated, they publish to the world that every kind of cruelty was committed against all sorts of people, regardless of age or sex. These claims can never be proven or substantiated. 

The Marquess of Pianezza had promised certain individuals from Villaro and Bobbio that he would find a way to obtain their pardon, consistent with a promise he had previously made to them. Because of this, they were inclined to receive and house <term>quarter</term> the soldiers in a peaceful manner. This is shown in a formal agreement <term>capitulation</term> signed by the heads of several households. 

<column-break/>

In this agreement, they were granted the practice of the "so-called" Reformed Religion <note>The Catholic author uses the phrase "pretended Reformed Religion" to refer to the Waldensian Protestant faith.</note>. It also specified the conditions of their pardon, subject only to the approval of His Royal Highness <note>S.A.R.: Sua Altezza Reale, the Duke of Savoy</note>. However, the Duke refused to grant his approval because the agreement was made only with a few specific individuals. Consequently, there was no security or assurance that the agreement would be properly followed by their side. 

Within a few days, many people left their homes, and many others voluntarily offered to become Catholics. These people were given a safe conduct <note>original Italian: *salvo condotto*</note> or protection to remain in their houses for two years. They were promised a full pardon at the end of that time, provided they did nothing against His Royal Highness and did not resume their rebellion. The same approach was taken with various others from other villages who voluntarily converted to the Catholic religion. This also applied to some who were being held as prisoners; they requested to be admitted as members of the Church so earnestly that their request could not be refused.

The district of Rorata, consisting of about 25 families or thereabouts, had not been interfered with at all before that time. The Marquess of Pianezza believed that they would not behave any worse than the people of Villar and Bobbio had done, and therefore he also granted them a <term>safeguard</term> <note>original: *Salvaguardia*; a legal document granting protection from military violence or looting</note>.

But Giosuè Ginavello <note>also known as Joshua Janavel, a famous leader of the Waldensian resistance</note>, resolving that his rebellion should exceed that of all the others, arrived with a troop of soldiers who were local inhabitants of that place. Even though that place had received nothing but grace and favors, the Marquess found the inhabitants so completely ungrateful <note>original: "insensible"</note> that he resolved to attack and break up Janavel’s troop (which he did). Some of the rebels were killed on the spot, and others escaped among the steep mountain cliffs. After that, he resolved to destroy this "den of assassins" by demolishing the village of Rorata, which was, by that time, already uninhabited.

As for the Valleys of San Martino and Perosa, which were the subjects of His Royal Highness, the Marquess of Pianezza could do no less than make them feel some part of the punishment due for their audacity. Despite never having been harmed or provoked in any way by His Royal Highness, they had taken up arms against their Sovereign merely to encourage and maintain the rebellion of the people in Luserna.

This is a true account <note>original: "Relation"</note> of what occurred in the Valley of Lucerna. By this, every man may see with what shamelessness <note>original: "impudence"</note> those rebels—who have forcibly brought destruction upon themselves—now intend to spread such strange reports as they do. They think to not only stir up the world’s compassion toward them for their well-deserved punishment <note>original: "chastisement"</note>, but also to create a negative <note>original: "sinister"</note> impression against those who have, with much moderation, inflicted that punishment upon them. These rebels behaved so barbarously and inhumanly—thinking themselves not inferior to their own Prince—against those persons over whom they had no authority at all. They used the most extravagant and unheard-of manner of revenge that was ever practiced against the most innocent people in the world: their own nearest countrymen and kinsmen, who had no knowledge of or part in the troubles that had happened.

<column-break/>

*...that no one escaped but one or two badly wounded men, which does not allow the facts to be established otherwise.* <note>original Italian: "non permetta che ne possa constare"</note>

*This is the true account of the events of the Valley of Lucerna, in which everyone can perceive with what boldness <note>original Italian: "con che fronte"</note> the rebels—who by force have brought ruin upon themselves—think to disseminate those strange stories which they are spreading. They do this to excite not only pity for their well-deserved punishment but a negative conception against those who have justly and moderately established it. Meanwhile, they have behaved with such barbarity and inhumanity, almost in competition with their Prince <note>original Italian: "quasi à gara del suo Principe"; implying they acted as if they held sovereign power</note> against people over whom they had no authority whatever, and mostly with the most extravagant and unheard-of form of vengeance that has ever been practiced against those most innocent and most closely joined to them by country and blood—even those who had no knowledge, let alone any part, in the troubles they brought upon themselves.*

</columns>

## A summary of the reasons and foundations by which His Royal Highness was moved to prohibit the heretics <note>original Italian: "Heretici"</note> of the Valley of Lucerna from living outside the tolerated limits.

->I.<-

The order of January 25, 1655, published by Auditor Gastaldo <note>Andrea Gastaldo was the official tasked with enforcing the boundaries between Catholic and Protestant lands in Savoy.</note> by the command of His Royal Highness <note>Charles Emmanuel II, Duke of Savoy.</note> against those of the so-called Reformed Religion <note>original Italian: "Religione pretesa Riformata"</note>, is so firmly based on justice, reason, and the terms of the gracious grants given by the most serene predecessors of His Royal Highness, that it cannot be disputed by anyone who considers its foundations.

->II.<-

The first document produced on this matter is dated July 5, 1561 <note>This refers to the Treaty of Cavour, which ended a period of warfare and established the first legal boundaries for Waldensian worship.</note>, signed (as is supposed) by Monsieur de Raconigi, Philip of Savoy, with a promise to have it ratified by the reigning Duke at that time, the most serene Duke Emmanuel Philibert. In this document, the limits for the practice of the so-called Reformed Religion were established—namely, for the Valleys of Lucerna (leaving aside the other valleys, which are not currently in dispute), Angrogna, Bobbio, Villar, Valguichiara, and Rorà, along with Tagliaretto and Rua de Bonetti in the territory of Torre Pellice.

<column-break/>

## A Summary of the Reasons and Grounds which moved His Royal Highness to prohibit the heretics of the Valley of Lucerna from living beyond their prescribed limits.

->I.<-

The Order of January 25, published by Auditor Gastaldo according to His Royal Highness's command against those of the <term>so-called Reformed Religion</term> <note>original: "pretended Reformed Religion." Catholic authorities used this legal phrase (Religion Prétendue Réformée) to indicate they did not recognize the Protestant church as a legitimate "reformed" body.</note>, is so well-grounded upon justice and reason, and so consistent with the gracious grants <note>original: "Concessions"</note> of the most serene predecessors of His Royal Highness, that it cannot be questioned by anyone who will duly weigh and consider its grounds.

->II.<-

The first document produced on this matter is dated July 5, 1561, signed (as is supposed) by Monsieur de Raconigi, Philip of Savoy, with a promise to see it ratified by His Highness then reigning, namely the most serene Duke Emmanuel Philibert. In this document, the limits were set within which the so-called Reformed Religion was to be practiced: these were the Valleys of Lucerna (not to mention the other valleys, about which there is currently no dispute), Angrogna, Bobbio, Villar, Valguichiara, and Rorà, together with Taglieretto and Rua de Bonetti in the territory of Torre Pellice <note>original: "La Torre"</note>.

->XXII.<-

Therefore, since the established facts mentioned above cannot be denied—as indeed they cannot—who could ever maintain that the Order of Auditor Gastaldo <note>Andrea Gastaldo was the official who issued the 1655 decree ordering the Waldensians to move to specific areas or convert to Catholicism within three days.</note> is not perfectly well-founded in every sense of equity and justice? ->XXIII.<-

If it is objected that the towns of San Giovanni and La Torre <note>Now Torre Pellice, the historic center of the Waldensian church.</note> were included in this order—even though residency was partially tolerated there—the response is that while this is true, the individuals of that religion living in those places (the first of which is a district and member of Lucerna) have shamelessly and contemptuously violated those laws. They did this by introducing public preaching, which is expressly forbidden by the first article of the Decree of February 25, 1602. By this act, they have incurred the penalty of death and the confiscation of their goods—not only those who performed the religious functions and preached, but even everyone who assisted or was present.
