using a church, which was strictly forbidden; also taking away the bells of the Catholics and failing to demolish those churches that were ordered to be destroyed according to many commands issued for that purpose; and having driven out all the Catholics living in the first of the places mentioned above, and almost all who were in the second, despite an express order to the contrary and the risk of the confiscation of their goods which they incurred by doing so. After all this, how can anyone raise the slightest question or doubt that their punishment was perfectly just? Simply moving from one place to another, between which there is such a very small distance, was the mildest punishment that could be inflicted upon them for such great stubbornness.

## XXIV.

Leaving aside only those of La Torre and San Giovanni, and speaking of all of them in general who received orders to vacate their homes <note>original: "disinhabit"</note>: who ever ventured to dispute or question whether a Prince has sufficient power to command one or more of his subjects to move and relocate from one territory to another within his dominions (whenever he judges it suitable for his service) and to sell the property they have in the place where they live? Who then can doubt the lawfulness of such a command, when it is only a matter of moving to a place two leagues <note>A league was roughly three miles.</note> away, or slightly more? This is especially true where the order is directed at individuals who are offenders, and who might for other reasons be most severely punished, but their Sovereign settles for only—

<column-break/>

*...and with the use of the church <note>original: "Tempio" — literally "Temple," often used for Protestant places of worship</note> which was also strictly forbidden, and by having taken the bells from the Catholics, and by not having demolished the churches according to the many commands received, and by having driven out all the Catholics from the first place and almost all from the second—buying their goods contrary to orders and despite the penalties of confiscation—who can doubt that it was very just to punish these people as well? And who can doubt that the punishment of simply moving one's residence from one place to another a very short distance away was the mildest that could be applied to such great persistence?*

## XXIV.

*But to speak not only of those of La Torre and San Giovanni, but of all those who had orders to vacate their homes, who has ever dared to question that a Prince cannot command one or many of his subjects to move their residence from one land to another within his states, if he judges it fits his service, and to sell their goods in the place from which they move? Who can doubt that it is lawful to do so, where it is a matter of moving only a distance of one, two, or a few more miles, and where the order is addressed to a criminal person who could otherwise be most severely punished, and the goodness of the Sovereign is content with this alone? And who finally—* <note>original Italian: "e chi final-" (the catchword "mente" on the next page completes "finalmente," meaning "finally").</note>

[Mi]nisters of His Royal Highness were sent into the said Valleys, not so much to impose upon them a burden of quartering soldiers <note>The practice of requiring civilians to provide housing and food for military troops.</note>—and even then, a burden that was in no way unbearable—as a kind of punishment for their obstinacy. They were also sent so that, being on the spot, they might confer with their syndics <term>local government officials or magistrates representing the community</term> and councilors in La Torre <note>Torre Pellice, the principal town and intellectual center of the Waldensian valleys.</note> to adjust (if possible) those differences without any further trouble. These men most unwisely took up arms against His Royal Highness in such a brutish, raging, and strangely rebellious manner that it deserved, on one side, a most severe and exemplary punishment; on the other side, it made them altogether unworthy of the favor of any state or sovereign prince, who ought to consider how dangerous a consequence it is to allow crimes of such a nature to go unpunished.

<note>original: "quando i Ministri di S. A. R. si sono portati nelle Valli..." (This column provides the Italian translation of the same argument.)</note>

When the ministers of His Royal Highness <note>S.A.R.: Sua Altezza Reale, referring to Charles Emmanuel II, Duke of Savoy.</note> went into the Valleys, it was not so much to give them the burden of a tolerable lodging <note>Referring to the quartering of soldiers mentioned in the previous column.</note> as some punishment for their stubbornness, as it was to be on the site where—without any other effort—speaking with the same syndics and councilors in La Torre, they could settle these differences. Instead, they very imprudently took up arms against His Royal Highness with a fury, a brutality, and a kind of rebellion that was as deserving of the most exemplary and severe punishment as it was unworthy of any assistance or protection from any sovereign or any state. Such a ruler must, without question, consider with what harmful consequences the people always view these kinds of crimes when they go unpunished.

## CHAPTER II.

### The Observations of some capable and knowledgeable Friends of the poor Protestants of the Valleys of Piedmont, regarding the Court of Savoy's Statement of Fact <note>original: "Factum"—a legal summary of the facts of a case.</note> and Reasons, set down at length in the preceding Chapters.

In the previous chapter, the *Christian Reader* has a faithful account of what the opposing party is able to claim, either for the justification of their own proceedings or the exaggeration of the others' offense and pretended rebellion. The truth is, they have handled this in such a skillful method and expressed it in such smooth language that ordinary people, in reading it without commentary, would certainly run a great risk of having their judgments warped and of swallowing the most notorious deceptions in the world as well-grounded and undoubted truths. 

Therefore, while on one hand I thought it appropriate—to avoid the accusation of bias—to insert the narrative and reasons of the Court of *Savoy* word-for-word in their own native language <note>The previous pages included the original Italian text alongside the translation.</note> in which they themselves published them to the world, so on the other hand, I believed it the duty of a faithful historian not to omit anything that might enlighten the understanding of those who read this work. This will give them the advantage of fully comprehending the very core of these subtle documents, which were composed for the express purpose of darkening and complicating the truth with Jesuitical <note>A term often used by Protestant writers of the time to describe reasoning they considered deceptive, hair-splitting, or morally flexible.</note> distinctions and evasions. No further introduction to this matter is needed.

...ing, as well as to leave their homes and the property they owned in other parts of the said Valley.

->Critique <note>original: "Animadversion"—a critical observation or remark.</note><-

Christian Reader, take heed and beware of who you are dealing with at this first encounter; it is the Devil appearing to you in human form, though he hides his cloven foot! The author of the text tells you that the poor Protestants were commanded to move themselves within three days, leaving their homes and goods, and so far he speaks the truth. But he leaves out the main part of the sentence—that wicked influence which poisons the whole situation—*namely, unless they prove to us within twenty days that they have become Catholics.* This can be seen in that famous "Order of Gastaldo" <note>Andrea Gastaldo was the official who issued the 1655 decree ordering the Waldensians to move or convert, which triggered the massacre.</note>, which is included in the Second Book of this history, Chapter 4.

->Court of Savoy<-

*In obedience to this command, those of the so-called <note>original: "pretended"—the Catholic court used this term to deny the legitimacy of the Reformed faith.</note> Reformed Religion accordingly withdrew within the prescribed limits.*

->Critique<-

A very strong argument for their profound obedience and respect toward their Prince, and for his severity toward his poor subjects.

->Court of Savoy<-

*Nevertheless, at the same time, they sent representatives to His Royal Highness, declaring this command to be contrary to their ancient concessions <note>Legal grants of religious and civil rights given by previous rulers.</note> and therefore petitioned for it to be revoked.*

->Critique<-

The Christian Reader is left to judge whether they had a just reason to do so or not, after remembering the concessions of the year 1621 (included in Chapter 3 of the Second Book) and carefully comparing them with the following authentic documents. These have been preserved by a miraculous providence, and the true original versions may be seen by those who are interested in the public library of the famous University of Cambridge <note>The author, Samuel Morland, personally deposited these historical Waldensian documents at Cambridge.</note>.

The truth is, this issue of *concessions* is the most essential point of all. Consequently, clarifying this at the start of the discussion will be of great use in better explaining and deciding the whole controversy.

### An Agreement of King Henry IV of France with the Evangelical Churches of the Valleys of Piedmont, Who Submitted Themselves to His Rule, November 1, 1592.

#### A highly authentic copy of the true original text, which can be seen in the Public Library of the famous University of Cambridge.

---

<note>The following text is presented in two columns, mirroring the original layout. The left column is modernized from the original French, and the right column is modernized from the 17th-century English translation.</note>

Inasmuch as the enemies of the most High, most Powerful, and most Victorious Prince, Henry the Fourth of this name, by the grace of God King of France and of Navarre, having for some years past, by force of arms and without just title, occupied his country and the Marquisate of Saluces <note>original: "Saluces" — modern Saluzzo in Italy</note>, as well as other lands and places belonging to His Majesty on this side of the mountains <note>The Alps</note>, which were ancient territories of the French Crown; for the recovery of which, and also to bring under his obedience and subjection the provinces and countries of Piedmont, Savoy, and others currently possessed by the enemies and usurpers of the said Marquisate of Saluces, His Most Christian Majesty sent here a strong and sufficient army under the command and leadership of the illustrious Lord François de Bonne, Lord of Lesdiguières, a counselor in his private State Council, Captain of one hundred men-at-arms of His Majesty’s regular forces <note>original: "ordonnances" — permanent military units</note>, and General Commander of the said army and country of Savoy on this side of the mountains for His Majesty's service; and the said Lord of Lesdiguières, having moved with the said army into Piedmont, has captured and brought under the obedience of His Ma-

<column-break/>

Inasmuch as the enemies of the most High, Mighty, and most Victorious Prince, Henry the Fourth of that name, by the grace of God King of France and Navarre, have of late years—by force of arms and without just title—usurped his country and the Marquisate of Saluces, with other lands and places belonging to His Majesty on this side of the mountains, which were ancient members of the Crown of France; for the recovery of which, as also to bring under his obedience and subjection the provinces and countries of Piedmont, Savoy, and others at present possessed by the said enemies and usurpers of the said Marquisate of Saluces, His Most Christian Majesty did send to this side of the mountains a good and sufficient army, under the leadership of the illustrious Lord Francis de Bonne, Lord of Lesdiguières, a Counselor in his private Council of State, Captain of one hundred men-at-arms of His Majesty’s trained bands <note>original: "trained Bands" — a term for organized local militia or regular troops</note>, and Commander General of the said army and country of Savoy on this side of the mountains for the service of his said Majesty; the which Lord of Lesdiguières, having traveled with his said army into Piedmont, took and brought under the obedi- <note>catchword: ence</note>

<summary>This page introduces a 1592 agreement where the Waldensian (Evangelical) churches of Piedmont submitted to King Henry IV of France. It details the military campaign led by the Lord of Lesdiguières to reclaim the Marquisate of Saluzzo and surrounding territories from those who had usurped them from the French Crown.</summary>

...presence of His Majesty, the towns and castles of Pérouse, Bricherasio, Torre Pellice, Mirabocco, Osasco, Massello, and Pradellina, and at the same time summoned the ministers and officers of the churches, the syndics <note>original: "Syndicks" — local government officials</note>, and the inhabitants of the Valleys of Angrogna, Bobbio Pellice, Villar Pellice, Tagliante, and Torre Pellice, and of another place named Torre Pellice, San Giovanni di Luserna, Massello, Rorà, Bibiana, Campiglione, and Fenile—all included and contained under the name of the Valley of Angrogna. Also the places of Rocheplatte, St. Barthélemy, and Prarustin, comprised under the jurisdiction of San Secondo; likewise the places of Pérouse, Saint-Germain-des-Portes, Pinache, Villar di Pinache, Pramollo, and Le Taluc, all included under the name of the Valley of Pérouse. Likewise the places of Frusase, as well as the places of Prali, Rodoretto, Perrier, Fayet, Massello, Saint Martin, Maneille, and Rioclaret, all comprised under the name of the Valley of Saint Martin. Likewise the places of Meana and Mattie, situated in the Valley of Susa. To this end, the said Lord of Lesdiguières <note>François de Bonne, a prominent French Protestant military leader</note> deputized and sent to them at several times Mr. Claude Perron, Minister of the Word of God in Pragela, to negotiate the means and conditions by which the said people and Valleys, and their inhabitants, might be brought out from the obedience and subjection of Charles Emmanuel, the current Duke of Savoy. They claim to have been under his power and sovereignty until the present, even from the beginning of the wars raised in France in the year 1585 and before. They now render and yield themselves under the obedience of His Majesty, taking the Oath of Allegiance to His said Majesty, in such...

...His Majesty, the cities and castles of Pérouse, Bricherasio, Torre Pellice, Mirabocco, Osasco, Massello, and Pradellina, and at the same time having summoned the ministers and church syndics, residents, and inhabitants of the Valleys of Angrogna, Bobbio Pellice, Villar Pellice, Tagliante, Torre Pellice, and another place named Torre Pellice, San Giovanni di Luserna, Massello, Rorà, Bibiana, Campiglione, and Fenile—all places comprised and contained under the name and title of the said Valley of Angrogna. Likewise the places of Rocheplatte, St. Barthélemy, and Prarustin under the name of the jurisdiction <note>original: "mandement"</note> of San Secondo. Likewise the places of Pérouse, Saint-Germain-des-Portes, Pinache, Villar di Pinache, Pramollo, and Taluc, all comprised under the name of the Valley of Pérouse. Likewise the place of Frusase, as well as the places of Prali, Rodoretto, Perrier, Fayet, Massello, Saint Martin, Maneille, and Rioclaret, all comprised under the name of the Valley of Saint Martin. Likewise the places of Meana and Mattie, situated in the Valley of Susa. To these ends, the said Lord of Lesdiguières has several times deputized Mr. Claude Perron, Minister of the Word of God in Pragela, to treat regarding the means and conditions under which the said peoples and Valleys, and their residents and inhabitants, might be induced to depart from the obedience and subjection of Charles Emmanuel, the current possessor of the Duchy of Savoy. They claim to have been under his power and sovereignty until now, even at the beginning of the wars raised in France in the year 1585 and before, and to reduce and restore themselves under the obedience of His said Majesty, pledging to him the oath of loyalty required in such a case...

## Chapter II. and the Protestants, 1592.

<columns>

...as the case required and was accustomed, into the hands of the said Lord of Lesdiguières <note>François de Bonne, Lord of Lesdiguières, was a prominent French Protestant military leader and later Constable of France</note>. To this, the said Ministers, Syndics <note>original: "Syndicks" — local government officials or magistrates</note>, and inhabitants of the said Valleys raised great opposition and difficulties. They argued that, according to the Word of God, it was not lawful for them to withdraw themselves or depart from the obedience and loyalty they owed to their natural and lawful Prince. They also noted that they had not been molested by him in the public, free, and general exercise of the Christian Reformed Religion, but had been maintained and preserved in it until the present time—both by the late Duke of Savoy and by his successor—through the treaties and agreements <note>original: "Capitulations"</note> made with them by the late Duke concerning religion after the war they fought against him in the year 1561.

<column-break/>

Upon this, the said Mr. Perron argued <note>original: "remonstrate"</note> to them that this current war was not a private war of the said Charles Emmanuel <note>Charles Emmanuel I, Duke of Savoy (reigned 1580–1630)</note> against the "Most Christian King" <note>A traditional title for the King of France, in this case, Henry IV</note>. On the contrary, he explained it was a general war involving many Princes of Christendom who had combined together to usurp the Kingdom of France, and particularly to uproot <note>original: "extirpate"</note> and totally ruin the Reformed Churches of France, England, Germany, and other states of Christendom. He argued that Charles Emmanuel was included in this combination and conspiracy. Under this pretext and name, the Duke had already usurped the state and Marquisate of Saluzzo <note>original: "Saluces"</note> and invaded by force of arms many towns and castles in the County of Provence. In every place he took, he abolished and drove out the practice of the Reformed Religion, as he had recently done in the bailiwicks <note>original: "Balliages" — administrative districts</note> of Gex, Thonon, and other places which the people of Berne had restored to his late father. In those places, his soldiers committed all manner of plunders, murders, and wicked acts.

</columns>

<summary>The Protestant inhabitants of the Piedmontese valleys refuse to switch their loyalty from the Duke of Savoy to France, citing religious freedom treaties. In response, the French negotiator Mr. Perron warns them that the Duke is part of a broader Catholic conspiracy intended to destroy Protestantism across Europe.</summary>

| ...erased and exterminated both the memory and the practice <note>original: "exercise"</note> of the Reformed Religion; and that the said Ministers and inhabitants of the said Valleys—who from time immemorial, even before the time of Luther, John Hus, and Wycliffe <note>original: "Wickliff"</note>, have belonged to the said Reformed Religion—found themselves (as ancient members of the Church) greatly concerned in this business. Upon this depends their utter ruin and overthrow if God by His mercy does not uphold the other Churches, including even those of the Kingdom of France. He likewise pointed out <note>original: "remonstrate"</note> to them the ancient alliance that existed between them and the Valley of Pragela <note>modern Pragelato, a Protestant stronghold in the Alps</note> and others under the authority <note>original: "obedience"</note> of His said Majesty. These had been joined and allied together from time immemorial for the maintenance of their religion, an alliance that was not made void by the treaty made with the late Duke of Savoy. On the contrary, the said treaty was made while saving and without prejudice to the said alliance. By virtue of this, since this war was undertaken on behalf of the said religion, they cannot—without making themselves treacherous <note>original: "perfidious"</note>—forsake those of Pragela, who are now at war with the said Charles Emmanuel for the preservation of the said religion. Whereupon the said Ministers and inhabitants of the said Valleys, who had taken up arms and put themselves on the defensive against the said Lord of Lesdiguières—and to that end had taken possession of many places and narrow mountain passes <note>original: "passages"</note> of their Valleys—were at length persuaded by the reasons mentioned above, as well as by other reasons alleged and proposed by the said Mr. Claude Perron. Seeing the said Lord of Lesdiguières in arms and ready to attack <note>original: "fall on"</note> them as enemies of His Majesty should they persevere and refuse... | ...erased and exterminated every mark and practice <note>original: "effacé & exterminé toute marque & exercice"</note> of the said Reformed Religion; and that the said Ministers and inhabitants of the said Valleys—who from all antiquity and from time immemorial, indeed even before the century of Luther, John Hus, and Wycliffe <note>original: "Huiclef"</note>, have been of the said religion—finding themselves, as ancient members of the Church, had a very great and very notable interest in this affair. Upon this depends their ruin and entire subversion, if God by His great mercy does not sustain the other Churches, even those of the Kingdom of France. He further pointed out to them the ancient alliance which exists between them and the Valley of Pragela, and others under the obedience of the said Majesty, joined and confederated at all times by the maintenance of their religion. This alliance had not been renounced by the treaty made with the late Duke of Savoy; rather, the said treaty had been passed saving and without prejudice to the said alliance. By virtue of which, since it concerns the matter of the said religion in this war, they cannot, without treachery <note>original: "perfidie"</note>, abandon those of Pragela, who are now at war with Duke Charles Emmanuel for the preservation of the said religion. Whereupon the said Ministers, residents <note>original: "manans"</note>, and inhabitants of the said Valleys had taken up arms and stood on the defensive against the said Lord of Lesdiguières, and for these purposes occupied several places, passages, and straits <note>mountain passes</note> of their Valleys. They were finally persuaded by the reasons mentioned above and others alleged and proposed by the said Mr. Claude Perron. And seeing the said Lord of Lesdiguières in arms and ready to assault them and treat them as enemies of His Majesty, in case they persevered in not wanting to recognize him... |

<summary>This page records the 1592 treaty where the Waldensian Valleys transferred their allegiance from the Duke of Savoy to King Henry IV of France, securing a promise of religious freedom in exchange for their loyalty. The French commander, Lesdiguières, granted these terms to avoid a long, costly mountain war against a people the Pope and Savoy had failed to defeat by force.</summary>

| Church discipline <note>original: "Discipline Ecclesiastique"</note> and everything that depends on it throughout all locations in the said Valleys where it currently exists, without any restriction or modification whatsoever. Just as in the past and from time immemorial, their churches have been extended and enlarged from one place to another within the said Valleys as the people gained knowledge of it—achieved through the zeal and affection that these people brought to it, and the tolerance and permission of their Princes and Magistrates—so also it shall be lawful for them to extend the preaching of the Word of God and the administration of the Sacraments in all places and areas of the said Valleys where there are people professing the said Reformed Religion. These people, as a body of the Church, may call their Ministers and Pastors without distinction or difference of location. They shall be permitted and allowed to assemble to hold their consistories, colloquies, and synods <note>These are the local, regional, and general administrative meetings of the Reformed church.</note> and to manage and conduct their ecclesiastical affairs whenever necessity requires, without being molested or hindered by anyone. His Majesty shall be most humbly petitioned to please found, establish, and maintain a college for the instruction of the youth of the said Valleys in such a place as shall be decided by the Commissioners, who shall be appointed for these purposes by his said Majesty. It has been agreed that his said Majesty shall allow the Churches and their Pastors to enjoy the same wages, statuses, pensions, and privileges that he has granted or shall grant hereafter to the Churches, Pastors, and Ministers of France, specifically those of Guienne, Languedoc, and Dauphiné <note>Provinces in Southern France with significant Protestant populations.</note>. And since the said people are almost all of the Reformed Religion, the Roman Catholics not making... | Church discipline, and that which depends on it, in all places of the said Valleys where it is at present, without any restriction or modification whatsoever. Those who, as a body of a church, shall call their Ministers and Pastors without distinction or difference of places, shall be permitted to assemble themselves to hold their consistories, colloquies, and synods, and to treat and order their church affairs at any time as the occasion requires, without being troubled or molested by anyone. His Majesty shall be most humbly prayed that he will be pleased to found, erect, and maintain a college for the instruction of the youth of the said Valleys in such a place as shall be advised by the Commissioners that shall be established by his Majesty for that purpose. It is concluded that his said Majesty shall permit the Churches and Pastors of the Valleys to enjoy the same wages, estates, pensions, and privileges that he has granted or shall grant hereafter to the Churches and Pastors of France, even those of Guienne, Languedoc, and Dauphiné. | [Modernized from the English] | [Modernized from the French] |
| :--- | :--- |
| the hundredth part <note>The meaning of "the hundredth part" likely refers to a specific proportion of officials or a fiscal arrangement mentioned on the preceding page.</note> among them, it is agreed at their earnest and urgent request—without which they would neither negotiate nor conclude the treaty—that to keep them in a greater union, and to give them reason to have even greater affection for His Majesty's service and to remain his good and loyal subjects, His Majesty and the Kings his successors shall allow them, now and hereafter, Officers of Justice of the highest rank. These shall be men of the said Reformed Religion <note>Protestantism, specifically the Waldensian/Calvinist faith.</note> and no other, considering that by their privileges, they have the right to elect the said judges and officers; that is to say, they shall choose three candidates, from whom the Prince shall choose one. All their franchises <note>original: "Franchises" — refers to specific legal rights or exemptions granted to a city or group.</note>, liberties, immunities, and privileges, both ancient and modern, shall be maintained and confirmed to them in Piedmont, Dauphiné, the Marquisate of Saluzzo, and the territories of France, in the same manner as they have by right used and enjoyed them previously. Italians and others, of whatever status they may be, who profess the Reformed Religion, shall have the power to retire to the said valleys if they think fit, to live there according to the Reformation of the said religion without being troubled, vexed, or harassed by anyone whatsoever. And the said valleys shall be and remain joined and incorporated into the State and Crown of France forever, without ever being separated, alienated, or taken away for any reason whatsoever. And if at any time it should happen that His Majesty and his successors should be forced to surrender them to the jurisdiction of any other, they shall be transferred with the same conditions, privileges, and qualities that shall be granted to them by the present treaty, to— | the hundredth part among them: It was agreed at their very great and urgent request <note>original: "tresgrande & instante requisition"</note>—without which grant they would not have been willing to negotiate or agree—that to maintain them in greater union and give them cause to be all the more devoted to His Majesty’s service and to remain his good and loyal subjects, His Majesty and the Kings his successors shall give them, now and hereafter, Officers of Justice in the first instance <note>A legal term referring to the court where a case is first heard.</note> from the said Reformed Religion and no other. This is especially granted since, by their privileges, they have the right to nominate three such judges and officers, from whom the Prince chooses one. All their franchises, liberties, immunities, and ancient and modern privileges shall be confirmed to them and inviolably observed and maintained, both in Piedmont and in the Dauphiné, the Marquisate of Saluzzo, and French lands, according to how they have properly and duly used them previously. Italians and others of whatever nation they may be who profess the said Reformed Religion may retire into the said valleys, if they see fit, to live there according to its Reformation without being harassed, disturbed, or investigated <note>original: "recerchés" — often implying a judicial inquiry or persecution.</note> by anyone. The said people and valleys shall be and remain perpetually annexed and incorporated into the state and Crown of France, without the possibility of being dismembered, alienated, or transferred for any cause or occasion whatsoever. <meta>This page continues the formal legal declaration of loyalty by the Waldensian communities and local magistrates of the Piedmontese valleys to King Henry IV of France in 1592.</meta>

# An Agreement between Henry IV. Book III.

| Modernized from the original English | Modernized from the original French <note>original: "nautés en general & particulier..."</note> |
| :--- | :--- |
| The said communities <note>original: "Communalties"</note> in general and in particular—as far as it does now, or may at any time hereafter, concern any of them respectively—have confessed and acknowledged, and do confess and acknowledge themselves to be vassals and liege subjects <term>A "liege subject" owed absolute and primary loyalty to a specific sovereign above all others.</term> of the most Christian and most serene Henry IV, by the grace of God King of France and Navarre, Dauphin of Viennois <note>The title of the heir to the French throne, also referring to the province of Dauphiné.</note>, Marquess of Saluzzo <note>original: "Saluces"</note>, their true and sovereign Lord. They are willing to hold in liege homage the said fiefs and jurisdictions, lordships and estates, with their appurtenances and dependencies, according to the lists or rolls which they shall respectively submit. Swearing and promising by their faith and oath taken upon the Holy Bible, lifting up their right hands to Heaven in the accustomed manner and according to the King’s ordinances, they promise both now and in the future to remain perpetually vassals and liege subjects to his said Majesty. They vow to yield to him forever all obedience, fidelity, submission, and service, as they were formerly accustomed to render to their sovereign prince. In short, they promise to do, say, and fulfill all that is contained in the new and ancient forms of loyalty <note>original: "fidelity"</note>, and particularly not to assist or counsel anyone who wishes to or may hurt—either in word or deed—his Majesty, his ministers, officers, or subjects. On the contrary, if they know of such threats, they will hinder them with all their power, or—not being able to hinder them—will give notice as soon as they can to his Majesty or his officers. If it should happen that any usurpation or wrong is done to the King's people or estates, they promise to help and aid them both in recovering what they have lost and in defending and maintaining what they possess. Knowing that his Majesty will justly resent... | ...communities <note>original: "nautés"</note> in general and in particular, as much as each of them is affected now or may be affected in the future respectively, have confessed and recognized—and do confess and recognize—that they are vassal men and liege subjects of the most Christian and most serene Henry IV, by the grace of God King of France and of Navarre, Dauphin of Viennois, Marquess of Saluzzo, etc. He is their true and sovereign Lord, from whom they hold (and wish to hold) in faith and liege homage the aforementioned fiefs, lands, jurisdictions, lordships, and goods, including their appurtenances and dependencies, according to the records <note>original: "denombremens"</note> they shall provide respectively. Swearing and promising by their faith and the oaths they have pledged—having touched the Holy Gospels of God and raised their right hands to heaven in the accustomed manner according to the King's ordinances—they promise from this time forward to be and remain perpetually vassal men and liege subjects of his said Majesty. They promise to pledge and render to him forever all obedience, loyalty, submission, and service that they were previously accustomed to render to their sovereign prince. In summary, they shall do, say, and carry out <note>original: "exploiter"</note> everything contained in the new and old forms of loyalty. Especially, they shall never provide counsel or aid to anyone who wishes to or could harm—by deed or word—his said Majesty, his ministers, officers, and subjects. Rather, knowing of such a thing, they shall prevent it with all their power, or if unable to stop it, they shall inform his Majesty or his officers as soon as possible. In the event that any wrong or usurpation is committed against their persons and property, they shall aid and assist them both in recovery and in their perpetual maintenance. And knowing that his said Majesty will justly take offense <note>original: "se ressentir"</note>... |

This was done by the Counts and Lords of the Fiefs <term>land held under the feudal system</term>, Counties, Jurisdictions, and Lordships, both in their own names and as legal representatives acting for their associates mentioned therein, and by the syndics and communities of Bricherasio and the aforementioned places and valleys. We do approve, ratify, and confirm the same by these presents, as if it had been made by us in our said Council, so that those agreed and concluded articles may be kept and maintained by us and by the Kings who succeed us, without violating them or allowing anyone else to violate them in any way or manner whatsoever. And we have received the said Counts and Lords in their respective names, as well as the syndics and communities, into the said faith and homage. In doing so, we have maintained them in the possession of all the said fiefs and counties... | ...to be sold or transferred for any cause or occasion whatsoever, and other charges and conditions amply declared in the act of the said treaty, made and passed at Bricherasio <note>original: Briqueiras</note> on the first day of November last; and yet under our good pleasure, and by means of the oath of loyalty that the said syndics, in the said names, would make into the hands of the said Lord of Lesdiguières, as they have done on the said day. We make it known that—having had shown to us in our Council, held in the assembly of the Princes of our Blood <note>original: Princes de nôtre Sang</note> and other great and notable figures of our said Council, the said treaty, accord, and convention, together with the act of the oath of loyalty, faith, and homage, made and given to us into the hands of the said Lord of Lesdiguières on the first day of November by the Counts, Lords, and Co-Lords of the Fiefs, Counties, Lordships, and Jurisdictions, both in their own names as representatives and acting for the associates named therein, and by the syndics and communities of Bricherasio and the aforementioned places and valleys—We have praised, approved, ratified, and confirmed the whole. **Y**our most humble and most obedient subjects, who profess the Reformed Religion in the valleys of Luserna, Angrogna, Perosa, San Martino, Roccapiatta, San Bartolomeo, Talucco, and other places in Piedmont subjected to your Crown, come to throw themselves at your Majesty’s feet. They do this to offer their faith and homage, along with all assurances of sincere fidelity and perfect obedience that subjects owe to their Sovereign—just as they have already done through the person of my Lord Cardinal Richelieu, your Majesty's General in Italy. <meta>This page continues the argument for the authenticity of the legal treaties between the Protestant inhabitants of the Piedmont valleys and King Henry IV of France. <page-num>456</page-num>
<header>*The aforementioned Agreement between* Henry IV, Book III.</header>

Now, to make it evident to the world that the treaty mentioned above between Henry IV and the inhabitants of the Valleys—along with its ratification and subsequent confirmation—is a genuine document and not a forgery by these poor people (as is usually alleged against them in such cases), we note the following: That very treaty, word for word, without any alteration other than the reordering of some sections and a few minor spelling differences which do not change the substance or meaning, was registered in the Parliament of Dauphiné <note>original: "Dauphine"; a high court of justice in southeastern France</note>. It was established as a permanent decree by the King and his successors, intended to be as unalterable as the "laws of the Medes and Persians" <term>Laws of the Medes and Persians: a biblical idiom (from the Book of Daniel) referring to a law that is absolute and cannot be changed or revoked</term>. 

To provide full and complete satisfaction to all who are curious, there follows here a most authentic extract and copy of that document, written by the hand of Maximin, one of the Secretaries of the Parliament. He is a person so well known that no record in the world could carry greater credit or authority.

The true original of this document can be seen, along with the others, in the public library of the famous University of Cambridge.

## Letters Patent of the King, regarding the homage paid to His Majesty by those who have returned to his obedience in Piedmont.

<margin>
(a) Osasco.
(b) Macello.
</margin>
Henry, by the grace of God, King of France and of Navarre, Dauphin of Viennois, Count of Valentinois and Diois, to all present and to come, greetings. Some time ago, we sent an army into Piedmont and Savoy, giving the general command and conduct of it to our beloved and loyal Counselor in our Private and State Council, and Captain of one hundred men-at-arms, François de Bonne, Lord of Lesdiguières. His mission was to use our forces to recover the Marquisate of Saluces <note>original: "Saluxes"; the Italian territory of Saluzzo</note>, which was usurped and invaded by the Duke of Savoy, to return it to our obedience, and to bring back under our rule the countries of Piedmont and Savoy. The said Lord of Lesdiguières, with the aforementioned army, advanced into Piedmont and brought under our obedience the towns and castles of Perosa, Bricherasio, Torre Pellice, Luserna, Mirabocco, (a) Osasco, (b) Macello, and Bradelens. 

At the same time, he summoned the churches, <term>Syndics</term> <note>Syndics: local government officials or chief magistrates in these alpine communities</note>, residents, and inhabitants of the valleys of Angrogna, Bobbio, Villar, Tagliaret de la Tour, and another place named Torre San Giovanni, as well as Luserna, Macello, Boras, Bibiana, Campiglione, Fenile—all places included under the name and title of the Valley of Angrogna. He also summoned the villages of Rocheplatte, Saint Barthélemy, and Prarostino under the name of the district of Saint Pion; the places of Perosa, Saint Germain, <margin>(c) Des Portes. (d) Pramollo. (e) Prussac. (f) Rodoretto. (g) Massello, or Macello. (h) Rioclaret.</margin> (c) Des Portes, Pinache, Villart de Pinache, (d) Pramollo, and Le Talluc, all included under the name of the Valley of Perosa; the village of (e) Prussac; as well as the places of Prali, (f) Rodoretto, Perrero, Faetto, (g) Massello, Saint Martin, Maneille, and (h) Rioclaret, all included under the name of the Valley of Saint Martin; and the villages of Meana and Mattie located in the Susa Valley, to return to our said obedience. 

To this end, he appointed capable persons of authority to meet with them on several occasions to negotiate the terms and conditions under which the said people, valleys, residents, and inhabitants could be induced to do so. Regarding this, after great opposition and difficulties on their part, and following the arguments, just causes, and considerations presented by the Lord of Lesdiguières—and after the matter was maturely deliberated by both sides—a treaty of peace, agreement, and convention was made between the said Lord of Lesdiguières, acting for and in our name, and the Syndics and deputies of the said Valleys, acting both in their own names and for their communities, residents, and inhabitants, their heirs, and successors. This was for the return of the specified places to our obedience, with the people and Valleys being forever annexed and incorporated into the State and Crown of France, without the possibility of being alienated or transferred for any cause or occasion whatsoever, along with other duties and conditions fully declared...

In the act of the said treaty, made and signed at Bricherasio <note>original: "Briqueiras"</note> on the first day of last November—all of which is subject to our royal approval and contingent upon the oath of loyalty that the said <term>Syndics</term> <note>local magistrates or community representatives</note>, in the aforementioned names, would swear to the Lord of Lesdiguières, as they had already done on that day:

In doing so, we have maintained them in the possession of all the said Fiefs, Counties, Jurisdictions, Seigniories, goods, and properties, with their rights, belongings, and dependencies, in accordance with their ancient and previous privileges and investitures <note>formal legal grants of land or office</note> which they have previously and duly enjoyed and continue to enjoy. Therefore, we command our beloved and faithful members of our Court of Parliament and the Chamber of Accounts <note>original: "Chambre des Comptes"; the sovereign court responsible for managing public finances</note> in our land of Dauphiné, the treasurers-general of France and our finances there, and our other Justices and Officers whom it may concern, to have these presents—together with the said articles and acts attached under the counter-seal of our Chancery—read, published, registered, maintained, kept, and observed inviolably forever, ceasing and causing to cease all troubles and hindrances to the contrary. We also command our officials of the Chamber of Accounts to register the said oath of loyalty, faith, and homage made and sworn to us (as stated above) in the archives of our said Chamber of Accounts without any difficulty, so that it may be referred to when necessary. For such is our pleasure; and to ensure this is a firm and stable matter forever, we have caused our seal to be placed on these presents, saving our rights in all things and the rights of others in all things.

<header>Chapter II. and the Protestants of the Valleys.</header>

<margin>
Taillare <note>modern: Tagliante</note>.

Since the enemies of the most high, most powerful, and most victorious Prince Henry IV, by the grace of God King of France and Navarre, have for several years occupied his land and the Marquisate of Saluzzo <note>original: "Marquisat de Salluces"</note>, along with other lands and places belonging to His Majesty on this side of the mountains—ancient members of the Crown of France—His Most Christian Majesty, for the recovery of these lands and to bring under his obedience and subjection the provinces and countries of Piedmont, Savoy, and others currently possessed by the said enemies and usurpers of the said Marquisate of Saluzzo, sent a good and sufficient army under the leadership of the Illustrious Lord François de Bonne, Lord of Lesdiguières. 

The Lord of Lesdiguières is a member of the King's Private and State Council, Captain of one hundred men-at-arms of his ordinances, and General Commander of the said army and the lands of Savoy and the regions on this side of the mountains. Having moved into Piedmont with his army, he took and brought under His Majesty’s obedience the towns and castles of Perosa <note>original: "la Perouse"</note>, Bricherasio <note>original: "Briqueras"</note>, Torre Pellice <note>original: "la Tour de Luserne"</note>, Mirabouc, Osasco <note>original: "Osase"</note>, Massel, and Pradelle. 

At the same time, he summoned the ministers, officers, churches, <term>syndics</term> <note>local magistrates or community representatives</note>, residents, and inhabitants of the Valleys of Angrogna, Bobbio, Villar, Taillare, and Torre; another place named Torre, San Giovanni di Luserna, Massel, Rorà, Bibiana, Campiglione, and Fenile—all places included under the name and title of the Valley of Angrogna. Also, the places of Rocheplatte, San Bartolomeo, and Prarostino under the name of the district <note>original: "mandement"</note> of San Secondo <note>original: "Sainct Sion"</note>. Also, the places of Perosa, San Germano Chisone, Pinasca, Villar Perosa, Pramollo, and Tallut, all included under the name of the Valley of Perosa. Also, the place of Frossasco, as well as the places of Prali, Rodoretto, Faetto, Massello, San Martino, Maneglia, and Rioclaret, all included under the name of the Valley of San Martino. Finally, the places of Meana and Mattie situated in the Val di Susa.

To this end, the said Lord of Lesdiguières has at various times sent to them Mr. Claude Perron, Minister of the Word of God in Pragelato <note>original: "Prajalla"</note>, to negotiate the means and conditions under which the said people and inhabitants of the Valleys might be induced to withdraw from the obedience and subjection of Charles Emmanuel, the current possessor of the Duchy of Savoy. They claim to have been under his power and sovereignty until now, even at the beginning of the wars raised in France in the year 1585 and before. They were invited to return and submit themselves to the obedience of His Majesty, swearing to him the oath of loyalty required and customary in such cases into the hands of the said Lord of Lesdiguières. 

To this, the said Ministers, Syndics, and inhabitants of the said Valleys formed great oppositions and difficulties. They argued that it was not permissible for them, by the word of God, to withdraw and depart from the obedience and loyalty they owed to their natural and legitimate Prince. They noted that they had not been disturbed by him in the public, free, and general exercise of the Reformed Christian Religion, but rather had been maintained and preserved up to the present—both by the late Duke of Savoy and by his successor—according to the treaties and <term>capitulations</term> <note>formal agreements or surrender terms</note> made by the late Lord Duke regarding religion following the war they had sustained against him.

<summary>This page describes how King Henry IV's general, Lesdiguières, captured key Piedmontese territories and attempted to persuade the local Protestant (Waldensian) communities to switch their allegiance from the Duke of Savoy to the French Crown. The inhabitants resisted, citing religious loyalty to the Duke who had granted them freedom of worship.</summary>

<header>The above-said Agreement between Henry IV and the Protestants. Book III.</header>

In the year 1561 <note>This refers to the Peace of Cavour, an earlier treaty between the Duke of Savoy and the Waldensians</note>, Master Perron pointed out to them that this present war was not merely a private conflict between the said Charles Emmanuel <note>Charles Emmanuel I, Duke of Savoy</note> and the Most Christian King <note>The traditional title for the King of France, here referring to Henry IV</note>. Rather, he argued it was a general war involving several Princes of Christendom, allied and banded together for the usurpation of the Kingdom of France and, specifically, for the total destruction and ruin of the Reformed Churches <note>original: "Eglises Reformées"</note> of France, England, Germany, and other states of Christendom. 

He explained that the said Charles Emmanuel is included in this league and conspiracy. Under this name and pretext, he has usurped the state of the Marquisate of Saluzzo <note>original: "Marquisat de Saluce"</note> and invaded several towns and castles of the County of Provence by force of arms. In these places, he has abolished and driven out the practice of the Reformed Religion, as he recently did in the districts of Gex and Thonon <note>original: "Baliages de Gey Thonon"</note> and others that the people of Bern had returned to his late father. In those regions, his soldiers have committed all sorts of looting, murder, and impieties, erasing and exterminating every mark and practice of the Reformed Religion.

Master Perron further argued that the said ministers and inhabitants of these Valleys have belonged to this religion since ancient times—indeed, from time immemorial, even before the era of Luther, Jan Hus, or Wycliffe <note>This is a significant claim by the Waldensians/Vaudois that their faith predated the 16th-century Protestant Reformation</note>. As ancient members of the Church, they have a very great and notable interest in this affair, upon which their entire ruin or survival depends. If God, through His mercy, does not allow the other Churches to survive—especially those in the Kingdom of France—they too will fall.

Beyond this, he reminded them of the ancient alliance between themselves and the Valley of Pragela <note>original: "Pragella"</note> and others under His Majesty’s obedience. These regions have been joined and confederated at all times for the maintenance of their religion. This alliance was not renounced in their treaty with the Duke of Savoy; rather, the treaty was signed without prejudice to the said alliance. By virtue of this bond, since this war concerns the survival of their religion, they cannot—without being treacherous—abandon the people of Pragela, who are now at war with Charles Emmanuel for the preservation of the said faith.

Upon hearing this, the ministers, residents, and inhabitants of the Valleys—who had taken up arms to defend themselves against the Lord of Lesdiguières and had occupied several places, passes, and straits in their Valley—were finally persuaded by the reasons mentioned above and others proposed by the said Mr. Claude Perron. Seeing the Lord of Lesdiguières in arms and ready to attack them as enemies of His Majesty if they continued to refuse to recognize him, they finally resolved to enter into the present treaty of peace. 

This accord was made and begun between the Lord of Lesdiguières, acting in the name of His Majesty through the mediation and diligence of Claude Perron, and the deputies of the said Valleys named hereafter:

### The abovesaid Agreement between Henry IV. Book III.

Regarding the year 1561 <note>original: "Iceluy en l’année mil cinq centz soizante un," likely referring to the Treaty of Cavour which previously established Vaudois rights</note>, whereupon the said Master Perron <note>Claude Perron, a negotiator for the French crown</note> pointed out to them that this current war was not a private conflict between the said Charles Emmanuel <note>Duke of Savoy</note> and the Most Christian King <note>Henry IV of France</note>. Rather, he argued it was a general war involving several Princes of Christendom allied and banded together for the usurpation of the Kingdom of France, and particularly for the total extermination and ruin of the Reformed Churches of France, England, Germany, and other states of Christendom.

He explained that the said Charles Emmanuel is included in this league and conspiracy; under this name and pretext, he has usurped the state of the Marquisate of Saluzzo <note>original: "Saluce"</note> and invaded several towns and castles of the County of Provence by force and armed hand. In these places, he has abolished and driven out the practice of the Reformed Religion everywhere, just as he recently did in the bailiwicks <term>bailiwick: a district under the jurisdiction of a bailiff or local officer</term> of Gex, Thonon, and others which the people of Bern had returned to his late father. In those places, his soldiers have committed all kinds of looting, murder, and impieties, erasing and exterminating every trace and practice of the Reformed Religion.

Master Perron further pointed out that the said ministers and inhabitants of these Valleys have been of this religion from all antiquity and time immemorial—even before the century of Luther, Jan Hus, or Wycliffe <note>these are the "morning stars" of the Reformation; the Vaudois claimed their faith descended directly from the early apostolic church</note>. As ancient members of the Church, they have a great and notable interest in this affair, upon which depends their entire ruin and subversion, unless God in His mercy allows the other Churches to survive, especially those in the Kingdom of France.

Beyond this, he reminded them of the ancient alliance that existed between them and the Valley of Pragela <note>original: "Pragella," a valley then under French control</note> and others under His Majesty's authority, which have been joined and confederated at all times for the maintenance of their religion. This alliance was not renounced by the treaty made with the Duke of Savoy; instead, that treaty was passed without prejudice to the said alliance. By virtue of this alliance, since this war concerns the matter of their religion, they cannot without treachery <note>original: "perfidie"</note> abandon those of Pragela, who are now at war with the said Charles Emmanuel for the preservation of the said religion.

Upon hearing this, the said ministers, residents, and inhabitants of these Valleys—who had taken up arms and were defending themselves against the said Lord of Lesdiguières, and for those ends had occupied several places, passes, and straits in their Valley—were finally persuaded by the reasons mentioned above and others proposed by the said Mr. Claude Perron. Seeing the said Lord of Lesdiguières in arms and ready to attack them as enemies of His Majesty if they persisted and refused to recognize him, they finally resolved to come to the present treaty of peace and agreement. This was begun between the said Lord of Lesdiguières, acting in the name of His Majesty through the mediation and diligence of the said Claude Perron, and the deputies of the said Valleys named hereafter:

<header>Chapter II. and the Protestants of the Valleys.</header>

...tin, Girardo Masette, and Michaella Velovecto of Saint Jean de Luserna <note>original: "Sainct Jean de Luserne"</note>; Valentino Valla, deputy of Bobbio <note>original: "Bubeanna"</note>; Stefano Bordoira and Costanzo Ramondetto, deputies of Campiglione <note>original: "Campillon"</note>; and Pietro Girardo for Micamia and Meana. These syndics <term>syndic: a local government official or magistrate</term> and deputies, along with several others not named in the present treaty, acting both in their own names and on behalf of their communities, residents, and inhabitants—as well as for their heirs and any successors—have agreed, settled, promised, and sworn to the articles and conventions that follow.

The Lord of Lesdiguières, out of his desire to bring these lands under the obedience of His Majesty <note>Henry IV of France</note>, and because he expected that failing this, the people would resolve to engage in a war that could only be long, difficult, and very harmful to His Majesty's service—given the location and natural strength of the country, composed of mountains and narrow passes <term>straits: narrow mountain passes or defiles</term>, whose ruggedness meant the late Duke of Savoy could never subjugate or reduce them by force, even when aided by the forces and funds of the Pope—has finally, in the name of His Majesty and subject to his approval, granted, agreed, sworn, and promised all the following conditions:

First, the inhabitants of the said Valleys will renounce the obedience and loyalty they previously swore and claim to owe naturally to the said Charles Emmanuel of Savoy. They will submit themselves to the obedience and subjection of the King of France and Navarre, to whom they shall take the oath of loyalty in the presence of the Lord of Lesdiguières, as is required in such cases and as good and loyal subjects must do toward their Sovereign Prince, according to the form drafted for this purpose. This oath of loyalty shall be sworn by the aforementioned syndics and deputies, and others if necessary.

Furthermore, the said people and their pastors shall be maintained and preserved in the free, public, and general exercise of the Christian Reformed Religion <note>Protestantism</note>, ecclesiastical discipline, and all that depends upon it, throughout all the places of the said Valleys where it currently exists, without any restriction or modification whatsoever. 

Just as in the past and from time immemorial their churches have extended and expanded from place to place within the Valleys as the people gained knowledge of the faith—driven by the zeal and affection the people brought to it and the tolerance and permission of their Princes and magistrates—so too shall it be lawful for them to expand throughout all areas and locations of the said Valleys where there are people professing the Reformed Religion who, as a church body, call for ministers and pastors. This shall be allowed without distinction or difference of location. 

They shall also be permitted and allowed to assemble to hold their **Consistories**, **Colloquies**, and **Synods** <note>various levels of administrative and governing bodies in the Reformed church</note> to manage and conduct their ecclesiastical affairs whenever necessity requires, without being hindered or harassed by anyone.

His Majesty shall be most humbly petitioned to please found, establish, and maintain a college for the instruction of the youth of the said Valleys, in such a place as shall be decided by the commissioners established by His Majesty for this purpose. 

It has been agreed that His Majesty will grant the churches and their pastors the same wages, status, pensions, and privileges that he has granted or shall grant hereafter to the churches and pastors of France—specifically those of Guyenne, Languedoc, and Dauphiné. 

And since the people are almost all of the Reformed Religion—with Roman Catholics not even making up a hundredth part of the population—it was agreed...

...agreed at their very great and urgent request, and without which grant they were unwilling to negotiate or agree: that in order to maintain them in greater unity, and to give them reason to be all the more devoted to the service of His Majesty and remain his good and loyal subjects, His Majesty and the Kings his successors will provide them, now and hereafter, with judicial officers of the first instance <term>first instance: the initial level of court where a case is heard</term> who are of the so-called Reformed Religion <note>original: "Religion pretenduë Reformée" — the standard legal term used in 16th-century France for Protestantism</note> and no others. This is granted especially since, by their privileges, they have the right to elect three candidates for the said judges and officers, from whom the Prince then chooses one. 

All their franchises, liberties, immunities, and privileges, both ancient and modern, will be confirmed and maintained for them—not only in Piedmont, Dauphiné, the Marquisate of Saluzzo <note>original: "Salluces"</note>, and the land of France, according to how they have well and duly used them in the past—but also that Italians and others of any nation or condition who profess the so-called Reformed Religion may take refuge in the said Valleys without being searched for or harassed by anyone. 

The said Valleys shall be and remain forever annexed and incorporated into the State and Crown of France without ever being separated, alienated <term>alienated: transferred to the ownership of another</term>, or transferred for any reason whatsoever. And if, by some forced events, His Majesty and his successors should be constrained to return or transfer them to another power, they shall be transferred with the same conditions, privileges, and qualities granted to them by this present treaty, along with their ancient privileges and immunities. These shall not be changed, innovated, or altered in any way by the said transaction. 

These written articles and conventions were granted, agreed, and conceded by the Lord of Lesdiguières, in the name of His Majesty and subject to his approval, in exchange for the oath of loyalty sworn this day to His Majesty into the hands of the said Lord. He further promises to report and deliver a declaration of His Majesty's approval of this treaty within a term of three months. In witness of this, he has signed these presents and caused the seal of his arms to be affixed to them. Done at Bricherasio <note>original: "Briqueras"</note> on the first of November, one thousand five hundred and ninety-two. Signed, **Lesdiguières**.

<header>The aforesaid Agreement between Henry IV Book III.</header>

...and raising their right hands toward heaven in the customary manner, following the King’s ordinances, they declare that they are now and shall forever remain liege vassals <term>liege vassal: a feudal subject bound to give absolute loyalty and military service to a superior lord</term> to His Majesty. They pledge to render him forever all obedience, loyalty, submission, and service that they were previously accustomed to give to their Sovereign Prince. In short, they swear to do, say, and carry out everything contained in both the new and old forms of fealty.

Specifically, they promise never to provide aid or counsel to anyone who wishes or might be able to harm His Majesty, his ministers, officers, or subjects, whether by deed or by word. Instead, should they learn of such a threat, they will prevent it with all their power; if they cannot prevent it, they will warn His Majesty or his officers as soon as they can. Should any wrong or usurpation be committed against their persons or property, they will help and support the recovery and perpetual maintenance of the same. Furthermore, knowing that His Majesty justly wishes to take offense at, avenge himself upon, or attack anyone, they promise to help and support him with everything required or within their power.

Moreover, if any secret of His Majesty is communicated to them, they shall not reveal it to anyone, nor allow it to be revealed. When they are requested for counsel for the service of His Majesty, they shall give him faithful, useful, and honest advice, according to their knowledge and conscience. They shall never, through their persons or property, do, say, or plot <note>original: "Machineront"</note> anything against the person, life, honor, or property of His Majesty, the Princes of his blood, or his officers.

In summary, in heart, word, and action, they shall observe everything that good and faithful liege vassals and subjects owe to their Sovereign Lord and absolute Prince, as they recognize His Majesty alone against all others, without any exception whatsoever. They humbly request and petition to be maintained, protected, preserved, and defended by His Majesty in the possession and use of all the said fiefs, counties, jurisdictions, lordships, goods, and properties, along with their rights and dependencies, according to their previous investitures <term>investiture: the formal ceremony or legal act of handing over a fief or office to a vassal</term>. They also request that this act of fealty performed now by the subjects of the community of Luserna, the Valley of Bricherasio, and other places shall not prejudice the rights of homage and fealty owed by the said subjects to their local lords <note>original: "Seigneurs particuliers"</note>. Rather, they ask that those rights be maintained, confirmed, and preserved for the Lords present here, with the respective subjects in agreement.

Upon this, my Lord of Lesdiguières <note>François de Bonne, Duke of Lesdiguières (1543–1626), a prominent French general and later Marshal of France who led the campaign in Piedmont.</note>, representing the person of His Majesty in this matter, first declares that this act of fealty shall be held and considered as performed and given according to the ancient forms used during the transfer or change of Sovereign Lords. This is done without prejudice to the individual rights of homage and fealty owed by the subjects to their "Useful Lords" <term>Seigneurs Utiles: the local lords who held the actual usage and rights of a fief, as opposed to the sovereign overlord</term>. 

Proceeding in order according to the power His Majesty gave him "beyond the mountains" <note>This refers to the French perspective of the territories on the Italian side of the Alps.</note>, he has received and admitted the said Lords, the Counts, Luserna and its valley, Saint Martin and its valley, and Bricherasio, as they appear in faith, homage, and liege vassalage to His Majesty. Likewise, he admits all these Lords, Counts, and other subjects of the aforementioned places into the liege subjection, loyalty, and obedience of His Majesty, for their respective fiefs and properties. # Chapter II: To the Protestants of the Valleys

| The Petition of the Valleys | The Duke’s Response |
| :--- | :--- |
| ->**The first.**<- | ->**To the first.**<- |
| First, may it please your Highness to cancel and declare null and void all harassment of any kind on account of religion, along with all the legal proceedings and confiscations that have been carried out. Specifically, we ask for the reversal of the alleged confiscation of the property of Lady Beatrice Solara and her children (she having lived in the Valley of Lucerna for over thirty years, and her children having been born there), and that they may all be restored to a state of peace. | His Highness does not intend for them to be harassed for their so-called religion <note>original: "pretended Religion," a legal term used by the Savoyard state to refer to Protestantism</note>, provided they refrain from practicing it outside the designated areas of the Valleys of Lucerna, San Martino, and Perosa. |
| ->**The second.**<- | ->**To the second.**<- |
| Furthermore, to grant them the free preaching and practice of their religion in all the Valleys of Lucerna, Perosa, San Martino, Roccapiata, San Bartolomeo, Talucco, Meana, Mattie, and the Marquisate of Saluzzo, in the places where it has been customary and usual until now. | Provided they do so only within the tolerated limits of the three aforementioned valleys, they shall not be harassed. |
| <column-break/> Additionally, that all those of this religion from these valleys may return and live in their homes, enjoy liberty of conscience, and practice their religion in the customary places. | As for those of the three valleys, they may return to live there; His Highness suspends, in their case, the order made against those who own property outside the designated limits. |
| Furthermore, that those of the said religion may hold and be admitted to all types of public offices in the aforementioned Valleys, and that they may trade throughout the entire state of His Most Serene Highness, harvest their crops, and thresh their grain <note>original: "Corn," which in this period referred to cereal crops in general</note> without harassment or investigation on account of their religion. Also, those who house and host them as assistants shall not be harassed. Similarly, those living in the valleys shall have all their usual privileges and concessions confirmed to them as they have been until now. | Regarding the holding of public offices, His Highness grants this within the three valleys only. He declares that they may go and harvest their crops and thresh their grain, provided that they refrain from preaching their doctrine while doing so. |

->Most Serene Princess,<-
<note>original: "Serenissima Principessa"; this likely refers to Margaret of France, Duchess of Savoy, who was known for her sympathetic stance toward the Waldensians and often acted as a mediator.</note>

The Valleys of Lucerne, Perosa, and San Martino—those of the Reformed Religion <note>original: "li della Religione"; a common contemporary term for Protestants, specifically the Waldensians in this region</note>—were required to provide a response to His Most Serene Highness regarding the concessions obtained from him in Cuneo on the ninth of April last, concerning the contents of the petition presented to him. Because they were unable to assemble for this response at the proper time due to various hindrances and causes, His Highness departed from Mondovì before they could arrive there. For this reason, he referred them to your Highness, so that by appealing to you, you might provide whatever seems appropriate. 

Therefore, the undersigned, elected and sent by the said Valley of Lucerne in the name of the said Valleys and the others mentioned above, first offer with all humility infinite thanks to His Most Serene Highness for the aforementioned concessions and favors granted to them regarding the contents of that petition, which they promise to fulfill and obey according to the mind of His Highness. However, because there are certain articles in these concessions which seem somewhat ambiguous:

They humbly petition you to be pleased to clarify these concessions and articles which, as stated above, seem somewhat ambiguous; and they will continually pray to the Lord God for the preservation of your Highness.

<header>Chapter II: To the Protestants of the Valleys.</header>

Regarding the second point: whether *Roccapiata*, *San Bartolomeo*, *Prarustino*, and *Talluco*—even though they are not technically part of the three Valleys—should be included in the said grants as has been the custom.

In the fourth article: that those who receive and host the harvest workers of the [Protestant] Religion, and those who thresh their grain, should incur no penalty for hosting them. If they should happen to be questioned regarding their faith, they wish to know in what manner they are permitted to answer such questions.

In the eighth article: that he [the Duke] would be pleased to declare to whom he grants a pardon, and that they may not be held liable regarding the matter of outlaws <note>original: "Banditi"; refers to those previously declared outlaws or banished during religious conflicts</note>, except according to the general orders published by His Most Serene Highness throughout his dominions.

*Chaberto Bodetti*, for *Bobbio*.
*Giacomo Fontana*, for *Villaro*.
*Chaberto Chialmitio*, for *La Torre*.
*Giovanni Oddino*, for *Angrogna*.
*Giovanni Appia*, for *San Giovanni*.
*Antonieto Mallanoto*, for *San Giovanni*.

<column-break/>

His Highness declares that *Roccapiata* shall be included within the three Valleys for the purpose requested in the petition. Regarding the places of *San Bartolomeo* and *Prarustino*, the residents may live there according to the answer given to the third point of the referenced memorial.

To the fourth article: His Highness declares that those who receive and host the harvest workers and threshers of the Religion shall incur no penalty. Furthermore, he forbids both the hosts and the workers from questioning others or answering questions regarding the "pretended religion" <note>original: "pretended Religion"; the official legal term used by Catholic authorities at the time to refer to Protestantism</note>, under penalty of fifty crowns for every person who acts to the contrary.

Regarding the eighth article: His Highness declares that he has granted grace and pardon to all those requested in the memorial, except for those specifically excluded in His Highness's previous answer. This is provided that they observe and fulfill the requirements contained in that answer. For this purpose, they must submit a formal obligation <note>a legal bond or written promise</note> from all the communities within the next ten days. Additionally, within the term of three months, they shall pay for all damages done to churches. These churches shall be quickly repaired and supplied with the items necessary for the saying of Mass and the celebration of Divine Service.

*Turin*, 14 *May* 1603. Signed,

-> *Margarita* <- 
<note>Likely Margaret of Savoy, acting on behalf of the ducal administration</note>
-> *V. F. Miller* <-

# Concessions of the Duke of Savoy, Book III. 476

### Copy of another Petition. <note>original: "Copia d'altra Supplica"</note>

->**Most Serene Lord,**<-

Your most humble and most faithful subjects, the people of the Valleys of Luserna, Angrogna, Perosa, San Martino, Meana, Mattie <note>original: "Matis"</note>, Talucco, Roccapiata, San Bartolomeo, and Prarustino, who profess the Reformed Religion, humbly represent to your Most Serene Highness: That whereas it pleased your Most Serene Highness, on the ninth of April last, to grant them certain articles <note>original: "cappi" / "heads"</note> concerning the liberty of their religion, its practice <note>original: "esercitio" / "exercise"</note>, and their conduct <note>original: "depertamenti" / "deportments"</note>; and these articles were further clarified and expanded on May 14th by the Most Serene Princess Margaret; and because, according to the format of these articles, all the communities were required to submit a formal obligation within the next ten days, which they could not fulfill because of the difficulty of the people of those Valleys gathering together; and also because the people refused to carry out the article concerning the restoration <note>original: "refectione"</note> of the churches which were assumed to be damaged <note>original: "dannificate"</note>, the people claiming they were not the cause of such damage, and therefore, according to their religion, they are not obligated to repair them; for which purpose they intend to appeal to your Most Serene Highness so that the said article might be removed, which—

<column-break/>

# Concessions of the Duke of Savoy, Book III.

<page-num>478</page-num>

<columns>

->I.<-

**First**, to confirm to the said petitioners the articles granted up to the present day, despite the expiration of the deadline given to them—given the obstacles encountered—restoring all natives and inhabitants to the freedom to stay, live, go, come, trade, and conduct business throughout every place in the said Valleys and in Your Highness's states without being harassed because of their religion. And where it is not legal to preach <note>original: "dogmatizare"</note>, let it at least be legal to respond to anyone who asks that they are of that religion.

->II.<-

**Second**, to free the said men and Valleys from the requirement to restore the said churches <note>This refers to Catholic churches damaged during the conflict</note> as a community, since they were not the authors or the cause of such damage.

->III.<-

**Third**, regarding the section on outlaws, to declare that they are not required to do anything except provide strong assistance <note>original: "dar braccio forte"</note> to the law for the capture of criminals when requested by each community's ordinary magistrate, while observing the usual privileges of each location.

->IV.<-

**Fourth**, for the public peace of the Valleys, to grant a pardon for every instance of carrying prohibited weapons and for every excess committed for the sake of the religion of the aforementioned, and...

<column-break/>

**First**, His Highness does not intend for them to be harassed for their claimed religion <note>original: "pretesa luoro Relligione"</note> as long as they refrain from practicing it outside the limits of the Valleys of Luserna, San Martino, and Perosa. If they do so only within the tolerated limits in these three Valleys, they may reside there again. Regarding those who have property outside the designated limits, His Highness suspends the order made against them, confirming the responses given to the articles of April 9th and May 14th last, despite the passage of time.

**Second**, His Highness frees the men and Valleys collectively <note>This grants the request to be exempt from the costs of rebuilding Catholic churches</note>.

**Third**, His Highness grants this.

**Fourth**, His Highness grants the requested general and individual grace and pardon <note>original: "abolitione"</note>, with the sole exceptions of Giovanni Fraschetto and Danielle Rollo of Angrogna,
