# Chapter II. To the Protestants of the Valleys.

<page-num>479</page-num>

<sig>Q q q</sig>

<columns>

### I.

**First**, to confirm for the said petitioners the articles granted up to this day, despite the expiration of the deadline given to them—due to the aforementioned obstacles—allowing all people, whether natives or inhabitants, full liberty to stay, live, travel, come, go, and conduct trade and commerce throughout all parts of the said Valleys and in Your Highness’s territories, without being harassed because of their religion. Furthermore, in places where they are not permitted to preach <note>original: "publish their doctrines"</note>, it should at least be lawful for them to answer anyone who asks them if they are of that religion.

### II.

**Secondly**, to exempt the said men and Valleys from the requirement to repair the churches, as this is not a collective responsibility since they were not the authors or the cause of the damage.

### III.

**Thirdly**, regarding the article on outlaws, to declare that they are not obligated to do anything except assist in the capture of criminals <note>original: "malefactors"</note> when they are required to do so—each community reporting to its ordinary magistrate—while preserving the usual privileges of each specific location.

### IV.

**Fourthly**, for the sake of public peace in the Valleys, to grant a pardon to the aforementioned people for all carrying of prohibited weapons and for all excesses committed regarding matters of religion; and as to the—

<column-break/>

**First**, His Highness does not intend for them to be harassed for their so-called <note>original: "pretended"</note> religion, provided they refrain from practicing it outside the Valleys of Luserna, San Martino, and Perosa. They must practice it only within the tolerated limits of these three Valleys, in which they may live again. Regarding those who own property outside the designated limits, the previous order is suspended. His Highness confirms the answers given to the articles of April 9th and May 14th last year, despite the time that has passed.

Regarding the **second** point, His Highness exempts the people and the Valleys in general.

His Highness grants the **third** request.

His Highness grants the **fourth** request regarding the pardon and general amnesty <note>original: "abolition"</note> and the specific points petitioned for, with the sole exceptions of Giovanni Fischetto and Daniele Rollo of Angrogna.

</columns>

<header>Concessions of the Duke of Savoy, Book III</header>

->Most Serene Lord,<-

The most faithful and humble subjects of Your Serene Highness <note>original: "V. A." or "Vostra Altezza"</note> of the Religion <note>This refers to the Waldensian Protestant faith</note> of the Valleys of Luserna, Perosa, and San Martino, and other places joined to them, having in times past obtained from the clemency of Your Highness, and also from the glorious memory of your Serene Father <note>This likely refers to Victor Amadeus I or Charles Emmanuel I, previous Dukes of Savoy</note>, certain kind concessions regarding the exercise of their religion, have always endeavored to live in a Christian manner according to those concessions, under the protection and obedience of Your Highness—a life they desire to continue in peace forever. 

Now, finding themselves troubled by certain edicts that contradict their aforementioned concessions—which are said to have been published in some places within the Valley of Luserna—and as the penalties contained in those edicts are being carried out with threats of even greater harm, they are certain that this does not proceed from the mind of Your Highness. From you alone, after the help of God, they expect their necessary deliverance, as from their most merciful and natural Prince. Therefore, they have decided to fall at your feet to humbly pray that you might be pleased, according to your habitual kindness, to forbid any harassment of these petitioners for the sake of their religion, restoring them to a peaceful state. To this end, they ask you to confirm and grant them the humble requests that follow.

<page-num>487</page-num>
<header>Chapter 2: To the Protestants of the Valleys.</header>
<sig>Rrr</sig>
<meta>catchword: Al; There is significant mirror-image ghosting/ink transfer from the facing page in the lower half of the leaf.</meta>

<image-desc>A horizontal row of decorative fleurons (printer's ornaments) divided into two groups by a central question mark symbol.</image-desc>

->Most Serene Lord,<-

The most faithful and most humble subjects of Your Most Serene Highness, who belong to the Religion <note>This refers specifically to the Waldensian Protestant faith, often called "The Religion" in official Savoyard documents</note> of the Valleys of Luserna, Perosa, and San Martino, and the other places joined with them, have in times past obtained certain favorable grants concerning the exercise of their said religion from the clemency of Your Highness, and also from your Most Serene Father of glorious memory <note>Duke Victor Amadeus I or Charles Emmanuel I</note>. They have always endeavored to live according to these grants in a Christian manner, under the protection and obedience of Your Highness, and they desire to continue doing so quietly forever.

However, they now find themselves troubled because of certain edicts that are contrary to their aforementioned grants, which are said to have been published in certain places in the Valley of Luserna. Furthermore, as proceedings are being taken to carry out the penalties contained in those edicts, along with threats of even greater damage, the subjects assure themselves that this does not proceed from the intention of Your Highness. From you alone, next to God, they expect their necessary deliverance, as from their natural and most gracious Prince. 

Therefore, they have thought it right to cast themselves at your feet, humbly beseeching that you would be pleased, according to your usual goodness, to forbid all harassment of your said petitioners for matters of religion, restoring them to a peaceful condition. For this purpose, they ask you to confirm and grant the following humble requests.

<header>Concessions of the Duke of Savoy, Book III.</header>

<columns>
<column>

To the first point: His Highness confirms and orders the observance of the concessions granted to the petitioners on April 9, May 14, and the second to last day of September 1603, regarding the Valleys of Luserna, San Martino, and Perosa, together with Roccapiatta, San Bartolomeo, Prarostino, and other places mentioned in the concessions as requested. These are to be observed within the graciously tolerated limits only, notwithstanding any other order to the contrary. 

Furthermore, His Highness grants them grace and pardon for all penalties incurred for violating his orders, and for other crimes and excesses committed before the general amnesty <note>original: "indulto generale"</note>, despite the previous sentences of the Captain of Justice and the Senate. In this regard, he overrides the provisions of the said amnesty. All this His Highness has done, and does as a special grace, also in consideration of a payment <note>original: "finanza"</note> of six thousand Ducats <note>A gold or silver coin used throughout Europe</note> to be paid proportionately according to the custom of the three aforementioned Valleys. This is granted with the condition, however, that the residents of San Giovanni must wall up the door of the newly built church, and not do otherwise or act in any other way.

To the second and last point: His Highness grants it to them. Given in Turin on June 20, 1620. Signed:

->**Charles Emmanuel**<-
->**V. Argentero, V. Cernusco, Carron**<-
->**Arnaldo Magalli, Secretary**<-

</column>
<column>

First, may it please you to confirm all the gracious concessions granted to them by both Your Most Serene Highness and your Most Serene Father of happy memory. This is so that they may continue in the free exercise of their religion in the places tolerated and used until the present, notwithstanding any order published or issued (or to be issued) to the contrary. 

We request the annulment of all legal proceedings, confiscations, declarations of penalties, fines, and investigations made on the occasion of said orders. We ask that all those troubled and harassed for these reasons be restored to a peaceful state, so that they may live in the future under the dominion of Your Highness. 

Furthermore, let the aforementioned requests be granted and ratified <note>original: "interinate"</note> for free, liberating the subjects from the *Quos* <note>original: "Quos" — a specific administrative fee or tax</note>, tithes, lodging taxes <note>original: "Albergo" — a duty to provide housing for officials or troops</note>, seal fees, signature fees, and other expenses. They hope to obtain this and will pray to the Lord for your happiness and that of the Most Serene Princes. 

Registered 3. 170. First Register 245. I say 245. Registered in the Chamber.

# Chapter II: To the Protestants of the Valleys.

<columns>
<column>

Regarding the first point, His Highness confirms it. He commands that the grants made to the petitioners on April 9, May 14, and the 29th of September 1603 <note>original: "last but one of September"</note> shall be observed in the Valleys of Luserna, San Martino, and Perosa, as well as Roccapiatta, San Bartolomeo, Prarostino, and the other places mentioned in the grants. This is to be done as requested, and only within the graciously tolerated limits, despite any other orders to the contrary. 

He also grants them pardon and remission for all penalties incurred for breaking his orders, and for other faults and excesses committed before the general pardon. This applies regardless of the sentences handed down by the Captain of Justice and the Senate, overriding that which the said pardon provides in this specific part. All this His Highness has done and continues to do as a special grace. This is also granted in consideration of a payment of six thousand ducatoons <term>ducatoons</term> <note>A large silver coin used throughout Europe in the 17th century</note>, to be paid by the three Valleys at the usual rate. This is granted on the condition that the people of San Giovanni shall wall up the door of the newly built church, and not otherwise, nor in any other manner.

Regarding the second and last points, His Highness grants them. Given in Turin on June 20, 1620. Signed:

->**Charles Emmanuel**<-

Seen by Argentero, Seen by Cernusco,
->**Carron**<-
Arnaldo Magalli, Secretary.

First, may it please you to confirm all the gracious grants made to them, both by Your Most Serene Highness and by your Most Serene Father of happy memory. This would allow them to continue the free exercise of their religion in the places tolerated and used until now, regardless of any orders already published or to be made to the contrary. 

We also ask that you annul all legal proceedings, confiscations, declarations of penalties, fines, and investigations made because of those orders. Restore all those who have been disturbed or harassed for these reasons to a peaceful condition, so that they may hereafter live under Your Highness’s rule. 

Furthermore, we request that you command that these requests be granted and <term>interinated</term> <note>original: "interinated"; meaning to be officially registered, ratified, or given the force of law</note> for them for free, exempting them from the payment of the *Quos*, *Decima*, *Albergo*, *Sigillo*, *Signattura* <note>original: "Quos, Decima, Albergo, Sigillo, Signattura." These were various administrative fees and taxes for legalizing documents, such as fees for seals, signatures, and tithes.</note>, and all other charges whatsoever. <header>Concessions of the Duke of Savoy, Book III</header>

### Copy of a Petition.

->Most Excellent Lords,<-

The communities and men of the Valleys of Lucerna, Perosa, San Martino, and other places of the Reformed Religion, have obtained from his most Serene Highness the articles and answers recited here. These documents confirm their ancient grants and the cancellation <note>original: "abolitions"</note> of certain criminal proceedings which were initiated against them at the request of your Highness’s Exchequer <note>the government office responsible for public revenue and legal-financial interests</note>, upon payment of six thousand Ducatoons <note>large silver coins; a very significant sum of money intended to settle the state's legal claims</note>. Since these specific details and cancellations have been admitted by the most Illustrious Chamber of Accounts without any difficulty—as appears by the patents duly sealed and signed by *Fassioti* on the seventeenth of August of this present year—and desiring to obtain the same formal registration <term>original: interination; the process of a high court or senate recording a decree to give it the full force of law</term> from the most Excellent Ducal Senate, they have thought it fit to appeal to your Excellencies;

Humbly beseeching you that you would be pleased to admit, approve, and formally register the said articles, answers, grants, and cancellations requested, fully and entirely, according to the form, intent, and tenor of the said articles and the things petitioned for. This was signed: **Reggis**, Advocate.

### A Copy of the Decree.

Let it be communicated to one of the Lords Advocates of the Exchequer, so that he may conclude it. At Turin, 30 August 1620. **V. Comes.**

<column-break/>

### Copy of the Petition.
<note>original: Copia di Supplica (Italian)</note>

->Most Excellent Lords,<-
<note>original: Excellentissimi Signori</note>

*The communities and men of the Valleys of Lucerna, Perosa, San Martino, and other places of the Reformed Religion have obtained from His Serene Highness the attached articles and responses, confirming their ancient grants and the cancellation of some criminal investigations that were being formed against them at the request of the Exchequer of Your Serene Highness, by means of a payment of six thousand Ducatoons. These articles and cancellations having been admitted by the most Illustrious Chamber of Accounts without any difficulty—as is evident by patents duly sealed and signed by* Fassioti *on the seventeenth of the current August of the present year—and desiring to obtain the same formal registration from the most Excellent Ducal Senate, they have decided to appeal to your Excellencies.*

*Humbly beseeching you to be pleased to admit, approve, and formally register the said articles, responses, grants, and cancellations requested in every part and entirely according to the form, mind, and tenor of the said articles and things requested; which was signed* Reggis, Advocate.

<page-num>493</page-num>
<header>Chapter II. To the Protestants of the Valleys.</header>

### Copy of the Conclusions.
<note>original Latin: "Copia di Conclusioni"</note>

I have seen these documents, and I do not object to the approval of the requested concession, provided that it does not apply to those condemned to pay a monetary fine; the rights of the officials must remain protected. In particular, the fiscal officers <note>original: "fiscalibus," government legal-financial agents</note> are prohibited from claiming their maximum fiscal tenth-part fee <note>original: "decima fiscali"</note>. Furthermore, those who are condemned to corporal punishment are required to present themselves for the formal registration <term>interination; the process of a high court recording a decree to give it the force of law</term> of the Pastor's Memorial.

### A Daily Memorial.
<note>original Italian: "Memoriale Dietim"</note>

In the year of our Lord 1620, on the fourth of September, judicially before the most Excellent Senate.

### Copy of a Petition.

#### Most Excellent Lords,

The communities and men of the Valleys of Luserna, Perosa, San Martino, and other places of the Reformed Religion, have obtained from his Most Serene Highness the articles and responses listed here. These documents confirm their ancient grants and the dismissal <note>original: "abolitions"</note> of several criminal legal proceedings that were being formed against them at the request of your Highness's Exchequer <term>the government office responsible for collecting and managing revenue and legal fines</term>, upon payment of six thousand ducatoons <note>a large silver coin used in several European countries</note>. These particulars and dismissals have been accepted by the Most Illustrious Chamber of Accounts without any difficulty, as shown by the patents duly sealed and signed by Fassioti on the seventeenth of August of the current year. Desiring to obtain the same legal registration <term>interination; the formal process of a high court recording a decree to give it the force of law</term> from the Most Excellent Ducal Senate, they have thought it right to appeal to your Excellencies;

Humbly beseeching you that you would be pleased to admit, approve, and register the said articles, responses, grants, and dismissals petitioned for, fully and entirely, according to the form, intent, and tenor of the said articles and the things requested. This was signed: Reggis, Advocate.

<header>Chapter II. To the Protestants of the Valleys.</header>

These same concessions were confirmed by Madame Royale <term>Madame Royale; the title of Christine Marie of France (1606–1663), who served as regent of Savoy</term> in the year 1638. They were confirmed again by His Royal Highness who is currently reigning, on June 30, 1649, on June 2, and on December 29 in the year 1653.

They requested that the aforementioned confirmation of the concessions be made, "without any restriction or alteration, notwithstanding any order made or to be made, or any other thing whatsoever to the contrary" <note>original Italian: "Senza alcuna restrittione, ne alteratione, non ostante qual si voglia ordine fatto, ò da farsi, ò qual si voglia altra cosa in contrario."</note>.

His Royal Highness answered at the bottom of their petitions in the following terms: "His Royal Highness declares that it is not his intention that the concessions which have been issued in due form—which the petitioners obtained from the late Duke Charles Emmanuel, his grandfather <note>original Italian: "avo suo"; the original English translation on this page mistakenly translated this as "uncle."</note>, and from his other most serene predecessors—should be enlarged or diminished. In Turin, December 29, 1653" <note>original Italian: "Dichiara Sua Altezza Royale non esser di mente sua, che per le risposte date al memoriale a capi delli 2 Giugno 1653. s'intendino ampliate ne diminuite le Concessione debitamente spedite, le quali hanno li supplicanti rapportate del fu Duca Carlo Emanuel avo suo, & de alteri suoi serenissimi Predecessori. <page-num>498</page-num>
<header>Observations upon the Book of the Court of Savoy, Book III.</header>

<image-desc>A decorative horizontal divider consisting of two rows of ornamental fleurons.</image-desc>

## Court of Savoy.

*His Royal Highness's answer to them was that this order was consistent both with justice and the intent of their former concessions; yet, he was nonetheless content to graciously hear what they could allege to the contrary. Furthermore, he would still be favorable to them if they would send deputies to Turin, provided with a full commission drawn up in a due and legal form, with whom, etc.*

*This admonition was repeated by various ministers of state and members of a committee established for that very purpose, consisting of the chief counselors of state and justice, as well as by the Marquess of Pianezza, etc.*

*Despite this, they always refused to send letters of proxy <term>original: "Letters of Procuration"; a legal document giving one person the power to act for another</term> in a proper form, etc.*

->**Observation**<-

1. Alas! What justice was there, or indeed could there be, in driving so many thousands of souls out of their ancient possessions and inheritances—and that within three days, in the very middle of winter, and under penalty of death—in case they would not damn their souls by becoming Catholics against their consciences? And to make amends, he promised to encourage them by hearing their reasons and requests afterward! If they had the least inclination to hear what they could say in their own defense, why did they first issue such a severe decree against them? The truth is, this proceeding is:

<margin>Genesis 3:9</margin>
1. Against the example of God himself, who, though he is the supreme and absolute Judge of the whole world (and who can say to Him, "What are you doing?"), yet we find that he first summoned Adam and gave him a fair trial before ever he turned him out of Paradise or passed that heavy sentence against him and his descendants.

<margin>Acts 25:16</margin>
<margin>Baldus in Conf. 327. 2. Vol.</margin>
2. Against the principles of common right. For as Festus told King Agrippa, *The law condemns no man before he who is accused has the accusers face to face and has permission to answer for himself concerning the crime laid against him.* Yes, and what is more, *restoration of possession is granted when a judge has proceeded against one who was not summoned.* <note>original Latin: "Restitutio poßeßionis datur quando Judex proceßit contra non citatum."</note> And all civil lawyers <term>original: "Civilians"; specialists in Roman Civil Law</term> agree on this: namely, *that a summons is required so that one can defend oneself, and therefore...* <note>original Latin: "Citationem requiri, ut quis se defendere poßit, & ideo..."</note>

<meta>The catchword "ideo" (therefore) indicates the legal argument continues on the next page.</meta>

<summary>This page critiques the Duke of Savoy's 1655 expulsion of the Waldensian Protestants, arguing that forcing people from their homes in winter before hearing their legal defense violates both divine example and established Roman civil law.</summary>
<keywords>Protestant persecution, Waldensians, Marquess of Pianezza, Turin, due process, religious liberty, 1655 decree, House of Savoy</keywords>

<header>Chapter II. Savoy’s Factum and Reasons.</header>

<margin>
Clementines, *Pastoralis* <note>A papal decree regarding legal procedures.</note> on the matter of the thing judged.

Portius in *Confessions* 2. n. 7.
</margin>
“Therefore, he who denies a summons is said to deny a defense; and since defense is granted by natural law, it ought not to be taken away from any man.” <note>original: "ideo negans citationem dicitur negare defensionem, quæ cum in re naturali concedatur, nomini auferri debet."</note> And to show that even a Prince cannot dispense with this right, they confess it to be by divine law: “Nor can a summons be taken away by a Prince, so much so that if a summons did not precede it, the act is rendered void.” <note>original: "Jure divino, Nec à Principe potest auferri citatio, adeo ut si non præcessit citatio, actus reddatur nullus."</note> Therefore, the Order of Gastaldo must necessarily be void, as it is repugnant and contrary to all human and divine institutions.

3. To whom were the poor people to address themselves in such a case? Was it not to the Council for the Uprooting of Heretics <note>original: "Council de extirpandis hæreticis"; likely referring to the local branch of the *Congregatio de Propaganda Fide*.</note>, from whom *good Lord deliver us!* and let all honest Protestants say, Amen! “O excellent guardians of sheep—wolves, as they say!” <note>original: "o præclaros ovium custodes, ut aiunt, lupos!"</note> What encouragement do the poor larks have to send their deputies to the hungry kites? Or the lambs to make their humble addresses to the ravenous evening wolves, who are hunting greedily after their prey? If it is replied that there never was such a Council established at **Turin**, we answer: it is true, there is only one great Council that bears that glorious title preeminently <note>original: "καθ' ἐξοχήν"</note>, and that is at **Rome**, which Petrarch rightly calls “A forge of deceits and a temple of heresy, etc.” <note>original: "Fuscina d’ingannai, et tempio d’ heresia, &c."</note> But it is just as true that under that great Council there are a large number of other great councils in the metropolitan and chief cities of those Kings and States who depend on the See of Rome, and which are subordinate to it. Indeed, the Auditor Gastaldo, while he styles himself, “General Conservator of the Holy Faith for the observation of Orders against the pretended Reformed Religion, etc.” <note>original: "Conservatore generale della santa fede per osservanza de' gli' Ordini contro la preteſa Religione Riformata, &c."</note> does he not declare plainly that he himself is a member of this congregation? The Marquess **Pianezza** likewise has been forced to confess that the assembly which had judged all those affairs sat in the house of the Archbishop of **Turin**, with the said Archbishop serving as President; and if so, what could this be but an ecclesiastical assembly?

3. What were the *Letters of Proxy* <term>original: "Letters of Procuration"; a legal document giving one person the power to act for another</term> which they refused to bring before this assembly? Alas! They were such as must have been drawn up by Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> notaries, by which the people would have been forced to accept everything his Royal Highness was pleased to ordain concerning them—renouncing and disclaiming all their ancient rights, privileges, and estates. No man can deny that the poor people used their utmost diligence to present their requests to his Royal Highness. Indeed, they longed for nothing more than for such an opportunity to inform their sovereign Prince of the truth of all things and, if possible, to remove those hard thoughts and sinister impressions which their malicious adversaries had so long labored to fill his mind with. But they could never obtain an audience, although all their deputies made three distinct voyages to Turin for that very purpose. They were always sent back to the Council for the Uprooting of Heretics, being thus tossed back and forth like balls between rackets, merely to confuse them and waste time until everything was ready for the slaughter of their brothers in the **Valleys**. If it is objected that these requests were not authentic, we affirm the contrary,

### Observation <note>original: "Animadversion"; a critical remark or commentary</note>

1. That the poor people had such recourse to other states and princes, as is specified above, is denied by them, and is not proved at all by the other party.

2. Although the ministers of Geneva might counsel them to yield obedience to His Royal Highness, yet surely they never counseled them to enslave themselves to the Council for the Uprooting of Heretics <note>original: "de extirpandis hæreticis"; a Catholic committee dedicated to eliminating Protestantism in the region</note>, or to suffer their throats to be cut like beasts, and to be thrown out of their houses and ancient habitations without knowing either the cause or reason for it. Certainly, the ministers of Geneva never counseled them to accept the Order of Gastaldo <note>The decree issued by Andrea Gastaldo in 1655 that triggered the massacre by forcing Protestants to move or convert</note>; but on the contrary, they exhorted them (if they did anything) to have recourse to His Highness, and there to complain of the cruelty and injustice of the same. And thus must these men’s text be read like Hebrew—that is, backward—in order to rightly understand it.

A poor proof indeed! And yet the Order did not respect Religion or Conscience at all? The truth is, the words very clearly allow for another interpretation: *the said Order respects neither Religion nor Conscience*. This means there is not even a trace of Religion or Conscience in that Order; it is that cruel, barbarous, and inhuman! 

What was the purpose and intent of this Order other than to force those poor people to renounce their faith <note>original: "apostatize"</note>? They were forced to either leave their houses and homes in the middle of winter—being confined to a region where it was impossible for them to survive, amidst a thousand other cruel circumstances—or else, against their own beliefs and the light of their consciences, become Catholics and risk their immortal souls. All these circumstances, and the bloody massacre that followed immediately after, plainly show that the plan was to destroy them as Protestants, root and branch, and to wipe their memory from the face of the earth.

# Chapter II. Savoy's Legal Statement <note>original: "Factum"</note> and Reasons.

### An Authentic Transcript of Count Bouchard's Letter to Mr. Lorenzo <note>original: "Laurentio"</note> and Mr. Malarot, Dated May 5, 1655.

Most honorable and dear Friends,

I have thought it best to warn you once again of the extreme danger which hangs over your heads, and how easily you may prevent it. If you refuse to apply a remedy, choosing instead to satisfy your reckless whim <note>original: "giddy fancy"</note> by watching the total destruction of our district <note>original: "Canton"</note>, and insist on acting like the only rebels <note>original: "Ranters"</note> in all the Valleys, I do protest—both in the names of the Lords, the Earls Vagnone and Verdina, and in my own—that we shall take our revenge even unto blood. You shall have no way to trade or conduct business, either in Pinerolo <note>original: "Pignerol"</note> or within our borders. Sooner or later you will repent of this error and the damage it brings. 

Therefore, consider what path you will take, and whether you will govern yourselves according to the example of Prali, Rodoretto, Salsa <note>original: "Salfa"</note>, Macello, and Maneglia. Those people have all turned Catholic and have made promises even for those who are absent. Otherwise, I swear to you by my holy Baptism that the Lord Marquess Galeazzo has orders to burn, root out, and demolish every house, as well as to cut down the vines and trees on the properties—not only of those now living, but also belonging to the children you have yet to bear. But if God does not enlighten you by His holy grace, and if you will not become Catholics, then—

*Most magnificent and my dearest friends,*

*Once again, I wish to warn you of the supreme evil that hangs over you and the ease with which you might avoid it. If you do not wish to remedy the situation, and prefer to see the extermination of our neighborhoods through your beautiful caprice—acting as the only "wild spirits" in the whole Valley—I protest to you, as much on behalf of the holy Counts Vagnone and Verdina as on my own, that we will avenge ourselves with blood. And if indeed God does not illuminate you with His holy grace, and you do not become Catholic, provided that...*

### An authentic extract of *Merolles’s* letter from *Turin*, 17 July 1655.

> You have understood from my previous letter the state of the valleys in *Piedmont*, and what has happened to the *heretics* <note>The term used by Catholic officials for the Waldensian Protestants.</note>. ...prohibited <note>original: "hibited" — the conclusion of the word "prohibited" from the previous page</note> (*notwithstanding they still acted through representatives <note>original: "by way of Deputation"</note>, as if they had no intention at all of a rebellion, etc.*)

### *Observation* <note>original: "Animadversion" — a critical commentary or remark</note>

1. And was it not high time for the poor people to hold a *General Assembly*, when their sworn adversary had fully and absolutely determined their destruction?
2. Again, is it not high time for men to *take up arms* in their own defense—men who never had the slightest thought of disobeying their natural Prince, and who had always been generous with their lives and fortunes in his service—once they saw themselves attacked by a barbarous generation of men? These attackers, contrary to all law and equity, attempted to cut their throats like beasts. Does not the very Law of Nature teach all men self-preservation in such a desperate time?
3. What if they did oblige themselves by an oath to preserve those small estates left to them by their ancestors, or what they had lawfully purchased according to the agreements <note>original: "concessions"</note> made in the year 1561, where that very right is granted to them? Anyone who knows anything of those affairs knows that it has been an ancient strategy of their Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> adversaries to buy out and purchase the lands and inheritances of the Protestants at any price. In the meantime, they prohibit the Protestants, under the strictest possible penalties, from purchasing even one foot of land from the Catholics, so that little by little they might utterly root them out of the Valleys. Surely the Bible story of *Naboth*, who would not sell his vineyard to King *Ahab* <note>original: "Achab"</note>, sufficiently justifies the behavior of these poor people in this case. It shows plainly that it was not lawful for magistrates—no, not even for the King himself—to compel *Naboth* to sell his vineyard. Furthermore, all the deceptive pretenses and legal formalities, along with the false witnesses used to overthrow him, were not able to hinder the *dogs from licking the blood of Ahab and Jezebel for shedding the blood of Naboth.* <note>Referencing 1 Kings 21, where King Ahab and Queen Jezebel illegally seized a subject's land, leading to divine judgment.</note>
4. What likelihood in the world was there, or what ground was there to believe, that those poor people would exhaust themselves and their small estates by keeping their deputies at Court at excessive charges to manage their affairs? Not only that, but why would they expose the lives of the deputies themselves—who were their chief leaders and principal men—to the fury of their adversaries (which in such a case would have been completely unavoidable) if they had any such design as they are accused of here: namely, of acting in an open and plain rebellion? On the contrary, was it not much rather an evident argument of their deep obedience and loyalty, accompanied by the greatest innocence? Even though they were treated harshly and rejected often, they would by no means stop presenting their petitions at the feet of their Sovereign, but still kept themselves within the bounds of that humility and respect which faithful and obedient subjects give to their Prince.

<summary>This page provides a point-by-point rebuttal to the Court of Savoy's claims of Waldensian rebellion, arguing that the Protestants acted only in self-defense and maintained legal representation at court as a sign of their continued loyalty to the Duke.</summary>

5. How could it be said that they returned *by their own authority*, when they were actually invited and lured there, like birds into a snare? For:

1. The majority of those who returned were tenants to certain Catholics, who commanded them to return and cultivate <note>original: "Till"</note> their grounds, faithfully promising them that everything would be settled and accommodated, and that not the slightest wrong in the world would be done to them. More particularly, they were promised that by doing so, they would not become liable to the penalties specified in the Order of *Gastaldo* <note>Andrea Gastaldo, the official who issued the 1655 decree ordering the Waldensians to leave their homes or convert.</note>.

2. When they complained of the wrongs and robberies mentioned earlier, they received this answer from the mouth of *Cristoforo Rorenco*, a gentleman of *Luserna* and a member of the *Council for the Propagation of the Faith* <note>original: "Council de Propaganda fide" — a Catholic committee established to convert Protestants</note>: That they should watch those thieves and identify them to the *President of the Province of Pinerolo*, who was appointed to do them justice. *And that in the mean time, they might also cultivate their grounds, provided they did not bring their families with them, and that the men should go back from time to time to stay in those other places where they had retired by order.* 

Whereupon those honest-meaning people, thinking their adversaries acted with the same sincerity of heart as they themselves did, and that it was not His Royal Highness's intention to drive them out of their ancient inheritances, returned based on the said *Rorenco's* word and promise. And yet, forsooth, this must be blamed on them as "rebellion." *It is easy to find a stick with which to beat a dog!* <note>original: "Facile est invenire baculum quo cedas canem!"</note> When someone who has power is resolved to do harm to an inferior, how easy it is for them to find or forge a grand and plausible pretext for even the most cruel and unhandsome action!

### Court of Savoy

His forces were admitted into Angrogna, Villar, and Bobbio without any opposition. 

The truth is, this was against the judgment of the wiser people, who would not have consented to let the troops in without resistance, except perhaps into the lower part of the community, which they thought would have been enough space to house them. But others, who were more trusting <note>original: "credulous"</note>, opposed this advice so strongly and so thoroughly convinced the rest that not the slightest resistance was made anywhere. Consequently, the troops advanced as far as the Alp of Soirian and La Vachère on the side of Angrogna, and into the Alps near Villar and Bobbio—all without a single shot being fired at them by those of the Reformed religion <note>original: "Reformed Religion." Referring to the Protestant Waldensians.</note>.

Now, these forces knew well what orders they had received. Seeing that most of the farmers <note>original: "Husbandmen"</note> had abandoned their homes, and realizing that on the day scheduled for the massacre they would have few throats to cut, the troops feared that those who had fled might return to cause trouble later. Therefore, for the next two days, they used every possible effort...

By using very civil and fair treatment toward those who stayed behind, they tried to entice the others to return. But on the third day, they put everyone to fire and sword, without any resistance except from a few countrymen. These men were pursued even into those places they had chosen for a sanctuary, thinking they were out of all danger. There, they did what they could to withstand the fury of those bloodthirsty men, while their poor wives and children made their escape through the snow. In many places, they fought—sometimes one man against a hundred, sometimes more—and with such wonderful and marvelous success that it plainly showed the hand of God was involved in preserving the remnant of his poor servants. And although it is true that Captain Janavel <note>original: "Fanavel." Referring to Joshua Janavel, a hero of the Waldensian resistance.</note>, his lieutenant, and their small company had far better success against those who intended to most cruelly murder them, their fellow believers knew nothing of it at the time. They were such a small handful that it is a miracle of Providence that a single soul of them ever escaped.

### The Declaration of *Mr. de Petit Bourg*, first Captain of the Regiment of *Grancey*, concerning the Cruelties that were exercised upon persons of all ages and sexes among the poor Protestants of the Valleys of *Piedmont*, signed with his own hand at *Pignerol*, November 27, 1655, in the presence of two other Commanders.

The true original of this document is to be seen, together with the rest, in the public library of the famous University of *Cambridge*.

I, Mr. de Petit Bourg, first Captain of the Regiment of Grancey, commanding it, and having orders from Prince Thomas to go join, etc. <note>original: "Je Sieur du Petit Bourg, premier Capitane au Regiment de Grancey, le commandant, & ayant en ordre de Monsieur le Prince Thomas d'aller joindre, &c."</note>

I, Mr. de Petit Bourg, first Captain of the Regiment of *Grancey*, who also commanded the same, received directions from Prince *Thomas* to go and join the Marquess of *Pianezza* and to receive his orders (the Marquess was then at *La Torre*). When I was just about to depart, the Ambassador sent for me and desired me to speak to Mr. de *Pianezza*. He asked me to use my best efforts to settle the troubles that had broken out among those of the Protestant religion <note>original: "those of the Religion." A common 17th-century term for the Reformed or Protestant faith.</note> in the Valleys of *Piedmont*. 

To that end, I then addressed myself to the Marquess, entreating him with great earnestness to let me undertake this peaceful settlement, which I believed I could have achieved. But he refused my request several times, despite all the arguments I could possibly use to persuade him. Instead of any mitigation of the situation—which my efforts or any other consideration might have produced—I was, on the contrary, a witness to many great acts of violence and extreme cruelties exercised by the bandits <note>original: "Banditi." Often irregular troops or outlaws recruited to assist the regular army in brutal tasks.</note> and soldiers of *Piedmont* upon people of every age, sex, and condition whatsoever. I myself saw them massacred, dismembered, hanged, and raped, amid many scenes of horrific chaos. 

It is far from the truth that these actions were done by virtue of orders given by me (as is falsely alleged in a certain official account <note>original: "Relation." Referring to the propaganda pamphlets published in French and Italian by the Court of Savoy to justify the massacre.</note> printed in *French* and *Italian*); rather, I beheld these events with horror and regret. And whereas it is said in that same account that the Marquess of *Pianezza* commanded me to treat the people peacefully, without hostility, and in the best manner I possibly could, the outcome clearly demonstrated that the orders he gave were altogether the opposite. It is most certain that, making no distinction between those who resisted and those who made no resistance, they were treated with every kind of inhumanity: their houses were burned, their goods plundered, and when prisoners were brought before the Marquess of *Pianezza*, I saw him give orders to give them no quarter <term>Give no quarter: A military term meaning to show no mercy and to kill prisoners rather than taking them captive.</term> at all. "Because," he said, "his Highness is resolved to..."

When once the mischief is done, and the cruelties are executed, and the world is likely to take notice of them to the everlasting shame (and perhaps prejudice) of the actors, then it is high time for them to endeavor to cover over their actions with the flimsy excuses <note>original: "untempered Morter," a biblical reference to Ezekiel 13:10, meaning a poorly made wall or a shaky, deceptive justification</note> of plausible pretexts. # CHAPTER III.

## *A Faithful and Most Authentic Narrative of the Continuation of the War in the Valleys of Piedmont, between the Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> and Protestant <note>original: "Reformed"</note> parties, following the Massacre.*

### ARTICLE I.

In the preceding account, the reader has seen confirmed all the notable events that occurred in the Valleys between the Catholic and the Protestant parties. This began with the first arrival of the Marquis of Pianezza's forces at San Giovanni around April 17, 1655, and continued until the fatal and bloody day of the massacre on the twenty-first of the same month.

By that time, the forces had caused such havoc among the poor people and such desolation throughout the Valleys that only the small community <note>original: "Communalty," referring to the local administrative district or township</note> of Rora could truly be said to remain entire and untouched. However, to ensure that the people of Rora suffered just like their brothers in the other churches—and to show the world that the destruction was designed to be universal—the Count of Christopher sent three hundred soldiers secretly by way of Villar Pellice <note>original: "Villaro"</note> on that very day to surprise them and put them all to the sword.

This party reached a certain small hill called Rumer, which belonged to Rora. There, they fortunately encountered some soldiers belonging to Captain Joshua Janavel <note>original: "Gianavel," a legendary leader of the Waldensian resistance</note>. God raised up Janavel in those days as a chosen instrument for the preservation of the poor, scattered remnant of his people.

Though these soldiers were only seven or eight in number, they had been placed in an ambush <note>original: "Ambuscado"</note> at a strategic post to prevent any incursion by the enemy. They took their opportunity to fire upon the attackers and, in truth, attacked them so vigorously that many were killed on the spot. The rest of the enemy, guessing by the great number of bullets flying about their ears that the men in ambush were six times more numerous than they actually were, fled back the way they came in great disorder and confusion. Seeing this, the defenders followed up their miraculous victory by falling upon the enemy's rear, and

chasing them for at least three-quarters of a league <note>original: "League"; a unit of distance roughly equal to three miles</note>, among the rocks and woods, killing many of them <note>original: "doing notable execution upon them"</note> as they were fleeing. And thus were three hundred of those murderers forced by seven or eight poor peasants to leave the country to their great shame and consternation, as well as the loss of many of their lives.

Now, because the common report at that time was that the soldiers sent by the Marquis of *Pianezza* (as mentioned above) had acted completely contrary to their orders in all their insolence, murders, massacres, and robberies, the members of this poor little Church soon after presented their complaints to the said *Marquis*. He, so that he might have a better advantage to deceive and surprise them a second time, gave them this answer: *that those of his soldiers who went to Rora were nothing more than thieves, robbers, and outlaws, and that they had completely disobeyed his orders in this; consequently, the peasants had done him a singular kindness in driving them out of their country.* He also claimed that he would take steps to prevent their disturbance in the future, and thereupon published an order by which he strictly <note>original: "straitly"</note> charged his soldiers not to give the people the least cause for future complaints or molest them in any way whatsoever.

But as promises made to heretics are not considered obligatory <note>This refers to the contemporary Catholic doctrine—often cited by Protestant writers of the era—that one was not required to keep faith with "heretics"</note> by men of the Marquis of *Pianezza’s* persuasion, he sent a party of five hundred chosen men the very next day to carry out his first bloody design. But as these men were passing over a little hill in *Rora* called *Cassulet*, they were so "saluted" by eleven musketeers of the *Protestants* and six men with slings—all under the command of Captain *Gianavel*, who had divided them into three squads and placed them strategically in the woods—that the enemy was soon put to flight. Afterward, this poor handful of "despicable" men pursued them for the space of a whole league, slaying a very great number of them, and all without the loss, or indeed even the injury, of so much as one man of their own party. By all of this, the reader may observe the admirable providence of the great *Lord of Hosts* <note>A biblical title for God, often used in the context of divine military protection</note> in preserving and prospering those who fight His battles.

The Marquis of *Pianezza*, despite having failed in his enterprise a second time, was resolved to try his fortune a third time. To this end, he made new promises and protestations that no injury in the world would be offered to them. He assured them further that the consideration shown by the Count <note>original: "Earl"</note> of *Christopher* of *Lucerna*, their Lord and Patron who had interceded for them, would have real effects for their preservation and protection. But whether the Marquis's memory was so short as to make him forget what he had promised, or whether his conscience and honor were troubled with a "looseness" <note>original: "looseness"; likely a play on words suggesting a lack of moral restraint or reliability</note>, the very next morning he sent a party of seven hundred soldiers. These troops first seized and secured all the mountain passes so that none might escape their bloody hands, and then most inhumanely burned and destroyed whatever they encountered throughout the entire community <note>original: "Communalty"</note> of *Rora*.

The common people <note>original: "communalty"</note> of **Rora**, whose hearts God had strengthened in a very significant manner for the battle to preserve their poor brothers, saw what treatment they could expect. They realized that nothing but death and destruction awaited them unless some wonderful act of providence prevented it. Calling to mind those many eminent and glorious deliverances God had granted to his people **Israel** in their greatest straits and emergencies, they were unanimously resolved to cast themselves, with their lives and fortunes, into the hands of the same God and Savior. They rested upon his gracious promises and freely submitted to his good will and pleasure for the success of all their undertakings.

The chief Captain and Commander of this valiant party was the previously mentioned Captain **Gianavel** <note>Joshua Gianavel (Giannello), a legendary Waldensian leader who led a small band of defenders against the ducal forces.</note>. Marching with his little troop near the enemy's quarters, he captured and carried away, in a most skillful manner, their entire guard post <note>original: "Court of Guard"</note> along with their sentry from a small hill belonging to a place called **Ramafiero**. At this bold exploit, the enemy was more than a little amazed and withdrew from their position. They resolved instead to march through a small meadow at the lower part of **Rora** called **Piampra**, hoping to reach **Villaro** or **La Torre**. However, they were not fast enough to achieve their goal; Gianavel’s men met them at **Piampra** and killed a great number of them without losing a single man of their own. They also recovered all the stolen cattle and other goods that the enemy had previously plundered from the inhabitants of the neighboring places.

Now the **Marquis of Pianezza** was significantly troubled that all his designs were being frustrated. He realized that all the fair words and hollow promises he could now offer these poor people were like telling a story to a deaf man <note>original: "surdo fabulam narrare"; a Latin proverb meaning to speak to deaf ears or waste one's breath.</note>, or rather acted as warning signals to bid them stay on their guard. He sent orders with all possible speed to all the men capable of carrying arms in **Lucerna**, **Bubbiana**, **Barges**, **Bagnol**, **Famolas**, **Cavour**, and the adjacent places. They were commanded to join a large part of his own army to surround those poor people on every side: namely, from the direction of **Villaro**, the mountains of **Bagnol**, and the side of **Lucerna**.

But as it is common for men to propose and for God to dispose <note>original: "men to decree, and for God to disappoint"</note>—making their plans foolish as he pleases—despite the meeting time <note>original: "Rendezvouz"</note> being punctually assigned, they arrived at least two hours too late. The only exception was the troop from **Bagnol**, which was led by a certain Captain **Mario**, a famous persecutor and notorious enemy of the Reformed Churches. This **Mario**, accompanied by a ragged regiment of outlaws, thieves, and robbers, as well as a great number of **Irish Rebels** <note>Irish Catholic soldiers who had fled to the Continent after the Cromwellian conquest and were serving as mercenaries for the Duke of Savoy.</note>, attacked the poor people on both the upper and lower parts of the district <note>original: "Canton"</note> of **Rumer**. To tell the truth, the defenders were only seventeen in number; but it pleased God to put so much courage into their hearts that they immediately climbed to the top of the mountain. There, after a long skirmish, they forced their enemies—no matter how full of fury and malice they were—to retreat and flee before them as far as the cliff called **Payro Capello**. # The War in Piedmont
### Book III

They also themselves admitted that they had lost sixty-five men, besides a great number who were wounded. Indeed, it could not have been otherwise, for many of them were so heavily burdened with plunder that the very weight of it caused them to tumble headlong as they fled among the rocky precipices, dashing themselves to pieces.

Now, those among them who—thanks to their lighter burdens and swifter feet—had reached the place called **Pairo Capello** <note>A rocky pass or peak in the mountains near Rora.</note>, found even greater difficulties there than they had faced before. Finding themselves closely pursued by the Reformed party <note>The Waldensians, or Vaudois Protestants.</note> and surrounded on every side, they were forced to take the very cords and ropes they had used to tie up their stolen goods and fasten them to shrubs growing on the side of the cliff. They used these to slide down, at least a hundred (or as some say, a hundred and fifty) at a time. From the end of the rope—which did not reach the river by at least the length of a pike <note>A pike was a long spear, usually between 10 and 20 feet long.</note>—they had to throw themselves into the water and swim for their lives. However, partly due to the violence of the current and partly due to the great confusion—with men falling on each other's necks and those who could not swim grabbing anyone nearby—the majority of them drowned. Their Captain, **Mario** <note>An officer in the Ducal army of Savoy.</note>, also threw himself into the river when his turn came. Had it not been for several soldiers—who were excellent swimmers and risked their lives to pull him out—he would have marched into the next world along with most of his troop. There, they would have received their full "payment" for the notable service they had performed for the Prince of Darkness <note>A sarcastic reference to the Devil.</note>.

This Captain **Mario** was afterwards brought into **Luserna** <note>Luserna San Giovanni, a town in the Piedmont region.</note> stripped to his shirt, without either a hat or shoes, like a man astonished and at his wits' end. Soon after, he fell into a desperate illness and died. Before his death, he often cried out in utter despair that he felt a burning within his bowels, which he saw as a just judgment of God upon him for having burned so many houses and so many innocent souls within them.

After this heroic and gallant action, the Reformed party felt somewhat tired from their hard service. As they were marching to find refreshment, they spotted another company coming from **Villar** <note>Villar Pellice.</note>. They immediately went into ambush <note>original: "Ambuscado"</note>. As the enemies drew near the place, they saw some of the men but were unable to distinguish who they were by any colors or marks. They called out to them for the password <note>original: "the Word"</note>. The Reformed party made no answer but beckoned for them to come closer. The enemy did so in a very careless manner, confident that they were meeting their own party. Suddenly, Gianavel’s men fired upon them, killing a very great number on the spot, and pursued the rest as far as the descent to **La Torre** <note>Torre Pellice.</note> and **Villar**. After this remarkable deliverance, Captain **Gianavel** <note>Joshua Gianavel (Giannello), the famed leader of the Rora resistance.</note> rallied his men together on a certain piece of high ground nearby. There, in the sight of his enemies, he had them all kneel down and, with a loud voice, give thanks to the Lord for the wonderful preservation He had granted them.

# Chapter III: The Catholic and Protestant Parties, 1655

<margin>Letter to Rora</margin>
About three days later, the Marquess of Pianezza, being highly enraged by this resistance from the Protestant party, sent an express messenger to the people of Rora with a letter. In it, he strictly ordered them to change their religion within twenty-four hours of receiving the notice, under penalty of death and having their houses burnt to the ground. To this letter, the poor people replied that they would much rather choose death than obey such an order. 

Seeing their steadfastness, the Marquess immediately dispatched no fewer than eight thousand men, in addition to the militia forces from the neighboring communities. Following his orders, these forces were divided into three squadrons: one to attack the poor people from the side of Villaro, another from the mountains of Bagnolo, and the third from the direction of Lucerna. They carried this out, not only putting men, women, and children to the sword, but also exercising all kinds of cruelties upon whomever they pleased. 

Those bloody wretches took much pleasure and delight in torturing those poor creatures. They snatched up young infants and hurled them through the air from the points of their pikes and halberds <note>A halberd is a historical pole weapon consisting of an axe blade topped with a spike.</note>. Their pitiful cries created such a mournful echo among the rocks that it would have melted the heart of any Christian soul to hear it. They also dashed the infants' brains against the rocks. In total, about one hundred and twenty-six people were killed, wounded, or taken prisoner in this encounter; the rest escaped the enemy’s hands through a miracle of Providence.

After this "great victory" of eight thousand soldiers over nineteen or twenty men (along with a few elderly people, women, and infants), and after they had sufficiently satisfied themselves with the plunder they found in the countryside and turned all the houses and dwellings to ashes, they sent their prisoners in triumph to Turin. Among these prisoners were the wife and children of Captain Gianavel <note>Joshua Janavel (or Gianavello), a famous Waldensian military leader known as the "Lion of Rora."</note>. The Catholic party then marched back to Lucerna with great joy and celebration.

Not long after, the Marquess of Pianezza wrote a very long and detailed letter to Captain Gianavel. On one hand, he promised him great rewards if he would only change his religion. On the other hand, he threatened that Gianavel’s wife and children would be burned, and a large sum of money would be given to anyone who brought in Gianavel, either dead or alive. He added that if Gianavel were ever taken prisoner, he could easily imagine how he would be treated. 

To this, Captain Gianavel immediately answered that there was no torment so violent, nor death so cruel, that he did not much prefer over the renunciation <note>original: "Abjuration"</note> of his religion, and that all the Marquess's promises and threats only served to fortify and strengthen his faith. Finally, he said that although the Marquess had his wife and children in his power and custody, he could do no more than kill their bodies; as for their souls, he committed them, along with his own, into the hands of God, should he ever fall into the Marquess's power. This was the direct and honest answer of Captain Gianavel, whose heroic actions should certainly be recommended to posterity, and—

<header>The War in Piedmont, Book III</header>

They themselves admitted that they had lost sixty-five men, in addition to a great number who were wounded. Indeed, it could not have been otherwise, for many of them were so heavily weighed down with plunder <note>Stolen goods or loot taken during the raid.</note> that the very weight of it, as they were fleeing among the precipices of the rocks, caused them to tumble headlong and dash themselves to pieces.

Now, those of them who—by reason of their lighter burdens and swifter feet—had reached the place called *Payro Capello* <note>A rocky pass in the Piedmont region.</note>, found much greater difficulties to contend with than before. Finding themselves closely pursued by the *Reformed* party <note>The "Reformed" refers to the Waldensians, a group of pre-Reformation Protestants living in the Alpine valleys.</note> and surrounded on every side, they were forced to take the very cords and ropes they had used to tie up their stolen goods and fasten them to some shrubs growing on the side of the cliff. They used these to slide down, at least a hundred (or as some say, a hundred and fifty) at a time. From the end of the rope, which did not reach within the length of a good pike <note>A long thrusting spear; a "pike's length" is about 10 to 15 feet.</note> of the river, they had to throw themselves into the water and swim for their lives. 

Between the violence of the rushing torrent and the great confusion among them—with one person falling on the neck of another, and those who could not swim grabbing hold of anyone near them—the majority of them drowned. Their captain, *Mario*, also threw himself into the river when his turn came. Had several of his soldiers (who were excellent swimmers) not risked their lives to pull him out, he would have marched along with the greater part of his troop into the other world, there to receive the full "pay" for the eminent service they had done for the Prince of Darkness <note>A rhetorical way of saying they served the Devil through their cruelty.</note>.

This Captain *Mario* was later brought into *Lucerna* <note>Modern day Luserna San Giovanni.</note> wearing only his shirt, without either a hat or shoes, like a man astonished and at his wit's end. Soon after, he fell into a desperate illness and died. Before his death, he often cried out in a state of utter despair, saying that he felt a burning within his bowels as a just judgment of God upon him for having burned so many houses and so many innocent souls within them.

After this heroic and gallant action, the *Reformed* party was somewhat tired from their hard service. As they were marching to find refreshment, they noticed another company of soldiers coming from *Villaro*. They immediately set an ambush <note>original: "Ambuscado"</note>. As the enemies drew near, they saw some of the Protestants but could not distinguish who they were by any colors or marks. They called out asking for the password <note>original: "the Word"</note>. The *Reformed* made no answer but gestured for them to come closer. The enemy approached carelessly, confident that these were their own men. Suddenly, the Protestants opened fire, killing a very great number of them on the spot and pursuing the rest as far as the slopes of *La Torre* and *Villaro*. 

After this remarkable deliverance, Captain *Gianavel* <note>Joshua Janavel, a famous Waldensian military leader.</note> gathered his men together on a certain high ground nearby. There, in the sight of his enemies, he had them all kneel down and, with a loud voice, give thanks to the Lord for the wonderful preservation He had granted them.

### Chapter III. The Popish and Protestant Parties, 1655.

About three days later, the Marquess of Pianezza—being deeply enraged by the resistance of the Protestant party—sent the people of *Rora* a letter by an express <note>original: "Express"; a specialized fast messenger</note>. In this letter, he strictly ordered them to change their religion within twenty-four hours after the delivery of his order, upon pain of death and having their houses burned to the ground. To this letter, the poor people replied that *they would much rather choose death than obey any such order.* 

Seeing their constancy, the Marquess immediately dispatched no fewer than eight thousand men, in addition to the militia forces of the neighboring communities. According to his orders, these were divided into three divisions: one to attack the poor people from the side of *Villaro*, the second from the mountains of *Bagnol*, and the third from the side facing *Lucerna*. This they carried out, not only putting to the sword every man, woman, and child, but also practicing all kinds of cruelties upon whomever they pleased. 

Those bloody wretches took great pleasure and delight in torturing those poor creatures. They took young infants—whose woeful cries created such a lamentable echo among the rocks—and hurled them through the air off the enemies' pikes and halberds <note>long spears and axe-like polearms used by infantry</note>, dashing their brains against the rocks. It would have melted the heart of any Christian soul to hear it. The number of those killed, wounded, and taken prisoner in this encounter was 126 in total; the rest, by a miracle of Providence, escaped the enemy's hands.

After this "great victory" of eight thousand over nineteen or twenty men (along with a few old men, women, and poor infants), and after they had sufficiently glutted themselves with the plunder they found in the country, they turned all the houses and dwellings to ashes. They sent their prisoners in triumph to *Turin* (among whom were the wife and children of Captain *Gianavel*). Afterward, the Popish <note>original: "Popish party"; referring here to the Roman Catholic forces of the Duchy of Savoy</note> party marched back to *Lucerna* with great joy and cheers.

Not long after, the Marquess of Pianezza wrote a very long and detailed letter to Captain *Gianavel*. On one hand, he promised him great advantages if he would only change his religion. On the other hand, he threatened him *that his wife and children would be burned, and a large sum of money would be given to anyone who brought in Gianavel, either dead or alive; and that if he were ever taken prisoner, he could easily imagine how he would be treated.* 

To this, Captain *Gianavel* immediately answered *that there was no torment so violent, nor death so cruel, that he did not prefer it over the renunciation of his religion, and that all the Marquess's promises and threats only served to further fortify and strengthen his faith. Finally, he stated that although the Marquess had his wife and children in his power and custody, he could do no more than kill their bodies; as for their souls, he commended them, along with his own, into the hands of God, should he ever happen to fall into the Marquess's power.* 

This was the true and direct <note>original: "naked Answer"</note> answer of Captain *Gianavel*, whose heroic actions ought certainly to be recommended to posterity, and

whose name ought to be recorded among the most famous heroes who ever drew a sword for the cause of Christ and his poor, distressed believers <note>original: "Members"; referring to the "members of the body of Christ," or the church</note>.

This Captain **Gianavel**, having gathered a small handful of men upon a part of the Alps called *La Pella des Faimets*, went out on the evening of May 22. He marched about nine miles <note>original: "three Leagues"</note> from that place, not far from **Bibiana** (a small town just below **Luserna**). There, he first sought God in prayer with his entire small troop. Afterward, he gathered information regarding the number and strength of the enemy. Finding that they were too numerous and powerful to be attacked by such a small handful of men as he had with him, he steered his course toward **Lucernetta**, a village belonging to **Bibiana**. There, he was attacked very furiously by the garrison of **Luserna**, but he resisted them most courageously without the loss of a single man. He himself received a shot in one of his legs from a soldier who had hidden behind a tree for that purpose; however, that soldier lost his life for his effort. As soon as the Captain realized where the shot had come from, though he was wounded, he quickly reached the man and killed him on the spot.

In the meantime, while these things were happening, it is worth observing that the **Irish rebels** <note>Catholic Irish soldiers who had fled to the Continent and were serving as mercenaries for the Duke of Savoy</note> attempted to make themselves masters of **Bibiana**, under the pretext of guarding it against the <term>Barbets</term> <note>a derogatory nickname given to the Waldensian Protestants by their Catholic opponents</note>. The local peasants took this opportunity to quarrel with the Irish and eventually drove them out, killing a great number of them.

### The Battles at Garzigliana, San Secondo, and Bricherasio.

On May 26, 1655, Captain **Joshua Gianavel** wrote several letters to Captain **Bartholomew Jahier** and to those who had retreated into **Val Luserna**, requesting a general rendezvous at **Angrogna**. This meeting took place very successfully. The following day, May 27, they all marched together to a certain place in the plain called **Garzigliana**. However, as they attempted to enter the town, they were met by a large party of cavalry and infantry. This small handful of men fought against them for a long time but was eventually forced to retreat. Nevertheless, they did not leave without a bounty of about six yoke of oxen and a large number of other smaller cattle, as well as some prisoners. One of these prisoners immediately offered them fifty <term>pistoles</term> <note>a type of gold coin</note> for his ransom. All of this was accomplished with the loss of only one man during their retreat.

### Chapter III. Catholic and Protestant Parties, 1655.

The organized <note>original: "formed"</note> party marched toward **San Secondo**. After first kneeling down and praying for a blessing upon their efforts, they rose up and encouraged one another in a wonderful manner. They attacked the place with incredible courage and bravery. To better approach the houses where the enemy had sheltered and fortified themselves, they used planks, barrels, and whatever else they could find to shield themselves from the bullets being fired at them constantly from the houses. 

They quickly made themselves masters of the doors of those houses, immediately set them on fire, and broke in by force, putting all the soldiers they found to the sword. In truth, they had been extremely provoked to this harshness and severity by the enemy's cruel treatment of their wives and children. This led them to seek revenge to some extent (especially since almost every room in those very houses they entered was stuffed and filled with the goods stolen from the **Protestants**). However, their fury and desire for revenge did not overcome them so much that they harmed any women or children, as they viewed them as not guilty of the crimes and cruelties committed by the others.

After this, they set fire to the entire town. They recovered supplies from the churches, which they found full of their own goods and cattle that the enemy had brought there some days before. They also carried away about seven of their church bells <note>original: "Mass-Bells"</note>.

In this great encounter, no fewer than 450 men from the Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> party died that very day, as was testified by a man who helped to bury them. Among others, an entire company of **Irish rebels** <note>mercenary soldiers serving the Duke of Savoy</note> perished; they chose to be burned alive rather than surrender and accept mercy <note>original: "take Quarter"</note>. This was seen as a just judgment from Heaven upon them for all their cruelties. On the Protestant side, only seven notable soldiers were killed: two from the Valley of **San Martino**, one from **La Torre**, one from **Roccapiatta**, two from **Angrogna**, and one from **San Giovanni**. About six or seven others were slightly wounded, but they soon recovered.

On Monday, June 4, Captains **Jahier**, **Laurentio**, **Gianavel**, **Genolat**, **Benet**, and other officers of the Reformed party went to **Angrogna**. Having called a Council of War, they decided to alarm the enemy the following day at **Bricherasio** <note>original: "Briqueras"</note> and **San Giovanni**. After doing so, Captains **Laurentio** and **Jahier** marched by way of **Roccapiatta** so they could more easily approach **Bricherasio** under the cover of the thick woods in that area, where they hid themselves. Having reached a small hill above the vineyards of **Bricherasio**, Captain **Laurentio** held his position to block any reinforcements that might have been sent from **San Secondo**. Meanwhile, Captain **Jahier** went down somewhat lower and set fire to several houses, barns, and neighboring buildings.

At the sight of this fire, the people of **Bricherasio** gave notice to those in **Cavour** <note>original: "Cavors"</note>, **Fenile**, **Bibiana** <note>original: "Bubiana"</note>, and **Campiglione**, along with all neighboring parts, that...

...so that they might take the alarm. At this, the enemy quickly advanced, but they were just as quickly repelled and driven back.

In the meantime, a party of about twenty cavalry arrived and took up their station at **San Secondo**. They did this for fear that the **Protestant** <note>original: "Reformed"</note> party might make a sudden attack <note>original: "Sally out"</note> that way, as they truly believed the Protestants intended to attack **Briqueras**. Upon seeing this, Captain **Jahier** marched with his company by way of **San Giovanni**, while Captain **Laurentio** took another path slightly higher up. They both met at the appointed place. There, Captain **Jahier** found Captain **Gianavel** engaged with the soldiers of **Lucerna** and **La Torre**, against whom he had defended himself with exceeding courage. Jahier charged them in the flank while Captain **Laurentio** advanced against their front at the same time. Laurentio seasonably positioned his company in the very spot where the enemies intended to surround Captain **Gianavel**. Consequently, the Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> party was put to flight in great disorder, losing a hundred men and suffering many wounded; meanwhile, only one man of the Protestant party was killed on the field.

On the second of June, three hundred enemy soldiers left **La Torre** to bring a supply convoy into the fort of **Mirebouc**, situated on the border between **Dauphiné** and **Piedmont**. Captain **Gianavel** was then at a place called **Malbec**. Although he had only nine soldiers with him, he fell upon them and fought them for a long time, to the astonishment of the enemy. In the end, he was forced to retreat toward **Ville Neuve**, but he did not lose a single man from his party, and only four were slightly wounded.

After this, Captain **Gianavel** marched with some small parties to a place called **La Pela des Gainets**. From there, he sent word to the residents of **Bobbio**, **Villar**, **La Torre**, and other places who had retreated to **Villar**: that all those of the **Protestant Religion** must leave that place (where the Catholic Mass was being celebrated) within twenty-four hours, or else be treated as enemies. He also declared that those who had renounced <note>original: "abjured"</note> their faith through weakness, but intended to persist in those renunciations, must also depart under the same penalties. 

Immediately after this, all the Catholics departed from **Villar**, and the Protestants came in to join Captain **Gianavel**. All those able to bear arms followed him cheerfully, while the others contributed what they could to maintain him and his troops. As for those who had renounced their religion through infirmity, they went over the mountain into the **Valley of Queyras**. However, not long after, they returned like so many wandering sheep to the "true Shepherd of their souls" <note>A biblical reference to Jesus Christ, implying they returned to their original Protestant faith.</note> and were accordingly received back into the bosom of the Church.
