Chapter III. Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> and Protestant Party, 1655.

## ARTICLE III.

### The Battles of Lucerna, La Torre, Crissolo <note>original: "Crusol"</note>, Angrogna <note>original: "Angrognia"</note>, and Osasco <note>original: "Osac"</note>, with several other incidents and encounters.

After the people of Lucerna had retreated, that very same day Captains Jahier and Gianavel, along with some other officers, held a Council of War. In this meeting, it was decided and resolved to make a sudden attack <note>original: "Sally out"</note> to surprise, if possible, the garrison at La Torre. A large portion of the troops there were Irish <note>The Duke of Savoy employed Irish Catholic mercenaries—many of whom were refugees from the Cromwellian conquest of Ireland—to suppress the Protestant Vaudois.</note>. However, the enemy received timely warning of the plan and killed the first and bravest of those who had crossed the bridge at Angrogna. This success so encouraged the rest of the Catholic party that they were satisfied with nothing less than attempting to surround the entire body of the Protestant party to trap and destroy them completely. But after making many unsuccessful assaults, they were finally forced to retreat back into La Torre, having lost a great number of their soldiers, while many others received very painful and dangerous wounds.

The next day, Captains Jahier and Gianavel marched toward La Torre. Upon their arrival, many of the soldiers there came out to fight them. However, because they did not have a suitable way to charge out as a single large unit <note>original: "sallying forth in a full Body"</note>, they were all killed on the spot as quickly as they emerged. When their captains and commanders—who also came out at the sound of the shooting—saw this, they realized how great the danger was. They decided it was more prudent to recall their soldiers rather than let them cross the bridge of Angrogna. Consequently, the Reformed <note>Protestant</note> party retreated toward Angrogna to a place called La Verné, where a few houses still remained unburnt.

The following day was spent reviewing their army and holding another Council of War. There, it was resolved to send a party against the community of Crissolo <note>original: "Crusol"</note>, because its inhabitants had made several raids against them and committed many atrocities <note>original: "Outrages"</note> at the beginning of the massacre. To achieve this, they marched all night (numbering 495 men) and passed above La Torre without being discovered by the people there. A little after midnight, they arrived safely at Crissolo, where they captured four hundred head of cattle, six hundred sheep and goats, and a large amount of other loot <note>original: "Booty"</note>. They did all this without the slightest resistance, as most of the inhabitants of Crissolo were so terrified by this sudden surprise that they threw themselves into the opening of a fearsome rock formation <note>original: "mouth of a most fearfull Rock"</note>, from which it was entirely impossible to retrieve them. Having finished this, the Protestants returned to one of the mountain pastures <note>original: "Alps"</note> of Villaro, where they arrived the next evening and divided the spoils among the soldiers.

A few hours after their departure, people arrived from Lucerna, Cavour <note>original: "Cavars"</note>, Bricherasio <note>original: "Briqueras"</note>, Barge <note>original: "Barges"</note>, Bagnolo <note>original: "Bagnol"</note>, Envie <note>original: "Famolase"</note>, and other neighboring places,

But Captain Janavel was then at a place called Malbec. Although he had only nine soldiers with him, he fell upon them and fought for a long time, to the amazement of the enemy. After this, Captain Janavel and some small parties marched to a place called La Pela des Gainets. From there, he sent word to the people of Bobbio <note>original: "Bobio"</note>, Villar <note>original: "Villaro"</note>, La Torre, and other places who had sought refuge in Villar. He declared that all those of the Protestant religion must leave that place (where the Mass was being celebrated) within twenty-four hours, or else be treated as enemies. He also warned that those who had renounced their faith <note>original: "abjured"</note> out of weakness, but who intended to persist in those conversions, must also leave under the same penalties. 

Because of this, all the Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note> immediately left Villar, and the Protestants joined Captain Janavel. All who were able to bear arms followed him cheerfully, while others contributed what they could toward the maintenance of him and his troops. As for those who had renounced their religion out of fear <note>original: "infirmity"</note>, they fled over the mountains into the Valley of Queyras <note>original: "Queires"</note>. However, not long after, they returned like wandering sheep to the true Shepherd of their souls, and accordingly were received again into the heart of the Church.

<header>Chapter III. *The Catholic and Protestant Parties, 1655.*</header>

### A R T I C L E III.

#### The Battles of Luserna, Torre Pellice, Crissolo, Angrogna, and Ofac, with several other Incidents and Encounters.

After the forces from Luserna <note>original: "Lucerna"</note> had retreated, on that very same day, Captains Jahier and Janavel <note>original: "Giannavel"</note>, along with other officers, held a Council of War. They resolved to launch a sortie <note>original: "Sally out"</note> to surprise the garrison at Torre Pellice <note>original: "La Torre"</note>, a large portion of whom were Irish <note>The "Irish" were Catholic mercenaries serving the Duke of Savoy, many of whom were refugees from Cromwell's campaigns in Ireland.</note>. However, the enemy received timely warning of the plan and killed the first and bravest of the Protestant soldiers who had crossed the bridge at Angrogna. This success so encouraged the Catholic party that they were satisfied with nothing less than attempting to surround the entire body of the Protestant party to wipe them out completely. However, after making many failed assaults, they were finally forced to retreat into Torre Pellice with the loss of a great number of their soldiers, in addition to many others who received very painful and dangerous wounds.

The next day, Captains Jahier and Janavel marched toward Torre Pellice. Upon their arrival, many of the soldiers there came out to fight them; however, because they could not emerge in a full formation, they were killed on the spot as quickly as they came out. When their captains and commanders—who also came out at the sound of the gunfire—saw this, they realized the greatness of the danger. They decided it was more prudent to call their soldiers back inside than to let them cross the bridge of Angrogna. Consequently, the Reformed <note>Protestant</note> party retreated toward Angrogna to a place called La Verné, where a few houses remained unburned.

The following day was spent reviewing their army and holding a Council of War. It was resolved to send a party against the community of Crissolo <note>original: "Crusol"</note>, because its inhabitants had made several raids against them and committed many outrages at the beginning of the massacre <note>This refers to the "Piedmontese Easter" massacre of April 1655.</note>. To this end, they marched all night (numbering four hundred ninety-five men) and passed above Torre Pellice without being discovered by the townspeople. A little after midnight, they arrived safely at Crissolo, where they captured four hundred head of cattle and six hundred sheep and goats, along with a great deal of other booty. They accomplished all of this without the slightest resistance, because most of the inhabitants of Crissolo were so terrified by this sudden surprise that they threw themselves into the mouth of a fearsome rock crevice, from which it was impossible to retrieve them. This being done, the soldiers returned to one of the high mountain pastures <note>term: Alps</note> of Villar Pellice <note>original: "Villaro"</note>, where they arrived the next evening and divided the spoils among themselves.

A few hours after their departure, people arrived from Luserna, Cavour <note>original: "Cavors"</note>, Bricherasio <note>original: "Briqueras"</note>, Barge, Bagnolo <note>original: "Bagnol"</note>, Famolasco <note>original: "Famolase"</note>, and other neighboring places,

...places, numbering 800 men, who had heard of the aforementioned plan against Crissolo <note>original: "Crusol"</note> and intended to reinforce them. But finding that the others were too far ahead to be overtaken, they resolved not to waste their efforts. They immediately began plundering the poor people in a manner ten times more cruel than the Reformed <note>The "Reformed" refers to the Protestant Waldensians.</note> had done before. Not only that, but they also fell into a dispute among themselves over the division of the loot and ended up destroying one another instead of inflicting the slightest harm on the Reformed party.

It is very remarkable that on the very same day as the action against Crissolo, the people of San Secondo <note>A town in the Piedmont region.</note>, having received word of it, came to burn the remaining houses of Roccapiatta. They had already advanced as far as the small hill of Angrogna <note>original: "Angrognia"</note> with the intent to surprise the remaining forces left in the camp under the command of Captain Lorenzo <note>original: "Laurentio"</note> and the brother and lieutenant of Captain Jahier. However, having received timely notice of this, the Reformed forces marched without delay to the top of the mountain with half of the soldiers. They left the other half under the prudent leadership of Captain Benet of San Germano, who also took his position on the aforementioned hill with seventeen of his men with all possible speed and placed the rest in ambush <note>original: "Ambuscado"</note>. But the enemies’ hearts failed them, and they retreated in a most shameful and cowardly manner. They performed no brave deed that day except for one: they captured Giovanni Pietro Ragio as he was coming from Pinache <note>original: "Pinachia," modern Pinasca</note>. Binding his head with a cord, they tightened it with such violence that it sank into his skull. After doing this, they sent him to Turin to be "cured"—which indeed he was a few days later by a lingering and miserable death.

About eight days later, Captain Janavel <note>original: "Gianavel"</note>, having waited in vain at Angrogna for three whole days for the arrival of Captain Jahier to join him in assaulting the town of Luserna <note>original: "Lucerna"</note>, resolved to undertake the attack himself. To this end, he began his march from Angrogna at nightfall and arrived at Luserna by daybreak. Upon arrival, he first cut the pipes that carried water into the town and broke down the bridge so that no reinforcements could reach them from Bibiana <note>original: "Bubbiana"</note>, Barge <note>original: "Barges"</note>, and Bagnolo <note>original: "Bagnol"</note>. Having done this, he assaulted the town and quickly defeated two of the outposts. However, because the regiment of Monsieur de Merolles and several other significant groups had entered the town the night before, Janavel was, to his great sorrow, forced to retreat and abandon the storming of the town. Had Captain Jahier arrived in time, they likely would have captured the place in a very short period.

The following Friday, June 8th, Captain Janavel was left alone in Angrogna with only his own company and a few men from Villar Pellice <note>original: "Villaro"</note>, Bobbio, Torre Pellice <note>original: "La Torre"</note>, San Giovanni, and Angrogna. He was assaulted at daybreak by the soldiers of Torre Pellice and others. Some of them had climbed to the top of the mountain, while others had taken the lower pass to seize the Gate of Angrogna by way of San Bartolomeo <note>original: "San Bartholomeo"</note>, thinking to fall suddenly

...suddenly upon Captain *Gianavel* and his forces, as a high-flying hawk does upon her prey. It pleased God to order affairs such that at the sound of the trumpet, when everyone should have attacked, Captain *Gianavel* quickly woke up. Having first sought God in prayer, he fell upon the enemy and gained the advantage of the terrain over them. After a short skirmish <note>original: "Dispute"</note>, he forced them to retreat, even though there were at least 2,500 of them and his entire company did not exceed 300. Not only that, but he also pursued them as far as the descent of *Angrogna* <note>original: "Angrognia"</note>, into the woods and steep rocky places, where he killed a very large number of them.

This fight lasted without any interruption until about two o'clock in the afternoon, at which time Captain *Jahier* <note>original: "Fahier"</note> arrived from *Pramollo* <note>original: "Pramol"</note> with his men. This was very timely for the relief of Captain *Gianavel* and his troops. These two joined their forces together (though Gianavel's group had been fighting for at least eight hours straight) and with incredible courage drove the enemy before them as far as the church <note>original: "Temple"</note> of *Chabas* in the commune of *San Giovanni*, and totally routed them. Some of the infantry fled toward *La Torre* and some into *Lucerna*. Many of the cavalry were also forced over cliffs and other dangerous places as they fled for their lives. In this combat, many significant officers and commanders of the Catholic party <note>original: "Popish party"</note> were killed. On the other side, Captain *Gianavel*, their chief commander, was severely wounded. His own soldiers, who loved him dearly, carried him back (though by force and much against his will), so that his wound would not become infected <note>original: "festered, or putrified"</note>. Such an infection would have been extremely dangerous for him and, consequently, for his entire company, whose lives and safety were, after God, dependent upon him.

Now Captain *Gianavel*, seeing that it was impossible for him to undertake anything further at that moment, urged Captain *Jahier* to stop for the day and take some time for himself and his soldiers to rest. But Captain *Jahier*, being at that time much more passionate than prudent, refused the sound and timely advice of Captain *Gianavel*. Taking about 150 chosen men whom he had selected from the whole army, he took his leave of Captain *Gianavel* (perhaps not thinking it would be his last) and immediately departed. He marched down into the plain, where he burned several houses belonging to those who had previously burned and destroyed so many of the Protestants' homes. He also took a significant amount of booty, including their cattle and other movable property.

### ARTICLE IV.

### The Sad and Much-Lamented Death of Captain Jahier and His Company.

Up until this point, Captain Jahier had been exceedingly successful in all his attempts and enterprises, even to the admiration and astonishment of his very enemies. However, as all our days are numbered, and the number of our months is determined by the Almighty—beyond which we cannot pass for even a single moment, nor is any human device or power able to turn aside His unalterable will—this was to be his end. 

This valiant Captain intended to crown his other notable achievements with one final high undertaking at the end of the day. As he was very near executing his design, a squadron of cavalry surrounded him and his forty-five men (for there were no more with him at that time) at a country house not far from the town of Ossac, which is about three miles <note>original: "a League"</note> distant from San Giovanni. Although he and his company did everything for their defense that could possibly be expected from the most valiant champions under the canopy of heaven—killing three captains along with the commander-in-chief of the squadron, besides a great number of others—he and thirty-five of his followers eventually lost their lives. As a token of everlasting triumph, the enemies afterward beheaded Captain Jahier and his sons. They carried the heads to Turin and presented them to the Duke and *Madam Royale* <note>Christina of France, the Duchess of Savoy and mother of Duke Charles Emmanuel II</note>, who gave them a reward of six hundred ducatoons <note>original: "Ducatoons"; a silver coin used in several European countries</note>.

<margin>A description of Captain Jahier’s character.</margin>
This man was certainly most worthy of remembrance, and his fame deserves to be renowned to all posterity. This is especially true for his great piety and zeal for the service of God and the preservation of His poor, afflicted Church and its members. He was a man whom the terrors of death and ten thousand torments could never frighten or cause to deny his Master. He was as bold as a lion in all his enterprises, and for his valor, another Achilles! Yet, he was as meek and humble as a lamb in the midst of his victories, always lifting up his hands toward heaven, from where his deliverance came. He frequently recited sweet and comfortable passages of the Scripture (in which he was amazingly well-versed) to the great encouragement of all his followers and the strengthening of their faith on all occasions. Besides all this, regarding his outward abilities and accomplishments, he was a man of good understanding and sound judgment. Above all, he possessed a marvelously active spirit; had he used this activity with more moderation, he would certainly have had few equals.

The death of this brave commander, together with the wounding of Captain Gianavel, at that particular moment greatly startled the Reformed party, as the reader may easily imagine. But, as necessity many times drives very ordinary <note>original: "inconsiderable"</note> men to take bold risks, those

The poor people did not lose their courage so much as to give up everything for lost; on the contrary, they took heart and assembled themselves shortly afterward at La Vachere, a mountain of Angrogna. From there, they went into the plain, where they were twice severely assaulted. The last of these assaults was a dangerous ambush <note>original: "Ambuscado"</note> by the enemy, who were at least six thousand in number, while the Protestants were no more than a hundred. But Providence so disposed all things, and so guided their hands and strengthened their hearts, that they killed a very great number of them. Among these were several significant officers, specifically a certain Bavarian who was a Lieutenant Colonel of infantry <note>original: "Foot"</note> and a man greatly mourned by all his soldiers. In contrast, the only losses for the Reformed party were Michele Bertino, a sergeant of Angrogna, and a single common soldier of Val Martino who was wounded.

It is remarkable that the son of the said Bertino, seeing his father fall dead at his feet, was so far from being dismayed (as many would have been) that he immediately stepped into his father's place, saying:

> *Though my father is dead, yet be of good courage, fellow soldiers, for God is a father to us all.*

The following Monday, they had a very sharp skirmish <note>original: "dispute"</note> at La Torre and around Tagliaretto, where they killed and wounded a great number of the enemy without the loss of any of their own men. It is true that the enemies during this time did reap their grain <note>original: "corn"</note> in the plains of San Giovanni and La Torre, but they were not able to carry it away without a considerable loss of their men.

At the same time, there arrived and stayed with them until the peace at Pignerol a certain Mr. Andrion, a Major of a cavalry <note>original: "Horse"</note> regiment, along with two other gentlemen who were foreigners <note>original: "strangers"</note>, followed by some volunteers. Their charitable visit to their poor afflicted brethren, and their good counsel and advice in such a critical moment, was extremely well received, as indeed it deserved to be. It was a singular means to strengthen and uphold the weak and fainting spirits of many a fragile brother, who—seeing others come to "the help of the Lord against the mighty" <note>A biblical reference to Judges 5:23</note>—went on with much more cheerfulness and speed, as the rest of this account will better demonstrate.

### The War in Piedmont between the... Book III.

The poor churches of the valleys, having heard that the enemies believed he had returned from his journey with arms, money, and ammunition—and thereby suspecting that the enemy would soon attempt a significant attack to prevent what they so much feared—went to Colonel *Andrion*, an exceedingly valiant captain, and urged him to carry out his plan.

The poor people did not yet have a standing army, but rather squadrons from each community stationed at great distances from one another. Certainly, very few days would have passed before every man of them was cut off, had their sentinels not been very watchful; but above all, they were saved because Captain *Chanforan* discovered the enemy in time on one side, and the poor people on the other side were greatly encouraged in the battle by the great valor and singular leadership of the Sieurs <note>original: "Sieurs," a title of respect similar to "Sirs" or "Messrs."</note> *Andrion*, *Michelin*, and *Leger*.

The enemy was very numerous at this time, having been reinforced with a great number of fresh troops who came to their assistance. These had encamped during the night within half a league <note>A league is roughly three miles.</note> of the *Reformed* party. In the morning at about dawn, they divided their army into four squadrons. Three of these attacked with remarkable determination in three different places at once: one below on the south side, another on the east side and in the front, and a third on the north side; the fourth stood still, ready to support the assailants if needed. This fight lasted at least four hours without intermission and was the sharpest that was ever fought in the open field. 

What made the attackers even more fierce was their hope of driving the *Reformed* back just one pistol-shot from a post they held—namely the *Chastelas*, or the *Bastion of the Classes*. If they could have done this once, they would have inevitably made themselves masters of the valleys of *Perosa*, *San Martino*, and *Lucerna*. But the poor people, having lifted up their hearts and voices to the Lord of Hosts <note>original: "Lord of Hoasts," a biblical title for God as the leader of heavenly armies.</note> through earnest prayers and supplications (as was their usual custom on all such occasions), Major *Andrion* and the other captains he had brought with him to assist the valleys issued the necessary orders. They encouraged the soldiers exceedingly, so that they held their ground and did not retreat a single foot—except for a few who were exhausted from heavy service or had grown weak from lack of food. 

There were also some who had no powder left, and others who had no flints in their muskets <note>original: "fire-locks"</note>. However, the Sieurs *Leger* and *Michelin* employed these men in rolling down great stones upon the enemies' heads as they came to attack them. This indeed proved very successful and did such execution upon the enemy that it made them lose much of their fury. Whereas in the beginning of the combat their cry was always, *"Advance, advance, you remnants <note>original: "Relicks"</note> of Jahier!"*, the *Reformed* party now began to cry out just as loudly, *"Advance, advance, you remnants of San Secondo!"* <note>The Regiment of San Secondo was the primary Catholic force involved in the massacre and subsequent battles.</note> 

With this, they ran upon those murderers like so many lions; the enemy turned their backs and fled toward *La Torre* and *Lucerna* with all possible speed, leaving behind fifty-five men who were killed on the spot, and

And about forty who were killed in the flight, besides many others who were carried either dead or sorely wounded to *Lucerna*. The enemies themselves confessed that they lost in this encounter at least three hundred men, among which were many officers of a *Bavarian* Regiment. Two soldiers of that regiment assured Captain *Laurentio* of *Val San Martino*, and many others of the *Reformed* Religion, that from their regiment alone, no fewer than one hundred and eighty died that day.

<margin>(a) That is, Protestants; for just as they are called Huguenots in France, they are called Barbets in these valleys.</margin>

It is very remarkable that at this time, when such multitudes of dead, wounded, and dying men were brought into *Lucerna*, the Syndic <note>A syndic was a local government official or magistrate.</note> of the place (named *Baptista Bianco*), an honest Roman Catholic but less superstitious than many others, happened to let slip the following words: *“In the past the wolves ate the Barbets, but now the Barbets eat the wolves.”* <note>original Italian: "Altre volte li lupi mangiavano li Barbetti, ma hora li Barbetti mangiano li lupi."</note> These words being soon after reported to Mr. *Marolles*, the chief commander at that time in *Lucerna*, he threatened him severely, saying he would put him in prison and give him the *strappado* <term>A form of torture where the victim’s hands are tied behind their back and they are hoisted up by a rope, then dropped abruptly to jerk the joints out of place.</term>. This so terrified the poor man that he fell sick and died within a short time after.

Two days after this fight at *La Vaschere*, the enemies, being much enraged by their great loss, spread themselves all over *Angrogna* and began to set the corn on fire. This was noticed by those of the Company of *La Torre*, who were at that time on the top of the Mountain of *Tagliaretto*. They gave speedy notice of it to those of *San Giovanni* and *Angrogna*, who immediately moved towards them and charged them so fiercely that they were forced to flee, leaving the greatest part of their ammunition behind them.

In the meantime, Captain *Belin* assaulted the town of *La Torre*, killed the sentinel and some of the soldiers on the fortifications, and gave the town such a heated alarm that almost all of them fled toward the River *Pelice*. It is truly believed by some who were eyewitnesses of that action that had he then had but a few more men with him, he certainly would have made himself master of *La Torre* that very day.

***

# CHAPTER IV.

## General Observations <note>original: "Animadversions"</note> of some capable and knowledgeable friends of the poor Protestants of the Valleys of Piedmont, regarding the Court of Savoy's grounds and reasons for justifying the Order of Gastaldo. <note>The "Order of Gastaldo," issued in January 1655 by Andrea Gastaldo, commanded the Waldensian Protestants to leave their homes in specific areas within three days or convert to Catholicism, which triggered the subsequent military actions and massacres.</note>

If it were not completely unnecessary—and if we were sure it would not be viewed as a work of mere supererogation <term>performing more work than is required by duty</term>—after such a clear refutation of every important article in the Court of Savoy’s *Factum* <note>original: "Factum" – a legal statement of facts</note> and the listing of so many authentic proofs and testimonies, some of which were signed and supported by significant people from their own side who were eyewitnesses to those horrific cruelties. Furthermore, these proofs were provided by the very people they themselves called as witnesses (being persons of honor and reputation), yet their testimonies clearly contradict everything the Court affirms and confirm everything the Court denies. We say, if we thought it necessary to make any additional observations on the rest of their argument, nothing would be easier in the world than to expose the same falsehoods and evasions in this section as in the previous part of their writings. But we are truly convinced that whoever seriously reads and thoroughly understands the refutation of that first document will never have the patience to even look at the second. By repeating and refuting the same points, we would only be raking up a foul dunghill <note>original: "noyfome Dunghil"</note> that would offend sincere readers. Therefore, all we will add is briefly this:

### II.

Their Popish adversaries hired (as is strongly presumed and generally believed) a company of thieves to rob the poor people of their original writings and legal documents <note>original: "Inſtruments"</note> as they were returning from Cavour <note>original: "Cavors"</note> where the treaty was concluded. Now, those same adversaries demand to know where those documents are. May the poor people not, with a much better case, demand of their adversaries what they have done with them?

### III.

The formal agreements <term>Capitulations</term> made by Henry IV with those of the Valleys in the year 1592—which we have already included, and which were registered in the Parliament of Dauphiné—plainly show that such concessions were granted to the people of the Valleys in the year 1561. Furthermore, these very same concessions are mentioned by a famous writer of their own, named Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a French historian known for his monumental history of his own times</note>, (whom the adversaries themselves cite in their apology for the House of Savoy, printed at Chambéry in 1631). They were permitted to hold sermons and celebrate their assemblies in designated places and within prescribed limits which they were not allowed to cross. **NOTWITHSTANDING THESE LIMITS**, the pastors were permitted to visit and console the sick and perform other duties of their religion, though they could not preach outside those areas. If they should happen to be questioned about their doctrine, they were to be free to answer without penalty to their property or their lives. Furthermore, all those who were away from home because of their religion were permitted to return home, embrace the religion handed down by their ancestors, and attend sermons and assemblies in the permitted manner and places—regardless of any previous promises or renunciations of their religion made before the war. <note>original: "Tandem conventum... # Chapter I: Favor of the Protestants in Piedmont

It has been reported to some among them that they must leave their homes and move elsewhere. Consequently, both as a community and as individuals, they have been subjected to great terrors, anxieties, and troubles. Because we share a common religion with these poor, afflicted people, we have been moved to deep compassion for their miserable condition. We have therefore decided to approach Your Royal Highness with all due respect to urgently intercede on their behalf. 

We do not doubt that you will graciously accept our petition. You have previously been pleased to assure us, in a neighborly manner, of your sincere affection and cooperation; we, for our part, have tried to reciprocate in every possible way with genuine actions whenever the occasion arose. We hope you will allow your subjects, who are our brothers in faith, to feel the gentle benefit of your favor. 

Therefore, we beg Your Royal Highness to look upon these subjects with an eye of compassion and to allow them to remain peacefully in their homes from now on. We ask you to favorably confirm their liberty of belief, especially considering that they have always conducted themselves peacefully and quietly. As all faithful subjects should, and as our Christian religion teaches, they have shown submission and obedience in all matters that do not affect their conscience (which is under the power and government of God alone). For this reason, they are worthy of continued favor. 

In granting this request, which we hope for, Almighty God will surely be pleased and will reward Your Royal Highness in a fatherly way. Likewise, it will bring joy and comfort to your greatly afflicted subjects and move them to pray even more fervently that God, the Governor of the world, will bless Your Royal Highness with all prosperity. We will also welcome this gracious grant with joy and acknowledge it as a special sign of your favor toward us. We shall not fail, to the best of our ability, to return all kinds of friendly and helpful services. In the meantime, heartily wishing Your Royal Highness increasing happiness, we remain,

->Your most affectionate servants, the Mayors <note>original: "Burgmasters"</note>, Chief Magistrates <note>original: "Advoyers" and "Landamans"</note>, and Councils of the confederate Protestant towns of Zurich, Berne, Glaris, Basle, Schaffhouse, and Appenzil.<-

# The Duke of Savoy's Letter to the Protestant Cantons, April 6, 1655.

### Translated from the *French copy*, which was provided to the author by *Mr. Schmidt*, Under-Secretary of State at *Zurich*.

->Magnificent Lords, most dear and special friends, allies, and confederates,<-

*Our subjects of the so-called Reformed Religion <note>original: "pretended Reformed Religion"; a legal term used by Catholic rulers to deny the legitimacy of Protestantism</note> have, for many years, committed an infinite number of excesses and transgressions. These acts were committed against both our orders and the orders of our most serene predecessors—even against the very conditions expressed in the concessions and privileges we granted them. The latest of these riots, occurring on Christmas Day in 1654, has forced us to take notice of such great insolence and to apply a suitable remedy.* 

*Nevertheless, this was done with such mildness and moderation that, instead of punishing them as their crimes and disobedience deserved, we were content only to command them to withdraw into those parts of our dominions where they were permitted to live by the aforementioned orders and concessions. We required them to leave those places where they were not permitted to inhabit. Thus, their punishment consists of no physical pain (though they deserved a heavy one), but simply a new order which we have issued to bring them into strict compliance with the previous edicts they were already bound to follow, even if they had committed no crime.* 

*In truth, they initially obeyed this order, but only for a few days. Soon after, failing to acknowledge the great mercy we had shown them, they returned to their former transgressions and disobedience. Not satisfied with that, they appealed to you under false pretenses to obtain the letter of recommendation you wrote to us on March 13/23 <note>Dual dating was common in this period; the first date follows the Julian calendar (Old Style) and the second follows the Gregorian calendar (New Style)</note>. They acted as if we had intentionally, or of our own accord, begun to trouble and harass them, and as if we had not treated them with the kindness and benevolence we should have.* 

*On the contrary, we were far from having any intention of forcing their consciences as they have claimed (something we never even considered). Our intention was only to require them to observe the orders established by us and our most serene predecessors. Under those terms, we would never have reduced the favors, privileges, and concessions...*

<meta>catchword: concessions,</meta>

<summary>In this letter, the Duke of Savoy defends his order for the Waldensians to relocate, framing it as a lenient response to their "insolence" rather than religious persecution. He accuses the Waldensians of deceiving the Swiss Cantons to gain diplomatic support.</summary>

# Chapter 1: To the Protestant Cantons

*...concessions which have been granted to them. We have been all the more eager to let you understand all these things in detail so that you might better know the high regard we have for your friendship and neighborly relations. We value your recommendations greatly; they would certainly have achieved the result you desired if the circumstances had been of such a nature that they permitted us to grant what you ask. On this occasion, we believe it is our duty to remind you that the disobedience of subjects toward their sovereigns—and the boldness they show in appealing to foreign states under false pretenses to justify that disobedience—is extremely harmful and has very dangerous consequences. Just as during the recent revolt of your own subjects, our horror at their rebellion moved us to deny them any help or favor, whether directly or indirectly; so likewise we hope that your own wisdom will lead you to show us the same loyalty. We trust you will refrain from giving any support or encouragement to people who have no reasonable basis for their vain and insolent defiance.*

*This is what we expect from the good correspondence between us, and from the ancient union and confederacy you have had with us. Our hearty prayers to God are that he would grant you a long and happy life under his blessed and holy protection.*

->From *Turin*, April 6, 1655.<-

->Magnificent Lords, most dear and special friends, allies, and<-
->confederates; your very good friend, ally, and confederate,<-

->The Duke of Savoy, King of Cyprus. <note>The Dukes of Savoy claimed the title "King of Cyprus" through their ancestry, though they did not rule the island.</note><-

->**CHARLES EMMANUEL**<-

---

On April 29th, being the Lord's Day, news of that horrific massacre <note>Known as the "Piedmontese Easter," this was a state-led slaughter of the Waldensian Protestants in the Alpine valleys.</note> was brought to the Council of *Zurich*. They immediately assembled and gave orders for a public day of humiliation <note>A day of fasting and collective repentance to seek God's favor.</note> throughout all their territories. They also ordered a collection of funds for the survivors' relief and shared the sorrowful news of the massacre with their *Protestant* neighbors.

Among others, they sent a letter to the *States General* <note>The governing body of the Dutch Republic.</note> dated April 30th. In it, they represented the tragic condition of these poor people to their *High and Mighty Lordships*, requesting that they consult together to find some way to resolve these affairs.

# The Protestant Cantons of Switzerland's Letter Book IV.

---

# Copy of a Letter from the *Protestant* Cantons of *Switzerland* to the *States General* of the *United Provinces*,

## **April 30, 1655.**

### Communicated to the Author by Mr. *Andrew Schmidt*, Under-Secretary of State at *Zurich*.

---

->Most Illustrious and Most Powerful Lords, our most respected Lords. <note>original: "Illustrissimi & Præpotentes Domini, Domini nostri plurimum observandi."</note><-

Having just now received the sad news concerning the most mournful state of our fellow believers in Piedmont, as you may see from the copy of the letter, etc. <note>original: "Triste jamjam nuntium accipientes de luctuosissimo statu fidei sociorum Pedemontanorum, ut ex copia literarum, &c."</note>

->*Most illustrious, most mighty, and our very much honored Lords,*<-

Having at this moment received sad news concerning the most lamentable state of our brethren of the faith in *Piedmont*, as you may see by the copy of the letter, etc., we thought ourselves obliged by the sacred rights of faith, union, and communion to acquaint your most illustrious and most mighty Lordships with the matter. We are very much assured that you will be pleased, according to your usual piety and Christian charity, to thoroughly consider and lay to heart this <term>affliction of Joseph</term> <note>A biblical reference to Amos 6:6, used here to describe the suffering of fellow believers that others should not ignore.</note>. This persecution is smoothed over with a very fair pretext by the opposing party; but in the meantime, there is no one who loves the Church of Christ who will not easily be convinced of the subtleties and treacheries which the adversaries use on both sides.

Being grieved and moved by a true, heartfelt, and most passionate sympathy, we beseech you again and again, most Mighty and most Illustrious Lords, that you would so favor, consider, and lay to heart the cause of those afflicted ones, that you would be pleased to provide those means which, according to your prudence and power, you shall judge helpful for relieving and saving those miserable and afflicted people. This should be done not only by prayers to the Father of Mercies for them, and by <term>alms</term> <note>Charitable donations or financial relief.</note> which their miseries earnestly cry for, but also by pacifying their Prince toward them, or at least by obtaining for them a liberty of <term>transmigration</term> <note>The right for the persecuted Waldensians to legally emigrate and move to a safer territory.</note>; which we also shall endeavor to do as much as lies in our power. May the sovereign Lord of all things have mercy upon his Church in all places, own their cause, and may his most mighty arm turn away all their miseries and adversities.

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the original page is "To," indicating the start of the address on the following page.</meta>

## CHAPTER II.

### *The Negotiation of Mr. Gabriel Weis, the Deputy of the Protestant <note>original: "Evangelical"</note> Cantons, at the Court of Savoy, on behalf of the poor distressed Protestants in the Valleys of Piedmont.*

On the fifth of May following, they sent Monsieur Gabriel Weis, the Captain General of Bern, in the capacity of their Deputy, with a letter to the Duke of Savoy on behalf of those, his poor afflicted and persecuted subjects.

On the eighteenth day of the same month, Monsieur Weis arrived at Rivoli, where His Royal Highness was then residing with his entire court. Having been granted an audience, he requested in very respectful <note>original: "respective"</note> terms the reinstatement of those who had survived the massacre, the enjoyment of their ancient privileges, the free exercise of their religion, and the release <note>original: "enlargement"</note> of their prisoners. This being done, he delivered the following letter into the hands of the Duke.

<header>Chapter II. In the Court of Savoy.</header>

## A Letter of the Six Protestant Cantons of Switzerland to His Royal Highness of Savoy, dated May 1655. Translated from the High Dutch <note>In this period, "High Dutch" referred to the German language.</note>.

An authentic copy of the true original, signed by Mr. Andrew Schmidt, the Under-Secretary of State of Zurich, is to be seen in the public library of the famous University of Cambridge.

Most Serene Prince and Lord. We offer our most willing service and all due honor to Your Royal Highness: Most Gracious Lord and Ally <note>original German: "Bundsgnoß"</note>. We have received Your Royal Highness's reply to our previous letter with due respect and have understood its contents. We could not, therefore, fail to write to Your Royal Highness regarding our own concerns and especially those of your Protestant <note>original German: "Evangelischer"</note> subjects, etc.

->Most Serene Prince, etc.<-

*We have with due respect received the letter which your Royal Highness was pleased to write to us in answer to ours, and have likewise understood its contents. By this, we consider ourselves obliged—both for our own duty <note>original: "discharge"</note> and the duty of your Royal Highness's subjects who profess the Reformed Religion—to tell you and to beseech your Royal Highness to receive and interpret kindly <note>original: "take and interpret in good part"</note> both our former and this present letter of intercession. Both have proceeded from an honest and good intention. We ask you to firmly believe that we have not been informed or sought out by your Royal Highness's said subjects to intercede on their behalf, but that we have received the news from other sources. The communion of faith and Christian compassion <note>original: "pity"</note>, together with our own natural inclinations, have moved us to intercede for them. As neighbors and allies <note>original: "Confederates"</note>, we have an ancient and singular confidence in your Royal Highness, and we would be very distressed <note>original: "sensible"</note> and much troubled if those poor people were to suffer, having committed no offense or given the least cause. Therefore, as we refuse to believe you would permit such a thing, we once more most earnestly and instantly beseech your Royal Highness to be pleased to continue to show grace to those subjects, honoring the concessions obtained from your predecessors of glorious memory. Thus, they may find, to their great comfort and consolation, the effects of our intercession.*

# A Letter from the Six *Protestant Cantons* of *Switzerland* to His Royal Highness of *Savoy*, May 1655. Translated from German <note>original: "High Dutch"</note>.

## An authentic copy of the true original, signed by Mr. *Andrew Schmidt* <note>original: "Smidt"</note>, the Under-Secretary of State of *Zurich* <note>original: "Zuric"</note>, is kept in the public library of the famous University of *Cambridge*.

Most Serene Prince and Lord. To your Royal Highness, we offer our most willing service with all honor: Most Gracious Lord and Confederate. Your Royal Highness's written response to our previous message has been received with due respect and its contents understood. We could not neglect to write to your Royal Highness for our own sake, and especially for your Evangelical subjects, etc. <note>original German: "Durchleuchtigister Fürst und Herr. Ur. Kon. Durchl. fuegen unser gantz gutwillige Dienst mit erbietung aller Ehren Zuvor : Gnedigister Herr und Bundsgnoss. Ihr. Kon. Durchl. Antwort Schreiben, uber was Unserige habend wie mit gebuhrenden Respect empfangen und inhaltlich verstanden, mochtens hieruber nicht unterlassen, Ur. Kon. Durchl. zu unserer und sonderlich deroselben Evangelischer Unterthanen, &c."</note>

->Most Serene Prince, etc.<-

*WE have received with due respect the letter which your Royal Highness was pleased to write to us in answer to our own, and we have likewise understood its contents. Because of this, we feel obliged—both for our own sake and for the sake of your Royal Highness's subjects who profess the Reformed Religion <note>the Protestant faith</note>—to ask your Royal Highness to kindly and favorably interpret both our former letter and this present letter of intercession <note>a plea or prayer on behalf of another</note>. Both have proceeded from an honest and good intention. We ask you to firmly believe that we have not been prompted or requested by your subjects to plead on their behalf. Rather, we received the news of their condition from other sources. Our shared faith and Christian compassion, together with our own natural inclinations, have moved us to intercede for them. As neighbors and allies <note>original: "Confederates"</note>, we have an ancient and unique confidence in your Royal Highness. We would be deeply affected and troubled if those poor people were to suffer, having committed no offense nor given the slightest cause for such treatment. Therefore, as we do not believe you would permit this to happen, we once more most earnestly and urgently beg your Royal Highness to be pleased to graciously continue the concessions <note>legal grants or privileges</note> obtained from your predecessors of glorious memory. By doing so, they may find great comfort and relief through the effects of our intercession.*

<page-num>548</page-num>
<header>Mr. Gabriel Weis’s Negotiations, Book IV.</header>

<margin>The answer of Madame Royale to Mr. Weis.</margin>
The answer which the Duke of Savoy (or rather Madame Royale, his mother <note>Madame Royale refers to Christine of France, the Duchess-regent and mother of Duke Charles Emmanuel II.</note>) gave to this letter, and to the message that *Major Weis* had delivered in person, was essentially this: *That although they were not obliged to give an account of their actions to any prince in the world, nevertheless, out of the respect they held for the friendship they had established with his masters, the Swiss Cantons, they had ordered the Marquess of Pianezza to inform him of the truth regarding all those affairs.*

Not long after, the same *Major Weis* spoke with the *Marquess of Pianezza*, who gave him a long narrative. In this speech, the Marquess endeavored to justify all his proceedings and everything done by the forces under his command. He attempted to place the entire burden and blame on the poor people <note>The Waldensian victims.</note>, protesting again and again *that he never had the slightest intention to impose upon their consciences or their religion, and that whatever reports had been spread abroad in the world concerning a massacre and strange cruelties exercised against them were mere fabrications and had no basis in truth.*

<margin>Discussion between the Marquess of Pianezza and Mr. Weis.</margin>
To this, *Major Weis* replied, *First, that as for the massacre, it was a thing so publicly known and evident that it could not possibly be concealed or denied. Secondly, as for the poor people’s right to live in the places in question, he believed it was founded on justice and equity; for it was not only granted to them in the concessions of Charles Emmanuel, the late Duke of Savoy, but also purchased from his Royal Highness for six thousand ducatoons <term>large silver coins used in Europe at the time</term>, which they had actually paid for that very reason.*

The *Marquess* told him that he did not deny their *legal documents* and *authentic records*, but argued that they were all *conditional*. For example, he claimed that the *Catholic religion* should have been freely practiced in all those places, which the inhabitants would never permit. In short, he argued that their continuous residence in the contested areas for ninety years could truly be called nothing other than a ninety-year rebellion and disobedience.

Mr. *Weis* continued to press him regarding the sad and miserable condition of those who had escaped the massacre, and the necessity of finding some way to reach a settlement, both regarding the release of prisoners and the restoration of everyone to future peace and quietness. The *Marquess* advised him to negotiate with the poor people and persuade them to stop their hostile acts, assuring him that they would find his *Royal Highness* disposed to accept all proposals of that nature.

*Monsieur Weis* accepted this offer and, for that purpose, traveled into the Valley of *Perosa*, which is within the dominions of the *King* of *France*.

Here, it should be observed that at this time—by the miraculous providence of God and His blessing upon the poor people's efforts to preserve the remnant of their wives and little ones—they had turned to face the enemy. They began to contest the matter with such successful results that their enemies began to fear where this business might lead, and what effects—

<meta>The catchword "fects" connects to the first word of the next page, "effects."</meta>

<summary>Major Weis confronts the Marquess of Pianezza over the Waldensian massacre, refuting the Marquess's claims of innocence by citing legal land rights and the public evidence of the atrocities. The Marquess characterizes the Waldensians' 90-year residency as a rebellion, but eventually suggests Weis negotiate a peace directly with the survivors who have begun to successfully fight back.</summary>

<header>Chapter II. In the Court of Savoy.</header>

[ef]fects it might produce. And therefore the **Marquess** had no better move to make than to get their swords out of their hands by such a strategy as this.

Upon **Mr. Weis’s** arrival at the place mentioned before, he proposed to the poor people <note>The "poor people" refers to the Waldensian Protestant refugees who survived the initial massacres.</note> what the **Marquess** had advised him (though for a more honest purpose than the **Marquess** intended it). But the poor people, having learned by long and woeful experience the **Marquess’s** schemes, gave him this answer: *That in case the Six Evangelical Cantons <note>The Protestant member states of the Swiss Confederacy.</note> would give their word that the proposed treaty would be carried out on honorable terms and, for that purpose, would advise them to a ceasefire, they were most ready to listen to it (as they returned most hearty thanks for what the Cantons had already done on their behalf). Otherwise, they were resolved never to trust those who had so often deceived and betrayed them, and whose principle was not to keep faith with those whom they consider heretics.* <note>The Protestant victims were referencing the contemporary belief that Catholic authorities were not religiously bound to honor promises or treaties made with "heretics."</note>

At this, **Mr. Weis**, having no instructions to enter into a treaty nor to give a categorical <note>original: "Categorick"</note> answer to the poor people’s demands, returned to the **Marquess of Pianezza** to obtain, if possible, the release of the prisoners, or at least permission to visit and speak with them. But since both requests were refused, he requested his second audience, which was granted on May 24th. He then returned home to his superiors with the following letter, which the **Duke of Savoy** sent with him in answer to theirs of May 6/16, 1655.

# The Duke of Savoy's Letter to the Protestant Cantons of Switzerland, May 23 / June 3, in answer to theirs of May 6 / 16, 1655.

## Translated from the French copy, which was shared with the author by Mr. Andrew Schmidt, Under-Secretary of State at Zurich.

<note>original French: "Magnifiques Seigneurs, Treschers & speciaux Amis Alliés & Confederés. Encore que les Princes ne foyent pas accoutumés de donner Compte des resolutions qu’ils prennent à l’egard de leurs Subjects, qu’à Dieu seul, toutesfois l’estime que nous faisons de vostre amitié nous à conviés à faire representer au Sr. Gabriel Weis, &c."</note>
Magnificent Lords, most dear and special Friends, Allies, and Confederates: 

Although Princes are not accustomed to give an account of the decisions they make regarding their subjects to anyone but God alone, nevertheless the high regard we have for your friendship has invited us to represent to Mr. Gabriel Weis, etc.

->*Magnificent Lords, most dear and special Friends, Allies, and Confederates.*<-

*Although it is not the custom for Princes to give an account of the decisions they make concerning their subjects to anyone but God alone, nevertheless the esteem we have for your friendship has invited us to present to Mr. Gabriel Weis—through a sincere and true account—the grounds for our proceedings against our subjects in the Valleys of Luserna, San Martino, and Perosa <note>These three valleys were the traditional home of the Waldensian (Vaudois) Protestants in the Piedmont region.</note>. We have also shown him the falsehoods with which they tried to cover their long-standing rebellion (which we have endured for a long time) under the cloak of religion, and the moderation we have shown toward them by inflicting only a fraction of the punishment they so justly deserved.*

*And although your deputy arrived at a time when they allowed themselves to be carried away by such strange and foolish <note>original: "sottish"</note> obstinacy and blindness, and consequently at a time when we were least obliged to listen to anything in their favor or on their behalf, yet we have assured him (in order to demonstrate how much influence your mediation has with us) that we would be inclined to listen to terms of moderation. These would show signs of our piety and mercy even toward those people who have least deserved it, provided that this in no way infringes upon or lessens our authority and the obedience and service due to us. Furthermore, justice—and the necessity of making an example of them—must retain the portion required by the rules of good government. However, since your deputy Mr. Weis appeared unwilling to involve himself in that affair, preferring instead to leave it...*

<summary>In this letter, the Duke of Savoy defends his violent suppression of the Waldensians to the Swiss Protestant Cantons, framing the massacre as a "moderate" response to "rebellion" and "falsehoods." He claims he is only willing to show mercy out of respect for the Swiss, provided his absolute authority is maintained.</summary>

...leaving it to be decided by others. We told him that we could not consent to negotiate with our rebellious subjects while they continued to act rebelliously and abuse our obedient subjects. We also stated that if they truly had any such intentions to negotiate, they ought first to put a stop to those acts of violence and aggression. We have always given good and sufficient proof of the high regard we have for your friendship and affection toward us by expressing reciprocal affection toward you on all occasions. So we pray that Almighty God will keep you under His protection.

->Most Magnificent [Lords], etc.<-

From Rivoli, June 3, 1655.

->*Your good Friend and Confederate,*<-
->*The Duke of Savoy, King of*<-
->*Cyprus.*<-

->CHARLES EMMANUEL<- <note>Charles Emmanuel II (1634–1675), Duke of Savoy, who oversaw the "Piedmontese Easter" massacre of the Waldensians in 1655.</note>

## CHAPTER III.

### The several passionate <note>original: "pathetick," meaning full of deep emotion or passion</note> *Letters* of his *Highness* the Lord PROTECTOR of the *Commonwealth* of *England*, etc., to his *Protestant* *Neighbors*, in favor of the poor distressed *Protestants* in the *Valleys* of *Piedmont*.

Mr. Weis, upon his return home, gave an account of his entire negotiation to his superiors whose deputy he was. Seeing that their intercession had no better results, they were discouraged from proceeding any further in the business, resolving instead to wait and see what would be done by other princes and states. The plain truth is that this affair would likely have been forgotten and come to nothing, had it not been awakened in a most lively and vigorous manner by his Highness the Lord Protector of England. As soon as the news was brought to him, he was so deeply affected by the poor people's calamities that he was often heard to say, *that it lay as near, or rather nearer, his heart than if it had concerned his nearest and dearest relations in the world.* Indeed, the effects of his charity and Christian compassion were not at all inferior to those zealous, earnest, and passionate expressions.

The first letters of advice brought to his Highness the Lord PROTECTOR of *England*, etc., regarding this business arrived in the month of *May* in the year 1655. At that time, he did not only seriously invite the good people of the nation to seek the Lord through prayer and humiliation <note>A religious practice involving fasting and penance to seek divine favor or mercy.</note> regarding their sad condition, but he also urged them by his own example and by a public declaration to provide a free and liberal contribution toward their rescue and support (as shall be specified in more detail later). Furthermore, he awakened all his Protestant neighbors who professed the same faith and religion as himself to join him in this work. # A Letter of His Highness the Lord Protector of England, etc., To the King of Sweden, on behalf of the poor Evangelical Churches in the Valleys of Piedmont.

## An authentic copy of the true original, which was shared with the author by the Right Honorable Mr. Secretary Thurloe. <note>John Thurloe (1616–1668) was the Secretary of State to the Protectorate and a key figure in Cromwell's intelligence and foreign policy network.</note>

->Most Serene King,<-

We are fully persuaded that the report of that most cruel decree has recently reached your kingdom, by which the Duke of Savoy has completely ruined his subjects in the Alps who profess the Reformed Religion. He ordered that they should be driven from their ancestral homes unless, within twenty days, they renounced their own faith and embraced Roman Catholicism. Because of this, many have been killed, while the rest have been robbed and left to face certain destruction. No one is unaware that the Kings of Sweden, your royal ancestors, have always joined their cause with those of the Reformed faith, even bringing their armies into Germany to defend the Protestant religion without distinction. It has reached our knowledge, and we did not wish to hide from Your Majesty how much grief we feel on their account. We have informed our other friends and allies of the same religion of this as well. We have already written our letters to the Duke of Savoy <note>original: *Sabaudiae Ducem*</note> with as much urgency as possible on behalf of these miserable people. We do not doubt that Your Majesty—out of your own hatred for such inhuman and barbarian cruelty, and your well-known devotion to religion—has already intervened with your authority, or will do so as soon as possible. We trust you will deal with the Duke of Savoy so that he might revoke that most cruel edict and command that the survivors of those most wretched men, whom sword and fire <note>original: *ferrum atque flamma*</note> have not yet consumed, may return to their homes and whatever remains of their property. Indeed, if there is any bond, any charity, or any communion of religion to be believed in and cherished, then such a great multitude of our most innocent brothers—a part of the body of Christ—cannot suffer these atrocities without the whole body suffering as well, feeling the same pain. We believe it is unnecessary to remind Your Majesty where these savage beginnings originate, what they aim at, or what they threaten us all with; your own wisdom and piety will naturally lead you to those plans which will be most suited to comforting and relieving these poor and calamitous people as soon as possible. We have written this not for the sake of advising Your Majesty, but so that you might understand how heavily we take the evils they endure, and how ready we are to share those plans with you which best pertain to their help and comfort, and to the sustaining and strengthening of the Protestant cause throughout the whole world. Meanwhile, we heartily commend Your Majesty to God, the Greatest and Best. Given from our Court at Westminster, May 25, 1655.

->*Your Majesty’s good Friend,*<-
->*OLIVER P.*<-

We have already written our letters in the most effective manner we could to the Duke of Savoy on behalf of these poor innocent men. And we do not doubt but your Majesty, detesting such inhuman and barbarous massacres, and out of your known zeal and love for religion, has already, or will also interpose your mediation, and apply yourself to the Duke of Savoy, for the revoking of that cruel edict, and for recalling back to their habitation and estates that small remainder of those poor men who are yet left unslaughtered <note>original: "unbutchered"</note>. # A Letter from his Highness the Lord Protector of England, to the King of Denmark, in favor of the poor Evangelical Churches of the Valleys of Piedmont, dated May 25, 1655.

## An authentic copy of the true original, which was communicated to the author by the Right Honourable Mr. Secretary Thurloe. <note>John Thurloe (1616–1668) was the Secretary of State to the Protectorate and headed the postal and intelligence networks.</note>

***

->*Most Serene King,*<-

| [English Column] | [Latin Column] |
| :--- | :--- |
| We suppose your Majesty has heard by now, by what a severe and merciless edict Emmanuel, Duke of Savoy, has—for the cause of religion—driven from their native country those subjects of his who inhabited the valleys of the Alps. These were harmless men who for many ages have been famous for holding to a purer religion. After very many were slain, he has exposed the rest, destitute and naked, to all kinds of hardships and miseries in desolate places. We believe you have consequently been affected with sorrow, as is fitting for such a great defender and prince of the Reformed faith <note>original: "Profession"</note>. For indeed, according to the rules of the Christian religion, if any number of our brothers suffer calamities and miseries, we all ought to be touched with the same feeling for them. Truly, if we are rightly informed of your piety and prudence, no one understands better than Your Majesty what danger the outcome and example of this act portends <term>portends</term><note>portends: serves as a warning of a momentous or calamitous event likely to happen</note> for the whole Protestant cause. # A Letter of His Highness the Lord Protector of England, etc.
## To the High and Mighty Lords, the States General of the United Provinces, in favor of the poor Protestants of the Valleys of Piedmont.

->An authentic copy of the true original, which was shared with the author by the Right Honorable Mr. Secretary Thurloe.<- 
<note>Secretary John Thurloe was Oliver Cromwell’s head of intelligence and managed his foreign correspondence.</note>

->High and Mighty Lords,<-

We assume that by this time, through various reports and messages from neighboring regions, you have heard of the late edict of the Duke of Savoy <note>Charles Emmanuel II</note> against his subjects dwelling in the valleys of Lucerna, Angrogna, and other places of his dominion. These people have been ancient professors of the Orthodox religion <note>the Waldensians, a proto-Protestant group whose origins date back to the 12th century</note>. By this edict, they were enjoined to quit their habitations, stripped and turned out of everything, unless they would embrace the Roman Catholic religion within twenty days. 

We have also heard with what rigor they have proceeded, by virtue of that edict, against men who are both innocent and helpless, and (which most nearly touches us) those who are our brothers in Christ. Very many of them have been slain by a party of soldiers sent against them; the rest have been plundered and driven out of their houses, so that they are forced, with their wives and children, to wander about in desolate mountains, exposed to the miseries of continual hunger and cold. Now, what trouble of mind and sense of—

<column-break/>

->High and Mighty Lords,<- 
<note>original: *Celsi ac præpotentes Domini*</note>

We believe that you have already learned—from rumors and frequent letters and messages from all surrounding places—of the very recent edict of the Duke of Savoy <note>original: *Ducis Subaudiæ*</note> against the inhabitants subject to him in Lucerna, Angrogna, and other valleys and places of his jurisdiction, who have anciently professed the Orthodox religion. By this edict, unless they embrace the Roman faith within twenty days, they are ordered to leave their ancestral homes, stripped of all their fortunes. 

We believe you also know with what great cruelty the authority of that edict has been carried out against innocent and needy men, and (which is most important) our brothers in Christ. Many were killed by a part of the army sent against them, and the rest were plundered and expelled from their homes. Consequently, they have long been forced to struggle with hunger and cold among the harshest mountains and perpetual snows, along with their wives and children. With what deep emotion of mind, with what sense of fraternal—
<note>The Latin text ends here with "fraterna," matching the English "sense of [fraternal...]"</note>

...how much these calamities have affected you, we can easily understand from our own grief, which is certainly most heavy <note>original: "gravissimus"</note>. For since we are joined by the same bond of Religion, why shouldn't we be moved by the same feelings in so heavy and shameful <note>original: "indigna"</note> a calamity of our brothers? And your piety toward the orthodox <note>Protestant believers</note>, wherever they are scattered and oppressed, has been proven and often recognized in many of the Church's difficulties and adversities. We certainly would rather be surpassed in anything else than in zeal and charity toward our brothers who are violated and afflicted for the sake of religion; indeed, we would gladly prefer the health and peace of the Churches even over our own safety.

Therefore, we have written to the Duke of Savoy <note>original: "Sabaudiæ Ducem"</note>, greatly requesting that he take up a more peaceful mind and will toward these most innocent men, who are both his subjects and his petitioners <note>original: "supplices"</note>. We have asked that he restore their homes and fortunes to these miserable people and also grant them their former freedom in religion. We have also written to the most serene King of the French <note>original: "serenissimum Gallorum Regem"; this refers to Louis XIV</note>, so that he might be willing to intercede with the Duke of Savoy on their behalf. 

Furthermore, just as we have written to you yourselves, we have also written to other Protestant princes and magistrates to whom we judged this most closely pertains, so that they might wish to join their efforts with ours in pleading with the Duke of Savoy. For if this dangerous example turns out well for its authors, there is no need to remind your wisdom how much religion is brought into danger. And if he should allow himself to be swayed and moved by our collective prayers, we will receive a noble and rich fruit from the labor we have undertaken...
</column>

...how much the calamity of our brethren has affected you, we can easily gather from our own sad apprehension. For, seeing that we are united by the same bond of Religion, it cannot be otherwise than that we must be moved with the same feelings in so heavy an oppression of our brethren. Your Lordships, for your part, have given ample testimony of your piety toward the professors of the true Reformed Religion, wherever they are scattered and oppressed in the most difficult and adverse times of the Church. 

And we, for our part, would rather be found to fall short in anything else than in our zeal and affection toward our brethren who suffer for the cause of religion, being ready to prefer the peace and prosperity of the Churches before our own ease and safety. For this cause, we have written to the Duke of Savoy <note>Charles Emmanuel II</note>, entreating him to bear a more favorable mind and inclination toward those innocent men, his petitioners and subjects, and that he would restore to them their houses and estates and grant them their ancient liberty in religion. 

We have also written to the King of France to mediate with the said Duke on their behalf; and we have likewise written both to yourselves and to other princes and states of the Protestant religion, whom we believe this case principally concerns, so that they might join their endeavors with ours in this intercession. For if an example of such evil consequence should take effect according to the intentions of those who devised it, we do not need to instruct your wisdom as to what danger religion will be reduced to thereby. And if the Duke can be persuaded and prevailed upon by our joint entreaties, it will be a good and satisfactory reward for the labor and...

# A Letter of His Highness the Lord Protector of *England*, etc. To the Cantons of the *Swiss* professing the *Reformed Religion*, in favor of the poor *Protestants* of the Valleys of *Piedmont*.

### An Authentic Copy of the true Original of which was communicated to the Author by the Right Honorable Mr. Secretary *Thurloe* <note>John Thurloe (1616–1668) was the postmaster general and head of intelligence for Oliver Cromwell.</note>.

->*Most Illustrious Lords,*<-
<note>original Latin: "Illustrissimi Domini"</note>

We do not doubt that the recent calamity of those Alpine people who profess our religion has reached your ears somewhat sooner than ours. Although they were under the loyalty and jurisdiction of the Duke of Savoy, they were commanded by an edict of their prince to leave their ancestral homes unless, within three days, they gave assurance that they would embrace the Roman Catholic religion. Soon after, they were attacked by force of arms and driven into exile by the army of their Duke, with very many also having been killed. Now, without a home, without a roof, naked, plundered, afflicted, and dying of hunger and cold, they wander most miserably through deserted mountains and snow with their wives and children. There is much less reason for us to doubt that these things, as soon as they were reported to you, affected you with a sense of such great miseries equal to our own—and perhaps even more severe pain because you are closer to their borders. For we are abundantly aware of your particularly excellent zeal for the orthodox faith <note>original Latin: "orthodoxæ fidei"</note>, and your great constancy in retaining it, as well as your courage in defending it. As we do not doubt that the late calamity of those people in the Alps, who are of the same religious profession as ourselves, has come to your knowledge sooner than to ours. These people, being under the dominion of the Duke of Savoy, were required by an edict of his to forsake their native country unless they would, within three days, give assurance of their embracing the Roman Catholic religion. Soon after, they were attacked by force of arms; many were slain, and others driven into banishment. They now miserably wander with their wives and children over desert and snowy mountains without house or shelter, in want and nakedness, ready to die of cold and hunger. So we have far less cause to doubt that you, as soon as the report of these things reached your ears, were affected with the same sense of such great calamity that we are; and perhaps with an even more sorrowful apprehension of their misery because you are closer to them than we are. For we know very well your singular zeal for the orthodox faith <note>In this context, "orthodox faith" refers specifically to the Reformed Protestant faith, which the Waldensians and the Swiss Cantons shared.</note>, together with your great constancy in maintaining it and your fortitude in defending its profession. <header>The Lord Protector's Letter, etc. Book IV.</header>

<columns>
<column>
...through the most intimate communion of religion, you, together with us, are brothers—or rather one body—with these afflicted men. Of this body, no member can suffer without the rest of the fellow-members feeling the pain, harm, and danger. We thought it right to write to you and to indicate how much we judge it the concern of us all to help and comfort our exiled and heartbroken <note>original: "disconsolate"</note> brothers by such means as shall be thought proper and convenient. In doing so, we provide not only for the removal of their present evils, but also prevent their further growth, or any danger which may happen to us all by the precedent <note>original: "example"</note> and consequence of this action.

Therefore, we have written letters to the Duke of Savoy, in which we have pleaded with him that, out of his mercy <note>original: "clemency"</note>, he would deal more gently with his faithful subjects and restore them (as they are now almost destroyed) to their estates and native lands. We hope that he will be persuaded <note>original: "intreated"</note> by our pleas, or rather by the joint pleas of us all, and that he will readily grant what we so earnestly desire. 

But if he appears otherwise minded, we are ready to consult with you about such means as may best lead to the relief <note>original: "redress"</note> of these poor innocent men, and our dear brothers in Christ, who groan under so many injuries and oppressions. We must preserve them from a most certain and groundless <note>original: "causless"</note> destruction; we are confident that their safety and preservation, in accordance with your usual piety, lies very near to your hearts. Given at our Palace at Westminster, the 25th of May, 1655.

->Your Lordship's good friend,<-
->OLIVER P.<- <note>The "P." stands for *Protector*, Cromwell's title as head of state.</note>
</column>

<column-break/>

<note>This column is a translation of the original Latin text.</note>

Therefore, through the closest shared faith <note>original Latin: "Religionis arctissima communione"</note>, you are brothers—or rather one body—with these miserable people, just as we are. No member of this body can be afflicted without a sense of pain, loss, and danger to the rest. We have decided that we must write to you about this matter to show how much we believe it concerns us all to help and comfort our exiled and destitute brothers through common aid, and by whatever means are found most convenient and suitable. We must look ahead in time, not only to remove their current evils and miseries, but also to ensure that the evil does not spread further, and that no danger is created for all of us by this example and its outcome.

We have indeed written letters to the Duke of Savoy, in which we have earnestly requested that, in his mercy, he act more gently with his most faithful subjects and restore those who are now nearly ruined to their homes and property. We hope that this Most Serene Prince will be moved by our prayers—or rather the combined prayers of all of us—and will easily grant what we have so greatly asked of him. 

However, if his mind is set otherwise, we are prepared to share counsel with you as to how we might best support and lift up these innocent men, so oppressed by injuries and harassed, who are our beloved brothers in Christ, and preserve them from a most certain and undeserved death. I trust that their safety and well-being are of the greatest concern to you, in keeping with your piety. Given from our Court at Westminster, the 25th day of May, in the year 1655.

->*Your Illustrious Lordships'*<-
->*good friend,*<-
->OLIVER P.<-
</column>
</columns>

<summary>In this concluding portion of his letter to the Swiss Cantons, Oliver Cromwell emphasizes the shared religious bond between all Protestants and urges a collective diplomatic response to save the persecuted Waldensians. He requests that if the Duke of Savoy refuses to show mercy, the Protestant powers must consult on further actions to prevent the total destruction of their "brethren in Christ."</summary>
