# CHAPTER IV.

## Mr. Morland’s *negotiation* as *His Highness's envoy* to the *King of France* and the *Duke of Savoy* in the year 1655.

On the twenty-third of May in the year 1655, Samuel Morland, Esq., received orders to prepare himself to carry a message from His Highness <note>Oliver Cromwell, the Lord Protector of England.</note> to the Duke of Savoy. His mission was to plead with the Duke to revoke that merciless edict or order issued by Gastaldo <note>original: "Gastaldo" — referring to Andrea Gastaldo, the auditor in the Duchy of Savoy who issued the decree that triggered the massacre by ordering the Protestant Vaudois to leave their homes or convert to Catholicism.</note> and to restore the survivors of his poor, distressed subjects to their ancient liberties and homes. Additionally, he was to deliver a letter on his way from His Highness to the King of France, to urge His Majesty to use his power and influence with the Duke for the same purpose.

In obedience to this command, Mr. Morland set out from London on the twenty-sixth of May, 1655. On the first of June, he arrived at La Fère, where the King and the Court of France were then residing. Immediately upon his arrival, and according to his instructions, he delivered the following letter from His Highness the Lord Protector to the King of France.

->**Translation of a Letter from His Highness the Lord Protector of England, etc., to the King of France in favor of the poor distressed Protestants in the Valleys of Piedmont.**<-

->**An authentic copy of the true original, which was communicated to the author by the Right Honorable Mr. Secretary Thurloe.** <note>John Thurloe (1616–1668) was the Secretary of State to the Protectorate and famously served as Oliver Cromwell’s spymaster.</note><-

<columns>2</columns>

->**Most Serene King,**<-

The sorrowful complaints which have been brought to us from those poor, distressed people who live in and profess the Reformed Religion in Luserna, Angrogna, and other valleys within the territories of the Duke of Savoy—who have recently been most cruelly massacred—as well as the frequent sad news we have received concerning the plundering and exile of others, have prompted us to write these letters to Your Majesty. This is especially true since we have also been informed (though how truthfully we do not yet know) that this massacre was carried out partly by some of your troops who had joined with other forces belonging to the Duke of Savoy. 

However, we have been very reluctant to believe these things, as they cannot be thought consistent with the goals and actions of either good princes or Your Majesty’s most prudent ancestors. They believed it to be primarily in their own interest, and also greatly conducive to the peace of their kingdom and of all Christendom, that their subjects professing that religion should be permitted to live in...

<column-break/>

->**Most Serene King,**<- <note>original: "Serenissime Rex"</note>

The groans of the most miserable men inhabiting Luserna, Angrogna, and also other valleys in the dominion of the Duke of Savoy, and professing the Reformed Religion—whose most bloody murders have lately occurred, and concerning the plundering and exile of the rest, very sad messages have frequently arrived—have drawn these letters from us to Your Majesty. This is especially so since it has also been reported to us (though how truthfully we have not yet sufficiently learned) that this slaughter was committed in part by some of your cohorts <note>original: "cohortibus," referring to military units or troops.</note> which had joined themselves with other forces of the Duke of Savoy <note>original: "Allobrogum Ducis" — Allobroges was the Latin name for the ancient people of the Savoy region.</note>. 

This, however, we would not rashly believe, since it seems consistent neither with the customs of good princes nor the most prudent ancestors of Your Majesty, who judged it to be primarily in their own interest, and to lead as much as possible to the peace of their own kingdom and of the entire Christian world, that they should allow their subjects practicing that religion to remain unharmed and safe under their rule and protection; which clemency... <note>original: "qua illi clementia" — the text continues on the next page.</note>

<columns>2</columns>

...moved by the kindness of their Kings, they have often performed excellent service for their Sovereigns in both peace and war. This same logic persuaded the Dukes of Savoy <note>original: *Allobrogum*, referring to the ancient inhabitants of the Savoy region</note> to treat the inhabitants of the Alpine Valleys subject to them with the same kindness; these people, in turn, were most ready to obey their Prince and never spared their own lives or fortunes. We have no doubt that Your Majesty has such a close relationship and authority with the Duke of Savoy that, through your intercession and expression of goodwill, peace, the right to return home, and their former liberty may be very easily obtained for these miserable people. This action will be worthy of Your Majesty and consistent with the wisdom and example of your most serene ancestors. It will not only greatly reassure your own subjects that they need never fear such treatment, but it will also bind your confederates and allies who follow the same religion to Your Majesty with even greater respect and goodwill. As for us, whatever favor is granted in this matter—whether to your own subjects or obtained through your influence for the subjects of others—will be no less pleasing to us; indeed, it will be more truly welcome and valued than any other profit or advantage we expect from Your Majesty’s friendship. Given from our Court at Westminster, 25 May 1655. <note>original: *Dab. ex Aula nostra Westmonasterii*</note>

->OLIVER, Protector<- <note>original: *OLIVER. P.*</note>

<column-break/>

...safe and free from injury under their government and protection. Being obliged by this mercy of their Kings, they have often performed eminent service for their Sovereigns in both peace and war. For the same reason, the Dukes of Savoy have also been induced to treat their subjects who inhabit the Alpine Valleys with the same favor; these people, being ready to serve their Prince whenever needed, have never spared their lives or fortunes. Now, we do not doubt that Your Majesty has such influence and authority with the Duke of Savoy that, by your intercession and the expression of your goodwill, peace may be very easily secured for those poor people, along with a return to their native country and their former liberty. Performing this would be an action worthy of Your Majesty and in keeping with the wisdom and example of your most serene predecessors. It would not only reassure the minds of your subjects so they need not fear similar harm in the future, but it would also engage your confederates and allies who profess the same religion with much greater respect and affection for Your Majesty. As for us, whatever favor is granted in this regard—either to your own subjects or obtained through your efforts for the subjects of others—it shall be no less acceptable to us. Indeed, it will be more acceptable and valuable than any other profit and advantage among the many we anticipate from Your Majesty's friendship. Given at our Palace at Westminster, 25 May 1655.

->OLIVER, Protector<-

<summary>In this concluding portion of his letter to Louis XIV, Oliver Cromwell argues that protecting religious minorities is a tradition of wise rulers and urges the French King to mediate a peace for the persecuted Waldensians in Savoy. He emphasizes that such an act of mercy would strengthen international alliances and ensure the loyalty of Protestant subjects across Europe.</summary>

About three days after his arrival at La Fère, Mr. Morland received the King’s answer to His Highness’s <note>Referring to Oliver Cromwell, the Lord Protector of England</note> letter regarding the affairs of the Valleys, as follows:

### The King of France to His Highness the Lord Protector, in answer to his letter of May 25, 1655.

->An authentic copy of the original was shared with the author by the Right Honorable Mr. Secretary Thurloe.<-

Lord Protector,

<note>original French: *Dès que je fus averti que le Duc de Savoie avait pris l’occasion du passage des troupes que j’envoyais en Italie pour assister le Duc de Modène dans l’invasion, etc.* — "As soon as I was informed that the Duke of Savoy had taken the opportunity of the passage of the troops I was sending to Italy to assist the Duke of Modena in the invasion, etc."</note>

Lord Protector,

Since I was informed <note>original: "advertised"</note> that the Duke of Savoy had used the passage of the troops I sent into Italy (to assist the Duke of Modena against the Spanish invasion of his country) as an opportunity to punish—as he has since informed me—the rebellion and disobedience of some of his subjects who practice the Protestant <note>original: "pretended Reformed"</note> Religion; and since those people had requested that I permit them to take shelter <note>original: "put themselves under covert"</note> from that persecution, which they say was carried out against them out of hatred for their religion, I immediately took action. 

As a testimony that I in no way approved of the conduct or course taken in employing my forces for a business of this nature without my command (even though it was done under the pretext of housing them in the Valley of Luserna), I immediately dispatched several of my officers to the Duke of Savoy to put a stop to the punishment or ill-treatment that was said to be continuing against those who still remained in his country. I also sent word to the Duke of Lesdiguières, Governor of my province of Dauphiné, to gather the refugees together and, by treating them kindly, to give them a sense of the benefits of my protection. 

And now that I have been informed by your letter, dated the twenty-fifth of last month, that you are moved by the calamity of these poor people, I am very glad that I have already anticipated <note>original: "prevented"</note> your request. I shall continue my urgent requests <note>original: "instances"</note> with that Prince for their relief and comfort, and to ensure that he would consent to their resettlement in their dwellings in the respective...

*...places of his dominions, which they enjoyed by concessions from the Dukes of Savoy, his predecessors. Indeed, I have gone so far as to even be answerable for their faithfulness and obedience in such a way that I have reason to hope that my mediation will not be fruitless <note>original: "unprofitable"</note>. I also have cause to applaud their faithfulness and zeal for my service, as they, for their part, never miss an occasion to give me proof of it, even beyond all that can be imagined, and contribute in all things to the welfare and success of my affairs. This is all I can say in answer to your letter. However, I shall not conclude without requesting you to be assured that, on all occasions, you shall find the high esteem I have for your person. From the bottom of my heart, I pray to the Divine Majesty that he would keep you in his holy and divine protection.*

->LOUIS.<-

->And signed below by D'Aumenie.<-

Mr. *Morland*, having received this letter from His Majesty and finished the business for which he was sent to that court, continued his journey toward *Savoy*. On the twenty-first of *June*, he arrived at *Rivoli* <note>original: "Rivole"</note>, which is about eight or ten miles on this side of *Turin*, where the Duke was then staying with *Madame Royale* <note>Christine Marie of France, the Duchess and mother of the Duke</note> and the entire court.

Upon his arrival at *Rivoli*, he requested an audience with His Royal Highness, according to his orders, in his capacity as the Lord Protector's envoy. The Duke accepted and directed him to travel to *Turin*, where he would be met by the Master of Ceremonies and conducted within a day or two back to *Rivoli* for his audience. Following these instructions, Mr. *Morland* went on to *Turin*. A few hours after he arrived there, the Master of Ceremonies came to his lodgings and, after a very civil greeting in the name of the Duke, his master, conducted him to specific lodgings appointed for him by the Duke’s special order. There he was very nobly entertained. About two days later, the Master of Ceremonies accompanied him in the Duke’s own coach to *Rivoli*, where he had his audience and spoke to the Duke in the presence of *Madame Royale*, his mother, in the following terms:

## Copy of Mr. Morland’s Speech to the Duke of Savoy, at his first Audience, in the role of *Envoy* from His Highness the Lord Protector of England, on behalf of the poor distressed Protestants in the Valleys of Piedmont <note>The Waldensians, or Vaudois, who were facing violent persecution.</note>.

->May it please your most Serene and Royal Highness,<-

I am sent by the most serene Prince *Oliver*, Lord Protector of the *Commonwealth* <note>The English government from 1649–1660, following the execution of King Charles I.</note> of *England*, *Scotland*, and *Ireland*, to your Royal Highness. He heartily salutes you and, with a very high and singular affection toward the person of your Serene Highness, wishes you life, a long reign, and prosperous success in all your affairs, together with the love and affection of your people. This respect is undoubtedly due to your merit, whether one considers the most noble character and royal lineage <note>original: "extraction"</note> of your Highness, along with the high expectations the world has from so many eminent virtues, or whether, by examining the records <note>original: "Monuments"</note> of the past, he recalls the ancient alliance of our Kings with the Royal family of *Savoy*. | [We hope that you] would not deviate from the example of your predecessors in this, but that you would repeal <note>original: "abrogate"</note> this edict, or any other that has been made for the disturbing of your subjects on account of the Reformed Religion. We ask that you would restore them to their native homes and properties; that you would confirm to them their ancient rights and former liberty, order that compensation be made for damages, and ensure that an end may be put to their harassment <note>original: "vexations"</note>. We shall regard your favor and mercy toward them as the effect and fruit of our mediation, which will obligate us to return the favor through all good deeds <note>original: "good Offices"</note>. This will be a means not only to lay a foundation for a good relationship <note>original: "correspondency"</note> and friendship, but also to increase it between this Commonwealth and your dominions. And this we expect from your justice and mercy, to which we desire God to incline your heart and mind. And so we heartily pray that He would confer on you and your people peace and truth, and prosperous success in all your affairs. Given at our Palace of Westminster, 25 May, 1655. | [We ask] that if any other order has been proposed for disturbing his subjects on account of the Reformed Religion, he might repeal it <note>original: "uti abroget"</note>, restore them to their ancestral homes and goods, confirm the rights granted and their original liberty, and command that the losses sustained be repaired and an end be put to their harassments. If your Royal Highness does this, you will have done a thing most acceptable to God; you will have raised up and refreshed those miserable and calamitous people, and you will find the greatest favor from all your neighbors, as many as follow the Reformed Religion—and especially from us, who will consider your kindness and mercy toward them as the fruit of our attention. This will obligate us to return all manner of duties, and will lay the firmest foundations not only for establishing but also for increasing the bond and friendship between this Commonwealth and your dominion. Nor indeed do we expect any less from your justice and moderation of mind. To which end we pray to God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Deum Opt. Max."</note>, that he might turn your mind and thoughts; and we heartily pray for peace, truth, and successful outcomes in all things for you and your people. Given from our Court at Westminster, 25 May, in the year 1655. |

# Chapter IV. Mr. Morland's Negotiation, etc.

After Mr. Morland had finished speaking and delivered this Letter into the hands of the Duke, his mother **Madame Royale** <note>Christine Marie of France, the Dowager Duchess and regent of Savoy</note> told him that, on one hand, she could not help but greatly applaud the singular charity and goodness of his Highness the Lord Protector toward their subjects, whose condition had been represented to him as so exceedingly sad and lamentable, as she perceived by his speech. 

On the other hand, however, she could not help but be extremely surprised that the malice of men should ever go so far as to characterize such fatherly and tender punishments <note>original: "chastisements"</note> of their most rebellious and insolent subjects in such a black and ugly way, intended to make them hateful to all neighboring Princes and States with whom they so much desired to maintain a good understanding and friendship—especially with so great and powerful a Prince as his Highness the Lord Protector. 

Furthermore, she said she did not doubt that when he was particularly and clearly informed of the truth of all that had occurred, he would be so fully satisfied with the Duke's proceedings that he would not give the least support <note>original: "countenance"</note> to those disobedient subjects. But regardless, for his Highness's sake, they would not only freely pardon their rebellious subjects for those most heinous crimes which they had committed, but would also grant <note>original: "accord"</note> to them such privileges and graces as would give the Lord Protector sufficient evidence of how great a respect they held for both his person and his mediation.

After this, Mr. Morland was accompanied back to **Turin** by the Master of Ceremonies, according to the special order of the Duke, where he was entertained with all the outward demonstrations of civility and respect imaginable during the time of his stay in that place.

Within a few days after his first audience, he was visited by the **Marquis of Saint Thomas** <note>original: "Marchio a Santo Thoma"</note>, the chief Secretary of State, who shared with him some Latin papers. These were the very same as the Duke of Savoy's **Statement of Facts and Reasons** <note>original: "Factum and Reasons"</note>, which are inserted in the third book of this history in the Italian language, except for a few additions and alterations, and the fact that these first pieces were not organized in quite as exact a method as the later ones were. The Secretary took the trouble to read these papers over himself to Mr. Morland, making large comments upon each article as he went, and ending with a long exhortation to Mr. Morland to give a favorable report of all the Duke his master's proceedings.

When Mr. Morland had heard all that the Secretary had to say, he told him that despite all he had either seen in those papers or heard from his mouth, there were very many difficulties which appeared to him not easy to be answered. And though he had no instructions to enter into any treaty concerning this affair, yet if the Marquis were pleased to leave the papers in his hands for a few days, he would make such critical observations <term>original: "animadversions"</term> upon several of the articles contained within them as the information he had received from others would enable him, so that the truth might better shine through by comparing contradictory accounts. <note>original Latin: "Contraria juxta se posita magis elucescerent," literally "Opposites placed next to each other become more clear."</note>

To this the Marquis replied that he would take the papers with him for the moment because they were not neatly written, and within two or three days he would send them in a more legible hand; which he accordingly did, enclosing them in the following letter.

# A Copy of a Letter from the Marquis of Saint Thomas, Chief Secretary of State, to Samuel Morland, Esq., His Highness’s Envoy to the Duke of Savoy.

## The original of which can be seen in the public library of the famous University of Cambridge.

Most Illustrious Lord,

I am sending to your Lordship <note>original: "Dominationi vestræ"</note> two documents: one which contains a true and exact account of the events that took place in the Valleys of Lucerna, and another which demonstrates the equity and justice of the Edict recently promulgated by the Auditor Gastaldo. There remains a third, shorter document containing some general notes on the previous two, which your Illustrious Lordship will receive today. Meanwhile, I would ask you to excuse the delay in sending them, as well as the handwriting, which is perhaps not neat enough. If, however, your Illustrious Lordship finds anything in these documents that requires further interpretation, please signify it to me in your kindness, and I will clear up every difficulty in my reply. In the meantime, I wish you every success with all my heart. From the castle of Rivoli <note>original: "castro Ripularum"</note>, July 10, 1655.

<note>original Latin: "Illustrissime Domine, Transmitto Dominationi vestræ duas scripturas, unam scilicet quæ continet veram, & exactam rerum gestarum in Vallibus Lucernensibus relationem, & alteram quæ Edicti nuper à Domino Auditore Gastaldo promulgati demonstrat æquitatem, & justitiam. Superest alia tertia Scriptura brevior, quæ quasdam annotationes generales continet super præmissis duabus, quam hodie Illustrissima Dominatio vestra habebit. Interea eam rogatum velim, ut dilationem missionis excuset, sicut & characterem, forfitan non satis concinnum, si quid verò in istis scripturis repererit F. D. V. quod egeat majori interpretatione, id pro sua humanitate mihi significabit, & responso meo omnem enucleabo difficultatem. Eidem interim facilitatem omnem toto cordis affectu auguror. Ex castro Ripularum die 10. Julii 1655."</note>

->Your Illustrious Lordship's<-
->Most devoted servant,<-
->Marquis of Saint Thomas.<-

***

Mr. Morland, upon the receipt of this letter and the enclosed papers (which were, as stated above, nothing other than the first and rough draft of the Court of Savoy’s *Factum* <term>a legal statement of the facts of a case</term> and *Reasons*, etc., which are inserted in the third book of this history), immediately drew up short *animadversions* <term>critical remarks or observations</term> upon all the important articles. He did this with the help of those papers of intelligence which he had received before and soon after his arrival at Turin. These *animadversions* (which it is completely unnecessary to repeat here, as they are effectively included in those general observations made by some knowledgeable friends of the Protestants, which are set down at length as an answer to the Court of Savoy’s *Factum* and *Reasons*) Mr. Morland sent to the Secretary of State, enclosed in the following letter.

### Copy of a Letter from Samuel Morland, Esq., His Highness's <note>Oliver Cromwell, the Lord Protector</note> Envoy, etc., to the Marquis of Saint Thomas <note>original Latin: "Marchio a Sancto Thoma"</note>, the Chief Secretary of State. Turin, July 2/12, 1655.

->Most Illustrious Lord,<- <note>original: "Illustrissime Domine"</note>

**IN** reviewing and re-examining <note>original: "evolvendis revolvendisque"</note> several papers written regarding the Protestant cause, some points occurred to me which seemed—if properly organized—to be suitable responses to almost every article included in your Illustrious Lordship’s own documents. Therefore, I decided that in order for the truth to shine more clearly, and also so that the Most Serene Protector of England might be satisfied in all things—yet with the greatest respect and due honor for his Royal Highness <note>The Duke of Savoy</note>—I should present these same points to your Illustrious Lordship for examination. Since these papers were originally written in French, I was unwilling to translate them into Latin, lest there be any suspicion that I had invented them myself, or that I might seem to have changed the proper and natural meaning of any word, or finally (which would be judged even more unfair), that I might seem to favor the opposing side too much. However, it is not my place to debate these matters or to fight with arguments; I come for this one thing alone: to ask his Royal Highness, with humble and repeated prayers, that he would be pleased to communicate to me in advance what and how much he intends to grant to these most miserable and afflicted subjects of his, out of favor to the Most Serene Protector.

From my lodgings in Turin,
July 2/12, 1655.
->Your Illustrious Lordship’s<-
->Most obedient servant,<-
->**SAMUEL MORLAND.**<-

***

About four days after this, the said Marquis sent me his reply to those annotations I had previously sent him, enclosed in the following letter.

*Most Illustrious Lord,* <note>original Latin: "Illustrissime Domine"</note>

*In this time of the army setting out against enemies, with business multiplied as is customary, I have been forced to postpone for several days the sending of the response to your annotations, which were collected from the booklets or papers of the Reformed <note>The Protestants/Waldensians</note> that are being circulated everywhere. Indeed, since these annotations are supported by no strength of reason or truth, they collapse on their own; therefore, it was easier for me to respond than if some new argument had come forth from your Illustrious Lordship’s great sharpness and insight in this matter. Thus, I fully believe that your Lordship will be convinced of the good faith and truth of the points I bring forward. I also believe you will be happy to hear of the supreme clemency of their Royal Highnesses <note>The Duke of Savoy and his mother, the Duchess Regent</note>—who do not disdain to turn a kind eye toward their rebel subjects out of regard for the Most Serene Protector of England <note>Oliver Cromwell</note>. They will experience this indulgence all the sooner in the treaty initiated—and even now being completed—in the name of His Most Christian Majesty <note>The King of France</note> by the most excellent Lord de Servien, his Ambassador. I thought it necessary to inform your Illustrious Lordship of this, as you will feel no small joy that the services you performed before their Royal Highnesses, in the name of the Most Serene Protector, have not been without the desired outcome. Meanwhile, I wish to assure you that their Royal Highnesses daily place a greater value on your merits, and that I, above all, am bound to you with every kind of respect and obedience. Dated at the Castle of Rivoli <note>original Latin: "Castro Ripularum"</note>, July 17, 1655.*

->*Your Illustrious Lordship's*<-
->*Most Devoted,*<-
->*The Marquess of San Tommaso.*<- <note>original: "Marchio à Sancto Thoma"</note>

<page-num>579</page-num>
<header>Chapter IV. in the Court of Savoy.</header>

Since the *Factum* <note>original: "ctum"; likely *Factum*, a legal statement of facts</note> and the reasons are already included in the third book of this history—except for some harsh and angry expressions—it will be a relief to the reader and a courtesy to their author not to include them here.

During the time of Mr. Morland’s stay in Turin, he had several serious meetings with the French Ambassador, Mr. Servient <note>Abel Servien (1593–1659), a high-ranking French diplomat</note>, regarding the massacre and the ancient privileges of the poor people <note>The Waldensian Protestants</note>. In one of these meetings, Mr. Servient told Mr. Morland—who was pressing him very hard to intervene on their behalf—*that he truly believed that Emanuel Philibert <note>Duke of Savoy from 1553 to 1580</note> had granted the concessions the people were demanding, specifically in the year 1561. He also believed that his Royal Highness and the Duchess Regent, his mother, could easily be reconciled with them and might be inclined to grant them the same or even greater privileges than his royal ancestors had done, if there were not certain powerful people in the Court whose zeal for the* Catholic Religion *prompted them to put the worst possible interpretation and representation on everything to their Prince. However, he advised Mr. Morland by all means not to add fuel to the fire, but rather to try to satisfy and appease his Highness the* Lord Protector <note>Oliver Cromwell</note> *with a gentle and moderate account of all these proceedings.*

He was also frequently visited and treated very politely by the Jesuits and other members of the clergy, who spared no effort to persuade him and make him believe that all the reports circulating in the world in favor of the poor people were pure fictions and fantasies <note>original: "chimaeras"</note>, having no foundation or hint of truth.

When Mr. Morland had stayed in Turin for his appointed time, he requested his formal dismissal, which was granted to him. Having taken his leave of the Duke in a second audience and received his response to the Lord Protector’s letter, he set out from Turin on July 19, 1655, toward Geneva, where he was commanded to go by his Highness’s order. The Duke’s answer to his Highness’s letter follows.

# CHAPTER 5.

## A brief account of the notable and famous collection in England, Wales, and Ireland for the relief of the poor, distressed Protestants in the valleys of Piedmont <note>original: Piemont</note> in the year 1655.

---

Soon after the departure of the mentioned Mr. Morland <note>Samuel Morland (1625–1695), a diplomat and mathematician sent by Cromwell to negotiate with the Duke of Savoy on behalf of the Waldensians.</note> from England to the Duke of Savoy, His Highness the Lord Protector <note>Oliver Cromwell</note> was not satisfied with merely saying to those who were naked and lacked daily food, *"Be warm and be filled"* <note>A biblical reference to James 2:16, criticizing those who offer kind words without practical help.</note>, without actually giving them the things necessary for the body. Therefore, he immediately published a declaration expressing his earnest desire that the good people under his rule might be grieved by the *afflictions of Joseph* <note>A biblical reference to Amos 6:6, used here to describe the suffering of fellow believers.</note> and might be moved to make a free and generous contribution toward the aid and support of their poor, distressed brethren. He also encouraged them by his own noble example, contributing no less than two thousand pounds sterling to the treasury from his own private funds.

Now, so that the *Christian reader* may be fully satisfied that all these pious intentions of his *Highness* had their blessed effects on both the hearts and spirits of his subjects, and also that the money collected was truly delivered to the poor people for whom it was intended—to feed the hungry, clothe the naked, and relieve the sick among them—the reader is invited to examine the following extract from a large and detailed account. This account was recently printed and published by special order of his *Highness* and the *Council*.

This declaration expressed his earnest desire that the people might be stirred up to a free and liberal contribution toward their aid and support. To manage this collection, certain instructions were also agreed upon and attached to the declaration. For the more effective promotion of the work, His Highness appointed a committee consisting of persons of known honor, fidelity, and integrity to consider and advise from time to time how the money that should be raised might be employed with the most advantage and certainty for the supply of those poor, distressed members of Christ, according to the true intention of the givers. Among these committee members, two selected individuals of very considerable wealth and reputation were appointed to be treasurers for receiving the money. ## CHAPTER V.

### A brief account of the notable and famous collection in England, Wales, and Ireland for the relief of the poor, distressed Protestants in the valleys of Piedmont, in the year 1655.

Soon after the departure of the mentioned Mr. Morland <note>Samuel Morland (1625–1695) was an English diplomat sent by Cromwell to protest the massacres.</note> from England toward the Duke of Savoy, his Highness the Lord Protector <note>Oliver Cromwell, who led the English Commonwealth at this time.</note>—not being satisfied with merely saying to those who were naked and destitute of daily food, *“Be warm and be filled,”* <note>original: "Be ye warm, and be ye filled"; a reference to the biblical Book of James 2:16, which rebukes those who offer words of comfort without providing physical aid.</note> without actually giving them the things necessary for the body—immediately published a declaration. He also encouraged them by his own princely example, donating no less than two thousand pounds sterling from his own private account.

This account was printed and published not long ago by special order of his Highness and the Council.

---

Nor was His Highness's <note>Oliver Cromwell</note> Christian care and tenderness left unanswered by the open hearts and hands of many charitable and compassionate souls, both of this nation and Ireland. Upon the publishing of the above-mentioned Declaration and Instructions, they most freely and cheerfully contributed toward the timely relief <note>original: "refreshing the bowels," a biblical idiom for providing comfort or satisfying the essential needs of the afflicted</note> of their poor, afflicted brethren.

It is true that there were some parishes and particular persons of note among whom a certain reluctance <note>original: "backwardness"</note> to this good work was observed at that time. Indeed, there are many to this very day who do not appear in the official records <note>original: "Returns"</note> to have contributed anything toward it. However, means were also used for supplying that defect through a subsequent Proclamation. This was later reinforced by His Highness's precise <note>original: "punctual"</note> orders to the Justices of the Peace in the various counties to examine their respective districts <note>original: "Divisions"</note> and find where no collections had been made. In cases where collections were made but the money had not been sent up, they were to cause a speedy delivery of the funds. 

By these means, through the great goodness of God and the blessing upon His Highness's endeavors, considerable sums were brought in within a short space of time. These were carefully lodged in the Treasury, ready to be issued and distributed as soon as ways and means were found for the safe transport of the money to the respective places where those poor people <note>original: "wretches," used here as a term of pity for those in a miserable state</note> were then living. Although, it may be justly feared that there were defaults in some places, and the money has not to this day been delivered to the Treasurers.

# Chapter V. For the Protestants in Piedmont.

*...which was in the clefts of ragged rocks, and in the caves of snowy mountains.*

To achieve this goal and purpose, His **Highness** <note>Oliver Cromwell, the Lord Protector of the Commonwealth</note> (continuing his care for carrying on this **Work**) simultaneously appointed **Mr. Pell** (his **Resident** <note>A diplomatic representative, similar to an ambassador</note> with the **Protestant Cantons** of **Switzerland**) and **Mr. Morland** as his **Joint-Commissioners Extraordinary** for the management of this **Affair** overseas. Morland had not long before been sent as his **Envoy** to the **King** of **France** and the **Duke** of **Savoy** on their behalf. They were also provided with suitable instructions and commands to ensure that, through their special oversight and care, the collected **money** might not only be sent from **England** to the **valleys** quickly, securely, and at the best exchange rates, but also that once conveyed, it might actually be distributed and spent on clothing the **naked**, feeding the **hungry**, and relieving the **sick**. This was to be done with all possible fairness and just proportion, giving due respect to the greatest **sufferers** and those in the most need among them.

This work was performed accordingly by the aforementioned **Mr. Pell** and **Mr. Morland**. Once the methods they proposed to His **Highness** and the **Council** were approved, the plan was immediately put into action. Based on advice received from time to time from the **Committee**, His **Highness** ordered the sending of several sums of **money** to the **valleys**. This was done first through both **Mr. Pell** and **Mr. Morland** together, and later through **Mr. Morland** alone. By order of His **Highness**, Morland resided in **Geneva** for an entire year (starting from November 20, **1655**) for that very purpose. He reported on the poor people's urgent needs as they arose so that funds could be sent during the most critical **seasons** and **circumstances** <note>original: "Conjunctures"</note>.

Upon **Mr. Morland's** return to **England**, he submitted an **Account** to the **Committee** this past **January** regarding the **money** sent overseas. A **Sub-Committee** was then appointed to receive and examine it (specifically **Sir Thomas Vyner, Sir Christopher Pack,** and **Mr. Cresset**). They were also authorized to hire anyone they thought fit as an **Auditor** to assist with the precise examination and balancing of the **Account**. On January 21, this **Sub-Committee** reported to the full **Committee** that they had thoroughly reviewed the **Account**, including both the **money** sent from England and the funds handled abroad. They found the entire record, as stated in the **Book** delivered by **Mr. Morland**, to be justly stated.

To provide public notice of how much **money** has been received through these **collections**, how much has been distributed and sent overseas, and what remains in the fund; and to ensure that all the good people of this **Commonwealth** are fully satisfied and assured that no part of these **collected funds** has been, or will ever be, diverted from the charitable intentions of the **donors**, but used solely for the very purposes for which they were originally intended, His **Highness** has decided to publish the following **Account**.

Regarding the money that still remains in the hands of the Treasurers, the good people of this nation are asked to believe and be assured that it has, until now, been His Highness's <note>Oliver Cromwell, the Lord Protector</note> exceeding great care that no part of the collected money might be distributed or delivered out except by the advice and through the hands of persons of known honor and approved integrity. Similarly, it shall be his constant endeavor that what remains now, or shall hereafter be collected and stored in the hands of the Treasurers (who are as ready now as ever to receive what shall be further collected), shall be used for the best advantage of those for whom it was (or shall be) solely intended.

For this end and purpose, His Highness—after careful consultation with both his commissioners at home and his public ministers abroad—has already caused some part of it to be invested for interest in secure hands (but in such a way that it may be called in upon urgent occasion). In the future, he will make such decisions as the necessities of those poor people and the circumstances of their condition require. Their condition (the Lord knows) is now as miserable as ever in many respects; without the same miraculous hand of Providence that has preserved them so far, they must in a short time inevitably perish. Therefore, if there are any charitable souls who have yet contributed nothing to the relief of their poor distressed brothers, let them please read the following discourse; perhaps they may find there such arguments as may awaken them and quicken their hearts to perform such a good and Christian work.

## CHAPTER VI.

### *The notable effects of the intercession of His Highness the Lord Protector of England, etc., for the poor, distressed Protestants in the valleys of Piedmont, upon the spirits of the neighboring princes and states of the Protestant profession; with several of their letters upon that subject, and the intended negotiation of the Commissioners Extraordinary from His Highness the Lord Protector and the States-General of the United Provinces.*

Having in the previous chapters given an account not only of *His Highness's* <note>Referring to Oliver Cromwell, the Lord Protector of England.</note> mediation and intercession with the King of *France* and Duke of *Savoy* on behalf of the poor, distressed churches in the *valleys of Piedmont*, but also his many serious and stirring <note>original: "pathetick"; in the 17th century, this meant deeply moving or emotional rather than "pitiful."</note> letters to his *Protestant* neighbors, urging them to join with him to obtain their re-establishment, it will not now be unwelcome to inform the world of the blessed fruits and effects of his Christian and princely endeavors, and how far they influenced the minds and hearts of those who share the same belief and profession as himself.

It would be an almost endless (or at least too massive) a task to recite here all the individual letters which were written in those days from one prince to another upon this occasion. I shall therefore limit myself to some of those which more immediately concern the carrying on of this present discourse, and which more naturally lead us to the subsequent events.

I shall begin with the letters from the *King of Sweden* and the

# A Letter from the King of Sweden to His Highness the Lord Protector of England, &c. dated June 23, 1655.

## An authentic copy of the true original, which was shared with the author by the Right Honorable Mr. Secretary Thurloe. <note>John Thurloe (1616–1668) was the Secretary of State under Oliver Cromwell and served as his primary advisor on foreign policy and intelligence.</note>

---

->WE, CHARLES GUSTAVUS, <note>original: "Nos Carolus Gustavus"</note> by the Grace of God King of the Swedes, Goths, and Vandals; Grand Prince of Finland; Duke of Estonia, Karelia, Bremen, Verden, Stettin, Pomerania, Cassubia, and Vandalia; Prince of Rügen; Lord of Ingria and Wismar; and Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, Jülich, Cleves, and Berg, etc. To our most Serene and High good friend, OLIVER, Lord Protector of the Commonwealth of England, Scotland, and Ireland and their dominions, greetings and all prosperity.<-

->Most Serene and High Lord Protector,<-
->Good Friend;<-

The reports we have received—partly through your Highness’s letters and partly by common rumor—concerning the slaughter and destruction of the Protestants in Savoy <note>The "Sabaudia" referred to here is the Duchy of Savoy, where the "Bloody Easter" massacre of the Vaudois (Waldensian) Protestants took place in April 1655.</note> have profoundly shaken us. For beyond the fact that basic humanity requires us to pity the unjust fate of the innocent and harmless, the shared name and cause of Protestants, as well as the equal hatred our enemies hold against us all, makes their joys and sorrows our own. 

Indeed, how much our ancestors, the Kings of Sweden, have labored to ensure that the rights of Protestants remain legally protected <note>original: "vigore constent"</note> is proven by the many years of war fought in Germany for this cause <note>A reference to the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), in which Sweden was the leading Protestant military power.</note>, and the Peace of Osnabrück <note>One of the treaties comprising the Peace of Westphalia (1648), which granted legal recognition to various Protestant groups within the Holy Roman Empire.</note> signed with our most serene and powerful brother, kinsman, and friend, the Emperor, and the Holy Roman Empire. It shall be no less our care to strive to equal our illustrious predecessors in this honor. 

Therefore, we promise from our hearts—out of our hatred for such inhuman cruelty—that we will intercede by writing to the Duke of Savoy. We will strive, as much as it lies within our power, to ensure he revokes or softens that cruel and harsh edict, and that he orders those who were driven from their homes to wander, and those who have survived the sword and flames, to return to their lands. In this way, we trust it will be clearly evident to your Highness how deeply we feel this calamity, and how much the Protestant <note>original: "Evangelicam"</note> religion of these most afflicted men...

...we are deeply affected by the sufferings of those who profess the same faith. Likewise, we do not doubt that your Highness will act and strive with a zeal equal to ours before the Holy Roman Emperor, so that those devoted to the Protestant <note>original: "Evangelicæ Religioni"</note> faith in Bohemia, Moravia, and Silesia do not remain perpetually exposed and vulnerable to the hatred of their persecutors, contrary to the Peace of Osnabrück <note>original: "pacta Osnabruggensia"; the 1648 treaty that ended the Thirty Years' War and established legal rights for certain religious groups</note> and the freedom of conscience. 

This duty is all the more urgent for both of us because we have certain proof that such savage beginnings by the opposing side aim at the total destruction of the Protestants. We are ready to share such counsel with your Highness as may serve to mitigate these evils and support the Protestant cause with our united help. 

In the meantime, we desire your Highness to be in the best of health, and we affectionately commend you to Divine protection. Given in our Royal Palace at Stockholm, on the 23rd day of June, 1655.

->Your good Friend,<-

# A Letter from the *States General* of the *United Provinces*, to His Highness the *Lord Protector* of *England*, etc. Bearing date *June* 12, 1655.

### An authentic copy of the true original, which was shared with the author by the Right Honourable Mr. Secretary *Thurloe*. <note>John Thurloe (1616–1668) was the secretary to the Council of State in Protectorate England and supervised the government's intelligence network.</note>

->Most Serene and Most High Lord Protector,<-
<note>original: "Serenissime & Celsissime Domine Protector"</note>

We received your letters written at Westminster on the 25th of last May a few days ago. In them, we certainly perceived with great joy the immense signs of your piety and Christian love and charity. It was no small comfort to us, in the midst of the afflicted and almost ruined affairs of our Piedmontese <note>original: "Taurinalpinorum"; referring to the inhabitants of the Alpine valleys near Turin, specifically the Waldensian Protestants</note> brothers, that your Highness has taken up their protection with such fire and zeal. 

Just as the savage slaughter and butchery of these most innocent people has struck our own hearts most bitterly, so, moved by that same zeal, we are most ready to consult with your Highness to determine what help or assistance can be given to these most miserable fellow members of our Reformed <note>original: "Orthodoxae"; in this context, it refers to the Protestant/Reformed faith rather than Eastern Orthodoxy</note> faith. Indeed, we must join our efforts to help the scattered and most cruelly dispersed flock of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that the unhappy multitude of wanderers and exiles may be restored to their possessions, homes, and former status. 

For this purpose, we have already given orders and are ready to give even more extensive ones as the situation requires. At the same time, our most distinguished and wise Ambassador, Willem Nieupoort <note>original: "Neportius"; Willem Nieupoort was the Dutch ambassador to England from 1653 to 1660</note>, will explain more fully to your Highness what we have already achieved in this matter. In closing,

->Most Serene and Most High Lord Protector, we pray to the Great and Good God that He may long preserve your Highness in safety for the promotion of the common good of the Reformed religion. Given at The Hague, June 12, 1655.<-

->G. Hoolck.<-

->Your Highness's most devoted good friends,<-

->The States General of the United Netherlands.<-

->By their command,<-

->MUYSSE.<-

# A Letter of the Evangelical Cantons of Switzerland to His Highness the Lord Protector of England, etc.
## June 17, 1655.

An authentic copy of the true original, which was shared with the author by the Right Honourable Mr. Secretary Thurloe.

---

->*Most Serene and Most High Lord Protector, Lord to be followed with the highest honor.*<-
<note>original: "Serenissime ac Celsissime Domine Protector, Domine summo honore prosequende."</note>

How piously and with what deep feeling your Highness has grieved over the most mournful affliction and need of our Piedmontese <note>original: "Taurinalpinorum"; referring to the Waldensian Protestants living in the Alpine valleys near Turin.</note> brothers, and how you have received their groans and tears with affection, and how greatly you have been moved by the atrocity of an act more than human in its cruelty—your Highness's letters written to us have given us abundant proof of all this. We have also seen this in the reports of your other letters sent to various Kings and States, and even to the Duke of Savoy himself. 

This extraordinary piety of your Highness, and your great zeal for the Orthodox <note>In this context, "Orthodox" refers to the Reformed or Protestant faith.</note> religion, deserves singular praise and glory among all who share our faith. It has also excited in us a desire and ardor to petition the Duke of Savoy himself through a formal embassy <note>original: "Legationem solennem"</note>, a goal we have so far been unable to achieve for these miserable, afflicted people, neither by letters nor by a simple messenger. To this end, a messenger <note>original: "praecursor"</note> set out today to notify the Duke of our intentions and, at the same time, to ask for a cessation of arms <note>A ceasefire.</note>. The ambassadors will follow him as quickly as possible on the eleventh day of the upcoming month of July, Old Style <note>The Julian calendar, then used in England and Switzerland, which was 10 days behind the Gregorian calendar used in Savoy.</note>. 

We earnestly ask your Highness, with the greatest affection we can, that out of your most pious and tender love for these fellow members of our faith, and your most ready desire to help them, you would deign to join your counsels with ours. We would welcome this either through some mission <note>original: "Ablegatione"</note> of your own, which we greatly desire, or at least by repeated letters, so that it may be much easier to return the exiled to their former homes and provide safely for their constant security. 

We are also revealing this same intent of ours to the States General of the United Netherlands, who we know will not deny their Christian and powerful help and labor to these innocent and most unworthily harassed brothers. In this happy hope and omen we conclude, praying from our hearts to God, the Greatest and Best, that He may command your Highness's endeavors and government to be perpetually successful, for the glory of His name, the consolation of the Church Militant <note>The term for the Christian church on earth, viewed as engaged in spiritual warfare against sin and persecution.</note>, and the joy of all good people. 

Dated the 17th day of June in the year 1655. Fortified with the seal of our beloved Confederates of the City of Zurich in the name of us all.

->*Your Highness's most devoted,*<-

->The Consuls, Mayors <note>original: "Sculteri"</note>, Landammen, and Senators of the Evangelical Cantons of Switzerland, namely: Zurich, Bern, Glarus, Basel, Schaffhausen, and Appenzell; as well as the Confederates of the same religion in Graubünden <note>original: "Rhætia"</note>, Geneva, St. Gall, Mulhouse, and Bienne.<-

<summary>The Protestant Cantons of Switzerland write to Oliver Cromwell to coordinate a diplomatic mission to the Duke of Savoy, seeking to end the persecution of the Waldensians and restore them to their homes.</summary>

<page-num>603</page-num>
<header>Chapter VI. The Lord Protector's Intervention.</header>

From the three previous letters, it can easily be seen how much his Highness's <note>Oliver Cromwell, the Lord Protector of England, who spearheaded the diplomatic rescue mission.</note> intervention had energized and moved the spirits of the King of Sweden and the two other states. If it were not a task too tedious, similar effects of this intervention could just as easily be demonstrated in the actions of the King of Denmark, the Prince Elector Palatine, the Elector of Brandenburg, the Duke of Württemberg, and all the other Protestant princes and states in those parts of the world. All of these, either through their letters to the Duke of Savoy or by other means, sufficiently declared their deep indignation <note>original: "resentment"</note> regarding that bloody massacre. This was especially true of the Landgrave of Hesse, whose letter to the said Duke is so full of passionate and moving <term>pathetic</term> expressions that I cannot help but recommend it to the Christian reader in a particular way.

---

### A Letter from the Landgrave of Hesse to the Duke of Savoy.
<note>The following is translated from the original Latin: "Literae Landgravii Hassiae ad Sabaudiae Ducem."</note>

->**Most Illustrious Prince, Kinsman, and Dearest Friend,**<-
<note>original: "Illustrissime Princeps, Consanguinee, & Amice charissime."</note>

Since we have been informed by certain and beyond-doubt reports of the most severe and harsh things that have recently been done against the inhabitants of the valleys of Lucerna, Perosa, and San Martino <note>The three main Waldensian valleys in Piedmont.</note>—people who follow the same Reformed religion as ourselves—we could not, out of a sense of shared humanity and the bond of our common faith, help but be most deeply affected by their misery and their extremely wretched condition. 

We had indeed hoped that your Highness’s innate clemency and justice would have provided a much milder remedy for your subjects' grievances. However, the news of such slaughter, of such widespread fire, and of such extreme cruelty used against these miserable and innocent people, has filled our heart with incredible sorrow...

### Translation of a Letter from the Landgrave of Hesse to the Duke of Savoy, July 23, 1655.
<note>Landgrave William VI of Hesse-Kassel was a prominent German Protestant prince who actively supported the Huguenots and Waldensians.</note>

#### An authentic copy of the true original, which was shared with the author during his stay in Geneva.

<note>original French: "Monſieur, Ayant appris n'a gueres le cruel Maſſacre commis ſur ceux de la Religion nommez Vaudois, habitants de vos Vallees d' Angrogne et Pragela en Piemont, je n'ay pu, &c."</note>
Sir, having recently learned of the cruel massacre committed against those of the religion called Waldensians, inhabitants of your valleys of Angrogna and Pragela in Piedmont, I could not... [etc.]

SIR,

Having lately received the news of that cruel massacre committed upon the Protestants, who are commonly known by the name of Waldensians <note>original: "Waldenses"; a group of pre-Reformation Christians in the Alps who faced intense persecution.</note>, inhabiting your valleys of Angrogna and Pragela in Piedmont, I could at first hardly be brought to believe such a sorrowful story. I was unable to imagine that their adversaries had ever been so bold <note>original: "audacious"</note> as to exercise such barbarous cruelties upon poor, innocent people who lived peaceably under the government of your Highness and in perfect obedience, without giving the least offense to anyone, and who for such a long time together have had protection and security both from you and from your ancestors. 

Indeed, I imagined this all the less because of my conviction <note>original: "persuasion"</note> that their enemies had learned by the experience of so many ages that persecutions and massacres <note>original: "Butcheries"</note> are not the means to suppress our religion, but rather to preserve and spread it abroad. But this news having been written and confirmed to me from so many places, and with circumstances altogether deplorable—so that I could no longer remain in doubt—it has seized me with horror. 

Consequently, being moved with compassion and pity toward so many thousands of souls in such extreme distress—who have been most cruelly robbed and despoiled of their lives and estates by the cruelty of their furious and sworn enemies, and that without distinction of either sex or age—I have thought it my duty as a Christian Prince with a stake <note>original: "intereſſed"</note> in the preservation of those of my religion to write this present letter to your Highness. I beseech you not only to command and permit the remainder of those poor, innocent people who have escaped the violence of their persecutors to be established in their lands, goods, and possessions which are still left to them after this great desolation, but also that they may find the effects of your powerful protection. To this end, I ask that you would be pleased to favor them hereafter by hearing their complaints and by examining their case yourself <note>original: "taking cognizance of them"</note> as a good and righteous prince, from whom they ought

> ...to expect all the effects of justice, clemency, and generosity <note>original: "bounty"</note>. Whereas those who call themselves the "Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith and for the Extirpation of Heretics" <note>This refers to the *Sacra Congregatio de Propaganda Fide*, a department of the Vatican established to spread Catholicism and suppress Protestantism.</note> are their declared enemies. Instead of turning souls to righteousness by the sword of the Word, they have employed the temporal sword, fire, the rope, and all the barbarous cruelties that outrageous men could possibly invent for the bodies of those poor creatures, to destroy them from the face of the earth. I most earnestly beseech your Highness to grant the requests mentioned above, and to be assured of my unbreakable affection for your interests and service. I shall consider it a happiness to have an opportunity to give you real testimonies of the same; as being, etc.

->Kassel, July 23, 1655. William, Landgrave of Hesse.<-

To all this might be added various consoling and Christian letters written from several individual churches in many places and parts of Europe to their poor, distressed brethren in the valleys of Piedmont: namely, from Frankfurt, Zurich, Hanau, Vlissingen <note>original: "Flushing"</note>, Middelburg, Clairac, Bergerac, and the like. These were sent together with large financial contributions according to their respective proportions and abilities. Authentic copies of many of these letters are to be seen, together with the rest of the original papers and manuscripts, in the public library of the famous University of Cambridge.

These were the first fruits of His Highness's <note>Referring to Oliver Cromwell, the Lord Protector of England.</note> intercession and mediation for those poor, afflicted churches. They were the good effects of that close union and communion of all the churches of Christ and His members throughout the Protestant world. This is especially worthy of our serious observation, as it would likely be very difficult to find a similar example of such sweet harmony and mutual agreement among so many different nations and states in any matter relating to religion in all the histories of former ages. 

Certainly, had these beginnings not been stifled at birth by that unhappy treaty concluded at Pinerolo <note>original: "Pignerol"</note> in the year 1655, God alone knows into how great a flame these little sparks might have been blown in time. Remarkable changes and alterations might have been produced throughout all Christendom for the advantage of the Church Militant <note>The "Church Militant" refers to the body of Christians on earth who are perceived as being in a state of spiritual warfare against sin and evil.</note>.

The expectations of all people were indeed raised to a very high pitch at this time. Their eyes were fixed upon all the Protestant princes of Europe to see whether they would tolerate such an open affront to their cause in general, or whether they would, with unanimous and joint consent, use their power and influence for the preservation and re-establishment of their poor, distressed brethren in Christ.

## Translation of a Letter from the Landgrave of Hesse
### to the Duke of Savoy, July 23, 1655.
### An authentic copy of the true original, which was shared with the author during his stay at *Geneva*.

Sir,
Having recently learned of the cruel massacre committed upon those of the religion called Waldensians <note>original French: "Vaudois"</note>, inhabitants of your Valleys of Angrogna and Pragela in Piedmont, I could not, etc. <note>The author provides the first lines in French before moving to a full English translation.</note>

SIR,
Having lately received the news of that cruel massacre committed upon the Protestants—who are commonly known by the name of *Waldensians*—inhabiting your Valleys of *Angrogna* and *Pragela* in *Piedmont*, I could not easily be brought at first to believe such a mournful story. I was unable to imagine that their adversaries had ever been so bold <note>original: "audaciously"</note> as to exercise such savage <note>original: "barbarous"</note> cruelties upon poor innocent people who lived peaceably under the government of your Highness and in perfect obedience, without giving the slightest offense to anyone, and who for so long a time have had protection and security both from you and from your ancestors.

Indeed, I imagined this even less because of my conviction that their enemies had learned from the experience of so many ages that persecutions and slaughters <note>original: "butcheries"</note> are not the means to suppress our religion, but rather to preserve and spread it abroad. But this news has been written and confirmed to me from so many places, and with circumstances so utterly deplorable that I could no longer doubt it. It has filled me with horror. 

Consequently, being moved with compassion and pity toward so many thousands of souls in such extreme distress—who have been most cruelly robbed and deprived of their lives and estates by the cruelty of their furious and sworn enemies, without distinction of sex or age—I have thought it my duty as a Christian Prince concerned in the preservation of those of my religion to write this letter to your Highness. I implore you not only to command and permit that the survivors of those poor innocent people, who have escaped the violence of their persecutors, be restored to their lands, goods, and possessions which are still left to them after this great desolation, but also that they may find the effects of your powerful protection. For this end, may it please you to favor them hereafter by hearing their complaints and by investigating their case <note>original: "taking cognizance of them"</note> yourself as a good and righteous Prince, from whom they ought to expect...

<summary>This page contains the opening of a diplomatic letter from the Landgrave of Hesse to the Duke of Savoy, protesting the 1655 massacre of the Waldensian Protestants and urging their restoration and protection.</summary>
<keywords>Landgrave of Hesse, Duke of Savoy, Waldensians, Piedmont, Angrogna, Pragela, religious persecution, 1655 massacre, Protestant history</keywords>

...to expect every outcome of justice, mercy, and generosity. On the other hand, those who call themselves members of the "Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith and for the Extirpation of Heretics" <note>The *Propaganda Fide*, a Vatican department founded in 1622 to coordinate missionary work and combat the spread of Protestantism.</note> are their declared enemies. Instead of converting souls to righteousness through the power of the Word, they have employed the physical sword, fire, the rope, and every savage cruelty that violent men could possibly invent to torture the bodies of those poor creatures and to wipe them off the face of the earth. I most earnestly beseech your Highness to grant the requests mentioned before and to be assured of my unwavering affection for your interests and service. I shall consider it a happiness to have an opportunity to give you real proof of the same; as being, etc.

->Kassel, July 23, 1655.<-
->William, Landgrave of Hesse.<-

To all this might be added various comforting and *Christian* letters written from several individual churches in many places and parts of *Europe* to their poor, distressed brothers in the Valleys of *Piedmont*. Specifically, these came from *Frankfurt*, *Zurich*, *Hanau*, *Vlissingen* <note>original: "Flushing"</note>, *Middelburg*, *Clairac*, *Bergerac*, and similar locations, together with large financial contributions according to their respective means and abilities. Authentic copies of many of these letters can be seen, along with the rest of the original papers and manuscripts, in the public library of the famous University of *Cambridge*.

These were the first fruits of *His Highness’s* <note>Referring to Oliver Cromwell, the Lord Protector of England.</note> intercession and mediation for those poor, afflicted churches. They represent the good effects of that close union and fellowship among all the churches of *Christ* and his members throughout the *Protestant* world. This is especially worthy of our serious attention because it would perhaps be very difficult to find, in all the histories of former ages, a similar example of such beautiful harmony and mutual agreement among so many different nations and states in any single matter relating to *religion*. Certainly, had these beginnings not been smothered in their infancy by that unfortunate treaty concluded at *Pinerolo* <note>original: "Pignerol"</note> in the year 1655, God alone knows how great a flame these little sparks might have eventually become, and what remarkable changes and alterations might have been produced throughout all *Christendom* for the advantage of the *Church Militant* <note><term>Church Militant</term> A Christian term for the body of believers on earth who are struggling or "warring" against sin, temptation, and spiritual enemies.</note>.

Indeed, the expectations of all people were raised to a very high level at this time. Their eyes were fixed upon all the *Protestant Princes* of *Europe* to see whether they would tolerate such an open insult to their cause in general, or whether they would, with a unanimous and joint consent, use their power and influence for the preservation and restoration of their poor, distressed brothers in *Christ*.

Neither was this expectation of the world at all lessened or diminished—

<page-num>605</page-num>

## The Good Effects of Book IV.

...[di]minished for several months together; but on the contrary, every day it was more and more heightened and enlarged. His Highness *the Lord Protector* of *England* [Oliver Cromwell] had already sent his *envoy* to the *King* of *France* and the *Duke* of *Savoy* on the poor people's behalf. He also openly declared that he would further support their cause with a more significant delegation if the necessity of their affairs required it. Accordingly, as soon as he had received Mr. *Morland's* report from *Geneva* regarding his negotiations at *Turin*, and fully understood the whole matter of fact, he appointed no fewer than three *commissioners extraordinary*. He gave them full instructions for undertaking a formal treaty with the *Duke* and for the effective re-establishment of his persecuted subjects. To all this may be added his frequent and most passionate <note>original: "pathetick" — meaning full of pathos or deep emotion</note> letters, in which he had invited all his *Protestant* neighbors (as has been already shown) to join with him in such a good and charitable work.

The *States General* <note>The governing body of the Dutch Republic.</note>, seeing how heartily their cause was supported from the very beginning by His Highness, had not only written a letter to the *Duke* of *Savoy* to entreat him to be favorable to the people, but had also appointed their own *commissioners extraordinary* to join with those of *His Highness* for the better achieving of the goals mentioned above.

And the *Evangelical <note>Protestant</note> Cantons* of *Switzerland*, so that a "threefold cord might not be easily broken," <note>A biblical reference to Ecclesiastes 4:12, suggesting that the alliance of England, the Netherlands, and Switzerland would be powerful.</note> being encouraged by the other two states, resumed their courage and chose four *ambassadors* to assist their commissioners in bringing this affair to a happy conclusion.

These four *ambassadors* (having the advantage of their country's proximity to that of the *Duke*) were the first to set out on this expedition. They began their journey about the beginning of *July* 1655. The plain truth is, as matters fell out, they "made much more haste than good speed" <note>An idiom meaning they acted too quickly to be effective.</note> in their negotiations, as will appear more particularly in the following chapter.

About the middle of *July* 1655, the Lord *Radulph D. Ommeren*, an ordinary commissioner at the Assembly of their High and Mighty Lordships from the province of *Gelderland*, received orders to travel to the Court of *Savoy* in the role of their *Commissioner Extraordinary*. He was also ordered to visit the *Evangelical Cantons* on his way. After making a serious representation in a public audience regarding their High and Mighty Lordships' deep indignation <note>original: "resentment"</note> over those barbarous cruelties which had been committed upon the poor *Protestants*, and giving an assurance of their readiness to join with the *Lord Protector* and the Swiss in any plans tending to their settlement and re-establishment, he was to deliver to their Lordships the following letter.

# Chapter VI. The Lord Protector's Intercession.

<image-desc>A horizontal row of decorative fleurons separates the header from the title text.</image-desc>

### A Letter from the High and Mighty Lords, the States General of the *United Provinces*, to the *Protestant <note>original: "Evangelical"</note> Cantons of Switzerland. July 14, 1655.*

*An authentic copy of the true original of which was shared with the author by* Mr. Andrew Schmidt, *Under-Secretary of State at Zurich.*

---

->Most Excellent, etc.<-

> We received your letters, secured with the seal of the city of Zurich and written on the seventeenth day of the month just past, only a few days ago. In these letters, you express your unique and truly brotherly affection for our afflicted brothers in the Alps near Turin <note>original Latin: "Amplissimi, &c. Literas vestras Civitatis Tigurinæ sigillo munitas, exaratasque decimo septimo mensis tum proxime præteriti, ante paucos admodum dies accepimus, quibus nos pro singulari et vere fraterno in afflictos fratres Taurinalpinos affectu, &c."</note>, etc.

->Most Excellent Lords,<-

> We have within these few days received your letters, sealed and dated at the *City of Zurich*, on the 17th day of the previous month. In these, according to your exceptional and indeed brotherly affection toward our afflicted brothers beyond the *Alps*, you urge us to provide them with some financial relief, but especially to strive through an embassy of our own as well, so that those poor exiles may be restored to their former homes, and that the necessary arrangements may be made for their safety in the future. 
> 
> In this business, as your piety is most commendable and to be praised by all, and your most Christian zeal has affected us with no small joy, we would not have your Lordships be unaware that we have, some days ago, chosen one of our Senate—a person distinguished for piety, wisdom <note>original: "Prudence"</note>, and high social standing <note>original: "Quality"</note>—who is preparing himself with all speed to travel very soon. He will declare to your Lordships the most intimate thoughts of our mind and our purpose concerning this whole affair, and join in counsel to determine how that most miserable multitude of poor exiled people may, through the mercy of God, be brought back again to their native country. 
> 
> So, concluding with this good hope and confidence of success, we pray to Almighty God that he will be pleased to crown your Lordships' plans with prosperous success in your affairs, and particularly for the benefit of our brothers living beyond the *Alps*, who are so cruelly persecuted.

Given at the *Hague*,
July 14, 1655.

# The Good Effects of Book IV.

Mr. D' Ommeren, having finished his negotiations with the Protestant <note>original: "Evangelical"</note> Cantons in Switzerland, traveled toward Geneva. There, Mr. Morland, the Lord Protector’s envoy, was then residing after his negotiations at Turin. This was done so that, according to his instructions, he might more conveniently communicate and coordinate with Morland regarding the future management of those affairs.

About the end of the month of July 1655, George Downing, Esquire <note>George Downing was a highly influential diplomat and the namesake of Downing Street in London.</note>, received orders from his highness the Lord Protector to hurry his journey to Geneva. There, he was to join Mr. Pell (his highness’s resident minister at Zurich), who was likewise commanded to be ready there, and Mr. Morland, who had been staying there for several weeks following his return from Turin. From Geneva, they were to go to the Duke of Savoy in the role of his highness’s **Commissioners Extraordinary**. Their goal was to join with the ministers of other Protestant states to settle and resolve those tragic <note>original: "unhappy"</note> affairs.

# A Letter from His Highness the Lord Protector of England, to the King of France, 31 July, 1655.

## An Authentic Copy of which was communicated to the Author, by the Right Honorable Mr. Secretary Thurloe. <note>John Thurloe was the Secretary of State under Oliver Cromwell and was famously in charge of the Protectorate's intelligence network.</note>

<column-break/>

->Most Serene and Most Potent King;<-

From your Majesty’s letter, in which you replied to mine dated the twenty-fifth of last May, I easily understand that I was not at all mistaken in my belief that those most inhuman massacres and the barbarous slaughter of those people who profess the Reformed Religion <note>The "Reformed Religion" here refers to the Waldensians, a proto-Protestant group in the Piedmont region who were being violently persecuted by the Duke of Savoy.</note> in Savoy <note>original: "Sabaudia"</note>, carried out by certain of your troops, happened without either your order or command. I was greatly rejoiced that you so promptly informed your Majesty’s military commanders (who had committed these inhuman acts by their own impulse without orders) of how much this displeased you, and that you warned the Duke of Savoy himself of such great cruelty. Finally, I am glad that you have used all your favor, influence, and authority with such sincerity and humanity to advocate for the return of those miserable exiles to the homes from which they were driven. Our hope was, indeed, that the Duke would have granted at least something in this matter in response to your Majesty’s will and prayers. But since neither by your efforts, nor those of other Princes... <note>The Latin text provided in the left column is a translation of the letter's opening, which matches the English text in the right column.</note>

<column-break/>

->Most Serene, and most Potent King;<-

I am inclined to believe, by the letter which your Majesty was pleased to write to me in answer to mine of the twenty-fifth of May last, that I was not deceived in my confidence that the inhuman and barbarous slaughters carried out by your troops against the followers of the Reformed Religion in Savoy were done without your orders. I was very glad to understand that your Majesty had so promptly expressed your dislike of this action to your own officers—as it was done without your command—and also that you had addressed this great cruelty with the Duke of Savoy. You have shown much goodness and humanity by interposing your favor, interest, and authority with him for the restoration of those poor exiled people to their homes and possessions from which they had been driven. Our hope truly was that the Duke would, at least in some measure, have listened to your mediation. However, I have been informed that your Majesty’s efforts on their behalf have yielded no real results, just as the efforts made by other states and princes have also failed...

# A Letter from His Highness the Lord Protector of England, to the King of France, 31 July, 1655.

## An Authentic Copy of which was communicated to the Author, by the Right Honorable Mr. Secretary Thurloe. <note>John Thurloe was the Secretary of State under Oliver Cromwell and was famously in charge of the Protectorate's intelligence network.</note>

->Most Serene and Most Potent King;<-

From your Majesty’s letter, in which you replied to mine dated the twenty-fifth of last May, I easily understand that I was not at all mistaken in my belief that those most inhuman massacres and the barbarous slaughter of those people who profess the Reformed Religion <note>The "Reformed Religion" here refers to the Waldensians, a proto-Protestant group in the Piedmont region who were being violently persecuted by the Duke of Savoy.</note> in Savoy <note>original: "Sabaudia"</note>, carried out by certain of your troops, happened without either your order or command. I was greatly rejoiced that you so promptly informed your Majesty’s military commanders (who had committed these inhuman acts by their own impulse without orders) of how much this displeased you, and that you warned the Duke of Savoy himself of such great cruelty. Finally, I am glad that you have used all your favor, influence, and authority with such sincerity and humanity to advocate for the return of those miserable exiles to the homes from which they were driven. Our hope was, indeed, that the Duke would have granted something more to your Majesty's influence and prayers. But seeing that neither your Majesty's mediation nor our own, nor that of other Princes, has yet been able to obtain any relief for those poor people, we have deemed it consistent with our duty and with Christian charity to send this gentleman, George Downing, as our Envoy Extraordinary to the Duke of Savoy. Our purpose is to present to him the deep sense we have of the extreme suffering of those people.
