| Regarding the same matter, I felt it necessary to send this Gentleman, our Special Commissioner <note>original: "Commissioner Extraordinary"</note>, to the <term>Duke of Savoy</term> to let him more fully know my feelings and concerns regarding the inhumane cruelty committed against those who share our faith, which was done out of hatred for the Religion they profess. And truly, I shall hope for better success in this matter if your Majesty is pleased to support your previous efforts with some more effective means for their relief. Just as your Majesty has already guaranteed the loyalty and obedience of those poor people to their Prince, I hope you will also be pleased to guarantee their security and protection, so that similar unjustifiable disasters and injuries are not inflicted upon them in the future. This being a just and noble act in itself, and consistent with the protection and freedom which you continue to provide with all sincerity and mercy to your own subjects of that religion, we cannot but expect it from your Majesty. Besides, you will gratify the followers of the same faith in your own dominions, who have given such great proof of their loyalty and zeal for your Majesty and the success of your affairs. Lastly, you will satisfy the world that the <term>French government</term> <note>original: "Counsels of France"</note> was not involved in this action, even though some of their ministers and commanders were. This is especially true if your Majesty properly punishes those officials and officers who have acted on their own authority and at their own pleasure to commit such horrible cruelties against innocent and blameless people. In the meantime, seeing that your Majesty declares how justly you detest this most barbarous massacre, we do not doubt but that you will give shelter... | At the request and urgency in the cause of these unfortunate people, so that I may see something accomplished, I have considered it consistent with my duty to send this noble man, commissioned as our Special Commissioner, to the <term>Duke of Savoy</term> <note>original: "Allobrogum Ducem"</note>; he is to explain more fully to the Duke the feelings with which I am affected by such great cruelty practiced against the worshipers of the same religion as ours, out of hatred for that very religion. And I shall hope for a more successful outcome of this embassy if it should please your Majesty once more, and with even greater urgency, to apply your authority and effort. Just as your Majesty has taken it upon yourself to ensure that those destitute people would be faithful and obedient to their Prince, so may you wish to watch over their safety and well-being, lest any such injury and atrocious calamity be further inflicted upon those who are innocent and peaceful. Since this is just and truly royal in itself, and highly consistent with your kindness and mercy—which keeps so many of your own subjects who follow that same religion safe and unharmed everywhere—we cannot but expect it from your Majesty, as is fitting. By this same action, you will bind more closely to yourself all the Protestants throughout your kingdoms, whose zeal and supreme loyalty toward you has often been observed and recognized in the greatest matters; and you will also convince all foreigners that the King’s council contributed nothing to this crime, whatever the King’s ministers and prefects contributed. Especially if your Majesty demands the due punishment from those leaders and ministers who dared to perpetrate such monstrous crimes on their own authority and according to their own lust. Meanwhile, since your Majesty testifies that you turn away from this most inhumane deed with the hatred it deserves, I do not doubt <note>original: "non dubito"</note>... |

<page-num>612</page-num>

# The Good Effects, etc. Book IV.

Mr. Downing had barely finished delivering his message at the French Court when he received news from Turin and other parts that the Swiss Ambassador had concluded (or at least consented to) a treaty. This treaty had been rushed through <note>original: "hudled up"</note> by the French Ambassador, Servient, between the Duke of Savoy and the Duke's poor subjects [the Waldensians]. This news made Downing hurry even faster on his journey to Geneva to consult with Mr. Pell and Mr. Morland and to fully inform himself of the truth of the matter.

Upon his arrival at Geneva in the beginning of September 1655, he met with Mr. Pell and Mr. Morland. After conferring with them, he soon found that the report he had heard on the road concerning the unfortunate Treaty of Pignerol was indeed true. The state of affairs was now completely altered, and everything was set upon a new footing <note>original: "Basis"</note>; consequently, after reviewing their joint instructions, he realized their negotiation was at an end. As the saying goes,
> What begins as a beautiful woman ends as a fish.
> <note>original Latin: "Desinit in piscem mulier formosa supernè," a quote from Horace’s *Ars Poetica* describing a promising start that leads to a disappointing or grotesque conclusion.</note>
> *And when men’s hopes and expectations are raised to the highest pitch, they are often frustrated and ruined in a moment. It is in the power of man to appoint, but it is God alone who disposes of the outcome of all things as He pleases.*

About eight days after Mr. Downing's arrival at Geneva, he received orders to return speedily to England. Mr. Pell and Mr. Morland received instructions to remain in that city to manage the money collected in England, Wales, and Ireland for the relief of the poor Protestants, of which the reader has already had a detailed account in the previous chapter.

Not many days after Mr. Downing’s departure (which was about September 12, 1655), Mr. D'Ommeren arrived. He was a Commissioner Extraordinary from the States General <note>the governing body of the Dutch Republic</note>, who had hoped to meet His Highness's [Cromwell's] commissioners there and accompany them from Geneva to Savoy. But alas, it was all in vain; he came too late for anything except to hear the sad stories and see the mournful faces of many honest and intelligent people regarding the recent treaty. This was indeed a business of no small consequence, and therefore it is appropriate that the reader receive a distinct and particular account of it in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER VII.

### *The Negotiations of the four Ambassadors of the Protestant <note>original: "Evangelical"</note> Cantons of Switzerland at the Court of Savoy, and the Treaty concluded at Pignerol. Together with a copy of the report <note>original: "Relation"</note> which they themselves sent to their superiors at that time.*

->An authentic copy of the true original of this report, signed by Mr. Andrew Schmidt (the Under-Secretary of State at Zurich) in his own hand, is to be seen in the public library of the famous University of Cambridge.<-

Having guided the kind and patient reader this far through a multitude of winding paths and difficult passages, and brought him safely to that famous and lovely city of Geneva—where he has rested and refreshed himself for a while—I have also introduced him to the public ministers of the two powerful states of England and the United Provinces <note>The Dutch Republic</note>. I must now ask the reader (though I fear he will be very reluctant to leave such good company behind) to take one more journey over the Alps. There, he may see things that will abundantly satisfy his curiosity, even if they do not meet his expectations.

It was in June 1655 that the Protestant <note>original: "Evangelical"</note> Cantons—now being assured that their appeals to the Court of Savoy would be supported by the other Protestant states, at least by England and the United Provinces—resolved to send an embassy to the Duke. In preparation for this, they appointed Major Weis to take a second journey to Turin to request both from the people and from their Prince a cessation of arms and all hostile acts. This was intended to ensure that affairs were in a better state of readiness for the arrival of their ambassadors. They also communicated this intent in a letter to the Duke, which they sent at the same time by the hands of Major Weis.

# A Letter from his Royal Highness the Duke of Savoy, in answer to that of the Protestant <note>original: "Evangelical"</note> Cantons, of June 17, 1655, delivered by the hands of their Deputy, Major Weis. Received by the Ambassadors at Aigle on July 10/19, 1655.

An authentic copy of the true original, signed by Mr. Andrew Shmidt (Under-Secretary of State at Zurich) in his own hand, is to be seen, together with the rest, in the public library of the famous University of Cambridge.

->Most noble Lords; Our most dear and special friends, Allies, and Confederates,<-

We have received your letter of the 17th day of last month by the hands of Major Weis, your deputy. Having declared his commission to us and expressed the good intentions of your Lordships regarding everything that concerns us and our interests, we could not help but return our thanks to you. We do so with the same demonstration of that good diplomatic relationship which we have always maintained and evidenced on our part. 

In the meantime, we are glad that we gave your Lordships undeniable proof of this during the first journey of Major Weis to these parts from this place. We were unable to make any progress with those rebels <note>original: "Rebells"; the Duke's derogatory term for his Waldensian subjects who were resisting religious persecution.</note> in anything that might lead to a treaty on their behalf, so great was their obstinacy and hardness of heart. 

The King of France has indicated his intentions to intercede for the pardon of those rebels. Because the respect we bear to his Majesty does not permit us to refuse his mediation, we have remitted the management of this business wholly and entirely into his hands. Therefore, since his Majesty is already engaged in the matter, we can by no means admit any competitors into an affair which he has undertaken alone without diminishing the respect we owe to him. 

Nonetheless, we shall be very glad if the rebels will give us an opportunity to do anything for them upon this occasion that may satisfy you. It shall always be close to our hearts to do so, and we would readily give you a guaranteed testimony of this by granting that truce which Major Weis has propound-

...presented to us, if it would be consistent with our dignity to accept such a thing from our rebellious subjects after they refused our first offer to them of the very same thing. Furthermore, the truce which your deputy proposes in preparation for the arrival of your ambassadors now seems completely unnecessary for any mediation for the reasons mentioned above (which we have explained to him more specifically in person). While such a request would be acceptable to us in any other circumstance, this truce would be of no use in this current situation <note>original: "Conjuncture"</note>, since the reason for that request is now void. 

To this we shall add that since his Most Christian Majesty <note>original: "his most Christian Majesty"; the traditional title for the King of France, in this case Louis XIV.</note> has taken full responsibility for this matter, we cannot accept the truce or anything else of that nature without offending the respect we owe him. You are so wise that, without question, you will agree with us and will recognize that we cannot act otherwise toward such a great King who is managing this business. All we can do is wait for the outcome and success of his efforts, just as we expect a resolution to the just complaints we made in our previous letter. 

We repeat those complaints now regarding the poor treatment of our subjects in your territories since the uprising of our rebels—indeed, even since the return of your deputy—which has happened without any basis in fairness or reason. We hope that you will provide us with proper and just reparations, and also severely punish the harmful actions of the physician Guerin. We have sent him back to you as a testimony of the esteem we have for that friendship and good diplomatic relationship <note>original: "Correspondence"</note> which we have strictly maintained with you. Therefore, we reasonably expect you to reciprocate in this situation for the preservation of our good union. The interruption of this union would have very dangerous consequences, as you can foresee in your wisdom.

And upon this ground we pray,

<page-num>618</page-num>
<header>The Negotiation Book. IV.</header>

From this letter by the Duke, it is very easy to guess that he strongly desired and intended to discourage the ambassadors from continuing their journey toward Turin. If they had not already begun their journey, we do not doubt that other plans might have been made; however, since the ambassadors were already at Aigle <note>original: "Aigle"; a town in the Swiss Canton of Vaud, then under the rule of Bern.</note> before receiving this letter, they resolved to continue toward Turin, where they arrived on July 14/24, 1655.

Upon their arrival, they found very few preparations—or rather, none at all—made for their mediation or for beginning a treaty with the Duke (as they had hoped). Furthermore, during that entire interval of time, Major Weis was unable to obtain permission to have any communication whatsoever with the poor people of the Valleys <note>The Waldensians (Vaudois), the Protestant inhabitants of the Alpine valleys of Piedmont.</note>. The only information they could gather was from the secretary of the French Ambassador, Monsieur Servient, who had recently returned from the Valleys and reported that he found the people in general very inclined toward peace and a settlement.

In truth, that secretary (I leave it to the reader to guess whose orders he was following) had taken a very effective approach to bring them to a "settlement" of this nature. At that very moment, he summoned the primary leaders of the poor people, who were then in the Valley of Perosa, in the name of his master the Ambassador, to meet with him. He claimed his purpose was to propose something (as he pretended) to the people in general. But while he was distracting them with such talk, the enemy’s entire army of cavalry and infantry furiously attacked the groups of poor people who had been left behind on the slopes of Angrogna without their commanders. If the execution of the attack had matched the intent of the plan, they would all have been miserably slaughtered.

About three days after arriving in Turin—having been treated very nobly in the meantime by the special order of the Duke and *Madam Royale* <note>original: "Madam Royale"; Christine of France, the Duchess of Savoy and sister of King Louis XIII of France, who acted as regent for her son.</note>—these ambassadors and their retinue were conducted by Count Miradour, the Master of Ceremonies, in two of the Duke's coaches to Rivoli. There they were granted an audience, and after a short speech, they presented His Royal Highness with the following proposal in writing, written in the French language.

### The Proposal of the Four Ambassadors of the Evangelical Cantons of Switzerland to the Duke of Savoy at their Audience on July 17/27, 1655.

An authentic copy of the true original, which was communicated to the author by Mr. *Andrew Schmidt*, Under-Secretary of State at *Zurich*.

->Most Serene Prince,<-

<note>original (French): "Avant toutes choses Nous sommes instruits au nom de Nos Seigneurs et Superieurs tous les Cantons Evangeliques en Suisse, de saluer avec toute sorte de respect et reverence Vostre Altesse Royale avec offre de leurs tres affectionnes Services, vraye amity, et bonne correspondence. Et en apres de lui representer deüement l’estat de ses pauures gens, &c."</note> First and foremost, we are instructed in the name of our Lords and Superiors—all the Evangelical Cantons in Switzerland—to greet your Royal Highness with every kind of respect and reverence, offering their most affectionate services, true friendship, and good relations. ->Most Serene Prince,<-

We are commanded, first and foremost, to greet your Royal Highness with all respect and reverence in the name and on behalf of all the *Evangelical Cantons of Switzerland, our Lords and Superiors, with an offer of their most affectionate services, true friendship, and good relations*. In the next place, we are to represent in an appropriate manner the condition of your poor subjects who profess the Reformed Religion <note>The "Reformed Religion" refers to the Protestant faith of the Waldensians.</note> in the *Valleys of Luserna, Angrogna, San Martino*, and the neighboring areas. 

The Evangelical Cantons were informed by letters from France this past February concerning that severe order which Auditor Gastaldo <note>Andrea Gastaldo, the official who issued the January 1655 edict ordering the Waldensians to abandon their homes or convert to Catholicism.</note> caused to be published against those who profess that religion. In this order, they were commanded under penalty of death to either abandon their houses and estates or to sell those estates to *Catholics* within three days, or else face confiscation of their property. 

Because of their shared faith, the Swiss Cantons have been moved to great pity for their condition, leading them to write your Royal Highness a *letter of intercession* on behalf of those subjects with all due respect. They were hopeful that, undoubtedly, considering the ancient friendship and understanding that has existed between the...

...between the most Serene House of *Savoy* and the *Commonwealth of Switzerland*, your *Royal Highness* would be pleased to favorably accept their mediation, as you expressed in your answer to our *superiors*. 

Furthermore, in that letter of yours, you seemed to imply that you had some cause for jealousy and suspicion—that your subjects in the *Valleys* had provided them with information about their condition and had otherwise sought help from foreign states, consequently making themselves guilty of treason and rebellion against their own natural Prince. The *Evangelical Cantons* have judged it appropriate—indeed, very necessary—to clear those poor, suspected subjects of yours before your *Royal Highness*. At the same time, they wish to repeat their plea for the subjects' re-establishment and restoration, along with the free enjoyment of those rights and concessions which your *ancestors* of glorious memory granted them, and which your *Royal Highness* has likewise confirmed.

In the meantime, it is notoriously evident how much rigor and violence some have used against those poor people. We do not attribute this to your *Royal Highness* (as it is so contrary to your *virtue*, *glory*, and *mercy*), but rather to those ill-intentioned persons who hunt for the ruin and total destruction of that little flock <note>original: "little flock" — a common biblical metaphor used by the Waldensians to describe their small, persecuted community.</note>. This extreme misery and affliction has so stirred the hearts of our people that our *superiors* have had great difficulty restraining several thousand of their subjects from rushing to the aid and relief of their distressed and oppressed brothers. We are also informed that a similar readiness has been observed among the subjects of other states. 

For this reason, and to prevent such a dangerous situation, they resolved to send us in our capacity as their *ambassadors* to your *Royal Highness*. We most earnestly and urgently entreat you (with all respect and reverence) to graciously consider the cause of those poor, afflicted *Christians* so that their property may be restored and they may receive compensation for their losses. This should be done in such a way that, in the future, they may enjoy these rights with security and liberty of conscience. 

We also ask that your *Royal Highness* be pleased to order the release of those poor prisoners detained in *Turin* or elsewhere. Please set at liberty both the persons and the consciences of those who have been taken away to various places in *Piedmont* and forced to renounce their religion since the beginning of the recent troubles, allowing them to return without facing any punishment. 

In doing this, your *Royal Highness* will perform an action worthy of your *greatness* (which will exalt the glory of your *mercy*). We are certain that your subjects will use this grace and mercy for no other purpose than to show their complete gratitude through constant humility and obedience to your commands, as the commands of their natural *Prince* and *Sovereign*. Indeed, should they fail in their duty toward you, we have already instructed them otherwise, and we shall use our utmost efforts to encourage their loyalty. We will perform every helpful service and apply every possible remedy to reach an agreement. To this end, we entreat your *Royal Highness* to permit us to send representatives to visit those poor people on our behalf, to learn of their current state and condition. And being fully persuaded that...

The proposal that the said *Ambassadors* then made to the *Duke* was as follows; a few days later—specifically <note>original: "viz." (videlicet)</note> on July 20/30, 1655—they were visited by the *Baron of Greisy*, a Counselor of State. He had also been authorized with a letter of credentials from his *Royal Highness* to negotiate with them. The *Baron of Greisy* brought with him the *Duke’s* written answer to the proposal mentioned above. The core substance of this reply was, in part, to level heavy accusations of *rebellion* and stubbornness against his subjects, which served to justify all the actions the Court of *Savoy* had taken against them. It also served to show them that, despite all this, his *Royal Highness*—due to the intervention of the *King of France* (to whom he had completely entrusted the matter)—had already offered those subjects a full pardon and *amnesty* for all the crimes and offenses they had committed, along with the free exercise of their religion within all their ancient borders and limits.

Furthermore, the *Ambassadors* were granted the liberty to travel into the *Valleys* and speak with the people there in person. Consequently, the next day, they went to *Pinerolo* <note>original: "Pignerol"</note> and there concluded (or rather, witnessed the conclusion of) a treaty, which will be included at the end of this chapter in its original language.

Now, because the handling and processing of this affair was somewhat complex and criticized by many, the author believes the best way to prove his impartiality and integrity to the discerning <note>original: "Judicious"</note> reader is to include the actual report <note>original: "Relation"</note> which those four *Ambassadors* sent to their superiors while they were still residing in those parts.

He let it be known that, because of significant and pressing business, he could no longer remain here. ...to remain firm in their resolutions, and that therefore the representatives of the Valleys <note>original German: "Talluth," likely referring to the leaders or deputies of the Waldensian communities</note> should go once more to the Lord Ambassador and urgently request that he advance their cause as quickly and effectively as possible. After we had spoken at length about the proposals made by the Lord Ambassador, we found that the exchange of lands (for the reasons mentioned previously) was not helpful and would also proceed very slowly. Furthermore, it was considered very dangerous to rely entirely on the Duchess's <note>Christina of France (1606–1663), the Duchess of Savoy, who was acting as regent.</note> mercy and mediation. Likewise, they did not even want to speak of submitting the affair to the decision of a foreign judge. After expressing their thanks and holding their own private discussion, the representatives of the Valleys shared their declaration with us: They were willing to leave Campiglione, Bibiana, and Fenile for the sake of more quickly obtaining a cherished peace, as they must always live in great worry and danger in those places and cannot enjoy religious freedom there. Regarding Luserna, they would have liked to keep it, especially because of the market and the tradesmen and craftsmen there. However, they were willing to surrender even that place rather than prevent peace. Indeed, in an extreme case, they would also give up Bricherasio. In return, however, they demand to keep La Torre and San Giovanni, and that the <term>free exercise of religion</term> <note>original Latin: "liberum religionis exercitium"</note> be granted to them there.

<column-break/>

...decided that we ought to stick to our former resolutions, and that therefore those of the Valleys should make another address to the Lord Ambassador and be very persistent <note>original: "importunate"</note> with him, so that their business might be advanced in the fastest and best way possible. Now, after a long conference about the proposals which the Lord Ambassador had made, we found that the exchanging of the lands would not be practical for the reasons previously mentioned, and would only delay the business. Likewise, it was very dangerous to throw themselves absolutely upon the mercy and mediation of the Duchess. Without even mentioning the referral of that affair to any foreign judge’s decision, those of the Valleys—having returned thanks and conferred privately among themselves—declared to us that, for the sake of more quickly obtaining a precious peace, they were ready to leave Campiglione, Bibiana, and Fenile. These were places where they would always have to live in great fear and anxiety, without being able to enjoy the liberty of their religion. But as for Luserna, they would gladly keep that, especially because of the market, the trade, and the manufacturing of that place. Nevertheless, they were ready to surrender even that place as well, rather than block the peace. Indeed, in a case of extreme necessity, they would give up Bricherasio to boot. But on the other hand, they desired to keep San Giovanni and La Torre, and to have the free exercise of their religion granted to them there.
</columns>

<summary>The Waldensian representatives decide to compromise on several of their ancestral lands, including Luserna and Bricherasio, to secure a faster peace treaty, provided they are allowed to keep La Torre and San Giovanni with guaranteed religious freedom.</summary>

# The Negotiation: Book IV.

<columns>
In the afternoon, the representatives of the Valleys <note>original: "Valley-men"</note> came to us again to inform us that Lord Truchi had met with the [French] Ambassador <note>Abel Servien (1593–1659), the French diplomat mediating the treaty</note>, and that their situation had not improved. This was because the Lord Ambassador refused to grant them Lucerna <note>Luserna San Giovanni</note> and would only permit half of the lands in question to be exchanged for others. As for the other half, they were to be paid for them, or else the matter would be referred to the Judge at Chambery <note>the location of the Sovereign Council of Savoy</note>. Consequently, the poor people feared that all of this was merely a strategy to frustrate them with delays.

Lords Truchi and Greisy visited us a second time and attempted to persuade us through a long speech that His Royal Highness [the Duke of Savoy] had sufficient cause to take La Torre <note>Torre Pellice</note> and San Giovanni from them, based on the grounds and reasons they provided in writing. We later shared these documents with the people, who refuted them.

On Friday the 27th, the Baron of Greisy brought us news that His Royal Highness would never voluntarily concede the matter of San Giovanni and La Torre, but would rather allow the business to be decided by foreign judges outside of Savoy. However, we could not advise the people to agree to this. They then declared that they would prefer to give up Lucerna as well, provided that La Torre and San Giovanni might remain entirely theirs.

Soon after this, we were visited by the Lord Ambassador, who proposed the same thing the Baron de Greisy had done earlier, representing that he had done everything in his power up to this point—

<column-break/>

After midday, the representatives <note>original German: "Talluth," a term for the Waldensian deputies</note> came back to us, reporting that Mr. Truchi had been with the Mr. Ambassador, and that the matter had not improved. This was because the Mr. Ambassador would in no way grant them Lucerna, and would only allow half of the abandoned properties to be exchanged for others, while the remaining half should be paid for, or else submitted to the judge at Chambery. They worried that the matter was being delayed indefinitely <note>original German: "uff den langen banck spillen," an idiom meaning to put something on the long bench/stall</note>.

Mr. Truchi and Greisy came once again and tried to claim through a lengthy discourse that the side of His Royal Highness <note>original Latin: "S. A. R." for Sua Altezza Reale</note> had enough cause to also take La Torre and St. Giovanni from them, according to the written reasons handed over, which were afterwards communicated by us to the representatives and refuted by them.

On Friday the 27th, Mr. Baron de Greisy brought us the news that His Royal Highness would not concede anything amicably regarding St. Jean and La Tour, but would rather have the matter decided by foreign judges outside of Savoy. However, we could not advise the representatives to do this; they then declared again that they would even let Lucerne go, if only La Tour and St. Jean remained purely theirs.

Immediately after this, we were visited by the Mr. Ambassador, who proposed exactly what Mr. Greisy had proposed, mentioning that he had indeed done his best until now—
</columns>

<columns>
However, it was believed on the Savoyard side that the people of the Valleys <note>original German: "Talluth" (Thalleute), referring to the Vaudois</note> must be punished for their heavy faults by the removal of San Giovanni <note>St. Jean</note> and La Torre <note>la Tour</note>. In return, they would be compensated for what they were leaving behind, half by exchanging the lands elsewhere and half by payment. Lucerna <note>Lucerne</note> was not to be kept at all. He again thought the best thing would be for them to submit to Madame Royale <note>Christina of France (1606–1663), the Duchess of Savoy</note> and seek her intercession, or to look for judges from elsewhere outside of both Savoy and Piedmont. Nevertheless, upon our very serious and earnest insistence, he would work to ensure that San Giovanni and La Torre might remain theirs, but without the exercise of their religion <note>original: "Religions exercice"</note>, which could not be granted to them. This was because in the year 1620 they had been forced to wall up the church at San Giovanni, and since then they have not been allowed to preach in either place; therefore, they would lose nothing regarding the exercise of religion in those areas.

On Saturday the 28th, Monsieur Leger and eight representatives from the Valleys reported that the Lord Ambassador had expressed anger toward them. He was displeased that the Lord Pianezza would not accept his proposal on their behalf. He also informed them that it would not be possible to exchange their property; rather, the Duke would prefer to pay them for everything as it stood. San Giovanni and La Torre would also have to be abandoned. However, because the Lord Ambassador saw that their request was not unreasonable, he intended to work further and would sooner write to his King...

<column-break/>

...power. But on the Duke's part, it was held necessary that those of the Valleys should be punished <note>original: "chastised"</note> for the serious offenses <note>original: "grievous enormities"</note> they had committed, by depriving them of San Giovanni and La Torre. As for the rest, half <note>original: "one moitie"</note> of their lands should be exchanged, and the other half paid for. Lucerna was not to be obtained under any terms, and he judged it their best course to yield themselves up entirely to Madame Royale and to beg for her intercession, or else to seek judges from both sides somewhere outside of Savoy and Piedmont. Nevertheless, by reason of our further serious and earnest requests <note>original: "instances"</note>, he would labor to ensure that San Giovanni and La Torre might remain with them, but without the exercise of their religion. This could not be granted to them because in the year 1620, they were forced to wall up the church at San Giovanni, and since then they have not had the liberty to preach in either of those places. Therefore, they are not being restricted at all regarding the exercise of their religion in those parts.

On Saturday the 28th, M<gloss>onsieu</gloss>r Leger and eight more from the Valleys came and informed us that the Ambassador had expressed great displeasure in their presence. He was frustrated that the Lord Pianezza <note>The Marquis of Pianezza, the Duke's chief minister and general</note> would not admit his proposal on their behalf. He also acquainted them with the fact that it was not possible to make an exchange for their lands. The Duke would rather buy them out altogether, and San Giovanni and La Torre must likewise be abandoned by them. But nevertheless, since the said Ambassador understood their request to be reasonable, he promised to make further requests, and would even write...
</columns>

...to the King his Master, and expect more effective orders. He also proposed that the matter might be brought before impartial judges of both one and the other religion. He added that it was no small act of graciousness <note>original: "condescension," meaning a voluntary waiver of a superior's rights</note> for a Prince to subject himself to foreign legal judgments.

On the Lord’s day in the morning, being the 29th, we were accompanied by some of the people of the Valleys to hear a sermon preached at Pinache <note>modern: Pinasca; original: Pinachia</note>. There we found a great multitude of the poor banished people of the Valleys, numbering about 1,600, young and old. We were met by about 60 musketeers <note>original: Musquetiers</note>, who also conducted us back again, together with several foreign gentlemen who, out of a zeal for religion, had joined those of the Valleys. They then and since have applied themselves to us, highly commending the valor and resolute courage of those of the Valleys, of whom there were about 1,000 in arms and 500 or 600 others. Those poor people were exceedingly rejoiced at our arrival, and we were hosted at the aforementioned Pinache.

On Monday, July 30, Lord Trucchi proposed another expedient <note>term: a practical, though perhaps temporary, solution</note>: namely, that at San Giovanni and La Torre, those of both religions should separate their habitations and lands. He proposed that each party, by way of exchange with one another, should keep their dwellings and lands separately. He hoped that in this way, all occasion for future strife—which for the most part proceeded from the cohabitation of those who were of different religions—might be prevented. Yet, notwithstanding this, the people of the Valleys should not only permit, but they themselves should also contribute to the repair of the Fort of La Torre...

<column-break/>

<note>The following is a modernization of the original German column</note>

...and expect more orders. He also proposed to let the matter come before impartial judges from both religions, mentioning that it was quite a significant step for a prince to go so far for his subjects and subject himself to foreign judgment.

On Sunday morning the 29th, in the company of several people of the Valleys <note>original German: "Talluten"</note>, we rode to Pinache for the sermon. There we met many exiled people of the Valley (said to be 1,600, young and old). About 60 musketeers <note>original German: "Fuseliers"</note> came toward us and escorted us back. Various brave gentlemen <note>original German: "Cavalters"</note>, who had joined those people out of religious zeal, reported to us then and afterward. They praised the bravery and heroic courage of the people of the Valleys, of whom about 1,000 were armed and another 500 or 600 others. The good people were very happy about our arrival, and we were hosted at the mentioned Pinache.

On Monday, July 30, Mr. Trucchi proposed another solution: namely, that at San Giovanni <note>original: St. Jean</note> and La Torre <note>original: la Tour</note>, those of both religions should separate themselves regarding their houses and goods. Each part should keep their houses and goods separately through exchange with one another. In this way, all cause for future disputes—which for the most part flowed from the cohabitation of those belonging to both religions—might be prevented. However, they should not only allow, but even contribute themselves to the repair of the fortress at La Torre...

### Extract of the second report <note>original: "Relation"</note>, which the Ambassadors of the Protestant <note>original: "Evangelical"</note> Cantons sent to their superiors from Pinerolo <note>original: "Pignerol"</note> on August 10/20, 1655.

->An authentic copy of the true original, signed by Mr. Andrew Schmidt, Under-Secretary of State of Zurich, which can be found in the public library of the famous University of Cambridge.<-

---

<columns>
->Right Honorable, etc.<-

By our letter dated August 1, your honors (we suppose) understood what had passed until that time regarding the business of the Protestant <note>original: "Evangelical"</note> believers <note>original: "professors"</note> in the Valleys of Piedmont, and how far the matter had then advanced. We do not doubt that through that report and what has happened since, your honors will see that we have exerted our best efforts according to our instructions and the letters sent to us from your honors. (The last of these, along with the mentioned papers dated July 28, was delivered to us last Sunday night via Aigle <note>A town in the Swiss canton of Vaud</note>). We have contributed everything we believed, based on the circumstances, might prove advantageous to those good people.

As an addition to that report, your honors may be pleased to take notice that on Thursday, the second of this month, Mr. Leger and Mr. Lepreux <note>Jean Léger and Mr. Lepreux were prominent Waldensian pastors and leaders</note>, together with some other people from the Valleys, came to us. They informed us that they had received news—namely, that their men were in a good position <note>original: "posture"</note> and that more were arriving daily...

<column-break/>

->Highly Respected, etc. <note>original German: "Hochgeachte, &c."</note><-

From the detailed report that we sent to Your Graces on August 1, you will undoubtedly have already understood what had occurred up to that time regarding the business of the Protestant <note>original German: "Evangelische"</note> Valleys in Piedmont, and the status of the matter then. We do not doubt that Your Graces will see from that report and what has followed since that we have, to the best of our ability and according to our instructions and the letters sent to us (the last of which, dated July 28 with the attachments, we received this past Sunday evening via Aigle), contributed our best efforts. We did what we believed, according to the state of affairs, would be beneficial for those good people.

Your Graces may further understand from this continuation of the report that on Thursday the 2nd of this month, Messrs. Leger and Lepreux, along with several other Valley people <note>original German: "Talluthen," referring to the Waldensians</note>, came to us and communicated the news they had received: that their people were in a good position and more were coming daily...
</columns>

# Chapter VII. Concerning the Swiss Ambassadors.

<columns>
[The troops] are in good formation, and more join them daily from neighboring areas. They can also expect more help to follow without fail if needed. They requested that several specific points be recommended to the French Ambassador. Consequently, we did not fail to visit the said Ambassador and recommend the points regarding the people of the Valleys <note>original: "Talluthen"</note> in the best possible manner. We received a fairly good response from him, as he offered to do his best regarding almost all points as far as possible. However, quite unexpectedly, Count Trucchi came to us immediately after, complaining about our dear fellow believers <note>fellow Protestants</note>. He claimed they were always bringing up new issues and trying to force the Prince to grant their wishes against all propriety. He said this could not be done; instead, they must submit various matters to the mercy of His Royal Highness. And although more favors might be shown to them, these could not be included in the formal agreement <note>original: "instrument"</note> by way of conditions <note>original: "per modum conditionis"</note> to legally bind His Royal Highness. Nevertheless, whatever His Royal Highness could do at our intercession (which he values highly) would occur outside of the formal agreement being drafted, etc.

Because of this, we not only impressed the necessity of the matter upon Count Trucchi ourselves, but also communicated it to Mr. Leger and Mr. Lepreux and their associates, and advised them to better inform Count Trucchi themselves regarding these issues.

On Friday the 3rd of this month, Mr. Leger and Mr. Lepreux, along with the other deputies <note>original: "usschützen," meaning delegates or representatives</note> of the Valleys, met with both Count Trucchi and the French Ambassador, presenting their...

<column-break/>

[...joined] in with them from the neighboring parts. Also, in case of necessity, they were sure of more supplies to follow. They entreated us to recommend certain proposals on their behalf to the French Ambassador. Whereupon we did not fail to visit the said Lord Ambassador and recommend the aforementioned proposals of these people to him to the utmost. We indeed found him fairly well-disposed, so that he engaged upon almost every point to do the best he possibly could on their behalf. But most unexpectedly, there arrived in an instant the Lord Count Trucchi, making great complaints to us against our dear friends of the same profession <note>meaning fellow Protestants</note>. He said they were always finding new devices and most improperly went about trying to force their business from the Prince according to their own wills; this was not to be obtained in this manner, but they must refer themselves in the particulars to His Royal Highness's clemency. And though more favors may be shown them, yet the same could not be inserted in the formal agreement <note>original: "Instrument"</note> by way of conditions to bind His Royal Highness thereby. Nevertheless, that which His Royal Highness should be able to do upon our intercession (which is of no small esteem with him) would be performed just as well, even if not inserted in the agreement, etc.

Upon this, we not only showed the necessity of it to the said Lord Count Truchi, but also shared it with Mr. Leger and Mr. Lepreux and their associates, and advised them to better inform the said Lord themselves.

On Friday, the 3rd of this month, Mr. Leger and Mr. Lepreux, with the rest of the deputies of the people of the Valleys, were with the Lord Count Truchi as also with the French Ambassador, making their formal statement <note>original: "Remonstrance"</note> and receiving thereupon...

...thereupon a written proposal <note>original: "project in writing"</note> of what was intended for them was presented, which did not satisfy them at all. Because of this, when they came to us for advice, we considered the matter and its circumstances. We advised them that, in our opinion, they should sit down together, weigh every article carefully, and put them into a proper written format. We told them that if they shared this with us afterward, we would be ready to advise them further. After supper, they returned to us and reported how they had presented those clarified articles to the Lord Ambassador and had most earnestly requested that they be granted. However, he refused to accept them and was quite angry with them. Immediately afterward, Baron de Grefy arrived, confirming this and saying that the Lord Ambassador and Count Truchi were almost resolved to abandon the treaty altogether and leave. He hinted that we had incited the people of the Valleys to demand these "innovations," as he called them. At this point, we not only explained the necessity of the matter to him ourselves, but also had the people of the Valleys explain themselves fully. This satisfied him at last, and the next morning early, the Ambassador sent his secretary to ask us to assist further in revising the agreement alongside Lords Truchi and Grefy, and to contribute our best efforts to the business.

After sending for the said deputies of the Valleys and impressing upon them the urgency <note>original: "Exigencie"</note> of the various points or articles, and understanding their individual and collective opinions, we went to the Lord Ambassador's quarters. # Chapter 7: Of the Swiss Ambassadors

Trucchi, Orenco, Grefy, Berroquin <note>original: "Perroquin" in German, "Berroquin" in English</note>, and several other distinguished gentlemen and persons of quality, along with the deputies of the Valleys <note>original: "Talluthen," a term for the Waldensian inhabitants of the Alpine valleys</note>, debated the matter point by point for three hours. We put it into writing, made four copies of the agreement, and sent one to the Court that same day for ratification.

Toward evening, the deputies of the Valleys came to us and kindly thanked us for the efforts we made that day. They asked us to remain mindful of the things that could not be fully resolved in the previous discussion, specifically:
* The status of the fort at La Torre.
* The specific number of years they should be exempt from all taxes and burdens.
* The guarantee that the value of the estates they must give up within the Pellice River area would be paid to them in cash <note>original: "bahrem geldt" / "ready money"</note> at a certain time, in case they cannot sell the properties themselves.

We promised to negotiate these matters for them.

On Sunday, August 15, we again attended worship services at Pinache.

On Monday evening, the official decree <note>original: "patent"</note> arrived from the Court. It was shared with the deputies of the Valleys, who brought it to us the next morning, Tuesday. They provided a detailed explanation of the points they found burdensome and asked for our advice. We advised them to immediately and diligently present their grievances to Count Trucchi and to humbly pray for redress and improvement. They did so, but were unable to obtain anything. Consequently, the French Ambassador asked us again through his secretary to come to him that afternoon to help finalize the settlement <note>original: "accommodation"</note>.

# The Negotiation Book IV.

<column>

...tion. Once we were fully informed about what was still missing, and having shared our advice with the people of the Valleys, we went at the scheduled hour to the Lord Ambassador. In his presence, and before most of the gentlemen mentioned above, the legal document <note>original: "Instrument," referring to the formal treaty</note> was read all over again. The deputies of the Valleys, a considerable number of whom were present, were heard regarding their objections. Matters were debated for three hours, arguing for and against <note>original: "pro and con"</note>, until the whole document was essentially corrected and amended to their satisfaction. 

The only exception was that after we had withdrawn, when nothing remained but for the people of the Valleys to sign, they refused to do so. Their reason was that the document made not the slightest mention of either our mediation or our intercession on their behalf. Consequently, after supper, the Baron de Gresy came to us to inform us of this and to explain how much the French were offended by it. He asked us to persuade the people to sign. He offered to help find a way to settle this business to our satisfaction and that of the Valley people, especially since the Lord Ambassador—acting on behalf of his King—would not allow anyone else to be mentioned in the peace document. We did not fail to give him the necessary response.

On Wednesday—yesterday morning—the deputies of the Valleys came to inform us of this in detail. They represented to us that since not only your Honors <note>referring to the Swiss Protestant authorities</note> from the beginning, but we also up to this point, had so faithfully supported and committed ourselves to them, they were prepared to reject the peace entirely if honorable mention were not made of your Honors or us in the document, as we deserved.

</column>

<note>The following is a contemporary German translation of the English text in the left column.</note>

After receiving a detailed report on what was still lacking, and after giving our opinion to the people of the Valleys <note>original: "Talluthen," the Waldensians</note>, we returned at the appointed hour to the Lord Ambassador. In front of him and most of the gentlemen mentioned above, the document was read once more. The deputies of the Valleys, who were present in significant numbers, were heard regarding their concerns. For three hours, they argued for and against <note>original: "pro & contra"</note> each other, and finally, almost everything was corrected and improved to their satisfaction. 

The only exception was that after our departure, when it came time for the people of the Valleys to sign, they refused to do so because the document did not mention our mediation or intercession in a single word. Therefore, only after supper did the Baron de Gresy come to us to reveal this and to say how angry the Lord Ambassador was about it. He requested that we lead the people of the Valleys to sign. He offered to help think of how this matter might be addressed to our and the Valleys' satisfaction, since the Lord Ambassador, on behalf of his King, would not tolerate anyone else in any way in the peace decree <note>original: "Friedenspatent"</note>. We did not fail to give him the necessary answer.

On Wednesday—yesterday morning—we were also informed of this at length by the deputies of the Valleys. They further declared that because not only your Honors from the beginning, but we also up to this time, had so faithfully burdened ourselves with their cause and accepted them, they would rather not accept the peace at all if your Honors or we were not mentioned in the document in an honorable and well-deserved manner.

### Chap. VII. Of the Swiss Ambassadors.

We replied to them that this request was indeed fair, and we would see for ourselves whether it could be formally established in a specific way. However, if that were not possible, we would not let it hinder the peace at all, but would wait to see how we might be acknowledged in other ways, as had been suggested. We then returned to the Lord Ambassador <note>The French Ambassador, representing King Louis XIV.</note> and discussed the necessity of this matter with him. He was quite offended on behalf of his Majesty, who—having taken on this task solely at the urging of the Lord Protector of England <note>Oliver Cromwell.</note>, the Lords States General of the Netherlands, and your Honours—felt it improper for anyone else to be included in this peace treaty at the same level as the King. Nevertheless, he offered to provide a letter to your Honours to give full testimony of our faithful efforts in these negotiations, and he asked for the same from us. We were also encouraged to hope that we would receive a similar acknowledgement from His Royal Highness <note>Charles Emmanuel II, Duke of Savoy.</note>. Therefore, we chose to be satisfied with this rather than delay the long-awaited peace any further and cause more expense and trouble for the people of the Valleys <note>original: "Talluthen," a reference to the Waldensians.</note>. During this visit with the Lord Ambassador, we also recommended the general cause of the people of the Valleys to him, specifically requesting that the fort at La Tour be dismantled <term>slighted: to demolish or dismantle a fortification so it can no longer be defended.</term> as soon as possible; he promised to do his best to ensure this.

Following this, we summoned the deputies of the Valleys and persuaded them to sign what had been decided yesterday. They then went with our Secretary to see Count Truchi and signed the document as requested. The official patents <note>The formal legal documents or decrees granting the peace terms.</note> were issued immediately, along with several copies (one of which we have kept in our possession...

To whom we replied, that indeed the thing was just, and we would endeavour ourselves to get it obtained in a certain way. But in case we should not prevail, yet we would by no means hinder the peace, but wait to see how we shall be otherwise considered, according to the intimation given. Hereupon we repaired to the Lord Ambassador, and had a conference with him about this matter. He resented it very highly on his Majesty’s behalf, who alone—upon the application of the Lord Protector of England, the Lords States General of the Netherlands, and of your Honours—had charged himself wholly with the business, and took it ill that anyone else in any kind whatsoever should be mentioned in this treaty of peace. Nevertheless, he offered us his letters to your Honours to give ample testimony of our faithful endeavours in this negotiation, desiring the like from us. Besides, hopes were given that we should receive a similar attestation on our behalf from his Royal Highness. For this cause we were content to acquiesce, rather than the happy peace should be delayed any longer, and more charge and trouble be brought upon the people of the Valleys. In the time of this visit to the Lord Ambassador, we likewise recommended the cause of the people of the Valleys in general, and especially desired that the fort at La Tour might speedily be dismantled <term>slighted: destroyed or made unusable for military purposes.</term>, wherein he promised his best endeavours.

During this time, we made several visits, including one to the French Ambassador, who also returned the visit. 

Regarding the prisoners: the monks and others belonging to the Duke who were held by the people of the Valleys were set free on Monday. On Tuesday morning, more than sixty Waldensians who had been imprisoned at Turin—including men, women, young women, and children—were also released. Forty of these individuals had previously renounced their faith out of weakness <note>original: "frailty," referring to forced conversions to Catholicism</note>, but they have since returned to our churches with great remorse. These people were provided with food and drink—better than the usual prison rations—and given a small amount of money. They were then brought on their way toward Pinerolo and presented to us. After we spoke to them kindly and dismissed them...

From this, your Excellencies will see how welcome the cooperation of the English and Dutch ambassadors would have been to us in this business, and for what reasons we, on our part, could not delay the execution of the peace according to Mr. Morland's request. But the reason we allowed the treaties to proceed so much sooner was, among other things, because the time of the arrival of the English and Dutch ambassadors could not be exactly known; nor was there any certain information available regarding them at this time. Since we saw that the peace was truly being implemented without further hindrance, we departed in God’s name on Wednesday morning, November 21st <note>original: "21/11"</note> of this month, from Pinerolo back to Turin. We were accompanied by the Baron de Gressy and were nobly entertained along the way at Orbassano <note>original: "Orbazan"</note> by order of His Royal Highness <note>Charles Emmanuel II, Duke of Savoy</note>. Even since our return here, our expenses continue to be paid by his appointment.

**As** soon as we arrived here that evening, an express messenger also came from Geneva with your Lordships' <note>The authorities of the Protestant Swiss Cantons</note> two letters from the 9th and 10th of this month, together with a copy of Mr. Morland's <note>Samuel Morland, the English envoy sent by Oliver Cromwell</note> letter, to which we responded according to the enclosed copy. In that letter, your Lordships shall see how gladly we would have welcomed the cooperation of the English and Dutch commissioners, and the reasons that prevented us, on our part, from delaying the implementation of the peace according to Mr. Morland's request. Indeed, our allowing the treaty to proceed this far was (among other things) because the arrival time of the English and Dutch commissioners could not be known exactly, nor was there any certain news yet concerning it. Besides, it was much to be feared that the business might have been delayed until winter, when it would have been impossible for the poor people of the valleys to have survived any longer in those mountains. And even if those commissioners had come, it is a question—

<column-break/>

[German Translation of the above]

With travel money <note>original: "zehrpfening"</note> also left to them by us, they thanked us most highly with weeping eyes, and after being received for a midday meal by the deputies at Pinerolo, they went to their own people with joy. Now that we have seen that the peace is achieving its implementation without hindrance, we departed on Wednesday morning the 21st of this month in God’s name from Pinerolo back toward Turin, accompanied by the Baron de Gressy. In the meantime, we were grandly entertained at Orbassano by order of His Royal Highness. Since our return here, the hospitality also continues.

**As** soon as we arrived here on the evening of the aforementioned day, a messenger <note>original: "Postilion"</note> from Geneva also arrived with your Lordships' two letters from the 9th and 10th of this month, as well as a copy of the attached letter from Mr. Morland, to which we responded as the attachment specifies. Your Lordships will see from this how dear the cooperation of the English and Dutch ambassadors would have been to us in this business, and for what reasons we, on our part, could not hold up the implementation of the peace according to Mr. Morland's request. That we allowed the negotiations to proceed so much sooner was, among other things, because the time of arrival of the English and Dutch ambassadors could not be known exactly, nor was there any certain information available at this time. Meanwhile, it was to be feared that the matter might be delayed until winter, when it would no longer have been possible for the valley people <note>original: "Thalleuthen," referring to the Waldensians</note> to remain in such mountains. Even if they had come, it would have been worth considering whether they might have faced the same [treatment] as us—

## Chapter VII. Of the Swiss Ambassadors

We considered whether their involvement <note>original: "Cooperation"</note> in the peace treaty might have been challenged—just as our own was—and whether the resulting exchange of letters and arguments might have dragged the matter out too long or caused other complications. This was a significant concern because His Royal Highness <note>Charles Emmanuel II, Duke of Savoy</note> had granted the role of mediator entirely to His Majesty <note>Louis XIV of France</note>, whom other states had also asked to take on this responsibility.

Furthermore, the French Ambassador openly stated that if the people of the Valleys <note>the Waldensians</note> did not agree to reasonable terms in these external matters, his King would withdraw all protection and refuge in France and would no longer tolerate or endure them there. We will omit other reasons for now, as they are better explained in person at a later time.

Since our return here to Turin, we have not failed to press for the fulfillment of the separate article <note>original: "articuls a parte"</note> regarding the dismantling <note>original: "slighting" or "demolition"</note> of the fort at La Torre. We have received strong assurances that this will be carried out. However, the process has been delayed by the court's mourning for the Duchess Dowager of Mantua <note>Margaret of Savoy, 1589–1655</note>, the former Governor of Portugal and sister to His Royal Highness’s late father. She passed away at this court during her journey from Spain. 

Additionally, the illness of the Duchess Royal <note>Christine of France, the Duke's mother and regent</note> has also hindered us; we could not press the matter further at court while she was unwell. Nevertheless, we are resolved to pursue this in earnest as soon as audiences are granted again. For this reason, we cannot yet give your Lordships a specific date for our departure. However, we remain confident that through our persistent requests, the business will soon be fully and correctly resolved, allowing us to begin our journey home in God's name.

# Copy of a Patent of Grace and Pardon, granted by His Royal Highness to His Subjects professing the Reformed Religion in the Valleys of Piedmont.

->Faithfully translated from the printed copy published in Turin according to special order, by Giovanni Sinibaldo, Printer to His Royal Highness and to the Most Honorable Chamber, 1655. This document may be seen in the public library of the famous University of Cambridge.<-

### A Patent of Grace and Pardon by His Royal Highness

Granted to the men professing the so-called <note>original: "pretended." The Catholic authorities used this term to indicate they did not recognize the Reformed faith as a legitimate religion.</note> Reformed Religion in the three Valleys of Luserna <note>original: "Lucerna"</note>, San Martino, and Perosa, along with the villages of San Bartolomeo, Roccapiatta, and Prarustino; provided that they meanwhile leave the areas beyond the Pellice <note>original: "Pelice"</note> River, observe the conditions specified in the said Patent of Grace, and do not stray from the obedience which they owe to His Royal Highness.

**CHARLES EMMANUEL**, By the Grace of God, Duke of Savoy, Prince of Piedmont, and King of Cyprus, etc.

**IT** is the role of a good and generous Prince, not only to defeat and suppress through the force of arms those enemies who violently oppose him, and to restrain the disobedience of the people through severe punishments to keep them within due...

*...duty, that with the sweetness of kindness toward those who, lying submissively prostrate at his feet having recognized the faults they committed, implore him with all humility.*

*Therefore, it follows that the men of the so-called <note>original: "pretesa," often translated as "pretended" in Catholic documents of this era to deny the legitimacy of the Protestant faith.</note> Reformed Religion of the three Valleys of Luserna, San Martino, and Perosa, and the places of Roccapiatta, San Bartolomeo, and Prarustino, had taken up arms against our forces and hostilely resisted the execution of our commands, making them targets of our indignation. And having now (while our right hand was armed to their detriment) represented with feelings and expressions of regret the infinite sorrow they have felt, and feel, for having contravened our orders by taking up arms, they have accordingly turned to our goodness and begged us to forgive the errors committed by restoring them to our good and entire grace, and also to grant them—following the example of our predecessors—certain articles concerning the practice of their religion. And likewise, since his Most Christian Majesty, the invincible King of France, through Monsieur de Servien—his ordinary Councilor in his Councils of State and his resident Ambassador to us—has been pleased to perform various offices <note>original: "ufficii," meaning diplomatic interventions or mediation.</note> so that we might deign to receive the aforementioned people back into our good grace: we wish to make known to the world with what tenderness of affection we love our people when they do not stray from their due obedience, and how much we defer to the intervention of His Majesty and the singular respect we profess for him. By these presents, of our certain knowledge, full power, and supreme au-*

<column-break/>

limits. But also, on the other hand, he must exercise acts of mercy with mildness and clemency toward those who, lying prostrate at his feet, do with the greatest submission and acknowledgment of their offenses, in all humility implore the same.

Wherefore, because the people of the so-called <note>original: "pretended"</note> Reformed Religion of the three Valleys of Lucerna, San Martino, and Perosa, and of the places of Roccapiatta, San Bartolomeo, and Prarustino, having taken up arms against our forces and in a hostile manner resisted the execution of our commands, thus rendering themselves liable <note>original: "obnoxious," meaning subject to or exposed to punishment.</note> to our indignation; and having now, with tokens and expressions of their regret, represented their exceeding sorrow for opposing our orders by taking up arms, and accordingly having had recourse to our goodness, and most earnestly entreated of us pardon for these offenses by them committed; and that we would be pleased to re-establish them entirely in our grace and favor, and according to the example of our predecessors to grant unto them certain articles concerning the exercise of their religion; and because it has pleased his most Christian Majesty the King of France, by Monsieur de Servien, his ordinary Commissioner in his Councils of State and his Ambassador Ordinary residing here with us, to perform several diplomatic offices to the end that we would vouchsafe to receive the said people into our grace and favor; we, being willing to manifest to the world that tenderness and affection which we bear to our people when they do not depart from their due obedience, and how much the intervention of his Majesty and that singular respect which we bear to him prevails with us; by these presents, of our certain knowledge, full power and sovereign author-

<meta>This page continues the documentation of the 1655 Treaty of Pinerolo (the "Patents of Grace"), specifically detailing the supplemental fourth article concerning the fortification at La Torre (Torre Pellice) and the role of Swiss mediation.</meta>

->The Negotiation Book IV.<-

<image-desc>A decorative horizontal bar composed of a series of repeating floral fleurons.</image-desc>

### Here follows a transcript of the fourth Article of the above-mentioned Agreement.

As to La Torre <note>modern-day Torre Pellice</note>, the inhabitants may live there as stated above, and within its borders they may have their religious services <note>original: "exercises"</note> just as they did in the past. His Royal Highness shall, however, retain the fortification. Regarding this fort, it is agreed that it should not be mentioned in the patent of pardon; instead, it is reserved for those of the so-called Reformed Religion <note>original: "Pretended Reformed Religion," the standard Catholic legal term for Protestantism at the time</note> to humble themselves before His Royal Highness and petition him. They shall pray that, as they demonstrate their obedience and faithfulness, he might be pleased to demolish the fort, or at least move it to the site of the old fortress. To this end, they declare that they will submit their requests through the Swiss Ambassadors, whom His Excellency <note>Abel Servien, the French Ambassador</note> promises to assist with his own influence <note>original: "good offices"</note>. Nonetheless, it is declared that whether His Royal Highness consents to the demolition or relocation or not, this agreement shall always remain in effect, even if His Royal Highness decides to refuse those requests.

->E. SERVIENT.<-

->By order of my Lord,<-
->C. F. Canon.<-

<column-break/>

### The content of the fourth Article of the aforementioned agreement follows.
<note>This is a translation of the Italian text in the right-hand column.</note>

Regarding La Torre, they may re-inhabit it as stated above, and within its territory have their religious practice <note>original: "esercitio"</note> as in the past. His Royal Highness, however, retains the fortification. Concerning this, it was stated that no mention should be made of it in the Patents of Pardon, but that it be reserved for those of the so-called Reformed Religion <note>original: "pretesa Religione riformata"</note> to appeal at the feet of His Royal Highness. They shall beg him that, once he is assured of their obedience and loyalty, he might be pleased to demolish it or at least move it to the site of the old fortress. Concerning this, they declare their intention to involve the petitions of the Swiss Ambassadors, to which His Excellency promises to add his own influence <note>original: "Ufficii"</note>. This is with the declaration, however, that whether His Royal Highness consents to the demolition or relocation or not, the agreement shall always remain in effect, even in the event that His Royal Highness chooses to reject the said petitions.

->E. SERVIENT.<-

->By order of my Lord,<-
->C. F. Canon.<-

<summary>This page records the fourth article of the 1655 agreement regarding the town of La Torre, stipulating that while the Waldensians may return and practice their religion, the Duke of Savoy retains his fort there unless persuaded otherwise by Swiss mediation.</summary>

<header>Chapter VII. Concerning the Swiss Ambassadors.</header>

The aforesaid Patent was arranged in Pinerolo <note>original: "Pinarolo"</note>, and before it was signed by His Royal Highness, the men professing the so-called Reformed Religion <note>original Italian: "pretesa Religione riformata," a legal term used by the Catholic authorities to refer to Protestantism</note> made the following act of submission before the Most Illustrious Lord Gian Giacomo Truchi <note>original: "Gio. <page-num>667</page-num>
<header>Chapter VII. Concerning the Swiss <note>original: "Switzer"</note> Ambassadors.</header>

At the very same time that the above-mentioned Treaty was concluded and ratified by both parties, Ambassador *Servient* <note>Abel Servien (1593–1659), a high-ranking French diplomat and diplomat at the Peace of Westphalia</note> himself dictated several letters of thanks to his secretary. This was confirmed to the author by several people who had seen his actual handwriting. These letters were written in the name of the poor people <note>The Waldensian survivors of the 1655 massacres</note> to the *Lord Protector of England* <note>Oliver Cromwell</note>, the *King of France*, the *States General* of the *United Provinces* <note>The Dutch Republic</note>, and others who had acted on their behalf. The deputies of the Valleys were later forced to copy these letters and sign them with their own hands, and they were then sent away as quickly as possible to their various recipients.

Now, what Ambassador *Servient’s* goal was in doing this—whether it was to gain favor with the *Duke of Savoy*, or (being a great zealot for his own religion) to please the entire *Catholic* party by such a notable and worthy service—I leave to the wise reader to decide by examining and comparing all the facts. Specifically, his goals may have been: first, to prevent further interference <note>original: "Interposition"</note> from those two powerful states, *England* and the *United Provinces*, at such a critical moment; or second, to make it impossible for the poor people ever to take back <note>original: "recanting"</note> what they had done. It is certain that he intended at the same time not only to satisfy the *King* his *Master* <note>Louis XIV of France</note> (who had given him very strict orders to use his best efforts to secure good and honorable conditions for the poor people) but also to satisfy his Highness the *Lord Protector of England*. This seems evident from the following letter, which was written by the four ambassadors of the *Evangelical Cantons* <note>The Protestant states of Switzerland</note> to his Highness at his earnest request.

## CHAP. VIII.

### *The many grievances and sad effects of the Treaty concluded at Pignerol, with a true description of the present state and condition of those poor people.*

These and similar things were the *glorious appearances* of the Treaty made at *Pignerol*. The poor people were led to believe that they had obtained a most happy peace, and that they would enjoy its blessed fruits and effects—they and their children's children—for as long as the sun and moon should endure. As for the *Swiss Ambassadors* (as appears by all their narratives and letters), they viewed themselves as having been instrumental in bringing about and perfecting a work of such importance that the entire Protestant world would have been extremely satisfied with it. And *Ambassador Servient* <note>Jean Servien (1598–1659), a French diplomat who mediated the treaty.</note> did not doubt that his negotiations (as he had now handled the matter) would certainly prove to be a very acceptable service to everyone involved.

In the meantime, as this Treaty was published to the world and more thoroughly examined by wise and sober men, it was found to be nothing other than a *leper dressed in rich clothing and fine attire!* It was a Treaty as full of *grievances* as poor *Lazarus was of sores* <note>A reference to the biblical parable in Luke 16.</note>. The greatest part of the Articles directly clashed with the people's interests and ancient privileges, and the remainder was made up of expressions that point in as many directions as there are points on a mariner's compass. In *short*, it cannot be more accurately compared to anything than to *Ezekiel's Scroll* <note>Ezekiel 2:10 describes a scroll with writing on both sides containing "lamentations, mourning, and woe."</note>, which, though it was as *sweet as honey in the mouths of the poor people*, had nothing written within it but *lamentation, mourning, and woe*. Indeed, the *Swiss Ambassadors* had no sooner turned their backs and departed toward their own country than a countless number of grievances and difficulties—almost inexpressible—came crawling out of the Treaty like so many hornets out of a rotten or hollow tree. From that very day to this, they have never

<header>Chapter VIII. concluded at Pignerol.</header>

...ceased stinging the poor people to death, as will be shown more particularly in the rest of this chapter.

The author will not attempt here to determine where the failure lay in the management of this affair; indeed, it is not a subject he finds pleasant enough to expand upon at length. He will only say this in general: it was a great misfortune that the ambassadors of the *Protestant Cantons* <note>original: Evangelical Cantons; referring to the Swiss Protestant states of the time.</note> allowed themselves to be so influenced by the persistence of Ambassador *Servien* <note>Jean Servien, the French mediator.</note> and the Court of *Savoy* that they did not delay concluding the treaty until the arrival of the *English* and *Dutch* commissioners. This is especially true since they had been so earnestly urged to do so by Mr. *Morland*, his Highness’s envoy. Morland was in *Geneva* at the time and had sent no fewer than three separate couriers <note>original: expresses</note> with letters in the name of his master, the Lord *Protector*, for that purpose (as the ambassadors themselves acknowledge in their own *account* <note>original: relation</note>). Some of these letters reached them in plenty of time, before anything was finalized.

Furthermore, one of those very *ambassadors*, Mr. *Johann Jakob Stockar*, had declared himself strongly against the treaty. This is evident from the following testimony of Mr. *Andreas Schmidt*, who was then the Secretary of the Embassy. Ambassador *Stockar* personally delivered this testimony to Mr. *Morland* in *Geneva* on his return home from *Turin*, very earnestly requesting him to communicate it to the Lord *Protector* of *England* with all possible speed.

## The Testimony of Mr. *Andrew Schmidt*, Secretary of the Embassy of the *Protestant Cantons of Switzerland* <note>original: "Evangelical Cantons"</note>, to the *Duke of Savoy*, in the year 1655. Delivered into the hands of Mr. *Morland* by Ambassador *Stockar*, on September 16, 1655.

->The true original document, both signed and sealed by the said Mr. *Andrew Schmidt*, can be seen in the public library of the famous University of *Cambridge*.<--

***

I, the undersigned, testify by this document that Mr. *Stockar*, Ambassador from the Town and Canton of *Schaffhausen* to his Royal Highness of *Savoy* during the Treaty at *Pinerolo* <note>original: "Pignerollo"</note>, repeatedly urged his fellow ambassadors not to hasten the said Treaty. Instead, he argued they should delay its conclusion until the arrival of the ambassadors from *England* and the *Netherlands* <note>original: "Holland"</note>. He explained to them through various arguments how dangerous and damaging this proceeding would be, not only to the inhabitants of the Valleys but also to the common cause of all Protestants. When, despite all this, they refused to listen to him, he formally protested that he would not be held responsible for whatever might follow. Done at *Geneva* this present September 17/27 <note>The double date reflects the difference between the Julian and Gregorian calendars.</note>, in the year 1655.

<margin>Place for the seal <note>original: "locus sigilli"</note></margin> **Andrew Schmidt**,
Secretary of the
Embassy.

<column-break/>

<note>The following is a translation of the original French version of the testimony provided in the second column.</note>

*I, the undersigned, bear witness by this document that Mr. Stockar, Ambassador of the City and Canton of Schaffhausen to His Royal Highness of Savoy during the Treaty of Pinerolo, made many requests to his colleagues, the Ambassadors, not to hasten the said Treaty, but rather to delay the conclusion until the arrival of the Ambassadors of England and the Netherlands. He demonstrated to them by all sorts of reasons how dangerous and prejudicial this procedure would be, not only to the inhabitants of the Valleys but also to the common cause of all Protestants; and when, notwithstanding all that, he was not heard, he made a protest that he did not wish to be responsible for what might follow. Done at Geneva this September 17/27, the year 1655.*

<margin>Place for the seal <note>original: "locus sigilli"</note></margin> **Andrew Schmidt**, Secretary of the said Embassy.
