<header>Chapter 8. Concluded at Pignerol.</header>

<sig>Rrrr 2</sig>

The day before Ambassador Stockar delivered the previous testimony into the hands of Mr. Morland, he held a conference with Mr. Morland and Mr. D’ Ommeren (the Commissioner Extraordinary of the States General <note>The governing body of the Netherlands.</note>). During this meeting, he told them that since he and his colleagues had finished their negotiations at the Court of Savoy and were now traveling home to their own country, he had a great desire to travel by way of *Geneva*. He wanted the opportunity to inform the Commissioners *Extraordinary* of his Highness the *Lord Protector* of *England* [Oliver Cromwell] and the *States General* about everything that had occurred during their entire negotiation. He was especially eager to do this because he had heard that the recent *Treaty* they had concluded had greatly displeased many honest people.

In short, he assured them that his colleagues had solemnly promised him that they would take the entire blame upon themselves for hurrying or precipitating the Treaty. They also promised to give him a signed statement testifying that he never consented to any of their actions. Therefore, he claimed he would clear himself before the whole world at the next General Assembly of the Cantons through a public protest <note>original: "remonstrance"</note> and wash his hands of all the evil consequences of that affair. He earnestly requested the two aforementioned Commissioners to communicate what he had told them to their masters, and to assure them of his innocence in this matter. He added that if his service were accepted, he would risk <note>original: "hazzard"</note> both his life and all that he possessed to correct this situation.

The next morning, at another conference, he repeated the same words. He added *that he had resisted the other three ambassadors to the utmost, to the point that they had almost come to blows many times. He said that when the time was right, he would declare things that he did not think convenient to speak or write at that moment.*

These statements by Ambassador *Stockar* to the commissioners and several of his friends raised the expectations of many. They hoped for great results at the next *Assembly* of the *Protestant* <note>original: "Evangelical"</note> *Cantons*, which was to be held at *Payerne* at the beginning of the following month, *October*. At that time and place, their ambassadors were ordered to give an account of their entire negotiation.

Attending this meeting were *John Pell*, Esquire (his Highness’s Resident at *Zurich*), and the aforementioned Mr. *D’ Ommeren*, acting on behalf of their masters. They came to see what further resolutions the *Protestant Cantons* would take regarding either the nullifying or the correcting of the recent *Treaty* of *Pignerol* <note>Modern Pinerolo.</note>, which was now being universally criticized by the entire *Protestant* party. In the end, after hearing the report of their ambassadors (where it should be noted that Ambassador *Stockar* never even appeared, despite all his recent protests), they delivered the following resolution to Mr. *Pell* and Mr. *D’ Ommeren*.

# The Grievances of the Treaty Book. IV.

How this resolution of the **Protestant Cantons** <note>original: "Evangelical Cantons"</note> was privately resented by the two other states, the Author will not take it upon himself here to determine. However, it is certain that the matter rested there and fell to the ground; there did not follow any such alliance of councils for an improvement <note>original: "melioration"</note> and clarification of the aforementioned Treaty, as was suggested in that resolution.

In the meantime, the poor people began to taste more and more of the bitter fruits of that unhappy Agreement. Continually, they were ready to despair under their grievous and intolerable oppressions, as shall be specified hereafter in greater detail. They were like poor **working heifers**; the **Patent** <note>The "Patent of Pignerol," the official decree or treaty document</note> was the cruel **yoke** that so painfully pinched their **chafed necks**; the **Articles** of the treaty were the **heavy burdens** laid upon their backs; and **Andrea Gastaldo** <note>The official auditor and magistrate responsible for enforcing the decrees against the Waldensians</note> was the **driver**. With his orders and injunctions, acting like so many sharp goads, he always pricked and pushed them forward to accept by force those miserable conditions offered to them.

About the end of **December** in the year 1655, Ambassador **Servient** <note>Abel Servien, a French diplomat and mediator of the treaty</note> began to write very harsh letters to the poor people of the **Valleys**. It is supposed that his private zeal prompted him to do this rather than any command from his Master, the King. The contents of these letters were intended to threaten them with many negative consequences if they refused to submit and be satisfied with the Treaty made at **Pignerol**.

About the 12th of **March** in the same year 1655 <note>Under the Old Style calendar used at the time, the new year began in late March; this likely refers to March 1656 in modern dating</note>, **Monsieur de Bais**, Lieutenant Colonel of the Regiment of **Lyons**, arrived in the **Valleys** as an envoy from the King of **France**. Upon his arrival, he called some of the leaders of the poor people to meet him at a place called **Cassina**, which lies between **San Giovanni** and **Pelice**. After he delivered a letter to them from the **Duke of Lesdiguieres** <note>François de Bonne, a prominent French military commander</note>, which strongly urged them to accept the Treaty, he told them the King had received information that they intended to start an insurrection against their sovereign Prince. He claimed they were being prompted to do this by foreigners with whom they held correspondence and who provided them with vast supplies of money. 

Because of this, his Majesty had commanded him to assemble the Deputies of the **Valleys** to understand their grievances and let them know his intentions: that the Treaty made at **Pignerol** should be strictly <note>original: "punctually"</note> executed by both sides, and that he would maintain the poor people in peace according to its terms.

In obedience to this command, the poor people held a general assembly several days later, where they made a full justification of their actions—

## A Letter of the Evangelical Churches of the Valleys of Piedmont to the Duke of *Lesdiguières*, 29 of *March*, 1656.

->An authentic copy of the true original, which was shared with the author during his stay in *Geneva*.<-

My Lord, we have received Monsieur de Bais with all the respect possible for us, etc. <note>original French: "Monseigneur, Nous avons receu avec tout le respect qui nous à esté possible Monsieur de Bais, &c."</note>

MY LORD,

We have received, with all the respect we could show, Monsieur de Bais, Field Marshal <note>original: "Mareschal de Camp"</note> and Commander of the Lyon Regiment, sent here by you according to the order of his most Christian Majesty <note>A traditional title for the King of France, in this case, Louis XIV.</note>. This is not the first time we have experienced the mercy <note>original: "experimented the clemency"</note> of that great Monarch, which is so great that it moves him to stoop to take notice of us, who are among the most insignificant people in the whole world. 

Neither is it the first time that we have observed signs of your Lordship’s goodwill toward us, shown by your sympathy for our miseries and desolation. We would be the most ungrateful of all men if we did not take particular care to prove to the world our desire not to act unworthily of that kindness. We certainly would be unworthy if we held even the slightest thought of the crime of rebellion and insurrection, of which some ill-intentioned men have not only accused us before His Royal Highness <note>The Duke of Savoy.</note>, but also before his most Christian Majesty. 

This is the reason we have taken the liberty of writing to him, to protest—as if in the presence of God, whose living image His Majesty is—that our conscience is clear. In all our actions regarding this matter, we are wholly innocent. We would rather suffer all sorts of outrages (as we have already done) than commit the slightest breach of the respect and obedience that good subjects owe to their Sovereign Prince. 

As we hope that our protests will find more credit with His Majesty than the slanders of our enemies, we shall continue to fulfill our duty toward His Royal Highness with such zeal and sincerity that he will not give the slightest credit to the false reports spread to harm our reputation for innocence. We know very well that we cannot justly deserve the anger of our Prince without <margin>incurring</margin>

...incurring God’s displeasure. *You see by this what our principles and intentions are. We have been so far from being turned away from them by the appeals and persuasions of any foreigners that, on the contrary, all those who have in any way supported our interests have greatly strengthened us in this design through their constant and powerful exhortations.*

My Lord, as for the excuse based on those alms <note>original: "Almes"; charitable relief funds donated by Protestants across Europe following the 1655 massacres.</note> which we have received from other countries, it has no foundation. Various good people in France of our communion—whom His Majesty recognizes as his faithful subjects and who hold his authority as inviolable as we do that of our own Prince—have given us their charitable benevolence in the sight and with the knowledge of the entire Court and with the approval of His Majesty. Indeed, no man was ever known to take offense when poor, miserable men—after losing their entire estates, after the burning of their houses and the plundering of their goods—should receive the charity of those who took pity on them to prevent them from perishing of hunger. We were reduced to such an extreme condition that, without such a supply, the lack of all things would have finished what the sword and fire had left behind.

All people who are not driven by passion may judge from this, my Lord, what advantage it could give us to rip open a wound afresh that was not yet perfectly healed. Our desires tend toward nothing other than peace, and we incessantly pray to the God of Peace that he would bestow upon us and preserve for us that rich treasure. We adore His Divine Providence, which has inspired His Most Christian Majesty <note>A traditional title for the King of France, here referring to Louis XIV.</note> with so much goodness and bounty that he is inclined to intervene for the correction of the grievances regarding the late treaty <note>The Treaty of Pignerol, signed in August 1655, which ended the open warfare but contained many clauses the Waldensians found restrictive or unfair.</note> and to secure our re-establishment. To show how much we value this benefit, we have sent a memorial representing these grievances along with the letter we wrote to His Majesty. We also entreat your Lordship to give life to that letter by the testimony you are able to give of our innocence and lamentable state, as well as the profound respect and reverence we have for His Majesty. This charitable act, which we hope for from your Lordship, will oblige us to continue our prayers for your prosperity and to remain faithfully as long as we live,

->My Lord,<-

# A Letter from the Evangelical Churches of the Valleys of Piedmont to the King of France, March 29, 1656.

## An authentic copy of which was shared with the author during his stay in Geneva.

Sire,

The greatest monarchs, and those whom heroic virtues have raised above all others, like suns among the stars, have always made it their glory to share their kind influences with the most miserable people, in imitation of the King of Kings, etc. <note>original: "Les plus grands Monarques, & ceux que les vertus heroiques ont relevés par dessus tous les autres, comme des soleils entre les estoilles ont tousjours fait gloire de communiquer leurs benignes influences aux personnes les plus miserables, à l'imitation du Roy des Roys, &c."</note>

Sir,

The greatest monarchs, and those whom their heroic virtues have exalted above all others—like so many suns among the lesser stars—have always counted it their glory to share their kind <note>original: "benigne"</note> influences with the most miserable sort of men. This is done in imitation of the King of Kings, who has his throne in the highest heavens and yet also dwells in the lowest hearts. This is exactly what your Majesty, who is the living image of the living God, has practiced toward us. This shall obligate us to be continually grateful to your Majesty and to offer most ardent and extraordinary prayers to the Almighty for your prosperity. We hope that since He has put thoughts of peace and charity for us into your heart, you will allow us to personally experience <note>original: "experimentally to taste"</note> the good fruits of those thoughts. 

We also hope that you will not be distracted from such intentions by those negative <note>original: "sinister"</note> impressions which either ignorant or ill-intentioned men have tried to fill you with against us. (We learned of these impressions through the letter which my Lord the Duke of Lesdiguières did us the honor of writing, and through the speech made by Monsieur de Bais, his envoy, by your Majesty's order.) We have been so far from ever having the slightest thought of taking up arms against our Sovereign (as we are accused) that we have always prevented our people from even forming negative impressions in their minds concerning those acts of violence and extortion <note>term: "extortions" here refers to the illegal or abusive seizure of property or money by officials.</note> which have been and are constantly committed against us without any remedy. These acts occur even against the intentions of His Royal Highness <note>The Duke of Savoy, the direct ruler of the Waldensian valleys.</note>, in an attempt to push our patience (if possible) until we cause some disorder.

<meta>catchword: We</meta>

<summary>In this letter to King Louis XIV, the Waldensian churches express their gratitude for the King's past favor and vigorously defend themselves against accusations of rebellion. They argue that their patience in the face of violent extortion proves their loyalty to their Sovereign and their desire for peace.</summary>

<page-num>68</page-num>
<header>Chapter 8 concluded at Pinerolo.</header>

*We will always persist in this same course, seeking a remedy for our suffering through respectful means—actions that are just and consistent with the principles we have held since childhood <note>original: "which we sucked in together with our milk"</note> and which are suitable to the duty that true subjects owe to their Prince. It has never happened that any foreign countries who were moved by our devastation, who poured oil into our wounds and championed our cause, ever incited us to rebellion. As for the charity <note>original: "Alms"</note> they have bestowed upon us, it was for no other purpose than to prevent hunger, cold, nakedness, and other hardships from killing those among us who had escaped the sword. Furthermore, they never made any pleas <note>original: "remonstrances"</note> that aimed at anything other than exhorting us to repent before God, to be patient toward those who mistreat us, and to show humility, loyalty, and obedience toward our Sovereign—all of which are duties that we shall never fail to perform, by God’s assistance. Meanwhile,* Sir, *we are confident that the Treaty made at Pinerolo <note>original: "Pignerol"</note> through the mediation <note>original: "interposition"</note> of your Majesty’s Ambassador, Lord de Servient, has not fulfilled the good intentions you have always had for securing a firm and sure peace for us. We hope to be restored to the same state and condition that the most Serene Predecessors of His Royal Highness always maintained us in, according to our ancient concessions. We ask that you please continue your powerful and gracious mediation with His Royal Highness to improve our conditions. We ask for the amendment of those articles that truly injure us, the clarification <note>original: "Elucidation"</note> of those that are obscure and ambiguous, and the addition of those that are known to be fair and necessary for public peace, according to the draft <note>original: "minute"</note> we have written and delivered to Monsieur de Bais at his request, to be presented to your Majesty on our behalf. This is especially important considering that the two most harmful details—namely the Preface and the Article concerning the Fort—were never signed by our Deputies, who instead opposed them. What they did sign, they signed without authority, contrary to our intentions, and without consulting us. Therefore, we cannot justly be deprived of what nature, the law of nations, centuries of possession, our legal concessions, and justice itself grant us. This is what we desire and hope for from the mercy and fairness of His Royal Highness, through your Majesty's powerful and gracious mediation.*

Sir, *in hope of this, we shall unswervingly continue in that loyalty and obedience which we owe to His Royal Highness (our natural Prince and Sovereign), and we shall pour out our souls before the Divine Majesty for the prosperity of your Royal Majesty, being with all possible respect,*

->**SIR,**<-

->Your most humble and most obedient servants, the<-
->Inhabitants of the Valleys of **Luserna**, **Angrogna**,<-
->**Perosa**, and **San Martino** in **Piedmont**, Professors<-
->of the **Christian Reformed Religion.**<-

->And for all, **FELIX LEGER**, etc.<-

## The Grievances of the Treaty made at Pinerolo <note>original: "Pignerol"</note>, Delivered into the hands of *Monsieur de Bais* to be sent to the King.

->Translated out of the French Copy.<-

First, in the Preface there is this harmful <note>original: "prejudicial"</note> point: it speaks of us as rebels, etc. <note>original: "Premierement en la Preface il y a ceci de prejudiciable, qu’elle parle de nous comme de Rebelles, &c."</note>

> “First, in the Preface there is this harmful point: it speaks
> “of us as *rebels* and disobedient subjects who have taken up arms
> “against His Royal Highness, our natural Prince and Sovereign.
> “Thus, as guilty persons worthy of his indignation, we are
> “required to ask pardon for those outrages which they claim we have
> “committed. In this way, we are clearly implicated in the crime of *rebellion*,

# Chapter 8. Concluded at Pinerolo.
<header>Chapter 8. concluded at Pinerolo.</header>

"...your Royal Highness. Nevertheless, seeing that contrary to the said concessions and the practice of all times, our adversaries have sometimes endeavored to extort contrary orders, and might do so again in the future, it would be just that this liberty of buying and selling all things from one another (at least in the said Valleys and those places that are annexed) should be more clearly specified. For seeing that the Roman Catholics buy from us freely, while we are indebted in great sums both to private men and to some communities <note>original: "Communaltyes"; refers to municipalities or collective local governments</note>, they would soon purchase all our best lands and inheritances, and so by degrees root us out of the country without recovery.

9. "In the 9th article: There should be added this, that if his Royal Highness insists that the Mass <note>The central act of worship in the Roman Catholic Church</note> be said in the places where <term>those of the Religion</term> <note>A standard historical term for Protestants, specifically the Waldensians in this context</note> inhabit, then it must not be performed within their private lands. All the concessions and the Patent <term>a formal legal document or decree issued by a monarch</term> itself free them from contributing anything toward the Mass or those who perform it; yet this particular has not been observed, as they seize the houses of private men against their will to celebrate the Mass in them, even if the owners oppose it.

10. "The eleventh article, which declares no more than that *our prisoners who are within the dominions of his Royal Highness shall be set at liberty when it is known where they are*, is also made void and of no effect. This is because our adversaries have transported many of our captives, especially young children, out of his Royal Highness’s dominions, or else have hidden or moved them to various places even within this land, so that no certain notice can be had of them; and there are others whom they flatly refuse to give back to us. Therefore, we most humbly petition that it please his Royal Highness to cause a proclamation to be made through all his dominions, enjoining all those who have any prisoners, or who detain any people from the Valleys, to deliver them immediately without any excuse or demand for payment of costs. Furthermore, they should be ordered to bring back and restore those who have been transported to other places within such a time as his Royal Highness shall be pleased to appoint, upon pain of death or other punishment, according to his pleasure.

11. "In the 12th article: That his Royal Highness would be pleased to admit the same expressions found in the old concessions—especially those of 1603—to be duly confirmed without altering or restraining them. By those expressions, it is declared absolutely that those of the Religion in the said Valleys shall be admitted 'to every kind of public office indifferently, just like the Roman Catholics' <note>original Italian: "ad ogni forte d' officio publico indifferentemente come li Catholici Romans"</note>, and not be bound to any act contrary to their religion, as appears by the Patents and the oaths taken by the attorneys and notaries, etc. Whereas, in the text of the late treaty, they have introduced some restrictions upon the offices of the notaries and tacitly deprived us of the others.

# The Grievances of the Treaty Book. IV.

“...and also from Meana and Mattie, even though they were included in the old agreements and were given the Valley of Luserna specifically as a place of refuge. Now they are being driven out of the best parts of it and forced to sell the estates they have owned since time immemorial. We have—and can always prove we have—the right to live there, not just by birth, but by all the grants made by the most serene predecessors of His Royal Highness. These rights were specifically confirmed in the first article of the Patent <term>a formal legal document or decree issued by a monarch</term>, and the order published by Auditor Gastaldo is a manifest violation of that.

5. “In the third article, they have taken away our freedom to preach in all the territories of San Giovanni, which we have always enjoyed openly before the whole world. In fact, he himself has always encouraged the people with the hope that he would restore its use to them, which is something they now expect from his justice and mercy.

6. “In the 6th article: The exemption from taxes for six years is not sufficient to help those people survive who are destitute of houses, goods, cattle, and linen, and who live only on charity. Therefore, we humbly pray that a full exemption may be continued for at least ten years. After that time, we ask that we be charged no more in taxes and duties than what is required of Roman Catholics. We ask this because the six-year period includes the year that has just passed, leaving only two years of full exemption remaining.

The ancient concessions do not name these places but refer instead to local custom and toleration. This often causes many difficulties. It should be added that we may have preaching in all the places where it was commonly practiced at the beginning of the troubles. It would also be necessary for those places to be specifically named to prevent any future disputes.

8. “In the 8th article: Although, if interpreted according to its true sense and meaning, it does not take away our right to buy, sell, or trade land and inheritances with Roman Catholics within the said Valleys—seeing as these things are included in the old concessions mentioned in the seventh and preceding articles—it rather confirms that liberty. # Chapter VIII. Concluded at Pignerol.

The King of France, upon receiving the aforementioned letter and list of grievances, was deeply moved by their sorrowful condition. If certain malicious individuals <note>original: "malignant spirits"</note> had not tried by every possible means to create negative impressions in his mind against them—such is the natural kindness and sincerity of that Prince’s character, and so inclined is he on all occasions toward acts of mercy (among his many other princely and heroic qualities)—he would undoubtedly have used his power and influence with the Duke of Savoy for their relief and restoration. 

Therefore, all the efforts made in those days by his Ambassador, Servient, and his Envoy, Monsieur de Bais, regarding the ratification of the treaty concluded at Pignerol, must be interpreted either as actions arising from the personal zeal of those two men, or as acts and decrees in which His Majesty was misled <note>original: "surprised"; in this context meaning the King was given a false impression or tricked into signing something contrary to his intent</note>, contrary to his own personal and princely inclination.

But regardless of how it happened, from that time until this very day, certain leading men in the Court of Savoy have used their best efforts to place even heavier burdens upon their backs than they ever did before.

In their orders of April 20 and October 6, 1656, and August 24, 1657, they summoned the poor people to pay their taxes for the year 1655 (which is contrary to the aforementioned treaty). Meanwhile, they exempted all the Catholic residents from the same tax. In the Duke's answer to their humble petition <note>original: "supplication"</note> of October 6, 1657, they were, among other things, absolutely forbidden from practicing their religion in San Giovanni, as appears in the following extract of the poor people's petition and the Duke's answer.

### Chapter VIII. concluded at Pignerol.

By an Order from the *Gastaldo* <term>Gastaldo: a high-ranking administrative or judicial official in the Duchy of Savoy</term> dated December 14, 1657, those individuals who did not appear at the appointed time and place to receive the payment for their goods and possessions (which they were no longer permitted to keep) were summoned to appear at another time and place for the same purpose. They were warned that if they failed to comply, they would be prosecuted and severely punished as defiant <note>original: "contumacious"</note> persons.

By another Order from the *Gastaldo* dated December 20, 1657, the members of the community of San Giovanni were summoned to Turin in the persons of their syndics <term>Syndics: local government officials or legal representatives</term> and counselors. They were summoned for continuing to perform ministerial duties and for the instruction of youth within that community. Great care was taken to ensure a double penalty would be applied if they failed to appear.

In the Duke's answer to a humble petition from the poor people, dated January 25, 1658, they were again (among other things) strictly forbidden from practicing their religion at San Giovanni, using the following terms: "Therefore, His Royal Highness wills that the aforementioned petitioners abstain from instruction and other religious exercises as stated above; otherwise, he will proceed with the prosecution already announced." <note>original: "Per ciò si vuole S. A. R. che i supti. s'astenghino dalla instruttione, & altri essercitii come sopra, altrimente farà proseguire la processura già communiciata."</note>

It would be almost endless to repeat all the edicts, orders, and commands issued against these poor people since that cruel Patent <note>The "Patent" refers to the formal royal decree of 1655 that preceded the massacre and subsequent restrictive treaties.</note> in the year 1655, along with all the related grievances. Therefore, I shall only present the reader with the following *Letters*, which provide the most authentic accounts of their current state and condition. With these, I shall close this discourse, which I fear some will judge to be too long and tedious.

### Copy of a Letter from the four Ambassadors of the Protestant <note>original: Evangelical</note> Cantons of Switzerland, to *Monsieur de Servient*, Ambassador of the *French* King to the Duke of *Savoy*: Dated November 30, 1657.

->Most Illustrious Lord,<-

Having heard with extreme grief concerning our most dear friends of the Reformed religion <note>original: "of the Religion"</note> in the Valleys of *Piedmont*—not so much from themselves as from the reports of others—that contrary to the Patent <term>Patent: a formal grant of rights or privileges issued by a sovereign</term> granted by His Royal Highness two years ago, they still suffer many great troubles and injuries in various ways. This is happening, without doubt, by the suggestion and persuasion of their adversaries. 

We recall that Your Excellency was not only present at the Treaty of *Pignerol* and helped advance its conclusion, and is therefore correctly informed of all the details that were transacted in it, but you have also always promised us to do your utmost to see the said Treaty punctually observed. Your goal was to ensure that these poor, afflicted people may be completely restored to peace. 

Therefore, because of the high regard we have for Your Excellency, we have thought it more fitting to trouble Your Excellency with this letter than to allow our Lords and Superiors to send their intercession directly to His Royal Highness. We are in great hope that Your Excellency has not only the power, but also the inclination to do good for those poor people. 

Based on this, we most humbly beseech Your Excellency not only to help them in general by causing the said Treaty to be better observed—so that these people may enjoy peace and, according to the express terms of the Patent, be restored to their former condition, the good will of their Prince, and his royal protection and safeguard as they were before—but also to most earnestly recommend to him the following points. 

Your Excellency may remember with what humility, submission, care, and pleading these people have desired, from time to time, to be freely exempted from the building of the new fort. They asked that His Royal Highness remain confident that they would prove themselves so obedient and submissive that it would clearly appear there was no need to restrain <note>original: "bridle"</note> them with such a fort, so that no ground would remain for any troublesome suspicion <note>original: "jealousie"</note> which might otherwise be directed toward them, and that they might also be delivered

“ Furthermore, since the 4th Article of the aforementioned Patent <term>Patent: an official document or decree issued by a monarch or government to grant a right, status, or title.</term> clearly grants—along with the free exercise of religion in general without limitation—liberty of conscience within all the locations included in the former concessions <term>concessions: rights or lands granted by a government to a specific group</term> (which should neither be restricted nor expanded further), we leave it to Your Excellency to consider whether they can rightfully deny liberty of conscience to strangers and others who wish to embrace our religion in those places, as they currently do. This act goes against the Article and the continuous practice of our religion. We also ask you to consider whether they can, contrary to all custom, give a new interpretation to the Patents—namely, that they are only meant to apply to those who were born into the Reformed <term>Reformed: a term for Protestant Christians, specifically those following the traditions of John Calvin.</term> faith?

“ But let Your Excellency especially consider this: according to what was granted to them regarding the free exercise of their religion in all previous agreements, they were always able to fill the needs of congregations when local ministers were unavailable by receiving others from neighboring areas. They have done this without contradiction or opposition, and they never needed to ask permission from His Royal Highness or his ministers. Although the said Patent did not speak against this practice in any way, this privilege was recently questioned and labeled an 'usurpation' and an 'abuse.' Furthermore, a few months ago, several ministers sent to them from the Synod of Dauphine <note>original: "Synod of Dauphine" — the regional governing body of the French Protestant church in the Dauphiné province.</note> were taken away and banished from the country. Similarly, a minister from the neighboring Valley of Cluson—who had served in the Holy Ministry among them for about thirty years within the dominions of His Royal Highness—was turned out and banished, along with a physician named Mr. Armand. By this means, many churches and congregations are deprived of both the 'food of their souls' <note>original: "Food of their Soul" — a reference to spiritual teaching and the sacraments.</note> and comfort for their bodies.

“ This happened even though they were promised that if they humbly requested permission—which they have done through five separate petitions using the most submissive and earnest language possible—it would be graciously granted to them. Nevertheless, we hear that after many rejections, they have only been given leave for one year to employ some of those foreign ministers. Among those they approved, they named a Mr. Saurin, who had actually retired to France a long time ago. Thus, these poor people are constantly facing new troubles and are exhausting themselves with expenses greater than they can bear.

“ We must also admit that we believed—as did the inhabitants of the Valleys—that according to the 6th Article, the remainder of the debts that had been forgiven <note>original: "remitted"</note> from the year 1655 should have included everything left unpaid up to that point. However, we see the opposite: they have been forced to pay all remaining debts right up to the time the treaties were made at Pignerol. This is despite many humble appeals made to the Court on their behalf, which were ignored. We hope, along with the people, that through the intercession of your...”

<header>Chapter VIII. concluded at Pignerol.</header>

"Your Excellency, they shall receive a reciprocal promise for the year 1659 regarding a payment or reimbursement for what may have been paid. And although those who live on the other side of the River Pellice <note>original: "Pelice"</note>—except for a few—have finally consented to this (namely, to receive the tax and the price of their estates according to the Patents <term>Patent: an official royal decree or grant of rights.</term>), they have nevertheless almost all been forced to lose a significant portion of their value. As a result, they are deprived of all hope and the means of buying other estates within the areas where they are allowed to live.

"In the meantime, Roman Catholics are forbidden from selling or leasing lands or houses to the Reformed <term>Reformed: Protestants, specifically the Waldensians.</term>, even within the limits where they are permitted to dwell. This is contrary both to the custom practiced until now and to the Patent, which does not deny them the right to buy any lands or inheritances outside the permitted places.

"We refrain from mentioning many other grievances and troubles they suffer without being able to obtain any relief through the law or otherwise. These include the seizure of their churchyards in some places and the cunning schemes used to strip them of their real estate—now this house, now that piece of ground, then another, and so on—especially in San Giovanni <note>original: "St. John"</note> and Torre Pellice <note>original: "La Tour"</note>. This is in addition to the many insults and shameful reproaches cast upon them, which would be too long and tedious to relate but are undoubtedly already well known to Your Excellency. All these things seem to be done for no other purpose than to gradually and completely deprive these poor people of the freedom of both their souls and bodies. They cannot seek a remedy in any court of justice; they have so little hope that cases will be handled without favoritism that, on the contrary, they have cause to mourn that, under the guise of justice, they are too often exposed to many intolerable injuries.

"Since the things mentioned above have happened so clearly and contrary to our expectations to our friends and associates of the faith, they touch our hearts all the more because we were present in the name of our Lords and superiors at the aforementioned Treaty, and because we are also to some extent invested in it. Nevertheless, we neither will nor can imagine that His Royal Highness or his ministers would seek the ruin of their most faithful and obedient subjects. Instead, we believe they intend that the Royal word given in the Patent shall be strictly observed. By virtue of that word, those poor oppressed people should be maintained under Royal protection and assurance, as they have been formerly. They should be effectively defended against all their adversaries (who maliciously endeavor to distort the true meaning of the Patents) so that they may at last experience the effects of his natural mercy.

"Therefore, we are all the more encouraged to humbly and affectionately plead with Your Excellency, as we do at this time,"

### Copy of a Letter from His Highness the *Lord Protector* of *England, etc.* to Lord *Lockhart*, His *Ambassador* Ordinary at the *French Court*, in favor of the poor *Protestants* of the *Valleys of Piedmont*, May 26, 1658.

->An authentic copy of the true original, which was shared with the author by the Right *Honorable* Mr. Secretary Thurloe.<-

The continual troubles and harassment of the poor people of Piedmont who profess the *Reformed Religion* are a matter of great sorrow to **Us**. This is despite your many serious appeals at the Court of *France* on their behalf, and our own heartfelt recommendations of their most miserable condition to *His Majesty* <note>King Louis XIV of France.</note> in **Our** name. His Majesty has been pleased on all such occasions to express deep sympathy <note>original: "resentments"</note> for their miseries and to give **Us** significant hope that he would use his power and influence with the *Duke of Savoy* to settle those affairs and restore those poor, distressed creatures to their ancient privileges and homes.

These matters lie so close to **Our** heart that, although we are fully satisfied with the many signs you have shown of your truly Christian zeal and tenderness toward them, the current state of their affairs and the misery daily added to their affliction give **Us** fresh reasons for pity. We view them not only as fellow men, but as the poor, distressed members of *Christ*. This moves **Us** at present to recommend their sad condition to your special care. We desire you to redouble your appeals to the *King* with such moving and affectionate language as may be appropriate to the greatness of their current sufferings and grievances, which, in truth, are almost impossible to express.

For the malice and fury of their Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> enemies is restless and relentless. It is as if they considered it a small matter to have previously shed the innocent blood of so many hundreds of souls, to have burned their houses, demolished their churches, plundered their goods, and driven the inhabitants across the *River Pelice* out of those ancient possessions which they had peacefully enjoyed for so many ages and generations. Now, they are resolved to fill their cup of *Affliction* to the brim and to heat the *Furnace* seven times hotter than before. Among other things:

1. First, they forcibly forbid all types of public religious services at *San Giovanni*, which the inhabitants have nonetheless enjoyed since time out of—

2. And because there are not enough men found among the natives in the said *Valleys* who are fitly qualified and have the ability for *ministerial functions* to supply even half of their *churches*, they are necessitated by this situation to hire some ministers from *France* and *Geneva*, who are the *Duke of Savoy’s* friends and allies. Their *Catholic* <note>original: "Popish"</note> enemies take advantage of this and use this strategy: namely, to banish and drive out the *shepherds* of the flocks so that the *wolves* may more easily come in and devour the *sheep*.

3. To this, we may add their strict prohibition of all *physicians* and *surgeons* <note>original: "Chirurgions"</note> of the *Reformed Religion* from living in the *Valleys*. Thus, they attempt not only to starve their souls for want of spiritual food and nourishment, but to destroy their bodies as well for lack of those outward conveniences and helps which God has allowed to all mankind.

4. As a *supplement* to the three previous *grievances*, those of the *Reformed Religion* are prohibited from all manner of commerce and trade with their *Catholic* neighbors, so that they may not be able to support and maintain their families. If they offend in the least regard in this matter, they are immediately *arrested* <note>original: "apprehended"</note> as *rebels*.

5. Moreover, to give the world a clear testimony of what their main design is in all these oppressions, they have issued orders to force the poor *Protestants* to sell their lands and houses to their *Catholic* neighbors, whereas the *Catholics* are prohibited, upon pain of *excommunication*, from selling any real estate <note>original: "immovable"</note> to the *Protestants*.

6. Besides this, the *Court of Savoy* has rebuilt the *Fort of La Torre*, contrary to the formal and express promise they made to the *ambassadors* of the *Evangelical Cantons* <note>The Protestant states of the Swiss Confederacy.</note>. There, they have also stationed *commanders* who commit Lord knows how many excesses and outrages in all the neighboring parts, without ever being called into question or compelled to make restitution for them.

7. If by chance any murder is committed in the *Valleys* (as is practiced far too often), and the authors are not discovered, the poor *Protestants* are immediately accused as being guilty of it, to render them more *hateful* <note>original: "odious"</note> to their neighbors.

8. Recently, several *troops of cavalry* <note>original: "Horse"</note> and *companies of infantry* <note>original: "Foot"</note> were sent into the *Valleys* to take up new quarters in all those parts, as is *claimed* <note>original: "pretended"</note>. This has caused the poor people—fearing a *massacre*—to send their wives and little ones, along with all who were feeble or sick among them, into the *Valley of Perosa* (under the *King of France’s* dominions) at great expense and difficulty.

These are, in short, the principal *grievances*, and this is the present state and condition of those poor people even at this very day. You are to use your utmost endeavors to make *His Majesty* <note>King Louis XIV of France.</note> thoroughly aware of this, and to persuade him to give speedy and effectual orders to *his ambassador* who resides in the *Duke’s court* to act vigorously on their behalf. <header>Chapter VIII concluded at Pignerol <note>modern: Pinerolo, a strategic fortress city in the Italian Piedmont</note>.</header>

The document which you shall present to his Majesty <note>King Louis XIV of France</note> for this end and purpose contains several reasons within it which we hope will move his heart to perform this charitable and merciful work. We desire you to support and encourage <note>original: "second and animate"</note> these reasons with your most earnest pleas, representing to him how much his own interest and honor are concerned in upholding that agreement <note>original: "Accord"</note> of Henry IV, his royal predecessor, made with the ancestors of these very people in the year 1592 by the Constable of Lesdiguières. This agreement is registered in the Parliament of Dauphiné, and you have an authentic copy of it in your own hands. By this document, the Kings of France bound themselves and their successors to maintain and preserve the people's ancient privileges and concessions. Besides that, winning the hearts of those people to himself by such a gracious and remarkable protection and deliverance might be of significant use in the future regarding Pignerol and the adjacent places under his dominion.

One of the most effective remedies which we believe is best to be applied at present is that the King of France would be pleased to make an exchange with the Duke of Savoy for those Valleys, giving up some other parts of his dominions to him in their place. This occurred in the reign of Henry IV, when the Marquisate of Saluzzo <note>original: "Saluces"</note> was exchanged with the Duke for Bresse <note>original: "La Bresse"</note>. This certainly could not fail to be of great advantage to his Majesty, both for the safety of Pignerol and for opening a passage for his forces into Italy. If those places were under the dominion and in the hands of so powerful a prince—combined with the natural strength of those locations due to their geography—they would surely be rendered impregnable.

By what we have already said, you see our intentions; therefore, we leave all other particulars to your special care and conduct, and remain,

---

May 26, 1658.

->**OLIVER P.**<-
<note>The "P" stands for *Protector*, the title used by Oliver Cromwell as head of the English Commonwealth.</note>

# A Letter from His Highness the Lord Protector of England, etc.
## To the King of France, May 26, 1658.

->An authentic copy of the true original, which was communicated to the author by the Right Honourable Mr. Secretary Thurloe.<-

->Most Serene and most Powerful King,<-

| Modernized English Text | Translated Latin Text |
| :--- | :--- |
| Your Majesty may remember that at the time when the treaty began concerning the renewal of the alliance between us (which, now happily entered upon, is sufficiently testified by the many advantages to both nations and the many inconveniences resulting to our common enemies), there occurred that miserable massacre of the people of the Valleys <note>the Waldensian Protestants of the Piedmontese Alps</note>. Their cause, being deserted and afflicted on every side, we recommended to your mercy and protection with the utmost passion and compassion. We do not think that your Majesty has yourself been lacking in any duty of such piety and humanity, making use of either that authority or influence by which you should prevail with the Duke of Savoy. As for our part, we and many other princes and states have not failed to intervene through embassies, letters, and pleas. At length, after a most inhumane slaughter of persons of both sexes and of every age, a peace was concluded—or rather, a more concealed course of hostility introduced under the name of peace. The conditions of peace were agreed upon in your town of Pinerolo <note>original: "Pignerol"</note>; they were harsh ones... | <note>original: "Serenissime, Potentissimeque Rex,"</note> Most Serene and Most Powerful King, <br><br> Your Majesty can remember at the time when negotiations were being held between us to renew the treaty—which, having begun under the best of omens, is proven by the many benefits to both peoples and the many troubles caused to our common enemies since then—that the miserable slaughter of the inhabitants of the Valleys <note>original: "Convallensium"</note> occurred. We recommended their cause, which was abandoned and suffering on all sides, to your mercy and protection with the greatest fervor of spirit and pity. We do not believe that your Majesty has personally failed in a duty so pious and indeed so human, given the authority or favor you ought to have with the Duke of Savoy. Certainly, we and many other princes and states have not been lacking, interceding with embassies, letters, and prayers. After the bloodiest slaughter of both sexes and every age, peace was finally granted, or rather a certain more concealed hostility was introduced under the name of peace. The conditions of peace were issued in your town of Pinerolo <note>original: "Pinarolii"</note>; they were indeed harsh... |

| ...but they were conditions which the wretched and poor people—having suffered all kinds of dreadful and monstrous outrages—would have easily accepted, provided that they were upheld, however harsh and unjust they might be. Yet they are not upheld. Instead, through a false interpretation of each condition and by various evasions, trust is eluded and violated. Many are driven from their ancient homes; many are forbidden their ancestral religion; new taxes are demanded; a new fortress is imposed upon their necks, from which soldiers frequently burst forth to either plunder or slaughter everyone they meet. Furthermore, new forces have recently been secretly prepared against them; and those who practice the Roman Catholic religion among them are ordered to move away for a time, so that everything now seems once again to point toward the extermination <note>original: "internecionem"</note> of those most miserable people who survived that previous butchery <note>original: "laniena"</note>. | ...indeed, but they were such conditions as those poor people, who have endured all manner of outrages and cruelties, would readily accept, even though they were hard and unjust, if only they were observed. But they are not observed; for by a false interpretation of each of them, and by several shifts, the true meaning is evaded and faith is violated. Many are cast out of their ancient possessions; many are prohibited from the exercise of their religion; new payments are demanded; a new fort is built to yoke them, from which the soldiers often break out, either plundering or killing everyone they meet. Moreover, new forces have lately been privately prepared against them, and those who profess the Roman Catholic religion among them are told to withdraw for a time; so that all things now again seem to point toward the slaughtering of those most miserable creatures who were left alive in the former butchery <note>original: "laniena"</note>. |

I entreat and beseech your Majesty not to allow this to happen, nor to permit such a license for cruelty—I do not say to any Prince (for such great cruelty cannot enter the heart of any Prince, much less befit the tender age of that Prince <note>Referring to the young Duke of Savoy, Charles Emmanuel II</note>, or the mind of his mother, the Duchess) — but do not permit it to those most savage murderers <note>original: "salvage murtherers"</note>. While they profess themselves to be the servants and followers of Christ our Savior, who came into this world to save sinners, they abuse His most merciful name and gentle teachings for the most cruel massacres of innocent people.

May your Majesty—who has the power, and being advanced to such a high position, is worthy of that power—rescue so many of your poor petitioners from the hands of bloodthirsty men. These men, having recently been drunk with blood, thirst for it again, and consider it their greatest craft to divert the ill-will <note>original: "envie"</note> of their own cruelty onto Princes.

The legal document of that surrender still exists in the public records of your kingdom, in which it was, among other things, excepted and guarded against, that the people of the Valleys <note>original: "Convallenses"</note> should never afterward be handed over to anyone, except under the same conditions by which your Majesty’s most invincible grandfather received them into his protection. This faith they now implore; as suppliants, they seek from the grandson what was granted by the grandfather. They would prefer and choose to be yours rather than his under whom they now live—perhaps by some exchange of territory, if it can be done. If that is not possible, let them at least have your patronage, compassion, and refuge. There are also political reasons which might urge your Majesty not to reject the people of the Valleys; but I would not want so great a king to be moved to defend these wretched people by any other reasons than the faith pledged by your ancestors, as well as by your own piety and the innate kindness and greatness of your royal mind. Thus, the praise and glory for this most beautiful act will be entirely and completely yours, and your Majesty may expect to find, as long as you live, prosperity and blessings from the Father of Mercies himself and from his Son, Christ the King, whose name and doctrine your Majesty [upholds]... |

# A Letter from His Highness the Lord Protector of England, etc.
## To the Evangelical Cantons of Switzerland, May 26, 1658.
### An authentic copy of the true original of which was communicated to the author by the Right Honourable Mr. Secretary Thurloe <note>John Thurloe (1616–1668), Cromwell’s Secretary of State and head of intelligence</note>.

| ->Most Illustrious and most Magnificent Lords,<- | ->Most Illustrious and most Magnificent Lords,<- <note>original: "Illustres atque Amplissimi Domini"</note> |
| :--- | :--- |
| Concerning your poor distressed neighbors of the Valleys <note>the Waldensians, or Vaudois</note>, and the grievous and intolerable things they have suffered from their Prince <note>the Duke of Savoy</note> on account of religion: just as we are astonished by the monstrous cruelty when we recall it, so we thought it unnecessary to write to you about it, as these matters are much better known to you. We have seen copies of the letters which your ambassadors—who were the mediators <note>original: "perswaders"</note> and witnesses of the peace recently made at Pignerol—wrote to the Duke of Savoy and the President of his Council at Turin. In these letters, they specifically demonstrate and prove that all the articles of peace have been broken, and that they have been used to deceive, rather than protect, those miserable people. Unless they will patiently endure that violation of the articles—which has continued from the very moment the peace was concluded until today, and grows worse daily—unless they lie down to be completely trampled and ruined... | Concerning your most afflicted neighbors of the Valleys, and how many grievous and intolerable things they have suffered from their Prince for the sake of religion: both because of the atrocity of the events themselves, our soul almost shudders to remember them, and we have deemed it unnecessary to write those things to you, to whom they are much better known. We have also seen copies of the letters which your ambassadors—the advisors and witnesses of the peace of Pignerol long ago—wrote to the Duke of the Savoyards and the President of that Council at Turin; in which they show and prove in detail that all the conditions of peace have been broken, and were a source of deception rather than security for those miserable people. This violation has continued from the very moment the peace was granted until this day, and grows more serious daily. Unless they endure it with a calm mind, unless they prostrate themselves to be plainly trampled and ruined... |

### A Letter of His Royal Highness the Duke of Savoy to the Evangelical Cantons of Switzerland, Turin, May 9, 1655.

*Magnificent Lords, Very dear and special Friends, Allies, and Confederates. Those who have informed you that our subjects of the Pretended Reformed Religion were unable to obtain the execution of the Patents we granted them in the year 1655, have informed you contrary to the truth, etc.* <note>original: "Magnifiques Seigneurs, Tres chers & speciaux Amiz, Alliez, & Confederez. Ceux qui vous ont donné advis que nos sujets de la Religion Pret. Reform. n'avoient pû obtenir l'execution des Patentes que nous leur accordames en l'année 1655, vous ont informé contre la verité, &c."</note>

->Most Magnificent Lords, Most dear and special Friends, Allies, and Confederates;<-

Those who have advised you that Our subjects of the Pretended Reformed Religion <note>original: "Religion Pretendue Reformée"—a Catholic term for Protestantism used to imply it was not "truly" reformed</note> could not obtain the fulfillment of that Patent <note>an official decree or charter</note> which we granted to them in the year 1655, have informed you contrary to the truth. For we have not failed them in one tittle <note>original: "title," meaning the smallest detail</note>, but have observed all things whatsoever We then granted to them, although We were not at all obliged to do so, since they on their part have failed so much. They still continue, even to this time, their failure and violation of many of the Articles of the said Patent, as you may see by the Answer that President Truchi <note>an official representative of the Duke</note> gave to your Deputies who came into Piedmont that same year. By this you may also know the reason why We delayed Our Answer. 

In that same answer, you may take notice of the enormous crimes of those in the said Valleys, together with the false and insulting slanders they use, and in short, of their formal rebellion and disobedience. And yet, notwithstanding all this, it has not been able to move us so far as to deprive them of the effects of Our Clemency, nor to inflict on them that punishment which they have deserved. Our patience is beyond all belief, since they—knowing how deeply they had provoked Us—believed that We intended to take up arms to reduce them to the obedience they owe Us, and so they took up arms themselves first. Knowing likewise how fruitless this resistance was likely to be, they sent their movable property <note>original: "moveables"</note> and their families out of the country, even though on Our side there was neither soldier nor peasant who had any order so much as to approach the Valleys. 

Indeed, there was no other sign of our displeasure that they could notice, except for the gentle prosecution (conducted through ordinary Justice) of the assassination and high treason committed by those of La Torre <note>Torre Pellice, the cultural and religious center of the Waldensians</note> in the murder of their Judge or chief Magistrate, while he was actually performing the duties of civil justice, as well as their other crimes and disobedience. What We now tell you is so publicly known to all those foreign 
<meta>catchword: Ministers</meta>

# Chapter VIII. *concluded at Pignerol.*

*...the Ministers who reside in Our Court, so that it would not be at all necessary to add that even they themselves could not doubt it in the least. Consequently—without Us revoking any Order, recalling any of Our Troops, or doing anything else of that nature, other than letting them see for themselves how groundless their fears of Us were (even though such actions on Our part would have been just and righteous, given the guilt <note>original: "conscience"</note> of their crimes)—they brought their families and household goods back over a month ago to their houses. No one has bothered them there at all, except as previously specified.*

*By this, you can now see how We have behaved, as well as how Our subjects have acted. To be honest, We have been extremely surprised to see that you are so inclined to support and adopt their unrighteous cause against Our own just cause. Instead of acknowledging Our great goodness toward them, you accept their slanderous <note>original: "calumnious"</note> complaints against Us as if they were based on solid reasons. Meanwhile, you have never taken the slightest notice of the complaints We made to you regarding the violations and disobedience of Our subjects in the Valleys. Though We asked and requested you to write to them and urge them to follow the Patent <note>an official decree or charter</note> of 1655, you have never done so in the least, even though Mr. Salomon Hirtzel <note>a Swiss diplomat and leader of the Protestant embassy to Turin</note>, the chief of your deputies, promised the Baron of Greisy in his letter of September 10/20, 1656, that he would do so. Furthermore, you never behaved as good friends and allies <note>original: "Confederates"</note> by giving Us any satisfaction regarding the libels printed in your cities, which are stuffed with countless shameful lies invented against Us. All these matters have weighed heavily on Us, and it grieves Us deeply to see that you do not reciprocate what We have done for you whenever the opportunity arose. For you know very well that when your own subjects took up arms against you, We had no communication with them whatsoever, much less did We assist them with recommendations, advice, or financial <note>original: "pecuniary"</note> supplies. In fact, We refused even to listen to the arguments your subjects made against your government. Even when you had your swords drawn against the Catholic Cantons <note>referring to the First War of Villmergen (1656), a religious conflict within the Swiss Confederacy</note> regarding matters of religion, We worked—and successfully so—through the mediation of Our Ambassador to restore peace and tranquility to your country. This is what We ask you to reflect upon, hoping that in the end, you will give Us reason to say that We are satisfied with the evidence of your friendship <note>original: "Amity"</note> and good relations. On this basis, We pray that God—*

> *Most Magnificent Lords, most dear and special Friends, Allies, and Confederates, will keep you in His holy safeguard and protection.*

From Turin, May 9, 1658.

->Your very good Friend, Ally, and<-
->Confederate,<-

->The Duke of Savoy,<-
->King of Cyprus,<-
->CHARLES EMANUEL.<-

He reminds them of his neutrality and help during their own religious wars to highlight what he views as their current lack of gratitude.</summary>

# The Grievances of the Treaty. Book IV.

### A Letter from His Royal Highness the Duke of Savoy to the Evangelical Cantons of Switzerland, Turin, May 9, 1655.

<note>original French: "Magnifiques Seigneurs, Tres chers & speciaux Amiz, Alliez, & Confederez, Ceux qui vous ont donné advis que nos sujets de la Religion Pret. Reform. n'avoient pû obtenir l'execution des Patentes que nous leur accordames en l'année 1655, vous ont informé contre la verité, &c."</note>

Magnificent Lords, Very dear and special Friends, Allies, and Confederates:
Those who have advised you that our subjects of the so-called <note>original: "Pretended"</note> Reformed Religion were unable to obtain the execution of the Patents <note>official decrees or charters</note> that we granted them in the year 1655, have informed you contrary to the truth, etc.

->Most Magnificent Lords, Most dear and special Friends, Allies, and Confederates;<-

*Those who have informed you that Our subjects of the so-called Reformed Religion could not obtain the execution of that Patent which We granted to them in the year 1655, have told you something contrary to the truth. In fact, We have not failed them in a single detail <note>original: "tittle"</note>, but have observed everything We granted to them at that time. We did this even though We were not at all obliged to do so, since they, on their part, have failed so significantly—and continue to fail even now—to follow many of the Articles of the said Patent. You may see this for yourselves in the Answer that President Truchi <note>Giovanni Battista Truchi, the Duke’s finance minister and diplomat</note> gave to your deputies who came to Piedmont that same year. From that document, you may also understand the reason why We delayed this, Our Answer.*

*In the same document, you may take note of the enormous crimes committed by those in the said Valleys, along with the false and harmful slanders they use—and, in short, of their formal rebellion and disobedience. Yet despite all this, it has not moved us so far as to deprive them of the effects of Our mercy <note>original: "clemency"</note>, nor to inflict on them the punishment which they have deserved. Our patience in this matter is beyond all belief. Knowing how deeply they had provoked Us, they believed We would have to take up arms to reduce them to the obedience they owe Us, and so they were the ones who took up arms first. Knowing likewise how useless this resistance was likely to be, they sent their property and their families out of the country. On Our side, there was neither soldier nor peasant who had any order even to approach the Valleys; indeed, there was no other sign of Our displeasure that they could have noticed, except for the mild prosecution (conducted through the ordinary course of justice) of the assassination and high treason committed by the people of La Torre. This involved the murder of their judge or chief magistrate while he was actually performing his duties of civil justice, as well as their other crimes and disobedience. What We are telling you now is publicly known to all those foreign*

<meta>The text continues with a mention of foreign ministers residing at the Duke's court who witnessed these events.</meta>

<summary>In this letter, the Duke of Savoy defends his actions against his Protestant subjects in the Valleys, claiming they rebelled and fled without provocation while he was merely seeking legal justice for the murder of a magistrate.</summary>

<header>Chapter VIII. concluded at Pignerol.</header>

Ministers who reside in *Our Court, that it would not be at all necessary to add, that even they themselves could not in the least doubt it. And hereupon (though We are revoking no Order, nor recalling any of Our Troops, nor doing any other thing of that nature, except letting them know for themselves the groundless foundation of their fear regarding any actions on Our part—which nonetheless would have been just and righteous, considering the guilt of their crimes) they have brought back their* Families *and* household goods <note>original: "houshold-stuff"</note> *over a* Month *ago into their houses, where no person has molested them at all, except as is specified above.*

*By this you now see what Our conduct has been, and also what has been the conduct of Our subjects. The truth is, we have been extremely surprised to see that you should be so inclined to support and adopt their unrighteous cause against Our just cause, and instead of acknowledging Our great goodness toward them, to receive their slanderous complaints against Us as if they were founded upon solid reasons. In the meantime, you have never taken the least notice in the world of those complaints which We made to you regarding the violations and disobedience of those subjects of Ours in the* Valleys. *And though We entreated and requested you to write to them and to exhort them to observe the* Patent of 1655 <note>A treaty, also known as the Mercy of Pignerol, which was supposed to guarantee the rights of the Waldensians after the 1655 massacres</note>, *yet you have never done so in the least, although* Mr. <note>original: "Sieur"</note> Salomon Hirtzel, *the chief of your* Deputies, *promised the* *Baron of Greisy in his Letter of the* <gloss>26th</gloss> *of* September 1656 *to do the same. Besides all this, you never prepared yourselves, as good friends and* Confederates, *to give Us any satisfaction at all for those* Libels <note>defamatory pamphlets or writings</note> *printed in your* Cities, *which are stuffed with an infinite number of insulting lies invented against Us. All these things have weighed heavily upon us, and it much grieves us to see that you do not reciprocate what We have done for you whenever the occasion has presented itself. For you know very well that when your subjects took up* Arms *against you, We had no communication at all with them, much less did We assist them with recommendations, advice, or financial supplies. In fact, we refused even to listen to those* Reasons *which your subjects alleged against your* Government. *But even then, when you had your sword drawn against the* Catholic Cantons <note>referring to the First War of Villmergen in 1656, a Swiss religious conflict</note> *concerning matters of* Religion, *We employed Our-self, and did so successfully through the mediation of Our Ambassador, to restore* Peace *and tranquility in your* Country. *This is what We entreat you to reflect on, hoping that in the end you will give Us cause to say that We are satisfied with the evidence of your* Friendship *and good correspondence. And upon this ground we pray* God,

> Most Magnificent Lords, most dear and special Friends, Allies, and Confederates, that he will keep you in his holy safeguard and protection.

From Turin, May 9, 1658.

-> Your very good Friend, Ally, and <-
-> Confederate, <-

-> *The Duke of Savoy,* <-
-> *King of Cyprus,* <-
-> C. EMANUEL <note>Charles Emmanuel II (1634–1675), Duke of Savoy</note>. <-

<page-num>708</page-num>

<header>The Grievances of the Treaty Book. IV.</header>

There were also some other letters written to the *Swiss Ambassadors* from the Court of *Savoy* for the same purpose, but I will refrain from including them here, as it is high time to bring this discourse to a close. To tell the truth, I have been somewhat lengthy because I hoped to conclude everything with the happy news of their deliverance after so many hundred years of *Egyptian* bondage <note>Egyptian bondage: A biblical metaphor for slavery or intense oppression, referring to the Israelites' time in captivity in Egypt.</note>. But unfortunately, I am forced to leave them where I found them: among the *potsherds* <term>broken pieces of pottery, often associated in the Bible with mourning and extreme poverty</term>, with sackcloth and ashes spread under them, lifting up their voices in weeping, in the words of *Job* when he was in the depths of his misery and anguish: "*Have pity on me, have pity on me, O you my friends, for the hand of God has touched me.*" <note>Job 19:21</note> *To this very hour they hunger and thirst, and are naked, and beaten, and have no certain dwelling place* (1 Corinthians 4:11). 

To this very day, they labor under the very heavy burdens laid upon their shoulders by those rigid *taskmasters* of the *Church of Rome*. To this very day, the enemies of the Truth "plow and make long furrows" upon the backs of those poor creatures: 

* By forbidding them every kind of trade <note>original: "traffique"</note> or commerce for their survival; 
* By robbing them of their goods and estates; 
* By driving them in a most savage manner from their ancient houses and homes, and forcing them to "sell their birthright for a bowl of stew" <note>original: "mess of pottage," an allusion to Esau in Genesis 25:29-34</note>; 
* By banishing their ministers, who are the shepherds of the flocks, so that the wolves may more easily come in and devour the sheep; 
* By raping <note>original: "ravishing"</note> their young women and girls; 
* Yes, by murdering many innocent souls as they travel the highways on their private business; 
* By cruel mocking and insults; 
* By continual threats of another massacre—possibly seven times more bloody than the last. 

What shall I say? The very valleys where they live today are, by the tireless efforts of their Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> adversaries, made into nothing less than a prison or dungeon, for which the Fort of *La Torre* serves as a door. Through this door, they can let in a troop of murderers whenever they please, to utterly destroy and exterminate those poor, simple people. 

To all this, I must add that despite all the large supplies of aid sent to them so far—from either *England* or foreign states—the number of these hungry people is so great, and the oppression of their Catholic enemies so severe (who lie in wait to rob them of whatever they are given and snatch every morsel of food that goes into their mouths), that truly, some of them are ready to eat their own flesh for want of bread. *The tongue of the nursing infant clings to the roof of its mouth, and the young children ask for bread, but no one gives it to them. And in many places, the young and the old lie on the ground in the streets.* <note>These descriptions of starvation are drawn from the biblical book of Lamentations.</note>

In summary: *Small sorrows speak, but great ones are struck dumb.* <note>original: "Cura leves loquuntur, ingentes stupent." From Seneca the Younger's tragedy Phaedra.</note>

Their miseries are more tragic and painful than words can express, and they are in a way dying while they still live: *No grapes in their vineyards, no cattle in their fields, no herds in their stalls, no grain in their barns, no flour in their barrel, no oil in their jug.* The funds <note>original: "stock"</note> which were gathered for them by the good people of this and other nations...

<summary>This page describes the ongoing persecution and starvation of the Waldensian Protestants in the Piedmont valleys despite international aid. The author concludes that their suffering is beyond description, characterized by constant threats of renewed massacre and total economic ruin.</summary>

<page-num>709</page-num>

<header>Chap. VIII. concluded at Pignerol.</header>

[The resources of these] nations are wasting away quickly, and once they are entirely spent, the people must inevitably perish—unless God, who *turns the hearts of Princes like the rivers of water* <note>A reference to Proverbs 21:1: "The king's heart is in the hand of the Lord, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will."</note>, is graciously pleased to incline the heart of their Sovereign Prince to take pity on his poor, harmless, and faithful subjects. These people are so far from any thoughts of *rebellion* or *disobedience* (as some would desperately force both him and his *Royal* Mother <note>Christine Marie of France (1606–1663), the Duchess Regent of Savoy, who was seen as a driving force behind the persecution.</note> to believe) that if they could only have some assurance of enjoying the freedom of their consciences in peace and quietness, they would be the first to sacrifice their lives and fortunes for the good and preservation of their *Royal Highnesses*. To them, I shall give this, my last and final farewell, in the same language that *Peter* once used to the scattered Churches in *Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia,* and *Bithynia*: 

> *Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his abundant mercy has begotten us again unto a living hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance incorruptible and undefiled, and that does not fade away, reserved in heaven for you, who are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation, ready to be revealed in the last time. In this you greatly rejoice, though now for a season (if need be) you are in heaviness through manifold temptations; so that the trial of your faith, being much more precious than gold that perishes, though it be tested with fire, might be found unto praise, and honor, and glory, at the appearing of Jesus Christ; to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.* <note>1 Peter 1:3-7</note>
